skills.title: u-substitution
method: Look for an inner function whose derivative sits outside: $\int f(g(x))\,g'(x)\,dx = \int f(u)\,du$ with $u = g(x)$.
Write $du = g'(x)\,dx$ and solve for what is in the integrand: $x\,dx = du/2$ for $u = x^2 + 4$. Constants come out front.
Linear inside: $\int f(ax + b)\,dx = \frac{1}{a}F(ax + b)$. Don't forget the $1/a$.
Numerator = derivative of denominator: $\int \frac{g'}{g}\,dx = \ln|g| + C$.
Back-substitute: the answer is in $x$, not $u$.

skills.title: Integration by parts
method: $\int u\,dv = uv - \int v\,du$. Choose $u$ by LIATE: Log, Inverse trig, Algebraic, Trig, Exponential.
Polynomial times $e^{ax}$ or $\sin/\cos$: $u$ = the polynomial. Degree $n$ means $n$ rounds; tabular: differentiate $u$ to 0, integrate $dv$, alternate $+,-,+$.
$\ln x$ or $\arctan x$ alone: $u = \ln x$, $dv = dx$.
$e^{ax}\sin bx$: parts twice, the integral comes back; solve for it: $\frac{e^{ax}(a\sin bx - b\cos bx)}{a^2 + b^2}$.

skills.title: Partial fractions
method: Degree on top $\ge$ degree below? Divide first.
Factor the denominator. Distinct linear $\frac{A}{x - a}$; repeated $\frac{A}{x - a} + \frac{B}{(x - a)^2}$; irreducible $\frac{Bx + D}{x^2 + k^2}$.
Cover-up for a simple root: $A = \left.\frac{N(x)}{\text{other factors}}\right|_{x = a}$. Compare coefficients for the rest.
Integrals: $\ln|x - a|$, $-\frac{1}{x - a}$, $\frac{1}{2}\ln(x^2 + k^2)$, $\frac{1}{k}\arctan\frac{x}{k}$.

skills.title: Complex roots & Euler's formula
method: Euler: $e^{i\theta} = \cos\theta + i\sin\theta$, so $re^{i\theta} = r\cos\theta + ir\sin\theta$.
Polar: $r = \sqrt{a^2 + b^2}$; pick $\theta$ from the signs of $a, b$ (quadrant), not $\arctan(b/a)$ alone.
De Moivre: $(re^{i\theta})^n = r^ne^{in\theta}$. Reduce $n\theta$ mod $2\pi$ before converting back.
Roots $\alpha \pm \beta i$: $e^{(\alpha + \beta i)x} = e^{\alpha x}(\cos\beta x + i\sin\beta x)$; real and imaginary parts are the two real solutions.

skills.title: Complex equations, regions, mappings and limits
Analytic and harmonic functions: Cauchy–Riemann
Complex integration, Taylor and Laurent series, zeros and poles
Conformal maps, Möbius maps and branches of log and powers
Contour integration, Cauchy's theorems, residues and real integrals
Shifting summation indices
method: To get $x^k$ from $x^{n + j}$: set $k = n + j$, so $n = k - j$. Replace every $n$, including the lower limit.
Differentiating $\sum a_nx^n$ kills the first term: $y' = \sum_{n=1}^\infty na_nx^{n-1} = \sum_{k=0}^\infty (k+1)a_{k+1}x^k$.
A factor $x^p$ in front just adds $p$ to the power. Line all sums up at the same $x^k$ and the same start before adding.

skills.title: Partial derivatives & exact differentials
method: $\partial f/\partial x$: differentiate in $x$, treating $y$ as a constant (and vice versa). $\partial_x(y^2e^{3x}) = 3y^2e^{3x}$.
Mixed partials agree: $f_{xy} = f_{yx}$. Watch $e^{kxy}$: $\partial_x e^{kxy} = ky\,e^{kxy}$.
Implicit curve $u(x, y) = c$: $dy/dx = -u_x/u_y$.
$M\,dx + N\,dy$ is exact (some $du$) exactly when $M_y = N_x$.

skills.title: Separable equations
Separable via substitution
Linear: integrating factor
Integrating factor + integration by parts
Bernoulli equations
Exact equations
method: Form $M\,dx + N\,dy = 0$. Test $\partial M/\partial y = \partial N/\partial x$ first.
$u = \int M\,dx + k(y)$; then $u_y = N$ gives $k'(y)$. Terms of $N$ already produced by $u_y$ don't go into $k$.
Solution $u(x, y) = c$ (implicit is fine). IVP: $c = u(x_0, y_0)$.
Trap: adding $\int M\,dx$ and $\int N\,dy$ double-counts the mixed terms.

skills.title: Integrating factors for exactness
method: Not exact: $P\,dx + Q\,dy = 0$ with $P_y \ne Q_x$. Look for $F$ making $FP\,dx + FQ\,dy$ exact.
$R = \frac{1}{Q}(P_y - Q_x)$ depends on $x$ only: $F(x) = \exp\int R\,dx$.
$R^* = \frac{1}{P}(Q_x - P_y)$ depends on $y$ only: $F^*(y) = \exp\int R^*\,dy$. Note the reversed order.
Then solve the exact equation; the solution is $u(x, y) = c$ for the new $M = FP$, $N = FQ$.

skills.title: Modeling: mixing, cooling, growth
method: Rate of change = in − out. Mixing: $y' = (\text{rate})(\text{conc in}) - (\text{rate})\,y/V$; limit $y \to (\text{conc in})V$.
Newton cooling: $T' = -k(T - T_A)$, $T = T_A + (T_0 - T_A)e^{-kt}$. One measurement fixes $k$.
Decay / growth: $y = y_0e^{\pm kt}$; half-life $H$: $k = \ln 2/H$, $y = y_0 2^{-t/H}$. $^{14}$C: $H = 5715$ yr.
Logistic $y' = Ay - By^2$: Bernoulli, $y = \frac{A/B}{1 + Ce^{-At}}$, $y \to A/B$.
Units: keep minutes with minutes; $\ln$ of a ratio has none.

skills.title: Which first-order method?
method: Separable: $y' = g(x)h(y)$ — factor first ($xy^2 + x = x(y^2 + 1)$).
Linear: $y' + p(x)y = r(x)$, $y$ to the first power only. Bernoulli: the same plus $g(x)y^n$.
Substitution: a function of $y/x$ (homogeneous) or of $ax + by + c$.
Exact: given $M\,dx + N\,dy = 0$, test $M_y = N_x$; if not, try an integrating factor.

skills.title: Solving a system by row reduction
method: Write the augmented matrix $[A\,|\,\mathbf b]$. Three legal moves: swap rows, scale a row, add a multiple of one row to another.
Clear below each pivot, left to right (echelon form), then back-substitute from the bottom row.
Check your answer in one original equation; arithmetic slips hide in the third row.

skills.title: Linear independence
method: Independent means $c_1\mathbf v_1 + \dots + c_p\mathbf v_p = \mathbf 0$ only for all $c_i = 0$.
$n$ vectors in $\mathbb R^n$: independent exactly when $\det[\mathbf v_1 \cdots \mathbf v_n] \ne 0$. Otherwise row-reduce: a pivot in every column means independent.
Shortcuts: a zero vector, or more vectors than entries, means dependent.

skills.title: Inverse of a 2×2 matrix
method: $A = \begin{bmatrix} a & b\\ c & d\end{bmatrix}$: $A^{-1} = \frac{1}{ad - bc}\begin{bmatrix} d & -b\\ -c & a\end{bmatrix}$. Swap the diagonal, negate the off-diagonal.
If $ad - bc = 0$, there is no inverse.
Check: $AA^{-1} = I$.

skills.title: 3×3 determinants (cofactor expansion)
method: Cofactor expansion: pick the row or column with the most zeros; signs follow the checkerboard $+\,-\,+$.
Each term: entry × sign × the $2\times2$ minor $ad - bc$ left after deleting its row and column.
Row operations: a swap flips the sign; adding a multiple of a row changes nothing; scaling a row scales $\det$.

skills.title: 2×2 eigenvalues
method: Solve $\det(A - \lambda I) = 0$. For $2\times2$: $\lambda^2 - (\operatorname{tr}A)\lambda + \det A = 0$.
Check: the eigenvalues sum to the trace and multiply to the determinant.
Triangular matrix: the eigenvalues are the diagonal entries.

skills.title: 2×2 eigenvectors
method: Solve $(A - \lambda I)\mathbf v = \mathbf 0$. The matrix is singular, so one row of a $2\times2$ is enough.
From $a v_1 + b v_2 = 0$, take $\mathbf v = (-b, a)$ or any nonzero multiple.
Check: $A\mathbf v = \lambda\mathbf v$.

skills.title: Rank and the null space
Orthogonality, projection and Gram–Schmidt
Least squares and the normal equations
Diagonalisation, symmetric matrices and singular values
Vector equations, span and solution sets
Matrix products, transposes and sizes
LU factorisation
Determinant properties: row operations, products, area and volume
Subspaces, bases and dimension
Coordinates and change of basis
Linear transformations: standard matrix, composition, kernel and range
Eigenvectors at work: powers, Markov chains, complex eigenvalues
Quadratic forms and constrained optimisation
The singular value decomposition and condition number
Characteristic equation (3 root cases)
method: Try $y = e^{\lambda x}$: $ay'' + by' + cy = 0$ becomes $a\lambda^2 + b\lambda + c = 0$.
Distinct real roots: $c_1e^{\lambda_1x} + c_2e^{\lambda_2x}$. Double root: $(c_1 + c_2x)e^{\lambda x}$. Complex $\alpha \pm \beta i$: $e^{\alpha x}(c_1\cos\beta x + c_2\sin\beta x)$.
IVP: write the general solution, then $y(0)$ and $y'(0)$ give two equations for $c_1, c_2$.
Check by plugging back in — especially the sign of $\alpha$.

skills.title: Reduction of order
method: Know one solution $y_1$? Put the ODE in standard form $y'' + p(x)y' + q(x)y = 0$ first — divide by the leading coefficient.
Then $y_2 = uy_1$ with $U = u' = \dfrac{1}{y_1^2}e^{-\int p\,dx}$, and $u = \int U\,dx$.
Drop constant factors and any multiple of $y_1$ in $y_2$; the general solution is $c_1y_1 + c_2y_2$.
Double root of the characteristic equation: $U = 1$, so $y_2 = xy_1$. Euler–Cauchy double root: $U = 1/x$, so $y_2 = y_1\ln x$.

skills.title: Euler–Cauchy equations
method: $x^2y'' + axy' + by = 0$: try $y = x^m$ to get the auxiliary equation $m^2 + (a - 1)m + b = 0$ — note the $a - 1$.
Distinct real roots: $c_1x^{m_1} + c_2x^{m_2}$. Double root: $(c_1 + c_2\ln x)x^m$.

Complex $m = \mu \pm 
u i$: $x^\mu\left[c_1\cos(
u\ln x) + c_2\sin(
u\ln x)ight]$.
IVPs are posed at $x = 1$, where $\ln 1 = 0$ and $(x^m)' = m$.

skills.title: The Wronskian
Mass–spring, undamped
Mass–spring, damped
Undetermined coefficients
method: $y = y_h + y_p$. Guess $y_p$ shaped like the right side: polynomial → full polynomial of the same degree; $Ke^{kx}$; $\cos\omega x$ or $\sin\omega x$ → both $K\cos\omega x + M\sin\omega x$.
Modification rule: if your guess already solves the homogeneous equation, multiply by $x$ (by $x^2$ for a double root).
Apply initial conditions to $y_h + y_p$, never to $y_h$ alone.
Check: $y_p'' + by_p' + cy_p$ must give back the right side exactly.

skills.title: Mass–spring, forced & resonance
method: $my'' + cy' + ky = F_0\cos\omega t$. Damped: the homogeneous part dies out, the steady state is $y_p = a\cos\omega t + b\sin\omega t$ — keep both terms.
Amplitude $C^* = F_0/\sqrt{(k - m\omega^2)^2 + c^2\omega^2}$; it peaks at $\omega_{\max}^2 = \omega_0^2 - c^2/(2m^2)$ when $c^2 < 2mk$.
Undamped, $\omega = \omega_0 = \sqrt{k/m}$: resonance, $y_p = \frac{F_0}{2m\omega_0}t\sin\omega_0t$ (modification rule).
Undamped, $\omega \ne \omega_0$, starting from rest: $y = \frac{F_0}{m(\omega_0^2 - \omega^2)}(\cos\omega t - \cos\omega_0t)$ — beats.

skills.title: Variation of parameters
method: Standard form first: $y'' + p y' + q y = r$ (divide an Euler–Cauchy equation by $x^2$).
Basis $y_1, y_2$, Wronskian $W = y_1y_2' - y_2y_1'$. Then $y_p = -y_1\int\frac{y_2r}{W}dx + y_2\int\frac{y_1r}{W}dx$.
Works for any $r$ — $\sec x$, $\csc x$, $e^x/x$, $\ln x$ — where undetermined coefficients fails.
Leftover multiples of $y_1$ or $y_2$ in $y_p$ solve the homogeneous equation; drop them (or keep them — still a particular solution).

skills.title: Higher-order characteristic equations
method: $y = e^{\lambda x}$ turns $y^{(n)} + \dots + a_0y = 0$ into a degree-$n$ polynomial. Integer roots divide $a_0$: test them, then divide out.
A root of multiplicity $k$ gives $e^{\lambda x}, xe^{\lambda x}, \dots, x^{k-1}e^{\lambda x}$; a pair $\alpha \pm \beta i$ gives $e^{\alpha x}\cos\beta x,\ e^{\alpha x}\sin\beta x$.
Order $n$ means $n$ constants. IVP: $y, y', \dots, y^{(n-1)}$ at $x_0$ give $n$ linear equations.

skills.title: 2×2 systems by eigenvalues
method: $\mathbf y' = A\mathbf y$: try $\mathbf y = \mathbf x e^{\lambda t}$, so $A\mathbf x = \lambda\mathbf x$. For $2\times2$: $\lambda^2 - (\operatorname{tr}A)\lambda + \det A = 0$.
Distinct real: $\mathbf y = c_1\mathbf x^{(1)}e^{\lambda_1t} + c_2\mathbf x^{(2)}e^{\lambda_2t}$.
Complex $\alpha \pm \beta i$: the real and imaginary parts of $\mathbf x e^{(\alpha + i\beta)t}$ are two real solutions.
Double $\lambda$, one eigenvector: second solution $(\mathbf x t + \mathbf u)e^{\lambda t}$ with $(A - \lambda I)\mathbf u = \mathbf x$.
IVP: solve $c_1\mathbf x^{(1)} + c_2\mathbf x^{(2)} = \mathbf y(0)$.

skills.title: Kinetics A → B → C as a 2×2 system
method: $A \to B \to C$: $\frac{d}{dt}([A],[B]) = M([A],[B])$ with $M = \begin{pmatrix}-k_1 & 0\\ k_1 & -k_2\end{pmatrix}$. C never feeds back, so the $2\times2$ block is the whole problem.
Triangular, so the eigenvalues are $-k_1, -k_2$; eigenvectors $(k_2 - k_1, k_1)$ and $(0, 1)$.
$[B] = \frac{k_1[A]_0}{k_2 - k_1}(e^{-k_1t} - e^{-k_2t})$ from pure A; $[C] = [A]_0 - [A] - [B]$ (mass balance).
Equal rate constants: a repeated eigenvalue, so a $te^{-kt}$ term appears. Peak of B: $t_{max} = \ln(k_1/k_2)/(k_1 - k_2)$.

skills.title: Phase portrait type
method: $p = \operatorname{tr}A$, $q = \det A$, $\Delta = p^2 - 4q$.
$q < 0$: saddle. $q > 0,\ \Delta \ge 0$: node. $q > 0,\ \Delta < 0$: spiral, or a center if $p = 0$.
Stable and attractive iff $p < 0,\ q > 0$; a center is stable but not attractive; $p > 0$ or $q < 0$ is unstable.
A second-order ODE $y'' + by' + cy = 0$: $y_1 = y,\ y_2 = y'$ gives $A = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ -c & -b \end{pmatrix}$.

skills.title: Ordinary vs. singular points
Power series: recurrence relation
Power series: first terms
Guaranteed radius of convergence
Frobenius: indicial roots
Frobenius: which case?
Legendre & Bessel recognition
method: Legendre: $(1 - x^2)y'' - 2xy' + n(n+1)y = 0$; polynomial solution $P_n$ of degree $n$.
Bessel: $x^2y'' + xy' + (x^2 - \nu^2)y = 0$; with $k^2x^2$ instead of $x^2$ the solution is $J_\nu(kx)$.
Euler–Cauchy $x^2y'' + axy' + by = 0$ looks similar but has no $x^2y$ term.
Divide out a common factor before matching (e.g. $-1$, or multiply $xy'' + y' + \dots$ by $x$).

Non-integer $
u$: $J_
u$, $J_{-
u}$ independent. Integer $n$: $J_{-n} = (-1)^nJ_n$, so use $Y_n$.

skills.title: Transforms from the table
method: Linearity first: $\mathcal{L}\{af + bg\} = aF + bG$, then look each piece up.
Core entries: $\mathcal{L}\{t^n\} = n!/s^{n+1}$, $\mathcal{L}\{e^{at}\} = 1/(s - a)$, $\mathcal{L}\{\cos\omega t\} = s/(s^2 + \omega^2)$, $\mathcal{L}\{\sin\omega t\} = \omega/(s^2 + \omega^2)$.
Hyperbolic: same shapes with a minus sign, $\mathcal{L}\{\cosh at\} = s/(s^2 - a^2)$, $\mathcal{L}\{\sinh at\} = a/(s^2 - a^2)$.
Not in the table? Rewrite first: $\sin^2\theta = \tfrac12(1 - \cos 2\theta)$, $\sin\theta\cos\theta = \tfrac12\sin 2\theta$.
Trap: $\sin$ carries $\omega$ in the numerator, $\cos$ carries $s$.

skills.title: Inverse transforms (partial fractions)
method: Factor the denominator. Simple real roots: partial fractions, each $A/(s - a) \to Ae^{at}$; cover-up gives $A$ at once.
Repeated root: write the numerator in powers of $(s - a)$; $1/(s - a)^2 \to te^{at}$.
Complex roots: complete the square, $(s - a)^2 + \omega^2$, and split the numerator into $(s - a)$ and a constant: $e^{at}\cos\omega t$, $e^{at}\sin\omega t$.
Irreducible quadratic next to $1/s$: $A/s + (Bs + C)/(s^2 + \omega^2)$; match coefficients.
Check: $f(0)$ equals $\lim_{s\to\infty} sF(s)$.

skills.title: s- and t-shifting, Heaviside
method: s-shifting: $\mathcal{L}\{e^{at}f(t)\} = F(s - a)$; a factor $e^{at}$ in $t$ is a shift $s \to s - a$.
t-shifting: $\mathcal{L}\{f(t - a)u(t - a)\} = e^{-as}F(s)$; a factor $e^{-as}$ in $s$ is a delay with a switch-on at $t = a$.
The function multiplying $u(t - a)$ must be written in $t - a$: $t\,u(t - a) = [(t - a) + a]u(t - a)$.
Piecewise: on at $a$, off at $b$ is $u(t - a) - u(t - b)$. Type the step as u(t-2).

skills.title: Solving IVPs by Laplace
method: Transform: $\mathcal{L}\{y''\} = s^2Y - sy(0) - y'(0)$, $\mathcal{L}\{y'\} = sY - y(0)$.
Solve the subsidiary equation (algebra!) for $Y$, then partial fractions, then invert.
The initial conditions enter at the start, so the answer has no arbitrary constants.
Check $y(0)$ and $y'(0)$ before you submit.

skills.title: Convolution
method: $(f * g)(t) = \int_0^t f(\tau)g(t - \tau)\,d\tau$, and $\mathcal{L}\{f * g\} = F(s)G(s)$.
Inverse of a product: split $H = FG$ into two table entries and convolve, or use partial fractions.
Integral equations: $\int_0^t k(t - \tau)y(\tau)\,d\tau$ transforms to $K(s)Y(s)$; solve for $Y$.
Inside the integral $t$ is a constant; integrate in $\tau$. $1 * g = \int_0^t g$, so $\mathcal{L}\{\int_0^t g\} = G/s$.

skills.title: Transfer function, poles & stability
method: Zero initial values: every $d/dt$ becomes a factor $s$. $ay'' + by' + cy = r$ gives $G(s) = Y/R = 1/(as^2 + bs + c)$.
Poles = roots of the denominator (after cancelling common factors with the numerator).
Stable: all poles with $\operatorname{Re} < 0$. Simple poles on the imaginary axis: marginal. Any $\operatorname{Re} > 0$, or a repeated imaginary pole: unstable.

skills.title: IVPs with switched (unit-step) forcing
method: Write the forcing with steps: on at $a$, off at $b$ is $K[u(t - a) - u(t - b)]$; $\mathcal{L}\{u(t - a)\} = e^{-as}/s$.
Keep each $e^{-as}$ as a label: invert $1/(s\,p(s))$ once (the step response $h$), then each term becomes $K\,h(t - a)u(t - a)$.
Check: before the first switch only the initial-condition part acts; $y$ and $y'$ are continuous at every switch.
Type steps as u(t-2), H(t-2), u_2(t) or heaviside(t-2); $\pi$ shifts as u(t-pi).

skills.title: Impulses: δ(t − a) and the impulse response
method: $\mathcal{L}\{\delta(t - a)\} = e^{-as}$. With zero initial state, $\delta(t)$ gives $Y = G(s)$: the impulse response is $g = \mathcal{L}^{-1}\{G\}$.
Response to $K\delta(t - a)$: $K\,g(t - a)u(t - a)$.
The impulse makes $y'$ jump by $K/a$ ($a$ the coefficient of $y''$); $y$ itself stays continuous.

skills.title: Differentiation of transforms: L{tf} = −F′(s)
method: $\mathcal{L}\{tf(t)\} = -F'(s)$: differentiate the transform and flip the sign.
Inverting $\ln$ or $\arctan$: differentiate $F$ to get a rational function, invert that to get $tf(t)$, then divide by $t$.
$\mathcal{L}\{t\sin\omega t\} = \frac{2\omega s}{(s^2 + \omega^2)^2}$, $\mathcal{L}\{t\cos\omega t\} = \frac{s^2 - \omega^2}{(s^2 + \omega^2)^2}$.

skills.title: Systems of ODEs by Laplace
method: Transform each equation: $sY_j - y_j(0)$ replaces $y_j'$; constants $k$ become $k/s$.
Solve the $2\times2$ algebraic system (Cramer or elimination); its determinant is the characteristic polynomial of $A$.
Partial fractions on each $Y_j$, then invert. Check both initial values.

skills.title: S–L: eigenvalues
S–L: eigenfunctions
S–L: self-adjoint form (p, q, r)
S–L: regular, periodic, or singular?
S–L: shifted eigenvalue y'' + (λ + c)y = 0
method: Substitute $\omega = \lambda + c$: now it's the plain problem $y'' + \omega y = 0$ with the same boundary conditions.
Run all three cases on $\omega$: $\omega < 0$ (cosh/sinh), $\omega = 0$ ($A + Bx$), $\omega > 0$ (cos/sin). Dirichlet–Dirichlet: only $\omega > 0$ survives; Neumann–Neumann adds $\omega = 0$.
Undo it: $\lambda_n = \omega_n - c$. Eigenfunctions don't change; eigenvalues shift, and some can go negative or land exactly on 0.

skills.title: Fourier series coefficients
method: Kreyszig: $f = a_0 + \sum(a_n\cos\frac{n\pi x}{L} + b_n\sin\frac{n\pi x}{L})$ with $a_0 = \frac{1}{2L}\int_{-L}^{L} f$ (the mean), $a_n = \frac1L\int f\cos$, $b_n = \frac1L\int f\sin$.
Symmetry first: odd $f$ has $a_0 = a_n = 0$; even $f$ has $b_n = 0$ and integrals twice those over $[0, L]$.
$\cos n\pi = (-1)^n$, $\sin n\pi = 0$. Integrate $x\cos$, $x\sin$, $x^2\cos$ by parts.
Half-range on $(0, L)$: sine series $b_n = \frac2L\int_0^L f\sin$ (odd extension); cosine series $a_0 = \frac1L\int_0^L f$, $a_n = \frac2L\int_0^L f\cos$.

skills.title: Green's functions and impulse responses
Random walks and the diffusion limit
Separation of variables (heat & wave equations)
method: $u = F(x)G(t)$: the BCs make $F'' + p^2F = 0$ an eigenvalue problem; Dirichlet $F_n = \sin\frac{n\pi x}{L}$, insulated $F_n = \cos\frac{n\pi x}{L}$ (with $n = 0$).
Heat $u_t = c^2u_{xx}$: $G_n = e^{-\lambda_n^2t}$, $\lambda_n = cn\pi/L$. Wave $u_{tt} = c^2u_{xx}$: $G_n = B_n\cos\lambda_nt + B_n^*\sin\lambda_nt$.
If $u(x,0)$ is already a finite sine (cosine) sum, read the coefficients off; each mode keeps its own rate.
Wave: $B_n$ from $u(x,0)$, $B_n^*\lambda_n$ from $u_t(x,0)$.
Nonzero end temperatures: subtract the steady line $U(x)$ first, then solve for $u - U$.

skills.title: Classify a PDE; check a solution
method: $Au_{xx} + 2Bu_{xy} + Cu_{yy} = F$: $AC - B^2 > 0$ elliptic, $= 0$ parabolic, $< 0$ hyperbolic. Halve the $u_{xy}$ coefficient to get $B$.
Heat is parabolic, wave hyperbolic, Laplace elliptic. Variable coefficients: the type can change from region to region.
Verifying a solution: compute the needed partials and substitute; match coefficients of the same function.

skills.title: d'Alembert: the infinite string
method: $u = \tfrac12[f(x + ct) + f(x - ct)] + \frac{1}{2c}\int_{x - ct}^{x + ct} g(s)\,ds$.
Displacement splits into two half-height waves moving left and right; the velocity enters through its antiderivative.
Check $u(x, 0) = f$ and $u_t(x, 0) = g$.

skills.title: Laplace's equation on a rectangle
method: One non-zero side at a time. The two zero sides perpendicular to it give $\sin\frac{n\pi x}{a}$; the opposite zero side picks $\sinh$ that vanishes there.
Data side $y = b$: $u = \sum A_n^*\sin\frac{n\pi x}{a}\sinh\frac{n\pi y}{a}$, $A_n^* = \frac{2}{a\sinh(n\pi b/a)}\int_0^a f\sin\frac{n\pi x}{a}\,dx$.
If the data are already a sine sum, read the coefficients off and divide by $\sinh$ at the data side.

Rate equations: conduction, convection, radiation
method: Three mechanisms, three laws: conduction $q''_x = k\,\Delta T/L$ (slab), convection $q'' = h(T_s - T_\infty)$, radiation $q''_{rad} = \varepsilon\sigma(T_s^4 - T_{sur}^4)$.
Flux $q''$ (W/m²) or rate $q = q''A$ (W)? Read which one is asked. For a rod, $A = \pi DL$, the lateral area.
Radiation in kelvin, always. $\sigma = 5.67\times10^{-8}\ \mathrm{W/m^2K^4}$.
$h_r = \varepsilon\sigma(T_s + T_{sur})(T_s^2 + T_{sur}^2)$ rewrites radiation as $h_r(T_s - T_{sur})$.
Lengths in metres: cm ÷ 100, mm ÷ 1000.

skills.title: Surface & control-volume energy balances
method: Draw the surface or control volume, then every arrow in and out: $\dot E_{in} - \dot E_{out} + \dot E_g = \dot E_{st}$. Steady means $\dot E_{st} = 0$.
A surface has no volume: no generation, no storage. Conduction in = convection out + radiation out.
Heated wire, per metre: $I^2R'_e = h\pi D(T_s - T_\infty) + \varepsilon\sigma\pi D(T_s^4 - T_{sur}^4)$.
Radiation terms in kelvin; convection differences can stay in °C.

skills.title: Heat equation & boundary conditions
method: 1-D, constant $k$: $\rho c_p\,\partial T/\partial t = k\,\partial^2T/\partial x^2 + \dot q$.
Given $T(x)$, just differentiate: flux $q''_x = -k\,dT/dx$ (positive in $+x$); steady generation $\dot q = -k\,d^2T/dx^2$.
Curvature tells the story: concave down ($T'' < 0$) means heat is being generated inside.
Transient: $\partial T/\partial t = (kT'' + \dot q)/(\rho c_p)$.

skills.title: Thermal resistance: plane & composite walls
method: Heat through layers in series is current through resistors: $q'' = \Delta T_{overall}/R''_{tot}$.
Per unit area: $R''_{conv} = 1/h$, $R''_{cond} = L/k$, contact $R''_{t,c}$. Add them; $U = 1/R''_{tot}$.
Interior temperatures: the same $q''$ crosses every layer, so walk through it: $T_{s,i} = T_{\infty,i} - q''/h_i$, then subtract $q''L/k$ per layer.
The biggest resistance takes the biggest temperature drop.

skills.title: Thermal resistance: cylinders & spheres, critical radius
skills.short: Thermal resistance: cylinders & spheres, critical radius
method: Area grows with $r$, so $L/k$ becomes: cylinder $R'_{cond} = \ln(r_2/r_1)/(2\pi k)$; sphere $R_{cond} = (1/r_1 - 1/r_2)/(4\pi k)$.
Outside convection uses the outer area: $R'_{conv} = 1/(2\pi r_2h)$; sphere $1/(4\pi r_2^2h)$.
Critical radius $r_{cr} = k/h$ (cylinder), $2k/h$ (sphere). Below it, more insulation means more heat loss.
Radii in metres; $r_2 = r_1 +$ insulation thickness.

skills.title: Conduction with heat generation
method: Overall balance first: everything generated leaves through the cooled surface. Wall $T_s = T_\infty + \dot qL/h$; rod $T_s = T_\infty + \dot qr_o/(2h)$.
Then the parabola: wall $T_{max} = T_s + \dot qL^2/(2k)$; rod $T_0 = T_s + \dot qr_o^2/(4k)$.
$L$ is the half-thickness of a wall cooled on both sides, but the full thickness if one face is insulated (the max sits on that face).

skills.title: Fins: temperature profile, efficiency, effectiveness
method: $m = \sqrt{hP/(kA_c)}$. Pin: $P = \pi D$, $A_c = \pi D^2/4$, so $m = \sqrt{4h/(kD)}$.
$M = \sqrt{hPkA_c}\,\theta_b$ with $\theta_b = T_b - T_\infty$.
Infinite: $q_f = M$. Adiabatic tip: $q_f = M\tanh mL$ and $\theta(L)/\theta_b = 1/\cosh mL$. If $mL > 2.65$, $\tanh mL \approx 1$: it's effectively infinite.
Efficiency $\eta_f = \tanh(mL_c)/(mL_c)$, corrected length $L_c = L + D/4$ (pin) or $L + t/2$ (straight fin).

skills.title: 2-D conduction shape factors
method: Between two isothermal surfaces in 2-D: $q = Sk(T_1 - T_2)$, with $S$ (in metres) from Table 4.1.
Buried cylinder $S = 2\pi L/\cosh^{-1}(2z/D)$; buried sphere $S = 2\pi D/(1 - D/4z)$; cylinder centred in a square $S = 2\pi L/\ln(1.08w/D)$.
$z$ is measured to the centre or centreline, not to the top of the pipe.

skills.title: Finite-difference node equations
method: Energy balance on the node's own cell: for each neighbour, $k\,(\text{face})\,(T_{nb} - T_m)/\Delta x$; add convection and $\dot q\,(\text{cell area})$; total $= 0$.
Interior, $\Delta x = \Delta y$: $T_m = \left(\sum T_{nb} + \dot q\Delta x^2/k\right)/4$.
Plane surface: half-faces to the two neighbours along the surface, convection over the full face $\Delta y$. External corner: quarter cell, two half-faces.
Sanity check: the node temperature lies between its neighbours and $T_\infty$.

skills.title: Lumped capacitance & the Biot number
method: Check first: $Bi = hL_c/k < 0.1$ with $L_c = V/A_s$ — sphere $D/6$, long cylinder $D/4$, plate cooled on both faces $t/2$.
Then $\dfrac{T - T_\infty}{T_i - T_\infty} = e^{-t/\tau}$, $\tau = \dfrac{\rho Vc}{hA_s} = \dfrac{\rho cL_c}{h}$; time to reach $T$: $t = \tau\ln\dfrac{T_i - T_\infty}{T - T_\infty}$.
Energy transferred by time $t$: $Q = \rho Vc\,(T_i - T_\infty)(1 - e^{-t/\tau})$.
Traps: using the radius instead of $V/A_s$; taking the log of a ratio upside down (gives a negative time).

skills.title: Transient conduction: one-term solutions
method: Bi here uses the half-thickness $L$ or the radius $r_o$, not $V/A_s$: $Bi = hL/k$ or $hr_o/k$. $Fo = \alpha t/L^2$ (or $\alpha t/r_o^2$).
One term is fine when $Fo > 0.2$: $\theta_0^* = C_1e^{-\zeta_1^2Fo}$ at the centre, $\theta^* = (T - T_\infty)/(T_i - T_\infty)$.
$\zeta_1$ is the first root of: wall $\zeta\tan\zeta = Bi$; cylinder $\zeta J_1(\zeta)/J_0(\zeta) = Bi$; sphere $1 - \zeta\cot\zeta = Bi$ (Table 5.1 lists $\zeta_1$, $C_1$).
Off-centre: wall $\theta^* = \theta_0^*\cos(\zeta_1x^*)$, cylinder $\theta_0^*J_0(\zeta_1r^*)$, sphere $\theta_0^*\sin(\zeta_1r^*)/(\zeta_1r^*)$ — radians.
If $Bi < 0.1$, lumped capacitance is simpler and just as good.

skills.title: Semi-infinite solid (erf solutions)
method: Surface suddenly held at $T_s$: $\dfrac{T(x,t) - T_s}{T_i - T_s} = \operatorname{erf}\eta$, $\eta = \dfrac{x}{2\sqrt{\alpha t}}$.
Surface flux $q''_s = \dfrac{k(T_s - T_i)}{\sqrt{\pi\alpha t}}$, falling as $t^{-1/2}$.
Depth or time for a given $T$: compute the ratio, invert erf (Table B.2) for $\eta$, then solve $\eta = x/(2\sqrt{\alpha t})$.
Two semi-infinite solids in contact: $T_s = \dfrac{(k\rho c)_A^{1/2}T_A + (k\rho c)_B^{1/2}T_B}{(k\rho c)_A^{1/2} + (k\rho c)_B^{1/2}}$, constant in time.
Valid while the far side has not felt the change — roughly $\eta \gtrsim 2$ at the back face.

skills.title: External flow correlations (plate, cylinder, sphere)
method: Film temperature $T_f = (T_s + T_\infty)/2$ for properties (Whitaker sphere: properties at $T_\infty$, $\mu_s$ at $T_s$).
Flat plate, $Re_L = u_\infty L/\nu$; laminar if $Re_L < 5\times10^5$: $\overline{Nu}_L = 0.664Re_L^{1/2}Pr^{1/3}$ (Eq. 7.31; local is $0.332$, half the average).
Cylinder: Churchill–Bernstein $\overline{Nu}_D = 0.3 + \dfrac{0.62Re_D^{1/2}Pr^{1/3}}{[1 + (0.4/Pr)^{2/3}]^{1/4}}\left[1 + (Re_D/282\,000)^{5/8}\right]^{4/5}$ ($Re_DPr > 0.2$).
Sphere: Whitaker $\overline{Nu}_D = 2 + (0.4Re_D^{1/2} + 0.06Re_D^{2/3})Pr^{0.4}(\mu/\mu_s)^{1/4}$. Then $\bar h = \overline{Nu}\,k/L$ — divide by the right length ($L$ or $D$).

skills.title: Internal flow: mean temperature, Nu correlations
method: $Re_D = \dfrac{4\dot m}{\pi D\mu}$; laminar below 2300. Laminar entry lengths: $x_{fd,h} \approx 0.05Re_DD$, $x_{fd,t} \approx 0.05Re_DPr\,D$.
Uniform $q''_s$: $T_m$ rises linearly, $T_{m,o} = T_{m,i} + q''_s\pi DL/(\dot mc_p)$; wall $T_s = T_m + q''_s/h$.
Uniform $T_s$: $\dfrac{T_s - T_{m,o}}{T_s - T_{m,i}} = \exp\left(-\dfrac{\pi DL\bar h}{\dot mc_p}\right)$ — exponential approach, never a straight line.
Laminar fully developed: $Nu_D = 4.36$ (uniform $q''_s$), $3.66$ (uniform $T_s$). Turbulent ($Re_D \gtrsim 10^4$): Dittus–Boelter $Nu_D = 0.023Re_D^{4/5}Pr^n$, $n = 0.4$ heating, $0.3$ cooling.

skills.title: Free convection correlations
method: $Ra_L = \dfrac{g\beta(T_s - T_\infty)L^3}{\nu\alpha}$; ideal gas $\beta = 1/T_f$ in kelvin. Properties at $T_f$.
Vertical plate, any $Ra_L$ (Eq. 9.26): $\overline{Nu}_L = \left\{0.825 + \dfrac{0.387Ra_L^{1/6}}{[1 + (0.492/Pr)^{9/16}]^{8/27}}\right\}^2$; laminar below $Ra_L \approx 10^9$.
Horizontal plate, $L = A_s/P$. Hot face up or cold face down: $0.54Ra_L^{1/4}$ ($10^4$–$10^7$), $0.15Ra_L^{1/3}$ ($10^7$–$10^{11}$). Hot face down or cold face up: $0.52Ra_L^{1/5}$ ($10^4$–$10^9$).

skills.title: Heat exchangers: LMTD & ε–NTU
method: Energy balance first: $q = C_h(T_{h,i} - T_{h,o}) = C_c(T_{c,o} - T_{c,i})$, $C = \dot mc_p$.

LMTD: $q = UA\,\Delta T_{lm}$, $\Delta T_{lm} = (\Delta T_1 - \Delta T_2)/\ln(\Delta T_1/\Delta T_2)$. Parallel: $\Delta T_1 = T_{h,i} - T_{c,i}$, $\Delta T_2 = T_{h,o} - T_{c,o}$. Counterflow: $\Delta T_1 = T_{h,i} - T_{c,o}$, $\Delta T_2 = T_{h,o} - T_{c,i}$.
Outlets unknown? Use ε–NTU: $NTU = UA/C_{min}$, $C_r = C_{min}/C_{max}$, $q = \varepsilon C_{min}(T_{h,i} - T_{c,i})$.
Parallel $\varepsilon = \dfrac{1 - e^{-NTU(1 + C_r)}}{1 + C_r}$; counterflow $\varepsilon = \dfrac{1 - e^{-NTU(1 - C_r)}}{1 - C_re^{-NTU(1 - C_r)}}$; 1-shell-pass: Eq. 11.30a.
Traps: the arithmetic mean instead of the log mean; $C_{max}$ in $NTU$; mixing up which end is which in counterflow.

skills.title: Radiation view factors
method: Reciprocity $A_iF_{ij} = A_jF_{ji}$; summation $\sum_jF_{ij} = 1$; a flat or convex surface has $F_{ii} = 0$.
Convex body 1 inside surface 2: $F_{12} = 1$, $F_{21} = A_1/A_2$, $F_{22} = 1 - A_1/A_2$ (spheres $(D_1/D_2)^2$, long cylinders $D_1/D_2$).
Long duct of three flat sides: $F_{ij} = (w_i + w_j - w_k)/(2w_i)$, from summation + reciprocity alone.
Cavities: close the opening with an imaginary surface, find one factor from a chart or Table 13.2, the rest by algebra.

skills.title: Radiation exchange in enclosures
method: Network: surface resistance $(1 - \varepsilon_i)/(\varepsilon_iA_i)$ between $E_{bi} = \sigma T_i^4$ and radiosity $J_i$; space resistance $1/(A_iF_{ij})$ between radiosities.

Two-surface: $q_{12} = \dfrac{\sigma(T_1^4 - T_2^4)}{\frac{1 - \varepsilon_1}{\varepsilon_1A_1} + \frac{1}{A_1F_{12}} + \frac{1 - \varepsilon_2}{\varepsilon_2A_2}}$; parallel plates per area: $\sigma(T_1^4 - T_2^4)/(1/\varepsilon_1 + 1/\varepsilon_2 - 1)$.
A shield adds $1/\varepsilon_{3,1} + 1/\varepsilon_{3,2} - 1$ to the denominator. Black surfaces: $q_{12} = A_1F_{12}\sigma(T_1^4 - T_2^4)$.
Reradiating (insulated) surface: $q_R = 0$, so $J_R = E_{bR}$ floats between the others — it is a node with no source.
Kelvin always; for the outer of two concentric surfaces use its own area $A_2$.

skills.title: Convection: boundary layers, dimensionless groups, analogies
method: $Re_x = u_\infty x/\nu$, $Pr = \nu/\alpha = \mu c_p/k$, $Nu = hL/k_f$: the $k$ of the fluid, not the wall (that would be a Biot number).
Transition on a flat plate at $Re_{x,c} = 5\times10^5$: $x_c = 5\times10^5\,\nu/u_\infty$.
Average $\bar h_L = \frac{1}{L}\int_0^L h_x\,dx$. Laminar $h_x \propto x^{-1/2}$ gives $\bar h_L = 2h_x(L)$, i.e. $\bar{Nu}_L = 0.664Re_L^{1/2}Pr^{1/3}$ from $Nu_x = 0.332Re_x^{1/2}Pr^{1/3}$.
Laminar plate: $\delta = 5x/Re_x^{1/2}$ and $\delta/\delta_t \approx Pr^{1/3}$ (so $\delta_t < \delta$ when $Pr > 1$).
Chilton–Colburn: $C_f/2 = St\,Pr^{2/3}$, $St = h/(\rho c_pu_\infty)$, $C_f = \tau_s/(\rho u_\infty^2/2)$; $0.6 < Pr < 60$. Drag $F_D$ → $\tau_s = F_D/A$.

skills.title: Flow across tube banks
method: Aligned: $V_{max} = \frac{S_T}{S_T - D}V$. Staggered: same, unless $S_D = \sqrt{S_L^2 + (S_T/2)^2} < (S_T + D)/2$, then $V_{max} = \frac{S_T}{2(S_D - D)}V$.

Zukauskas (Eq 7.58): $\bar{Nu}_D = C_2CRe_{D,max}^mPr^{0.36}(Pr/Pr_s)^{1/4}$; $C$, $m$ from Table 7.5 by $Re_{D,max}$; $C_2 < 1$ only if $N_L < 20$ (Table 7.6). $Pr_s$ at the wall, everything else at the mean fluid temperature.
Outlet (Eq 7.62): $\frac{T_s - T_o}{T_s - T_i} = \exp\left(-\frac{\pi DN\bar h}{\rho VN_TS_Tc_p}\right)$ with $V$, $\rho$ at the inlet; then $q' = N\bar h\pi D\,\Delta T_{lm}$ per unit length.
Reynolds number uses $V_{max}$, never the approach velocity $V$.

skills.title: Boiling: nucleate flux, critical heat flux
method: Excess temperature $\Delta T_e = T_s - T_{sat}$. Water at 1 atm: free convection $\lesssim 5$ K, nucleate 5–30 K, transition 30–120 K, film beyond.

Rohsenow (Eq 10.5): $q''_s = \mu_lh_{fg}\left[\frac{g(\rho_l - \rho_v)}{\sigma}\right]^{1/2}\left(\frac{c_{p,l}\Delta T_e}{C_{s,f}h_{fg}Pr_l^n}\right)^3$; $C_{s,f}$, $n$ from Table 10.1 ($n = 1$ for water). Nucleate regime only.
The flux goes as $\Delta T_e^3/C_{s,f}^3$: a 10 % slip in $C_{s,f}$ is a 30 % slip in $q''_s$. Inverting for $\Delta T_e$ takes a cube root.
Critical flux (Eq 10.6): $q''_{max} = Ch_{fg}\rho_v\left[\frac{\sigma g(\rho_l - \rho_v)}{\rho_v^2}\right]^{1/4}$, $C = 0.149$ for large horizontal surfaces; $\propto g^{1/4}$.

skills.title: Film condensation (Nusselt)
method: Modified latent heat $h'_{fg} = h_{fg} + 0.68c_{p,l}(T_{sat} - T_s)$; liquid properties at $T_f = (T_{sat} + T_s)/2$, $\rho_v$ and $h_{fg}$ at $T_{sat}$.
Vertical plate, laminar (Eq 10.30): $\bar h_L = 0.943\left[\frac{g\rho_l(\rho_l - \rho_v)k_l^3h'_{fg}}{\mu_l(T_{sat} - T_s)L}\right]^{1/4}$. Horizontal tube: $0.729$ and $D$ in place of $L$.
$q = \bar hA(T_{sat} - T_s)$, condensate $\dot m = q/h'_{fg}$ (use $h'_{fg}$, not $h_{fg}$).
Check $Re_\delta = 4\dot m/(\mu_lb) \le 30$ for the laminar wave-free result; above that use the wavy-laminar or turbulent correlations.

skills.title: Radiation: blackbody, band fractions, emissivity & absorptivity
method: Kelvin everywhere. Wien: $\lambda_{max}T = 2898\ \mu\mathrm{m\cdot K}$ (µm, not m). $E_b = \sigma T^4$, $E = \varepsilon\sigma T^4$.
Band fraction $F_{(\lambda_1\to\lambda_2)} = F_{(0\to\lambda_2T)} - F_{(0\to\lambda_1T)}$ from Table 12.2 in $\lambda T$; $F_{(\lambda\to\infty)} = 1 - F_{(0\to\lambda T)}$.
Band-wise surfaces: $\varepsilon = \sum\varepsilon_iF_i$ weighted at the surface $T$; solar $\alpha_S = \sum\alpha_iF_i$ weighted at 5800 K.
Opaque: $\alpha + \rho = 1$. Gray and diffuse: $\alpha = \varepsilon$ (Kirchhoff). Radiosity $J = \varepsilon E_b + \rho G$; net out $q''_{rad} = \varepsilon E_b - \alpha G = J - G$.
Sunlit surface: absorb solar with $\alpha_S$, long-wave sky with $\alpha = \varepsilon$, emit with $\varepsilon$.

skills.title: Diffusion mass transfer: Fick's law, stationary media, evaporation
method: Fick: $J^*_A = -CD_{AB}\,dx_A/dx$ (molar) or $j_A = -\rho D_{AB}\,dm_A/dx$ (mass). kmol × $\mathcal M_A$ (kg/kmol) = kg.
Ideal gas $C = p/(\mathcal RT)$ with $\mathcal R = 8.314$ kJ/kmol·K and $p$ in kPa gives kmol/m³.
Stationary medium or equimolar counterdiffusion: linear profile, $N''_A = D_{AB}(C_{A,1} - C_{A,2})/L$. Gas–solid interface: $C_{A,s} = Sp_A$.
Evaporation through stagnant B (Stefan flow): $N''_A = \frac{CD_{AB}}{L}\ln\frac{1 - x_{A,L}}{1 - x_{A,0}}$, $x_{A,0} = p_{sat}/p$; bulk motion matters as $x_{A,0}$ grows.
First-order reaction, impermeable bottom: $C_A = C_{A,0}\cosh m(L - x)/\cosh mL$, $m = \sqrt{k_1/D_{AB}}$; surface flux $D_{AB}C_{A,0}m\tanh mL$.

skills.title: Convective mass transfer & the heat–mass analogy
method: Rate: $n_A = \bar h_mA(\rho_{A,s} - \rho_{A,\infty})$, $\rho_{A,s} = \rho_{A,sat}(T_s)$, $\rho_{A,\infty} = \phi_\infty\rho_{A,sat}(T_\infty)$.
Analogy: $\bar{Nu}/Pr^n = \bar{Sh}/Sc^n$ ⇒ $\bar h/\bar h_m = k/(D_{AB}Le^{1-n})$ (Eq 6.92), $\approx \rho c_pLe^{2/3}$ for $n = 1/3$, $Le = \alpha/D_{AB}$, $Sc = \nu/D_{AB}$.
Correlations carry over with $Nu \to Sh$, $Pr \to Sc$: laminar plate $\bar{Sh}_L = 0.664Re_L^{1/2}Sc^{1/3}$; sphere $\bar{Sh}_D = 2 + 0.6Re_D^{1/2}Sc^{1/3}$.
Evaporative cooling / wet bulb: $\bar h(T_\infty - T_s) = \bar h_mh_{fg}(\rho_{A,s} - \rho_{A,\infty})$.

skills.title: Exam: true/false & multiple-choice concepts (Ch 1–5)
method: Radiation needs no medium; $k$ can depend on direction (anisotropic); fin effectiveness $> 1$ means the fin helps; fin efficiency is at most 1.
Is $T(x,y,z)$ possible (steady, no $\dot q$, constant $k$)? Check $\nabla^2T = 0$. Cross terms like $xy$ drop out; only $x^2, y^2, z^2$ count: $2(a+b+c) = 0$.

Cylindrical: $
abla^2(r^2) = 4$, $
abla^2(z^2) = 2$, $
abla^2(\ln r) = 0$, and $
abla^2(rz) = z/r$, which is never zero.
Series layers carry the same $q$, so $\Delta T_i = qR_i$: the bigger temperature drop marks the bigger resistance (smaller $k$ for equal $L$).
Series/parallel: blocks in series carry the same rate $q$; blocks in parallel share the same $\Delta T$. Flux $q'' = q/A$: a block twice as tall carries half the flux for the same rate.

skills.title: Exam: short answers (wall point, rod in slab, two spheres, pot)
method: Inside one layer (1-D, steady, no $\dot q$) $T$ is linear: halfway through layer 1 is $(T_1 + T_2)/2$, a quarter of the way is $\tfrac34T_1 + \tfrac14T_2$.
Rod midway between two isothermal planes (Table 4.1 case 5, $z = y$): $R'_t = \ln(8z/\pi D)/2\pi k$. With generation, $q' = \dot q\,\pi D^2/4$ must equal $\Delta T/R'_t$.
Two equal spheres: the midplane is isothermal at the mean temperature. Each sphere is case 1 with $z$ = centre to midplane: $S = 2\pi D/(1 - D/4z)$, $q = Sk(T_1 - T_{mid})$. Use the medium's $k$.
Pot bottom: $T'' = 0$, $-kT'(0) = q''$, $-kT'(L) = h[T(L) - T_\infty]$. So $T(L) = T_\infty + q''/h$ and $T(0) = T(L) + q''L/k$; raising $q''$ steepens the line.
Units: W/cm² × $10^4$ = W/m²; mm × $10^{-3}$ = m. The exam rounds to whole numbers with no partial credit, so carry digits.

skills.title: Exam: finite-difference node with Δx ≠ Δy, convection & radiation
method: Draw the node's cell: interior full, surface half, corner quarter. Every face gets a term; assume all heat flows into the node and set the sum to 0.

Conduction to a neighbour: $k \times$ (face length it crosses) $\times (T_{nb} - T_n)/$(distance to that neighbour). With $\Delta x \ne \Delta y$ the face is the perpendicular spacing (halved on a boundary cell).
Exposed face: $h\,\ell(T_\infty - T_n)$, plus $h_r\,\ell(T_{sur} - T_n)$ for radiation, with $\ell$ the exposed length ($\Delta x$, $\Delta y$, or half of one at a corner). Insulated: no term.
Solve: $T_n = \sum G_iT_i/\sum G_i$ with conductances $G_i$. Check: with $\Delta x = \Delta y$, an interior node is the average of its four neighbours.

skills.title: Fundamental equation & intensive variables
method: Entropy representation: $\frac1T = \left(\frac{\partial S}{\partial U}\right)_{V,N}$, $\frac PT = \left(\frac{\partial S}{\partial V}\right)_{U,N}$, $\frac{\mu}{T} = -\left(\frac{\partial S}{\partial N}\right)_{U,V}$.
Energy representation: $T = \partial U/\partial S$, $P = -\partial U/\partial V$, $\mu = \partial U/\partial N$. Watch the minus sign on $P$.
Power laws differentiate in one line: $\partial(AU^gV^b)/\partial U = gS/U$. Dividing two derivatives cancels $A$.
Euler (extensivity): $U = TS - PV + \mu N$. Gibbs–Duhem: $S\,dT - V\,dP + N\,d\mu = 0$, so at fixed $T$, $d\mu = v\,dP$.

skills.title: First law, work & heat for reversible paths
method: $\Delta U = q + w$, $w$ = work done ON the gas, $\delta w = -P\,dV$. Expansion: $w < 0$.
Isothermal ideal gas: $\Delta U = 0$, $w = -nRT\ln(V_2/V_1)$, $q = -w$.
Reversible adiabatic: $q = 0$, $T_2 = T_1(V_1/V_2)^{R/C_V}$, $w = nC_V(T_2 - T_1)$. $C_V = \tfrac32R$ monatomic, $\tfrac52R$ diatomic.
Isobaric: $w = -nR\Delta T$, $q = nC_P\Delta T$, $C_P = C_V + R$. Isochoric: $w = 0$, $q = nC_V\Delta T$.
Litres to m³: divide by 1000. Temperatures in kelvin.

skills.title: Legendre transforms & free energies
method: Each Legendre term swaps a pair: $-TS$ ($S \to T$), $+PV$ ($V \to P$), $-\mu N$ ($N \to \mu$). $F = U - TS$, $H = U + PV$, $G = H - TS$.
To get $F(T, V, N)$: solve $T = \partial U/\partial S$ for $S$, then substitute into $U - TS$. An answer still containing $S$ is not in natural variables.
Derivatives back out: $dF = -S\,dT - P\,dV + \mu\,dN$, $dG = -S\,dT + V\,dP + \mu\,dN$.
Gibbs–Helmholtz: $H = G + TS = G - T(\partial G/\partial T)_P$.

skills.title: Maxwell relations
method: Pick the potential whose natural variables are the two in the derivative (the one held fixed and the one varied): $(T, V) \to F$, $(T, P) \to G$, $(S, V) \to U$, $(S, P) \to H$.
Equal mixed partials: $(\partial S/\partial V)_T = (\partial P/\partial T)_V$, $(\partial S/\partial P)_T = -(\partial V/\partial T)_P$.
Measurables: $\alpha = \frac1V(\partial V/\partial T)_P$, $\kappa_T = -\frac1V(\partial V/\partial P)_T$; triple product gives $(\partial P/\partial T)_V = \alpha/\kappa_T$.
Internal pressure: $(\partial U/\partial V)_T = T(\partial P/\partial T)_V - P$. Zero for an ideal gas; $a/V^2$ for van der Waals.

skills.title: Stability conditions
method: Stable means $S(U, V)$ is concave: $S_{UU} < 0$ ($C_V > 0$), $S_{VV} < 0$, and $S_{UU}S_{VV} - S_{UV}^2 > 0$.
Mechanical stability: $\kappa_T > 0$, i.e. $(\partial P/\partial V)_T < 0$. van der Waals: $(\partial P/\partial V)_T = -RT/(V-b)^2 + 2a/V^3$.
The unstable region first appears at the critical point, where $P_V = P_{VV} = 0$: $V_c = 3b$, $T_c = 8a/(27Rb)$.
$C_V = (\partial U/\partial T)_V$: write $U(T, V)$ first by inverting $1/T = \partial S/\partial U$.

skills.title: Phase equilibrium & Clapeyron
method: Coexistence: $\mu_\alpha = \mu_\beta$ along the line, so $dP/dT = \Delta H/(T\Delta V)$ (Clapeyron).
Vapor ideal, liquid volume neglected: $\ln(P_2/P_1) = -\frac{\Delta H_{vap}}{R}\left(\frac1{T_2} - \frac1{T_1}\right)$.
Order matters: $1/T_2 - 1/T_1$ with the same labels as $P_2/P_1$. Kelvin only; $\Delta H$ in J/mol with $R = 8.314$.
Melting: $\Delta V$ is small and can be negative (ice), so $dP/dT$ is huge and can be negative.

skills.title: Solutions: ideal mixing, activity, Raoult/Henry
method: Ideal: $\mu_i = \mu_i^* + RT\ln x_i$. $\Delta G_{mix} = RT\sum n_i\ln x_i$, $\Delta S_{mix} = -R\sum n_i\ln x_i$, $\Delta H_{mix} = 0$.
Raoult (solvent): $p_i = x_iP_i^*$; Henry (dilute solute): $p_i = K_Hx_i$. Vapor composition: $y_i = p_i/P$.
Real: $a_i = \gamma_ix_i$, so $\gamma_i = p_i/(x_iP_i^*)$. $\gamma > 1$ is a positive deviation.
Regular solution: $RT\ln\gamma_A = Wx_B^2$ — the OTHER component's mole fraction.

skills.title: Chemical equilibrium constants
method: $\Delta G^\circ = -RT\ln K$; $\Delta G = \Delta G^\circ + RT\ln Q$. $Q < K$: runs forward.
Units: $\Delta G^\circ$ in kJ/mol × 1000 before dividing by $RT$.
van 't Hoff: $\ln(K_2/K_1) = -\frac{\Delta H^\circ}{R}\left(\frac1{T_2} - \frac1{T_1}\right)$. Exothermic: $K$ falls as $T$ rises.
Extent: write moles of each species in terms of $\xi$, then $p_i = (n_i/n_{tot})P$, plug into $K$, solve for $\xi$ (between 0 and $n_0$).

skills.title: Probability & combinatorics for counting states
method: Order matters (labelled places, distinguishable objects)? $n!/(n-k)!$. Only which ones? $\binom{n}{k} = \frac{n!}{k!(n-k)!}$.
Sequences with repeats: $\frac{N!}{n_A!\,n_B!\cdots}$ — divide out swaps of identical items.
Exactly $k$ of $n$ independent trials: $\binom{n}{k}p^k(1-p)^{n-k}$.
"At least one" = $1 - P(\text{none}) = 1 - (1-p)^n$. Much easier than adding cases.

skills.title: Multiplicity & S = k ln W
method: Two-state: $W(N, n) = \binom{N}{n}$. Einstein solid, $q$ quanta on $N$ oscillators: $W = \binom{q + N - 1}{q}$ (stars and bars).
$S = k_B\ln W$, so $\Delta S = k_B\ln(W_2/W_1)$ — a ratio, never a difference of $W$s.
Lattice gas: $W = M^N$ with $M \propto V$, so $\Delta S = Nk_B\ln(V_2/V_1) = nR\ln(V_2/V_1)$.
Two solids in contact: every microstate of the combined system is equally likely, $P(q_A) = W_A(q_A)W_B(q - q_A)/W_{tot}$.

skills.title: Boltzmann distribution & populations
method: $\frac{N_j}{N_i} = \frac{g_j}{g_i}e^{-(E_j - E_i)/k_BT}$ — degeneracies multiply, energies sit in the exponent.
Molar energies use $R$; per-molecule use $k_B$. Wavenumbers: $\Delta E = hc\tilde\nu$ with $c$ in cm/s.
Fractions need the whole sum: $p_i = g_ie^{-E_i/k_BT}/q$.
Solving for $T$: $T = \Delta E/[k_B\ln(g_jN_i/(g_iN_j))]$.

skills.title: Partition functions → U, F, S, Cv
method: $q = \sum_i g_ie^{-\beta E_i}$; then $U = -N\,\partial\ln q/\partial\beta$, $F = -Nk_BT\ln q$ (localized), $S = (U - F)/T$.
Two-level: $q = g_0 + g_1e^{-x}$ with $x = \beta\varepsilon$; $U/N\varepsilon$ is just the excited-state probability.
Oscillator: $q = 1/(1 - e^{-x})$ from the ground state, $U/N\varepsilon = 1/(e^x - 1)$ (add $\tfrac12$ for zero-point).
Shifting every energy by a constant changes $U$ and $F$ by that constant but leaves $S$, $C_V$ and populations alone.

skills.title: Ideal gas: translational, rotational, vibrational q
method: Translation: $q = V/\Lambda^3$, $\Lambda = h/\sqrt{2\pi mk_BT}$ — mass in kg ($M$ in g/mol × $1.661\times10^{-27}$).
Rotation (diatomic): $\theta_{rot} = \hbar^2/(2Ik_B)$, $I = \mu r^2$; for $T \gg \theta_{rot}$, $q_{rot} = T/(\sigma\theta_{rot})$, $\sigma = 2$ if homonuclear.
Vibration: $\theta_{vib} = hc\tilde\nu/k_B$; from the ground state $q_{vib} = 1/(1 - e^{-\theta_{vib}/T})$, excited fraction $e^{-\theta_{vib}/T}$.
Usually $\theta_{rot} \ll T \ll \theta_{vib}$: rotations classical, vibrations frozen.

skills.title: Temperature & heat capacity from q
method: Equipartition: $\tfrac12R$ per quadratic term. Translation 3, rotation 2 (linear) or 3, each active vibration 2 (kinetic + potential).
Vibrational modes: $3N - 5$ (linear) or $3N - 6$ (nonlinear).
Quantum mode: $C/k_B = x^2e^x/(e^x - 1)^2$ with $x = \theta/T$; Einstein solid $C_{V,m} = 3R$ times that.
From $U(x)$: $C_V/Nk_B = -x^2\,d(U/N\varepsilon)/dx$, since $dx/dT = -x/T$.

skills.title: Energy fluctuations in the canonical ensemble
method: $\sigma_E^2 = \langle E^2\rangle - \langle E\rangle^2 = \partial^2\ln Q/\partial\beta^2 = k_BT^2C_V$.
Two-level: $\sigma_E^2 = \varepsilon^2p_1(1 - p_1)$. Compute $\langle E^2\rangle$ with the same weights as $\langle E\rangle$.
Ideal gas: $\sigma_E/\langle E\rangle = \sqrt{2/(3N)}$ — relative fluctuations die as $N^{-1/2}$.
Molar: $\sigma_{E,m} = \sqrt{RT^2C_{V,m}}$ with $C_V$ in J, not kJ.

skills.title: Other ensembles (grand canonical, isobaric)
method: Grand canonical: $\Xi = \sum_{N,i}e^{-\beta(E_i - \mu N)} = \sum\lambda^Ne^{-\beta E_i}$, $\lambda = e^{\beta\mu}$.
$\langle N\rangle = \lambda\,\partial\ln\Xi/\partial\lambda$; $\sigma_N^2 = \lambda\,\partial\langle N\rangle/\partial\lambda$.
List the states with their weights, then average — independent sites factor: $\Xi = \xi^M$.
Isobaric: weight $e^{-\beta(E + pV)}$; $p\Delta V$ in J/mol needs Pa × m³/mol (1 bar = $10^5$ Pa, 1 mL = $10^{-6}$ m³).

skills.title: Binding & cooperativity (Langmuir, Hill)
method: Langmuir site: weights 1 (empty) and $Kp$ (bound), so $\theta = Kp/(1 + Kp)$; in solution $\theta = c/(K_d + c)$.
Half coverage at $p = 1/K$ (or $c = K_d$).
Hill: $\theta = \frac{(c/K_{1/2})^{n_H}}{1 + (c/K_{1/2})^{n_H}}$; $n_H$ = slope of $\ln\frac{\theta}{1-\theta}$ vs $\ln c$.
$\Delta G^\circ_{bind} = RT\ln(K_d/1\,\mathrm{M})$ — negative for tight binding.

skills.title: Rates & transition-state theory
method: Arrhenius pair: $\ln\frac{k_2}{k_1} = \frac{E_a}{R}\left(\frac{1}{T_1} - \frac{1}{T_2}\right)$ — temperatures in kelvin, $E_a$ in J/mol.
Eyring: $k = \frac{k_BT}{h}e^{-\Delta G^\ddagger/RT}$, $\Delta G^\ddagger = \Delta H^\ddagger - T\Delta S^\ddagger$; $k_BT/h \approx 6.2\times10^{12}\,\mathrm{s^{-1}}$ at 298 K.
Invert: $\Delta G^\ddagger = RT\ln\frac{k_BT}{hk}$.
Rule of thumb: $E_a \approx 50$ kJ/mol roughly doubles $k$ per 10 °C near room temperature.

problems.prompt: What is the order of {{ka}} in the additive group Z_{{kn}}?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Adding a to itself first returns to 0 at the least common multiple of a and n, which is n/gcd(a, n) additions

problems.prompt: How many elements of order {{kd}} are there in the cyclic group Z_{{kn}}?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: A cyclic group has exactly one subgroup of each order dividing n, and that subgroup has φ(d) generators

problems.prompt: A group of order {{kg}} has a subgroup of order {{kh}}. How many left cosets does the subgroup have?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: The cosets partition the group into pieces of equal size, so there are |G|/|H| of them

problems.prompt: How many elements has the group of units modulo {{kn}}?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: A residue is a unit exactly when it is coprime to n, so the order is φ(n)

problems.prompt: Is the group of units modulo {{kn}} cyclic?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Cyclic only for 1, 2, 4, odd prime powers and twice odd prime powers. Modulo 8 every unit squares to 1, so no element has order 4

problems.prompt: What is the order of the permutation {{sh}}?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Each cycle returns to the identity after its own length, so the whole permutation does after the least common multiple

problems.prompt: Let σ = {{s1}} and τ = {{s2}}. Where does στ (apply τ first, then σ) send {{kx}}?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Follow the point through the right-hand permutation first, then through the left-hand one

problems.prompt: What is the sign of the permutation {{sh}}? Answer 1 for even, −1 for odd.

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Add up (length − 1) over the cycles: an even total is an even permutation

problems.prompt: How many elements has the alternating group A_{{kn}}?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Multiplying by a fixed transposition pairs each even permutation with an odd one, so exactly half are even

problems.prompt: How many conjugacy classes has the symmetric group S_{{kn}}?

parts.label: v

problems.prompt: A model scores three possible next tokens {{z1}}, {{z2}} and {{z3}}. Softmax turns the scores into probabilities. What is the probability of the first token?

parts.label: a
parts.explain: Softmax: raise e to each score, then divide by the total, so the results are positive and add to 1. Only differences between scores matter, and a lead of one point multiplies the odds by e ≈ 2.7

problems.prompt: Two candidate tokens score {{z1}} and {{z2}}. At temperature {{t}} (divide each score by the temperature, then softmax), what is the probability of the first?

parts.label: a
parts.explain: Dividing by a low temperature stretches the gaps, so the favourite wins almost every time (near-deterministic output). A high temperature shrinks the gaps and flattens the odds (more varied, more error-prone output)

problems.prompt: About how many gigabytes do the weights of a {{nb}}-billion-parameter model take at {{by == 2 ? "16-bit" : (by == 1 ? "8-bit" : "4-bit")}} precision?

parts.label: a
parts.explain: Parameters × bytes per parameter: 16-bit is 2 bytes, 8-bit 1 byte, 4-bit half a byte, and a billion bytes is a gigabyte. Running the model needs more memory than this for the context (the KV cache) and activations. Quantizing to fewer bits is how big models fit on smaller machines

cases.s: learning to tell cats from dogs from photos labelled by people
predicting tomorrow's demand from past days with known outcomes
grouping customers into segments nobody has named
learning to play a game from points won and lost
a robot learning to walk by trial and reward
pretraining a language model to predict the next word of web text

problems.prompt: What kind of learning is {{s}}?

parts.label: a
choice: Unsupervised: find structure with no answers given
Reinforcement: learn from rewards for actions
Self-supervised: the data supplies its own answers
parts.explain: Supervised learning needs labels; unsupervised learning has none and looks for patterns; reinforcement learning acts and is scored. Next-word prediction is self-supervised, a kind of supervised learning where the label (the next word) comes free with the text, which is why it can use the whole web

cases.s: reads trillions of tokens of general text to learn to predict the next token
continues training on a smaller set of example conversations or task answers
uses people's (or a model's) ratings of which answer is better to shape behaviour
happens every time someone sends a prompt, and changes no weights

problems.prompt: Which stage of building a chat assistant {{s}}?

parts.label: a
choice: Reinforcement learning from feedback (RLHF and similar)
parts.explain: Pretraining makes a model that can continue any text; fine-tuning on examples teaches it to follow instructions and act as an assistant; feedback-based reinforcement learning tunes it toward answers people prefer. Using the model afterward is inference: it learns nothing from your chat unless that data is later used for training

problems.prompt: A weight is {{w}}, the gradient of the loss with respect to it is {{g}}, and the learning rate is {{lr}}. What is the weight after one gradient-descent step?

parts.label: a
parts.explain: Step against the gradient: w − (learning rate) × gradient. A positive gradient means the loss rises as w rises, so w goes down. Too big a learning rate overshoots; too small crawls

problems.prompt: A model predicts {{p1}}, {{p2}}, {{p3}}; the true values are {{t1}}, {{t2}}, {{t3}}. What is the mean squared error?

parts.label: a
parts.explain: Square each error, then average. Squaring makes every error count positively and punishes big misses more than small ones. Training is the search for weights that make this loss small

problems.prompt: A model trains on {{nex}} examples in batches of {{bs}} for {{ep}} epochs, with one weight update per batch. How many updates is that?

parts.label: a
parts.explain: One epoch is one pass through all the data: {{nex}} ÷ {{bs}} batches. Multiply by the number of epochs

cases.s: training loss keeps falling but validation loss has started rising
it scores 99% on its training examples and 60% on new ones
both training and validation loss stay high
training and validation loss fall together and level off close to each other

problems.prompt: A model is being trained and {{s}}. What is happening?

parts.label: a
choice: Overfitting: memorizing the training data instead of the pattern
Underfitting: too simple or too little training to capture the pattern
parts.explain: Judge a model on data it has not trained on. A widening gap between training and validation performance is overfitting (cure: more data, regularization, stop earlier). Poor performance on both is underfitting (cure: a bigger model, better features, more training)

cases.s: the examples the weights are fitted to

problems.prompt: Which split of the data is {{s}}?

parts.label: a
parts.explain: Fit on the training set, tune on the validation set, and look at the test set once. Every time the test set influences a choice, it stops being an honest estimate of performance on new data

problems.prompt: A spam filter flags {{tp + fp}} emails: {{tp}} really are spam and {{fp}} are not. It misses {{fn}} spam emails. What is its precision?

parts.label: a
parts.explain: Precision = true positives ÷ everything flagged: of what it called spam, how much was spam. Recall = true positives ÷ all real spam: of the spam, how much it caught. Raising the threshold usually trades recall for precision

problems.prompt: A screening model flags {{tp + fp}} patients: {{tp}} have the disease and {{fp}} do not. It misses {{fn}} who do. What is its recall?

parts.label: a
parts.explain: Recall (sensitivity) = true positives ÷ everyone who really has it = {{tp}} ÷ ({{tp}} + {{fn}}). For screening, missed cases are costly, so recall usually matters more than precision

cases.s: Which task is a language model most reliable at?
cases.o1: Exact arithmetic on long numbers without a tool
cases.o2: Quoting a specific page from memory
cases.o4: Rewording or summarizing text you give it

parts.label: a
parts.explain: A language model generates what is likely given its training and context; fluency is not evidence of truth. It is strongest working on material in front of it, weakest recalling exact facts, figures and citations from memory. Ground it with sources or tools and check anything that matters

problems.prompt: You prompt a chatbot and {{s}}. Which change fixes that best?

parts.label: a
choice: Give context: who it is for, what you know, what you are trying to do
State the output format exactly (columns, length, structure)
Include one or two examples of what good looks like
Break it into steps, or ask for one part at a time
parts.explain: The model only knows what is in the context, so a good prompt reads like a brief to a capable colleague: the goal, the background, the constraints, the format and, where taste matters, examples. Iterate: tell it what was wrong with the last answer

parts.label: a
choice: No: it is not in the training data or the context
Yes: it is in the context window or a tool can fetch it
parts.explain: A model knows two things: what it absorbed in training, up to its knowledge cutoff, and whatever is in its context window right now (your messages, attachments, tool results). Anything else it can only guess at

problems.prompt: In an AI agent, which part {{s}}?

parts.label: a
parts.explain: A chatbot answers once. An agent wraps the model in a harness: tools it can call, memory it can read and write, and a loop that feeds each result back so the model can choose its next move, step after step, toward a goal

problems.prompt: In an agent's loop, what comes right after this: {{s}}?

parts.label: a
choice: The harness runs the tool with the arguments the model chose
Its result is put back into the model's context
The model decides the next step: another tool call, or a final answer
parts.explain: The model never runs anything itself: it writes a request, the harness carries it out and returns the result as new context. Knowing when to stop, or to ask a person, is part of the design

problems.prompt: In retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), what comes right after this: {{s}}?

parts.label: a
choice: The embeddings are stored in a searchable index (a vector database)
The chunks with the most similar embeddings are retrieved
They are pasted into the prompt and the model answers from them
parts.explain: RAG answers from your documents without retraining: embed and index the documents once; for each question, embed it, fetch the most similar chunks, and give them to the model as context. Quality depends on what gets retrieved, so a wrong chunk gives a wrong answer

choice: The largest, most capable model available
A multimodal model that accepts images

problems.prompt: An API charges {{pin}} dollars per million input tokens and {{pout}} dollars per million output tokens. A job sends {{tin}} million tokens in and gets {{tout}} million back. What does it cost, in dollars?

problems.prompt: What is the name for {{s}}?

parts.label: a
parts.explain: Scaling laws are why labs train ever-larger models; alignment is the work of making those models do what is intended, including when they are more capable than the people checking them. AGI has no single agreed definition, which is one reason forecasts of it differ so widely

problems.prompt: Training compute is roughly 6 × parameters × training tokens. About how many floating-point operations does training a {{nb}}-billion-parameter model on {{dt}} trillion tokens take, in units of 10²¹?

parts.label: a
parts.explain: 6 × {{nb}} × 10⁹ × {{dt}} × 10¹² = {{6*nb*dt}} × 10²¹. The 6 counts about two operations per parameter per token forward and four backward. It is an estimate that ignores attention's extra cost

problems.prompt: The Chinchilla rule of thumb says a compute-optimal model trains on about 20 tokens per parameter. How many billion tokens is that for a {{nb}}-billion-parameter model?

parts.label: a
parts.explain: Hoffmann et al. (2022) found that for a fixed compute budget, parameters and data should grow together, about 20 tokens per parameter. Models meant for cheap use are often trained well past this, because a smaller model trained longer costs less to run

cases.q: [H₃O⁺] is
[OH⁻] is

problems.prompt: At 25 °C, {{q}} ${{m}}\times10^{-{{e}}}$ M. What is the pH?

parts.label: r
parts.explain: pH $= -\log[\mathrm{H_3O^+}]$, pOH $= -\log[\mathrm{OH^-}]$, and pH + pOH = 14 at 25 °C because $K_w = 1.0\times10^{-14}$. A mantissa above 1 makes the pH a little below the exponent

problems.prompt: What is the pH of ${{c}}$ M {{f}}?

parts.label: r
parts.explain: Strong acids (HCl, HBr, HI, HNO₃, HClO₄, H₂SO₄ for its first proton) and group 1 and heavy group 2 hydroxides ionize completely, so the ion concentration is ${{k}} \times {{c}}$ M. Remember the 2 in Ba(OH)₂

problems.prompt: What is the pH of ${{c}}$ M {{f}} ($K_a = {{Ka}}$), and what percent of it is ionized?

parts.label: r
parts.explain: $K_a = \dfrac{x^2}{c - x}$ with $x = [\mathrm{H_3O^+}]$. When $x$ is small next to c, $x \approx \sqrt{K_a c}$; the exact root is $x = {{(-Ka + sqrt(Ka^2 + 4*Ka*c))/2}}$ M

parts.label: p
parts.explain: Percent ionization $= x/c \times 100$. It rises as the acid is diluted, even though the pH also rises

problems.prompt: What is the pH of ${{c}}$ M {{f}} ($K_b = {{Kb}}$)?

parts.label: r
parts.explain: Same ICE table as a weak acid, but $x$ is [OH⁻]: $K_b = x^2/(c - x)$. Find pOH $= -\log x$, then pH = 14 − pOH. Getting a pH below 7 for a base means you forgot that last step

problems.prompt: A ${{c}}$ M solution of a weak acid HA has pH ${{pH}}$. What is $K_a$?

parts.label: r
parts.explain: $[\mathrm{H_3O^+}] = [\mathrm{A^-}] = 10^{-\text{pH}} = {{10^(-pH)}}$ M, and $[\mathrm{HA}] = c - x$. Then $K_a = \dfrac{x^2}{c - x}$

problems.prompt: {{a}} has $K_a = {{Ka}}$. What is $K_b$ of {{b}}?

parts.label: r
parts.explain: For a conjugate pair $K_a K_b = K_w = 1.0\times10^{-14}$ (equivalently p$K_a$ + p$K_b$ = 14). The weaker the acid, the stronger its conjugate base

problems.prompt: ${{Va}}$ mL of ${{Ca}}$ M HCl is mixed with ${{Vb}}$ mL of ${{Cb}}$ M NaOH. What is the pH?

parts.label: r
parts.value: Va*Ca > Vb*Cb ? -log10((Va*Ca - Vb*Cb)/(Va + Vb)) : 14 + log10((Vb*Cb - Va*Ca)/(Va + Vb))
parts.explain: Neutralise first: mmol H⁺ $= {{Va*Ca}}$, mmol OH⁻ $= {{Vb*Cb}}$. Whatever is left over, divided by the total volume ${{Va + Vb}}$ mL, sets the pH

expect.r: (-log((Va*Ca - Vb*Cb)/(Va + Vb), 10)) if Va*Ca > Vb*Cb else (14 + log((Vb*Cb - Va*Ca)/(Va + Vb), 10))

problems.prompt: ${{na}}$ mmol of acetic acid is mixed with ${{nb}}$ mmol of NaOH. What is in the flask?

parts.label: a
choice: A buffer: acetic acid and acetate both remain
Only acetate (the salt): the equivalence point, basic
Excess OH⁻ with acetate: the strong base sets the pH
parts.explain: The strong base reacts completely with the weak acid. Less base than acid leaves some HA beside its conjugate base: a buffer, with pH = pKa exactly at half-neutralization. Equal amounts leave only A⁻; more base leaves free OH⁻

choices.a: 0 if nb < na else (1 if nb == na else 2)

problems.prompt: Is a solution of {{f}} acidic, basic or neutral?

parts.label: a
parts.explain: Ask where each ion came from. The conjugate of a strong acid or base (Cl⁻, NO₃⁻, Na⁺, K⁺) does nothing. The conjugate base of a weak acid (F⁻, acetate, CN⁻, CO₃²⁻) makes OH⁻; the conjugate acid of a weak base (NH₄⁺) and small highly charged metal ions (Fe³⁺, Al³⁺) make H₃O⁺

problems.prompt: ${{Va}}$ mL of ${{Ca}}$ M weak acid ($K_a = {{Ka}}$) is titrated with ${{Cb}}$ M NaOH. What is the pH at the equivalence point?

parts.label: r
parts.explain: At equivalence all HA has become A⁻: ${{Ca*Va}}$ mmol in ${{Va + Ca*Va/Cb}}$ mL. A⁻ is a weak base with $K_b = K_w/K_a$, so $[\mathrm{OH^-}] \approx \sqrt{K_b[\mathrm{A^-}]}$. The pH is above 7; at half-equivalence it equals p$K_a$

cases.q: acetic acid titrated with NaOH (equivalence pH 8.7)
HCl titrated with NaOH (equivalence pH 7.0)
ammonia titrated with HCl (equivalence pH 5.3)
HF titrated with KOH (equivalence pH 8.1)
pyridine titrated with HNO₃ (equivalence pH 3.4)

problems.prompt: Which indicator suits {{q}}?

parts.label: a
parts.explain: Pick an indicator whose pKa sits near the equivalence pH, so its color changes on the steep part of the curve. Weak acid with strong base: basic equivalence. Weak base with strong acid: acidic. Strong with strong: 7

choices.a: 0 if ph < 6 else (1 if ph < 8 else 2)

problems.prompt: A solution of {{f}} (p$K_a$ = {{pk}}) is titrated with NaOH; the first equivalence point comes at ${{V1}}$ mL. At what volume is the second equivalence point, and what is the pH at ${{V1/2}}$ mL?

parts.label: r
parts.explain: Each proton takes the same amount of base, so the equivalence points are evenly spaced: the second needs twice the base of the first

parts.label: p
parts.explain: Halfway to the first equivalence point [H₂A⁻] = [H₃A] (or the first pair), so pH = p$K_{a1}$. Halfway between the first and second equivalence points pH = p$K_{a2}$

problems.prompt: Which is the stronger acid: {{a}} or {{b}}?

parts.label: a
parts.explain: Down a group, weaker H–X bonds win (HI > HF). Across a period, a more electronegative atom holds the H less tightly (H₂O > NH₃). For oxyacids, more O atoms and a more electronegative central atom pull electron density away and stabilise the conjugate base. (p$K_a$ {{pa}} and {{pb}})

problems.prompt: In {{rx}}, which species is the Lewis acid?

parts.label: a
parts.explain: A Lewis acid accepts an electron pair; a Lewis base donates one. Metal cations, electron-deficient molecules (BF₃, AlCl₃) and molecules with polar multiple bonds (CO₂) accept; lone-pair species (NH₃, H₂O, OH⁻, CN⁻, Cl⁻) donate

problems.prompt: An acid HA has p$K_a$ = ${{pka}}$. Which form predominates at pH ${{ph}}$?

parts.label: a
parts.explain: $\text{pH} - \text{p}K_a = \log\dfrac{[\mathrm{A^-}]}{[\mathrm{HA}]} = {{ph - pka}}$. Below the pKa the solution is acidic enough to keep the proton on; above it, the proton comes off. At pH = pKa the two are equal

cases.q: an acetic acid/acetate buffer
an acetic acid/acetate buffer
an NH₃/NH₄⁺ buffer
an NH₃/NH₄⁺ buffer
an H₂PO₄⁻/HPO₄²⁻ buffer

problems.prompt: Some {{add}} is added to {{q}}. Which net ionic equation shows how the buffer absorbs it?

parts.label: a
parts.explain: A buffer holds a weak acid and its conjugate base. Added strong acid is used up by the base component, added strong base by the acid component, each turning a strong species into a weak one. The ratio shifts only a little, so the pH does too

problems.prompt: A {{pair}} buffer (p$K_a$ = ${{pka}}$) has ${{a}}$ M of the acid and ${{b}}$ M of the base. What is its pH?

parts.label: r
parts.explain: Henderson–Hasselbalch: pH = p$K_a$ + $\log\dfrac{[\text{base}]}{[\text{acid}]}$. More base than acid puts the pH above the pKa. Moles work as well as concentrations, since the volume cancels

problems.prompt: A buffer holds ${{na}}$ mol acetic acid and ${{nb}}$ mol acetate (p$K_a$ = 4.74). What is the pH after ${{ad}}$ mol of {{w == 0 ? "HCl" : "NaOH"}} is added?

parts.label: r
parts.explain: Do the stoichiometry first, in moles: added {{w == 0 ? "H⁺ turns acetate into acetic acid" : "OH⁻ turns acetic acid into acetate"}}. Then use Henderson–Hasselbalch with the new amounts

expect.r: Rational(474, 100) + log(((nb - ad)/(na + ad)) if w == 0 else ((nb + ad)/(na - ad)), 10)

problems.prompt: Using the {{pair}} pair (p$K_a$ = ${{pka}}$), what base-to-acid mole ratio gives a buffer of pH ${{pka + d}}$?

parts.label: r
parts.explain: $\log\dfrac{[\text{base}]}{[\text{acid}]} = \text{pH} - \text{p}K_a = {{d}}$, so the ratio is $10^{ {{d}} }$. Choose a pair whose pKa is within 1 of the target; a buffer works best with a ratio between 0.1 and 10

problems.prompt: Buffer 1 has ${{a1}}$ mol HA and ${{b1}}$ mol A⁻; buffer 2 has ${{a2}}$ mol HA and ${{b2}}$ mol A⁻. Which can absorb more added {{w == 0 ? "strong acid" : "strong base"}} before its pH changes sharply?

parts.label: a
parts.explain: Capacity against added acid is set by how much base component there is, and against added base by the acid component. More of both, in a ratio near 1, makes a buffer that resists in both directions

choices.a: 0 if (b1 if w == 0 else a1) > (b2 if w == 0 else a2) else 1

problems.prompt: Is {{f}} more soluble in acidic solution than in pure water?

parts.label: a
choice: Yes: acid removes the anion and pulls the dissolving equilibrium forward
No: the anion is too weak a base to react with H₃O⁺
parts.explain: If the anion is the conjugate base of a weak acid (F⁻, CO₃²⁻, PO₄³⁻, S²⁻, OH⁻), H₃O⁺ protonates it, lowering Q below Ksp so more solid dissolves. Anions of strong acids (Cl⁻, Br⁻, I⁻) are unaffected

problems.prompt: What is the sign of ΔS for {{q}}?

parts.label: a
parts.explain: Entropy rises with more ways to spread matter and energy: solid → liquid → gas, more moles of gas, mixing, dissolving a solid, higher temperature. Count gas moles first; they dominate

problems.prompt: A reaction has $\Delta H^\circ = {{dH}}$ kJ/mol and $\Delta S^\circ = {{dS}}$ J/(mol·K). What is $\Delta G^\circ$ at ${{T}}$ K, in kJ/mol?

parts.label: r
parts.explain: $\Delta G^\circ = \Delta H^\circ - T\Delta S^\circ$; divide ΔS by 1000 to put it in kJ. Negative ΔG° means thermodynamically favorable as written

problems.prompt: For {{q}}, $\Delta H^\circ = {{dH}}$ kJ/mol and $\Delta S^\circ = {{dS}}$ J/(mol·K). Above or below what temperature, in K, is it favorable?

parts.label: r
parts.explain: Set $\Delta G = 0$: $T = \Delta H/\Delta S$. Both positive: favorable above it (entropy wins when hot). Both negative: favorable below it. Opposite signs have no crossover

A mixture of H₂ and O₂ can sit for years without reacting.

problems.prompt: Why? {{q}}

parts.label: a
choice: Thermodynamically favorable but kinetically slow: the activation energy is high
parts.explain: ΔG° says whether a process can go, not how fast. A favorable reaction with a high barrier can be infinitely slow at room temperature until heat, a spark or a catalyst gets it over the hump. An unfavorable one will not go however long you wait

problems.prompt: {{f}} dissolves readily in water. What drives it?

parts.label: a
choice: Entropy: dispersal of the ions outweighs an endothermic enthalpy change
Enthalpy: hydration releases more energy than breaking the lattice costs
parts.explain: Dissolving costs the lattice energy and returns the hydration energy. If the solution cools, the process is endothermic and can only be favorable because ΔS is positive enough. If it warms, hydration wins and enthalpy helps

problems.prompt: A biosynthetic step has $\Delta G^\circ = +{{dG}}$ kJ/mol. ATP hydrolysis has $\Delta G^\circ = -30.5$ kJ/mol. What is the smallest whole number of ATP that must be coupled to make the step favorable?

parts.label: r

problems.prompt: A concentration cell has the same metal in ${{ch}}$ M and ${{ch/k}}$ M solutions of its ion (charge ${{n}}$+). What is its potential at 298.15 K, in V?

problems.prompt: {{q}} Is the process exothermic or endothermic?

parts.label: a
choice: Exothermic: heat flows out of the system, q negative
Endothermic: heat flows into the system, q positive
parts.explain: The thermometer reads the surroundings. If they warm, the system gave heat away (exothermic, ΔH < 0); if they cool, the system took heat in (endothermic, ΔH > 0). Breaking bonds or attractions takes energy; forming them releases it

problems.prompt: On an energy diagram the reactants sit at ${{Hr}}$ kJ and the products at ${{Hp}}$ kJ on the same scale. What is ΔH, in kJ?

parts.label: r
parts.explain: $\Delta H = H_\text{products} - H_\text{reactants}$. Products below reactants: energy was released, exothermic. Products above: endothermic

cases.q: Heat flows from a hot block to cold water because faster particles transfer kinetic energy in collisions.

problems.prompt: True or false: {{q}}

parts.label: a
parts.explain: Heat moves from higher to lower temperature (higher to lower average kinetic energy), not from more to less total energy: a bathtub of warm water holds more energy than a hot nail. Energy is conserved, so $q_\text{lost} = -q_\text{gained}$, and transfer stops when the temperatures match

problems.prompt: How much heat, in J, raises ${{m}}$ g of {{mat}} ($c = {{c}}$ J/(g·K)) by ${{dT}}$ °C?

parts.label: r
parts.explain: $q = mc\Delta T$. A change of 1 °C equals a change of 1 K, so no conversion is needed for ΔT. Water's large specific heat is why it buffers temperature

problems.prompt: ${{m1}}$ g of water at ${{T1}}$ °C is mixed with ${{m2}}$ g of water at ${{T2}}$ °C. What is the final temperature, in °C?

parts.label: r
parts.explain: Heat lost = heat gained: $m_1c(T_1 - T_f) = m_2c(T_f - T_2)$. With the same c it is a mass-weighted average, and it must land between the two starting temperatures

problems.prompt: ${{V}}$ mL of ${{C}}$ M HCl and ${{V}}$ mL of ${{C}}$ M NaOH are mixed in a coffee-cup calorimeter and warm by ${{dT}}$ °C. Taking the solution as water (1.00 g/mL, 4.184 J/(g·K)), what is ΔH per mole of water formed, in kJ/mol?

parts.label: r
parts.explain: Heat absorbed by the solution: $q = (2 \times {{V}}\text{ g})(4.184)({{dT}})$ J. The reaction released it, so $q_\text{rxn} = -q$. Divide by moles of water, ${{C*V/1000}}$ mol, and convert to kJ

problems.prompt: How much heat, in kJ, does it take to {{q}} ${{m}}$ g of water at its {{H < 10 ? "melting" : "boiling"}} point? ($\Delta H = {{H}}$ kJ/mol, $M = 18.015$ g/mol)

parts.label: r

problems.prompt: How much heat, in kJ, turns ${{m}}$ g of ice at ${{T1}}$ °C into liquid water at ${{T2}}$ °C? (ice 2.09 J/(g·K), water 4.184 J/(g·K), ΔH_fus = 6.01 kJ/mol, 18.015 g/mol)

parts.label: r
parts.explain: Three legs of the heating curve: warm the ice to 0 °C, ${{m*2.09*(0 - T1)}}$ J; melt it, ${{m/18.015*6010}}$ J; warm the water to {{T2}} °C, ${{m*4.184*T2}}$ J. The flat leg (melting) is usually the biggest

problems.prompt: For {{rx}}, $\Delta H = {{dH}}$ kJ. What is the heat change, in kJ, {{w == 0 ? "when " : "for the reverse reaction when "}}${{m}}$ g of {{A}} ($M = {{M}}$) {{w == 0 ? "takes part" : "is used up"}}?

parts.label: r
parts.explain: ΔH is per mole of reaction as written, which involves {{rt}} mol of {{A}}: scale by $({{m}}/{{M}})/{{rt}}$. Reversing a reaction flips the sign of ΔH

problems.prompt: Estimate ΔH, in kJ, for {{rx}} from average bond enthalpies (kJ/mol): {{data}}.

parts.explain: $\Delta H \approx \sum(\text{bonds broken}) - \sum(\text{bonds formed}) = ({{br}}) - ({{fo}})$. Breaking costs energy, forming releases it; count every bond, including each one in a coefficient's worth of molecules

problems.prompt: A gas absorbs ${{q}}$ J of heat (negative means it gives heat off) while its volume changes by ${{dV}}$ L against a constant ${{P}}$ atm. What is ΔU, in J? (1 L·atm = 101.325 J)

problems.prompt: At one instant a reversible reaction runs forward at ${{rf}}$ M/s and in reverse at ${{rr}}$ M/s. What happens next?

problems.prompt: What is the $K_c$ expression for {{rx}}?

parts.label: a
parts.explain: Products over reactants, each raised to its coefficient. Pure solids and liquids (including water as the solvent) are left out because their concentration does not change. $K_p$ is the same with partial pressures of the gases

problems.prompt: For N₂O₄ ⇌ 2 NO₂, $K_c = {{K}}$. A mixture has [N₂O₄] = ${{a}}$ M and [NO₂] = ${{b}}$ M. Which way does it shift?

parts.label: a
choice: Toward products: Q is less than K
Toward reactants: Q is greater than K
parts.explain: $Q = \dfrac{[\mathrm{NO_2}]^2}{[\mathrm{N_2O_4}]} = \dfrac{ {{b}}^2}{ {{a}} } = {{b^2/a}}$. If Q < K there is too little product and the reaction runs forward; if Q > K it runs back

problems.prompt: At equilibrium for H₂(g) + I₂(g) ⇌ 2 HI(g): [H₂] = ${{h}}$, [I₂] = ${{i}}$ and [HI] = ${{hi}}$ M. What is $K_c$?

parts.label: r
parts.explain: $K_c = \dfrac{[\mathrm{HI}]^2}{[\mathrm{H_2}][\mathrm{I_2}]}$. Use only equilibrium concentrations. Here the moles of gas do not change, so $K_p = K_c$

problems.prompt: ${{a}}$ M each of H₂ and I₂ are mixed. At equilibrium [HI] = ${{2*a*f}}$ M. What is $K_c$ for H₂ + I₂ ⇌ 2 HI?

parts.label: r
parts.explain: ICE: HI went up by $2x = {{2*a*f}}$, so $x = {{a*f}}$ and each of H₂ and I₂ fell to ${{a - a*f}}$ M. Then $K = \dfrac{(2x)^2}{(a - x)^2}$

problems.prompt: For {{rx}} (all gases unless marked), $K_c = {{Kc}}$ at ${{T}}$ K. What is $K_p$? ($R = 0.08206$)

parts.label: r
parts.explain: $K_p = K_c(RT)^{\Delta n}$, where $\Delta n$ is moles of gaseous products minus gaseous reactants: here ${{dn}}$. If $\Delta n = 0$ the two are equal

problems.prompt: A reaction has $K = 10^{ {{e}} }$. What does the equilibrium mixture look like?

parts.explain: K is products over reactants. Much greater than 1 (about $10^3$ or more): products dominate. Much less than 1: reactants dominate. Near 1, both are present in similar amounts. K says nothing about how fast equilibrium is reached

problems.prompt: A reaction has $K = {{K}}$. What is K when the equation is {{q}}?

parts.label: r
parts.explain: Reversing inverts K; multiplying the coefficients by $n$ raises K to the $n$th power; adding reactions multiplies their Ks. Here $K^{ {{p}}/{{d}} }$

problems.prompt: For A(aq) ⇌ B(aq) + C(aq), $K = {{K}}$. Starting with ${{c}}$ M A only, what is [B] at equilibrium, in M? Use the small-x approximation.

parts.label: r
parts.explain: ICE: $K = \dfrac{x^2}{c - x} \approx \dfrac{x^2}{c}$, so $x = \sqrt{Kc}$. Check: $x/c = {{100*sqrt(K*c)/c}}$ percent is under 5 percent, so dropping $x$ beside $c$ was fine

problems.prompt: For A ⇌ B + C, $K = {{K}}$ and A starts at ${{c}}$ M. The small-x approximation fails here. What is [B] at equilibrium, in M?

parts.label: r
parts.explain: $\dfrac{x^2}{c - x} = K$ gives $x^2 + Kx - Kc = 0$, so $x = \dfrac{-K + \sqrt{K^2 + 4Kc}}{2}$ (the positive root). The approximation fails when $x$ is more than about 5 percent of $c$, which happens when K is not much smaller than c

problems.prompt: A particle diagram of the equilibrium A₂(g) + B₂(g) ⇌ 2 AB(g) shows ${{a}}$ A₂, ${{b}}$ B₂ and ${{ab}}$ AB molecules in the box. What is K?

parts.label: r
parts.explain: Moles of gas are the same on both sides, so the box volume cancels and particle counts can stand in for concentrations: $K = \dfrac{ {{ab}}^2}{ {{a}} \times {{b}} }$. A diagram with a different ratio is not at equilibrium

problems.prompt: The molar solubility of {{f}} is ${{s}}$ M. What is its $K_{sp}$?

parts.label: r
parts.explain: Each mole that dissolves gives {{a}} mol cation and {{b}} mol anion: $K_{sp} = ({{a}}s)^{ {{a}} }({{b}}s)^{ {{b}} }$. Forgetting the coefficient inside the parentheses is the usual slip

problems.prompt: $K_{sp}$ of {{f}} is ${{Ksp}}$. What is its molar solubility, in M?

parts.label: r

problems.prompt: Equal volumes of ${{c1}}$ M AgNO₃ and ${{c2}}$ M NaCl are mixed. Does AgCl ($K_{sp} = 1.8\times10^{-10}$) precipitate?

parts.label: a
parts.explain: Mixing equal volumes halves each concentration. $Q = [\mathrm{Ag^+}][\mathrm{Cl^-}] = ({{c1/2}})({{c2/2}}) = {{c1*c2/4}}$. A precipitate forms only when Q is larger than Ksp

problems.prompt: What is the molar solubility of {{f}} ($K_{sp} = {{Ksp}}$) in ${{c}}$ M {{ion}}? (Assume the dissolved salt adds a negligible amount of the common ion.)

parts.label: r
parts.explain: The anion is already at about ${{c}}$ M, so $K_{sp} = s \cdot c^{ {{b}} }$ and $s = K_{sp}/c^{ {{b}} }$. The common ion pushes the dissolving equilibrium back, so the salt is far less soluble than in pure water
