problems.prompt: {{el}} has two isotopes, {{a}} (${{ma}}$ u) and {{b}} (${{mb}}$ u), and an average mass of ${{avg}}$ u. What percent is {{a}}?

problems.prompt: On a phase diagram, what is the point where {{q}}?

parts.label: a
parts.explain: Lines are two-phase equilibria and areas single phases: solid at low T and high P, gas at high T and low P. CO₂'s triple point is above 1 atm, so at 1 atm it sublimes. Water's solid–liquid line leans left because ice is less dense than liquid water

problems.prompt: ${{n}}$ mol of gas fills a ${{V}}$ L flask at ${{T}}$ K. What is the pressure, in atm? ($R = 0.08206$ L·atm/(mol·K))

parts.label: r
parts.explain: $P = nRT/V$. Match R to the units: 0.08206 L·atm/(mol·K) for atm and L; 8.314 J/(mol·K) for Pa and m³. Temperature must be in kelvin

problems.prompt: A gas at ${{P1}}$ atm, ${{V1}}$ L and ${{t1}}$ °C is changed to ${{P2}}$ atm and ${{t2}}$ °C. What is its new volume, in L?

parts.label: r
parts.explain: $\dfrac{P_1V_1}{T_1} = \dfrac{P_2V_2}{T_2}$ with T in kelvin: ${{t1 + 273.15}}$ K and ${{t2 + 273.15}}$ K. Using °C is the classic slip. Volume goes up with T (Charles) and down with P (Boyle)

problems.prompt: A ${{V}}$ L sample of an unknown gas weighs ${{P*V/(0.08206*T)*M}}$ g at ${{T}}$ K and ${{P}}$ atm. What is its molar mass, in g/mol?

parts.label: r
parts.explain: $n = PV/RT$, then $M = m/n$; in one step $M = \dfrac{mRT}{PV}$. The gas is {{g}}. The same rearrangement gives density: $d = PM/RT$

problems.prompt: Hydrogen is collected over water at {{t}} °C, where water's vapor pressure is ${{pw}}$ mmHg. The total pressure is ${{Pt}}$ mmHg. What is the partial pressure of H₂, and the mole fraction of water vapor?

parts.label: r
parts.explain: Dalton: partial pressures add, $P_\text{total} = P_{\mathrm{H_2}} + P_{\mathrm{H_2O}}$, so subtract the water's vapor pressure

parts.label: f
parts.explain: $\chi_i = P_i/P_\text{total} = {{pw}}/{{Pt}}$

problems.prompt: ${{m}}$ g of {{f}} ($M = {{M}}$ g/mol) is dissolved to make ${{V}}$ mL of solution. What is the molarity?

problems.prompt: What volume of ${{M1}}$ M stock, in mL, is diluted to make ${{V2}}$ mL of ${{M2}}$ M solution?

parts.label: r

problems.prompt: An aqueous solution is ${{w}}$ percent {{f}} by mass ($M = {{M}}$ g/mol). What is its molality?

problems.prompt: In a particle diagram of an aqueous solution, which end of each surrounding water molecule points toward a {{ion}} ion?

problems.prompt: On a paper chromatogram the solvent front moved ${{f}}$ cm and a dye spot ${{d}}$ cm. What is the R$_f$ of the dye?

problems.prompt: A Beer's-law calibration curve has slope ${{m}}$ M⁻¹ and intercept ${{b}}$. An unknown reads $A = {{A}}$. What is its concentration, in M?

problems.prompt: ${{n2}}$ mol of a nonvolatile solute is dissolved in ${{n1}}$ mol of a solvent whose vapor pressure is ${{P0}}$ mmHg. What is the solution's vapor pressure, in mmHg?

problems.prompt: By how much, in °C, does a ${{m}}$ m aqueous solution of {{f}} freeze below pure water? ($K_f = 1.86$ °C·kg/mol; assume complete dissociation.)

problems.prompt: ${{mg}}$ mg of a protein in ${{V}}$ mL of solution has an osmotic pressure of ${{(mg/1000/M)/(V/1000)*0.08206*298*760}}$ mmHg at 298 K. What is the protein's molar mass, in g/mol?

problems.prompt: ${{mN}}$ g of N₂ (28.014 g/mol) reacts with ${{mH}}$ g of H₂ (2.016 g/mol) by N₂ + 3 H₂ → 2 NH₃. What is the theoretical yield of NH₃ (17.031 g/mol), in g?

problems.prompt: A reaction is order {{n}} overall, with concentrations in M and time in s. What are the units of $k$?

parts.label: a
parts.explain: Rate is always M/s, and rate $= k[\,]^n$, so $k$ has units of $\mathrm{M}^{1-n}\,\mathrm{s}^{-1}$. Reading the units of a given $k$ is the fastest way to tell the order

problems.prompt: Rate $= k[\mathrm{A}]^{ {{a}} }[\mathrm{B}]^{ {{b}} }$. If [A] is multiplied by ${{f}}$ and [B] by ${{g}}$, by what factor does the rate change?

parts.label: r
parts.explain: Each concentration factor is raised to its order: ${{f}}^{ {{a}} } \times {{g}}^{ {{b}} } = {{f^a*g^b}}$. A zero-order reactant has no effect at all

problems.prompt: A zero-order reaction has $k = {{k}}$ M/s and starts at ${{A0}}$ M. How long, in s, until [A] = ${{A0*f}}$ M?

parts.label: r
parts.explain: Zero order: [A] falls in a straight line, $[\mathrm{A}] = [\mathrm{A}]_0 - kt$, so $t = ([\mathrm{A}]_0 - [\mathrm{A}])/k$. First order: $\ln[\mathrm{A}] = \ln[\mathrm{A}]_0 - kt$; second order: $1/[\mathrm{A}] = 1/[\mathrm{A}]_0 + kt$

problems.prompt: Mechanism: {{q}}. What order in {{s}} does it predict?

parts.label: a
parts.explain: When the first step is slow, the overall rate law is that step's rate law. Reactants that only enter after the slow step do not appear in it, so their order is zero. If the observed rate law matches, the mechanism is consistent (not proven)

problems.prompt: Mechanism: {{q}}. Eliminating the intermediate, what is the overall order of the predicted rate law?

parts.label: r
parts.explain: Write the slow step's rate law, which contains the intermediate. The fast step is at equilibrium, so solve its K expression for the intermediate and substitute. Here rate $= {{law}}$

problems.prompt: A reaction energy profile has ${{h}}$ peaks. How many elementary steps and how many intermediates does the mechanism have?

parts.label: r
parts.explain: Each peak is a transition state, one per elementary step

parts.label: n
parts.explain: Each valley between two peaks is an intermediate. The rate-determining step is the one whose peak sits highest above the starting reactants

problems.prompt: True or false: {{q}}

parts.label: a
parts.explain: A catalyst offers a different mechanism with a lower barrier. It speeds both directions equally, so K, ΔH and the equilibrium position stay put; only the time to get there changes. It is regenerated, though it takes part in the steps

problems.prompt: At 25 °C, which liquid has the highest vapor pressure?

parts.label: a
parts.explain: Weakest intermolecular forces escape most easily: highest vapor pressure and lowest boiling point go together. Hydrogen bonding (water, alcohols, HF) holds molecules back; HCl, with no H-bonding and the fewest electrons of the HX, is the most volatile

problems.prompt: In a gas mixture at ${{P}}$ torr, the partial pressure of O₂ is ${{p}}$ torr. What is the mole fraction of O₂?

parts.label: r
parts.explain: Dalton: $P_i = \chi_i P_{\text{total}}$, so $\chi = {{p}}/{{P}} = {{p/P|3}}$. Mole fraction and pressure fraction are the same thing for ideal gases

problems.prompt: An unknown gas effuses ${{ratio}}$ times as fast as {{known}} ($M = {{M1}}$ g/mol). What is its molar mass?

parts.label: r
parts.explain: Graham: $r_x/r_k = \sqrt{M_k/M_x}$, so $M_x = M_k/(r_x/r_k)^2 = {{M1}}/{{ratio}}^2 = {{M1/ratio^2|4}}$ g/mol. Faster means lighter, by the square

problems.prompt: What volume (mL) of ${{C1}}$ M stock is needed to make ${{V2}}$ mL of ${{C2}}$ M solution?

parts.label: r
parts.explain: Moles of solute stay the same: $C_1V_1 = C_2V_2$, so $V_1 = {{C2}} \times {{V2}} / {{C1}} = {{C2*V2/C1|4}}$ mL, then dilute to {{V2}} mL (acid into water)

problems.prompt: Equal 0.10 M solutions: which has the highest total concentration of dissolved particles?

parts.label: a
parts.explain: Count the ions per formula unit of a strong electrolyte; a nonelectrolyte stays as one molecule. Most particles means the lowest freezing point and highest boiling point and osmotic pressure

problems.prompt: The solvent front moves ${{front}}$ cm. How far does a spot with $R_f = {{rf}}$ travel?

parts.label: r
parts.explain: $R_f$ = spot distance ÷ solvent distance, so ${{rf}} \times {{front}} = {{rf*front}}$ cm. A higher $R_f$ means the compound prefers the mobile phase

problems.prompt: At ${{P1}}$ atm a gas's solubility is ${{S}}$ g/L. At the same temperature, what is it at ${{P2}}$ atm?

parts.label: r
parts.explain: Henry's law: solubility ∝ partial pressure, so ${{S}} \times {{P2}}/{{P1}} = {{S*P2/P1|4}}$ g/L. (Opening a soda drops the CO₂ pressure, and it fizzes)

problems.prompt: Which equation is balanced?

parts.label: a
parts.explain: Count every element on both sides, coefficient times subscript. Balance elements that appear once on each side first, and O and H last in combustions

problems.prompt: From {{eq}}: how many grams of {{reac}} are needed to make ${{g}}$ g of {{prod}}? ({{prod}} ${{Mp}}$, {{reac}} ${{Mr}}$ g/mol)

parts.label: r
parts.explain: Grams of product → moles (÷ molar mass) → moles of reactant (mole ratio from the coefficients) → grams (× molar mass)

problems.prompt: For {{eq}}, you start with ${{nA}}$ mol {{A}} and ${{nB}}$ mol {{B}}. Which is limiting?

parts.label: a
parts.explain: Divide each amount by its coefficient: ${{nA}}/{{cA}} = {{nA/cA|3}}$ vs ${{nB}}/{{cB}} = {{nB/cB|3}}$. The smaller runs out first. The reactant with fewer moles is not always limiting

choices.a: 0 if Rational(nA, cA) < Rational(nB, cB) else 1

problems.prompt: The theoretical yield is ${{th}}$ g and the percent yield is ${{py}}$%. What mass was actually collected?

parts.label: r
parts.explain: Actual = percent ÷ 100 × theoretical = ${{py/100}} \times {{th}} = {{th*py/100}}$ g

problems.prompt: What volume (mL) of ${{Cb}}$ M {{base}} reaches the equivalence point with ${{Va}}$ mL of ${{Ca}}$ M {{acid}}?

parts.label: r
parts.explain: Moles of acid ${{Va*Ca|3}}$ mmol; the mole ratio makes it ${{Va*Ca*k|3}}$ mmol of base; ÷ ${{Cb}}$ M $= {{Va*Ca*k/Cb|4}}$ mL. Count the H⁺ each acid gives and the OH⁻ each base takes

problems.prompt: In which species does {{el}} have an oxidation number of ${{t}}$?

parts.label: a
parts.explain: O is −2 (except peroxides), H is +1 with nonmetals, F is −1; the oxidation numbers sum to the charge. So in an ion, solve for the one unknown

problems.prompt: Which cation, added as its nitrate, forms a precipitate with {{ion}}?

parts.label: a
parts.explain: Group 1 and ammonium salts and all nitrates are soluble. Chlorides are soluble except Ag⁺, Pb²⁺, Hg₂²⁺; sulfates except Ba²⁺, Pb²⁺, Ca²⁺ (slightly) and Sr²⁺; carbonates and hydroxides are insoluble except group 1 and NH₄⁺ (Ba(OH)₂ dissolves)

problems.prompt: What is the {{what}} of {{sp}}?

parts.label: a
parts.explain: A conjugate pair differs by exactly one H⁺: remove one for the base (charge drops by 1), add one for the acid (charge rises by 1). Amphiprotic species like H₂PO₄⁻, HCO₃⁻ and water have both

problems.prompt: For {{eq}}, {{P}} forms at ${{r}}$ M/s. How fast (M/s) is {{R}} being used up?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Rates scale with the coefficients: $-\dfrac{1}{ {{cr}} }\dfrac{d[\text{ {{R}} }]}{dt} = \dfrac{1}{ {{cp}} }\dfrac{d[\text{ {{P}} }]}{dt}$, so ${{r}} \times {{cr}}/{{cp}} = {{r*cr/cp|4}}$ M/s

problems.prompt: Multiplying [A] by ${{f}}$ (others fixed) multiplies the initial rate by ${{g}}$. What is the order in A?

parts.label: n
parts.explain: rate ∝ [A]ⁿ, so ${{f}}^n = {{g}}$ and $n = \ln {{g}}/\ln {{f}} = {{log(g)/log(f)|3}}$. A half order (rate up √f times) happens too

problems.prompt: After ${{t}}$ {{unit}}, ${{pct}}$% of a first-order reactant remains. What is its half-life ({{unit}})?

parts.label: h
parts.explain: Each half-life halves what is left: ${{pct}}\% = (1/2)^{n}$ with $n = {{log(100/pct)/log(2)|3}}$ half-lives, so $t_{1/2} = {{t}}/{{log(100/pct)/log(2)|3}} = {{t*log(2)/log(100/pct)|4}}$ {{unit}}

problems.prompt: What is the overall order of the rate law for the elementary step {{step}}?

parts.label: n
parts.explain: For an elementary step only, the rate law comes straight from the molecularity: each reactant's exponent is its coefficient. For an overall reaction it must be measured

problems.prompt: A rate constant has units of {{u}}. What is the overall order?

parts.label: a
parts.explain: Rate is always M/s, so k carries M^(1−n) s⁻¹: zero order M s⁻¹, first s⁻¹, second M⁻¹ s⁻¹, third M⁻² s⁻¹

problems.prompt: A reaction has a forward activation energy of ${{Ea}}$ kJ/mol and ΔH = ${{dH}}$ kJ/mol. What is the activation energy of the reverse reaction?

parts.label: e
parts.explain: On the energy profile, $E_{a,\text{rev}} = E_{a,\text{fwd}} - \Delta H = {{Ea}} - ({{dH}}) = {{Ea - dH}}$ kJ/mol. Exothermic reactions have the larger barrier going back

problems.prompt: Does adding a catalyst change {{s}}?

parts.label: a
parts.explain: A catalyst offers a lower-barrier path for both directions, so both rates rise and equilibrium is reached sooner; the start and end energies, ΔH and K, are untouched

problems.prompt: ${{m1}}$ g of water at ${{T1}}$ °C is mixed with ${{m2}}$ g of water at ${{T2}}$ °C. What is the final temperature (°C), ignoring heat loss?

parts.label: t
parts.explain: Heat lost by the hot water = heat gained by the cold: ${{m1}}(T - {{T1}}) = {{m2}}({{T2}} - T)$, so $T$ is the mass-weighted average, ${{(m1*T1 + m2*T2)/(m1 + m2)|4}}$ °C

problems.prompt: ΔH_fus of ice is 6.01 kJ/mol (H₂O 18.015 g/mol). How many grams of ice at 0 °C does ${{q}}$ kJ melt?

parts.label: m
parts.explain: Moles $= {{q}}/6.01 = {{q/6.01|3}}$ mol, × 18.015 g/mol $= {{q/6.01*18.015|4}}$ g. During melting the temperature stays at 0 °C

problems.prompt: CH₄ + 2 O₂ → CO₂ + 2 H₂O, ΔH = −890 kJ. What mass of CH₄ (16.043 g/mol) must burn to release ${{q}}$ kJ?

parts.label: m

problems.prompt: A reaction has ΔH = ${{dH}}$ kJ. What is ΔH for the same reaction {{how}}?

parts.label: h
parts.explain: ΔH is extensive: scale it with the coefficients, and flip its sign when the reaction is reversed. ${{k}} \times ({{dH}}) = {{k*dH}}$ kJ

problems.prompt: A system's internal energy changes by ${{dU}}$ kJ while it absorbs $q = {{q}}$ kJ of heat. What is the work w (kJ), chemistry sign convention?

parts.label: w
parts.explain: ΔU = q + w, so w = ΔU − q = {{dU}} − ({{q}}) = {{dU - q}} kJ. Negative w means the system did work on the surroundings (expanded)

problems.prompt: For {{eq}}, ΔH = ${{dH}}$ kJ at ${{T}}$ K. What is ΔU (kJ)? (R = 8.314 J/mol·K)

parts.label: u
parts.explain: ΔH = ΔU + Δn_gas RT, so ΔU = ${{dH}} - ({{dn}})(8.314)({{T}})/1000 = {{dH - dn*8.314462618*T/1000|5}}$ kJ. Only gas moles count: Δn here is {{dn}}

problems.prompt: When {{salt}} dissolves in water in a coffee-cup calorimeter, the temperature {{d}}. What is the sign of ΔH for dissolving?

parts.label: a
parts.explain: The water is the surroundings. If it cools, the system took heat from it (ΔH > 0, a cold pack); if it warms, the system gave heat to it (ΔH < 0, a hot pack)

problems.prompt: For a reaction mixture, Q = ${{Q}}$ and K = ${{K}}$. Which way does it shift to reach equilibrium?

parts.label: a
parts.explain: Q < K: too few products, so the forward reaction runs. Q > K: too many products, so the reverse runs. Q = K: at equilibrium

problems.prompt: For {{eq}}, Kp = ${{Kp}}$ at ${{T}}$ K. What is Kc? (R = 0.08206 L·atm/mol·K)

parts.label: k
parts.explain: $K_p = K_c(RT)^{\Delta n}$ with Δn = gas moles of products − reactants = {{dn}}, so $K_c = K_p/(RT)^{ {{dn}} } = {{Kp/(0.082057366*T)^dn|3}}$

problems.prompt: Which has the higher molar solubility in pure water?

parts.explain: Compare molar solubilities, not Ksp values, when the formulas differ: for MₐXᵦ, $K_{sp} = a^a b^b s^{a+b}$. Ag₂CrO₄ has the smaller Ksp but the larger s, because s enters cubed

problems.prompt: The container of {{eq}} is compressed to half its volume. Which way does the equilibrium shift?

parts.explain: Higher pressure favors the side with fewer moles of gas (count only gases); equal moles means no shift. K itself does not change; only temperature changes K

problems.prompt: A solution has pH ${{pH}}$. What is [H₃O⁺] (M)?

parts.label: h
parts.explain: $[\text{H}_3\text{O}^+] = 10^{-\text{pH}} = 10^{-{{pH}}} = {{10^(-pH)|3}}$ M. Each pH unit is a factor of 10

problems.prompt: A ${{c}}$ M HCl solution is diluted ${{f}}$-fold. What is the new pH?

parts.label: p
parts.explain: Strong acid: [H₃O⁺] = concentration = ${{c/f}}$ M, so pH $= -\log({{c/f}}) = {{-log10(c/f)|3}}$. Each tenfold dilution raises pH by 1, until it nears 7

problems.prompt: Which is the strongest base?

parts.label: a
parts.explain: $K_aK_b = K_w$: the weakest acid (smallest Ka) has the strongest conjugate base

problems.prompt: Using the small-x approximation, what is the percent ionization of ${{c}}$ M {{acid}} (Ka ${{Ka}}$)?

parts.label: p
parts.explain: $x \approx \sqrt{K_a C}$, so percent $= x/C \times 100 = \sqrt{K_a/C} \times 100 = {{sqrt(Ka/c)*100|3}}\%$. Diluting a weak acid raises its percent ionization

problems.prompt: Is a solution of {{salt}} acidic, basic or neutral?

parts.label: a
parts.explain: Ask what each ion came from. A weak acid's anion (F⁻, acetate, carbonate) is basic; a weak base's cation (NH₄⁺) or a small highly charged metal ion (Al³⁺) is acidic; ions of strong acids and bases are spectators

problems.prompt: The pKa of {{acid}} is ${{pKa}}$. At pH ${{pH}}$, which form predominates?

parts.label: a
parts.explain: Below the pKa protons are plentiful, so the acid form wins; above it, the base form. At pH = pKa they are equal, and each pH unit away is a factor of 10

problems.prompt: What base-to-acid ratio [A⁻]/[HA] gives a {{pair}} buffer (pKa ${{pKa}}$) a pH of ${{pH}}$?

parts.label: r
parts.explain: Henderson–Hasselbalch: $\text{pH} = \text{p}K_a + \log([\text{A}^-]/[\text{HA}])$, so the ratio is $10^{ {{pH}} - {{pKa}} } = {{10^(pH - pKa)|3}}$. Blood (bicarbonate) runs about 11 to 1

problems.prompt: In a titration of a weak acid with NaOH, the pH at the half-equivalence point is ${{pH}}$. What is Ka?

parts.label: k
parts.explain: Halfway to equivalence, half the acid has become its conjugate base, so [HA] = [A⁻] and pH = pKa: $K_a = 10^{-{{pH}}} = {{10^(-pH)|3}}$

problems.prompt: Which has the highest standard molar entropy at 25 °C?

parts.label: a
parts.explain: Gas ≫ liquid > solid; then more atoms and heavier, floppier molecules have more ways to store energy. Rigid diamond has almost none

problems.prompt: For {{what}}, ΔH° = ${{dH}}$ kJ/mol and ΔS° = ${{dS}}$ J/mol·K. At what temperature (K) does ΔG° change sign?

parts.label: t
parts.explain: ΔG° = ΔH° − TΔS° = 0 at $T = \Delta H°/\Delta S° = {{dH*1000}}/{{dS}} = {{dH*1000/dS|4}}$ K (convert kJ to J). Same signs for ΔH and ΔS mean favorable only above (both +) or below (both −) this temperature

problems.prompt: A reaction has K = ${{K}}$ at 298 K. What is the sign of ΔG°?

parts.label: a
parts.explain: ΔG° = −RT ln K: K > 1 gives ln K > 0 and ΔG° < 0; K < 1 gives ΔG° > 0; K = 1 gives 0

problems.prompt: A galvanic cell is built from {{A}} (E° = ${{eA}}$ V) and {{B}} (E° = ${{eB}}$ V). What is E°cell (V)?

parts.label: e
parts.explain: The higher reduction potential is the cathode; the other is oxidized at the anode. E°cell = E°cathode − E°anode, always positive for a galvanic cell. Do not multiply E° by coefficients

problems.prompt: A cell reaction transfers ${{n}}$ mol of electrons with E° = ${{E}}$ V. What is ΔG° (kJ)? (F = 96,485 C/mol)

problems.prompt: How many minutes at ${{I}}$ A does it take to plate ${{m}}$ g of {{metal}} from {{ion}} ({{M}} g/mol)?

problems.prompt: A reaction has $E_a = {{Ea}}$ kJ/mol. By what factor does the rate constant grow from ${{T1}}$ K to ${{T2}}$ K? ($R = 8.314$ J/(mol·K).)

"C₂H₆ + 3.5 O₂ → 2 CO₂ + 3 H₂O" : "C₃H₈ + 5 O₂ → 3 CO₂ + 4 H₂O")}}, with ΔH°f of CO₂ = −393.5 and H₂O(l) = −285.8 kJ/mol. What is ΔH°f of the hydrocarbon, in kJ/mol?

problems.prompt: A gas reaction has $K_c = {{Kc}}$ at ${{T}}$ K, and the moles of gas change by ${{dn}}$ from reactants to products. What is $K_p$? ($R = 0.08206$ L·atm/(mol·K).)

problems.prompt: For A + B ⇌ C + D with $K = {{K}}$, you start with ${{c}}$ M each of A and B and nothing else. What is [C] at equilibrium, in M?

problems.prompt: For A ⇌ B + C with $K = {{K}}$ and ${{c}}$ M A at the start, the small-x approximation gives x. What percent of A is that?

parts.label: y
parts.explain: $\dfrac{x^2}{c - x} = K$ gives $x^2 + Kx - Kc = 0$. Take the positive root. Dilute solutions react a larger fraction

problems.prompt: A reaction has ΔH° = ${{dH}}$ kJ/mol. By what factor does K change from ${{T1}}$ K to ${{T2}}$ K? ($R = 8.314$ J/(mol·K); assume ΔH° is constant.)

problems.prompt: Which is the largest?

problems.prompt: The accepted value is ${{t}}$. A student's result was high, with a percent error of ${{pe}}$%. What did the student measure?

parts.explain: CSS pace per 100 is half the difference between the 400 and 200 times, which is why the test is worth doing

problems.prompt: A swimmer's CSS pace is {{css}} s per 100. What is the target pace per 100 for a set at {{pct}} per cent of CSS speed?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: A percentage of CSS speed divides the pace, it does not multiply it: 95 per cent of CSS speed is a slower pace

cases.q: CSS approximates:
cases.o1: The highest speed sustainable without a continuous rise in blood lactate

cases.q: CSS from a 400 and 200 test tends to be least reliable when:
cases.o1: The swimmer paces one of the two trials badly
cases.o4: The trials are on the same day

cases.q: CSS is usually computed for freestyle because:
cases.o1: In butterfly, form breaks down before the aerobic limit is reached, so the line is not the same quantity
cases.o2: Butterfly is not an Olympic stroke
cases.o3: Freestyle is the only stroke tested

cases.q: Two swimmers with the same CSS may still differ in:
cases.o1: Sprint speed, efficiency and how long they can hold CSS

parts.label: v
parts.explain: CSS is one number from two trials: useful for setting paces, not a full physiological profile

problems.prompt: A set is {{n}} x {{d}} m on a send-off of {{so}} s, and the swimmer holds {{hold}} s per repeat. What is the rest per repeat, in seconds?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Rest is the send-off minus the swim; it is the rest, not the distance, that decides which system the set trains

problems.prompt: A repeat takes {{hold}} s with {{rest}} s rest. What is the work:rest ratio (work divided by rest)?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: A ratio near or above 4:1 keeps the set aerobic; ratios below 1:1 point at speed or lactate-production work

cases.q: 10 x 100 at threshold pace on 15 seconds rest trains mainly:
cases.o1: The aerobic threshold and lactate clearance

cases.q: 6 x 50 maximum effort on 3 minutes trains mainly:
cases.o1: Speed and the phosphagen system, with near-full recovery

cases.q: 8 x 200 easy on 20 seconds rest trains mainly:
4 x 100 best effort on 8 minutes rest trains mainly:
cases.o1: Lactate tolerance, with enough rest to repeat near-maximal efforts

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Read the rest interval first, then the intensity: those two name the system

cases.q: The main reason rest interval, not distance, sets which system a repeat trains:
cases.o1: Rest decides how far the system recovers before the next effort, which sets the intensity that can be repeated
cases.o2: Distance does not matter at all

cases.q: Shortening the rest on a fixed set of repeats usually:
cases.o1: Pushes it toward aerobic and threshold work

cases.q: Lengthening the rest to near-full recovery lets the swimmer:
cases.o1: Repeat near-maximal efforts, which trains speed rather than endurance

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Two sets of identical distance train different systems if their rest differs

problems.prompt: A week has {{d1}} sessions of {{v1}} m and {{d2}} sessions of {{v2}} m. What is the week's volume in kilometres?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Weekly volume by category is the number a training plan is actually balanced against

problems.prompt: A taper starts at {{v0}} km a week and cuts volume by {{pct}} per cent each week. What is the volume in week {{wk}} of the taper (km)?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: An exponential taper multiplies each week, so week n is v0 x (1 - cut)^n

cases.q: During a taper, the element to keep rather than cut is:
cases.o1: Intensity: volume falls while intensity is maintained
cases.o2: Intensity, which should fall with volume

cases.q: Taper duration for a trained swimmer is usually about:
cases.o1: Two to three weeks, tuned to the individual

cases.q: Cutting training frequency sharply during a taper risks:
cases.o1: Losing feel for the water and timing

cases.q: The purpose of a taper is to:
cases.o1: Shed accumulated fatigue while keeping the fitness already built

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Volume down, intensity held, frequency largely kept

cases.q: In an event with a difficulty requirement, the 10 points are divided into:
cases.o1: Three parts: execution quality, overall performance and difficulty
cases.o3: One score from the head judge

cases.q: The judging panel is organised so that:
cases.o1: Different groups of judges score different components independently

cases.q: The head judge's role includes:
cases.o1: Applying deductions that are not a judge group's job, such as time and other procedural faults

cases.q: Difficulty is scored differently from execution because:
cases.o1: Difficulty is declared in advance and confirmed, while execution is judged as performed

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Separating execution, performance and difficulty is what lets three judge groups work independently

problems.prompt: Five judges give {{a}}, {{b}}, {{c}}, {{d}}, {{e2}}. The panel drops the highest and the lowest and averages the rest. What is the score?

parts.label: v
parts.value: (a + b + c + d + e2 - max(a, b, c, d, e2) - min(a, b, c, d, e2))/3
parts.explain: Trimming the extremes and averaging the rest is the standard way a panel's marks become one score

problems.prompt: Using the rule printed here — a routine shorter than the minimum loses 0.1 for each full {{inc}} seconds short — a routine runs {{act}} s against a minimum of {{mn}} s. What is the time deduction?

parts.label: v

problems.prompt: A performance scores {{aa}} for execution, {{bb}} for overall performance and {{cc}} for difficulty, with a head-judge deduction of {{dd}}. What is the final score?

parts.label: v

cases.q: The Duanwei system is organised into:
cases.o1: Three tiers of three duan each, from elementary through middle to advanced
cases.o2: A single ladder of five levels

cases.q: Progressing through Duanwei levels adds:
cases.o1: More demanding technical requirements and, at higher tiers, teaching and theory

cases.q: The Duanwei system is administered by:

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Three tiers of three, with teaching and theory entering at the higher tiers

problems.prompt: An exchange is timed with the outgoing swimmer's feet leaving {{gap}} s after the incoming touch. Relay reaction differentials are reported in hundredths: what is this one in hundredths of a second?

parts.explain: A positive differential is legal; coaches chase a small positive number, because zero is where a disqualification starts

problems.prompt: A relay's four legs are {{l1}}, {{l2}}, {{l3}} and {{l4}} s. What is the final time (s)?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Legs are cumulative differences on the result sheet; only the first leg is a flat start, which is why legs 2 to 4 are usually faster

cases.q: A stroke judge reports an infraction. The next step is:
cases.o1: The referee decides whether to disqualify

cases.q: Two officials disagree about whether an infraction occurred. The usual resolution:
cases.o1: No disqualification, because the swimmer gets the benefit of the doubt
cases.o3: The senior official's view wins automatically

cases.q: A disqualification is recorded with:
cases.o1: The rule or infraction it was called under

parts.label: v
parts.explain: The referee decides; doubt favours the swimmer; the reason is recorded

problems.prompt: A 50 takes {{tm}} s in total, of which the clean-swimming 30 m took {{clean}} s. How long did the start and finish segments take together (s)?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: The reverse split: separating start and finish from clean swimming is what makes two swimmers comparable

parts.label: v
parts.explain: A faster swim is not always the more efficient one: stroke index is what separates speed from economy

problems.prompt: To hold velocity while stroke rate falls by {{dn}} per cent, by what percentage must distance per cycle rise?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: The compensation is not equal to the loss: a 20 per cent rate drop needs 25 per cent more distance per cycle

problems.prompt: A 200 target is {{goal}} s with the front half {{fh}} s. What must the back half be (s)?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: The other half of the race plan, and the number the swimmer actually has to hold when it hurts

cases.o1: Broken 200s with the third 50 at race pace, so that segment is rehearsed under fatigue

cases.q: A swimmer takes the first 50 of a 200 far too fast every time. A sensible response:
cases.o1: Practise the opening 50 to a pace clock until the target feels slow

cases.q: A flat middle in a 400 is best addressed by:
cases.o1: Pace-controlled sets that hold target speed through the middle repeats

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Rehearse the segment that fails, at the pace it must be held

problems.prompt: At a CSS pace of {{css}} s per 100 and a set at {{pct}} per cent of CSS speed, what is the target time for a {{d}} m repeat (s)?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Convert the zone pace, then scale to the repeat distance: this is how a CSS test becomes a written set

cases.q: The practical value of knowing CSS is that it:
cases.o1: Gives a pace to write threshold sets around, rather than guessing

cases.q: CSS should be retested:
cases.o1: Periodically, because it moves with training

cases.q: A swimmer's CSS pace is faster than their actual 400 pace. That means:
cases.o1: Something is wrong with the trials: CSS should be slower than 200 pace and near 400 pace

parts.label: v
parts.explain: CSS is a pace to train at, retested as fitness moves

problems.prompt: A set is {{n}} x {{d}} m. What is the set's distance in metres?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: The simplest number on the board, and the one a week's volume is built from

problems.prompt: A set of {{n}} x {{d}} m runs on a send-off of {{so}} s. How many minutes does the set take?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Send-off times the repeats gives the clock time, which is what makes a session fit the lane time available

problems.prompt: Of a {{tot}} km week, {{part}} km is threshold work. What percentage of the week is that?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Balance between categories, not total volume, is what a plan is judged on

problems.prompt: A taper cuts volume from {{v0}} km to {{v1}} km at {{pct}} per cent reduction per week. How many weeks does that take (rounded up)?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Solving the exponential taper for its length: a two-to-three week answer is the usual range

problems.prompt: A taper week of {{v}} km is spread over {{d}} sessions. What is the average session in metres?

parts.label: r
parts.explain: Frequency is kept during a taper even as volume falls, so the sessions get shorter rather than fewer

cases.q: Judges are divided into groups so that:
cases.o1: Each group concentrates on one component rather than scoring everything at once
cases.o3: The head judge has less work

cases.q: A declared difficulty list is confirmed rather than scored freely because:
cases.o1: It is checked against what was actually performed, element by element

cases.q: The score a competitor receives is:
cases.o1: The components added, less any head-judge deductions
cases.o3: The average of all marks including extremes

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Independent groups, a confirmed difficulty list, and deductions off the total

problems.prompt: Five judges give {{a}}, {{b}}, {{c}}, {{d}}, {{e2}}. What is the spread between the highest and lowest mark?

parts.label: v
parts.value: max(a, b, c, d, e2) - min(a, b, c, d, e2)
parts.explain: A wide spread is what panel supervision looks for: it suggests the judges are not applying the criteria the same way

expect.v: Max(nsimplify(a), nsimplify(b), nsimplify(c), nsimplify(d), nsimplify(e2)) - Min(nsimplify(a), nsimplify(b), nsimplify(c), nsimplify(d), nsimplify(e2))

cases.q: A practitioner wanting a recognised teaching qualification in wushu would pursue:
cases.o1: The higher Duanwei levels, where teaching and theory are examined

cases.q: The Duanwei examinations are organised around:
cases.o1: Set technical requirements per level, with its own textbook series

cases.q: The baoquan li salute is part of wushu practice because:
cases.o1: Martial ethics (wude) are taught alongside technique
cases.o2: It is a competition difficulty element

parts.label: v
parts.explain: The ladder examines technique, then teaching and theory; etiquette is taught with it

problems.prompt: With {{gc}} seconds left in a quarter and a {{sc}}-second shot clock, by when must a team shoot to be sure of getting the ball back (seconds on the game clock)?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: A two-for-one needs the shot up with more than a shot clock plus a few seconds left, so the opponent cannot hold the ball to the horn; shooting with the shot clock exactly on is too late

problems.prompt: At {{gc}} seconds with a {{sc}}-second clock, how many seconds wide is the window in which shooting still earns the two-for-one, taking the latest useful shot as shot clock plus 3?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: The window is wider than teams use: taking a worse shot early to get a second possession pays only if the second possession's expected points exceed what the shot quality gave up

problems.prompt: A leading team has the ball with {{gc}} seconds left and a {{sc}}-second shot clock. How many full shot clocks can they use, and how many seconds are left over?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: If the leftover is less than a shot clock the trailing team must foul before that last possession starts, which is the calculation that sets the moment to start fouling

problems.prompt: Trailing with {{gc}} seconds left against a {{sc}}-second shot clock, after how many seconds of the opponent's possession must a foul come, to leave one possession (take a possession as {{pp}} seconds)?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: The trailing team's own possession has to fit after the opponent's shot clock runs, so the foul has to come earlier than it feels: waiting for the shot clock to expire has already lost the game

cases.q: A last shot of a quarter should go up with:
cases.o1: A few seconds left, so a rebound can be put back
cases.o4: As soon as the set is run

cases.q: Holding the ball for the very last second costs:
cases.o1: Any chance at an offensive rebound

cases.q: A last shot of the game, trailing by one, should go up:
cases.o1: Early enough to rebound, since a miss ends the game otherwise

cases.q: A last shot of a quarter when tied should go up:
cases.o1: At or just before the horn, so the opponent gets nothing back

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Tied at the end of a quarter, leave no time; trailing at the end of a game, leave a rebound

problems.prompt: Leading by 3 with {{gc}} seconds left, fouling concedes two free throws at {{ft}} per cent. What is the chance the opponent makes both?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Fouling up three trades a three-point attempt for two free throws and the ball back; the case rests on the opponent's three-point rate against their free-throw rate and on how cleanly the foul can be given

cases.q: Fouling up three late is most defensible when:
cases.o1: The opponent shoots threes well and free throws poorly, and the foul can be given cleanly

cases.q: The main risk of fouling up three is:
cases.o1: A foul on the shot, giving three free throws or a four-point play

cases.q: Defending up three means accepting:
cases.o1: A three-point attempt that ties the game

cases.q: The decision is a close one because:
cases.o1: The two probabilities are similar at typical rates, so it turns on personnel and execution
cases.o2: The evidence is clear for fouling
cases.o3: The evidence is clear for defending

parts.label: v
parts.explain: A genuinely close call: the evidence does not strongly favour either, so personnel and the cleanness of the foul decide it

problems.prompt: Trailing by 2 with one possession: a three makes {{p3}} per cent, a two makes {{p2}} per cent and overtime is won {{ot}} per cent of the time. What is the win probability of going for two (per cent)?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Going for two is a conditional: make it, then win overtime. Going for three wins outright at its make rate, so the comparison is the three's rate against the two's rate times the overtime chance

problems.prompt: With the same numbers, by how many percentage points does going for three beat going for two?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: At typical rates the three usually wins by a few points, and it wins by more the worse the team expects to be in overtime: that is why a road underdog shoots the three

problems.prompt: Fouling a {{f1}} per cent shooter rather than a {{f2}} per cent shooter in the two-shot bonus saves how many expected points?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Half a point a foul is large late in a game, which is why the worst free-throw shooter on the floor is the target; in a one-and-one the saving is larger still

problems.prompt: In a one-and-one, a {{ft}} per cent shooter's expected points from the trip are what?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: The second shot is conditional on the first, so a one-and-one concedes far less than two shots: a sixty per cent shooter gives up under a point. NCAA men is the only level above high school still using it

problems.prompt: A team has {{tf}} team fouls with the bonus starting at the {{bn}}th. How many fouls can they give before conceding free throws?

cases.q: A foul to give is most useful for:

cases.q: A foul to give should be committed:

cases.q: A team with no fouls to give must:
cases.o1: Defend without contact, since any foul sends the opponent to the line

cases.q: The commonest error with fouls to give is:
cases.o1: Not knowing the count, so a free one is wasted or a costly one is given

parts.label: v
parts.explain: A free stoppage, used early in the possession and away from a shot; the error is always not knowing the count

cases.q: After a defensive rebound late, trailing, playing on is better when:
cases.o1: The defence is unset and a numbers advantage exists now

cases.q: Calling the timeout costs:
cases.o1: The transition advantage, in exchange for a set play against a set defence

cases.q: With a set play needed and the defence already organised, the timeout:
cases.o1: Buys an inbound at a chosen spot and a designed action

cases.q: Advancing the ball on a timeout matters where:
cases.o1: The level's rules allow it, which changes what the inbound can be

parts.label: v

parts.label: v

cases.q: Switching everything on a last-second inbound:
cases.o1: Prevents a screen creating separation, accepting a mismatch that has no time to be exploited

cases.q: Denying the first option rather than guarding the ball is right when:

cases.q: Fouling on a last-second inbound when leading by 3 or more is:
cases.o1: Usually wrong, since it stops the clock and concedes free throws for nothing

parts.explain: Time left decides it: under a second the inbound is the play, with several seconds the second option is

A foul on a missed two-point shot gives:

cases.o1: A shot after the horn, which is the commonest last-second error

parts.label: v
parts.explain: The clock sets the menu: a tip, a catch-and-shoot, or a pass and a catch-and-shoot

problems.prompt: Guarding the inbounder leaves {{nd}} defenders for {{no}} receivers. How many receivers are unguarded?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Guarding the inbounder costs a body, so it is right only when the entry itself is the danger — under a second on the clock, or against a long pass

problems.prompt: A closely guarded count reaches {{cc}} seconds against a limit of {{lm}}. How many seconds past the limit is that?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: The counts are short and the official's count is what matters, not the clock: a ball handler who feels he has time usually does not

problems.prompt: In a one-and-one, a {{f1}} per cent shooter yields how many fewer expected points than two shots for the same shooter?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: The gap is largest for a poor shooter, which is why the one-and-one rewards fouling a weak shooter far more than the two-shot bonus does

problems.prompt: A made two plus a free throw at {{ft}} per cent has what expected value (points)?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: An and-one at a good free-throw rate is worth nearly three, which is why drawing contact on a finish is worth more than the shot quality lost

problems.prompt: An unsportsmanlike foul gives two shots at {{ft}} per cent plus possession worth {{pp}} points. What is the expected cost (points)?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Around two and a half points against a possession of about one: the penalty is roughly a two-possession swing, which is why a late-game grab is far worse than a clean foul

problems.prompt: A restricted area of radius {{rr}} feet under the basket covers what area (square feet)?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: The half-disc is small, which is the point: it removes the defender's right to the spot only directly under the basket, and a step outside it restores the charge

problems.prompt: Goaltending on a {{sv}}-point attempt awards how many points?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: The score is awarded as if the shot had gone in, so goaltending on a three concedes three; the ball being on its downward flight above ring level is the trigger

problems.prompt: A three-person crew divides the court into primary areas. If each official's area covers about a third, what percentage of the court is any one official's primary (per cent)?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Each official sees a third as primary and the rest as secondary, which is why an action in the wrong third gets a late or no call: the angle, not the effort, is what is missing

problems.prompt: From a box score: {{fga}} FGA, {{to}} turnovers, {{fta}} FTA and {{orb}} offensive rebounds. How many possessions, using FGA + 0.44*FTA - ORB + TO?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: The 0.44 coefficient approximates how many free-throw attempts end a possession, since and-ones and technicals do not; the estimate is what makes per-possession comparison possible at all

problems.prompt: A team used {{ps}} possessions in {{mn}} minutes. What is its pace per 40 minutes?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Normalising to 40 minutes is what makes an overtime game comparable, and pace is the number that makes two teams' per-game scoring incomparable without it

problems.prompt: A team scored {{pts}} points in {{ps}} possessions. What is its offensive rating (points per 100)?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: A rating around 100 is average at most levels, so the figure is read directly as a comparison; net rating is the difference between the two teams' ratings, which in one game is symmetric

problems.prompt: Offensive rating {{off}} and defensive rating {{dff}} give what net rating (points per 100)?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Net rating is the one number that survives pace, which is why it rather than margin per game compares a fast team with a slow one

problems.prompt: Team A scores {{p1}} points on {{s1}} possessions, Team B {{p2}} on {{s2}}. Which has the better offence, and by how much per 100 possessions?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Points per game ranks the faster team higher at equal efficiency, so a fast team's scoring and a slow team's defence are both flattered: the per-possession figure removes the illusion

problems.prompt: With {{fgm}} field goals made including {{tpm}} threes, on {{fga}} attempts, what is eFG (per cent)?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Crediting a three as one and a half makes made shots comparable in points, which is why eFG exceeds FG for any team that makes threes and equals it for one that makes none

problems.prompt: For the same line, by how many percentage points does eFG exceed raw FG?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: The gap is half the three-point make rate on total attempts, so it is a direct measure of how much a team's shot profile is worth: two teams at the same FG can differ by ten points of eFG

problems.prompt: With {{pts}} points on {{fga}} field-goal attempts and {{fta}} free-throw attempts, what is true shooting (per cent)?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: True shooting counts free throws, so it is the measure that rewards a player who gets to the line; the true shot attempts in the denominator are field-goal attempts plus 0.44 of free-throw attempts

cases.q: Comparing a rim finisher with a three-point shooter is best done with:
cases.o1: True shooting or eFG, since raw FG per cent favours the finisher

cases.q: A player who draws many fouls is best measured by:
cases.o1: True shooting, which is the only one of the three counting free throws

cases.q: Raw field goal percentage is the right measure when:
cases.o1: Comparing two players who take the same shot types, for instance two post players

cases.q: A player with high eFG and low true shooting:
cases.o1: Shoots well but gets to the line rarely or shoots free throws poorly

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Three measures of the same thing at three levels of completeness; the gap between two of them is itself informative

problems.prompt: A team had {{to}} turnovers in {{ps}} possessions. What is its turnover rate (per cent)?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Turnover rate is the second of the four factors and the one a team controls most directly; a rate in the low teens is good and the low twenties loses games on its own

problems.prompt: A team grabbed {{orb}} offensive rebounds against the opponent's {{drb}} defensive rebounds. What is its offensive rebound percentage?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Rebounding is a percentage of available rebounds, not a count, because a team that misses more shots gets more chances; the third factor is this percentage, not the raw total

problems.prompt: Weighting shooting 40, turnovers 25, rebounding 20 and free throws 15 per cent, a team leads by {{d1}}, {{d2}}, {{d3}} and {{d4}} standardised points on the four. What is its weighted edge?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Shooting carries about twice the weight of turnovers and four times the free-throw factor, so a team can lose the other three and still win on shooting: that ordering is the useful part of the model

cases.q: A deficit in the shooting factor points first at:
cases.o1: Shot selection and the quality of looks created, before shooting mechanics

cases.q: A deficit in the turnover factor points at:
cases.o1: Ball security and decision-making under pressure, usually in specific actions

cases.q: A deficit in the rebounding factor points at:
cases.o1: How many players are sent to the glass, which is a scheme decision

cases.q: A deficit in the free-throw factor points at:
cases.o1: Attacking the rim and drawing contact more often

cases.q: Chasing the factor with the largest deficit is wrong when:
cases.o1: It is the lowest-weighted one, and a smaller shooting deficit costs more

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Each factor has its own lever, and the weights decide which deficit is worth chasing

problems.prompt: A {{sv}}-point shot makes {{pm}} per cent of the time. What are its expected points?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: A corner three at 38 per cent is worth 1.14 and a long two at 45 per cent is 0.90, which is the whole analytic case for the shot profile the modern game has adopted

problems.prompt: At what three-point percentage does a three equal a two that makes {{p2}} per cent?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Two thirds of the two's percentage is the breakeven, so a three beats a 60 per cent layup only above 40 per cent: the comparison has to be against the two actually available, not against an average two

problems.prompt: A shot makes {{pm}} per cent for {{sv}} points, and a miss is rebounded by the offence {{orb}} per cent of the time for a further {{nv}} expected points. What is the total expected value?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Offensive rebounding adds most to the shots that miss most, which narrows the gap between a three and a two and is part of why crashing changes shot selection

problems.prompt: A shooter is {{mk}} of {{at}} from three. What is the width of the 95 per cent interval on his rate (percentage points), using 1.96 standard errors on the binomial?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Twenty attempts give an interval tens of points wide, which is why a hot or cold start says almost nothing; the interval narrows with the square root of attempts, so it takes hundreds to resolve a few points

cases.q: 'Our defence is better when player X is in' is confounded by:
cases.o1: Who X plays against and alongside, and when he plays

cases.q: A lineup's net rating over 40 minutes is:
cases.o1: Far too small a sample to separate from noise

cases.q: A late-game clutch statistic is unreliable mainly because:
cases.o1: The sample is tiny and the situations are not comparable

cases.q: Role confounding means:
cases.o1: The player's number reflects what he was asked to do, not only how well he did it

cases.q: The fix for both is:
cases.o1: Comparing like with like, and treating small-sample numbers as hypotheses

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Who, against whom, and how often: the three questions that turn a lineup number from a finding into a hypothesis

cases.q: A right-hand-dominant driver with no left hand is defended by:
cases.o1: Forcing him left, with help positioned on that side

cases.q: A shooter who cannot drive is defended by:
cases.o1: A long closeout with high hands, since the drive is not a threat

cases.q: A driver who cannot shoot is defended by:
cases.o1: A short closeout that takes away the drive, conceding the jumper

cases.q: A non-threat is defended by:
cases.o1: Playing off him to help elsewhere, which is where the extra defender comes from

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Every key is a trade: whatever the player cannot do is what the defence concedes, and the help comes from the non-threats

problems.prompt: Of five opponents, {{nt}} are genuine threats. How many defenders are free to help, and what percentage of the opponent's lineup can be played off?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Help has to come from somewhere, so the number of non-threats is the defence's budget: against five threats there is no help, which is what a fully spaced lineup is for

cases.q: An offence that reads the same first three actions every possession is:
cases.o1: Running a base set, which can be scouted and jumped

cases.q: An after-timeout tendency is worth scouting because:
cases.o1: It is chosen, so it is the clearest signal of what a coach believes works

cases.q: An offence that produces different actions from the same entry is:
cases.o1: Read-based, so the scout is the reads rather than the sets

cases.q: The most useful scouting output on an offence is:
cases.o1: What they do in their first option and what their counter is when it is denied

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Scout the first option and the counter; a list of every set is unusable in a timeout

cases.q: A big who stays near the level of the screen and retreats is in:
Two defenders committing to the ball handler is:
cases.o1: A blitz, which concedes a four-on-three behind it

cases.q: An on-ball defender forcing the handler away from the screen toward the sideline is:
The counter to a drop is usually:
cases.o1: The pull-up or the pocket pass, since the pass to the roller is covered

cases.q: The counter to a blitz is usually:
cases.o1: Getting the ball out quickly to the short roll and playing four-on-three

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Each coverage has a counter, and identifying the coverage from film is what lets the counter be prepared rather than discovered

problems.prompt: An action was run {{nr}} times for {{pt}} points. What is its points per possession, and how does it compare with a team average of {{av}}?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: An action well below the team average is a candidate to cut, but eighteen possessions is a small sample: the useful move is to look at why rather than to cut on the number alone

problems.prompt: An action at {{p1}} points per possession over {{n1}} possessions would need how many possessions to halve the width of its confidence interval?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Halving an interval takes four times the sample, so an action run twenty times will not be resolved this season: judgment from film has to carry what the sample cannot

cases.q: A player who cannot yet execute a skill under light defensive pressure is at:
cases.o1: The introductory level, where skills are built before being contested

cases.q: A player who executes skills under pressure but not yet while reading a defence is at:
Level is set by:
cases.o1: What the player can do, not by age or team

cases.q: Teaching a concept above a player's level produces:
cases.o1: Execution without understanding, which fails as soon as the defence changes

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Level is a description of capability, which is why two players of the same age are often at different ones

problems.prompt: At a training-to-competition ratio of {{rt}} to 1 with {{ng}} games a season, how many training sessions is that?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Younger levels carry a higher ratio because development happens in training, not in games; a season with more games than sessions is a season of no development

cases.q: Which comes first in a teaching sequence?
cases.o1: Spacing and the ability to play one-on-one, before any five-on-five concept

cases.q: Help-side defence should enter:
cases.o1: Once players can guard the ball one-on-one, since help covers a beaten defender

cases.q: Fixing positions should happen:
cases.o1: Late, after players have played several roles

cases.q: Teaching set plays before reads produces:
cases.o1: Players who run the set and cannot play when it breaks down

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Reads before sets, one-on-one before help, and positions last: each layer assumes the one below it

cases.q: A drill teaching drive-and-kick reads must include:
cases.o1: Live defenders making real choices, since the read is of a defender

cases.q: A drill with no defence teaches:
cases.o1: The motion, not the read, which is the part the game requires

cases.q: A constraint such as 'no dribble after the catch' is used to:
cases.o1: Force the read the drill is teaching rather than letting a habit substitute

cases.q: Scoring a drill competitively does what?
cases.o1: Makes the players care about the outcome the read is supposed to produce

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Live defenders, a constraint that forces the read, and a score: a drill without all three teaches something else

problems.prompt: A {{mn}}-minute practice gives {{nb}} blocks with {{tr}} minutes of transition between each. How long is each block (minutes)?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Transitions eat ten to twenty minutes of a practice, so a plan with too many blocks loses its time to moving between them: counting it is what makes a plan honest

cases.q: A good teaching cue names:
cases.o1: An observable action the player can check

cases.q: 'Be more aggressive' fails as a cue because:
cases.o1: Nothing observable tells the player whether they did it

cases.q: 'Two feet in the paint before you pass' works because:
cases.o1: The player and the coach can both see whether it happened

cases.q: A cue naming the outcome rather than the action:
cases.o1: Leaves the player to guess which action produces it

parts.label: v
parts.explain: The test is whether a bystander could say yes or no: a cue that fails it is an instruction to try harder

problems.prompt: A player made the correct read on {{nc}} of {{nt}} tagged possessions. What is his decision rate (per cent)?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Separating the read from the result is what lets a player be developed: a correct read that missed is a good possession, and tagging reads rather than outcomes is the only way to see it

problems.prompt: Of {{nc}} correct reads, {{nm}} produced points. What percentage of correct reads were converted?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: The conversion rate is a shot-making measure and the read rate is a decision measure; conflating them is how a good decision-maker in a cold stretch gets coached out of the right read

problems.prompt: A team's turnover rate is {{t1}} per cent against a league average of {{t2}}. By what percentage must it improve to reach the average?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Setting season goals on the four factors gives a target that is trackable per game and that the team controls, which is what a goal of winning a number of games is not

cases.q: Points per game favours a fast team because:
cases.o1: It has more possessions, so the same efficiency produces more points

cases.q: Points allowed per game favours a slow team because:
cases.o1: Fewer possessions means fewer points allowed at the same efficiency

cases.q: Pace is:
cases.o1: Neither good nor bad on its own; it multiplies whatever efficiency a team has

cases.q: The cleanest comparison of two teams at different paces uses:
cases.o1: Points per 100 possessions on both ends

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Pace is a multiplier on both ends, so per-game numbers rank teams by how fast they play as much as by how well

problems.prompt: With {{fga}} field-goal attempts and {{fta}} free-throw attempts, how many true shot attempts is that?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: True shot attempts is the denominator true shooting divides by, and the 0.44 is there because not every free-throw attempt ends a possession

problems.prompt: Player A has a true shooting of {{a1}} per cent and an eFG of {{a2}}; player B {{b1}} and {{b2}}. Whose free-throw contribution is larger, and by how many points of difference?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: The gap between true shooting and eFG is a player's free-throw contribution, so comparing the two gaps says who earns points at the line that their shooting alone would not give

problems.prompt: Two teams differ on the four factors by {{d1}}, {{d2}}, {{d3}} and {{d4}} standardised points, weighted 40, 25, 20 and 15. Which single factor contributed the most, and how much did it contribute?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: The largest weighted contribution, not the largest raw difference, is what decided the game: a big rebounding edge at weight twenty can lose to a modest shooting edge at forty

problems.prompt: Closing a turnover-rate gap of {{gp}} percentage points over {{ps}} possessions saves how many turnovers a game?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Two or three fewer turnovers a game is worth around two or three points, which is how a factor target becomes a number a team can see on the stat sheet

problems.prompt: A corner three makes {{p3}} per cent and a long two {{p2}}. By how many expected points does the three beat the two?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: A tenth or two of a point a shot, over eighty shots, is a dozen points a game: that is the size of the shot-profile effect and why it changed the sport

cases.q: A three at 34 per cent against a layup at 60 per cent is:
cases.o1: Worse, since the breakeven against a 60 per cent two is 40 per cent

cases.q: The breakeven rises when:
cases.o1: The two available is a better shot

cases.q: Comparing a three against an average two rather than the available two:
cases.o1: Flatters the three, because the available two in that situation may be a layup

cases.q: A contested long two is almost always worse than a three because:
cases.o1: Its percentage is below two thirds of nothing: it is a low-percentage shot worth less

parts.label: v
parts.explain: The comparison is always against the two actually available, which is why a layup beats a three and a long two loses to one

problems.prompt: A quick shot is worth {{q1}} expected points; working the clock gives {{q2}} but costs a {{tr}} per cent chance of a turnover worth 0. Which is better, and by how much?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Working for a better shot is only worth it if the turnover risk of the extra actions is smaller than the improvement; a team that turns the ball over on a fifth of its late-clock possessions should shoot earlier

problems.prompt: To halve the width of a shooter's confidence interval from {{at}} attempts, how many attempts are needed?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Four times the attempts for half the width is why a three-point percentage takes most of a season to resolve: twenty attempts cannot distinguish a good shooter from a poor one

problems.prompt: A lineup played {{mn}} minutes at about {{pp}} possessions a minute. How many possessions is that, and is it near the hundreds a rating needs?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: A rating per 100 possessions computed from 25 possessions is an extrapolation by a factor of four, which is why most lineup net ratings in a season are noise

problems.prompt: An opponent takes {{nr}} of {{nt}} drives to his right. What percentage go right, and which way should he be forced?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: A tendency above about two thirds is worth building help around; near fifty per cent the scout is something else, because forcing a direction he is comfortable going both ways in concedes the help position for nothing

cases.q: Help against a non-shooter's man comes from:
cases.o1: His own defender, who can leave to help without consequence

cases.q: Against a lineup of five shooters, help must come from:
cases.o1: Nowhere without conceding a three, which is why spacing is the offence's main weapon

cases.q: A post player who cannot shoot from distance changes the defence by:
cases.o1: Freeing his defender to sit in the lane

cases.q: The commonest scouting error on help rules is:
cases.o1: Leaving a player who has improved his shooting since the last meeting

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Help comes out of the non-threats, so the scout has to be current: a player who added a shot removes the defence's help

problems.prompt: An opponent ran the same action on {{na}} of {{nt}} after-timeout possessions. What percentage is that, and is it worth preparing for?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: A third or more is worth a specific preparation, because the coach has chosen it in exactly the situation you will be in; below that the preparation costs more attention than it buys

problems.prompt: Against a drop, a pull-up makes {{p1}} per cent for two and a pocket pass yields {{p2}} expected points. Which is the better counter, and by how much (points)?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: The counter follows from the personnel: a good pull-up shooter beats the pocket pass against a drop, and a poor one does not, which is why the same coverage is attacked differently by different teams

problems.prompt: A squad of {{ns}} has {{n1}} introductory, {{n2}} foundational and the rest advanced players. How many are advanced?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: A squad spread across levels cannot be coached as one group, which is the practical reason practice is run in stations rather than as a whole-team walk-through

cases.q: At the introductory level, position policy should be:
cases.o1: Every player learns every role, since fixing positions early limits development

cases.q: A high training-to-competition ratio at young levels exists because:
cases.o1: Development happens in training and games mostly reveal it

cases.q: Fixing a tall young player at centre costs:
cases.o1: The ball skills he would have built in other roles, which he will need later

cases.q: As the level rises, the ratio:
cases.o1: Falls, as competition becomes part of the development

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Train more than you compete and fix positions late: both get reversed when a season's results start to matter to adults

problems.prompt: A progression runs one-on-one, two-on-two, three-on-three and five-on-five, with {{wk}} weeks at each. How many weeks to reach five-on-five?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Reaching five-on-five takes weeks, not a session, and a team that starts there skips the layers the five-on-five concepts assume

problems.prompt: A small-sided drill gives each of {{np}} players {{nr}} reps in {{mn}} minutes. How many reps a minute does the group get?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Small-sided drills multiply reps, which is the main argument for them over five-on-five: the same ten minutes gives each player several times the touches

problems.prompt: A practice gives {{t1}}, {{t2}}, {{t3}} and {{t4}} minutes to the four stages of a progression. What percentage is spent below five-on-five?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Most of a developmental practice belongs below five-on-five, and the percentage is the quickest audit of whether a plan matches what the coach says it is for

expect.v: 100*Rational(t1 + t2 + t3, t1 + t2 + t3 + t4)

problems.prompt: Of {{nc}} cues in a practice plan, {{no}} name an observable action. What percentage need rewriting?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Auditing a plan's cues against the observable test usually finds most of them wanting, because the natural way to write a cue is to name the outcome

cases.q: Season goals set on the four factors are better than a win target because:
cases.o1: The team controls them and can track them every game

cases.q: The factor to set a goal on first is:
cases.o1: The one with the largest weighted deficit, usually shooting

cases.q: Tracking a factor goal per game does what?
cases.o1: Makes a season-long aim actionable in the next practice

cases.q: A factor goal that the team meets while losing:
cases.o1: Still shows the plan is working on that factor, and points at which other factor to take next

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Factors are controllable and trackable, which is what a win total is not

cases.q: Two offensive players in one corner is a spacing error because:
cases.o1: One defender guards both, freeing a helper

cases.q: A player standing on the drive's path is a spacing error because:
cases.o1: His defender is already in help position without moving

cases.q: The usual spacing rule of thumb is:
cases.o1: Twelve to fifteen feet between adjacent offensive players

cases.q: A big standing in the short corner on a drive from the same side:
cases.o1: Shortens his defender's help distance to nothing

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Every spacing error has the same consequence: a defender guards two players, so the advantage the drive created disappears

problems.prompt: With {{no}} off-ball offensive players, {{nc}} of them crowded so one defender covers two, how many defenders are free to help?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Each pair of crowded players frees one defender, which is the whole arithmetic of spacing: perfect spacing leaves the defence with nobody spare

cases.q: On a drive from the wing in a 5-out alignment, the help usually comes from:
cases.o1: The defender one pass away on the drive side, who has the shortest closeout back

cases.q: In a 4-out-1-in alignment, a drive at the rim is met by:
cases.o1: The post defender, who is already inside

cases.q: In a 3-out-2-in alignment, a drive concedes:
cases.o1: Less room, since two defenders already sit inside

cases.q: The reason 5-out is harder to help in is:
cases.o1: Every helper has a long closeout back to a shooter
cases.o4: Defenders are further from the ball

parts.label: v
parts.explain: The alignment decides who can help and what the help costs: 5-out makes every help a long closeout

cases.q: An off-ball player above the drive on the same side should:
cases.o1: Lift toward the arc, keeping his defender from dropping in

cases.q: An off-ball player below the drive on the same side should:
cases.o1: Drift to the corner, widening the help distance

cases.q: A weak-side player whose defender is helping should:
cases.o1: Fill to the open spot his defender vacated, to be the kick-out target

cases.q: The player directly in the drive's path should:
cases.o1: Cut away or through, rather than stay

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Lift, drift, fill, cut: each is a specific response to where the drive is relative to the player

cases.q: Which of these creates an advantage by forcing two defenders to decide?
A post touch creates an advantage by:
cases.o1: Drawing help from a perimeter defender, opening a kick-out

cases.q: An isolation creates an advantage only when:
cases.o1: The matchup is genuinely favourable, since no second defender is forced to decide

cases.q: An off-ball screen creates an advantage by:
cases.o1: Forcing two defenders to communicate and choose a coverage

cases.q: Passing the ball around the perimeter without any of these:
cases.o1: Creates no advantage, which is why offences that do it stall

parts.label: v
parts.explain: An advantage is two defenders having to decide: anything that does not force that creates none

cases.q: On a catch with the closeout late, the read is:
On a catch with the closeout high and fast, the read is:
On a catch with the help already rotated across, the read is:
cases.o1: Pass to the player the helper left

cases.q: Holding the ball on a catch costs:
cases.o1: The advantage, since the defence recovers in the time taken to decide

cases.q: The reason the read must be made before the catch is:
cases.o1: The advantage lasts under a second, less time than deciding takes

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Three reads, chosen on what the defence has already committed to, and decided before the ball arrives

problems.prompt: A mismatch raises a possession's expected points from {{p1}} to {{p2}}. Over {{nt}} possessions attacking it, how many extra points is that?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: A mismatch is worth a fraction of a point a possession, so it pays only if attacked repeatedly; hunting it once and abandoning it wastes the advantage of having found it

parts.label: r

problems.prompt: A cross is expected to give a {{r}} : 1 ratio. Of ${{n}}$ offspring, ${{n*r/(r + 1) + d}}$ show the first phenotype and ${{n/(r + 1) - d}}$ the second. What is χ²? (Critical value at p = 0.05 with 1 df: 3.84)

parts.explain: Expected counts: ${{n*r/(r + 1)}}$ and ${{n/(r + 1)}}$. $\chi^2 = \sum (o - e)^2/e$. Degrees of freedom = categories − 1. If χ² exceeds the critical value, reject the hypothesis that the data fit the ratio

How do fungi get food?
What dominates most fungal life cycles?
What partnership do mycorrhizae form?

parts.label: a
choice: A network of hyphae called a mycelium
A haploid stage; the diploid zygote is brief
Fungi trade minerals and water for a plant root's sugars
parts.explain: Fungi are heterotrophs with chitin walls, closer to animals than to plants. They are key decomposers and partners (mycorrhizae, lichens), and some are pathogens

cases.q: Plasmodium, which causes malaria
Diatoms with glass walls
Amoebas that move with pseudopodia
Euglena with a flagellum and chloroplasts
Why is Protista not a natural group?

parts.label: a
choice: Its members do not share a single common ancestor that excludes plants, animals and fungi
parts.explain: Modern trees split protists among several supergroups, so "protist" is a grade, not a clade. Classify them by structure, movement and nutrition

cases.q: Mosses: no vascular tissue; the dominant stage is
Ferns: vascular tissue but no seeds; the dominant stage is
Conifers added which innovation?
Flowering plants added which innovation?
In alternation of generations, the haploid multicellular stage is the

parts.label: a
parts.explain: Plant evolution, in order of innovation: bryophytes (land), seedless vascular plants (vascular tissue), gymnosperms (seeds, pollen), angiosperms (flowers, fruit). Through that series the sporophyte grows to dominate

cases.q: Sponges
Jellyfish
Flatworms
Earthworms and snails
Sea stars and vertebrates

problems.prompt: How is the body plan of {{q}} classified?

parts.label: a
choice: Bilateral, three germ layers, no body cavity (acoelomate)
Bilateral, coelomate protostomes (mouth from the blastopore)
parts.explain: Animal phylogeny branches at tissues, symmetry, germ layers, body cavity, and protostome versus deuterostome development (spiral vs radial cleavage, mouth vs anus first). Echinoderms are deuterostomes, which is why they are our close invertebrate relatives

cases.q: Features every chordate has at some stage
Amniotic egg
Hair and mammary glands
Feathers and hollow bones
Jaws and paired fins, but no lungs or limbs in most

problems.prompt: Which group is defined by: {{q}}?

parts.label: a
choice: Chordates: notochord, dorsal hollow nerve cord, pharyngeal slits, post-anal tail
parts.explain: Vertebrate classes are nested by innovations: jaws, lungs and limbs (tetrapods, amphibians), the amniotic egg (reptiles including birds, and mammals), then feathers or hair and milk

problems.prompt: An outbreak has R = {{R}} and a generation interval of {{Tg}} days (treat it as fixed). What is the doubling time, in days?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: r = ln R / T_g, then T_d = ln 2 / r: the same R doubles faster with a shorter generation interval

problems.prompt: Cases double every {{Td}} days and the generation interval is {{Tg}} days (fixed). What is R?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: R = e^{rT_g} with r = ln 2 / T_d, which is 2^{T_g/T_d}: R doublings per generation

problems.prompt: A pathogen has R₀ = {{R0}}. What fraction of the population must be immune for herd protection, in %?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Spread stops once each case infects fewer than one: R₀(1 − p) < 1

problems.prompt: Herd protection against a pathogen needs {{h}}% of the population immune. What R₀ does that imply?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: p = 1 − 1/R₀, so R₀ = 1/(1 − p): measles-like thresholds (~95%) mean R₀ near 20

problems.prompt: {{d}} deaths follow {{c}} confirmed cases, but only {{a}}% of infections were confirmed. What is the infection fatality ratio, in %?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: IFR = CFR × ascertainment: counting only the sick inflates apparent lethality

cases.q: Early in an outbreak, mild infections are rarely tested. How does that bias the case fatality ratio?
cases.o1: Upward: the denominator misses mild infections

cases.q: Deaths lag cases by weeks. Dividing deaths to date by cases to date during rapid growth biases the CFR how?
cases.o1: Downward: recent cases have not yet had time to die

cases.q: Which ratio uses all infections, including those never tested, as its denominator?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Ascertainment inflates the CFR; reporting lag deflates it during growth

cases.q: In which year did the WHO certify the eradication of smallpox?
The 1979 anthrax outbreak at Sverdlovsk was later traced to what?
cases.o1: An accidental release from a military facility

cases.q: In which year was the Biological Weapons Convention opened for signature?
The 1925 Geneva Protocol did what?
cases.o1: Banned the use (not the development or stockpiling) of chemical and biological weapons in war

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Use was banned in 1925; development and stockpiling only in 1972, and without verification

cases.q: Which came first?
Which came last?
Which happened between the BWC's entry into force (1975) and smallpox eradication (1980)?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: 1925 Geneva Protocol · 1972/1975 BWC · 1979 Sverdlovsk · 1980 smallpox · 2001 letters · 2004 UNSCR 1540 · 2005 IHR · 2025 Pandemic Agreement

cases.q: A virus jumps from bats to people through an intermediate animal at a market. Which kind of risk is this?
A researcher is infected through a needle-stick and carries an agent out of the lab. Which kind?
A group seeks to cause harm by releasing an agent. Which kind?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Natural, accidental and deliberate risks need different layers: surveillance and One Health, biosafety, and nonproliferation

cases.q: Which combination most raises a biological event toward global catastrophe?
cases.o1: High transmissibility, high severity and poor countermeasures
cases.o4: A well-understood pathogen with a vaccine stockpile

cases.q: Why do biosecurity planners worry about 'stealth' spread?
cases.o1: Long presymptomatic spread defeats symptom-based detection

cases.q: Which factor most improves society's ability to respond?
cases.o1: Time between detection and wide spread

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Scale depends on the pathogen and on our response: detection time and countermeasures are levers

cases.q: What does the BWC lack that the Chemical Weapons Convention has?
Which BWC article contains the core prohibition on developing, producing and stockpiling?
What are the BWC's confidence-building measures?
cases.o1: Annual voluntary declarations of relevant facilities and activities

cases.q: Roughly how many States Parties does the BWC have (2026)?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: The BWC rests on national implementation, consultation and transparency, not inspection

cases.q: A State Party suspects another of breaching the Convention. Which route does the BWC itself provide?
cases.o1: Consult bilaterally, then lodge a complaint with the UN Security Council (Article VI)
cases.o4: Impose sanctions itself under Article I

cases.q: A State Party wants to share vaccine technology for peaceful purposes. Which article supports this?
A State Party passes laws making BWC violations crimes for individuals. Which obligation is it meeting?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Articles I–IV are obligations; V–VI consultation and complaint; VII assistance; X peaceful use; XII review

cases.q: What is the Australia Group?
cases.o1: An informal forum that harmonises national export controls on chemical and biological items

cases.q: What does UN Security Council Resolution 1540 (2004) require of every state?
cases.o1: Laws and controls keeping WMD and related materials from non-state actors
cases.o4: Reporting every outbreak to the WHO

cases.q: Export controls on dual-use equipment chiefly aim to…
cases.o1: Make it harder for proliferators to acquire it while allowing legitimate trade
cases.o2: Stop all trade in lab equipment

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Supply-side controls work through national licensing, coordinated lists and catch-all clauses

cases.q: Which instrument binds every UN member state, party or not?
Which instrument is a political arrangement, not a treaty?
Which instrument obliges states to notify the WHO of potential public health emergencies?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Treaties bind parties; Security Council resolutions bind all members; the Australia Group coordinates

cases.q: Gene synthesis screening checks which two things?
cases.o1: The ordered sequence against sequences of concern, and the customer's legitimacy

cases.q: Why do screening frameworks worry about benchtop DNA synthesisers?
cases.o1: They move synthesis outside the provider's central screening

cases.q: Why screen short sequence windows, not just whole genes?
cases.o1: Orders can be split into fragments that are assembled later

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Screening is a chokepoint: sequence, customer and fragment-splitting all have to be covered

cases.q: An order matches a regulated sequence and the customer is an unverified individual. What does good practice do?
cases.o1: Hold the order and escalate for customer verification and review

cases.q: An order matches a sequence of concern but comes from a verified vaccine lab with a legitimate need. What happens?
cases.o1: It can proceed after review, with records kept
cases.o4: The lab is reported to police automatically

cases.q: A flagged sequence turns out to be a harmless housekeeping gene that shares a short motif. What is that?
cases.o1: A false positive, which review should clear
cases.o3: A screening failure that must ship
