problems.prompt: A two-electron cell has E° = {{Ec}} V at 298 K and dE°/dT = {{d}} mV/K. What is ΔH°, in kJ/mol? ($F = 96485$)

parts.label: v
parts.explain: ΔG° = −nFE°; ΔS° = −(∂ΔG°/∂T) = nF dE°/dT; then ΔH° = ΔG° + TΔS°. A cell whose voltage falls with temperature has ΔS° < 0

problems.prompt: A cell reaction with n = {{nn}} has ΔS° = {{dS}} J/(mol·K). What is dE°/dT, in mV/K?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: ΔS° = nF(dE°/dT): a cell with negative ΔS° loses voltage as it warms

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Two independent measurements give ΔG° and ΔH°; their difference is TΔS°. Neutralising ions releases ordered hydration water, so ΔS° is often positive

problems.prompt: K = {{K1}} at {{T1}} K and ΔH° = {{dH}} kJ/mol (constant). What is K at {{T2}} K?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: ln(K₂/K₁) = −(ΔH°/R)(1/T₂ − 1/T₁): heating favours the endothermic direction

problems.prompt: Goldschmidt's tolerance factor for perovskite ABO₃ is t = (r_A + r_O)/(√2 (r_B + r_O)). With r_A = {{rA}} pm, r_B = {{rB}} pm and r_O = 140 pm, what is t?

parts.explain: t near 1 gives the cubic perovskite; t < 1 tilts the octahedra, t > 1 favours hexagonal stacking

cases.q: A rotamer library lists:

cases.q: A backbone-dependent rotamer library conditions those probabilities on:

cases.q: Which residue has no χ angles at all?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: A probability maps to an energy by −kT ln p, so a tenfold rarer rotamer costs about 1.4 kcal/mol at room temperature

cases.q: A Pose holds the conformation primarily as:

cases.o2: A list of Cartesian coordinates only

cases.q: Pose numbering runs:

cases.o2: The same as the PDB numbering

cases.o1: Smaller than the PDB numbers, because nothing was inserted for missing residues

cases.o1: Waters, ligands, alternate conformations and insertion codes can break the numbering or the chemistry
cases.o2: The file is too large otherwise

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Pose indices are contiguous; PDB numbering is whatever the depositor chose

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Pose numbering is contiguous across chains, so the index is the offset of the preceding chains plus the position within the chain

cases.q: In the centroid representation, each side chain is replaced by:
cases.o1: A single pseudo-atom carrying its size and polarity

cases.q: Centroid mode is used for:
cases.o1: Fast, aggressive search of conformational space
cases.o3: Computing hydrogen bonds between side chains

cases.q: Full-atom mode is used for:
cases.o1: Local refinement and final discrimination between models

cases.q: The usual multi-resolution pattern is:
cases.o1: Coarse-grained global search, then all-atom refinement

cases.q: Side-chain hydrogen bonds cannot be scored in centroid mode because:
cases.o1: The side-chain atoms are not represented
cases.o2: The energy function has no hydrogen-bond term
cases.o3: They do not matter for folding
cases.o4: They are computed separately by MD

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Two resolutions, two jobs: search wide and cheap, then refine and rank

problems.prompt: A {{n}}-residue protein averages {{a}} atoms per residue in full atom and {{b}} interaction centres per residue in centroid. By what factor does the number of pairwise interactions fall?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Pair work scales with the square of the number of centres, which is why coarse-grained search is affordable

cases.q: fa_atr and fa_rep come from:
cases.o1: The Lennard-Jones potential, split at its minimum into attractive and repulsive parts

cases.q: fa_sol implements:
lk_ball_wtd adds what the isotropic solvation term misses:
cases.o1: Direction: it penalises burying a polar atom where its ideal water sites are blocked

cases.q: fa_elec uses a distance-dependent dielectric that:
cases.o1: Rises from a low value in the core toward that of bulk solvent
cases.o4: Depends on the residue type only

cases.q: Which of these is a knowledge-based term fitted to structural statistics?
cases.o1: p_aa_pp, the propensity of an amino acid at given φ/ψ

cases.q: rama_prepro differs from a plain Ramachandran term by:
cases.o1: Using a separate map when the next residue is proline

cases.q: The repulsive part of the Lennard-Jones term is softened at very short distances to:
cases.o4: Allow atom overlap in the final model

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Physics-based terms carry weight 1.0; the statistical terms are fitted and weighted down

problems.prompt: A residue's unweighted term energies are fa_atr {{atr}}, fa_rep {{rep}}, fa_sol {{sol}} and fa_dun {{dun}} kcal/mol. With weights 1.0, 0.55, 1.0 and 0.7, what is the weighted total?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: The score is a weighted linear sum; fa_rep at 0.55 and fa_dun at 0.7 are the published weights

cases.q: The reference energy (ref) stands for:
cases.o1: A constant per amino-acid type approximating its unfolded-state energy
cases.o2: The energy of the native structure
cases.o4: The lowest score seen so far

cases.q: The reference energies were fitted to:
cases.o1: Maximise recovery of native sequences in design

cases.q: For a fixed sequence, ref contributes:
cases.o1: A constant offset that cancels in any comparison of conformations

cases.q: Without reference energies, design would:
cases.o1: Favour whichever residues the other terms happen to score well, biasing composition

cases.q: ref matters for design because design compares:
cases.o1: Different sequences on the same backbone
cases.o2: Different backbones with the same sequence

parts.label: v
parts.explain: ref is how a fixed-backbone score stands in for a folding free energy

problems.prompt: Two designs on the same backbone score {{ea}} and {{eb}} kcal/mol before reference energies, with reference sums {{ra}} and {{rb}}. Which is predicted more stable, and by how much (kcal/mol, magnitude)?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Subtract each design's reference sum before comparing, or composition bias decides the winner

cases.q: The current all-atom energy function is parameterised in:
cases.o1: kcal/mol, rather than arbitrary Rosetta Energy Units

cases.q: For the paper's worked mutation, the computed stabilisation was about four times the measured value. The lesson:
cases.o1: Trust the sign and the ranking more than the magnitude

cases.q: Comparing total scores between two different proteins is:
cases.o1: Not meaningful, because the total scales with size and composition
cases.o2: The standard way to rank designs

cases.q: A score of −450 for one structure and −300 for another of the same sequence and length means:
cases.o1: The first is predicted more favourable under this function
cases.o2: The first is more stable in reality, certainly

cases.q: A large positive fa_rep in one residue usually means:
cases.o1: A steric clash that should be relieved by repacking or minimisation

parts.label: v
parts.explain: The function is calibrated but approximate: rankings survive, absolute magnitudes often do not

problems.prompt: A mutation changes fa_atr by {{d1}}, fa_rep by {{d2}}, fa_sol by {{d3}} and fa_elec by {{d4}} kcal/mol (unweighted). Using weights 1.0, 0.55, 1.0 and 1.0, what is the weighted ΔΔG?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Decomposing by term tells you which interaction drove the change, which a single total never does

cases.q: A Monte Carlo move that raises the score by ΔE is accepted with probability:
Uphill moves are accepted so that the search can:
cases.o1: Escape local minima that gradient descent cannot leave

cases.q: A move that lowers the score is accepted with probability:
Gradient-based minimisation finds:
cases.o1: The nearest local minimum, which need not be the global one

cases.q: Simulated annealing lowers the temperature during the run so that:
cases.o1: Early moves explore widely and later moves settle into a minimum

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Metropolis with a falling temperature is the search behind both folding and packing

problems.prompt: At {{t1}} K a Monte Carlo move raises the score by {{de}} kcal/mol. By what factor does its acceptance probability fall when the temperature drops to {{t2}} K?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: The acceptance ratio is exp(−ΔE/kT); cooling multiplies the exponent, so the same uphill move becomes far less likely

cases.q: The packer optimises:
cases.o1: Which rotamer sits at each allowed position, by simulated annealing over the discrete set

cases.q: Minimisation differs from packing in that it:
cases.o1: Moves continuous degrees of freedom downhill rather than choosing discrete rotamers

cases.q: Relax is used because:
cases.o1: Alternating packing and minimisation settles a structure without letting it drift far
cases.o3: It is faster than packing alone

cases.q: A task that accidentally allows every position to design will:
cases.o1: Change the whole sequence rather than only the intended positions

cases.q: Packing requires a precomputed table of:
cases.o1: One-body rotamer energies and two-body rotamer pair energies

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Discrete packing and continuous minimisation do different jobs; relax interleaves them

problems.prompt: Packing {{n}} positions with {{k}} rotamers each needs how many two-body pair-energy entries (all position pairs, all rotamer combinations)?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: n(n−1)/2 position pairs times k² rotamer combinations each: the table, not the annealing, is usually the cost

cases.q: A design specification sets, per position:
cases.o1: Whether it is fixed, repacked only, or designed, and to which residues

cases.q: 'Repack only' at a position means:
cases.o1: Its rotamer may change but its residue identity may not

cases.q: Restricting a surface position to polar residues is a way to:
cases.o1: Encode design intent the energy function would not impose on its own

cases.q: Positions not mentioned in a design specification are usually:
cases.o1: Left at a default behaviour set by the file's header, which must be checked

cases.q: A common cause of a nonsense design is:
cases.o1: A task that allowed design where repacking was intended

parts.label: v
parts.explain: The task specification is the design: it decides what the packer is even allowed to try

problems.prompt: A design allows all 20 residues at {{n1}} positions and a restricted set of {{a}} residues at {{n2}} positions. How large is the sequence space? Give log₁₀.

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Alphabets multiply across positions; restricting an alphabet is the cheapest way to shrink the search

cases.q: A saturation point-mutation scan at one position tries:
cases.o1: The 19 substitutions other than the wild-type residue
cases.o2: All 20 residues including wild type twice

cases.q: Each candidate mutation is scored after:
cases.o1: Local repacking (and usually minimisation) around the site

cases.q: A positive computed ΔΔG for a mutation means it is predicted:
The output of a scan should be treated as:
cases.o1: A ranked shortlist to test, not a verdict

cases.q: Running each mutation several times with different random seeds is done to:
cases.o1: Separate a real energy difference from packing noise

parts.label: v
parts.explain: A scan ranks candidates; the laboratory decides

problems.prompt: A saturation scan covers {{n}} positions, with {{r}} independent trials per mutation. How many scoring jobs is that?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: 19 substitutions per position times the trials; the wild type is scored separately as the reference

problems.prompt: A redesign of {{n}} positions returns the native residue at {{h}} of them. What is the native sequence recovery (per cent), and how does it compare with the roughly 5 per cent expected by chance?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Recovery well above the roughly 1-in-20 chance level is the standard check that an energy function and protocol are working

cases.q: Dead-end elimination differs from simulated annealing in that it:
cases.o1: Prunes rotamers that provably cannot be in the optimum, so it can return the true optimum

cases.q: Simulated annealing returns:
cases.o1: A good solution with no proof of optimality

cases.q: A genetic algorithm searches by:
cases.o1: Recombining and mutating a population of candidate sequences

cases.q: Mean-field methods approximate the problem by:
cases.o1: Replacing each position's neighbours with an average, then iterating to self-consistency

cases.q: Why is exact optimisation of the packing problem hard in general?
cases.o1: It is combinatorial: the rotamer choices couple through pair energies
cases.o4: It needs more memory than exists for any protein

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Know which method gives a guarantee and which gives a good answer fast

cases.q: The usual docking strategy is:
cases.o1: A global rigid-body search followed by local high-resolution refinement

cases.q: A funnel plot shows:
cases.o1: Score against RMSD to a reference, which should funnel toward low RMSD

cases.q: Fourier-transform-based docking is used because it:
cases.o1: Scans translations and rotations of rigid bodies very fast

cases.q: If a funnel plot is flat, the likely conclusion is:
cases.o1: The score function does not discriminate near-native from decoy poses here

cases.q: High-resolution refinement after docking adjusts:
cases.o1: Side-chain rotamers and small rigid-body and backbone moves at the interface

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Search wide, refine locally, then ask whether the score can tell near-native from decoy

problems.prompt: A complex scores {{ec}} kcal/mol; the two partners alone score {{ea}} and {{eb}}. What is the interface energy?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Interface energy is the complex minus its separated partners, each scored in the same function; a negative value is favourable binding under the model

cases.q: Designing a ligand-binding pocket usually proceeds by:
cases.o1: Placing the ligand, designing the surrounding shell, then repacking and minimising
cases.o2: Designing the whole protein first, then adding the ligand

problems.prompt: A campaign made and screened {{nn}} designs and obtained {{k}} successes. What hit rate (per cent) should the next campaign assume?

cases.q: A design is stable but binds nothing. The most likely gap:

A designed loop is disordered in the structure. The usual explanation:
cases.o1: Loops are irregular and flexible, and are poorly captured by the score

problems.prompt: A {{n}}-residue loop is rebuilt. Its backbone has two free dihedrals per residue, and closure consumes {{c}} of them. How many free backbone degrees of freedom remain?

parts.label: v

cases.q: In a symmetric model, moves and energies are applied to:
cases.o1: One asymmetric unit, then replicated by the symmetry definition
cases.o4: The whole assembly atom by atom

problems.prompt: An assembly has {{nc}} identical chains of {{m}} residues. Under exact symmetry, how many residues' degrees of freedom does the search actually handle?

cases.q: Fitting a model into experimental density adds:
cases.o1: A restraint from evidence, scored alongside the energy function

cases.q: In a region where the map is unresolved, density fitting:
cases.o1: Cannot settle the conformation, so confidence stays low there

cases.q: A model that fits the density well but scores badly suggests:
cases.o1: Either a real strained feature or a modelling error worth inspecting
cases.o3: The energy function is always right

cases.q: Density-guided refinement is valuable mainly because:
cases.o1: It anchors the model to measurement rather than to the score alone
cases.o4: It removes the need for refinement

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Experimental density is evidence the score does not contain

cases.q: A refinement protocol alternates:
cases.o1: Small backbone moves, side-chain repacking and minimisation

cases.q: Ramping the repulsive weight during refinement lets:
cases.o1: Clashed regions pass through each other before the full weight is restored

cases.q: Refinement is restrained to the starting structure so that:
cases.o1: It settles locally instead of drifting to an unrelated conformation

cases.q: Refinement should be judged by:
cases.o1: Whether the score improves without the structure drifting far from the start

cases.q: A refinement run ends 6 Å from its starting structure. The likely reading:
cases.o1: It escaped the intended fold; tighten the restraints

cases.q: A refinement run improves the score by 0.2 units over hundreds of steps. The reading:
cases.o1: The structure was already near a local minimum

cases.q: Minimising without first repacking after a backbone move tends to:
cases.o1: Leave side chains in now-wrong rotamers that minimisation cannot escape

parts.label: v

cases.q: Antibody variable domains can be modelled from templates because their:
cases.o1: Frameworks are structurally conserved across antibodies

cases.q: Which complementarity-determining loop is hardest to predict?
cases.o1: CDR H3, the longest and most variable

cases.q: Most CDR loops other than H3 can be assigned to:
cases.o1: A small set of canonical conformational classes

cases.q: An antibody model with a confident framework and a poorly resolved H3 should be used:
cases.o1: With the caveat that the binding loop itself is the least certain part

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Graft the conserved framework; the variable loops, above all H3, are the uncertainty

cases.q: Antibody design is a one-sided problem because:
cases.o1: The epitope on the target cannot be redesigned

cases.q: Antibody design optimises:
cases.o1: CDR sequence and loop length against a chosen epitope

cases.q: Antibody design is especially hard because it combines:
cases.o1: One-sided interface design with flexible-loop modelling

cases.q: Choosing which epitope to target matters because:
cases.o1: Binding the wrong surface can give affinity with no function
cases.o2: Any epitope gives the same result

parts.label: v
parts.explain: The two hardest problems in the field meet in antibody design

cases.q: A membrane protein is set up in a bilayer by:
cases.o1: Embedding it with its hydrophobic span across the membrane and fixing its depth and orientation
cases.o4: Scoring it as a soluble protein

cases.q: The energy function must change for a membrane protein because:
cases.o1: The membrane interior is nonpolar, so burying a polar residue there costs differently than in water

cases.q: Scoring a membrane protein with a water-based solvation model would:
cases.o1: Misscore residues buried in the bilayer

cases.q: Predicting the ΔΔG of a point mutation in a membrane protein needs:
cases.o1: A membrane-aware score, because the residue's environment is the bilayer
cases.o2: The same protocol as a soluble protein

cases.q: Running one protocol to produce thousands of independent decoys is:
cases.o1: Embarrassingly parallel: each job is independent

cases.q: Running many different protocols across many inputs is best handled by:
cases.o1: A job system that tracks which protocol ran on which input

cases.q: A mutational scan parallelises best as:
cases.o1: Independent jobs, one per mutation and trial

cases.q: The reason a generative design pipeline needs a job system is:
cases.o1: Its stages differ in cost and each stage's output feeds the next

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Match the parallel pattern to the shape of the work

problems.prompt: A campaign runs {{ni}} input structures through {{np}} protocols with {{nd}} decoys each. How many output models is that?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Inputs × protocols × decoys; the lowest-scoring model of too small a set is noise, which is why decoy counts are large

cases.q: To reproduce a design run exactly you must record:
cases.o1: The random seed, the protocol and version, the input and every option

cases.q: Two runs of the same stochastic protocol with different seeds should:
cases.o1: Differ, which is why many decoys are run and the set is analysed

cases.q: Reporting only the single best-scoring decoy from a run is misleading because:
cases.o1: The best of a small stochastic set can be noise rather than signal

cases.q: A protocol's version matters to reproducibility because:
cases.o1: Score-function defaults and movers change between releases

parts.label: v
parts.explain: A result you cannot regenerate is not a result

cases.q: A model is refined into a 3.5 Å map. At that resolution you can place:
cases.o1: Backbone and secondary structure reliably, side chains far less so

cases.q: Overfitting a model to density means:
cases.o1: The model reproduces noise in the map rather than real features

cases.q: Density and the energy function are combined rather than used alone because:
cases.o1: Each covers what the other misses: evidence and chemistry

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Resolution sets what the map can decide; the score supplies the chemistry

problems.prompt: An antibody Fv has how many complementarity-determining loops in total across its heavy and light chains?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Three CDRs per chain (H1-H3 and L1-L3) make six loops; H3 is the longest and hardest to model

cases.q: A designed antibody binds the target with good affinity but also binds a close homologue. The missing step:
cases.o2: More positive design for the target

cases.q: Grafting a CDR with a known binding conformation onto a new framework assumes:
cases.o1: The framework does not change the loop's conformation much
cases.o2: The loop is rigid in all contexts

cases.q: Lengthening CDR H3 in a design is a way to:
cases.o1: Reach into a recessed epitope, at the cost of entropy and predictability

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Specificity needs negative design; loop length buys reach and costs certainty

problems.prompt: A single transmembrane α-helix must cross a hydrophobic core about {{d}} Å thick. At 1.5 Å rise per residue, how many residues is that?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: About 20 residues span a bilayer core, which is why a run of roughly 20 hydrophobic residues flags a membrane span

problems.prompt: {{nj}} independent jobs of {{tm}} minutes each run on {{nw}} workers. What is the wall-clock time in hours (perfect parallelism)?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Embarrassingly parallel work divides cleanly, so the only questions are worker count and queue time

problems.prompt: A reaction follows $-r_A = k\,C_A^{ {{n}} }$ with $k = {{k}}$ (in mol, L, min units). What is the rate at $C_A = {{C}}$ mol/L, in mol/(L·min)?

parts.label: r
parts.explain: Substitute: ${{k}} \times {{C}}^{ {{n}} }$. The order is the exponent on the concentration, not the stoichiometric coefficient

problems.prompt: What are the units of the rate constant for a reaction of order ${{n}}$ (concentration in mol/L, time in s)?

parts.label: a
parts.explain: The rate is always mol/(L·s), so $k$ carries (mol/L) to the power $1 - n$ per second. The units of a quoted $k$ tell you the order

problems.prompt: Doubling the concentration of A multiplies the rate by ${{fac}}$. What is the order in A?

parts.label: r
parts.explain: $2^n = {{fac}}$. Doubling doubles a first-order rate, quadruples a second-order one, and leaves a zero-order rate alone

problems.prompt: A first-order reaction has $k = {{k}}$ min⁻¹. What is its half-life, in minutes?

parts.label: r
parts.explain: $C = C_0e^{-kt}$, so $t_{1/2} = \dfrac{\ln 2}{k} = \dfrac{0.693}{ {{k}} }$. For first order it does not depend on the starting concentration

problems.prompt: A reaction has $E_a = {{Ea}}$ kJ/mol. By what factor does the rate constant increase when the temperature goes from ${{T1}}$ °C to ${{T1 + dT}}$ °C? Use $R = 8.314$ J/(mol·K).

parts.label: r
parts.explain: $\dfrac{k_2}{k_1} = \exp\!\left[\dfrac{E_a}{R}\left(\dfrac1{T_1} - \dfrac1{T_2}\right)\right]$ with kelvin and joules. Around room temperature and $E_a \approx 50$ kJ/mol, ten degrees roughly doubles the rate

problems.prompt: A rate constant increases by a factor of ${{fac}}$ between ${{T1}}$ °C and ${{T1 + dT}}$ °C. What is the activation energy, in kJ/mol? Use $R = 8.314$ J/(mol·K).

parts.label: r
parts.explain: Take logs of the Arrhenius ratio: $E_a = \dfrac{R\ln(k_2/k_1)}{1/T_1 - 1/T_2}$, temperatures in kelvin

problems.prompt: A first-order liquid reaction ($k = {{k}}$ min⁻¹) runs in a batch reactor. How long to reach ${{X*100}}\%$ conversion, in minutes?

parts.label: r
parts.explain: $\dfrac{dC_A}{dt} = -kC_A$ gives $1 - X = e^{-kt}$, so $t = \dfrac{1}{k}\ln\dfrac{1}{1 - X}$. Each extra "nine" of conversion costs another $\ln 10/k$

problems.prompt: A second-order liquid reaction, $-r_A = kC_A^2$ with $k = {{k}}$ L/(mol·min), starts at $C_{A0} = {{C0}}$ mol/L in a batch reactor. How long to reach ${{X*100}}\%$ conversion, in minutes?

parts.label: r
parts.explain: $\dfrac{dC_A}{dt} = -kC_A^2$ integrates to $\dfrac1{C_A} - \dfrac1{C_{A0}} = kt$, so $t = \dfrac{X}{kC_{A0}(1 - X)}$. Unlike first order, the starting concentration matters

problems.prompt: A first-order liquid reaction ($k = {{k}}$ min⁻¹) is run in a CSTR fed at ${{v0}}$ L/min. What volume gives ${{X*100}}\%$ conversion, in L?

parts.label: r
parts.explain: CSTR balance: in $-$ out $=$ consumed, with the rate evaluated at the exit concentration: $v_0C_{A0}X = kC_{A0}(1 - X)V$. So $V = \dfrac{v_0X}{k(1 - X)}$

problems.prompt: A first-order reaction ($k = {{k}}$ min⁻¹) runs in a CSTR with space time $\tau = {{tau}}$ min. What is the conversion?

parts.label: r
parts.explain: $X = \dfrac{k\tau}{1 + k\tau}$, where $k\tau = {{k*tau}}$ is the Damköhler number. $Da = 1$ gives 50%, $Da = 9$ gives 90%

problems.prompt: A first-order liquid reaction ($k = {{k}}$ min⁻¹) is run in a plug-flow reactor fed at ${{v0}}$ L/min. What volume gives ${{X*100}}\%$ conversion, in L?

parts.label: r
parts.explain: PFR design equation: $V = F_{A0}\displaystyle\int_0^X\dfrac{dX}{-r_A} = \dfrac{v_0}{k}\int_0^X\dfrac{dX}{1 - X} = \dfrac{v_0}{k}\ln\dfrac{1}{1 - X}$. Always smaller than the CSTR volume for the same job

problems.prompt: A first-order reaction ($k = {{k}}$ min⁻¹) runs in two equal CSTRs in series, each with $\tau = {{tau}}$ min. What is the overall conversion?

parts.label: r
parts.explain: Each tank multiplies the concentration by $\dfrac{1}{1 + k\tau}$, so after two $\dfrac{C_A}{C_{A0}} = \dfrac{1}{(1 + k\tau)^2}$. Many small tanks in series approach a PFR

expect.r: 1 - [s[Symbol('c2')] for s in solve([Eq(1 - Symbol('c1'), k*tau*Symbol('c1')), Eq(Symbol('c1') - Symbol('c2'), k*tau*Symbol('c2'))], [Symbol('c1'), Symbol('c2')], dict=True)][0]

cases.q: For a positive-order reaction, which reactor needs the smaller volume for the same conversion?
In which reactor is the composition everywhere equal to the exit composition?
Which reactor behaves like a batch reactor with time replaced by space time?
For a zero-order reaction, which reactor needs the smaller volume for the same conversion?
An infinite number of tiny stirred tanks in series behaves like which reactor?

parts.label: a
parts.explain: A CSTR runs everywhere at the low exit concentration, so a positive-order reaction is slow throughout. A PFR starts at the feed concentration and works its way down. If the rate does not depend on concentration (zero order), the two are the same size

problems.prompt: For $A \to B \to C$ in a batch reactor, both steps first order with $k_1 = {{k1}}$ and $k_2 = {{k2}}$ min⁻¹, at what time is the concentration of the intermediate B highest, in minutes?

parts.label: r
parts.explain: $C_B = \dfrac{k_1C_{A0}}{k_2 - k_1}\left(e^{-k_1t} - e^{-k_2t}\right)$. Setting its derivative to zero gives $t_{max} = \dfrac{\ln(k_1/k_2)}{k_1 - k_2}$. Stop the batch here if B is the product

problems.prompt: A reacts by two parallel paths: to the desired D at $r_D = {{k1}}\,C_A^{ {{a1}} }$ and to the undesired U at $r_U = {{k2}}\,C_A^{ {{a2}} }$. What is the instantaneous selectivity $r_D/r_U$ at $C_A = {{C}}$ mol/L?

parts.label: r
parts.explain: $S = \dfrac{k_1}{k_2}C_A^{\,{{a1}} - {{a2}} }$. The sign of the exponent tells you whether to run at high or low $C_A$

problems.prompt: In parallel reactions the desired path is order ${{a1}}$ in A and the undesired path is order ${{a2}}$. How should the reactor be run to favour the desired product?

parts.label: a
choice: Keep the concentration of A high: PFR or batch, concentrated feed
Keep the concentration of A low: CSTR, diluted feed
parts.explain: Selectivity goes as $C_A^{\,a_D - a_U}$. If the desired reaction has the higher order, high concentration helps it more; if it has the lower order, starve both and the undesired one suffers more

problems.prompt: A gas adsorbs on a catalyst following the Langmuir isotherm with $K = {{K}}$ atm⁻¹. What fraction of the sites is covered at $P = {{P}}$ atm?

parts.label: r
parts.explain: Adsorption rate $\propto P(1 - \theta)$ balances desorption $\propto \theta$: $\theta = \dfrac{KP}{1 + KP}$. Half coverage at $P = 1/K$; saturation at high pressure

cases.q: What does a catalyst change?
What does a catalyst leave unchanged?
In heterogeneous catalysis, what happens between diffusion to the surface and diffusion away?
A surface reaction follows Langmuir–Hinshelwood kinetics. At very high pressure of the reactant, the apparent order in it approaches

parts.label: a
choice: The pathway: a lower activation energy, so a faster rate
The equilibrium constant and the heat of reaction
parts.explain: A catalyst speeds forward and reverse reactions alike, so equilibrium does not move. On a solid: reactants diffuse in, adsorb, react on the surface, and the products desorb and diffuse out. Once every site is occupied, more reactant cannot raise the rate

cases.s: How many 4-character PINs use the digits 0–9 with repetition allowed?
How many ways can 3 of 8 runners finish first, second and third?
How many 3-person committees can be chosen from 10 people?
How many distinct arrangements are there of the letters of BANANA?
How many integers from 1 to 100 are divisible by 3 or 5?
How many 8-bit strings contain exactly three 1s?
How many ways can 5 identical cookies be shared among 3 children (some may get none)?

parts.label: a
parts.explain: Order matters and repeats allowed: nᵏ. Order matters, no repeats: n!/(n − k)!. Order does not matter: C(n, k). Repeated letters divide out their own orderings. "Or" needs inclusion–exclusion (subtract the overlap). Identical items into bins: stars and bars, C(n + k − 1, k − 1)

problems.prompt: With {{r}}, what is T({{nn}})?

parts.label: a
parts.explain: Unroll the recurrence: adding n each step sums 1 + 2 + … + n = n(n + 1)/2; adding a constant gives a line; doubling gives 2ⁿ⁻¹; adding the odd numbers gives n²

problems.prompt: {{nk}} keys are hashed uniformly at random into {{m}} slots. What is the expected number of colliding pairs (two keys in the same slot)?

parts.label: a
parts.explain: Linearity of expectation: one indicator per pair of keys, each pair colliding with probability 1/m, so the expectation is C(n, 2)/m, whether or not the pairs are independent. The birthday problem is this with m = 365

problems.prompt: An intrusion detector catches {{tpr*100}}% of real attacks and falsely alarms on {{fpr*100}}% of normal sessions. {{base*100}}% of sessions are attacks. When it alarms, what is the probability the session really is an attack?

parts.label: a
parts.explain: Bayes: true alarms ÷ all alarms = P(A)·TPR ÷ (P(A)·TPR + P(not A)·FPR). With rare attacks, false alarms from the huge normal majority swamp the true ones: the base-rate fallacy

cases.s: n log n vs n^1.5
2ⁿ vs n¹⁰⁰
log₂ n vs √n
n! vs 2ⁿ
(log n)³ vs n^0.1
log₂ n vs log₁₀ n

problems.prompt: For large n, which grows faster: {{s}}?

parts.label: a
choice: Neither: same order (they differ by a constant factor)
parts.explain: Order: constants < logs < powers of logs < nᶜ for any c > 0 < polynomials < exponentials < factorials. Any polynomial eventually loses to any exponential, however large its degree. Logs in different bases differ by a constant factor, so the base does not matter in big-O

cases.code:
for (int i = 0; i < n; i++)
  for (int j = 0; j < n; j++) work();

for (int i = 0; i < n; i++)
  for (int j = i; j < n; j++) work();
for (int i = 1; i < n; i *= 2) work();

for (int i = 0; i < n; i++)
  for (int j = 1; j < n; j *= 2) work();

for (int i = n; i > 0; i /= 2)
  for (int j = 0; j < i; j++) work();

for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) work();
for (int j = 0; j < n; j++) work();

problems.prompt: How many times does work() run, in big-O terms?

parts.label: a
parts.explain: Multiply nested independent loops, add sequential ones. A loop variable that doubles or halves runs log n times. A triangular inner loop still gives n²/2, which is O(n²). The halving outer loop with an inner loop to i sums n + n/2 + n/4 + … < 2n, so O(n)

problems.prompt: Solve {{r}} by the master theorem.

parts.label: a
parts.explain: Compare f(n) with n^(log_b a). If f is smaller (by a polynomial factor), the leaves win: Θ(n^(log_b a)). If equal, multiply by log n. If f is bigger (and regular), the root wins: Θ(f). Merge sort is 2T(n/2) + n = Θ(n log n); binary search is T(n/2) + 1 = Θ(log n)

problems.prompt: A dynamic array starts with capacity 1 and doubles when full; copying an element costs 1 and writing the new element costs 1. What is the total cost of {{nops}} appends?

parts.label: a
parts.explain: Copies happen at sizes 1, 2, 4, …, n/2, which add up to n − 1, plus n writes: under 2n in all, so each append is O(1) amortized even though a single append can cost O(n)

cases.s: reading element i of an array
inserting at the front of a singly linked list
inserting at the front of an array of n elements
reading element i of a linked list
searching a balanced binary search tree
extract-min from a binary heap
looking up a key in a hash table (expected, low load)
looking up a key in a hash table when every key collides

problems.prompt: What does {{s}} cost?

parts.label: a
parts.explain: Arrays give O(1) access by index but must shift to insert in front; linked lists insert at a known spot in O(1) but must walk to find it. Balanced trees and heaps keep height log n. Hash tables are O(1) only on average: a bad hash or a full table degrades to a list

problems.prompt: Keys {{ks}} are inserted in that order into a 10-slot table with h(k) = k mod 10 and linear probing (try the next slot up, wrapping around). What does the table hold, slots 0 to 9 ("-" empty)?

parts.label: a
parts.explain: Each key goes to its home slot, or the next free one after it; keys that land in a run make the run longer (primary clustering), so later keys with nearby home slots get pushed further along. The probe sequence wraps from slot 9 to slot 0

problems.prompt: In a linear-probing hash table at load factor α = {{alpha}}, an unsuccessful search takes about ½(1 + 1/(1 − α)²) probes. How many is that?

parts.label: a
parts.explain: Load factor = keys ÷ slots. Probe counts in open addressing blow up as α nears 1 (at 0.9, about 50 probes), which is why such tables resize around 0.5–0.75; chaining degrades only linearly, about 1 + α

problems.prompt: Keys {{ks}} are inserted in that order into an empty binary search tree. What is its {{kind}}-order traversal?

parts.label: a
parts.explain: Build the tree first (smaller keys left, larger right). Pre-order visits the node, then its left and right subtrees; in-order visits left, node, right, which always gives sorted order; post-order visits both subtrees before the node, so the root comes last

problems.prompt: Keys {{ks}} are inserted in that order into an empty binary min-heap (stored as an array), then extract-min runs {{ex}} time{{ex == 1 ? "" : "s"}}. What is the array?

parts.label: a
parts.explain: Insert appends at the end and sifts up, swapping with the parent at (i − 1)/2 while smaller. Extract-min moves the last element to the root and sifts it down, swapping with the smaller child. A heap is only partly ordered: each parent ≤ its children, nothing more

problems.prompt: A B+-tree index has a fan-out of {{fan}} (each node points to {{fan}} children). About how many leaf pages can {{lev}} levels below the root reach?

parts.label: a
parts.explain: Each level multiplies the reach by the fan-out, so height is about log_fanout(n). With fan-out in the hundreds, three or four levels cover billions of rows: a lookup costs a handful of page reads, and the top levels usually sit in memory. That is why databases use B+-trees, not binary trees

problems.prompt: Symbols occur with frequencies {{fs}}. How many bits does the Huffman-coded message take in all?

parts.label: a
parts.explain: Repeatedly merge the two smallest weights. Each merge adds one bit to every symbol beneath it, so the total length is the sum of all the merged weights. Equal frequencies give a fixed-length code

cases.p:
Saliva, the Overlooked Defender

(1) Saliva rarely gets credit for anything. Patients notice it only when there is too much of it during a dental procedure or too little of it on a dry, anxious morning. Yet the roughly half to one and a half litres that the salivary glands secrete each day do more to protect the teeth than any single product sold to clean them. Saliva is not merely water: it is a dilute, carefully regulated solution of ions, proteins and enzymes, and almost every one of its components has a job.

(2) The first job is mechanical. Saliva lubricates the mouth, coats food so that it can be swallowed, and washes sugars and acids away from the teeth. Researchers describe this as salivary clearance, and it can be measured: after a sugary rinse, the sugar concentration in the mouth falls over the following minutes at a rate set largely by how fast saliva flows. A person with a brisk flow clears the sugar quickly; a person with a slow flow keeps it bathing the teeth far longer.

(3) The second job is chemical. When bacteria in dental plaque ferment sugar, they release acids that lower the pH at the tooth surface. Enamel, which is mostly a calcium phosphate mineral, begins to dissolve once the pH falls below a critical value, usually placed near 5.5. Saliva resists this fall. Its bicarbonate acts as a buffer, and the concentration of bicarbonate rises steeply when flow is stimulated, by chewing for example. Saliva is also supersaturated with calcium and phosphate, so that once the pH recovers, minerals can return to the enamel surface. A tooth is therefore not a static object but the site of a daily contest between loss and repair, and saliva is the referee.

(4) The third job belongs to the proteins. Some, such as statherin, keep calcium phosphate dissolved in saliva so that it does not precipitate prematurely as tartar. Others bind to the clean enamel within minutes of brushing and form a thin film, the acquired pellicle, which both protects the surface and serves as the first foothold for bacteria. Still others, including lysozyme and lactoferrin, restrain the growth of microbes directly. The same saliva that feeds the first colonizers of the tooth also limits how far they can spread.

(5) The value of all this becomes obvious when saliva fails. Hundreds of commonly prescribed medicines, radiation therapy to the head and neck, and certain autoimmune diseases reduce salivary flow. Patients with severe dry mouth can develop decay at unusual sites, such as the necks of the teeth near the gums and even the tips of the lower front teeth, places that are normally well protected. Their dentures may fit poorly and their mouths may burn. Saliva substitutes help with comfort, but none reproduces the full set of functions of natural saliva, and most clinicians treat them as a supplement rather than a replacement.

(6) For this reason some researchers argue that saliva deserves a more central place in prevention. Measuring flow and buffering capacity takes only a few minutes and costs little, yet it is seldom done in routine care. Chewing sugar-free gum after meals, which stimulates flow and raises bicarbonate, has modest but consistent support in the research literature. None of this replaces fluoride or brushing; rather, it acknowledges that the mouth already contains a sophisticated protective system, and that much of good dental care consists of not getting in its way.

cases.p:
How Teeth Learned to Hold On

(1) For most of the twentieth century, a dentist who wanted a filling to stay in a tooth had one reliable tool: geometry. Amalgam and gold do not stick to enamel or dentin, so the cavity was cut into a shape that locked the restoration mechanically, with walls that converged, grooves and undercuts. The rule, taught to generations of students, was to extend the preparation into sound tooth so that the restoration would be retained and future decay prevented. A great deal of healthy tooth was removed in the process, but there seemed to be no alternative.

(2) The alternative began with an observation from industry. In the 1950s a dental researcher, Michael Buonocore, noticed that paints and adhesives held better to metal surfaces that had first been treated with acid. He applied a weak phosphoric acid to enamel and found that resin bonded to the treated surface far more strongly than to untreated enamel. The acid dissolved the enamel selectively, leaving a microscopically rough, porous surface into which liquid resin could flow and harden, forming countless tiny tags. The bond was mechanical, but at a scale no drill could produce.

(3) For a time the discovery had little practical effect. The resins of the day shrank and stained, and they could not withstand the forces of chewing. A second advance was needed, and it came in the early 1960s, when Rafael Bowen developed a new monomer, now known as Bis-GMA, that could be combined with finely ground glass treated to bond chemically with the resin. The result was a composite material that was stronger and more stable than earlier resins. Combined with acid-etched enamel, it allowed a filling to be bonded rather than merely wedged in place.

(4) Dentin proved a much harder problem. Unlike enamel, it is a living, wet tissue riddled with tiny tubules and built around a scaffold of collagen. When acid is applied to dentin, the mineral dissolves and leaves the collagen exposed; if this soft network is dried, it collapses and the resin cannot penetrate it. It took decades of research, much of it in Japan, to show that resin could be made to infiltrate the moist, demineralized collagen and form what came to be called the hybrid layer. Some later systems added molecules that bond chemically to the calcium remaining in the tooth, improving the durability of the joint.

(5) These developments changed the philosophy of the profession as much as its materials. If a restoration could be held by adhesion, the cavity no longer needed to be shaped for retention, and the dentist could remove only the decayed tissue. The term 'minimally invasive dentistry' summarizes the shift. Small lesions could be sealed rather than drilled, and broken front teeth could be rebuilt without crowns.

(6) Adhesive dentistry is not without problems. Bonded restorations are sensitive to technique: contamination with saliva or blood, overdrying of dentin, or an incompletely cured resin can each weaken the bond. Over years in the mouth, the hybrid layer can degrade, and enzymes released from the dentin itself may contribute. Researchers continue to argue about how long bonded restorations last compared with the older materials they replaced. Still, few dentists would return to the era of extension for prevention, when the healthiest tooth structure was often sacrificed to hold a filling in place.

problems.prompt: Sketch one full period of $y = {{A == 1 ? "" : A}}{{tex}} {{D > 0 ? "+" : "-"}} {{abs(D)}}$ starting at $x = 0$. Mark the midline, the highest and lowest points, and where the period ends.

problems.prompt: Sketch $y = {{=a*(x - h)^2 + k}}$. Mark the vertex, the axis of symmetry and the $y$-intercept.

parts.ask: Draw it on paper, then compare
parts.label: a
parts.explain: Vertex $({{h}}, {{k}})$, axis $x = {{h}}$, opens {{a > 0 ? "up" : "down"}}. One step either side of the vertex the height changes by ${{a}}$. The $y$-intercept is $y(0) = {{a*h^2 + k}}$

problems.prompt: Sketch $y = {{=mn/md*x + b}}$. Mark the $y$-intercept and one more point found from the slope.

parts.ask: Draw it on paper, then compare
parts.label: a
parts.explain: Start at the intercept $(0, {{b}})$. Slope ${{=mn/md}}$: run ${{md}}$ to the right and rise ${{mn}}$ to reach $({{md}}, {{b + mn}})$, then rule the line through both

problems.prompt: Sketch $y = {{=a*abs(x - h) + k}}$. Mark the corner and show the slope of each arm.

parts.ask: Draw it on paper, then compare
parts.label: a
parts.explain: A V with its corner at $({{h}}, {{k}})$, opening {{a > 0 ? "up" : "down"}}. The right arm has slope ${{a}}$ and the left arm slope ${{-a}}$

problems.prompt: Sketch $y = {{=sqrt(x - h) + k}}$. Mark where it starts and two more exact points.

parts.ask: Draw it on paper, then compare
parts.label: a
parts.explain: It starts where the radicand is zero, at $({{h}}, {{k}})$, and exists only to the right. Go $1$, $4$, $9$ to the right for rises of $1$, $2$, $3$: steep at first, then flattening

problems.prompt: Sketch $y = {{=a*b^x}}$. Mark the $y$-intercept, one more exact point and the asymptote.

parts.ask: Draw it on paper, then compare
parts.label: a
parts.explain: Through $(0, {{a}})$ and $(1, {{a*b}})$: each step right multiplies the height by ${{b}}$. The $x$-axis is the asymptote, approached on the {{b > 1 ? "left" : "right"}}, and the curve never crosses it

problems.prompt: Sketch $y = \log_{ {{b}} }({{=x - h}})$. Mark the asymptote, the $x$-intercept and one more exact point.

parts.ask: Draw it on paper, then compare
parts.label: a
parts.explain: Vertical asymptote where the argument is zero, $x = {{h}}$. The argument is $1$ at $x = {{h + 1}}$ (height $0$) and ${{b}}$ at $x = {{h + b}}$ (height $1$). It is the exponential reflected in $y = x$: always rising, ever more slowly

problems.prompt: Sketch $y = {{=a/(x - h) + k}}$. Mark both asymptotes and one point on each branch.

parts.ask: Draw it on paper, then compare
parts.label: a
parts.explain: Asymptotes $x = {{h}}$ and $y = {{k}}$. One step right of the vertical asymptote the curve sits ${{a}}$ from the horizontal one, at $({{h + 1}}, {{k + a}})$; one step left it is at $({{h - 1}}, {{k - a}})$. The branches lie in opposite corners

problems.prompt: Sketch $y = {{=s*(x - r1)*(x - r2)*(x - r3)}}$. Mark the three zeros and the $y$-intercept, and get the end behaviour right. The turning points need only be on the correct side of the axis.

parts.ask: Draw it on paper, then compare
parts.label: a
parts.explain: Zeros at ${{r1}}$, ${{r2}}$ and ${{r3}}$, each crossed once. The leading term is ${{s > 0 ? "x^3" : "-x^3"}}$, so the graph {{s > 0 ? "falls to the left and rises to the right" : "rises to the left and falls to the right"}}. At $x = 0$ the height is ${{-s*r1*r2*r3}}$

problems.prompt: The graph of $f$ is shown. Sketch $f'$ on the same axes: get its zeros and its sign right.

parts.ask: Draw it on paper, then compare
parts.label: a
parts.explain: $f'$ is zero where $f$ has a horizontal tangent (${{ztex}}$), positive where $f$ rises and negative where it falls. The steeper $f$ is, the further $f'$ is from the axis (dashed: $f$; solid: $f'$)

problems.prompt: Draw the unit circle and the angle $\theta = {{rad}}$ in standard position. Mark the point where it meets the circle and write its coordinates.

parts.explain: ${{rad}}$ is ${{deg}}^\circ$. The point is $(\cos\theta, \sin\theta) = \left({{cx}}, {{cy}}\right)$: the reference triangle (dashed) gives the sizes and the quadrant gives the signs

problems.prompt: Draw an angle of ${{deg}}^\circ$ freehand, then check it against the picture (or a protractor).

problems.prompt: A small sphere settles slowly through a liquid (Stokes regime). Its diameter is multiplied by ${{f}}$. By what factor does its settling velocity change?
