parts.label: r
parts.explain: $v = \sqrt{2gh}$: velocity goes as the square root of the head. Four times the depth only doubles the jet

problems.prompt: A surface at ${{T1}}$ K is heated to ${{T1*f}}$ K. By what factor does the power it radiates change?

parts.label: r
parts.explain: $E = \varepsilon\sigma T^4$ with $T$ in kelvin: the ratio is $({{T1*f}}/{{T1}})^4$. Radiation is negligible near room temperature and dominant in a furnace for this reason

problems.prompt: A wall is made ${{f}}$ times as thick and the temperature difference across it is multiplied by ${{g}}$. By what factor does the heat flux change?

parts.label: r
parts.explain: Fourier: $q'' = k\,\dfrac{\Delta T}{L}$, proportional to the driving force and inversely to the thickness. Think of $L/k$ as a resistance

problems.prompt: A small metal sphere cools in air with a fixed heat-transfer coefficient (lumped behaviour). Its diameter is multiplied by ${{f}}$. By what factor does its cooling time constant change?

parts.label: r
parts.explain: $\tau = \dfrac{\rho cV}{hA}$ and $V/A = D/6$ for a sphere, so $\tau \propto D$: heat stored grows as volume, heat lost as surface. Small things reach the surrounding temperature fast

problems.prompt: Heat (or a solute) takes a certain time to diffuse through a slab. The slab is made ${{f}}$ times as thick. By what factor does the time change?

parts.label: r
parts.explain: The Fourier number $\alpha t/L^2$ must reach the same value, so $t \propto L^2$. Ten times as thick takes a hundred times as long: the reason small cells need no circulatory system and a thick roast needs hours

problems.prompt: In turbulent pipe flow the Nusselt number goes as $Re^{0.8}$ (Dittus–Boelter). The velocity is multiplied by ${{f}}$. By what factor does the heat-transfer coefficient change?

parts.label: r
parts.explain: $h \propto v^{0.8}$: a little less than proportional. The pressure drop meanwhile goes as $v^2$, so pushing flow harder buys heat transfer at a steep pumping price

problems.prompt: A reaction has $E_a = {{Ea}}$ kJ/mol. By what factor does its rate constant rise when the temperature goes from ${{T}}$ K to ${{T + 10}}$ K?

parts.label: r
parts.explain: $\dfrac{k_2}{k_1} = \exp\!\left[\dfrac{E_a}{R}\left(\dfrac1{T_1} - \dfrac1{T_2}\right)\right]$. "Doubles every ten degrees" is only true near room temperature for $E_a$ around 50 kJ/mol; a higher barrier is more sensitive and a hotter reaction less

problems.prompt: A first-order batch reaction is run hotter so that its rate constant is ${{f}}$ times larger. By what factor does the time to reach 90% conversion change?

parts.label: r
parts.explain: $t = \dfrac{1}{k}\ln\dfrac{1}{1 - X}$: for a fixed conversion, time is inversely proportional to $k$. For first order it does not depend on the starting concentration at all

problems.prompt: A second-order reaction, rate $= kC^2$, is started at ${{f}}$ times the concentration. By what factor does its half-life change?

parts.label: r
parts.explain: $t_{1/2} = \dfrac{1}{kC_0}$ for second order: more concentrated, faster. Compare first order, where the half-life does not move, and zero order, where it grows with $C_0$. How the half-life responds to dilution tells you the order

problems.prompt: A first-order reaction runs in a CSTR at ${{X1*100}}\%$ conversion. By what factor must the volume grow to reach ${{X2*100}}\%$ at the same feed rate?

parts.label: r
parts.explain: $k\tau = \dfrac{X}{1 - X}$ for a first-order CSTR, so the volume goes as $\dfrac{X}{1 - X}$. The last few percent are expensive because the whole tank sits at the low exit concentration; a plug-flow reactor needs only $\ln\dfrac{1}{1 - X}$

expect.r: solve(Eq(x/(1 + x), nsimplify(X2)), x)[0]/solve(Eq(x/(1 + x), nsimplify(X1)), x)[0]

problems.prompt: An object is scaled to ${{f}}$ times its size in every direction. By what factor does its surface area per unit volume change?

parts.label: r
parts.explain: Area goes as $L^2$, volume as $L^3$, so area per volume goes as $1/L$. Everything that happens at a surface (heat loss, dissolution, catalysis, drag on small particles) gets relatively stronger as things get smaller

problems.prompt: A gas is compressed to ${{fp}}$ times the pressure and heated from ${{T1}}$ K to ${{T2}}$ K. By what factor does its density change?

parts.label: r
parts.explain: $\rho = \dfrac{PM}{RT}$: density follows pressure and goes against absolute temperature. Always kelvin

problems.prompt: A liquid has $\Delta H_{vap} = {{dH}}$ kJ/mol. By what factor does its vapour pressure rise from ${{T}}$ K to ${{T + 10}}$ K?

parts.label: r
parts.explain: Clausius–Clapeyron: $\ln\dfrac{P_2}{P_1} = \dfrac{\Delta H_{vap}}{R}\left(\dfrac1{T_1} - \dfrac1{T_2}\right)$, the same form as Arrhenius with the heat of vaporisation in place of the activation energy. Near room temperature, ten degrees is very roughly a factor of 1.5

cases.q: an exothermic reaction is heated
an endothermic reaction is heated
an exothermic reaction is cooled
an endothermic reaction is cooled

problems.prompt: What happens to the equilibrium constant when {{q}}?

parts.label: a2
parts.explain: van 't Hoff: $\dfrac{d\ln K}{dT} = \dfrac{\Delta H^\circ}{RT^2}$. $K$ moves with temperature in the direction of the sign of $\Delta H^\circ$: heat is a reactant of an endothermic reaction. A catalyst or a pressure change does not move $K$ at all

problems.prompt: What is the highest possible efficiency of a heat engine working between ${{Th}}$ K and ${{Tc}}$ K?

parts.label: r
parts.explain: $\eta = 1 - \dfrac{T_c}{T_h}$, in kelvin. Raising the hot side helps less and less; no engine, however clever, beats this number

problems.prompt: Compared with gas A, gas B is at ${{fT}}$ times the absolute temperature and its molecules are ${{fM}}$ times as heavy. What is the ratio of B's rms speed to A's?

parts.label: r
parts.explain: $v_{rms} = \sqrt{\dfrac{3RT}{M}} \propto \sqrt{T/M}$. Hydrogen at room temperature moves four times as fast as oxygen

problems.prompt: ${{V1}}$ mL of a ${{C1}}$ mol/L solution is diluted to ${{V1*f}}$ mL. What is the new concentration, in mol/L?

parts.label: r
parts.explain: The moles of solute do not change: $C_1V_1 = C_2V_2$. Diluting to ${{f}}$ times the volume divides the concentration by ${{f}}$. This is a material balance with no reaction and one stream

problems.prompt: An ideal gas expands reversibly at constant temperature. Expanding to ${{r2}}$ times the volume does how many times the work of expanding to ${{r1}}$ times the volume?

parts.label: r
parts.explain: $w = -nRT\ln\dfrac{V_2}{V_1}$: work goes as the logarithm of the volume ratio, so each doubling yields the same work as the one before

problems.prompt: Two ions of charge numbers {{z1}} and {{z2}} sit {{r}} nm apart in {{med}} (ε = {{er}}). What is the magnitude of the force between them, in pN? (e = 1.602 × 10⁻¹⁹ C, k_B = 1.381 × 10⁻²³ J/K, ε₀ = 8.854 × 10⁻¹² F/m, N_A = 6.022 × 10²³)

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Coulomb's law (1.1) with k_e = 1/(4πεε₀): the solvent's permittivity is what lets ions separate in water at all

problems.prompt: At what separation, in nm, does the Coulomb energy between ions of charge numbers {{z1}} and {{z2}} in {{med}} (ε = {{er}}) equal k_BT at 25 °C? (e = 1.602 × 10⁻¹⁹ C, k_B = 1.381 × 10⁻²³ J/K, ε₀ = 8.854 × 10⁻¹² F/m, N_A = 6.022 × 10²³)

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Inside this distance electrostatics beats thermal motion: under a nanometre in water, tens of nanometres in oil, which is why ions dissociate in water and pair up in oil

problems.prompt: A Helmholtz layer {{d}} nm thick has an inner dielectric constant of {{er}}. What capacitance per area does the parallel-plate model give, in μF/cm²? (e = 1.602 × 10⁻¹⁹ C, k_B = 1.381 × 10⁻²³ J/K, ε₀ = 8.854 × 10⁻¹² F/m, N_A = 6.022 × 10²³)

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Helmholtz pictured all counterions on one plane: a molecular capacitor. Reduced permittivity of oriented water near the wall (ε ~ 6–10) gives the tens of μF/cm² seen at electrodes

problems.prompt: A surface carries {{s}} μC/cm² in contact with water (ε = 78.4). What electric field acts in the liquid right at the surface, in MV/m? (e = 1.602 × 10⁻¹⁹ C, k_B = 1.381 × 10⁻²³ J/K, ε₀ = 8.854 × 10⁻¹² F/m, N_A = 6.022 × 10²³)

parts.label: v
parts.explain: σ = −εε₀(∇ψ·n) (equation 1.10): even modest surface charges give fields of tens of MV/m, which is why the first water layers orient

cases.reg: particles at low surface potential (z⁻² law)

problems.prompt: Compared with a monovalent counterion, by what factor is the critical coagulation concentration lower for a counterion of valence {{z}}, for {{reg}}?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: DLVO reproduces both laws (chapter 1): z⁻⁶ when the surface potential is saturated, z⁻² when the Debye–Hückel limit applies

problems.prompt: A sol coagulates at {{c1}} mM of a monovalent counterion. Under the z⁻⁶ Schulze–Hardy law, what concentration, in mM, of a counterion of valence {{z}} does the same?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Trivalent ions coagulate at about 1/729 of the monovalent dose: alum (Al³⁺) clears water at micromolar levels

cases.q: Ions as charged spheres in a structureless dielectric continuum. Which model class?
Ions and neutral solvent spheres with excluded volume and van der Waals attraction, but no solvent dipoles. Which model class?
Ions and solvent molecules carrying dipoles, so ion–dipole and dipole–dipole forces act. Which model class?
Which early model first added a layer of finite-size ions with specific adsorption next to the wall, keeping Gouy–Chapman beyond it?
Who first analysed neutral solvent molecules in the layer next to the wall?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: The book's argument is that the solvent, usually far denser than the ions, sets the structure near the wall: only semi-primitive and civilized models can show it

cases.q: What is the simplest model class that can show solvent layering (density oscillations) next to a wall?
Which model class is needed for the solvent near the wall to orient (polarise) in the field?
In the primitive model, what stands in for the solvent?
cases.o4: Nothing: the ions are in vacuum

cases.q: What makes a primitive model 'restricted'?
cases.o1: All ions have the same diameter

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Each step up the hierarchy adds a feature the simpler model cannot show: packing (semi-primitive), then orientation (civilized)

problems.prompt: A surface has its isoelectric point at pI = {{pI}} and the bulk pH is {{pH}}. What is the Nernst potential ψ_N at 25 °C, in mV? (e = 1.602 × 10⁻¹⁹ C, k_B = 1.381 × 10⁻²³ J/K, ε₀ = 8.854 × 10⁻¹² F/m, N_A = 6.022 × 10²³)

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Equation (2.7): the PDI concentration sets ψ_N. A real surface reaches only part of it because its charge also depends on site density and the double layer (charge regulation)

problems.prompt: A charge-regulating surface with pI = {{pI}} sits at Nernst potential ψ_N = {{psi}} mV at 25 °C. What is the bulk pH? (e = 1.602 × 10⁻¹⁹ C, k_B = 1.381 × 10⁻²³ J/K, ε₀ = 8.854 × 10⁻¹² F/m, N_A = 6.022 × 10²³)

parts.label: v
parts.explain: About 59 mV per pH unit at 25 °C; a negative potential means the pH lies above the isoelectric point

problems.prompt: A surface has Γ = {{G}} sites/nm² and δ = 2√(K₋/K₊) = {{d}}. With ψ_N − ψ_s = {{dp}} mV, what surface charge does the linear regulation law give, in μC/cm²? (e = 1.602 × 10⁻¹⁹ C, k_B = 1.381 × 10⁻²³ J/K, ε₀ = 8.854 × 10⁻¹² F/m, N_A = 6.022 × 10²³)

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Equation (2.9) is the small-argument limit of σ = eΓδ sinh[e(ψ_N − ψ_s)/kT]: the charge follows the potential difference linearly (the small-argument limit of the sinh law)

problems.prompt: A regulating surface has Γ = {{G}} sites/nm² and δ = {{d}}. What potential drop ψ_N − ψ_s, in mV, gives σ = {{s}} μC/cm² under the linear regulation law? (e = 1.602 × 10⁻¹⁹ C, k_B = 1.381 × 10⁻²³ J/K, ε₀ = 8.854 × 10⁻¹² F/m, N_A = 6.022 × 10²³)

parts.label: v
parts.explain: σ = (e²Γδ/kT)(ψ_N − ψ_s): a small δ (few, strongly bound sites) keeps the surface close to its Nernst value

problems.prompt: An ion with charge number {{z}} adsorbs at a Stern plane at potential {{psi}} mV. Its non-electrostatic adsorption energy is {{phi}} kT and v₀ρ = {{vr}}. What fraction of Stern sites does it occupy (one species, 25 °C)? (e = 1.602 × 10⁻¹⁹ C, k_B = 1.381 × 10⁻²³ J/K, ε₀ = 8.854 × 10⁻¹² F/m, N_A = 6.022 × 10²³)

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Equation (2.13): specific (non-Coulombic) attraction and the Stern potential both enter the Boltzmann factor; counterions crowd a strongly charged plane

problems.prompt: A single ion species of charge number {{z}} occupies a fraction θ = {{th}} of Stern sites, with adsorption energy {{phi}} kT and v₀ρ = {{vr}}. What is the Stern-plane potential, in mV (25 °C)? (e = 1.602 × 10⁻¹⁹ C, k_B = 1.381 × 10⁻²³ J/K, ε₀ = 8.854 × 10⁻¹² F/m, N_A = 6.022 × 10²³)

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Invert the modified Langmuir isotherm: θ/(1 − θ) = v₀ρ e^{−φ − zeψ/kT}

problems.prompt: What is the Debye length of a {{z}}:{{z}} salt at {{c}} mol/L in water (ε = 78.4) at 25 °C, in nm? (e = 1.602 × 10⁻¹⁹ C, k_B = 1.381 × 10⁻²³ J/K, ε₀ = 8.854 × 10⁻¹² F/m, N_A = 6.022 × 10²³)

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Screening length falls as 1/(z√c): 9.6 nm at 1 mM 1:1, 0.96 nm at 0.1 M. It is the one length scale of the continuum theory

problems.prompt: A 1:1 salt solution is concentrated by a factor {{f}} and its salt replaced by a {{z}}:{{z}} salt at the same molarity. By what factor does the Debye length change?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: κ⁻¹ ∝ 1/(z√c): a hundredfold concentration shrinks the double layer tenfold

problems.prompt: A flat surface sits at ψ_s = {{psi}} mV in {{c}} M 1:1 salt (ε = 78.4, 25 °C). What surface charge does Gouy–Chapman give, in μC/cm²? (e = 1.602 × 10⁻¹⁹ C, k_B = 1.381 × 10⁻²³ J/K, ε₀ = 8.854 × 10⁻¹² F/m, N_A = 6.022 × 10²³)

parts.label: v
parts.explain: From the first integral (3.7): dψ̃/dz = −κ√(2(cosh ψ̃ − 1)) = −2κ sinh(ψ̃/2). Charge grows exponentially with potential once ψ̃_s > 2

problems.prompt: A flat surface carries σ = {{s}} μC/cm² in {{c}} M 1:1 salt (ε = 78.4, 25 °C). What surface potential does Gouy–Chapman give, in mV? (e = 1.602 × 10⁻¹⁹ C, k_B = 1.381 × 10⁻²³ J/K, ε₀ = 8.854 × 10⁻¹² F/m, N_A = 6.022 × 10²³)

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Grahame inverted: the potential grows only logarithmically with charge once eψ/kT ≫ 1, and adding salt lowers it at fixed charge

problems.prompt: A flat double layer has reduced surface potential ψ̃_s = eψ_s/kT = {{ps}} (1:1 salt). What is ψ̃ at κz = {{kz}}?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Far out the profile decays like 4γ e^{−κz}: a highly charged wall looks, from afar, like one at ψ̃ = 4 at most (potential saturation)

problems.prompt: A Gouy–Chapman double layer has ψ̃_s = {{ps}}. At what κz has the reduced potential fallen to half its surface value?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Near a highly charged wall the potential drops much faster than e^{−κz}: half of it is gone well within one Debye length

problems.prompt: For ψ̃_s = {{ps}}, by what percentage does the linear Debye–Hückel profile ψ̃_s e^{−κz} misstate the exact Gouy–Chapman potential at κz = {{kz}}? (Give (exact − linear)/exact × 100.)

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Equation (3.15): the linear theory overshoots near a highly charged wall (negative error) and undershoots far away (positive), because nonlinear screening is stronger close in

problems.prompt: Far from a wall at ψ̃_s = {{ps}}, the Gouy–Chapman profile looks like ψ̃_eff e^{−κz}. What is ψ̃_eff?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: The effective potential saturates at 4 (about 100 mV): beyond that, extra surface charge is invisible from far away

problems.prompt: Between two identical plates in {{c}} M 1:1 salt at 25 °C, the reduced midplane potential is ψ̃_m = {{pm}}. What is the disjoining pressure, in kPa? (e = 1.602 × 10⁻¹⁹ C, k_B = 1.381 × 10⁻²³ J/K, ε₀ = 8.854 × 10⁻¹² F/m, N_A = 6.022 × 10²³)

parts.label: v
parts.explain: At the midplane the field vanishes, so the pressure is just the excess osmotic pressure of the ions there (3.25): the mutual repulsion is an osmotic effect

problems.prompt: Two plates in {{c}} M 1:1 salt at 25 °C repel with a disjoining pressure of {{P}} kPa. What is the reduced midplane potential ψ̃_m? (e = 1.602 × 10⁻¹⁹ C, k_B = 1.381 × 10⁻²³ J/K, ε₀ = 8.854 × 10⁻¹² F/m, N_A = 6.022 × 10²³)

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Π = 2ρ₀kT(cosh ψ̃_m − 1): the midplane is a free-standing reservoir excess osmotic pressure

problems.prompt: Two plates at ψ̃_s = {{ps}} face each other at κh = {{kh}} in 1:1 salt. What is the weak-overlap pressure, in units of ρ₀kT?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Each plate alone contributes 4γ e^{−κh/2} at the midplane; doubling it and using cosh ψ̃_m − 1 ≈ ψ̃_m²/2 gives 64γ².

problems.prompt: In the weak-overlap limit, by what factor does the double-layer pressure change when the plates' potential goes from ψ̃_s = {{p1}} to {{p2}} and the gap widens by {{n}} Debye lengths?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Π ≈ 64ρ₀kT γ² e^{−κh}: a fourfold potential rise gains less than the factor e lost per Debye length

problems.prompt: Two plates held at the same low potential approach to κh = {{kh}}. What fraction of its isolated-plate charge does each keep (linear PB)?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: At constant potential the surfaces shed charge as the layers overlap; at constant charge the potential rises instead. Real surfaces regulate in between

problems.prompt: Two plates with fixed (low) surface charge approach to κh = {{kh}}. By what factor has each plate's surface potential risen over its isolated value (linear PB)?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: At constant charge the potential climbs as coth(κh/2); at constant potential the charge falls as tanh(κh/2). Real surfaces regulate between the two

problems.prompt: A sphere of radius {{R}} nm at ψ_s = {{psi}} mV sits in salt with κ⁻¹ = {{kd}} nm (ε = 78.4). What surface charge does the linearised theory give, in μC/cm²? (e = 1.602 × 10⁻¹⁹ C, k_B = 1.381 × 10⁻²³ J/K, ε₀ = 8.854 × 10⁻¹² F/m, N_A = 6.022 × 10²³)

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Curvature adds the 1/R term: small particles need less charge for the same potential, and as κR → ∞ the flat-plate result σ = εε₀κψ_s returns

problems.prompt: A sphere of radius {{R}} nm and a flat plate sit at the same low potential in salt with κ⁻¹ = {{kd}} nm. How many times more charge per area does the sphere carry?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: The Yukawa field of a sphere has an extra 1/r term: small particles need more charge for the same potential

problems.prompt: Two flat surfaces have interaction free energy {{f}} mJ/m² at separation h. What force, in nN, acts between spheres of radii {{R1}} and {{R2}} μm at the same closest separation?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Equations (3.61)–(3.63): valid when the range of the force is small compared with the radii. A sphere near a flat wall (R₂ → ∞) gets 2πR

problems.prompt: Two identical spheres of radius {{R}} μm feel a force of {{F}} nN at closest separation h. What interaction energy per area, in mJ/m², do two flat plates have at the same h?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: F = 2πR_eff W with R_eff = R₁R₂/(R₁ + R₂) = R/2 for equal spheres: the surface-force apparatus reads W this way

problems.prompt: Two spheres of radius {{R}} nm with Hamaker constant {{A}} × 10⁻²⁰ J are {{h}} nm apart (h ≪ R). What is their van der Waals energy, in kT at 25 °C? (e = 1.602 × 10⁻¹⁹ C, k_B = 1.381 × 10⁻²³ J/K, ε₀ = 8.854 × 10⁻¹² F/m, N_A = 6.022 × 10²³)

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Integrating the plate law −A/(12πh²) with Derjaguin's weighting gives −AR/(12h) for equal spheres; DLVO adds the double-layer repulsion to this (3.70)

problems.prompt: Two spheres of radius {{R}} nm have Hamaker constant {{A}} × 10⁻²⁰ J. At what separation, in nm, does their van der Waals energy reach −k_BT at 25 °C (h ≪ R)? (e = 1.602 × 10⁻¹⁹ C, k_B = 1.381 × 10⁻²³ J/K, ε₀ = 8.854 × 10⁻¹² F/m, N_A = 6.022 × 10²³)

parts.label: v
parts.explain: V = −AR/12h for equal spheres: large colloids feel attraction worth kT from tens of nanometres, so the double layer must hold them off

problems.prompt: A particle with ζ = {{z}} mV moves in water (ε = 78.4, η = 0.89 mPa·s) under {{E}} V/cm. Using the {{lim}} limit, what is its speed, in μm/s? (e = 1.602 × 10⁻¹⁹ C, k_B = 1.381 × 10⁻²³ J/K, ε₀ = 8.854 × 10⁻¹² F/m, N_A = 6.022 × 10²³)

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Henry's function f_H(κR) interpolates between 2/3 (Hückel) and 1 (Smoluchowski); both assume the double layer is not polarised by the field

problems.prompt: A large particle (κa ≫ 1) in water (ε = 78.4, η = 0.89 mPa·s) has electrophoretic mobility {{u}} μm·cm/(V·s). What is its zeta potential, in mV (Smoluchowski)? (e = 1.602 × 10⁻¹⁹ C, k_B = 1.381 × 10⁻²³ J/K, ε₀ = 8.854 × 10⁻¹² F/m, N_A = 6.022 × 10²³)

parts.label: v
parts.explain: μ = εε₀ζ/η: 1 μm·cm/(V·s) is about 12.8 mV in water at 25 °C

problems.prompt: A particle of radius {{R}} nm is in salt with Debye length {{kd}} nm. Which limit applies?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Compare the particle with the double layer: a thin layer hugging a big particle behaves like flat-wall electroosmosis seen in reverse

problems.prompt: A particle of radius {{a}} nm sits in salt with κ⁻¹ = {{kd}} nm. Which electrophoresis formula applies?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Compute κa first: thin double layers give Smoluchowski, thick ones Hückel, and Henry's function bridges them

problems.prompt: A doped semiconductor has carrier density {{N}} × 10²⁴ m⁻³ and effective mass {{mr}} m_e. What is its Fermi temperature, in K? (ħ = 1.0546 × 10⁻³⁴ J·s, m_e = 9.109 × 10⁻³¹ kg, k_B = 1.381 × 10⁻²³ J/K)

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Well above T_F the Fermi integral reduces to the Boltzmann exponential (3.78), and the space-charge layer obeys PB; below it, degeneracy matters

problems.prompt: Above what carrier density, in 10²⁴ m⁻³, does the Fermi temperature of carriers with effective mass {{mr}} m_e exceed {{TF}} K? (ħ = 1.0546 × 10⁻³⁴ J·s, m_e = 9.109 × 10⁻³¹ kg, k_B = 1.381 × 10⁻²³ J/K)

parts.label: v
parts.explain: k_F = (3π²n)^{1/3}: once T_F ≫ T, Boltzmann statistics (and so PB) no longer describe the carriers

problems.prompt: A fluid has ρĉ(k = 0) = {{rc}}. What is its structure factor S(0) = 1 + ρĥ(0)?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: The OZ convolution becomes a product in k-space (4.5). Dense liquids have large negative ρĉ(0) and small S(0): they are nearly incompressible

problems.prompt: A fluid has structure factor S(0) = {{S0}}. What is ρĉ(k = 0)?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: OZ in Fourier space: S = 1/(1 − ρĉ). Dense liquids have S(0) ≪ 1 and large negative ρĉ(0); near a critical point S(0) blows up

problems.prompt: What is βp/ρ for hard spheres at packing fraction η = {{eta}} from the {{route}}?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: The virial route is 1 + 4ηg(d) with the PY contact value (1 + η/2)/(1 − η)²; the two PY routes disagree, and Carnahan–Starling sits between them, close to simulation

expect.v: 1 + 4*nsimplify(eta)*(1 + nsimplify(eta)/2)/(1 - nsimplify(eta))**2 if w == 0 else ((1 + nsimplify(eta) + nsimplify(eta)**2)/(1 - nsimplify(eta))**3 if w == 1 else (1 + nsimplify(eta) + nsimplify(eta)**2 - nsimplify(eta)**3)/(1 - nsimplify(eta))**3)

problems.prompt: At packing fraction η = {{eta}}, by how much does the Carnahan–Starling βp/ρ exceed the Percus–Yevick virial-route value?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: CS sums the virial series with coefficients n² + 3n and lies between the PY virial (below) and compressibility (above) routes

cases.q: Which closure sets c(r) = −βφ(r) outside the core and g(r) = 0 inside?
Which closure writes c(r) = g(r) − 1 − ln y(r)?
Which closure writes c(r) = f(r)y(r) and gives an analytic solution for hard spheres?
Why does the OZ equation need a closure at all?
cases.o1: It relates two unknown functions, h and c
cases.o2: It has no solution for hard spheres
cases.o4: It only applies to ideal gases

parts.label: v
parts.explain: For electrolytes, HNC handles the long-range Coulomb tail best; MSA gives analytic thermodynamics used later in DFT (section 7.4)

cases.q: Which closure sets c(r) = −βu(r) outside the hard core?
Which closure neglects the bridge function entirely: g = exp(−βu + h − c)?
Which closure gives an analytic solution for hard spheres (Wertheim, Thiele)?
Why does the Ornstein–Zernike equation need a closure?
cases.o1: It is one equation for two unknown functions, h and c
cases.o4: It applies only to ideal gases

parts.label: v
parts.explain: OZ defines c; a closure ties c back to u and h. Charged systems usually take HNC or MSA, hard cores PY

problems.prompt: A solvent modelled as hard spheres of diameter {{d}} nm has number density {{rho}} nm⁻³. What is its packing fraction?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: η is the fraction of space filled; liquids sit near 0.4–0.5 and hard spheres freeze above 0.494

problems.prompt: A hard-sphere solvent model must have packing fraction η = {{eta}} at number density {{rho}} nm⁻³. What diameter, in nm?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Water at 33.4 nm⁻³ with η ≈ 0.4 gives d ≈ 0.28 nm, close to its real size

problems.prompt: A square-well fluid has core diameter d, well width λ = {{lam}} and depth βε = {{be}}. What is B₂ in units of the hard-sphere value 2πd³/3?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: The core adds excluded volume, the well subtracts with weight e^{βε} − 1; B₂ changes sign at the Boyle temperature

problems.prompt: A square-well fluid has well width λ = {{lam}}. At what reduced temperature kT/ε does B₂ vanish (the Boyle temperature)?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Below T_B attraction wins (B₂ < 0); wider wells raise the Boyle temperature

problems.prompt: In reduced van der Waals units, what is p̃ at ρ̃ = {{r}} and T̃ = {{t}}?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Mean-field attraction (−aρ²) on top of a hard-core pressure; below T̃ = 1 the isotherm has a loop, cured by the equal-area rule (5.41)

problems.prompt: In reduced van der Waals units, what is the compressibility factor Z = pv/RT at ρ̃ = {{r}} and T̃ = {{t}}?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Z = 1/(1 − bρ) − aρ/RT, with bρ = ρ̃/3 and aρ/RT = 9ρ̃/8T̃: Z_c = 3/8 at the critical point

problems.prompt: In the Weiss mean-field Ising model at zero field, what is the spontaneous magnetisation m at T/T_c = {{t}}?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: A transcendental equation solved graphically or numerically (figure 5.7); near T_c, m ∝ (1 − T/T_c)^{1/2}, the mean-field exponent β = ½

problems.prompt: Above T_c the mean-field Ising susceptibility follows χ ∝ 1/(T − T_c). By what factor does χ fall when T/T_c rises from {{t1}} to {{t2}}?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Linearise m = tanh((m + h)/t) at small h: m = h/(t − 1). The Curie–Weiss divergence is mean field's γ = 1

problems.prompt: In a hard-sphere fluid at η = {{eta}}, what is the reversible work βW to open a cavity that excludes sphere centres from a radius σ/2?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Small cavities hold at most one centre, so p₀ is exact up to σ/2 (5.71); integrating ρG4πλ² reproduces −ln(1 − η)

problems.prompt: What βp/ρ does scaled-particle theory give for hard spheres at η = {{eta}}?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: SPT reproduces the PY compressibility equation of state; Z = 1 + η ∂(βf_ex)/∂η from the SPT free energy

expect.v: 1 + nsimplify(eta)*diff(-log(1 - Symbol('y')) + 3*Symbol('y')*(2 - Symbol('y'))/(2*(1 - Symbol('y'))**2), Symbol('y')).subs(Symbol('y'), nsimplify(eta))

problems.prompt: Hard rods of length σ on a line have linear density ρσ = {{rs}}. What is βp/ρ?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Exact in 1D: the virial route βp/ρ = 1 + ρσG(σ) with G = (1 − ρσ)⁻¹ (5.102). No phase transition occurs in one dimension

problems.prompt: Hard rods at linear density ρσ = {{rs}}: what is their excess free energy per rod, in kT?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: βf_ex = ∫₀^ρ (Z − 1) dρ'/ρ': each rod loses a fraction ρσ of the line, so the free length is L(1 − ρσ)

problems.prompt: A Lennard-Jones fluid has σ = {{s}} nm. Where does the WCA theory split the potential into repulsive and attractive parts, in nm?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: WCA keeps all the repulsive force in the reference fluid, so the perturbation is smooth; first-order Zwanzig then works well (5.19)

expect.v: Max(*[q for q in solve(diff((nsimplify(s)/x)**12 - (nsimplify(s)/x)**6, x), x) if q.is_positive])

problems.prompt: In the WCA split of a Lennard-Jones potential, what is the repulsive reference u₀(r), in units of ε, at r = {{f}}σ?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: u₀ = u_LJ − u_LJ(r_min) inside r_min = 2^{1/6}σ and zero beyond: purely repulsive, continuous, and close to hard spheres

problems.prompt: An ideal fluid feels an external potential of {{V}} kT at a point. What is its density there relative to the bulk?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: The Euler–Lagrange equation kT ln(Λ³ρ) + V_ext = μ: for point ions with V = zeψ this is the Boltzmann distribution behind Poisson–Boltzmann (7.15)

problems.prompt: An ideal gas at bulk density {{rb}} nm⁻³ meets a wall with a square attractive well of depth {{w}} kT and width {{d}} nm. What is the surface excess, in nm⁻²?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Minimising the ideal functional gives ρ = ρ_b e^{−βV}; the excess is the integral of the enhancement

problems.prompt: Near a wall a species follows ρ(z) = ρ_b(1 + {{A}}e^{−z/λ}) with ρ_b = {{rb}} nm⁻³ and λ = {{lam}} nm. What is its surface excess, in nm⁻²?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Equation (6.57); the Gibbs adsorption sum rule links it to −∂Ω^ex/∂μ (6.79), so DFT gives adsorption two ways that must agree

problems.prompt: A species near a wall follows ρ(z) = ρ_b(1 + {{A}}e^{−(z/λ)²}) with ρ_b = {{rb}} nm⁻³ and λ = {{lam}} nm. What is its surface excess, in nm⁻²?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Γ = ∫(ρ − ρ_b)dz: a depleted layer (A < 0) gives negative adsorption, as for ions at an air–water surface

problems.prompt: At some distance the radial distribution function is g = {{g}}. What is the potential of mean force there, in kJ/mol at 25 °C? (R = 8.314 J/mol·K)

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Fixing one particle as a 'wall' turns the density profile into g(r) (6.72); W includes all the averaged effects of the other molecules

problems.prompt: Two ions have a potential of mean force of {{w}} kJ/mol at some separation, at 25 °C. What is g(r) there? (R = 8.314 J/mol·K)

parts.label: v
parts.explain: g = e^{−βw}: a 5.7 kJ/mol well makes contact pairs ten times more likely than in the bulk

problems.prompt: A wall–vapour excess free energy is {{wv}} mJ/m², the wall–liquid one {{wl}} mJ/m², and the liquid–vapour tension {{g}} mJ/m². What contact angle results, in degrees?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Equation (6.69): c-DFT gives all three excess free energies from density profiles, so solvophilic or solvophobic walls (chapter 10) come out of the model

expect.v: Min(*[q for q in solve(Eq(cos(x*pi/180)*g, wv - wl), x) if q.is_positive])

problems.prompt: A liquid with surface tension {{g}} mJ/m² wets a wall at contact angle {{th}}°. What is the work of adhesion, in mJ/m²?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Young–Dupré: W = γ_lv(1 + cos θ). Mercury on glass (θ ≈ 140°) adheres weakly

problems.prompt: In Thomas–Fermi theory, by what factor does the kinetic-energy density change if the local electron density rises by a factor {{f}}?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: The first orbital-free functional (6.8): kinetic energy written directly as a functional of density, the idea c-DFT inherits

problems.prompt: A fixed number of electrons is compressed into a volume {{f}} times smaller, at uniform density. By what factor does the Thomas–Fermi kinetic energy rise?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: T ∝ ∫ρ^{5/3}dV = N^{5/3}/V^{2/3}: the degeneracy pressure that resists compression

problems.prompt: What is the Bjerrum length in a solvent with ε = {{er}} at 25 °C, in nm? (e = 1.602 × 10⁻¹⁹ C, k_B = 1.381 × 10⁻²³ J/K, ε₀ = 8.854 × 10⁻¹² F/m, N_A = 6.022 × 10²³)

parts.label: v
parts.explain: The distance at which two unit charges interact with kT; in low-ε solvents it is long, and ions pair

problems.prompt: With Bjerrum length {{lb}} nm and a 1:1 salt at {{rho}} ion pairs per nm³, what is the Debye length, in nm?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: κ² = 4πλ_BΣz²ρ is the same screening as in chapter 3, rewritten with the Bjerrum length (equation 7.16 in reduced units)

problems.prompt: A wall with σ = {{s}} μC/cm² faces {{c}} M 1:1 point-ion salt (ε = 78.4, 25 °C). What is the total ion density at contact, in mol/L? (e = 1.602 × 10⁻¹⁹ C, k_B = 1.381 × 10⁻²³ J/K, ε₀ = 8.854 × 10⁻¹² F/m, N_A = 6.022 × 10²³)

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Equation (7.21): the contact density balances the bulk pressure plus the Maxwell stress of the field. The check uses the Grahame surface potential and 2c cosh ψ̃_s, a different route

problems.prompt: At a charged wall in {{c}} M 1:1 point-ion salt (ε = 78.4, 25 °C), the total ion density at contact is {{rc}} M. What is |σ|, in μC/cm²? (e = 1.602 × 10⁻¹⁹ C, k_B = 1.381 × 10⁻²³ J/K, ε₀ = 8.854 × 10⁻¹² F/m, N_A = 6.022 × 10²³)

parts.label: v
parts.explain: kTρ(0) = p_bulk + σ²/2εε₀: the contact density is a direct read-out of the surface charge

problems.prompt: What is the Carnahan–Starling excess free energy per particle, in kT, at packing fraction η = {{eta}}?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Integrating (Z − 1)/η from zero density gives (7.31), the local-density hard-sphere term the first electrolyte DFTs used before FMT

expect.v: integrate(((1 + Symbol('ee') + Symbol('ee')**2 - Symbol('ee')**3)/(1 - Symbol('ee'))**3 - 1)/Symbol('ee'), (Symbol('ee'), 0, nsimplify(eta)))

problems.prompt: What is the Carnahan–Starling excess chemical potential βμ_ex at packing fraction η = {{eta}}?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: μ_ex = f_ex + p_ex/ρ: at η = 0.45 inserting a solvent sphere costs about 11 kT, which is why ions crowd where solvent packs loosely

cases.q: Which FMT weighted density is the local packing fraction?
Which weight function is a delta shell δ(R − |r − r′|)?
cases.o4: None: all FMT weights are smooth

cases.q: What does FMT reproduce exactly for a uniform hard-sphere mixture (Rosenfeld form)?
cases.o1: The Percus–Yevick compressibility equation of state
cases.o3: The virial expansion to all orders

cases.q: Why add tensor weights (White Bear, Tarazona) to Rosenfeld's functional?
cases.o1: To get freezing and strongly confined (0-D) limits right

parts.label: v
parts.explain: FMT builds the excess free energy from a few geometric averages of the density, which is why it handles layering next to walls, the solvent structure chapters 8–13 rely on

cases.q: Which Rosenfeld weighted density is the local packing fraction?
Which FMT weight is a delta function on the sphere's surface?
For a uniform fluid, Rosenfeld's original FMT reproduces which hard-sphere equation of state?
The White Bear versions of FMT were built to reproduce which equation of state?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: FMT builds the hard-sphere free energy from the geometric measures of a sphere: volume, surface, mean curvature and Euler characteristic

problems.prompt: In the restricted primitive model with ion diameter d and κd = {{kd}}, what is Γd from the MSA?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Γ plays the role of κ/2 but includes ion size: for κd ≪ 1, Γd ≈ κd/2; MSA energies feed the electrostatic correlation functionals of section 7.4

problems.prompt: In the restricted primitive model at κd = {{kd}}, what is the ratio of the MSA screening parameter Γ to its Debye–Hückel limit κ/2?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Γ → κ/2 at low concentration; at high κd the finite ion size makes screening weaker than Debye–Hückel predicts

problems.prompt: A surface site binds a cation with dissociation constant K = {{K}} mM. If the cation density at the surface plane is {{rs}} mM, what fraction of sites is bound?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: It is the local density at the wall, not the bulk one, that sets the surface reaction (7.86); that density comes out of the DFT, which is how solvent and ion structure reach the surface charge

problems.prompt: A fraction {{th}} of surface sites is bound when the cation density at the surface plane is {{rs}} mM. What is the dissociation constant, in mM?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Half occupancy at ρ_s = K; the surface density, not the bulk one, enters the law

cases.q: Why does the book treat the solvent as the most important species for EDL structure?
cases.o1: Its density is far greater than the ions', so it dominates packing and layering
cases.o2: It carries most of the charge
cases.o4: It is the only species that reacts with the surface

cases.q: The surface chemical reaction involves only the PDIs. What decides how many PDIs reach the wall?
cases.o1: Every species in the solution, through structure and interactions

cases.q: What does the solution structure couple to in a charge-regulating EDL?
cases.o1: The surface reaction, and hence the surface charge and potential
cases.o3: Nothing: structure and charge are independent

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Chapter 8's conclusion: an accurate surface chemistry and an accurate near-wall solution structure are both needed

problems.prompt: How many water molecules are there per ion in {{c}} M 1:1 salt? (Water: 997 g/L, 18.02 g/mol)

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Even at 1 M there are about 28 water molecules per ion: the solvent sets the packing that the ions must fit into

cases.q: The potential-determining ions are poorly solvated. What happens to a negatively charged regulating surface?
cases.o1: PDI density at the wall rises and the charge is partly neutralised
cases.o4: The surface becomes positive in all cases

cases.q: The potential-determining ions are strongly solvated. What happens to the negative surface charge?
cases.o1: Its magnitude increases, since fewer PDIs reach the wall

cases.q: How do non-PDI ions affect the surface charge?
cases.o1: Indirectly: their local density attracts or repels the PDIs and shifts the surface equilibrium
cases.o2: Directly, by reacting with surface sites

cases.q: Solvent–solvent attraction is weak. What happens near the surface?
cases.o1: The wall layer saturates with solvent and excluded volume expels the PDIs
cases.o2: PDIs accumulate and neutralise the surface
cases.o3: The solvent leaves the wall entirely

cases.q: Solvent–solvent attraction is strong. What happens?
cases.o1: It favours partial neutralisation of the surface by PDIs
cases.o3: It has no effect on charge

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Chapter 9: solvation shifts local densities, and the mass-action law at the surface turns that into a change of charge

problems.prompt: PDIs are at {{rb}} mM in the bulk and bind surface sites with K = {{K}} mM. Packing raises their contact density by a factor g = {{g}}. What fraction of sites is bound?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Poorly solvated PDIs pack at the wall (g > 1) and neutralise more of it; well-solvated ones (g < 1) leave the charge high

cases.q: Glass is hydrophilic toward water. Toward mercury it is…
cases.o1: Solvophobic: wettability depends on the pair of materials

cases.q: Why do non-Coulombic wall interactions change the surface charge?
cases.o1: PDIs compete with every other species for the finite space at the wall
cases.o3: They change the solvent's dielectric constant everywhere
cases.o4: They don't: only Coulomb forces matter

cases.q: Non-Coulombic attraction between ions and the wall mainly changes…
cases.o1: Adsorption, and so the Stern-layer composition
cases.o4: The solvent's density far from the wall

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Chapter 10: the wall–liquid interaction energy is a material property that also sets wetting and contact angles

problems.prompt: A liquid has γ_lv = {{g}} mJ/m² and wets a wall with W_adh = {{W}} mJ/m². What contact angle results, in degrees?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Stronger wall–liquid attraction raises W and lowers θ; W ≥ 2γ means complete wetting, as for a solvophilic wall

cases.q: How does the book get the potential profile from c-DFT?
cases.o1: Feed the DFT fluid charge density into Poisson's equation (1.8)
cases.o2: Solve Poisson–Boltzmann with a corrected κ

cases.q: Which classical quantities does the molecular charge profile give an interpretation to?
cases.o1: The Helmholtz planes, the Stern and Grahame layers, and the plane of shear

cases.q: Compared with Poisson–Boltzmann, what does the molecular potential profile show near the wall?
cases.o1: Structure (oscillations, layer-by-layer features) from solvent and ion packing
cases.o4: A discontinuity at the Debye length

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Chapter 11: once the charge density is known in molecular detail, Poisson's equation alone gives the potential; no Boltzmann closure is needed

problems.prompt: A Stern layer of {{CH}} μF/cm² sits in series with a diffuse layer in {{c}} M 1:1 salt at low potential (ε = 78.4, 25 °C). What is the total capacitance, in μF/cm²? (e = 1.602 × 10⁻¹⁹ C, k_B = 1.381 × 10⁻²³ J/K, ε₀ = 8.854 × 10⁻¹² F/m, N_A = 6.022 × 10²³)

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Capacitors in series: the smaller one dominates. At low salt the diffuse layer limits; at high salt the Stern (Helmholtz) layer does

cases.q: Why do EDL properties depend on which specific ions are present, not just ionic strength?
cases.o1: Ions differ in charge, size and non-Coulombic interactions with solvent, wall and each other
cases.o4: Only valence enters PB, so they don't

cases.q: Multivalent counterions in a double layer typically…
cases.o1: Screen and neutralise the surface charge far more effectively than monovalent ones
cases.o2: Have no effect beyond ionic strength

cases.q: Which classic empirical rule reflects the strong effect of counterion valence on colloid stability?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Chapter 12: valence sets Coulomb interaction strength, and its interplay with excluded volume and solvation shapes the profiles

problems.prompt: At a wall with reduced potential |ψ̃_s| = {{ps}}, by what factor is a {{z}}-valent counterion more enriched at contact than a monovalent one at the same bulk concentration (Boltzmann)?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Enrichment e^{z|ψ̃|} rises steeply with valence: multivalent counterions take over the wall even when they are minor in the bulk

cases.q: According to chapter 13, what mainly drives ion-size effects in the EDL?
cases.o1: Excluded volume and packing constraints near the charged wall
cases.o2: Changes in the bulk dielectric constant

cases.q: How do ion-size effects reach the surface charge?
cases.o1: They change the local density of the PDIs at the regulating surface
cases.o2: They change the number of surface sites
cases.o3: They change the surface pKa directly

cases.q: What nonphysical result does ignoring ion size in PB give near a highly charged wall?
cases.o1: Counterion densities far above close packing

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Chapter 13: size is another non-Coulombic effect, and it couples to the charge regulation reaction through packing

problems.prompt: PB puts counterions at c_b e^{ψ̃} at a wall. For c_b = {{c}} M and |ψ̃_s| = {{ps}}, how many times the simple-cubic close-packed concentration of {{d}} nm ions is that?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Values above 1 are impossible: point-ion PB overfills the wall, which is what excluded-volume theories correct

problems.prompt: A Monte Carlo trial move changes the energy by {{dU}} kT. With what probability is it accepted?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Downhill moves are always taken; uphill ones with the Boltzmann weight, which samples the canonical ensemble

problems.prompt: Half of the trial moves raise the energy by {{a}} kT and half lower it by {{a}} kT. What is the average Metropolis acceptance rate?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Downhill moves always pass; uphill ones pass with e^{−βΔU}. Step sizes are tuned for a rate near 30–50%

problems.prompt: Random test-particle insertions give ⟨e^{−βΔU}⟩ = {{w}}. What is βμ_ex?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: The potential distribution theorem (14.23); in an inhomogeneous fluid ln ρ(z) − ln⟨e^{−βU_t}⟩ must be constant, a check on any simulation

problems.prompt: A point test particle (zero size) is inserted into a hard-sphere fluid at η = {{eta}}. What is its βμ_ex?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: ⟨e^{−βΔU}⟩ is just the free-volume fraction 1 − η: the Widom estimate fails at high density because almost every insertion overlaps

problems.prompt: Two hard spheres with contact distance σ = {{s}} are {{r}} apart along x and approach head-on with relative speed {{v}} (consistent units). When do they collide?

parts.label: y
parts.explain: Event-driven MD jumps straight from collision to collision, solving this quadratic for every approaching pair

expect.y: Min(*[t for t in solve(Eq((nsimplify(r) - nsimplify(v)*x)**2, s**2), x) if t > 0])

problems.prompt: Two hard spheres with contact distance σ = {{s}} are {{dx}} apart along x and {{dy}} along y. They approach along x with relative speed {{v}}. When do they collide?

parts.label: r
parts.explain: Solve |r + vt| = σ for the smaller root; an impact parameter above σ means they miss

problems.prompt: A one-component plasma of charge Z = {{Z}} has Wigner–Seitz radius {{a}} nm at {{T}} K (vacuum). What is its coupling parameter Γ? (e = 1.602 × 10⁻¹⁹ C, k_B = 1.381 × 10⁻²³ J/K, ε₀ = 8.854 × 10⁻¹² F/m, N_A = 6.022 × 10²³)

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Γ > 1 means Coulomb energy beats thermal energy and the plasma becomes liquid-like; it crystallises near Γ ≈ 175

problems.prompt: A one-component plasma of charge Z = 1 has number density {{n}} nm⁻³ at {{T}} K (vacuum). What is its coupling parameter Γ? (e = 1.602 × 10⁻¹⁹ C, k_B = 1.381 × 10⁻²³ J/K, ε₀ = 8.854 × 10⁻¹² F/m, N_A = 6.022 × 10²³)

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Γ = l_B/a with a the Wigner–Seitz radius: Γ ≫ 1 means strongly coupled, where mean-field (PB) theory fails

problems.prompt: What is the mean activity coefficient of a {{zp}}:{{zm}} salt at ionic strength {{I}} M in water at 25 °C (limiting law)?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Simulations of the restricted primitive model test where this limiting law fails, typically above a few mM for 2:2 salts

problems.prompt: What is the ionic strength, in M, of a {{c}} M solution of {{salt}}?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: I = ½Σc_iz_i²: a 2:2 salt has four times the ionic strength of a 1:1 salt at the same molarity

problems.prompt: A Picard iteration has x^k = {{xk}} and g(x^k) = {{g}}. With mixing parameter α = {{a}}, what is x^{k+1}?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Small α trades speed for stability; strongly coupled Poisson and Euler–Lagrange equations often need α of a few percent, which is why Newton methods win (16.1.3)

problems.prompt: A Picard map is linear, g(x) = {{s}}x + {{b}}. What mixing parameter α makes the damped iteration x ← (1 − α)x + αg(x) converge in one step?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: The error shrinks by |1 − α + αs| per step; strongly negative slopes (oscillating maps) need small α

problems.prompt: To find ψ̃ with 2 sinh(ψ̃/2) = {{s}} (Grahame, reduced), take one Newton step from ψ̃₀ = {{p0}}. What is ψ̃₁?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Newton converges quadratically near the root; in c-DFT the Jacobian couples densities, potential and nonlocal weighted densities (16.17–16.22)

problems.prompt: Newton's method solves 2 sinh(ψ̃/2) = {{s}}. What root does it converge to?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: ψ̃ = 2 asinh(s/2): a closed form exists here, which is how a Newton solver is tested before it meets a problem without one

problems.prompt: For [[{{a}}, {{b}}], [{{c}}, {{d}}]]·[x₁, x₂] = [{{p}}, {{q}}], eliminate x₁ with the Schur complement. What is x₂?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: The book's real-space Newton solver splits off the density unknowns this way and solves the smaller Schur system with GMRES (16.24–16.26)

problems.prompt: For [[{{a}}, {{b}}], [{{c}}, {{d}}]]·[x₁, x₂] = [{{p}}, {{q}}], after finding x₂ from the Schur complement, back-substitute. What is x₁?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: x₁ = (p − b x₂)/a: in coupled DFT solvers the Poisson block is eliminated the same way

problems.prompt: An ion of charge number {{z}} (D = {{D}} × 10⁻⁹ m²/s) has local concentration {{c}} mol/m³, gradient {{dc}} mol/m⁴ and reduced potential gradient dψ̃/dx = {{dp}} m⁻¹. What is its flux, in μmol/(m²·s)?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Flux follows the gradient of the electrochemical potential, J = −(Dc/kT)∇(μ + zeψ) (16.3), which for an ideal solution splits into diffusion and migration

problems.prompt: An ion of charge number {{z}} at {{c}} mol/m³ sits where dψ̃/dx = {{dp}} m⁻¹. What concentration gradient, in mol/m⁴, makes its Nernst–Planck flux zero?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Zero flux means diffusion balances migration: the Boltzmann profile c ∝ e^{−zψ̃}, the equilibrium PB assumes

problems.prompt: Two well-mixed tanks of {{V}} L each are in series with flow {{qf}} L/min. Both start with clean water; at t = 0 the feed to tank 1 switches to {{c0}} g/L.

parts.label: tau
parts.explain: τ = V/q: each tank is a first-order lag

parts.ask: Concentration in tank 1 at t = {{T}} min (g/L)
parts.label: ca
parts.explain: c₁ = c₀(1 − e^(−t/τ))

parts.ask: Concentration in tank 2 at t = {{T}} min (g/L)
parts.label: cb

problems.prompt: A cylindrical pipe wall (k = {{kc}} W/m·K, length {{Lp}} m) runs from r = {{ri}} cm to {{ro}} cm with a temperature drop of {{dT}} K across it. What heat flows through it, in W?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Q = −k·(2πrL)·dT/dr is the same at every r: 2πkLΔT/ln(r_o/r_i)

problems.prompt: Compute ∇·(r^{{n}} e_r) at r = {{r0}} in {{geo}} coordinates.

parts.label: v
parts.explain: r^n e_r is r^(n−1) times the position vector; its Cartesian divergence matches (1/r)(r·rⁿ)′ or (1/r²)(r²·rⁿ)′

problems.prompt: A steady radial flux F(r) e_r has zero divergence in a {{geo}} geometry. It is {{F1}} at r = {{r1}}. What is it at r = {{r2}}?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Zero divergence means r·F (cylinder) or r²·F (sphere) is constant: the same total flow spreads over more area

problems.prompt: Two point charges of ${{q1}}$ µC and ${{q2}}$ µC are ${{r}}$ m apart. What is the magnitude of the force between them, in N? ($k = 8.99 \times 10^9$ N·m²/C².)

parts.label: r2
parts.explain: $F = \dfrac{kq_1q_2}{r^2}$. Microcoulombs squared give $10^{-12}$, so the answer is $8.99 \times 10^{-3}\,q_1q_2/r^2$ with the charges in µC. Halving the distance quadruples the force

problems.prompt: What is the electric field ${{r}}$ m from a point charge of ${{q}}$ nC, in N/C? ($k = 8.99 \times 10^9$.)

parts.label: r2
parts.explain: $E = \dfrac{kq}{r^2}$; with $q$ in nC, $kq = 8.99q$ N·m²/C. The field is the force per unit charge and points away from a positive charge

problems.prompt: What is the electric potential ${{r}}$ m from a point charge of ${{q}}$ nC, in volts, taking $V = 0$ far away?

parts.label: r2
parts.explain: $V = \dfrac{kq}{r}$: one power of $r$, not two, and a scalar, so potentials from several charges simply add

problems.prompt: Two parallel plates ${{d}}$ mm apart have ${{V}}$ V across them. What is the field between them, in V/m?

parts.label: r2
parts.explain: $E = V/d$ for a uniform field. A volt per metre is the same thing as a newton per coulomb

problems.prompt: How much energy is stored in a ${{C}}$ µF capacitor charged to ${{V}}$ V, in mJ?

parts.label: r2
parts.explain: $U = \tfrac12CV^2$, which is also $\tfrac12QV$: the average voltage while charging is half the final one

problems.prompt: Capacitors of ${{C1}}$ µF and ${{C2}}$ µF are connected in {{ser == 1 ? "series" : "parallel"}}. What is the equivalent capacitance, in µF?

parts.label: r2
parts.explain: Capacitors combine the opposite way to resistors: they add in parallel (more plate area) and combine as product over sum in series (a wider gap)

expect.r2: 1/(Rational(1, C1) + Rational(1, C2)) if ser == 1 else C1 + C2

problems.prompt: Resistors of ${{R1}}$ Ω and ${{R2}}$ Ω are connected in {{ser == 1 ? "series" : "parallel"}}. What is the equivalent resistance, in Ω?

parts.label: r2
parts.explain: Series adds. Parallel is product over sum and is always less than the smaller resistor, because a second path can only make it easier for current to flow

expect.r2: R1 + R2 if ser == 1 else 1/(Rational(1, R1) + Rational(1, R2))

problems.prompt: What power does a ${{R}}$ Ω resistor dissipate with ${{V}}$ V across it, in watts?

parts.label: r2
parts.explain: $P = IV = \dfrac{V^2}{R} = I^2R$. Pick the form that uses what you are given

problems.prompt: What is the time constant of a ${{R}}$ kΩ resistor with a ${{C}}$ µF capacitor, in ms?

parts.label: r2
parts.explain: $\tau = RC$, and kΩ times µF is ms. After one time constant a charging capacitor has reached 63%; after five it is done for practical purposes

problems.prompt: A discharging capacitor has been going for ${{n}}$ time constant{{n > 1 ? "s" : ""}}. What fraction of its initial voltage remains?

parts.label: r2
parts.explain: $V = V_0e^{-t/\tau}$: 37% after one, 14% after two, 5% after three, under 1% after five

problems.prompt: A proton ($e = 1.60 \times 10^{-19}$ C) moves at ${{v}} \times 10^6$ m/s at ${{th}}^\circ$ to a ${{B}}$ T field. What is the force on it, in units of $10^{-13}$ N?

parts.label: r2
parts.explain: $F = qvB\sin\theta$. The force is perpendicular to both the velocity and the field, so it turns the particle without changing its speed

problems.prompt: A charged particle circles in a magnetic field. Its speed is multiplied by ${{fv}}$ and the field by ${{fB}}$. By what factor does the radius of its path change?

parts.label: r2
parts.explain: $qvB = \dfrac{mv^2}{r}$ gives $r = \dfrac{mv}{qB}$: faster or heavier means a wider circle, a stronger field a tighter one. The period, $2\pi m/qB$, does not depend on speed at all, which is what makes a cyclotron work

problems.prompt: What is the magnetic field ${{r}}$ cm from a long straight wire carrying ${{I}}$ A, in µT? ($\mu_0 = 4\pi \times 10^{-7}$ T·m/A.)

parts.label: r2
parts.explain: $B = \dfrac{\mu_0I}{2\pi r} = 2 \times 10^{-7}\,\dfrac{I}{r}$. It falls as $1/r$, not $1/r^2$, and circles the wire by the right-hand rule. For scale, the Earth's field is about 50 µT

problems.prompt: A solenoid has ${{N}}$ turns over ${{L}}$ cm and carries ${{I}}$ A. What is the field inside, in mT?

parts.label: r2
parts.explain: $B = \mu_0nI$ with $n$ the turns per metre. It is uniform inside and does not depend on the radius

problems.prompt: The field through a ${{N}}$-turn coil of area ${{A}}$ cm² changes by ${{dB}}$ T in ${{dt}}$ s. What is the average emf, in volts?

parts.label: r2
parts.explain: $\mathcal{E} = N\dfrac{\Delta\Phi}{\Delta t}$ with $\Phi = BA$. What matters is how fast the flux changes; Lenz's law says the induced current opposes that change

the north pole of a magnet moves away from a loop
the field through a loop is increasing
a loop is pulled out of a field region

problems.prompt: What does the induced current in the loop do when {{q}}?

parts.label: a
choice: Opposes the applied field: the loop repels the change
Points the same way as the applied field: the loop tries to keep the flux it had
parts.explain: Lenz's law: the induced current opposes the change in flux, not the flux. Growing flux is opposed; shrinking flux is propped up. It is energy conservation: otherwise the change would feed itself

problems.prompt: A closed surface encloses a net charge of ${{q}}$ nC. What is the electric flux through it, in N·m²/C? ($\varepsilon_0 = 8.85 \times 10^{-12}$.)

parts.label: r2
parts.explain: $\Phi = Q_{enc}/\varepsilon_0$, whatever the shape or size of the surface and wherever the charge sits inside it. Charges outside contribute nothing

problems.prompt: An electromagnetic wave has a peak electric field of ${{E}}$ V/m. What is its peak magnetic field, in µT? ($c = 3.00 \times 10^8$ m/s.)

parts.label: r2
parts.explain: $E = cB$. The magnetic field of a light wave looks tiny in tesla only because of the units; the two fields carry equal energy

problems.prompt: In an LC circuit the inductance is multiplied by ${{fL}}$ and the capacitance by ${{fC}}$. By what factor does the resonant frequency change?

parts.label: r2
parts.explain: $f = \dfrac{1}{2\pi\sqrt{LC}}$: the electrical twin of $\sqrt{k/m}$ for a mass on a spring, with $L$ playing mass and $1/C$ playing stiffness

parts.label: v

problems.prompt: z has modulus {{kr}} and argument {{kd}}°. Find the real part of z^{{kn}}.

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Each step multiplies by 1 + hk, so n steps give (1 + hk)ⁿ, against the exact e^(nhk)

problems.prompt: For {{ka}}y dx + x dy = 0, (M_y − N_x)/N depends on x alone. Find the integrating factor μ(x), normalised to μ(1) = 1, at x = 2.

No guarantee at all (f is not continuous there)

problems.prompt: A {{km}} kg mass on a {{kk}} N/m spring starts at y = {{k0}} m with speed {{kv}} m/s. Find the amplitude of the motion, in m.

problems.prompt: A {{km}} kg mass hangs on a {{kk}} N/m spring. What damping constant c makes it critically damped?

problems.prompt: A {{km}} kg mass on a {{kk}} N/m spring is driven sinusoidally. Above what damping constant c does the amplitude curve lose its resonance peak?

problems.prompt: A series RLC circuit has L = {{kl}} H and C = {{kf}} F. What resistance makes it critically damped, in Ω?

problems.prompt: Find the Wronskian of e^({{ka}}x), e^({{kb}}x) and e^({{kg}}x) at x = 0.

problems.prompt: In A → B → C with rate constants k₁ = {{k1}} and k₂ = {{k2}} per minute, starting from pure A, when is the amount of B largest?

parts.label: v

problems.prompt: (x² − {{ks}})y″ + xy′ + y = 0. Where is its positive singular point?

parts.label: y
parts.explain: Kepler's third law from gravity: $T = 2\pi\sqrt{a^3/GM}$. The orbiting mass drops out, so a satellite and the Moon at the same radius would share a period

parts.label: y
parts.explain: Kinetic energy must cover the gravitational well: ½v² = GM/R, so $v = \sqrt{2GM/R}$, √2 times the speed of a circular orbit at the surface

problems.prompt: {{star}} has a surface temperature of about {{T}} K. At what wavelength (nm) does its spectrum peak?

parts.label: y
parts.explain: Wien's law: $\lambda_{\max} = b/T$ with $b = 2.898\times10^{-3}$ m·K. Hot stars peak in the blue or UV, cool ones in the red or IR, which is how colour gives temperature

problems.prompt: Find the luminosity of {{star}} (radius {{Rs}} m, T = {{T}} K) in units of the Sun's, L☉ = 3.828×10²⁶ W.

parts.label: y
parts.explain: Stefan–Boltzmann over the whole surface: $L = 4\pi R^2\sigma T^4$. Temperature enters to the fourth power, so a small hot star can outshine a big cool one

problems.prompt: If luminosity scales as M³·⁵, how long does a {{M}} M☉ star live on the main sequence, relative to the Sun?

parts.label: y
parts.explain: Lifetime ∝ fuel ÷ burn rate ∝ M/L ∝ M/M³·⁵ = M⁻²·⁵. Massive stars live millions of years, not billions; red dwarfs outlast the present age of the universe

parts.label: y

problems.prompt: Where were {{k}} made?

parts.label: y
choice: neutron capture in AGB stars, supernovae and mergers
parts.explain: Big Bang: H, He, a little Li. Stars fuse up to Fe. Beyond iron, neutron capture: slow (s) in AGB stars, rapid (r) in supernovae and neutron-star mergers. Li, Be and B are mostly from cosmic rays splitting heavier nuclei

problems.prompt: What kind of plate boundary is {{k}}?

parts.label: y

problems.prompt: A mineral holds radiogenic daughter and parent in the ratio D/P = {{ratio}} for {{iso}}, with no daughter at the start. How old is it (years)?

parts.label: y

problems.prompt: What is the radiative-equilibrium temperature (K) of {{planet}}: solar constant {{S}} W/m², albedo {{alb}}, no greenhouse effect?

parts.label: y
parts.explain: Absorbed S(1 − α)πR² equals emitted 4πR²σT⁴, so $T_e = [S(1-\alpha)/4\sigma]^{1/4}$. Earth's 255 K against an actual 288 K is the 33 K greenhouse effect; Venus's 230 K against 735 K is a runaway one

problems.prompt: Model {{planet}} (S = {{S}} W/m², albedo {{alb}}) with one atmospheric layer that absorbs all infrared and is transparent to sunlight. What is the surface temperature (K)?

parts.label: y
parts.explain: The layer radiates σT_a⁴ both up and down; balancing the top gives T_a = T_e, balancing the layer gives σT_s⁴ = 2σT_a⁴, so $T_s = 2^{1/4}T_e$. Too warm for Earth (303 K), because the real atmosphere absorbs only part of the infrared

problems.prompt: With radiative forcing ΔF = 5.35 ln(C/C₀) W/m² and climate sensitivity λ = {{lam}} K per W/m², how much warming (K) does CO₂ at {{C1}} ppm give relative to {{C0}} ppm, at equilibrium?

parts.label: y
parts.explain: Forcing grows with the logarithm of concentration, so each doubling adds the same 3.7 W/m². ΔT = λΔF; λ ≈ 0.8 gives about 3 K per doubling, the middle of the IPCC range

problems.prompt: How many gigatonnes of carbon correspond to {{ppm}} ppm of CO₂ in the atmosphere (air mass 5.148×10¹⁸ kg, 28.97 g/mol)?

parts.label: y
parts.explain: Moles of air × mole fraction × 12.011 g/mol: about 2.13 GtC per ppm. Fossil emissions of ~10 GtC per year would add ~4.7 ppm if it all stayed; about half does

problems.prompt: A population or a resource demand grows {{pct}}% a year. How many years does it take to double?

parts.explain: (1 + r)ᵗ = 2, so t = ln 2 / ln(1 + r) ≈ 70/(percent growth): the rule of 70. Steady growth means each doubling consumes as much as all the history before it

problems.prompt: Cost of goods sold was {{cogs}}; inventory was {{inv0}} at the start of the year and {{inv1}} at the end. On average, how many days is inventory held (365-day year)?

problems.prompt: Net income was {{ni}}. Preferred dividends declared were {{pref}}, and weighted-average common shares outstanding were {{sh}}. What is basic EPS?

problems.prompt: Year-end receivables are {{ar}}, and {{rate*100}}% is expected to be uncollectible. Before adjusting, the allowance has a {{old}} {{side == 0 ? "credit" : "debit"}} balance. What is bad debt expense for the year?

problems.prompt: Receivables are aged: {{c1}} current ({{r1*100}}% expected to be uncollectible), {{c2}} 31–90 days ({{r2*100}}%), and {{c3}} over 90 days ({{r3*100}}%). What should the allowance for doubtful accounts be?

problems.prompt: Beginning inventory: {{q1}} units at {{k1}}. Purchases: {{q2}} at {{k2}}, then {{q3}} at {{k3}}. {{sold}} units were sold. What is ending inventory under periodic {{m == 0 ? "FIFO" : (m == 1 ? "LIFO" : "weighted average")}}?

problems.prompt: A FIFO company holds {{n}} units that cost {{cost}} each. They sell for {{price}} each, with selling costs of {{sell}} each. At what total amount are they carried?

problems.prompt: Inventory was destroyed in a fire. Beginning inventory was {{bi}}, purchases {{pur}}, sales {{sales}}, and the usual gross margin is {{gm*100}}% of sales. Estimate the inventory lost.

parts.label: a
parts.explain: Goods available − estimated cost of goods sold, where COGS = sales × (1 − gross margin). Used for insurance claims and interim estimates, never for annual statements

problems.prompt: Equipment costs {{cost}}, has a salvage value of {{cost*sv}} and a {{life}}-year life. What is annual straight-line depreciation?

parts.label: a
parts.explain: Straight line spreads the depreciable base (cost − salvage) evenly over the life

problems.prompt: Equipment costs {{cost}}, has a salvage value of {{cost*sv}} and a {{life}}-year life. What is double-declining-balance depreciation in year 2?

parts.label: a
parts.explain: DDB applies twice the straight-line rate (2 ÷ life) to the book value at the start of each year, ignoring salvage until book value would fall below it. Year 1 = cost × 2/n; year 2 = (cost − year 1) × 2/n

problems.prompt: Equipment costs {{cost}}, has a salvage value of {{cost*sv}} and a {{life}}-year life. What is sum-of-the-years'-digits depreciation in year {{yr}}?

parts.label: a
parts.explain: SYD multiplies the depreciable base by (remaining life at the start of the year) ÷ (1 + 2 + … + n). For a 5-year life the fractions are 5/15, 4/15, 3/15, 2/15, 1/15

problems.prompt: A machine that cost {{cost}}, with accumulated depreciation of {{acc}}, is sold for {{proc}}. What is the gain (positive) or loss (negative)?

parts.label: a
parts.explain: Proceeds − book value, where book value = cost − accumulated depreciation (brought up to the date of sale first)

problems.prompt: An asset cost {{cost}}, no salvage, and has been depreciated straight-line over a {{life}}-year life for {{used}} years. Management now expects it to last {{rem}} more years. What is depreciation for the current year?

parts.label: a
parts.explain: A change in estimate is prospective: no restatement. Spread the remaining book value over the remaining life from now on

problems.prompt: While building its own warehouse, a company's weighted-average accumulated expenditures were {{waae}}. The applicable interest rate is {{rate*100}}%, and actual interest incurred in the year was {{actual}}. How much interest is capitalized?

parts.label: a
parts.explain: Capitalize avoidable interest (weighted-average accumulated expenditures × rate), but never more than the interest actually incurred

problems.prompt: A reporting unit carries goodwill of {{gw}}. Its total carrying amount is {{carry}} and its fair value is {{fv}}. What goodwill impairment loss is recognized?

parts.label: a
parts.explain: Goodwill is not amortized (except under the private-company alternative); it is tested for impairment. The loss is the excess of the unit's carrying amount over its fair value, capped at the goodwill itself

30% of another company's voting stock, giving significant influence

problems.prompt: How are {{s}} measured after purchase?

parts.label: a
choice: Fair value, changes through net income
Fair value, unrealized changes through other comprehensive income
parts.explain: Debt securities: trading (FV-NI), available for sale (FV-OCI), held to maturity (amortized cost). Equity securities are at fair value through net income unless the investor has significant influence (about 20–50%, equity method) or control (consolidate)

problems.prompt: An investor pays {{cost}} for {{pct*100}}% of a company and gains significant influence. That year the investee earns {{nii}} and pays {{div}} in dividends. What is the investment's carrying amount at year end?

parts.label: a
parts.explain: Under the equity method the investment rises by the investor's share of income (recognized as income) and falls by its share of dividends (a return of investment, not income)

problems.prompt: A {{prin}} note payable at {{rate*100}}% annual interest was signed {{mo}} months before year end; interest is paid at maturity. How much interest is accrued at year end?

parts.label: a
parts.explain: Principal × annual rate × fraction of the year elapsed. The accrual records the expense in the period it is incurred, before any cash is paid

problems.prompt: A company issues 100,000 of bonds paying {{cr*100}}% interest annually for {{n}} years, when the market rate is {{mr*100}}%. What do the bonds sell for?

parts.label: a
parts.explain: Price = present value of the face amount + present value of the coupon annuity, both at the market rate. Coupon above market → premium; below → discount

problems.prompt: Bonds with a 100,000 face pay {{cr*100}}% annually. Their carrying amount at the start of the year is {{carry}}, and the market rate at issue was {{mr*100}}%. Under the effective interest method, by how much does the carrying amount change this year (increase positive)?

parts.label: a
parts.explain: Interest expense = carrying amount × market rate at issue; cash paid = face × coupon rate. The difference amortizes the discount (carrying amount rises toward face) or the premium (it falls toward face)

problems.prompt: A company with {{sh}} shares outstanding ({{par}} par) declares a {{pct*100}}% stock dividend when the market price is {{mp}}. By how much does retained earnings fall?

parts.label: a
parts.explain: A small stock dividend (under about 20–25%) is recorded at the shares' fair value; a large one at par. Total equity does not change: retained earnings move into common stock and paid-in capital

problems.prompt: Retained earnings started the year at {{re0}}. Net {{ni > 0 ? "income" : "loss"}} was {{abs(ni)}}, cash dividends declared were {{div}}{{ppa == 0 ? "" : ", and an error from a prior year required a correction"}}{{ppa == 0 ? "" : (ppa > 0 ? " increasing" : " decreasing")}}{{ppa == 0 ? "" : " opening retained earnings by "}}{{ppa == 0 ? "" : abs(ppa)}}. What is ending retained earnings?

parts.label: a
parts.explain: Opening balance, adjusted for any prior-period error correction (net of tax), plus net income, minus dividends declared. Error corrections go straight to opening retained earnings, never through current income

problems.prompt: How is {{s}} reported?

parts.label: a
choice: Change in principle: retrospective, prior periods recast
Change in estimate: prospective, current and future periods only
Error correction: restate prior periods, adjust opening retained earnings
parts.explain: Principles are applied retrospectively so periods are comparable; estimates change prospectively because new information does not make the old estimate wrong. A change in depreciation method is a change in estimate effected by a change in principle, so it is prospective. Errors are restatements

problems.prompt: Under US GAAP, what does a company do when {{s}}?

parts.label: a
choice: Accrue the loss and disclose it
Accrue the low end of the range and disclose the range
Nothing until it is realized (disclosure allowed, without misleading)
parts.explain: Accrue a loss contingency only when probable and reasonably estimable; within a range accrue the best estimate, or the minimum if none is better. Reasonably possible losses are disclosed; remote ones are not, except guarantees. Gain contingencies are not recognized until realized

identify the performance obligations
determine the transaction price
allocate the transaction price to the performance obligations

problems.prompt: In the five-step revenue model (ASC 606), what step comes right after: {{s}}?

parts.label: a
choice: Allocate the price to the performance obligations
Recognize revenue when (or as) each obligation is satisfied
parts.explain: Contract → performance obligations (distinct goods or services) → transaction price (including variable consideration, constrained) → allocate by relative standalone selling price → recognize at a point in time or over time as control transfers

problems.prompt: A phone and a one-year service plan are sold together for {{price}}. Sold separately, the phone goes for {{s1}} and the plan for {{s2}}. How much of the price is allocated to the phone?

parts.label: a
parts.explain: Allocate the transaction price in proportion to standalone selling prices: price × s1 ÷ (s1 + s2). The phone's share is recognized at delivery; the plan's over the year

problems.prompt: A contract's bonus depends on results: {{v1}} with probability {{p1}}, {{v2}} with probability {{p2}}, {{v3}} with probability {{p3}}. Using the expected value method (before any constraint), what variable consideration is estimated?

parts.label: a
parts.explain: Expected value = Σ probability × amount, suited to many similar contracts; the most likely amount suits two or so outcomes. Either way, include it only to the extent a significant reversal is not probable (the constraint)

problems.prompt: A 1,000,000 construction contract recognizes revenue over time by costs incurred. By the end of year 2, costs to date are {{cc}} and total costs are now estimated at 800,000. Revenue recognized in year 1 was {{r1}}. How much revenue is recognized in year 2?

parts.label: a
parts.explain: Cumulative revenue = (costs to date ÷ estimated total costs) × contract price; this year's revenue is cumulative revenue minus what earlier years already recognized. A change in total estimated cost is a change in estimate, caught up in the current year

cases.s: faster depreciation on the tax return than in the books
installment sales taxed when cash is collected
a warranty expense accrued in the books, deductible when paid

problems.prompt: Is {{s}} a temporary or a permanent difference, and what does it create?

parts.label: a
choice: Temporary: a deferred tax liability (taxable later)
Temporary: a deferred tax asset (deductible later)
parts.explain: Temporary differences reverse: when book income runs ahead of taxable income now (tax deductions sooner, income taxed later) the company owes tax later, a liability; when taxable income runs ahead (expenses deducted later, revenue taxed sooner) it gets a deduction later, an asset. Permanent differences never reverse

problems.prompt: At year end, equipment's book value exceeds its tax basis by {{diff}}. The tax rate is {{rnow*100}}% this year, and the rate enacted for the years when the difference reverses is {{rfut*100}}%. What deferred tax liability is reported?

parts.label: a
parts.explain: Deferred taxes use the enacted rate for the years the difference will reverse, not the current rate. Rates that have only been proposed are ignored until enacted

a lawsuit about a year-ago accident is settled after year end for more than was accrued
a warehouse burns down a month after year end

parts.label: a
parts.explain: If the event gives evidence about conditions that existed at the balance-sheet date, adjust. If the condition arose after that date, do not adjust; disclose it when leaving it out would mislead

problems.prompt: In the fair value hierarchy, which level is {{s}}?

parts.label: a
choice: Level 1: quoted price for the identical item in an active market
Level 2: observable inputs other than Level 1 prices
parts.explain: Fair value is an exit price between market participants. The hierarchy ranks inputs, not assets: use the highest level available, and disclose more (including a roll-forward) for Level 3 measurements

problems.prompt: Under ASC 842, a lessee finds that {{s}}. How is the lease classified?

parts.label: a
parts.explain: Any one of five tests makes a finance lease: ownership transfers, a purchase option reasonably certain, a term for the major part of the economic life (about 75%), payments worth substantially all of fair value (about 90%), or a specialized asset. Both classes put a right-of-use asset and a lease liability on the balance sheet; they differ in the expense pattern

problems.prompt: A lease requires {{n}} annual payments of {{pmt}}, each paid at the {{due == 1 ? "start" : "end"}} of the year; the discount rate is {{r*100}}%. What lease liability is recognized at commencement?

parts.label: a
parts.explain: The liability is the present value of the payments not yet made. Payments at the start of each year are an annuity due: worth (1 + r) times the same payments at year end, because each arrives a year sooner

problems.prompt: A not-for-profit receives {{kx}} restricted by the donor to a programme and spends {{ky}} on that programme in the same year. By how much do net assets with donor restrictions rise for the year?

problems.prompt: A public company's consolidated external revenue is {{kx}}. Its reportable segments must together account for at least how much external revenue?

problems.prompt: Under the cash basis a business reports {{kc}} collected from customers. Accounts receivable rose from {{ka}} to {{kb}} during the year. What is revenue on the accrual basis?

parts.label: v

problems.prompt: Weighted-average accumulated expenditures on a self-built asset were {{kw}}. A {{ks}} construction loan carries {{k1}}%, and other debt averages {{k2}}%. Actual interest for the year was higher than the result. How much interest is capitalized?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Use the specific loan's rate up to its amount and the weighted rate of other debt on the rest; the total can never exceed actual interest

problems.prompt: A reporting unit carries goodwill of {{kg}}. Its total carrying amount is {{kc}} and its fair value is {{kf}}. What goodwill remains on the balance sheet after the impairment test?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: The loss is the excess of carrying amount over fair value, but never more than the goodwill itself

problems.prompt: Year-end accrued interest on a {{kr}}% note signed {{km}} months before year end is {{ki}}. What is the note's principal?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Interest = principal × annual rate × months/12, read backwards
