problems.prompt: A vessel carries a corrosion allowance of {{al}} mm at a measured rate of {{rt}} mm a year. What life does the allowance buy (years)?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: A design life follows from allowance over rate, which works only for uniform attack: pitting goes through a wall while the average thickness barely moves, so an allowance is no defence against it

problems.prompt: A {{yr}}-year life at a corrosion rate of {{rt}} mm a year needs what allowance (mm)?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: The reverse: at half a millimetre a year a twenty-five year life needs more than a centimetre of extra steel, which is usually the point at which a better material is cheaper than the thickness

cases.q: Austenitic stainless steel under tensile stress in a hot chloride solution is at risk of:
cases.o1: Stress-corrosion cracking, which needs stress, a susceptible alloy and that environment together

cases.q: Hydrogen service at high temperature and pressure threatens steel through:
cases.o1: Hydrogen attack and embrittlement, which the alloy is selected against

cases.q: Copper is excluded from some service not because it corrodes but because it:
cases.o1: Catalyses decomposition of the fluid or contaminates the product

cases.q: A compatibility chart must be read at:
cases.o1: The service temperature, since ratings change with it

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Compatibility covers cracking, embrittlement, catalysis and contamination, not just dissolution

problems.prompt: A coupon of area {{ar}} cm2 loses {{ml}} mg over {{dy}} days. With a density of {{dn}} g/cm3, what is the corrosion rate (mm/year)?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Mass loss becomes a thickness by dividing by density and area, and a rate by dividing by time; a coupon measures the uniform rate only, so pitting has to be looked for separately

problems.prompt: An inspection finds {{th}} mm of wall lost after {{yr}} years. What rate is that (mm/year), and how long until a further {{rm}} mm goes?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Extrapolating a measured rate is how an inspection interval is set, and it assumes the mechanism and the conditions have not changed since the wall was new

cases.q: Deep isolated holes in an otherwise sound stainless wall indicate:
cases.o1: Pitting, usually initiated by chloride on the passive film

cases.q: Attack concentrated under a gasket and nowhere else indicates:
cases.o1: Crevice corrosion, where the trapped solution cannot be replenished with oxygen

cases.q: Branching cracks in a stressed component with no general thinning indicate:
Thinning concentrated just downstream of an elbow indicates:
cases.o1: Erosion-corrosion, from high velocity and entrained solids

cases.q: Attack confined to where two different metals are bolted together indicates:

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Each mechanism leaves its own geometry, which is why a failure is diagnosed from where the metal went rather than from how much

problems.prompt: A galvanic couple has a cathode of {{ac}} cm2 and an anode of {{aa}} cm2. By what factor is the anode's current density raised over an equal-area couple?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: The cathode sets the total current and the anode carries it over its own area, so a small anode next to a large cathode corrodes fast: a steel bolt in a stainless plate fails, the reverse pairing does not

cases.q: In a couple of carbon steel and 316 stainless in seawater, which corrodes?
cases.o1: The carbon steel, as the less noble member

cases.q: In a couple of zinc and steel, which corrodes?
cases.o1: The zinc, which is why it is used as a sacrificial anode

cases.q: Galvanic attack needs:
cases.o1: Two different metals, an electrolyte and an electrical connection

cases.q: Breaking the electrical connection with an insulating gasket:
cases.o1: Stops the galvanic current and so the attack
cases.o4: Changes which metal is the anode

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Less noble corrodes, and the couple needs all three of metals, electrolyte and connection, so removing any one stops it

problems.prompt: A structure of {{ar}} m2 needs a protection current density of {{cd}} mA/m2. What total current is that (A)?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: The duty scales with the exposed area, so coating the structure first and protecting cathodically only the coating holidays is what makes the anode or rectifier small

problems.prompt: A sacrificial anode of {{ms}} kg delivers {{cap}} A-hours per kg at a current of {{cu}} A. How many years does it last?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: An anode's life is its charge capacity over the current drawn, so the replacement interval and the protection duty are the same calculation read two ways

cases.q: A coating with a small holiday is worse than no coating in one respect:
cases.o1: Attack concentrates at the holiday, since the small bare area carries all the current

cases.q: A corrosion inhibitor fails when:
cases.o1: Its concentration falls below what is needed, which can be worse than none if it leaves partial coverage

cases.q: A passive film on stainless steel is broken down by:
cases.o1: Chloride, especially where oxygen cannot reach to repair the film

cases.q: A passive film repairs itself only where:
cases.o1: Oxygen can reach the surface, which is why crevices and deposits are dangerous

cases.q: Cathodic protection makes the protected structure:
cases.o1: The cathode of the cell, so it no longer dissolves

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Each control measure has its own failure mode, and a partly failed barrier concentrates attack rather than halving it

problems.prompt: With a maximum specific growth rate of {{mx}} per hour and a half-saturation constant of {{ks}} g/L, what specific growth rate does a substrate concentration of {{ss}} g/L give (per hour)?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Monod kinetics is Michaelis-Menten for a whole organism: well above the half-saturation constant growth is at its maximum and substrate concentration no longer matters, which is the regime a batch spends most of its time in

problems.prompt: A culture grows at a specific rate of {{mu}} per hour. What is its doubling time (hours)?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Doubling time is the natural logarithm of two over the specific rate, so a culture at 0.4 per hour doubles in under two hours while one at 0.08 takes nearly nine

problems.prompt: A target of {{tt}} g/L of cells at a yield of {{yx}} g cells per g substrate needs how much substrate (g/L), if {{s0}} g/L must be left at the end?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: The yield coefficient converts the target titre into a substrate charge; it leaves out maintenance, so a slow fermentation uses more substrate per gram of product than the coefficient predicts

problems.prompt: A batch consumed {{ds}} g/L of substrate and produced {{dx}} g/L of cells. What yield coefficient is that (g/g)?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Measuring the yield from the batch rather than assuming it is how maintenance and by-product formation show up, as a yield below the theoretical value

problems.prompt: A chemostat of volume {{vv}} L runs on a feed of {{qq}} L/h. What is its dilution rate (per hour), and does it exceed a maximum growth rate of {{mx}} per hour? Give the dilution rate.

parts.label: v
parts.explain: At steady state the specific growth rate equals the dilution rate, so a dilution rate above the maximum growth rate washes the culture out: the highest usable feed rate sits just below it

problems.prompt: What feed rate (L/h) sets a dilution rate of {{fr}} times the maximum growth rate of {{mx}} per hour in a {{vv}} L vessel?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Running near the washout point maximises productivity and minimises the margin for upset, which is why continuous culture is run at a fraction of the maximum rather than at it

problems.prompt: A culture of {{xx}} g/L has a specific oxygen uptake of {{qo}} mmol per g per hour in {{vv}} L. What is the oxygen demand (mmol/h)?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Demand scales with cell mass, so the oxygen a fermentation needs rises through the batch and peaks late: the transfer system is sized for the peak, not the average

problems.prompt: To meet an oxygen demand of {{dm}} mmol/(L h) with a saturation of {{cs}} mmol/L and a dissolved concentration held at {{cl}} mmol/L, what transfer coefficient is needed (per hour)?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Because oxygen's saturation concentration is tiny, the driving force is tiny and the required coefficient is large: oxygen transfer, not kinetics, is usually what limits a fermentation's scale-up

cases.q: A substrate that inhibits growth at high concentration argues for:
cases.o1: Fed-batch, feeding it at the rate the culture consumes it
cases.o2: Batch with the whole charge at the start

cases.q: The highest volumetric productivity, accepting the risks, comes from:

cases.q: The main risks of a long continuous run are:
cases.o1: Contamination and genetic drift of the strain

cases.q: A defined, traceable lot for a regulated product argues for:
Perfusion differs from simple continuous culture by:
cases.o1: Retaining the cells while product is removed

parts.label: v
parts.explain: The mode follows the constraint: inhibition, productivity, contamination risk or lot definition

problems.prompt: A sterilisation must achieve {{nl}} log reductions with a decimal reduction time of {{dv}} minutes. What hold time is needed (minutes)?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Thermal death is first order in viable count, so each decimal reduction time removes a factor of ten and the hold is simply the product; the basis is the probability of a single survivor in the batch

problems.prompt: A starting load of {{n0}} organisms must be brought to a survival probability of 1 in {{pp}}. How many log reductions is that?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: The reductions needed span from the starting load down past one to the accepted survival probability, which is why a pharmaceutical basis asks for twelve logs rather than six

cases.o1: Feedforward on that disturbance, trimmed by feedback
cases.o2: Feedback alone with a higher gain

cases.q: A slow temperature loop whose valve is upset by changing steam pressure argues for:
cases.o1: Cascade, with a fast inner pressure or flow loop inside the temperature loop
