Feedforward alone is risky because:
cases.o1: It corrects only for what it measures and models, and never checks the result
cases.o4: It cannot be combined with feedback

cases.q: Feedback's inherent limitation is that:
cases.o1: It acts only once the output has already moved
cases.o4: It requires a fast inner loop

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Each strategy answers a different question: when the disturbance is known, when the valve is unreliable, and when two streams must track

cases.q: Which action leaves a steady offset after a load change?
Which action removes the offset but can wind up when the valve saturates?
Which action anticipates but amplifies measurement noise?
A noisy flow loop is usually tuned as:
Reset windup is prevented by:
cases.o1: Limiting or freezing the integral while the output is saturated

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Three actions with three costs, and the loop's noise and speed decide which are used

problems.prompt: A proportional-only loop has a loop gain of {{kg}}. What fraction of an unmeasured load change remains as offset?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Offset is the load change over one plus the loop gain, so it falls with gain but never reaches zero; integral action is what removes it, at the cost of lag

problems.prompt: What loop gain reduces a proportional-only offset from {{f1}} to {{f2}} of the load change?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Cutting the offset by a factor of five means raising one plus the gain by five, which is also five times the sensitivity to noise: the trade is why integral action exists

problems.prompt: A valve must pass {{qq}} US gallons per minute of a liquid of specific gravity {{sg}} with {{dp}} psi across it. What flow coefficient is needed, using Cv = Q*sqrt(SG/dP)?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: The coefficient is printed as its defining equation because valve-standard tables were not read. Flow goes as the square root of the drop, so a valve given only a small share of the system's drop has little authority over the flow

problems.prompt: A valve takes {{dv}} psi of a system whose total drop is {{dt}} psi. What percentage of the drop is across the valve?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Valve authority is its share of the total drop; below about a quarter the installed characteristic distorts badly and the loop becomes hard to tune at any gain

cases.q: A valve taking most of the system's pressure drop suits:
A valve in a line that takes most of the drop suits:
cases.o1: An equal-percentage characteristic, so the installed behaviour comes out closer to linear

cases.q: A fuel gas valve is usually specified to:
cases.o1: Fail closed on loss of air

cases.q: A cooling water valve on an exothermic reactor is usually specified to:
cases.o1: Fail open on loss of air

cases.q: The installed characteristic differs from the inherent one because:
cases.o1: The pressure drop across the valve changes as it opens and the line takes more

parts.label: v
parts.explain: The characteristic is chosen for the installed behaviour, and the failure position is chosen from what is safe on air loss

problems.prompt: A transmitter is ranged {{lo}} to {{hi}} degrees Celsius on a 4 to 20 mA output. What does {{ma}} mA mean (degrees Celsius)?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: The signal maps linearly onto the calibrated range, so a wrong range makes a loop control to the wrong value while every indication looks healthy

problems.prompt: The same transmitter, ranged {{lo}} to {{hi}} degrees Celsius, reads {{tv}} degrees. What current does it send (mA)?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: The reverse conversion, and the reason the zero is at 4 mA rather than 0: a broken wire reads 0 and is distinguishable from a genuine bottom-of-range reading

problems.prompt: Carbon steel for a vessel costs {{k1}} dollars; the alloy that resists the service costs {{fm}} times as much in material. If material is {{mf}} per cent of the installed cost, what does the upgrade add to the installed cost (per cent)?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: The alloy premium only applies to the material fraction, so a four-fold material price rise on a vessel that is 40 per cent material adds 120 per cent, not 300: that arithmetic is what decides upgrade against allowance against lining

problems.prompt: A component is stressed to {{sv}} MPa against a stress-corrosion threshold of {{th}} MPa in this environment. What percentage of the threshold is that?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Stress-corrosion cracking needs stress above a threshold in that specific environment, so a stress-relief heat treatment or a lower design stress removes the risk without changing the alloy

problems.prompt: Uniform attack runs at {{ur}} mm a year while pits grow {{pf}} times faster. A wall of {{wt}} mm fails by pitting in how many years?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: The number is why an allowance is no defence against pitting: at twenty-five times the uniform rate a wall is through long before the average thickness has moved, and only inspection for pits catches it

problems.prompt: A coating covers all but {{hp}} per cent of a surface. By what factor is the current density on the bare metal raised, compared with the whole surface being bare?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: A nearly perfect coating concentrates the whole cell's current into the holidays, which is why a coated pipeline still needs cathodic protection and why a small defect perforates fast

problems.prompt: A fed-batch holds substrate at the consumption rate. With {{xx}} g/L of cells in {{vv}} L at a specific consumption of {{qs}} g per g per hour, what feed of a {{cf}} g/L solution is needed (L/h)?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Feeding at the consumption rate is what keeps substrate low enough to avoid inhibition and repression; because cell mass grows, the feed has to rise with it, which is why fed-batch profiles are exponential

problems.prompt: An outer loop has a time constant of {{to}} minutes and the inner loop {{ti}} minutes. By what factor is the inner loop faster, and is the usual rule of at least three times met? Give the factor.

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Cascade works only when the inner loop settles well inside the outer loop's response, usually a factor of three or more; below that the two loops interact and tuning either one upsets the other

problems.prompt: A controller's integral action is set as a reset time of {{tr}} minutes per repeat. What is the reset rate in repeats per minute?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: The same integral setting is quoted both ways by different makers, and confusing them turns a sluggish loop into an oscillating one: more repeats per minute is more integral action, more minutes per repeat is less

problems.prompt: An equal-percentage valve has an inherent rangeability of {{rg}}. What fraction of maximum flow does it pass at {{op}} per cent open, if flow goes as R to the power of (opening minus one)?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: An equal-percentage valve passes a small fraction of full flow at half open, which is what compensates a line whose own drop rises with flow: the installed characteristic is the product of the two

problems.prompt: For {{fl}}, $\mu = {{mu}}$ Pa·s and $\rho = {{rho}}$ kg/m³. What is the kinematic viscosity in mm²/s (centistokes)?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: $\nu = \mu/\rho$ in m²/s, then $\times 10^6$ for mm²/s. Water is about 1, air about 15: air is the more "viscous" of the two per unit mass

problems.prompt: What is the gauge pressure ${{h}}$ m below the free surface of {{fl}} (SG ${{sg}}$), in kPa? Use $g = 9.81$ m/s².

parts.label: v
parts.explain: $P = \rho g h = {{sg*1000}} \times 9.81 \times {{h}}$ Pa. Ten metres of water is about one atmosphere

problems.prompt: A U-tube manometer filled with {{man}} ($\rho = {{rm}}$ kg/m³) connects two points in a line carrying {{line}}. The legs differ by ${{h}}$ cm. What is the pressure difference, in kPa? Use $g = 9.81$.

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Walk round the U-tube: the process fluid fills the leg above the manometer fluid, so only the density difference counts: $\Delta P = (\rho_m - \rho_f)\,g\,h$ with $h = {{h/100}}$ m

problems.prompt: {{body}} floats in {{fl}}. What percent of its volume is submerged?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Floating means weight equals buoyancy: $\rho_b V = \rho_f V_{sub}$, so the submerged fraction is the ratio of specific gravities

problems.prompt: {{fl}} ($\rho = {{rho}}$ kg/m³, $\mu = {{mu}}$ Pa·s) flows at ${{v}}$ m/s in a pipe of diameter ${{D}}$ m. What is the Reynolds number?

parts.label: r
parts.explain: $Re = \dfrac{\rho v D}{\mu}$: inertia over viscous force. Below about 2100 pipe flow is laminar; above about 4000 it is turbulent

problems.prompt: Pipe flow at $Re = {{Re|9}}$. Which regime?

parts.label: a
parts.explain: For flow in a pipe: laminar below about 2100, turbulent above about 4000, and unreliable in between

choices.a: 0 if Re < 2100 else (2 if Re > 4000 else 1)

problems.prompt: A rectangular duct is ${{a}}$ m by ${{b}}$ m and runs full. What is its hydraulic diameter, in m?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: $D_h = \dfrac{4 \times \text{area}}{\text{wetted perimeter}} = \dfrac{4({{a}})({{b}})}{2({{a}} + {{b}})}$. For a round pipe this gives back $D$

problems.prompt: A viscous liquid ($\mu = {{mu}}$ Pa·s) flows in laminar flow at ${{v}}$ m/s (mean) through ${{L}}$ m of ${{D}}$ m pipe. What is the pressure drop, in kPa?

parts.label: r
parts.explain: Hagen–Poiseuille: $\Delta P = \dfrac{32\,\mu L v}{D^2}$. The same thing as $f = 64/Re$ in the Darcy equation; density cancels

cases.q: inertial force to viscous force
inertial force to gravity force (open channels, waves)
inertial force to surface-tension force (drops, sprays)
flow speed to the speed of sound
pressure force to inertial force

problems.prompt: Which dimensionless group is the ratio of {{q}}?

parts.label: a
parts.explain: Reynolds: inertia/viscous. Froude: inertia/gravity. Weber: inertia/surface tension. Mach: speed/sound speed. Euler: pressure/inertia

problems.prompt: Water flows at ${{v1}}$ m/s in a ${{D1}}$ m pipe that narrows to ${{D2}}$ m. What is the velocity in the narrow section, in m/s?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Incompressible, so $A_1v_1 = A_2v_2$ and area goes as $D^2$: $v_2 = v_1(D_1/D_2)^2$. Halve the diameter, quadruple the speed

problems.prompt: Water ($\rho = 1000$ kg/m³) speeds up from ${{v1}}$ m/s to ${{v1*k}}$ m/s through a horizontal, frictionless contraction. By how much does the pressure fall, in kPa?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Bernoulli at one height: $P_1 + \tfrac12\rho v_1^2 = P_2 + \tfrac12\rho v_2^2$, so $P_1 - P_2 = \tfrac12\rho(v_2^2 - v_1^2)$

problems.prompt: A large open tank drains through a small hole ${{h}}$ m below the surface. Ignoring friction, what is the exit velocity, in m/s? Use $g = 9.81$.

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Bernoulli from the surface (at rest, atmospheric) to the jet (atmospheric): $g h = \tfrac12 v^2$, so $v = \sqrt{2gh}$, the speed of free fall from that height

problems.prompt: A pitot tube in {{fl}} ($\rho = {{rho}}$ kg/m³) reads a stagnation-minus-static pressure of ${{dP}}$ Pa. What is the flow velocity, in m/s?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: The flow stops at the probe tip, turning all its kinetic energy into pressure: $\Delta P = \tfrac12\rho v^2$

problems.prompt: Water flows at ${{v}}$ m/s through ${{L}}$ m of ${{D}}$ m pipe with Darcy friction factor $f = {{f}}$. What is the friction head loss, in m? Use $g = 9.81$.

parts.label: r
parts.explain: Darcy–Weisbach: $h_f = f\dfrac{L}{D}\dfrac{v^2}{2g}$. $L/D$ counts the pipe in diameters; $v^2/2g$ is the velocity head

cases.fit: a sudden exit into a tank

problems.prompt: Water passes through {{fit}} (loss coefficient $K = {{K}}$) at ${{v}}$ m/s. What head is lost, in m? Use $g = 9.81$.

parts.label: r
parts.explain: $h_L = K\dfrac{v^2}{2g}$: $K$ velocity heads. A globe valve costs tens of times what a gate valve does

problems.prompt: A pump lifts water from an open tank with its surface at ${{z1}}$ m to an open tank with its surface at ${{z2}}$ m. Friction losses in the line total ${{hL}}$ m. What head must the pump supply, in m?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Mechanical energy balance surface to surface: both are at atmospheric pressure and at rest, so the pump supplies the lift plus the losses: $h_p = (z_2 - z_1) + h_L$

problems.prompt: A pump delivers ${{Q}}$ L/s of water against a head of ${{H}}$ m at ${{eta*100}}\%$ efficiency. What shaft power does it need, in kW? Use $g = 9.81$.

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Power to the fluid is $\rho g Q H = 1000 \times 9.81 \times {{Q/1000}} \times {{H}}$ W. The shaft must supply more: divide by the efficiency

cases.q: What happens when the pressure at a pump inlet falls to the vapour pressure of the liquid?
To avoid cavitation, the available NPSH must be
Two identical pumps in series, at the same flow, give
Two identical pumps in parallel, at the same head, give

parts.label: a
choice: Cavitation: vapour bubbles form and collapse
Greater than the NPSH the pump requires
parts.explain: Net positive suction head is the margin of inlet pressure above the vapour pressure, in metres of liquid; the pump needs a minimum. Pumps in series add head, in parallel add flow

problems.prompt: A venturi meter in a water line ($\rho = 1000$ kg/m³) has a throat of ${{D2}}$ m, half the pipe diameter, and a discharge coefficient of ${{Cd}}$. It reads $\Delta P = {{dP}}$ kPa. What is the flow, in L/s?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Continuity gives $v_1 = v_2\beta^2$ with $\beta = 0.5$; Bernoulli then gives $v_2 = \sqrt{\dfrac{2\Delta P}{\rho(1 - \beta^4)}}$. Multiply by the throat area and by $C_d$

expect.v: Cd*pi*D2**2/4*1000*Max(*[s[x] for s in solve([Eq(Symbol('u'), x*Rational(1, 4)), Eq(dP*1000/1000, (x**2 - Symbol('u')**2)/2)], [x, Symbol('u')], dict=True)])

cases.q: Which meter measures a local velocity from the difference between stagnation and static pressure?
Which meter is a thin plate with a hole: cheap, but with a large permanent pressure loss?
Which meter has a smooth converging–diverging section and recovers most of the pressure?
Which meter is a float in a tapered vertical tube, read by its height?

parts.label: a
parts.explain: Pitot: point velocity. Orifice and venturi: flow from a pressure drop across a constriction, the venturi with far less permanent loss. Rotameter: a variable-area meter at constant pressure drop

problems.prompt: What is the speed of sound in {{gas}} ($\gamma = {{gam}}$, $M = {{M}}$ g/mol) at ${{T}}$ °C, in m/s? Use $R = 8.314$ J/(mol·K).

parts.label: v
parts.explain: $a = \sqrt{\gamma R T / M}$ with $T$ in kelvin and $M$ in kg/mol. Light gases carry sound fast: air about 343 m/s at 20 °C, helium about three times that

problems.prompt: Air flows at ${{v}}$ m/s where the speed of sound is 340 m/s. How should the flow be treated?

parts.label: a
choice: Ma < 0.3: incompressible is a good approximation
parts.explain: $Ma = v/a = {{v/340}}$. Below about 0.3 the density changes by only a few percent, so Bernoulli still works

choices.a: 0 if v*10 < 3*340 else (1 if v < 340 else 2)

cases.q: Water or air
A power-law fluid with n = 1
Paint, ketchup or a polymer solution: thinner the faster it is sheared
A power-law fluid with n = 0.6
A thick cornstarch suspension: stiffer the faster it is sheared
A power-law fluid with n = 1.4
Toothpaste: it will not flow until a yield stress is exceeded, then flows

problems.prompt: What kind of fluid? {{q}}.

parts.label: a
parts.explain: Power law: stress $= K(\text{shear rate})^n$. $n = 1$ is Newtonian, $n < 1$ shear-thinning, $n > 1$ shear-thickening. A Bingham plastic needs a yield stress before it moves at all

problems.prompt: A power-law fluid has $\tau = {{K}}\,\dot\gamma^{ {{n}} }$ (SI units). What is its apparent viscosity at a shear rate of ${{gd}}$ s⁻¹, in Pa·s?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Apparent viscosity is stress over shear rate: $\eta = K\dot\gamma^{\,n-1}$. With $n < 1$ it falls as the shear rate rises; with $n > 1$ it climbs

problems.prompt: An oil has kinematic viscosity {{nu}} cSt (mm²/s) and specific gravity {{sg}}. What is its dynamic viscosity, in mPa·s?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: μ = ρν: with ν in mm²/s and ρ in g/cm³ the numbers multiply straight into mPa·s

problems.prompt: A {{V}} L block of density {{rho}} kg/m³ floats in water (1000 kg/m³). What downward force, in N, holds it fully submerged? (g = 9.81 m/s²)

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Fully submerged, buoyancy is the weight of the whole displaced volume; the push makes up the difference from the block's weight

problems.prompt: {{fl}} ($\nu$ = {{nu}} mm²/s) flows in a {{D}} mm pipe. Up to what mean speed, in m/s, does the flow stay laminar (Re ≤ 2300)?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Water goes turbulent at a few cm/s in ordinary pipes, which is why most water flow is turbulent and most oil and syrup flow is not

problems.prompt: A pump draws water at {{T}} °C (vapour pressure {{pv}} kPa, ρ = 1000 kg/m³) from an open tank at 101.3 kPa. The water surface is {{z}} m {{dir}} the pump inlet and suction losses are {{hl}} m. What NPSH is available, in m?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Positive z is a flooded suction (surface above the pump). Hot water's vapour pressure eats the margin fast; if NPSH_A falls below the pump's NPSH_R it cavitates

problems.prompt: An orifice of diameter {{d}} mm in a {{D}} mm water pipe (C_d = 0.61) shows a pressure drop of {{dp}} kPa. What is the flow rate, in L/s?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Bernoulli plus continuity between the pipe and the vena contracta gives the ideal flow; C_d absorbs the contraction and losses. Orifices are cheap but waste most of that pressure drop

problems.prompt: A water jet ({{A}} cm², {{V}} m/s) strikes a flat plate head-on while the plate recedes at {{u}} m/s. What force acts on the plate, in N?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: In the plate's frame the jet arrives at V − u and the mass reaching the plate per second shrinks too, so force goes as (V − u)²

problems.prompt: A vane turns a water jet (ρQ = {{mq}} kg/s, speed {{V}} m/s, unchanged in magnitude) through {{th}}°. What is the magnitude of the force on the vane, in N?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: The force is ṁ times the vector change in velocity; turning the jet back on itself (180°) doubles the head-on force

problems.prompt: Oil ($\mu$ = {{mu}} Pa·s) fills a {{h}} mm gap; one plate slides at {{V}} m/s. What power per square metre is dissipated, in W/m²?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: The work done by the shear stress, τV, all turns into heat: viscous dissipation μ(du/dy)² integrated over the gap

problems.prompt: Water ($\mu$ = 1.0 mPa·s, ρ = 1000 kg/m³) runs down a vertical wall at {{G}} kg/s per metre of width in laminar flow. How thick is the film, in mm?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Integrating the half-parabola gives Γ = ρ²gδ³/(3μ): thickness grows only as the cube root of the flow

problems.prompt: A 2-D flow has u = {{a}}x + {{b}}y and v = {{c}}x + {{d}}y. Could it be an incompressible flow?

parts.label: v
choice: No: the divergence is not zero
parts.explain: Incompressibility is a zero divergence; the cross terms (b, c) only shear and rotate the fluid

choices.v: 0 if diff(a*Symbol('xx') + b*Symbol('yy'), Symbol('xx')) + diff(c*Symbol('xx') + d*Symbol('yy'), Symbol('yy')) == 0 else 1

problems.prompt: Estimate the hydrodynamic entry length, in pipe diameters, for turbulent flow at Re = {{Re}} using $L_e/D \approx 4.4\,Re^{1/6}$.

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Turbulent mixing develops the profile in 20–40 diameters, far shorter than the laminar 0.05 Re

problems.prompt: Find the exponent b that makes {{grp}} dimensionless.

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Balance mass, length and time exponents: these build the Euler, Froude, Weber and force-coefficient groups

problems.prompt: A ship {{Lp}} m long is tested as a 1:{{s}} model. With Froude similarity, what model speed, in m/s, matches a full-scale speed of {{Vp}} m/s?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Wave-making is gravity-driven, so Froude number is matched and Reynolds number is not; the friction part is corrected separately

problems.prompt: A {{d}} cm sphere in a wind tunnel at {{V}} m/s (air 1.2 kg/m³) feels a drag of {{F}} N. What is its drag coefficient?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: C_D uses the frontal area; for a sphere around 10⁴ < Re < 10⁵ it sits near 0.4–0.5

problems.prompt: Particles of density {{rp}} kg/m³ settle in water (1000 kg/m³, μ = 1.0 mPa·s). Up to what diameter, in μm, does Stokes' law hold (Re ≤ 1)? (g = 9.81)

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Re grows as d³ under Stokes settling: sand stays in the Stokes regime only below about 100 μm

problems.prompt: Laminar flow splits between two parallel pipes: pipe 1 is {{d1}} mm and {{L1}} m, pipe 2 is {{d2}} mm and {{L2}} m. What fraction goes through pipe 1?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Equal pressure drop across both; Hagen–Poiseuille resistance ∝ L/D⁴, so diameter dominates

problems.prompt: A pump makes {{H1}} m of head at {{N1}} rpm. What speed, in rpm, gives {{H2}} m (same impeller, similar operating point)?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Head ∝ N², flow ∝ N, power ∝ N³: a small speed change shifts power a lot

problems.prompt: At its operating point a pump delivers {{Q}} L/s of water against {{H}} m with efficiency {{eta}}%. What shaft power does it need, in kW?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Hydraulic power ρgQH divided by efficiency

problems.prompt: A vertical rectangular gate {{h}} m tall has its top edge {{d0}} m below the water surface. How deep, in m, is its centre of pressure?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Pressure grows with depth, so the resultant acts below the centroid: at 2h/3 when the gate reaches the surface, approaching the centroid as it sinks deeper

expect.v: integrate(Symbol('yy')**2, (Symbol('yy'), nsimplify(d0), nsimplify(d0) + h))/integrate(Symbol('yy'), (Symbol('yy'), nsimplify(d0), nsimplify(d0) + h))

problems.prompt: A water jet ($\rho = 1000$ kg/m³), ${{d}}$ cm across, hits a fixed flat plate head-on at ${{v}}$ m/s and spreads out sideways. What force does it put on the plate, in N?

parts.label: r
parts.explain: Momentum in, none out in the jet direction: $F = \dot m v = \rho A v^2$, with $A = \pi d^2/4$. Doubling the speed quadruples the force

problems.prompt: A jet of ${{m}}$ kg/s at ${{v}}$ m/s is turned through ${{th}}°$ by a fixed vane, without losing speed. What is the force on the vane in the original jet direction, in N?

parts.label: r
parts.explain: $F_x = \dot m (v_{in,x} - v_{out,x}) = \dot m v(1 - \cos\theta)$. A 180° turn doubles the force of a flat plate: the fluid's momentum is reversed, not just stopped

problems.prompt: A plate of area ${{A}}$ m² slides at ${{U}}$ m/s over an oil film ${{h}}$ mm thick ($\mu = {{mu}}$ Pa·s) on a fixed surface. What force keeps it moving, in N?

parts.label: r
parts.explain: Couette flow: the profile is linear, $u = Uy/h$, so $\tau = \mu U/h$ everywhere in the gap and $F = \tau A$

problems.prompt: Laminar flow in a tube of radius ${{R}}$ mm and length ${{L}}$ m under a pressure drop of ${{dP}}$ Pa, $\mu = {{mu}}$ Pa·s. What is the volumetric flow rate, in mL/s?

parts.label: r
parts.explain: Hagen–Poiseuille: $Q = \dfrac{\pi R^4\Delta P}{8\mu L}$. The fourth power is the point: halve the radius and the flow drops 16-fold

cases.geo: a wide slit between parallel plates

problems.prompt: Fully developed laminar flow in {{geo}} has mean velocity ${{V}}$ m/s. What is the centreline velocity, in m/s?

parts.label: r
parts.explain: The profile is a parabola. Averaged over a circle it gives $u_{max} = 2\bar u$; over a slit, $u_{max} = 1.5\bar u$. Turbulent profiles are much flatter (about $1.2\bar u$)

expect.r: nsimplify(V)*(1 - 0**2)/(integrate((1 - x**2)*2*x, (x, 0, 1)) if k == 2 else integrate(1 - x**2, (x, 0, 1)))

problems.prompt: A liquid film ${{d}}$ mm thick runs down a vertical wall ($\rho = {{rho}}$ kg/m³, $\mu = {{mu}}$ Pa·s, $g = 9.81$). What is its mean velocity, in mm/s?

parts.label: r
parts.explain: Bird, Stewart & Lightfoot 2.2: gravity balanced by shear gives a half-parabola with zero stress at the free surface, $u_{max} = \rho g\delta^2/2\mu$ and $\bar u = \rho g\delta^2/3\mu$

problems.prompt: A steady incompressible 2-D flow has $u = {{a}}x + {{b}}y$ and $v = 0$ on the wall $y = 0$. Find $v$ at $y = {{y0}}$ (any $x$).

parts.label: r
parts.explain: Continuity: $\partial u/\partial x + \partial v/\partial y = 0$, so $\partial v/\partial y = -{{a}}$ and $v = -{{a}}y$. A flow that speeds up in $x$ must draw fluid in from $y$

problems.prompt: Laminar flow at $Re = {{Re}}$ enters a tube of diameter ${{D}}$ cm. Using $L_e \approx 0.05\,Re\,D$, how far downstream, in m, is the flow fully developed?

parts.label: r
parts.explain: Laminar entry lengths are long: tens to hundreds of diameters. Turbulent flow develops in roughly $10$–$60$ diameters, so most turbulent pipes can ignore it

cases.q: drag F on a sphere depends on ρ, μ, V and D
pressure drop ΔP in a pipe depends on ρ, μ, V, D, L and roughness ε
pump head gH depends on flow Q, speed N, diameter D, ρ and μ
period T of a pendulum depends on its length L, mass m and g
heat transfer coefficient h depends on k, ρ, μ, c_p, V and D
the frequency f of a vibrating string depends on its length L, tension T and mass per length m

problems.prompt: If {{q}}, how many dimensionless groups does the Buckingham pi theorem give?

parts.label: r
parts.explain: Count the variables (including the one you want), subtract the independent dimensions they use (M, L, T, and Θ when heat appears). The pendulum has one group, $T\sqrt{g/L}$, so the mass cannot matter

cases.fl: water (prototype) to a fluid with five times the kinematic viscosity (model)

problems.prompt: A 1:{{s}} scale model is tested to match the Reynolds number of a prototype moving at ${{V}}$ m/s, going from {{fl}}. What speed must the model run at, in m/s?

parts.label: r

problems.prompt: A body with drag coefficient $C_D = {{CD}}$ and frontal area ${{A}}$ m² moves at ${{V}}$ m/s through air ($\rho = 1.2$ kg/m³). What is the drag force, in N?

parts.label: r
parts.explain: $F_D = C_D\cdot\tfrac12\rho V^2\cdot A$: the coefficient scales the dynamic pressure acting on the frontal area. Power to overcome drag is $F_DV \propto V^3$

problems.prompt: A sphere ${{d}}$ µm across, density ${{rp}}$ kg/m³, settles in water ($\rho = 1000$ kg/m³, $\mu = {{mu}}$ Pa·s, $g = 9.81$). Assuming Stokes drag, what is its terminal velocity, in mm/s?

parts.label: r
parts.explain: Weight minus buoyancy equals Stokes drag $3\pi\mu dv$: $v_t = \dfrac{(\rho_p - \rho)gd^2}{18\mu}$. Check $Re = \rho v d/\mu < 1$ afterwards, or Stokes does not apply

problems.prompt: Two pipes run in parallel between the same two points with the same friction factor. Pipe B has ${{r}}$ times the diameter and ${{l}}$ times the length of pipe A. What is $Q_B/Q_A$?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Parallel pipes share the head loss. With $h_f = f\dfrac{L}{D}\dfrac{v^2}{2g}$ and $v = 4Q/\pi D^2$, $h_f \propto LQ^2/D^5$, so $Q \propto D^{5/2}/\sqrt L$

cases.q: flow rate
head
shaft power

problems.prompt: A centrifugal pump running at ${{N1}}$ rpm is changed to ${{f*N1}}$ rpm. By what factor does its {{q}} change?

parts.label: r
parts.explain: Affinity laws for one pump: $Q \propto N$, $H \propto N^2$, $P \propto N^3$. That cube is why a variable-speed drive saves so much energy compared with throttling

problems.prompt: A pump curve is $H = {{H0}} - {{a}}Q^2$ and the system curve is $H = {{Hs}} + {{b}}Q^2$ ($H$ in m, $Q$ in m³/s). At what flow does the system run, in m³/s?

parts.label: r
parts.explain: The operating point is where the head the pump supplies equals the head the system demands. $Q = \sqrt{(H_0 - H_s)/(a + b)}$; the static lift $H_s$ is spent before any flow begins

problems.prompt: A vertical rectangular gate ${{w}}$ m wide and ${{h}}$ m tall has its top edge ${{t}}$ m below the surface of water ($\rho = 1000$ kg/m³, $g = 9.81$). What is the total water force on it, in kN?

parts.label: r
parts.explain: Pressure grows linearly with depth, so the force is the pressure at the centroid times the area: $F = \rho g h_c A$ with $h_c = {{t}} + {{h}}/2$. It acts lower than the centroid, at the centre of pressure

problems.prompt: Water ($\mu = {{mu}}$ mPa·s) flows under a pressure gradient of {{G}} Pa/m through the annulus between a rod of radius {{k}}R and a pipe of radius R = {{Rc}} cm. What is the volumetric flow rate, in mL/s?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: The profile is $v = \frac{GR^2}{4\mu}[1 - (r/R)^2 + (1-\kappa^2)\ln(r/R)/\ln(1/\kappa)]$; integrating $2\pi r v$ gives the bracket in the BSL result. As κ → 0 it tends to Hagen–Poiseuille

problems.prompt: At the same pressure gradient and outer radius, what fraction of the Hagen–Poiseuille flow passes through an annulus whose inner radius is {{k}}R?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Even a thin rod costs a lot: at κ = 0.1 the no-slip core removes far more than the 1% of area it blocks

problems.prompt: A cylinder of radius {{k}}R turns at {{Om}} rad/s inside a fixed cylinder of radius R = {{Rc}} cm, with oil of viscosity {{mu}} Pa·s between them. What torque per metre of length, in mN·m/m, keeps it turning?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Only $A r + B/r$ satisfies the θ-momentum equation; the shear $\tau_{r\theta} = -\mu r\,d(v_\theta/r)/dr$ comes from the $B/r$ part alone. A rigid rotation ($Ar$) carries no stress

problems.prompt: In circular Couette flow (inner cylinder radius {{k}}R turning at {{Om}} rad/s, outer fixed), what is the shear rate at the inner wall, in s⁻¹?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Narrow gaps approach plane Couette flow, γ̇ ≈ ΩκR/((1 − κ)R); rheometers use them for a nearly uniform shear rate

problems.prompt: Two discs of radius {{Rc}} cm approach at {{V}} mm/s with a {{h}} μm film of oil ($\mu$ = {{mu}} Pa·s) between them. What force, in N, resists the motion?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: The gap enters as h⁻³: halving it multiplies the force by eight, which is why squeeze films cushion so well and why joints and bearings stay lubricated

problems.prompt: Two discs of radius {{Rc}} cm are pressed together by {{F}} N through oil ($\mu$ = {{mu}} Pa·s). How long, in s, does the film take to thin from {{h1}} μm to {{h2}} μm?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Setting F = 3πμR⁴V/(2h³) with V = −dh/dt and integrating: the film never quite reaches zero thickness in finite force

problems.prompt: Air ($\rho$ = 1.2 kg/m³, $\nu = 1.5\times10^{-5}$ m²/s) flows at {{U}} m/s along a flat plate {{L}} m long. What is the friction drag on one side per metre of width, in mN? (Flow stays laminar.)

parts.label: v
parts.explain: The wall stress falls as $x^{-1/2}$ because the layer thickens as $\sqrt{x}$; integrating doubles the local coefficient 0.664 to 1.328

problems.prompt: A laminar flat plate is lengthened by a factor {{f}} at the same speed (still laminar). By what factor does the friction drag rise?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: The added length sits under a thicker boundary layer with lower wall stress, so drag grows only as √L

problems.prompt: In inviscid flow past a circular cylinder, what is the pressure coefficient $C_p$ at {{th}}° from the front stagnation point?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: From $w = U(z + a^2/z)$. $C_p$ = 1 at the stagnation points, −3 at the shoulders, and symmetric front to back, so the net drag is zero (d'Alembert)

problems.prompt: Air ($\rho$ = 1.2 kg/m³) flows at {{U}} m/s past a cylinder. In potential flow, how much lower is the pressure at the shoulders (90°) than at the front stagnation point, in Pa?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: The surface speed doubles at the shoulders, so the dynamic pressure there is four times the free stream's

problems.prompt: A power-law fluid (m = {{m}} Pa·sⁿ, n = {{n}}) flows through a tube of radius {{Rc}} mm under ΔP/L = {{G}} kPa/m. What is the flow rate, in mL/s?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Shear stress is linear in r whatever the fluid; a shear-thinning fluid (n < 1) has a blunter profile and a flow rate that rises faster than linearly with pressure

problems.prompt: A power-law fluid has m = {{m}} Pa·sⁿ and n = {{n}}. What is its apparent viscosity at a shear rate of {{g}} s⁻¹, in Pa·s?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: η = τ/γ̇ = m γ̇^{n−1}: a shear-thinning fluid (n < 1) is a hundred times thinner at 1000 s⁻¹ than at 1 s⁻¹ when n = 1/3

problems.prompt: One plate of a {{h}} mm gap filled with {{fl}} ($\nu$ = {{nu}} mm²/s) starts moving suddenly. How long, in s, until the slowest transient term has decayed to 1% of its initial size?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Momentum diffuses with ν, so the time scale is $h^2/\nu$; viscous fluids reach steady flow faster, not slower

problems.prompt: A plate in {{fl}} ($\nu$ = {{nu}} mm²/s) suddenly moves at speed U. What fraction of U has the fluid {{y}} mm away reached after {{t}} s?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Stokes' first problem: momentum diffuses a distance of order √(νt), the same similarity solution as heat into a semi-infinite solid

problems.prompt: In turbulent water flow ($\rho$ = 1000 kg/m³, $\nu = 10^{-6}$ m²/s) the wall stress is {{tw}} Pa. What is the mean velocity {{y}} mm from the wall, in m/s?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Check y⁺ > 30 before using the log law; nearer the wall (y⁺ < 5) the viscous sublayer has u⁺ = y⁺

problems.prompt: Water ($\nu = 10^{-6}$ m²/s) flows with friction velocity {{us}} m/s. In which region of the wall layer is a point {{y}} μm from the wall?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Wall units y⁺ = yu*/ν decide the region; in the sublayer u⁺ = y⁺, in the log layer the log law, in between neither fits well

choices.v: 0 if Rational(y, 10**6)*nsimplify(us)*10**6 < 5 else (1 if Rational(y, 10**6)*nsimplify(us)*10**6 < 30 else 2)

problems.prompt: A drop with viscosity ratio λ = {{lam}} (drop to surrounding fluid) settles in creeping flow. By what factor is its terminal velocity higher than a rigid sphere of the same size and density?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Internal circulation lets the interface move, cutting drag; a gas bubble (λ = 0) falls 1.5 times faster. Traces of surfactant immobilise the surface and bring it back to Stokes

problems.prompt: A small air bubble of radius {{a}} μm rises in water ($\mu$ = 1.0 mPa·s, Δρ = 998 kg/m³). With a clean, mobile surface (Hadamard–Rybczynski, λ = 0), what is its terminal speed, in mm/s?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Drag 4πμaU instead of 6πμaU: 1.5 times faster than a rigid sphere. Real bubbles in tap water often behave as rigid because surfactants immobilise the surface

problems.prompt: A solute (D = {{Dm}} × 10⁻⁹ m²/s) is carried at mean speed U through a capillary of radius {{a}} μm. At what U, in mm/s, does Taylor dispersion double the effective diffusivity?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Shear spreads the solute along the tube and radial diffusion evens it out, so faster diffusion means less dispersion: K grows as 1/D

problems.prompt: A solute with D = {{Dm}} × 10⁻⁹ m²/s flows at mean speed {{U}} mm/s through a tube of radius {{a}} μm. What is the Taylor dispersion coefficient, in 10⁻⁹ m²/s?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: The convective term usually dominates in microchannels: dispersion can exceed molecular diffusion by orders of magnitude

problems.prompt: A lubricant ($\mu$ = {{mu}} Pa·s, k = {{k}} W/m·K) is sheared in a {{h}} mm gap by a wall moving at {{V}} m/s; both walls are held at the same temperature. What is the maximum temperature rise, in K?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: The gap cancels: dissipation μ(V/h)² over a conduction length h². The Brinkman number μV²/(kΔT) says when viscous heating matters

problems.prompt: A lubricant ($\mu$ = {{mu}} Pa·s, k = {{k}} W/m·K) is sheared by a wall moving at {{V}} m/s; the stationary wall is at T₀ and the moving wall is insulated. What is the temperature rise at the insulated wall, in K?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: With one wall insulated all the dissipated heat must leave through the other: four times the rise of the two-cold-walls case

problems.prompt: Water at 0 °C freezes onto a plate held at {{dT}} °C below freezing. Ice: k = 2.2 W/m·K, ρ = 917 kg/m³, L = 334 kJ/kg. How long, in minutes, until the ice is {{d}} mm thick? (Neglect the ice's sensible heat.)

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Time grows as thickness squared: the ice it has already made insulates the front. Fine when the Stefan number cΔT/L is small

problems.prompt: Water at 0 °C freezes onto a plate {{dT}} °C below freezing (ice k = 2.2 W/m·K, ρ = 917 kg/m³, L = 334 kJ/kg). How thick is the ice, in mm, after {{t}} min?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: δ ∝ √t: the second half-hour adds less than half as much ice as the first

problems.prompt: Ion diffusivities (10⁻⁹ m²/s): {{ion1}} {{dp}}, {{ion2}} {{dm}}. What is the diffusion coefficient of dilute {{salt}} in water, in 10⁻⁹ m²/s?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: The fast ion runs ahead and sets up a field that drags the slow one and holds itself back; the pair moves at a harmonic mean, close to the slower ion

expect.v: nsimplify(dp)*(1 + solve(Eq(nsimplify(dp)*(1 + x), nsimplify(dm)*(1 - x)), x)[0])

problems.prompt: For dilute {{salt}} ({{ion1}} {{dp}}, {{ion2}} {{dm}} × 10⁻⁹ m²/s), what fraction of the current does the cation carry (its transference number)?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Mobility ∝ D (Nernst–Einstein), so current splits in proportion to D for a 1:1 salt. KCl's near-equal split is why it fills salt bridges

problems.prompt: Gas A diffuses through a {{dl}} mm film to a catalyst where it reacts instantly by A → 2B. With c = {{c}} mol/m³, D = {{Dm}} × 10⁻⁵ m²/s and bulk mole fraction y_A = {{y}}, what is the flux of A, in mol/(m²·s)?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: The B flowing back opposes the A: N_A(1 + y_A) = −cD dy_A/dz. Compare stagnant B, where the factor is 1/(1 − y_A) and the flux is larger

problems.prompt: With bulk mole fraction y_A = {{y}} and zero at the catalyst, how does the flux of A for A → 2B compare with diffusion through stagnant B (same film)? Give N(A → 2B)/N(stagnant).

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Counterflow of B fights A; a stagnant B lets the bulk flow help A along. The difference vanishes for dilute A

problems.prompt: Naphthalene sublimes from a plate {{L}} cm long into air at {{U}} m/s ($\nu = 1.5\times10^{-5}$ m²/s, D = 6.1 × 10⁻⁶ m²/s, laminar). What is the average mass-transfer coefficient, in mm/s?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: The heat–mass analogy: Sc replaces Pr. The local coefficient falls as $x^{-1/2}$, so the leading edge does most of the transfer

problems.prompt: On a laminar flat plate, the local mass-transfer coefficient at the trailing edge is what fraction of the plate-average coefficient?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: k ∝ x^{−1/2}, whose average over the length is twice the end value; the leading edge carries the transfer

problems.prompt: {{g}} has van der Waals constants a = {{a}} Pa·m⁶/mol² and b = {{b}} × 10⁻⁵ m³/mol. What critical temperature does the equation predict, in K? ($R = 8.314$)

parts.label: v
parts.explain: The critical point is where the isotherm's maximum and minimum merge into an inflection. vdW gets $T_c$ roughly right but predicts $Z_c$ = 0.375, well above real fluids' ≈ 0.27–0.29

problems.prompt: {{g}} has $T_c$ = {{Tc}} K and $P_c$ = {{Pc}} MPa. What van der Waals b does that give, in 10⁻⁵ m³/mol? ($R = 8.314$)

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Fitting a and b to the critical point is the usual way to set them; b is roughly the excluded volume per mole

problems.prompt: Using the Peng–Robinson equation, find Z for {{sp}} {{ph}} at {{T}} K and {{Pm}} MPa ($T_c$ = {{Tc}} K, $P_c$ = {{Pcm}} MPa, ω = {{om}}).

parts.label: v
parts.explain: $A = aP/(RT)^2$, $B = bP/RT$, with $a$ scaled by α(T, ω). Where there are three real roots, the middle one is unphysical; which of the outer two is stable is decided by fugacity

expect.v: gc_pr_z(Tc, Pcm*10**6, om, T, Pm*10**6, vap)

problems.prompt: In the Peng–Robinson equation, what is α(T) for a fluid with ω = {{om}} at reduced temperature $T_r$ = {{tr}}?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: α = 1 at the critical temperature; it grows below T_c so the attraction term strengthens, and ω tunes the slope so vapour pressures come out right

problems.prompt: A binary liquid follows $g^E/RT = A x_1 x_2$ with A = {{A}}. Is a mixture at x₁ = {{x1}} stable against splitting into two liquids?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Stability is curvature: Δg_mix must curve upward. The one-constant Margules model first splits at A = 2, at x₁ = ½ (the critical solution point)

choices.v: 0 if diff(Symbol('q')*log(Symbol('q')) + (1 - Symbol('q'))*log(1 - Symbol('q')) + nsimplify(A)*Symbol('q')*(1 - Symbol('q')), Symbol('q'), 2).subs(Symbol('q'), nsimplify(x1)) > 0 else 1

problems.prompt: For $g^E/RT = Ax_1x_2$, what is the smallest A at which a mixture with x₁ = {{x1}} becomes unstable (lies on the spinodal)?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: The spinodal bounds the region where tiny fluctuations grow; it touches A = 2 only at x₁ = ½

expect.v: solve(diff(Symbol('q')*log(Symbol('q')) + (1 - Symbol('q'))*log(1 - Symbol('q')) + x*Symbol('q')*(1 - Symbol('q')), Symbol('q'), 2).subs(Symbol('q'), nsimplify(x1)), x)[0]

problems.prompt: A gas has B(T) = {{b0}} − {{b1}}/T (cm³/mol, T in K). What is its residual enthalpy $H^R$ at {{T}} K and {{P}} bar, in J/mol?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: From $H^R/RT = -T\int_0^P (\partial Z/\partial T)_P\,dP/P$ with $Z = 1 + BP/RT$. Attractions (negative B) make $H^R$ negative: the real gas holds less enthalpy

problems.prompt: A gas with second virial coefficient B = {{B}} cm³/mol is at {{T}} K and {{P}} bar. What is its fugacity coefficient?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: ln φ = ∫(Z − 1)dP/P = BP/RT: attractions (B < 0) give φ < 1, an 'escaping tendency' below the pressure

problems.prompt: In an ideal liquid, A ⇌ B ($K_1$ = {{k1}}) and B ⇌ C ($K_2$ = {{k2}}) both reach equilibrium. What is the mole fraction of C?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Every species' amount follows from A's through the chain of K's; the mole balance fixes A. With independent reactions the order of writing them does not matter

expect.v: solve([Eq(Symbol('b'), nsimplify(k1)*Symbol('a')), Eq(Symbol('c'), nsimplify(k2)*Symbol('b')), Eq(Symbol('a') + Symbol('b') + Symbol('c'), 1)], [Symbol('a'), Symbol('b'), Symbol('c')])[Symbol('c')]

problems.prompt: In an ideal liquid, A ⇌ B ($K_1$ = {{k1}}) and A ⇌ C ($K_2$ = {{k2}}). What is the equilibrium mole fraction of A?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Isomers share one pool: each takes a share in proportion to its K relative to A

expect.v: solve([Eq(Symbol('b'), nsimplify(k1)*Symbol('a')), Eq(Symbol('c'), nsimplify(k2)*Symbol('a')), Eq(Symbol('a') + Symbol('b') + Symbol('c'), 1)], [Symbol('a'), Symbol('b'), Symbol('c')])[Symbol('a')]

problems.prompt: A reaction has K = {{K0}} at 298.15 K, ΔH° = {{dH}} kJ/mol and ΔCp = {{dCp}} J/(mol·K) (constant). What is K at {{T}} K? ($R = 8.314$)

parts.label: v
parts.explain: With ΔCp ≠ 0, ln K is not linear in 1/T; the extra term is ΔCp[ln(T/T₀) + T₀/T − 1]/R, small over modest ranges

problems.prompt: A reaction has K = {{K0}} at 298.15 K and ΔH° = {{dH}} kJ/mol (take ΔH° and ΔS° constant). At what temperature is K = 1, in K? ($R = 8.314$)

parts.label: v
parts.explain: K = 1 where ΔG° = 0, i.e. T = ΔH°/ΔS°: above it an endothermic reaction favours products, below it an exothermic one does

problems.prompt: A binary follows $g^E/RT = A x_1x_2$ with A = {{A}}; at the temperature of interest $P_1^{sat}/P_2^{sat}$ = {{r}}. At what x₁ is the azeotrope?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: With ln γ₁ = A x₂² and ln γ₂ = A x₁², the condition is linear in x₁. Positive deviations (A > 0) give a maximum-pressure azeotrope when A exceeds |ln(P₁/P₂)|

problems.prompt: A binary follows $g^E/RT = Ax_1x_2$ with A = {{A}}; $P_2^{sat}$ = {{p2}} kPa and $P_1^{sat}/P_2^{sat}$ = {{r}}. What is the azeotrope pressure, in kPa?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: At the azeotrope P = γ₁P₁^sat = γ₂P₂^sat; positive deviations make it a pressure maximum (a minimum-boiling azeotrope)

expect.v: exp(nsimplify(A)*(1 - solve(Eq(log(nsimplify(r)) + nsimplify(A)*(1 - x)**2 - nsimplify(A)*x**2, 0), x)[0])**2)*nsimplify(r)*p2

problems.prompt: At a steady state of a first-order exothermic CSTR, $k\tau$ = {{kt}}, the adiabatic rise $\Delta T_{ad}$ = {{J}} K, $E_a$ = {{Ea}} kJ/mol and T = {{T}} K. The heat-removal line R(T) has slope {{Rs}} (in G's units). Is the steady state stable?

parts.label: v
choice: Unstable (it moves to another steady state)
parts.explain: G(T) = ΔT_ad·kτ/(1 + kτ), so dG/dT = ΔT_ad·kτ/(1 + kτ)²·E/RT². The middle of three steady states always fails this test

choices.v: 0 if diff(J*Symbol('kk')/(1 + Symbol('kk')), Symbol('kk')).subs(Symbol('kk'), nsimplify(kt))*nsimplify(kt)*Ea*1000/(Rational(8314, 1000)*T**2) < nsimplify(Rs) else 1

problems.prompt: For a first-order exothermic CSTR at a steady state with kτ = {{kt}}, $\Delta T_{ad}$ = {{J}} K, $E_a$ = {{Ea}} kJ/mol and T = {{T}} K, what heat-removal slope (in the same units) would put it exactly on the stability boundary?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: dG/dT peaks at kτ = 1; cooling must be steeper than that slope to hold a steady state in the middle of the S-curve

problems.prompt: A ⇌ B: forward $A_1$ = {{a1}} s⁻¹, $E_1$ = {{e1}} kJ/mol; reverse $A_2$ = {{a2}} s⁻¹, $E_2$ = {{e2}} kJ/mol. At conversion X = {{X}}, which temperature maximises the net rate, in K? ($R = 8.314$)

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Too cold and the forward rate is slow; too hot and equilibrium pulls X back. The optimum falls as conversion rises, which is why staged reactors cool between beds

problems.prompt: A ⇌ B: forward $A_1$ = {{a1}} s⁻¹, $E_1$ = {{e1}} kJ/mol; reverse $A_2$ = {{a2}} s⁻¹, $E_2$ = {{e2}} kJ/mol. Above what temperature, in K, can conversion {{X}} not be reached at all?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Equilibrium conversion falls with temperature for an exothermic reaction; the optimum temperature always lies below this line

problems.prompt: A first-order reaction runs in spherical pellets with Thiele modulus φ = {{phi}} and mass Biot number $Bi = k_cR/D_e$ = {{Bi}}. What is the overall effectiveness factor Ω (rate over k C_bulk V)?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Resistances in series: the film sets the surface concentration, the pellet works at η of that. Large φ and small Bi together make the film control

problems.prompt: Spherical pellets have Thiele modulus φ = {{phi}} and mass Biot number {{Bi}} (first order). What is the surface concentration as a fraction of the bulk?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: C_s near 1: the film is negligible. Near 0: external mass transfer controls and the pellet interior hardly matters

problems.prompt: A gas dissolves into a liquid where it reacts (pseudo-first order, k = {{k}} s⁻¹, D = {{Dm}} × 10⁻⁹ m²/s, $k_L$ = {{kl}} × 10⁻⁴ m/s). What is the enhancement factor E?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Ha < 0.3: slow reaction, bulk liquid matters, E ≈ 1. Ha > 3: reaction finishes inside the film and E ≈ Ha, so the rate no longer depends on k_L

problems.prompt: Gas absorption with pseudo-first-order reaction: k = {{k}} s⁻¹, D = {{Dm}} × 10⁻⁹ m²/s, $k_L$ = {{kl}} × 10⁻⁴ m/s. Which regime applies?

parts.label: v
choice: Slow (Ha < 0.3): reaction in the bulk liquid
parts.explain: Ha² compares reaction in the film to diffusion across it; in the fast regime interfacial area, not liquid volume, sets the rate

problems.prompt: In a slurry reactor, the dissolved-gas concentration at saturation is {{ci}} mol/m³. Gas absorption $k_ba_b$ = {{kb}} s⁻¹, liquid-to-particle $k_ca_p$ = {{kc}} s⁻¹ and surface reaction $\eta k a_p$ = {{kr}} s⁻¹ (all per reactor volume). What is the overall rate, in mol/(m³·s)?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: At steady state the same rate crosses every step, so the driving forces add and the resistances add. The largest 1/k term is the one to attack

expect.v: solve([Eq(Symbol('rr'), nsimplify(kb)*(ci - Symbol('cb'))), Eq(Symbol('rr'), nsimplify(kc)*(Symbol('cb') - Symbol('cs'))), Eq(Symbol('rr'), nsimplify(kr)*Symbol('cs'))], [Symbol('rr'), Symbol('cb'), Symbol('cs')])[Symbol('rr')]

problems.prompt: In a slurry reactor, gas absorption $k_ba_b$ = {{kb}}, liquid-to-particle $k_ca_p$ = {{kc}} and surface reaction $\eta ka_p$ = {{kr}} s⁻¹. What fraction of the total resistance is gas absorption?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Plotting C_i/r against 1/(catalyst loading) separates the absorption term (intercept) from the particle terms (slope)

problems.prompt: A batch reaction is first order (k = {{k}} h⁻¹) on a catalyst whose activity decays first order ($k_d$ = {{kd}} h⁻¹). What conversion is reached after {{t}} h?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Conversion levels off at 1 − e^{−k/k_d} however long you wait: once the catalyst is dead, time buys nothing

problems.prompt: A first-order batch reaction (k = {{k}} h⁻¹) runs on a catalyst decaying with $k_d$ = {{kd}} h⁻¹. What is the highest conversion it can ever reach?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: The catalyst can do only k/k_d 'first-order lifetimes' of work; to go further you must regenerate or replace it

problems.prompt: A first-order process with τ = {{tau}} min gets a step input. How long, in minutes, until the output has made {{p}}% of its final change?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: The fraction remaining decays as e^{−t/τ} whatever the gain or the step size

problems.prompt: A first-order process (K = 1, τ = {{tau}} min) is driven by a ramp input. Once transients die out, by how many minutes does the output lag the input?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: A first-order lag follows a ramp at the same slope but τ behind: a quick way to read τ from plant data

problems.prompt: A second-order process with damping ratio ζ = {{z}} gets a step. What is its fractional overshoot?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Overshoot depends only on ζ; τ stretches time but not height. ζ = 0.5 gives about 16%, a common tuning target

problems.prompt: A second-order process overshoots by {{os}}% after a step. What is its damping ratio ζ?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Invert OS = exp(−πζ/√(1 − ζ²)); reading ζ from a step test is how a process is identified

problems.prompt: A first-order process (gain K = {{K}}) is under proportional control with $K_c$ = {{Kc}}. After a unit setpoint step, what fraction of the step remains as steady-state offset?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: A proportional controller needs an error to hold any output, so some offset remains; integral action removes it

problems.prompt: A first-order process has gain K = {{K}}. What proportional gain $K_c$ keeps the setpoint offset at {{e}}% of the step?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Offset falls as 1/(1 + KK_c), but high gain costs stability once lags and dead time are present

problems.prompt: A process $G = K/[({{t1}}s + 1)({{t2}}s + 1)({{t3}}s + 1)]$ is under proportional control. Above what loop gain $K K_c$ does the loop go unstable?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Routh gives the same: with $a_3s^3 + a_2s^2 + a_1s + 1 + KK_c$, stability needs $a_1a_2 > a_3(1 + KK_c)$. Three equal lags give 8

problems.prompt: A process $K/[({{t1}}s + 1)({{t2}}s + 1)({{t3}}s + 1)]$ runs under proportional control with loop gain $KK_c$ = {{kk}}. Is the closed loop stable?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Compare with the ultimate gain from Routh or s = iω; well-separated lags allow a much higher gain than equal ones

choices.v: 0 if kk < gc_ultimate(t1, t2, t3) else 1

problems.prompt: For $G = K/[({{t1}}s + 1)({{t2}}s + 1)({{t3}}s + 1)]$ (times in min) under proportional control, what is the ultimate period, in minutes? (Ziegler–Nichols would then set the PI reset time to P_u/1.2.)

parts.label: v
parts.explain: At the ultimate gain the loop oscillates steadily at the frequency where the phase lag is 180°

problems.prompt: For $G = K/[({{t1}}s + 1)({{t2}}s + 1)({{t3}}s + 1)]$ (min), what reset time τ_I, in minutes, do the Ziegler–Nichols PI rules give (τ_I = P_u/1.2)?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Ziegler–Nichols tunes from the ultimate gain and period; it gives quarter-decay responses, aggressive by modern standards

problems.prompt: A first-order process (K = {{K}}, τ = {{tau}} s) is driven by a sinusoid of {{w}} rad/s. What is the amplitude ratio?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Replace s by iω and take the modulus. Well above the corner frequency 1/τ the process filters the input out

problems.prompt: A first-order process (τ = {{tau}} s) is driven at {{w}} rad/s. What is the phase lag of the output, in degrees?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: A first-order lag never exceeds 90°; 45° at the corner frequency ω = 1/τ

problems.prompt: A process $e^{-{{th}}s}/({{tau}}s + 1)$ (times in min) is under proportional control. At what frequency, in rad/min, is the phase lag 180°?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Dead time adds lag without lowering the amplitude, so it limits how hard the loop can be pushed: the ultimate gain is $\sqrt{1 + \omega_u^2\tau^2}/K$

problems.prompt: A process $Ke^{-{{th}}s}/({{tau}}s + 1)$ (min) under P control: what is the ultimate loop gain $KK_{cu}$?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: At the crossover frequency the loop gain must be 1/AR; dead time lowers the crossover and so the allowable gain

problems.prompt: A still holds a binary with relative volatility α = {{al}} at light-key mole fraction {{x0}}. Simple batch distillation continues until the liquid is at {{x1}}. What fraction of the original charge remains?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Each bit of vapour leaves richer than the liquid, so the pot strips the light key gradually; a small α needs most of the charge boiled off

problems.prompt: Batch distillation with α = {{al}} takes the still from {{x0}} to {{x1}}. What is the average light-key mole fraction of the collected distillate?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: A light-key balance on the whole batch: what left the still is the distillate

expect.v: (nsimplify(x0) - nsimplify(x1)*gc_rayleigh(al, x0, x1))/(1 - gc_rayleigh(al, x0, x1))

problems.prompt: A gas with {{yin}}% solute is scrubbed to {{yout}}% with solute-free liquid; equilibrium is y = {{m}}x. What is the minimum L/G?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: At minimum flow the liquid leaving is in equilibrium with the gas entering: a pinch at the rich end and infinitely many stages. Practice uses 1.2–1.5 times the minimum

problems.prompt: An absorber takes y from {{yin}}% to {{yout}}% with solute-free liquid at 1.5 times the minimum L/G (equilibrium y = {{m}}x). What is the exit liquid mole fraction?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: More liquid than the minimum leaves it less loaded: here at two-thirds of the equilibrium value

problems.prompt: A column runs at reflux ratio R = {{R}} with distillate $x_D$ = {{xd}}. The feed (z = {{z}}) is {{f}}% vapour by moles. At what x do the q-line and the rectifying line cross?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: q is the liquid fraction of the feed (1 − vapour fraction). Saturated liquid (q = 1) gives a vertical q-line at x = z; saturated vapour a horizontal one at y = z

expect.v: solve(Eq((1 - Rational(f, 100))*x/(-Rational(f, 100)) - nsimplify(z)/(-Rational(f, 100)), nsimplify(R)*x/(nsimplify(R) + 1) + nsimplify(xd)/(nsimplify(R) + 1)), x)[0]

problems.prompt: A feed is {{f}}% vapour (by moles), saturated. What is the slope of its q-line on the McCabe–Thiele diagram?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: q = 1 − vapour fraction; the q-line is vertical for saturated liquid, horizontal for saturated vapour, and negative in between

problems.prompt: A channel of length {{L}} cm carries a solution at {{U}} cm/s; the solute diffusivity is {{D}}e-5 cm²/s. What is the Péclet number UL/D?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Pe compares convection with diffusion over the whole length. Large Pe does not license dropping diffusion outright: it confines it to a boundary layer, which is the distinction between a regular and a singular limit

problems.prompt: At Pe = {{pe}}, what is the ratio of the diffusive term to the convective term in the scaled equation?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: One over Pe multiplies the diffusive term once the equation is scaled on the channel length. A tiny coefficient on the highest derivative is the warning that the limit is singular, not regular

problems.prompt: A solute of diffusivity {{D}}e-5 cm²/s sits in a flow of {{U}} cm/s. Below what length, in micrometres, does diffusion carry more than convection?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: The crossover length is where the dimensionless group is one. Every scaling argument is this: a group of order one marks the length, time or concentration at which the physics changes hands

problems.prompt: Over a length of {{L}} micrometres, above what velocity, in cm/s, does convection beat diffusion for a solute of diffusivity {{D}}e-5 cm²/s?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: The same balance read the other way. In a microchannel the crossover velocity is high enough that diffusion often wins, which is why mixing there has to be engineered

problems.prompt: Flow over a plate of length {{L}} cm has Re_L = {{Re}}. From the scaling δ/L ~ Re^(-1/2), how thick is the momentum boundary layer at the trailing edge, in millimetres?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Scaling gets the exponent and the order of magnitude for free; the Blasius solution only fixes the constant (δ ≈ 5.0 L/√Re). Knowing which part needs the full solution is the point

problems.prompt: At Pr = {{pr}}, what is the ratio of the thermal to the momentum boundary-layer thickness, taking $\delta_T/\delta \sim Pr^{-1/3}$?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: A liquid metal (small Pr) carries heat far outside the momentum layer; an oil (large Pr) keeps it well inside. The exponent comes from the scaling, not from a correlation

problems.prompt: The root near 1 of $x^2 + \varepsilon x - 1 = 0$ is expanded as $x = x_0 + \varepsilon x_1 + O(\varepsilon^2)$. For ε = {{ep}}, what does the two-term expansion give?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: A regular perturbation works because the ε → 0 problem has the same character as the full one. The exact root is $(-\varepsilon + \sqrt{\varepsilon^2 + 4})/2$, so the error is $O(\varepsilon^2)$

problems.prompt: For $x^2 + \varepsilon x - 1 = 0$ at ε = {{ep}}, by how much does the two-term expansion $1 - \varepsilon/2$ differ from the exact root $(-\varepsilon + \sqrt{\varepsilon^2 + 4})/2$?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: The error falls as ε², so halving ε quarters it. Checking an expansion against a case you can solve exactly is how you learn to trust it where you cannot

problems.prompt: In $\varepsilon y'' + y' + y = 0$ on $0 \le x \le 1$ with ε = {{ep}}, the inner variable is $X = x/\varepsilon$. Over what fraction of the domain, as a percentage, does the inner layer span three inner units?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Setting ε = 0 drops the second derivative and with it one boundary condition, which is the signature of a singular limit. The lost condition is recovered in a layer whose thickness is the ε that multiplies the highest derivative

problems.prompt: An inner layer of thickness ε = {{ep}} (dimensionless) carries a unit change in y. What is the gradient dy/dx across it?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Thin layers mean steep gradients, which is why a uniform mesh resolves a singular problem badly: the grid has to be refined where the layer is, and knowing where that is comes from the scaling rather than from the solver

problems.prompt: A species of diffusivity {{D}}e-5 cm²/s diffuses into a quiescent half-space for {{tm}} minutes. Taking the penetration depth as √(4Dt), how deep is it in millimetres?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Two variables collapse into one because the half-space has no length scale of its own. The depth going as √t, not t, is the whole content of the similarity solution

problems.prompt: How long, in seconds, does a species of diffusivity {{D}}e-5 cm²/s take to penetrate {{dm}} mm, taking the depth as √(4Dt)?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Time goes as depth squared, so ten times the depth costs a hundred times the wait. That scaling is why diffusion-limited processes are run thin

problems.prompt: A slab of half-thickness {{h}} mm has diffusivity {{D}}e-5 cm²/s. Beyond what time, in seconds, does the semi-infinite similarity solution stop applying?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Every similarity solution rests on there being no length scale to compare with. This is the assumption IChemE Level F asks to be checked: past this time the slab is finite and an eigenfunction expansion takes over

problems.prompt: A slab of half-thickness h has diffusivity D. At the moment √(4Dt) first reaches h, what is the Fourier number $Dt/h^2$?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: The semi-infinite and one-term treatments meet near Fo of a few tenths: below it the series needs many terms and similarity is easier, above it one term suffices. Neither description is good at Fo ≈ 0.25, which is where numerical work earns its place

problems.prompt: A sphere of radius {{R}} mm with diffusivity {{D}}e-5 cm²/s is released into a bath. What is the time constant $R^2/(\pi^2 D)$ of its slowest mode, in seconds?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: In a sphere the substitution u = rc turns the problem Cartesian, so the eigenvalues are nπ/R in closed form. A cylinder has no such luck: its eigenvalues are the zeros of J₀, which have to be looked up or computed

problems.prompt: A sphere of radius R and a slab of half-thickness R share a diffusivity. What is the ratio of the slab's slowest time constant to the sphere's?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: The slab's slowest eigenvalue is π/(2R) and the sphere's is π/R, and the time constant goes as the inverse square, so the slab is four times slower. More surface per unit volume empties faster

problems.prompt: In a slab's eigenfunction expansion the terms carry $\exp(-n^2\pi^2 Fo/4)$. At Fo = {{fo}}, what is the ratio of the second term's exponential to the first's?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: The series is its own error estimate. Early in the transient every term matters and the series converges slowly, which is exactly when the similarity solution is the right tool instead

problems.prompt: Terms in a slab expansion carry $\exp(-n^2\pi^2 Fo/4)$. At Fo = {{fo}}, what is the smallest n whose exponential falls below {{tolp}}% of the first term's?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Early in a transient the series needs many terms, and a one-term formula applied there is simply wrong. Asking how many terms a tolerance costs is the habit that stops that

problems.prompt: A linear system has eigenvalues −{{lf}} and −{{ls}} per second. What is the largest forward-Euler step, in milliseconds, that stays stable?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: The slow mode sets how long you must integrate and the fast one sets how small each step may be; their ratio is the stiffness. This is why a stiff problem needs an implicit solver rather than a smaller tolerance

problems.prompt: A system has eigenvalues −{{lf}} and −{{ls}} per second. How many forward-Euler steps does covering three slow time constants take, at the stability limit?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: The step count is three halves of the stiffness ratio, so a ratio of 1e5 means millions of steps for an answer that is nearly constant. That is the whole case for implicit methods

problems.prompt: A linear system has condition number 1e{{k}} and the arithmetic carries about 16 significant digits. Roughly how many correct digits remain in the solution?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: The solver did not fail and will report no error: it returns a full set of digits, most of them meaningless. Recognising that a result is conditioning-limited rather than wrong is the Level F skill, since the software cannot tell you

problems.prompt: A solve returns a relative residual of 1e-{{r}} on a system with condition number 1e{{k}}. What is the bound on the relative error in the solution, as a power of ten (give the exponent)?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: A small residual does not mean a small error: the condition number sits between them. Software reports the residual because it can compute it, and reports nothing about the error because it cannot

problems.prompt: A forward difference is evaluated in arithmetic with machine epsilon 1e-{{e}}. At roughly what step h, as a power of ten (give the exponent), is the total error least?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Shrinking h past this point makes the answer worse, which surprises people who expect smaller steps to be strictly better. A central difference has error O(h²) + O(ε/h) and does better, at h ≈ ε^(1/3)

problems.prompt: Halving the step takes the error from {{e1}}e-4 to {{e2}}e-5. What is the observed order of convergence?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Measuring the order on two grids checks the implementation against the method's claim. An order that comes out below the advertised one usually means a boundary condition is only first-order accurate

problems.prompt: Two points on a sphere of radius {{kr}} km subtend an angle of {{kd}}° at the centre. Find the great-circle distance between them.

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Arc length is radius times angle in radians. Any two points that are not antipodal lie on exactly one great circle

problems.prompt: Two great circles on a sphere of radius {{kr}} meet at an angle of {{kd}}°. Find the area of one of the lunes between them.

parts.label: v
parts.explain: A lune is the fraction θ/2π of the whole sphere's area 4πR², which is 2θR²

problems.prompt: A triangle on a sphere of radius {{kr}} has angles {{k1}}°, {{k2}}° and {{k3}}°. Find its area.

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Area = excess × R², with the excess α + β + γ − π in radians. The octant with three right angles has excess π/2 and is one eighth of the sphere

expect.v: solve(Eq((k1 + k2 + k3)*pi/180, pi + Symbol('m')/kr**2), Symbol('m'))[0]

problems.prompt: A triangle on the unit sphere has area {{ka}} and two angles of {{k1}}° and {{k2}}°. Find the third angle in degrees.

parts.label: v
parts.explain: The three angles sum to π plus the area on a unit sphere, so the third angle is π + A minus the other two

expect.v: solve(Eq((k1 + k2 + Symbol('m'))*pi/180 - pi, nsimplify(ka)), Symbol('m'))[0]

cases.q: Every orientation-preserving isometry of the sphere is:
cases.o2: A reflection in a great circle

cases.q: The antipodal map x ↦ −x of the 2-sphere is:
The rotation group of the cube has order:
The rotation group of the icosahedron is isomorphic to:
Besides cyclic and dihedral groups, how many finite rotation groups of the sphere are there?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: The five Platonic solids give only three groups, because the cube and octahedron are dual, as are the dodecahedron and icosahedron

problems.prompt: A sphere is tiled by congruent spherical triangles with angles π/2, π/3 and π/{{kn}}. How many triangles are there?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Each triangle has area equal to its excess on the unit sphere, and together they cover 4π. The counts 24, 48 and 120 are the orders of the full symmetry groups of the tetrahedron, cube and icosahedron

problems.prompt: In the upper half-plane model, find the hyperbolic distance between the points {{ka}}i and {{kb}}i.

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Along the vertical geodesic the length element is dy/y, so the distance is ln(b/a). Equal Euclidean steps count for more the closer they are to the boundary

cases.q: In the upper half-plane model, the geodesics are vertical lines and:
cases.o1: Semicircles centred on the real axis
cases.o4: Circles tangent to the real axis

cases.q: In the Poincaré disc model, the geodesics are diameters and:
cases.o1: Circular arcs meeting the boundary circle at right angles

cases.q: Both Poincaré models are conformal, meaning that they show correctly:
The boundary of the Poincaré disc is, in hyperbolic terms:
cases.o1: Infinitely far from every interior point

cases.q: The isometries of the upper half-plane that preserve orientation are the Möbius maps z ↦ (az + b)/(cz + d) with a, b, c, d:

parts.label: v
parts.explain: The models distort lengths but not angles, which is why hyperbolic triangles can be read off a picture

problems.prompt: A triangle in the hyperbolic plane has angles {{k1}}°, {{k2}}° and {{k3}}°. Find its area.

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Area = π minus the angle sum, in radians. Unlike in the plane, the angles determine the size: similar triangles are congruent

expect.v: solve(Eq((k1 + k2 + k3)*pi/180, pi - Symbol('m')), Symbol('m'))[0]

problems.prompt: Through a point not on a given line, how many lines never meet the given line in {{gm}}?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Any two great circles meet, so the sphere has no parallels. In the hyperbolic plane there are two limiting parallels and infinitely many ultraparallels between them

problems.prompt: On the unit sphere, find the circumference of a circle of geodesic radius {{kr}}.

parts.label: v
parts.explain: At polar angle r the circle of latitude has Euclidean radius sin r. The circumference grows until the equator and then shrinks

problems.prompt: In the hyperbolic plane, find the circumference of a circle of geodesic radius {{kr}}.

parts.label: v
parts.explain: The hyperbolic circumference is 2π sinh r, which grows exponentially with the radius: most of a hyperbolic disc is near its edge

problems.prompt: Find the Gaussian curvature of a sphere of radius {{kr}}.

parts.label: v
parts.explain: K = 1/R². The same number comes out of how much a small circle's circumference falls short of 2πr: K = lim 3(2πr − C)/(πr³)

cases.sf: a cone away from its tip
the outer rim of a torus
the inner rim of a torus

problems.prompt: The Gaussian curvature of {{sf}} is:

parts.label: v
parts.explain: A cylinder and a cone unroll flat without stretching, so their Gaussian curvature is zero although they look curved. Gaussian curvature is what a flat map cannot remove

problems.prompt: Find the total curvature ∫ K dA of a closed orientable surface of genus {{kg}}.

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Gauss-Bonnet: the total is 2π times the Euler characteristic 2 − 2g, whatever the surface's shape

problems.prompt: A geodesic triangle of area {{ka}} lies on a surface of constant curvature {{kc}}. Find the sum of its angles in degrees.

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Angle sum = π + K × area. Positive curvature opens triangles up, negative curvature pinches them

problems.prompt: Two towns lie on the same meridian of a sphere of radius {{kr}} km, at latitudes {{k1}}° N and {{k2}}° N. Find the great-circle distance between them.

parts.label: v
parts.explain: A meridian is a great circle, so the central angle is the difference in latitude

problems.prompt: Find the central angle in degrees between the points at latitude {{k1}}°, longitude {{o1}}° and latitude {{k2}}°, longitude {{o2}}° on a sphere.

parts.label: v
parts.explain: cos c = sin φ₁ sin φ₂ + cos φ₁ cos φ₂ cos Δλ

problems.prompt: Find the length of the circle of latitude {{kd}}° on a sphere of radius {{kr}}.

parts.label: v
parts.explain: The parallel is a circle of radius R cos φ

problems.prompt: Two points lie at latitude 60° on a unit sphere, {{kd}}° of longitude apart. How much longer is the route along the parallel than the great-circle route?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Along the parallel the length is cos 60° × Δλ; the great-circle route is the central angle, which is shorter

problems.prompt: Find the area of the cap of a sphere of radius {{kr}} lying within angular radius {{kd}}° of the north pole.

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Integrate the area element R² sin θ dθ dφ, or use 2πR × height with height R(1 − cos θ)

problems.prompt: What fraction of a sphere's surface lies north of latitude {{kd}}°?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: By Archimedes the area between two latitudes is proportional to the difference of their heights sin φ

problems.prompt: In the upper half-plane with metric (dx² + dy²)/y², find the length of the horizontal segment from ({{ka}}, {{ky}}) to ({{kb}}, {{ky}}).

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Along a horizontal line y is constant, so every Euclidean length is divided by y

problems.prompt: In the upper half-plane, find the hyperbolic length of the vertical segment from height {{ka}} to height {{kb}}.

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Integrate dy/y. Halving both heights leaves the length unchanged, which is why the boundary is infinitely far away

problems.prompt: In the upper half-plane, the geodesic through ({{k1}}, {{k2}}) and ({{k3}}, {{k4}}) is a semicircle centred on the real axis. Find the x-coordinate of its centre.

parts.label: v
parts.explain: The centre is the point of the real axis at equal Euclidean distance from both points

expect.v: solve(Eq((k1 - Symbol('m'))**2 + k2**2, (k3 - Symbol('m'))**2 + k4**2), Symbol('m'))[0]

problems.prompt: In the upper half-plane, the geodesic through ({{k1}}, {{k2}}) and ({{k3}}, {{k4}}) is a semicircle centred on the real axis. Find its Euclidean radius.

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Find the centre on the real axis first, then the radius is its distance to either point

problems.prompt: In the upper half-plane, find the hyperbolic area of the region {{ka}} ≤ x ≤ {{kb}}, y ≥ {{kh}}.

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Integrate dx dy / y²: the y-integral from h to infinity is 1/h, so the area is width/h, finite even though the region is unbounded

problems.prompt: A geodesic {{kn}}-gon in the hyperbolic plane has every interior angle equal to {{kd}}°. Find its area.

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Cut the polygon into n − 2 triangles: its area is the Euclidean angle sum (n − 2)π minus the actual angle sum

problems.prompt: A geodesic triangle on a surface of constant curvature has angles summing to {{ks}}° and area {{ka}}. Find the curvature.

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Excess (in radians) equals curvature times area; an angle sum below 180° gives negative curvature

problems.prompt: Surveyors on a spherical planet measure a triangle of area {{ka}} km² whose angles sum to {{ks}}°. Find the planet's radius in km.

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Area = excess × R², so R = √(area/excess) with the excess in radians

problems.prompt: On a surface, a geodesic circle of radius {{kr}} has circumference {{kc}}. Estimate the curvature from K ≈ 3(2πr − C)/(πr³).

parts.label: v
parts.explain: The formula inverts C ≈ 2πr(1 − Kr²/6). A circumference short of 2πr means positive curvature

problems.prompt: On a sphere of radius {{kb}}, a circle is drawn with geodesic radius {{kr}}. By what fraction is its circumference shorter than 2πr?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: The circle's true radius in space is R sin(r/R), so its circumference is 2πR sin(r/R); for small r the shortfall is about r²/(6R²)

A C4 axis, four perpendicular C2 axes and a horizontal mirror
A regular octahedron

parts.label: a
parts.explain: {{why}}

problems.prompt: How many symmetry operations are in ${{g}}$ (the order $h$ of the group)?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: $C_{nv}$ and $C_{nh}$ have $2n$ operations, $D_{nh}$ and $D_{nd}$ have $4n$; $T_d$ has 24, $O_h$ 48, $C_s$ 2. $h$ is what you divide by when reducing a representation

problems.prompt: How many mirror planes does a molecule in ${{g}}$ have?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: $C_{nv}$: $n$ vertical planes. $C_{nh}$: the one horizontal plane. $D_{nh}$: $n$ vertical plus one horizontal. $D_{nd}$: $n$ dihedral. $T_d$ has 6 and $O_h$ has 9

problems.prompt: In $C_{2v}$ (water, $C_2$ along $z$): which single operation equals ${{ta}}$ followed by ${{tb}}$?

parts.label: a
parts.explain: Track a point $(x, y, z)$: $C_2$ flips the signs of $x$ and $y$, $\sigma_v(xz)$ flips $y$, $\sigma_v'(yz)$ flips $x$. Apply both and see which single operation gives the same signs. Every operation here is its own inverse

problems.prompt: In $C_{2v}$ a reducible representation has characters $\chi(E) = {{g1}}$, $\chi(C_2) = {{g2}}$, $\chi(\sigma_v) = {{g3}}$, $\chi(\sigma_v') = {{g4}}$. How many times does ${{irr}}$ appear? (${{irr}}$ has characters $1, {{c2}}, {{c3}}, {{c4}}$.)

In $C_{3v}$ (classes $E$, $2C_3$, $3\sigma_v$) a reducible representation has characters ${{g1}}$, ${{g2}}$, ${{g3}}$. How many times does ${{irr}}$ appear? (${{irr}}$ has characters ${{d}}, {{c2}}, {{c3}}$.)

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Weight each class by its size, with $h = 6$: $\tfrac16\left[1({{g1}})({{d}}) + 2({{g2}})({{c2}}) + 3({{g3}})({{c3}})\right]$

problems.prompt: How many vibrational normal modes does {{m}} have?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: $3N$ coordinates, less 3 translations and 3 rotations: $3N - 6$. A linear molecule has only 2 rotations, so $3N - 5$. Here $N = {{N}}$

cases.why: Symmetric stretch and bend are both A1; the antisymmetric stretch is B2 (with the molecule in the yz plane)
Two totally symmetric modes and two doubly degenerate pairs: 2 + 2(2) = 6
One A1, one doubly degenerate E and two triply degenerate T2: 1 + 2 + 2(3) = 9
Symmetric stretch, antisymmetric stretch, and a doubly degenerate bend: 1 + 1 + 2 = 4

problems.prompt: Symmetries of the vibrational modes of {{m}}?

parts.label: a
parts.explain: {{why}}. Check the count: the degeneracies must add up to the number of modes

cases.why: The dipole stays zero but the polarizability changes. CO2 has a centre of inversion, so no mode is both
The dipole changes; with a centre of inversion an IR-active mode is Raman-inactive
Bending creates a dipole perpendicular to the axis; mutual exclusion makes it Raman-inactive
A1 in C2v transforms like z and like x², y², z², and there is no centre of inversion
A homonuclear diatomic has no dipole at any bond length, but its polarizability changes
The dipole and the polarizability both change with bond length
Totally symmetric modes are always Raman-active; g modes in a centrosymmetric molecule are never IR-active
In Td only T2 modes transform like x, y, z, so A1 is IR-inactive; it is Raman-active
T2 in Td transforms like (x, y, z) and like (xy, xz, yz)

problems.prompt: Is {{m}} IR-active, Raman-active, or both?

parts.label: a
parts.explain: {{why}}. IR needs a mode that transforms like x, y or z (a changing dipole); Raman needs one that transforms like a product such as x² or xy (a changing polarizability)

cases.q: The wrist is ____ to the elbow.
The nose is ____ to the ears.
The sternum is ____ to the vertebral column.
The knee is ____ to the ankle.
