problems.prompt: Three criteria weigh {{w1}}, {{w2}} and {{w3}} per cent. A project scores {{s1}}, {{s2}} and {{s3}} out of 10. What is its weighted score out of 10?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: A weighted model makes the trade-off explicit, which is its only real benefit: the weights are the decision and the scores are evidence, so the weights are agreed before the scores are seen

problems.prompt: Projects cost {{c1}}, {{c2}} and {{c3}} thousand with weighted scores {{v1}}, {{v2}} and {{v3}}. Under a budget of {{bg}} thousand, what is the highest total score obtainable?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Ranking by score alone overspends; ranking by score per unit cost is a good heuristic but not always optimal, which is why a small portfolio is worth enumerating

expect.v: Max(nsimplify(v1) + nsimplify(v2) if c1 + c2 <= bg else 0, nsimplify(v1) + nsimplify(v3) if c1 + c3 <= bg else 0, nsimplify(v2) + nsimplify(v3) if c2 + c3 <= bg else 0, nsimplify(v1) if c1 <= bg else 0, nsimplify(v2) if c2 <= bg else 0, nsimplify(v3) if c3 <= bg else 0)

cases.q: Decisions made by business-unit leaders without central IT are the:
Decisions made jointly by IT and one business group are the:
IT infrastructure decisions are usually best placed with:
cases.o1: IT, because the decision is about shared capability rather than one unit's needs

cases.q: Application-needs decisions are usually best placed with:
cases.o1: The business unit that will use the application, with IT input

cases.q: Letting every unit decide its own IT principles produces:
cases.o1: Anarchy, with incompatible choices nobody can integrate later

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Five domains and five archetypes; the useful question is which combination a firm actually uses, against which it says it uses

cases.q: A board wants assurance that IT decisions are governed and measured. Which framework addresses it?
A service desk needs defined incident, problem and change practices. Which?
A firm wants a certifiable information security management system. Which?
A firm wants a common language for describing and improving its cybersecurity posture, not a certificate. Which?
A firm needs a method for developing an enterprise architecture. Which?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Each framework answers one question; naming the wrong one is how a governance programme becomes a documentation exercise

cases.q: A RACI row with no A is defective because:
cases.o1: Nobody is accountable, so the task has no owner when it slips

cases.q: A RACI row with two A's is defective because:
cases.o1: Accountability is shared, which in practice means neither holds it

cases.q: A RACI row with no R is defective because:
cases.o1: Nobody is doing the work, only overseeing it
cases.o4: It is fine if A exists

cases.q: A RACI with everyone marked C on everything signals:
cases.o1: A process that will be slow, because consultation is unbounded

cases.q: Exactly one A per row matters because:
cases.o1: It names the single person answerable for the outcome

parts.label: v
parts.explain: One A, at least one R, and consultation kept bounded: the defects are what the matrix exists to expose

cases.q: A canonical data model belongs to which architecture domain?
A capability map belongs to:
A network topology diagram belongs to:
Which ADM phase establishes the architecture vision?
cases.o1: The phase that comes immediately after the preliminary phase

cases.q: An architecture requirements document is produced:
cases.o1: Across the method, since requirements management runs through every phase

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Four domains for four kinds of artefact, and requirements management runs through all of it

problems.prompt: A capability map scores {{nc}} capabilities; {{nh}} are both high-value and low-maturity. If investment goes only to those, what fraction of the map is funded (per cent)?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Heat-mapping is a way of refusing to fund everything: the point of the map is that most capabilities are adequate and should be left alone

cases.q: An application of high business value and poor technical fit should be:
cases.o1: Migrated, keeping the value and replacing the platform

cases.q: An application of low business value and good technical fit should be:
cases.o1: Tolerated: it works and is not worth touching

cases.q: An application of high business value and good technical fit should be:
An application of low business value and poor technical fit should be:

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Value against fit gives four verdicts, and the useful one is Tolerate: most of a portfolio should be left alone

problems.prompt: Connecting {{nn}} systems point to point needs how many more links than connecting each to one hub?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Point-to-point links grow as the square and hub links linearly, which is the whole argument for a broker or a bus; the hub's cost is that it becomes a single point of failure and a bottleneck for change

cases.q: Two systems needing a reliable hand-off with neither available at the same time argue for:
cases.o1: Messaging, which decouples them in time

cases.q: A nightly bulk extract to a reporting system argues for:
cases.o1: File transfer, which is simple and adequate

cases.q: Many consumers each needing the same stream of state changes argue for:
cases.o1: Event streaming, where consumers read at their own pace

cases.q: A shared database between two applications is discouraged because:
cases.o1: Neither can change its schema without breaking the other

cases.q: A synchronous API call couples the caller to:

parts.label: v
parts.explain: The style is chosen on coupling: in time, in schema, and in availability

cases.q: Moving a virtual machine to the cloud unchanged is:
Moving to a managed database without changing the application code is:
Rewriting an application as cloud-native services is:
Replacing an in-house application with a SaaS product is:
Switching an application off because nobody uses it is:
cases.o1: Retiring, and it is often the highest-return move in a migration

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Six verdicts, and the two that cost nothing — retire and retain — are the ones a migration plan should start with

cases.q: In BPMN, a pool represents:
cases.o1: A participant or organisation in the process

cases.q: An exclusive gateway means:
cases.o1: Exactly one outgoing path is taken

cases.q: A hand-off between two lanes typically causes delay because:
cases.o1: Work waits in a queue for the other party to pick it up

cases.q: A parallel gateway means:
cases.o1: All outgoing paths are taken and must rejoin
cases.o3: The process waits for a message

parts.label: v
parts.explain: The notation matters less than the hand-offs it exposes: queue time between lanes is where process cycle time actually goes

cases.q: A well-formed acceptance criterion is:
cases.o1: Testable, so that it can be shown to pass or fail

cases.q: A use case's extensions capture:
cases.o1: The alternative and exception flows, not the happy path

cases.q: A user story that says what the user wants but not why is missing:
cases.o1: The benefit, which is what lets the team propose a cheaper way to get it

cases.q: Preconditions in a use case state:
cases.o1: What must be true before the flow can start

parts.label: v
parts.explain: The format is a prompt for the parts that get left out: the why, the exceptions, and how anyone will know it is done

cases.q: In MoSCoW, a Must is defined by:
cases.o1: The release having no value without it

cases.q: If every requirement is a Must, the prioritisation has:
cases.o1: Failed, because nothing can be dropped when the schedule slips

cases.q: In the Kano model, a feature whose absence angers users but whose presence is unremarked is:
A Kano delighter is characterised by:
cases.o1: Raising satisfaction when present but not reducing it when absent

cases.q: The point of prioritising is to decide:
cases.o1: What falls out of the release when time runs short

parts.label: v
parts.explain: A priority order is only real if it survives a schedule slip, which is the test a list of all-Musts fails

problems.prompt: Activities A ({{a}} days) then B ({{b}}) then D ({{d}}) run in parallel with A then C ({{c}}) then D. What is the project duration (days)?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: The duration follows the longest path, so shortening the shorter branch changes nothing: that is what slack means, and why crashing the wrong activity buys no time

problems.prompt: On the same network, how much slack does the shorter of the two parallel branches have (days)?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Slack is how much an activity can slip before it joins the critical path; an activity with zero slack is on it, and a network where almost everything has zero slack has no room anywhere

problems.prompt: A project reports planned value {{pv}}, earned value {{ev}} and actual cost {{ac}} thousand. What is its cost performance index?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Below one means the work done cost more than it was budgeted at; the schedule index compares earned with planned, and a project can be ahead on one and behind on the other

problems.prompt: With earned value {{ev}}, actual cost {{ac}} and a total budget of {{bac}} thousand, what is the estimate at completion assuming current efficiency continues (thousand)?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Dividing the budget by the cost performance index projects today's efficiency to the end, which is the forecast a steering group should be given rather than the original budget restated

cases.q: Releasing to a small fraction of users first and watching the metrics is:
Running the new and old systems side by side on the same inputs is:
cases.o1: Parallel running, which is expensive but lets results be compared

cases.q: Keeping two identical production environments and switching traffic between them is:
A big-bang cutover is chosen when:
cases.o1: Running two versions at once is impossible, for instance with a single shared ledger

cases.q: A hybrid delivery approach suits a project where:
cases.o1: Some parts have fixed requirements and others need discovery

parts.label: v
parts.explain: The strategy follows what can run in parallel and what has to be switched, not team preference

cases.q: A domain of highly interrelated entities with heavy transaction integrity needs:
cases.o1: A relational database with enforced constraints

cases.q: Sensor readings arriving continuously and queried by time window need:
A domain whose queries are mostly about relationships several hops deep needs:
A conceptual model differs from a logical model by:
cases.o1: Naming entities and relationships without committing to a technology

parts.label: v
parts.explain: The access pattern picks the technology; the conceptual model is written before any of that is decided

problems.prompt: A table of {{nr}} rows has {{nb}} rows with a blank required field, {{ni}} with an invalid value and {{nd}} duplicates. What is its completeness (per cent)?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: The four dimensions are measured separately because they have different causes: completeness points at capture, validity at the form, uniqueness at matching, and timeliness at the pipeline

problems.prompt: The same table: {{nr}} rows with {{nd}} duplicates. What is its uniqueness score (per cent)?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Duplicates are the dimension that silently inflates every count built on the table, which is why they are found by matching rules rather than by a constraint

cases.q: Who decides who may access a data domain and for what purpose?
cases.o1: The data owner, who is accountable for the domain

cases.q: Who maintains the definitions, quality rules and metadata of a domain?
Who operates the systems that store and protect the data?
A programme with stewards but no named owners fails because:
cases.o1: Nobody can decide the questions the steward has to escalate

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Three roles with three different decisions; the owner is the one most often left unnamed

cases.q: The first thing to declare when designing a fact table is:
cases.o1: Its grain: exactly what one row represents

cases.q: A fact table whose grain is one row per order line cannot answer:
cases.o1: Questions needing a finer level than an order line

cases.q: Mixing two grains in one fact table causes:
cases.o1: Double counting when the measures are added up

cases.q: A degenerate dimension is:
cases.o1: An identifier such as an order number kept in the fact table with no dimension of its own

parts.label: v
parts.explain: The grain is the design; measures and dimensions follow from it, and a mixed grain is the error that survives into the reports

cases.q: An attribute whose history does not matter and is simply corrected uses:
An attribute whose history must be preserved for reporting as of a date uses:
cases.o1: Type 2, adding a new row with effective dates

cases.q: An attribute where only the previous value is needed alongside the current uses:
Using Type 1 where history mattered means:
cases.o1: Past reports can no longer be reproduced

cases.q: Type 2 costs:
cases.o1: More rows and the need to join on the date the fact occurred

parts.label: v
parts.explain: The question is always whether a past report has to be reproducible; that decides the type, and the cost follows

cases.q: A dashboard that must reflect events within seconds needs:
A large volume of varied semi-structured data to be transformed after landing argues for:
A modest volume of well-understood structured data for daily reporting argues for:
cases.o1: ETL into a warehouse, which is simplest

cases.q: Streaming is more expensive to operate because:
cases.o1: The pipeline must be always available and correct under reordering and replay

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Latency need against volume and variety, with the simplest option that meets the latency winning

problems.prompt: A fact table has {{nr}} order lines across {{nc}} customers. A GROUP BY on customer returns how many rows at most?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: A grouped query returns one row per distinct group, so the result size follows the dimension's cardinality and not the fact table's; that is what makes a star schema queryable at scale

cases.q: A question asking what happened last quarter is:
cases.o1: Descriptive analytics, answered by a dashboard

cases.q: A question asking why churn rose is:
cases.o1: Diagnostic analytics, answered by cohort or driver analysis

cases.q: A question asking which customers will churn next month is:
cases.o1: Predictive analytics, answered by a classifier

cases.q: A question asking how to allocate a retention budget to minimise churn is:
Jumping to a predictive model when the question was diagnostic produces:
cases.o1: A model that forecasts well and explains nothing the business can act on

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Four kinds of question with four methods; matching them is most of what makes an analytics request answerable

problems.prompt: A classifier flags accounts: {{tp}} true positives worth {{gp}} each saved, {{fp}} false positives costing {{cp}} each. What is the expected profit?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: A model is worth using only when the value of its true positives beats the cost of its false ones, which is why the threshold is set from these costs rather than from accuracy

problems.prompt: With a gain of {{gp}} per true positive and a cost of {{cp}} per false positive, what precision does a campaign need to break even (per cent)?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: The breakeven precision follows from the two costs alone, so a cheap intervention on a valuable save is worth running at very low precision: that is the calculation that decides where to set the threshold

cases.q: A metric that rises steadily and cannot fall, such as cumulative registrations, is:
cases.o1: A vanity metric: it reports activity without informing a decision

cases.q: A well-formed KPI definition includes:
cases.o1: A formula, a target, an owner and a data source
cases.o2: A formula and a target only

cases.q: A KPI with no owner fails because:
cases.o1: Nobody is accountable for moving it, so it becomes reporting rather than management

cases.q: Choosing a metric the team can move but that does not affect the objective produces:
cases.o1: Local optimisation that leaves the objective where it was

parts.label: v
parts.explain: A metric earns its place by changing a decision; formula, target, owner and source are the four things that make that possible

problems.prompt: A system cuts cost per order from {{c1}} to {{c2}} dollars on {{no}} orders a year. What annual saving is that (thousand dollars)?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: A cost-leadership system's case is this number against its total cost of ownership; the strategic classification is useful only once it is priced

problems.prompt: A portfolio of {{na}} applications has {{ns}} strategic, {{nf}} factory and {{nt}} turnaround. What percentage is support?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Most portfolios are mostly support, and the grid's value is making that visible: a firm spending equally on all four quadrants is not managing the portfolio

problems.prompt: Five decision domains each assigned to one of {{nk}} archetypes gives how many possible governance patterns?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: The count is why governance is described domain by domain rather than as one label: a firm is usually a different archetype in each domain, and the mismatch between stated and actual is where governance fails

problems.prompt: Two frameworks list {{n1}} and {{n2}} controls with {{ov}} in common. How many distinct controls does adopting both require?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Mapping overlapping frameworks once is what keeps a compliance programme from implementing the same control three times under three names

problems.prompt: A RACI for {{nt}} tasks across {{nr}} roles has how many cells, and how many A's should it contain?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: One A per task means the number of A's equals the number of tasks, whatever the matrix's size; counting them is the quickest audit of a RACI

problems.prompt: An architecture cycle of {{np}} phases is run {{nc}} times a year with {{dw}} weeks a phase. What fraction of the year is spent in the method (per cent)?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: A full method run costs most of a year, which is why architecture is usually done iteratively on a scoped domain rather than as a complete cycle

cases.q: A capability differs from a process by:
cases.o1: Describing what the organisation can do, not how it does it

cases.q: Capability maps are stable over reorganisations because:
cases.o1: What a business must be able to do changes less often than who does it
cases.o3: They are approved by the board

cases.q: Heat-mapping a capability map shows:
cases.o1: Where current maturity falls short of the value at stake

parts.label: v
parts.explain: A capability is the stable noun under the changing verbs of process and org chart

problems.prompt: Eliminating {{ne}} of {{na}} applications each costing {{cm}} thousand a year saves what percentage of a {{tb}} thousand run cost?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Retiring the low-value, poor-fit quadrant is the cheapest money in an IT budget, and it is also the hardest politically, which is why portfolios accumulate

problems.prompt: Of {{na}} applications, {{nr}} are rehosted, {{np}} replatformed, {{nf}} refactored and {{nq}} repurchased. How many are retired or retained?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: The retire-or-retain remainder is where a migration saves money without any engineering, which is why it is counted first rather than last

problems.prompt: A process has {{ns}} steps of {{wt}} minutes work each, with {{nh}} hand-offs that queue {{qt}} hours each. What fraction of cycle time is work (per cent)?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Work is usually a few per cent of cycle time and queueing is the rest, so removing a hand-off beats making any step faster: that ratio is the reason to model the process at all

problems.prompt: A use case with {{nm}} main-flow steps and {{nx}} extensions becomes how many stories, if each extension is its own story plus one for the main flow?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: The extensions are where the work is: a use case that looks small because its main flow is short usually hides most of its cost in exception handling

problems.prompt: A release has {{nM}} Musts of {{pM}} points, {{nS}} Shoulds of {{pS}} and {{nC}} Coulds of {{pC}}. Capacity is {{cap}} points. How many points must fall out?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: The overflow is what the priority order exists to allocate; if the Musts alone exceed capacity the prioritisation has not been done, whatever the labels say

problems.prompt: A canary release goes to {{cp}} per cent of {{nu}} users. If the defect rate is {{dr}} per thousand users, how many users does the canary expose?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: The exposure is the whole point of a canary: the same defect at full release hits a hundred times as many people, and the canary's cost is the delay

cases.q: A conceptual model is written before the technology because:
cases.o1: The entities and relationships are a property of the domain, not of the database

cases.q: Choosing the database first tends to produce:
cases.o1: A model shaped by the tool's limits rather than by the domain

cases.q: A logical model adds:
cases.o1: Keys, attributes and types, still independent of a product

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Three levels, and skipping the conceptual one is how a schema ends up describing the tool instead of the business

problems.prompt: A programme has {{nd}} data domains and {{nst}} stewards, each able to maintain {{cap}} domains properly. How many domains go unstewarded?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Stewardship fails by arithmetic more often than by design: naming a steward for forty domains with eight people is a plan to steward sixteen of them

problems.prompt: A fact table at one row per order line grows by {{nl}} lines a day. How many rows after {{yr}} years?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Declaring the grain also declares the growth rate, which is what decides partitioning and whether the grain is affordable at all

problems.prompt: A Type 2 dimension of {{nr}} members sees {{nc}} attribute changes a year each. How many rows after {{yr}} years?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Type 2's cost is this row growth, which is the honest comparison against Type 1's loss of history: a volatile attribute on a large dimension can dominate the warehouse

problems.prompt: A pipeline must deliver within {{bd}} minutes. Extraction takes {{t1}}, transformation {{t2}} and load {{t3}} minutes. How much headroom is left?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: A negative headroom says the architecture cannot meet the requirement, however it is tuned: that is the calculation that forces the move from batch to streaming

problems.prompt: A fact table of {{nf}} rows joins a dimension of {{nd}} rows on its key. How many rows does the inner join return, if every fact matches exactly one dimension row?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: A conformed-dimension join preserves the fact row count, which is the check that catches a duplicated dimension key: a join that returns more rows than the fact table has a cardinality bug

problems.prompt: A dashboard shows {{nm}} metrics of which {{na}} are acted on. What percentage is reporting rather than management?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: A dashboard's value is in the metrics someone changes behaviour over; the rest costs attention every time it is looked at

problems.prompt: A KPI stands at {{cv}} against a target of {{tv}} and has moved {{mv}} per period. How many periods to the target?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: A target with no arrival date is not a target: this arithmetic is what turns a KPI into a commitment, and it often shows the target is unreachable at the current rate

problems.prompt: A workload peaks at {{pk}} requests a second; one instance serves {{ps}}. With {{hd}} per cent headroom, how many instances are needed?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Sizing is always at peak with headroom, because an instance count that just meets the average fails every day at the busy hour; the headroom is what absorbs a failed instance as well as growth

problems.prompt: Cloud instances cost {{ch}} dollars an hour; owned hardware costs {{hw}} thousand over {{yr}} years. How many instance-hours a year make them equal?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: There are 8766 hours in a year, so a crossover well above that means cloud always wins and well below it means steady load should be owned: the comparison is about utilisation, not price

cases.q: Under IaaS, who patches the guest operating system?
Under PaaS, who patches the runtime and the operating system?
cases.o3: The customer for the runtime only

cases.q: Under SaaS, what does the customer still manage?
cases.o1: Identities, access and the data itself

cases.q: Data classification and access control are the customer's responsibility:
cases.o1: Under every service model, including SaaS

cases.q: A system needing a specific unsupported OS kernel module argues for:
cases.o1: On-premises or IaaS, where the customer controls the OS

parts.label: v
parts.explain: The line moves with the model; what never moves is responsibility for identities, access and the data

cases.q: Transaction-cost reasoning says to keep a function in house when:
cases.o1: It is highly asset-specific, so a contract cannot capture what is needed

cases.q: A highly standardised, measurable function with many suppliers argues for:
cases.o1: Outsourcing, since the market will price it well

cases.q: The hidden cost of outsourcing a function is:
cases.o1: Co-ordination and monitoring, which rises with how hard the output is to specify

cases.q: Offshoring differs from outsourcing by:
cases.o1: Being about where the work is done, not who does it

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Asset specificity and measurability decide it; the cost that gets forgotten is the cost of supervising the contract

cases.q: A service is down for users. This is:
The underlying cause of repeated incidents is:
A user asking for access to a system is:
A pre-approved, low-risk, routine change is:
A change that must bypass the usual approval because a service is down is:
cases.o1: An emergency change, authorised and documented after the fact

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Incident restores service, problem removes the cause, request is business as usual, and change is the controlled alteration

problems.prompt: A service was down {{dm}} minutes in a {{dy}}-day month. What was its availability (per cent)?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Three nines allows about 43 minutes a month and four nines about four, so the difference between them is an architecture decision rather than a tuning one

problems.prompt: An incident log shows {{ni}} incidents with total downtime {{td}} minutes. What is the mean time to restore (minutes), and what availability does that give over {{dy}} days?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Mean time to restore and incident frequency multiply to downtime, so an SLA can be met by having fewer incidents or by restoring faster; the two need different investments

problems.prompt: On a matrix where priority is impact plus urgency on a 1-to-3 scale (1 highest), an incident of impact {{im}} and urgency {{ur}} gets what priority number?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: The matrix exists so that priority is not argued case by case: impact is how many are affected and urgency is how fast it worsens, and the two together, not the loudest caller, set the queue

problems.prompt: Four criteria weigh {{w1}}, {{w2}}, {{w3}} and {{w4}} per cent; a vendor scores {{s1}}, {{s2}}, {{s3}} and {{s4}} out of 5. What is its weighted score out of 5?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: The weights are agreed before the responses are opened, which is the only thing that makes a weighted evaluation defensible when the losing bidder asks

cases.q: Which contract term most protects a customer's ability to leave?
cases.o1: Data portability in a documented, usable format at no extra charge

cases.q: Source-code escrow protects against:
cases.o1: The vendor failing, not the vendor performing badly

cases.q: Service credits are weak protection because:
cases.o1: They refund a fraction of the fee, not the business loss

cases.q: A transition-assistance clause matters because:
cases.o1: Leaving needs the incumbent's cooperation, which it has no incentive to give without one

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Exit is designed at signature: portability, escrow and transition assistance, since none of them can be negotiated once the relationship has failed

problems.prompt: On a 5-by-5 matrix, a risk of likelihood {{lk}} and impact {{ip}} scores what, and does it exceed a tolerance of {{tl}}? Give the score.

parts.label: v
parts.explain: The product ranks risks for attention; what the matrix cannot do is compare a high-likelihood nuisance with a low-likelihood catastrophe, which is why the tolerance line is drawn on impact as well

cases.q: A risk whose activity the firm can simply stop doing is treated by:
Buying insurance against a risk is:
cases.o1: Transfer, which moves the financial consequence and not the risk itself

cases.q: A risk below tolerance whose controls would cost more than the exposure is treated by:
Insurance leaves the firm exposed to:
cases.o1: The operational consequences, which money does not undo

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Four treatments, and transfer is the one most often mistaken for removal

problems.prompt: A loss event costs {{sle}} thousand and occurs {{aro}} times a year on average. What is the annualised loss expectancy (thousand)?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Single loss expectancy times annual rate of occurrence is the figure a control has to beat; both inputs are estimates, so the number is for ranking rather than for budgeting to the dollar

problems.prompt: A control costing {{cc}} thousand a year cuts an annualised loss expectancy from {{a1}} to {{a2}} thousand. What is its return on security investment (per cent)?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: A negative return means the control costs more than the loss it removes, which is a legitimate reason to accept a risk; what it does not cover is a loss the firm could not survive

cases.q: A firewall rule blocking traffic is:
A log review that finds a breach after the fact is:
Restoring from backup after an incident is:
A security policy requiring annual training is:
A locked server-room door is:

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Two axes: when the control acts, and what kind of thing it is; a programme with only preventive controls has no way to know when one has failed

problems.prompt: A process loses {{lp}} thousand an hour when down, and a recovery option costing {{rc}} thousand a year cuts the recovery time from {{t1}} to {{t2}} hours. How many outages a year does it take to pay for itself?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Recovery objectives are derived from the cost of downtime, not chosen: if it takes three outages a year to justify a hot site, and outages happen once every three years, the objective is wrong

cases.q: A recovery time objective of under an hour generally requires:
cases.o1: A hot site or active-active operation

cases.q: A recovery point objective of near zero requires:
The recovery point objective is about:
cases.o1: How much data may be lost, which backup frequency decides

cases.q: A cold site is adequate when:
cases.o1: The process can be down for days, which is true of more processes than people expect

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Time objective picks the site, point objective picks the backup or replication scheme; they are set independently per process

problems.prompt: A full backup runs Sunday and differentials nightly. A failure occurs on {{dd}} with the last differential from the night before. How many backup sets must be restored?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: A differential scheme always restores the full plus one differential, whatever the day; an incremental scheme restores the full plus every incremental since, which is faster to write and slower to restore

problems.prompt: Backups run every {{bh}} hours. What is the worst-case data loss (hours), and what recovery point objective does that support?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Worst case is a failure just before the next backup, so the recovery point objective can never be better than the backup interval: a four-hour objective on nightly backups is not an objective, it is a wish

cases.q: Establishing risk appetite and accountability for cybersecurity belongs to which function?
Maintaining an asset inventory belongs to:
Access control and training belong to:
Continuous monitoring belongs to:
Restoring services and incorporating lessons learned belongs to:

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Six functions since the 2.0 revision added Govern, which is the one that makes the other five somebody's job

cases.q: A user who can both create a vendor and approve a payment to it has:
cases.o1: A segregation-of-duties conflict allowing fictitious payments

cases.q: A developer with production deployment rights creates the risk that:
cases.o1: Code can reach production without independent review

cases.q: When a conflict cannot be removed because the team is too small, the answer is:
cases.o1: A compensating control, such as independent after-the-fact review of every such transaction

cases.q: The commonest compensating control for a small team is:
cases.o1: Independent review of a complete log of the conflicting activity

parts.label: v
parts.explain: The conflict is the pair of rights, not the person; in a small organisation the answer is detection rather than prevention

cases.q: A system users find useful but too hard to operate will fail on:
A system that is easy but does not help users do their job fails on:
The intervention that raises ease of use most reliably is:
cases.o1: Changing the interface and the workflow, since training works around a problem rather than removing it

cases.q: Facilitating conditions means:
cases.o1: Whether the resources and support to use the system exist

cases.q: Social influence matters most:
cases.o1: Early in adoption, before a user has direct experience

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Two core beliefs plus the context around them; the useful part is that each points at a different intervention

cases.q: A change announced and implemented with no attempt to build urgency is likely to fail at:
cases.o1: Kotter's first step, establishing a sense of urgency

cases.q: A change where people know what to do but lack the skill fails at which ADKAR element?
A change that reverts to the old way after a few months failed at:
cases.o1: Refreezing, or reinforcement in ADKAR terms

cases.q: Lewin's unfreezing stage corresponds to:
cases.o1: Making the case that the current state is not acceptable

cases.q: ADKAR is individual where Kotter is organisational, which means:
cases.o1: ADKAR diagnoses which person is stuck and where

parts.label: v
parts.explain: The models name the step that was skipped, which is almost always urgency at the start or reinforcement at the end

problems.prompt: Innovators and early adopters are about {{ea}} per cent of a market. Of {{ms}} thousand potential users, how many remain beyond the chasm?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: The great majority of the market sits beyond the chasm and buys for different reasons: references from their own segment and a whole product rather than a promising technology. The percentage is printed because the diffusion figures were not read from a source

cases.q: Early adopters buy a technology for:
cases.o1: The advantage of being first, accepting an incomplete product

cases.q: The early majority buys for:
cases.o1: References from their own segment and a complete, reliable product

cases.q: Crossing the chasm usually means:
cases.o1: Dominating one narrow segment to earn the references the next one needs
cases.o2: Broadening the market as widely as possible

cases.q: A whole product means:
cases.o1: Everything the mainstream buyer needs to get the promised benefit, including services and integrations

parts.label: v
parts.explain: The chasm is a change in what the buyer wants, which is why the marketing that won early adopters stops working

cases.q: The riskiest assumption on a new venture's canvas is usually:
cases.o1: That the customer segment has the problem badly enough to pay
cases.o4: That the cost structure is right

cases.q: A canvas with a vague value proposition and precise cost figures indicates:
cases.o1: Effort spent where it is easy rather than where the risk is

cases.q: The point of filling a canvas is:
cases.o1: To make the assumptions explicit so the riskiest can be tested first

parts.label: v
parts.explain: The canvas is a list of guesses; its value is in ordering them by how fatal being wrong would be

problems.prompt: A subscription earns {{mr}} dollars a month at {{gm}} per cent gross margin with {{ch}} per cent monthly churn. What is the customer lifetime value (dollars)?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Lifetime value is margin divided by churn, so churn is the dominant term: cutting monthly churn from three per cent to one triples the value of every customer acquired

problems.prompt: Acquiring a customer costs {{cac}} dollars and they contribute {{mr}} dollars a month at {{gm}} per cent margin. What is the payback period (months)?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Payback in months is the figure that decides whether growth is self-funding: below about a year a business can grow from its own gross profit, above it growth consumes capital

cases.q: A messaging app where each new user makes it better for existing users has:
A marketplace where more sellers attract more buyers has:
In a two-sided market, the side to subsidise is generally:
cases.o1: The more price-sensitive side, whose presence the other side values more

cases.q: Negative network effects appear when:
cases.o1: More users degrade the experience, as with congestion or spam

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Which side to subsidise follows from which side's price sensitivity and which side the other values, and getting it backwards is how a platform stalls

cases.q: A US university handling student education records is governed by:
A US healthcare provider's patient records are governed by:
A firm processing the personal data of people in the EU, wherever the firm sits, is governed by:
California residents' personal information held by a qualifying business is governed by:
Processing personal data for a purpose other than the one it was collected for generally requires:
cases.o1: A compatible purpose or a fresh lawful basis

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Regime follows the data subject and the sector, not where the company is; a flow can be covered by more than one at once

cases.q: A data-protection impact assessment is required when processing:
cases.o1: Is likely to result in a high risk to people's rights, such as large-scale profiling
cases.o3: Is done by a public body only

cases.q: Privacy by design means:
cases.o1: Building the protections into the system rather than adding them afterwards

cases.q: Data minimisation means:
cases.o1: Collecting only what the stated purpose needs

cases.q: The commonest privacy-by-design failure is:
cases.o1: Collecting fields because they might be useful later

cases.q: Pseudonymisation differs from anonymisation by:
cases.o1: Being reversible with additional information, so the data is still personal data

parts.label: v
parts.explain: The assessment is triggered by risk to people, and the design measures are about what is collected and kept rather than about how it is secured

cases.q: Utilitarian reasoning about a system asks:
cases.o1: Which option produces the greatest total benefit across everyone affected
cases.o3: What a virtuous person would do

cases.q: Rights-based reasoning asks:
cases.o1: Whether anyone's rights are violated, however large the aggregate benefit

cases.q: A stakeholder analysis is used to:
cases.o1: Identify everyone affected, including those with no voice in the decision

cases.q: A decision that maximises total benefit while violating a small group's rights is:
cases.o1: Defensible on utilitarian grounds and not on rights-based grounds, which is why both are applied

cases.q: Applying more than one lens is useful because:
cases.o1: They disagree in exactly the cases that are hard, which is where the reasoning has to be shown
cases.o2: It always gives the same answer

parts.label: v
parts.explain: The lenses are tools for showing the reasoning, not a procedure for producing an answer

problems.prompt: Keeping {{nf}} machines costs {{eu}} kWh each a year; replacing them costs {{em}} kg CO2 embodied each and cuts use to {{e2}} kWh. At {{gi}} g CO2 per kWh, how many years before replacement breaks even on carbon?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Embodied emissions are most of a laptop's footprint, so a refresh for efficiency alone often never pays back: on a clean grid the breakeven is longer still, because the saving is worth less carbon

problems.prompt: The same fleet of {{nf}} machines: replacement costs {{cu}} dollars each and saves {{sv}} dollars a year each in energy and support. What is the simple payback (years)?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: The carbon and the cash payback rarely agree, and saying which one the decision was made on is the honest part of the analysis

problems.prompt: A platform has {{nv}} virtual machines, {{nc}} managed containers and {{ns}} SaaS applications. Under the shared-responsibility model, how many operating systems must the customer patch?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Only the IaaS layer leaves the guest OS with the customer, which is the practical reason a platform move reduces patching work: the containers and SaaS do not add to the count

problems.prompt: Outsourcing a function quoted at {{qp}} thousand a year needs {{nm}} staff at {{sc}} thousand to manage the contract. What is the true annual cost (thousand)?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: The retained management cost is what makes a cheap-looking contract expensive, and it rises with how hard the output is to specify: that is transaction-cost reasoning as a number

problems.prompt: A month saw {{nst}} standard, {{nnm}} normal and {{nem}} emergency changes. What percentage were emergency, and what does a high figure suggest?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: A high emergency share means changes are being forced by incidents rather than planned, so the fix is upstream in testing and release practice rather than in the change process itself

problems.prompt: Three incidents have impact and urgency ({{i1}},{{u1}}), ({{i2}},{{u2}}) and ({{i3}},{{u3}}) on a 1-to-3 scale with 1 highest. What is the best (lowest) priority number among them?

parts.label: v
parts.value: min(i1 + u1, min(i2 + u2, i3 + u3)) - 1
parts.explain: The matrix orders the queue without argument, which matters most when three people each believe theirs is the urgent one

problems.prompt: A programme has {{np}} preventive, {{nd}} detective and {{nc}} corrective controls. What percentage are detective?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: A programme that is almost all preventive has no way of knowing when a control has failed, which is why the detective share is a health measure in its own right

problems.prompt: A firm has controls mapped to {{nf}} of the six NIST CSF 2.0 functions. What percentage of the functions is covered, and which is most often the gap?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Govern, added in the 2.0 revision, is the function most often unmapped, because it is about accountability and risk appetite rather than about anything technical

problems.prompt: A system has {{nr}} roles of which {{nx}} pairs are defined as conflicting. If a user holds {{nh}} roles at random, how many pairs do they hold?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: The pairs a user holds grow as the square of their roles, which is why access accumulates into conflicts silently: nobody grants a conflict, they grant one more role

problems.prompt: A mandated system is used by {{nu}} of {{nt}} staff after {{wk}} weeks. What is adoption (per cent), and what rate per week would reach {{tg}} per cent by week {{tw}}?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Measured adoption rather than licences issued is what tells you whether the usefulness or the ease-of-use problem is the one to fix, and a mandate moves the number without moving either

problems.prompt: A programme has completed {{nc}} of Kotter's {{nt}} steps in {{mo}} months. At that rate, how many more months to finish?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: The arithmetic is a reminder that organisational change takes as long as it takes: a programme that declares success at step four has skipped the two that make it stick

problems.prompt: A venture holds {{cs}} thousand and burns {{bn}} thousand a month. How many months of runway, and how many does it need to test its riskiest assumption in {{tt}} months?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Runway against the time to test the riskiest assumption is the number that decides what to build first: an assumption that takes longer to test than the runway allows has to be tested another way

problems.prompt: A platform charges one side {{p1}} dollars and the other {{p2}}. If {{n1}} thousand join the charged side and {{n2}} thousand the other, what is total revenue (thousand dollars)?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: A subsidised side at zero price still carries the revenue, because its size is what the paying side buys: the arithmetic shows why giving one side away can be the whole business model

problems.prompt: A data flow touches EU residents, California residents and US patient records. How many of the four main regimes named in this unit apply?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Regimes stack rather than exclude one another, so a single flow can owe duties under several at once; the design has to satisfy the strictest of each requirement, not pick one

problems.prompt: A form collects {{nf}} fields of which {{nn}} are needed for the stated purpose. What percentage should be removed under data minimisation?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Minimisation is usually a large fraction of a real form, because fields accumulate on the chance of being useful later; every one removed is a field that cannot leak or be misused

problems.prompt: A decision affects {{ng}} groups of which {{nv}} have a voice in making it. What percentage of affected groups are unrepresented?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: The unrepresented share is the reason a stakeholder analysis is done at all: the groups with no voice are the ones a utilitarian calculation quietly trades away

problems.prompt: An augmented matrix has echelon form $\left(\begin{array}{ccc|c} 1 & {{a}} & {{b}} & {{c}} \\ 0 & 1 & {{d}} & {{e}} \\ 0 & 0 & {{f}} & {{g}} \end{array}\right)$. How many solutions does the system have?

parts.label: a
parts.explain: Read the last row. A pivot in every variable column means one solution. A row $0 = 0$ leaves a free variable, so infinitely many. A row $0 = c$ with $c \neq 0$ is a contradiction: no solution

problems.prompt: The coefficient matrix of a consistent system row-reduces to $\begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 & {{a}} & {{b}} \\ 0 & 1 & {{c}} & {{d}} \\ 0 & 0 & {{e}} & 0 \end{pmatrix}$. How many free variables does the solution have?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Free variables are the columns without a pivot: four columns minus the number of pivots

parts.label: a
parts.explain: Substitute into every equation. The first gives ${{a*s + b*t + u}}$; the second gives ${{c*s - t + d*u}}$. One failed equation is enough to reject the point

choices.a: 0 if Matrix([[a, b, 1], [c, -1, d]])*Matrix([s, t, u]) == Matrix([a*s + b*t + u, c*s - t + d*u + e]) else 1

problems.prompt: For which $h$ are $\begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ {{a}} \end{pmatrix}$ and $\begin{pmatrix} {{b}} \\ h \end{pmatrix}$ linearly dependent?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Two vectors in the plane are dependent exactly when one is a multiple of the other, which is when the determinant $h - {{a}}\cdot{{b}}$ is zero

problems.prompt: Is $\begin{pmatrix} {{s}} \\ {{s*a + t}} \\ {{s*b + t*c + e}} \end{pmatrix}$ in the span of $\begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ {{a}} \\ {{b}} \end{pmatrix}$ and $\begin{pmatrix} 0 \\ 1 \\ {{c}} \end{pmatrix}$?

parts.label: a
parts.explain: Solve $x_1v_1 + x_2v_2 = b$. The first entry forces $x_1 = {{s}}$, the second then forces $x_2 = {{t}}$; the third entry is the test. In general: $b$ is in the span exactly when the augmented matrix has no pivot in its last column

choices.a: 0 if Matrix([[1, 0], [a, 1], [b, c]]).rank() == Matrix([[1, 0, s], [a, 1, s*a + t], [b, c, s*b + t*c + e]]).rank() else 1

problems.prompt: $A$ has ${{n}}$ columns, $Ax = b$ with $b \neq 0$ is consistent, and $\dim \operatorname{Nul} A = {{k}}$. What is the solution set of $Ax = b$?

parts.label: a
choice: A line not through the origin
A plane not through the origin
parts.explain: Every solution is one particular solution plus a solution of $Ax = 0$, so the solution set is $\operatorname{Nul} A$ shifted off the origin. It has the dimension of the null space; it misses the origin because $A0 = 0 \neq b$

problems.prompt: $A = \begin{pmatrix} {{a1}} & {{a2}} & {{a3}} \\ 2 & 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix}$, $B = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & {{b1}} \\ 0 & {{b2}} \\ -1 & {{b3}} \end{pmatrix}$. Find the entry of $AB$ in row 1, column 2.

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Row 1 of $A$ dotted with column 2 of $B$: ${{a1}}\cdot{{b1}} + {{a2}}\cdot{{b2}} + {{a3}}\cdot{{b3}}$. Nothing else in either matrix enters

problems.prompt: $A$ is ${{m}} \times {{n}}$ and $B$ is ${{n}} \times {{p}}$. How many rows does $B^{T}A^{T}$ have?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: $B^TA^T = (AB)^T$. $AB$ is ${{m}} \times {{p}}$, so its transpose is ${{p}} \times {{m}}$. The reversed order is what makes the inner sizes match

problems.prompt: $A^{-1} = \begin{pmatrix} {{a}} & {{b}} \\ {{c}} & {{d}} \end{pmatrix}$. Solve $Ax = \begin{pmatrix} {{p}} \\ {{q}} \end{pmatrix}$: what is $x_1$?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: $x = A^{-1}b$, so $x_1$ is row 1 of $A^{-1}$ dotted with $b$: ${{a}}\cdot{{p}} + {{b}}\cdot{{q}}$. No need to find $A$ itself

problems.prompt: Is $\begin{pmatrix} {{d}} & {{bb}} \\ {{-c}} & {{a}} \end{pmatrix}$ the inverse of $\begin{pmatrix} {{a}} & {{b}} \\ {{c}} & {{d}} \end{pmatrix}$? (Hint: compute the determinant first.)

parts.label: a
parts.explain: The determinant is ${{a}}\cdot{{d}} - {{b}}\cdot{{c}} = {{a*d - b*c}}$. The inverse is $\dfrac{1}{\det}$ times the matrix with the diagonal swapped and the off-diagonal negated. Check by multiplying: the product must be $I$

choices.a: 0 if Matrix([[a, b], [c, b*c + 1]])*Matrix([[b*c + 1, -b if e == 0 else b], [-c, a]]) == Matrix([[1, 0], [0, 1]]) else 1

problems.prompt: Factor $A = \begin{pmatrix} {{a}} & {{b}} \\ {{k*a}} & {{c}} \end{pmatrix} = LU$ with $L$ unit lower triangular. What is $u_{22}$?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: The multiplier is $\ell_{21} = {{k*a}}/{{a}} = {{k}}$; it goes into $L$. Subtracting ${{k}}$ times row 1 from row 2 leaves $u_{22} = {{c}} - ({{k}})({{b}})$

problems.prompt: With $A = LU$ and $L = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0 \\ {{l}} & 1 & 0 \\ {{m}} & 2 & 1 \end{pmatrix}$, the first step of solving $Ax = b$ is $Ly = b$. For $b = ({{b1}}, {{b2}}, 0)$, find $y_2$.

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Forward substitution: $y_1 = {{b1}}$, then ${{l}}y_1 + y_2 = {{b2}}$. Then $Ux = y$ by back substitution. The factorisation is reused for every new $b$

cases.q: Ax = 0 has only the trivial solution.
The columns of A span Rⁿ.
A has n pivot positions.
Aᵀ is invertible.
The map x ↦ Ax is one-to-one.
det A = 0.
0 is an eigenvalue of A.
Ax = b has infinitely many solutions for some b.
rank A = n − 1.
The rows of A are linearly dependent.

problems.prompt: $A$ is $n \times n$. If {{q}}, is $A$ invertible?

parts.label: a
parts.explain: The invertible matrix theorem: for a square matrix, invertible, n pivots, independent columns, columns span, only the trivial solution of Ax = 0, one-to-one, onto, det ≠ 0 and 0 not an eigenvalue all stand or fall together. Any statement that one of them fails means A is singular

problems.prompt: Find $\det \begin{pmatrix} {{a}} & {{b}} & {{d}} \\ 0 & {{c}} & {{e}} \\ 0 & 0 & {{f}} \end{pmatrix}$ by inspection.

parts.label: v
parts.explain: A triangular matrix has determinant equal to the product of its diagonal: ${{a}}\cdot{{c}}\cdot{{f}}$. The entries above the diagonal never matter. Row reduction to triangular form is how large determinants are found

problems.prompt: $A$ is ${{n}} \times {{n}}$ with $\det A = {{d}}$. Find $\det\!\left({{k}}A^{T}A^{-1}A\right)$.

parts.label: v
parts.explain: $A^TA^{-1}A$ has determinant $d\cdot\dfrac1d\cdot d = d$; the scalar ${{k}}$ multiplies each of the ${{n}}$ rows, so it comes out as ${{k}}^{ {{n}} }$. The trap is writing ${{k}}d$

problems.prompt: $\det A = {{d}}$ ($3 \times 3$). $B$ is made by swapping rows 1 and 2, multiplying the new row 2 by ${{k}}$, then adding ${{m}}$ times row 1 to row 3. Find $\det B$.

parts.label: v
parts.explain: A swap flips the sign, scaling a row scales the determinant by the same factor, and adding a multiple of one row to another changes nothing: $-{{k}}\cdot{{d}}$

problems.prompt: $T(x) = \begin{pmatrix} {{a}} & {{b}} \\ {{c}} & {{d}} \end{pmatrix}x$ maps a region of area ${{R}}$. What is the area of its image?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: A linear map scales every area by $|\det|$, here $|{{a*d - b*c}}|$. A negative determinant only flips orientation

problems.prompt: $A$ is ${{m}} \times {{n}}$ and $\dim \operatorname{Nul} A = {{k}}$. What is $\dim \operatorname{Row} A$?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Row rank equals column rank equals rank, and rank + nullity = number of columns: ${{n}} - {{k}}$

cases.q: all x with $x_1 + 2x_2 - x_3 = 0$
all x with $x_3 = 3x_1$
the span of (1, 2, 0) and (0, 1, 1)
the null space of a 2 × 3 matrix
all x with $x_1 + x_2 = 1$
all x with $x_1x_2 = 0$
all x with $x_1 \ge 0$
all vectors $(t, 2t, t^2)$
all x with $|x_1| = |x_2|$

problems.prompt: Is {{q}} a subspace of $\mathbb{R}^3$?

parts.label: a
parts.explain: Three checks: contains 0, closed under addition, closed under scaling. Solution sets of homogeneous linear equations and spans always pass. A constant on the right misses 0; products, squares, absolute values and inequalities break closure

problems.prompt: What is the dimension of the span of $\begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ {{a}} \\ 0 \\ {{b}} \end{pmatrix}, \begin{pmatrix} 0 \\ 1 \\ {{c}} \\ {{d}} \end{pmatrix}, \begin{pmatrix} {{s}} \\ {{s*a + t}} \\ {{t*c + e}} \\ {{s*b + t*d}} \end{pmatrix}$?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: The first two are independent. The third is ${{s}}v_1 + {{t}}v_2$ in its first two entries; check whether the remaining entries agree. Dimension counts only the independent vectors

expect.v: Matrix([[1, a, 0, b], [0, 1, c, d], [s, s*a + t, t*c + e, s*b + t*d]]).rank()

problems.prompt: $\mathcal{B} = \left\{ \begin{pmatrix} {{a}} \\ {{c}} \end{pmatrix}, \begin{pmatrix} {{b}} \\ {{d}} \end{pmatrix} \right\}$. Find the second $\mathcal{B}$-coordinate of $x = \begin{pmatrix} {{s*a + t*b}} \\ {{s*c + t*d}} \end{pmatrix}$.

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Solve $c_1b_1 + c_2b_2 = x$, that is $P_{\mathcal{B}}[x]_{\mathcal{B}} = x$: $c_1 = {{s}}$, $c_2 = {{t}}$. Coordinates are the weights, not the entries

expect.v: Matrix([[a, b], [c, d]]).LUsolve(Matrix([s*a + t*b, s*c + t*d]))[1]

problems.prompt: In the basis $\mathcal{B} = \left\{ \begin{pmatrix} {{a}} \\ {{c}} \end{pmatrix}, \begin{pmatrix} {{b}} \\ {{d}} \end{pmatrix} \right\}$, $[x]_{\mathcal{B}} = \begin{pmatrix} {{s}} \\ {{t}} \end{pmatrix}$. What is the second standard coordinate of $x$?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: $x = P_{\mathcal{B}}[x]_{\mathcal{B}} = {{s}}b_1 + {{t}}b_2$: the change-of-coordinates matrix has the basis vectors as columns. Going the other way needs $P_{\mathcal{B}}^{-1}$

problems.prompt: A linear map $T: \mathbb{R}^2 \to \mathbb{R}^2$ has $T(e_1) = \begin{pmatrix} {{a}} \\ {{c}} \end{pmatrix}$ and $T(e_2) = \begin{pmatrix} {{b}} \\ {{d}} \end{pmatrix}$. Find the first entry of $T\begin{pmatrix} {{s}} \\ {{t}} \end{pmatrix}$.

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Linearity: $T(x) = {{s}}T(e_1) + {{t}}T(e_2)$. That is why the standard matrix has $T(e_1)$ and $T(e_2)$ as its columns

problems.prompt: $T$ rotates the plane 90° counterclockwise; then $S$ multiplies $x$-coordinates by ${{k}}$ and $y$-coordinates by ${{m}}$. Find $(S \circ T)\begin{pmatrix} {{a}} \\ {{b}} \end{pmatrix}$, first entry.

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Rotation sends $(x, y)$ to $(-y, x)$, so $({{a}}, {{b}})$ goes to $({{-b}}, {{a}})$; then the $x$-coordinate is scaled by ${{k}}$. As matrices, $S \circ T$ is $ST$: the map applied first stands on the right

problems.prompt: $A$ is ${{m}} \times {{n}}$ with rank ${{r}}$. Is $x \mapsto Ax$ one-to-one, onto, both or neither?

parts.label: a
parts.explain: One-to-one means no free variables: a pivot in every column, rank = n. Onto $\mathbb{R}^m$ means a pivot in every row, rank = m. Both needs a square invertible matrix

choices.a: 2 if (r == n and r == m) else (0 if r == n else (1 if r == m else 3))

problems.prompt: $T(p) = p^{({{k}})}$ (the ${{k}}$-th derivative) maps $\mathbb{P}_{ {{n}} }$, the polynomials of degree at most ${{n}}$, to itself. What is the dimension of the range of $T$?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: $\dim \mathbb{P}_{ {{n}} } = {{n + 1}}$. The kernel is the polynomials of degree below ${{k}}$, dimension ${{k}}$. Rank–nullity: ${{n + 1}} - {{k}}$

problems.prompt: $T(p)(x) = p(x + {{h}})$ on $\mathbb{P}_2$ with basis $\{1, x, x^2\}$. For $p = {{a}} + {{b}}x + {{c}}x^2$, what is the $x$-coordinate (the middle entry) of $[T(p)]$?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: $[T] = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & {{h}} & {{h^2}} \\ 0 & 1 & {{2*h}} \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix}$, whose columns are $T(1), T(x), T(x^2)$ in coordinates. Row 2 times $({{a}}, {{b}}, {{c}})$ gives ${{b}} + {{2*h}}\cdot{{c}}$

problems.prompt: What is the largest eigenvalue of $\begin{pmatrix} {{a}} & {{b}} & {{d}} \\ 0 & {{c}} & {{e}} \\ 0 & 0 & {{f}} \end{pmatrix}$?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: For a triangular matrix $\det(A - \lambda I)$ is the product of the diagonal entries minus $\lambda$, so the eigenvalues are the diagonal entries. Row reduction changes eigenvalues, so this only works on a matrix that is already triangular

expect.v: Max(*Matrix([[a, b, d], [0, c, e], [0, 0, f]]).eigenvals().keys())

problems.prompt: $A = \begin{pmatrix} {{a}} & {{-b}} \\ {{b}} & {{a}} \end{pmatrix}$ has complex eigenvalues. By what factor does $A$ scale every vector it rotates, i.e. what is $|\lambda|$?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: The eigenvalues are ${{a}} \pm {{abs(b)}}i$. A matrix of this form is a rotation through $\arg\lambda$ times a scaling by $|\lambda| = \sqrt{a^2 + b^2}$; powers of $A$ grow or decay as $|\lambda|^k$

problems.prompt: A two-state Markov chain has transition matrix $P = \begin{pmatrix} {{1 - p/10}} & {{q/10}} \\ {{p/10}} & {{1 - q/10}} \end{pmatrix}$ (columns sum to 1). In the long run, what fraction of the time is spent in state 1?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: The steady state is the eigenvector for $\lambda = 1$, scaled so its entries sum to 1. Balance the flows: ${{p/10}}q_1 = {{q/10}}q_2$, so $q_1 = \dfrac{ {{q/10}} }{ {{p/10}} + {{q/10}} }$

expect.v: (Matrix([[1 - Rational(p, 10), Rational(q, 10)], [Rational(p, 10), 1 - Rational(q, 10)]]) - Matrix([[1, 0], [0, 1]])).nullspace()[0][0]/((Matrix([[1 - Rational(p, 10), Rational(q, 10)], [Rational(p, 10), 1 - Rational(q, 10)]]) - Matrix([[1, 0], [0, 1]])).nullspace()[0][0] + (Matrix([[1 - Rational(p, 10), Rational(q, 10)], [Rational(p, 10), 1 - Rational(q, 10)]]) - Matrix([[1, 0], [0, 1]])).nullspace()[0][1])

problems.prompt: $A\begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix} = {{l1}}\begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix}$ and $A\begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ -1 \end{pmatrix} = {{l2}}\begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ -1 \end{pmatrix}$. Find the first entry of $A^{ {{k}} }\begin{pmatrix} {{c1 + c2}} \\ {{c1 - c2}} \end{pmatrix}$.

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Write $x = {{c1}}v_1 + {{c2}}v_2$. Each eigenvector is only scaled: $A^{ {{k}} }x = {{c1}}({{l1}})^{ {{k}} }v_1 + {{c2}}({{l2}})^{ {{k}} }v_2$. No matrix powers needed

problems.prompt: Find the distance between $u = ({{a}}, {{b}}, {{c}})$ and $v = ({{a + s*p}}, {{b - s*q}}, {{c + r}})$.

expect.v: sqrt((Matrix([a, b, c]) - Matrix([a + s*p, b - s*q, c + r])).dot(Matrix([a, b, c]) - Matrix([a + s*p, b - s*q, c + r])))

problems.prompt: $W$ is the line spanned by $(1, {{a}}, {{b}})$. For which $h$ is $(h, {{c}}, 1)$ in $W^{\perp}$?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: $W^\perp$ is everything orthogonal to the spanning vector: $h + {{a}}\cdot{{c}} + {{b}} = 0$. For a line in $\mathbb{R}^3$ that is a plane, of dimension $3 - 1 = 2$

problems.prompt: $A = \begin{pmatrix} {{p}} & {{u}} \\ {{q}} & {{w}} \end{pmatrix} = QR$ by Gram–Schmidt, with $R$ upper triangular and positive diagonal. Find $r_{12}$.

parts.label: v
parts.explain: $q_1 = a_1/\lVert a_1\rVert$ with $\lVert a_1\rVert = {{sqrt(p^2 + q^2)}} = r_{11}$. Then $r_{12} = q_1 \cdot a_2 = \dfrac{ {{p*u + q*w}} }{ {{sqrt(p^2 + q^2)}} }$, the component of $a_2$ along $q_1$

problems.prompt: A symmetric $2 \times 2$ matrix has eigenvector $({{p}}, {{q}})$ for $\lambda = {{l1}}$. Its eigenvector for $\lambda = {{l2}}$ is a multiple of $(h, 1)$. Find $h$.

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Eigenvectors of a symmetric matrix for different eigenvalues are orthogonal: ${{p}}h + {{q}} = 0$. In the plane there is only one orthogonal direction, so the second eigenvector is fixed without knowing the matrix

expect.v: solve(Eq((Integer(l1)*Matrix([p, q])*Matrix([p, q]).T + Integer(l2)*Matrix([-q, p])*Matrix([-q, p]).T)*Matrix([x, 1]), Integer(l2)*(p**2 + q**2)*Matrix([x, 1])), x)[x]

parts.label: a
parts.explain: The matrix is $\begin{pmatrix} {{a}} & {{b}} \\ {{b}} & {{c}} \end{pmatrix}$ (half the cross coefficient off the diagonal). Its eigenvalues decide: both positive, both negative, or mixed signs. For $2 \times 2$: $\det < 0$ means mixed; $\det > 0$ means the sign of $a$

choices.a: 0 if Min(*Matrix([[a, b], [b, c]]).eigenvals().keys()) > 0 else (1 if Max(*Matrix([[a, b], [b, c]]).eigenvals().keys()) < 0 else 2)

problems.prompt: What is the largest value of $Q(x) = {{a}}x_1^2 + ({{2*b}})x_1x_2 + {{a}}x_2^2$ on the unit circle $\lVert x \rVert = 1$?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: On unit vectors, $x^TAx$ ranges between the smallest and largest eigenvalue of $A$, reached at the eigenvectors. Here $A = \begin{pmatrix} {{a}} & {{b}} \\ {{b}} & {{a}} \end{pmatrix}$ has eigenvalues ${{a}} \pm {{abs(b)}}$, at $(1, \pm 1)/\sqrt2$

problems.prompt: $A = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & {{s1}} & 0 \\ {{s2}} & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & {{-s3}} \end{pmatrix}$. What is its condition number $\sigma_{max}/\sigma_{min}$?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Singular values are lengths, so signs and the order of the columns do not matter: here ${{s1}}, {{s2}}, {{s3}}$. $\kappa = {{s1}}/{{s3}}$. A large condition number means small errors in $b$ can become large errors in $x$

problems.prompt: $A = uv^{T}$ with $u = ({{p}}, {{s*q}})$ and $v = ({{m}}, {{-m}}, {{m}}, {{-m}})$. What is its nonzero singular value?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: A rank-one matrix $uv^T$ has one nonzero singular value, $\lVert u\rVert\,\lVert v\rVert = {{sqrt(p^2 + q^2)}}\cdot{{2*m}}$: it sends $v/\lVert v\rVert$ to $\lVert v\rVert u$

problems.prompt: For which value of k are the vectors (1, 2, 0), (0, 1, {{a}}) and (k, 0, 1) linearly dependent?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Three vectors in R³ are dependent exactly when the determinant of the matrix with them as columns is zero

problems.prompt: A set has {{m}} vectors in R^{{n}} whose matrix has rank {{r}}. How many of the vectors can be removed, at most, without shrinking the span?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: The span has dimension r, so r independent vectors carry it and the other m − r are redundant

problems.prompt: What is the dimension of the span of (1, 2, {{a}}), (2, 4, {{b}}) and (0, 0, 1)?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: The first two vectors agree in their first two entries up to the factor 2, and (0, 0, 1) fills in the third: the span is a plane

problems.prompt: Vectors in R³ form a matrix of rank {{r}}. What does their span look like? (Answer 0 for a point, 1 for a line through the origin, 2 for a plane through the origin, 3 for all of R³.)

parts.label: v
parts.explain: The span is a subspace of dimension equal to the rank: lines and planes always pass through the origin

problems.prompt: Fit y = b + mx by least squares to the points (0, {{y0}}), (1, {{y1}}), (2, {{y2}}), (3, {{y3}}). What is the slope m?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Normal equations AᵀA c = Aᵀy; with x = 0, 1, 2, 3 the slope is Σ(x − x̄)(y − ȳ)/Σ(x − x̄)²

problems.prompt: A least-squares line with an intercept is fitted to {{n}} points; the first {{k}} residuals sum to {{s}}. What is the sum of the remaining residuals?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: The residual vector is orthogonal to the column of ones, so all residuals sum to zero

problems.prompt: A is a ${{m}} \times {{n}}$ matrix of rank ${{r}}$. What is the dimension of its null space?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Rank plus nullity is the number of columns: ${{n}} - {{r}}$. The number of rows does not enter

problems.prompt: What is the rank of $\begin{pmatrix} {{a}} & {{b}} & 1 \\ {{c}} & {{d}} & 0 \\ {{s*a + t*c}} & {{s*b + t*d}} & {{s + e}} \end{pmatrix}$?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: The first two rows are independent (neither is a multiple of the other). Test the third: is it ${{s}}$ times row 1 plus ${{t}}$ times row 2? Check the last entry

expect.v: Matrix([[a, b, 1], [c, d, 0], [s*a + t*c, s*b + t*d, s + e]]).rank()

problems.prompt: The projection of $y = \begin{pmatrix} {{k*a - t*b}} \\ {{k*b + t*a}} \end{pmatrix}$ onto $u = \begin{pmatrix} {{a}} \\ {{b}} \end{pmatrix}$ is $c\,u$. Find $c$.

parts.label: v
parts.explain: $c = \dfrac{y\cdot u}{u\cdot u} = \dfrac{ {{(k*a - t*b)*a + (k*b + t*a)*b}} }{ {{a^2 + b^2}} }$

expect.v: Matrix([k*a - t*b, k*b + t*a]).dot(Matrix([a, b]))/Matrix([a, b]).dot(Matrix([a, b]))

problems.prompt: Gram–Schmidt with $v_1 = \begin{pmatrix} {{a}} \\ {{b}} \end{pmatrix}$ and $x_2 = \begin{pmatrix} {{k*a - t*b}} \\ {{k*b + t*a}} \end{pmatrix}$: $v_2 = x_2 - \dfrac{x_2\cdot v_1}{v_1\cdot v_1}v_1$. What is the first entry of $v_2$?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: The coefficient is $\dfrac{x_2\cdot v_1}{v_1\cdot v_1} = {{k}}$, so $v_2 = x_2 - {{k}}v_1 = \begin{pmatrix} {{-t*b}} \\ {{t*a}} \end{pmatrix}$. Check: it is orthogonal to $v_1$

expect.v: (Matrix([k*a - t*b, k*b + t*a]) - Matrix([k*a - t*b, k*b + t*a]).dot(Matrix([a, b]))/Matrix([a, b]).dot(Matrix([a, b]))*Matrix([a, b]))[0]

problems.prompt: Are $u = \begin{pmatrix} {{a}} \\ {{b}} \\ {{c}} \end{pmatrix}$ and $v = \begin{pmatrix} {{c}} \\ {{c + e}} \\ {{-(a + b)}} \end{pmatrix}$ orthogonal?

parts.label: a
parts.explain: $u\cdot v = {{a*c + b*(c + e) - c*(a + b)}}$. Orthogonal means the dot product is exactly zero

choices.a: 0 if Matrix([a, b, c]).dot(Matrix([c, c + e, -(a + b)])) == 0 else 1

problems.prompt: Fit $y = \beta x$ (a line through the origin) by least squares to the points $(1, {{k + t}})$, $(2, {{2*k + t}})$, $(3, {{3*k - t}})$. Find $\beta$.

parts.label: v
parts.explain: One unknown, so the normal equation is a single line: $\beta = \dfrac{\sum x_i y_i}{\sum x_i^2} = \dfrac{ {{(k + t) + 2*(2*k + t) + 3*(3*k - t)}} }{14}$

cases.q: Which equation does the least-squares solution of Ax = b satisfy?
In least squares, the residual b − Ax̂ is orthogonal to which space?
When is the least-squares solution unique?
What is Ax̂ geometrically?

parts.label: a
choice: When the columns of A are linearly independent
The orthogonal projection of b onto the column space of A
parts.explain: Least squares projects b onto Col A. The leftover b − Ax̂ is perpendicular to every column, which is exactly Aᵀ(b − Ax̂) = 0; AᵀA is invertible when the columns are independent

problems.prompt: $A = \begin{pmatrix} {{a}} & 1 \\ {{c}} & {{d}} \end{pmatrix}$. Without multiplying matrices, find the trace of $A^3$.

parts.label: v
parts.explain: The eigenvalues are ${{l1}}$ and ${{l2}}$ (sum ${{a + d}}$, product ${{a*d - c}}$). $A^3$ has eigenvalues $\lambda^3$, and the trace is their sum: ${{l1^3}} + {{l2^3}}$

cases.q: A real symmetric matrix has real eigenvalues.
A real symmetric matrix is diagonalizable.
Eigenvectors of a symmetric matrix belonging to different eigenvalues are orthogonal.
An n × n matrix with n distinct eigenvalues is diagonalizable.
A matrix with a repeated eigenvalue is diagonalizable.
An invertible matrix is diagonalizable.
A matrix with determinant 0 is invertible.
A singular value of a matrix is negative.
A matrix with 0 as an eigenvalue is invertible.

problems.prompt: Always, sometimes or never? {{q}}

parts.label: a
parts.explain: Symmetric matrices are the safe case: real eigenvalues, orthogonal eigenvectors, always diagonalizable. In general a matrix is diagonalizable exactly when it has n independent eigenvectors; distinct eigenvalues guarantee that, repeated ones may or may not. Invertibility is a separate question: it fails exactly when 0 is an eigenvalue. Singular values are square roots of eigenvalues of AᵀA, so never negative

problems.prompt: What is the largest singular value of $\begin{pmatrix} {{p}} & 0 \\ {{q}} & 0 \end{pmatrix}$?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: $A^{\mathsf T}A = \begin{pmatrix} {{p^2 + q^2}} & 0 \\ 0 & 0 \end{pmatrix}$, so the singular values are $\sqrt{ {{p^2 + q^2}} }$ and $0$: the length of the one nonzero column

problems.prompt: A matrix has singular values {{s1}}, {{s2}} and {{s3}}. What is the 2-norm error of its best rank-{{kk}} approximation?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Eckart–Young: truncating the SVD after k terms is best, and the leftover's largest singular value is σ_(k+1)

expect.v: (Matrix.diag(nsimplify(s1), nsimplify(s2), nsimplify(s3)) - Matrix.diag(*([nsimplify(s1), nsimplify(s2), nsimplify(s3)][:kk] + [0]*(3 - kk)))).singular_values()[0]

problems.prompt: A matrix has singular values {{s1}}, {{s2}}, {{s3}}. What fraction of its squared Frobenius norm does the best rank-1 approximation keep?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: ‖A‖_F² = Σσᵢ², and the rank-1 truncation keeps σ₁²: the 'energy' a principal component captures

problems.prompt: Let A = [[1, 0], [0, 1], [{{a}}, {{b}}]] and b = (1, 2, {{c}}). Using x = A⁺b with A⁺ = (AᵀA)⁻¹Aᵀ, find x₁.

parts.label: v
parts.explain: With independent columns the pseudo-inverse gives the least-squares solution of Ax = b

problems.prompt: A 3 × 2 matrix has SVD with singular values {{s1}} and {{s2}}. What are the singular values of A⁺? Give the larger one.

parts.label: v
parts.explain: A⁺ = VΣ⁺Uᵀ inverts each nonzero σ, so the smallest singular value of A becomes the largest of A⁺

problems.prompt: T acts on polynomials by T(p) = {{op}}. What is the eigenvalue for the eigenvector p(x) = x^{{k}}?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Apply T to the monomial and read off the multiple: x·d/dx counts the degree

expect.v: simplify([x*diff(x**k, x), x**k + x*diff(x**k, x), 2*x*diff(x**k, x) - x**k][m]/x**k)

problems.prompt: D = d/dx acts on polynomials of degree at most {{n}}. What is the {{what}} of D?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: On P_n, D lowers degree by one: its matrix is nilpotent with rank n, and D^(n+1) kills every polynomial, so 0 is its only eigenvalue

expect.v: [Matrix(n + 1, n + 1, lambda i, j: j if j == i + 1 else 0).rank(), n + 1][w]

problems.prompt: For which $h$ is the system $x_1 + {{a}}x_2 = {{b}}$, ${{c}}x_1 + hx_2 = {{d}}$ inconsistent?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Row 2 − c·row 1 leaves (h − ac)x₂ = d − cb: no solution when the left side vanishes and the right does not

problems.prompt: A homogeneous system has {{m}} equations in {{nv}} unknowns. At least how many free variables must it have?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: At most one pivot per row, so at least n − m columns have none

problems.prompt: For which $h$ is $\begin{pmatrix} {{k}} \\ h \\ {{k*b}} \end{pmatrix}$ in the span of $\begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ {{a}} \\ {{b}} \end{pmatrix}$?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: The span of one vector is its multiples: the scale is fixed by the first entry

expect.v: solve(Eq(Matrix([1, a, b]).cross(Matrix([k, x, k*b]))[2], 0), x)[0]

problems.prompt: $Ax = b$ is consistent, $A$ has {{nv}} columns and rank {{r}}. What is the dimension of the solution set (a shifted subspace)?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Every solution is p + (null space), and the null space has dimension n − rank

problems.prompt: $A^{-1} = \begin{pmatrix} {{a}} & {{b}} \\ {{c}} & {{d}} \end{pmatrix}$. What is the (1, 2) entry of $(A^T)^{-1}$?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: (Aᵀ)⁻¹ = (A⁻¹)ᵀ, so its (1, 2) entry is A⁻¹'s (2, 1) entry

cases.q: A is 4×4 and Ax = 0 has only the trivial solution. Which must also be true?
cases.o1: Ax = b has a unique solution for every b
cases.o4: The columns of A are dependent

cases.q: A is square and its columns span ℝⁿ. Which must be true?
A is square and 0 is an eigenvalue. Which must be true?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: For a square matrix every statement of the invertible matrix theorem stands or falls together

problems.prompt: $A = \begin{pmatrix} {{a}} & {{b}} \\ {{c}} & {{d}} \end{pmatrix}$. What is the (1, 2) entry of $A^2$?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Row 1 of A dotted with column 2 of A: ab + bd

problems.prompt: How many scalar multiplications does the standard algorithm use to multiply a {{m}}×{{k}} matrix by a {{k}}×{{p}} matrix?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Each of the m·p entries is a dot product of length k

problems.prompt: $A = LU$ with $L$ unit lower triangular and $U$ upper triangular with diagonal {{u1}}, {{u2}}, {{u3}}. What is $\det A$?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: det L = 1 and det U is the product of its diagonal: the pivots

problems.prompt: $L = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ {{l}} & 1 \end{pmatrix}$. Solving $Ly = \begin{pmatrix} {{p}} \\ {{q}} \end{pmatrix}$, what is $y_2$?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Forward substitution: y₁ = p, then y₂ = q − l·y₁

problems.prompt: $A$ and $B$ are 3×3 with $\det A = {{a}}$ and $\det B = {{b}}$. What is $\det({{k}}A^{-1}B^T)$?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: det(kM) = k³ det M for 3×3; det A⁻¹ = 1/det A; det Bᵀ = det B

problems.prompt: $B$ is made from a 3×3 matrix $A$ by swapping two rows and then multiplying one row by {{k}}. If $\det B = {{dB}}$, what is $\det A$?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Undo the operations: divide by k and flip the sign

problems.prompt: What is the area of the triangle with vertices ({{x1}}, {{y1}}), ({{x2}}, {{y2}}) and ({{x3}}, {{y3}})?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Half the parallelogram spanned by two edge vectors: ½|det|

cases.q: Which is a subspace of ℝ³?
Which is a subspace of the 2×2 matrices?
Which is a subspace of the polynomials of degree ≤ 3?
cases.o4: {p : p has a positive leading coefficient}

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Test the zero vector first, then closure under addition and scaling

problems.prompt: What is the dimension of the span of $(1, {{a}}, 0)$, $(0, 1, {{b}})$ and $({{1}}, {{a + k}}, {{k*b + e}})$?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: The third vector is v₁ + k·v₂ exactly when its last entry is k·b; otherwise it leaves the plane

problems.prompt: Using the orthogonal basis $\{(1, 1), (1, -1)\}$, what is the first coordinate of $x = ({{p}}, {{q}})$?

parts.label: v

parts.label: v

parts.label: v

parts.label: v

problems.prompt: For which $h$ is $(1, h, 2)$ orthogonal to $({{a}}, {{b}}, {{c}})$?

parts.explain: Orthogonal means the dot product is zero

problems.prompt: $A$ has first column $({{a}}, {{b}}, {{c}})$. In $A = QR$ (Gram–Schmidt, positive diagonal), what is $R_{11}$?

problems.prompt: What is the larger eigenvalue of $\begin{pmatrix} {{a}} & {{b}} \\ {{b}} & {{a}} \end{pmatrix}$?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Eigenvectors (1, 1) and (1, −1), orthogonal as for any symmetric matrix, give a ± b

problems.prompt: A well-mixed ${{V}}$ L tank of brine is flushed with pure water at ${{q}}$ L/min (same flow out, constant volume). How long until the salt concentration falls to $1/{{k}}$ of its starting value, in minutes?

parts.explain: Salt balance on a stirred tank: $V\dfrac{dC}{dt} = -qC$, so $C = C_0e^{-t/\tau}$ with $\tau = V/q = {{V/q}}$ min. Set $e^{-t/\tau} = 1/{{k}}$: $t = \tau\ln {{k}}$

problems.prompt: A stirred tank is flushed at constant volume. After ${{n}}$ residence time{{n > 1 ? "s" : ""}} ($t = {{n}}\tau$), what percent of the original solute is still in the tank?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: First-order washout: $e^{-t/\tau}$. Worth knowing cold: 37% after one $\tau$, 14% after two, 5% after three, under 1% after five

problems.prompt: A well-insulated tank holds ${{m}}$ kg of water ($c_p = 4.18$ kJ/(kg·K)) at ${{T1}}$ °C. A ${{Q}}$ kW heater is switched on. How long until it reaches ${{T2}}$ °C, in minutes?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Closed system, no losses: $m c_p\dfrac{dT}{dt} = \dot Q$, a constant rate. Energy needed is ${{m*4.18*(T2 - T1)}}$ kJ; at ${{Q}}$ kJ/s that takes ${{m*4.18*(T2 - T1)/Q}}$ s

problems.prompt: Two streams of a {{nc}}-component mixture merge into one. Of the {{tot}} stream variables (three flows and their compositions) {{known}} are given. How many degrees of freedom remain? (Negative means over-specified.)

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Unknowns minus independent equations: a non-reactive unit gives one balance per component. Zero means the problem can be solved

problems.prompt: In parallel reactions A → D (desired) and A → U, conversion of A is {{X}} and the fractional yield of D (moles D per mole A fed) is {{Yd}}. What is the selectivity, moles D per mole U?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: A consumed = D + U formed (one to one here); yield counts D against A fed, selectivity against U

problems.prompt: A reactor converts {{Xs}} of its feed per pass; unreacted A is separated completely and recycled, so overall conversion is 100%. For {{F}} mol/h of fresh A, what is the recycle flow, in mol/h?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Everything fed must eventually react: (F + R)X_sp = F. Low single-pass conversion means a large recycle and a big separator

problems.prompt: Water at {{Th}} °C is mixed adiabatically with {{mc}} kg/s of water at {{Tc}} °C. What flow of the hot water, in kg/s, gives a mixture at {{Tm}} °C? (Constant c_p.)

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Heat lost by the hot stream equals heat gained by the cold one: the lever rule on temperature

problems.prompt: A reaction has ΔH°(298 K) = {{dH}} kJ/mol and ΔC_p = {{dCp}} J/(mol·K), constant. What is ΔH at {{T}} K, in kJ/mol?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Kirchhoff's law: carry reactants down to 298 K, react, carry products back up

problems.prompt: A tank of cross-section {{A}} m² drains through an orifice of {{a}} cm² (discharge coefficient 0.6). How long, in s, for the level to fall from {{h1}} m to {{h2}} m? (g = 9.81 m/s²)

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Outflow ∝ √h (Torricelli), so draining slows as the level drops; the last bit takes longest

problems.prompt: A stirred batch ({{m}} kg, c_p = 4.18 kJ/(kg·K)) at {{T0}} °C is heated by steam at {{Ts}} °C through a coil with UA = {{UA}} W/K. How long, in min, to reach {{T}} °C?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: The driving force shrinks as the batch warms, so the approach is exponential with time constant mc_p/UA
