parts.explain: K changes by exp(ΔΔG/RT): 1 kcal/mol is about 5.4-fold and 1.36 kcal/mol tenfold at room temperature

cases.q: In favourable cases, alchemical binding predictions reach an RMS error of about:

parts.explain: Independent cycles = E − N + 1 (a star map, with E = N − 1, has none, so it cannot be checked by closure)

cases.o4: Only ligands with the same charge

cases.o1: Large sets, because they use the fewest edges

cases.q: For N ligands, a star map has how many edges?

cases.o1: Unphysically strong electrostatics with no steric repulsion
cases.o3: Too few λ states for electrostatics

cases.o2: Insert as many atoms as possible

cases.o4: Make the ligand bind tighter in reality

cases.o1: Left unconstrained, with a timestep of about 1 fs

cases.o2: Changing a methyl to an ethyl

cases.q: Single topology uses a ___ maximum common substructure than dual topology:

cases.o1: Check what it supports before planning the perturbations

cases.o1: A relative calculation mutating the substituent

Boresch restraints restrain:
cases.o1: All six rigid-body degrees of freedom of the ligand relative to the protein

cases.q: Absolute binding free energies are reported relative to a standard state of:

cases.o1: Well-defined, rigid parts of the ligand and protein

cases.q: Restraints can reduce sampling, but they can also:
cases.o3: Remove the need for a standard-state correction

cases.o3: A single replica moving through λ

cases.q: Independent fixed-λ runs are acceptable when:

parts.explain: Replica exchange is the robust default

Each λ state should be equilibrated:

cases.o1: Different states get different errors that distort ΔG

cases.o1: Automated and kept under version control

cases.o1: Maximises the number of effectively uncorrelated samples

parts.explain: Neighbouring overlap below about 0.03 is unreliable: add or respace states there

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Independent uncertainties add in quadrature; the complex leg usually dominates

problems.prompt: Three independent repeats give ΔΔG = {{a}}, {{b}} and {{c}} kcal/mol. What is the standard error of their mean?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Sample standard deviation over √n: the error that independent copies reveal, which MBAR's own error bar often understates

parts.label: v
choice: Not consistent: the error bars are too small
parts.explain: Differences between repeats bigger than the propagated error mean the error bars underestimate the real uncertainty

parts.label: v
parts.explain: A state function sums to zero around a closed cycle; a large residual points to undersampled edges

problems.prompt: Predicted versus experimental ΔG (kcal/mol) for four ligands: ({{p1}}, {{e1}}), ({{p2}}, {{e2}}), ({{p3}}, {{e3}}), ({{p4}}, {{e4}}). What is the mean unsigned error?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: MUE and RMSE are the headline errors for relative results; correlation statistics depend on the sign convention

cases.q: For relative free energies, report errors as:
cases.o1: RMSE and MUE (correlation depends on the sign convention)

cases.o1: At least three, from uncorrelated starting points

cases.o1: Add or tighten a restraint and correct for it

parts.label: v

cases.o1: Quantum interaction energies with water, and condensed-phase properties

cases.o4: The temperature is wrong at constant pressure

cases.o2: All of its interactions, internal ones included

cases.o1: Relative, as a perturbation network among the analogues
cases.o2: Absolute, one ligand at a time
cases.o3: With a single long MD run

cases.q: Comparing two chemically unrelated ligands calls for:
cases.o1: Absolute calculations, since no sensible atom mapping exists

cases.q: A charge-changing modification within a series argues for:
cases.o1: Extra care: a finite-size correction either way, and relative only if the correction is applied

cases.q: Relative calculations are usually cheaper because:
cases.o1: The shared scaffold's error cancels, so less of the molecule has to be transformed
cases.o2: They use fewer lambda windows by definition

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Chemical similarity is what decides: a mapping that cancels most of the system is the whole advantage of a relative calculation

problems.prompt: propka predicts pKa values {{p1}}, {{p2}}, {{p3}} and {{p4}} for four acidic residues. At an experimental pH of {{ph}}, how many are protonated?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Below its pKa a residue is protonated, above it deprotonated. The T4 lysozyme sites are run at the paper's two experimental pH values, and the states chosen here are what goes in the methods section

expect.v: (1 if nsimplify(p1) > nsimplify(ph) else 0) + (1 if nsimplify(p2) > nsimplify(ph) else 0) + (1 if nsimplify(p3) > nsimplify(ph) else 0) + (1 if nsimplify(p4) > nsimplify(ph) else 0)

cases.q: In lambda dynamics, lambda is:
cases.o1: An extra dynamical variable with its own mass and momentum, propagated with the atoms
cases.o2: A fixed parameter set once per window

cases.q: The advantage over fixed-lambda windows is that:
cases.o1: One simulation samples the whole alchemical space, so several end states are compared at once

cases.q: A lambda particle given too small a mass will:
cases.o1: Move so fast that the spatial coordinates cannot follow it adiabatically

cases.q: Free energies come out of a lambda-dynamics run from:
cases.o1: The relative populations of the end states

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Making lambda dynamical turns a set of separate windows into one trajectory whose populations carry the answer

cases.q: In the MSλD potential, which terms are scaled by a single substituent's lambda?
cases.o1: That substituent's own bonded and nonbonded terms with the environment

cases.q: Which terms carry a product of two lambdas?
cases.o1: Interactions between substituents at two different sites
cases.o4: Bonded terms within the common core

cases.q: Substituents at the same site do not interact because:
cases.o1: They occupy the same space, so their mutual interactions are excluded

cases.q: The common core's self-interaction is:
cases.o1: Unscaled, since it is present in every end state
cases.o2: Scaled by the sum of lambdas
cases.o3: Scaled by the product of lambdas

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Which power of lambda multiplies a term follows from how many alchemical groups the term involves

cases.q: Which ALF bias term is a fixed offset that equalises the end-state free energies?
cases.o1: The fixed term, applied per substituent

cases.q: What does the endpoint bias term do?
cases.o1: Pushes population into the physical end states, where lambda is near 0 or 1
cases.o2: Flattens the middle of the profile

cases.q: Why is any bias needed at all?
cases.o1: Barriers between substituents make transitions rare, so the run would not interconvert them

cases.q: The biases affect the final free energies how?
cases.o1: Not at all: they are subtracted out, they only change how fast it converges
cases.o3: They scale the answer by lambda

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Each term flattens a different feature of the landscape; the answer is bias-independent, the convergence is not

problems.prompt: A block setup has {{nb}} blocks. How many more pairwise bias potentials must be allocated under the newer nine-per-pair scheme than under the older five-per-pair scheme?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Both schemes allocate a fixed number of potentials per ordered pair of blocks, so the count grows as nblocks squared; the newer scheme's extra terms are what let it handle around twenty substituents

cases.q: A Result.txt entry is nan. The reading:
cases.o1: That substituent was never sampled, so no free energy could be estimated
cases.o4: The estimator failed on good data

cases.q: The usual first response to a nan in the penultimate production run is:
cases.o1: Repeat a production of that length, since it suggests the biases have not converged
cases.o2: Extend straight to the final length
cases.o4: Reduce the number of substituents to one

cases.q: Very noisy but finite entries suggest:
cases.o1: Marginal sampling of that substituent: more flattening or longer production
cases.o4: A box that is too large

cases.q: Extending a long production from poor biases gives:
cases.o1: Poor results: refine the biases on shorter runs first
cases.o2: Good results, since length fixes everything

parts.label: v
parts.explain: A nan is a sampling report, not a crash: it says the bias schedule, not the run length, is what needs work

cases.q: What does one ALF cycle consist of?
cases.o1: A short simulation, reweighting of recent cycles, profiles fitted, and the biases updated
cases.o2: A full production run and a final analysis

cases.q: Why does a cycle reweight several recent runs rather than only the last?
cases.o1: To use more data while still discarding biases that are now stale
cases.o3: Because the last run is always wrong

cases.q: If a cycle fails with an error, runflat:
cases.o1: Retries that cycle until it succeeds

cases.q: Relaunching runflat after a crash:
cases.o1: Checks how far it got and resumes at the first incomplete cycle

parts.label: v
parts.explain: The cycle is short-run, reweight, fit, update; the fault tolerance is what makes a hundred-cycle schedule practical on a preemptable queue

cases.q: A flattened 1-D profile along one substituent's lambda should look like:
cases.o1: Roughly flat, with population reaching both end states
cases.o4: A straight line with large slope

cases.q: A profile with a deep minimum in the middle means:
cases.o1: The run is trapped between end states and the biases need more work

cases.q: Biases that are still moving between cycles indicate:
cases.o1: More flattening cycles are needed before production

cases.q: Starting production from unconverged biases costs:
cases.o1: A long run that samples some substituents badly, giving nan or noisy entries
cases.o4: A systematic shift in every answer

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Flattening is judged on the profiles and on whether the biases have stopped moving, not on cycle count alone

problems.prompt: A flattening cycle is to run {{ps}} ps at a {{dt}} fs timestep, discarding the first quarter. How many sampling steps does that make?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Numerical experiments found discarding the first quarter optimal, so the sampling argument is three times the equilibration argument; the example run files use 13000 and 39000 steps for a cycle of about 104 ps and 125000 and 375000 for 1 ns

problems.prompt: A system mutates site 1 to {{m1}} alternatives and site 2 to {{m2}} alternatives, each site also keeping its native residue. What value of nblocks does alf_info.py compute?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: nsubs counts the native plus each mutation at a site, and nblocks is the sum over sites, which is what alf_info.py prints; the p38 example has nsubs 16 and 12 and so nblocks 28

cases.q: For a site-saturation system with about twenty substituents, the recommended bias scheme is:
cases.o1: The newer nine-term scheme, which was designed for that many

cases.q: For a two-substituent perturbation, the recommended bias scheme is:
cases.o1: The older five-term scheme, which is best for two

cases.q: Current best practice for the loss function is:
cases.o1: The nonlinear loss, not the older linearized one

cases.q: Current best practice for implicit constraints is:
cases.o1: The piecewise constraint, which samples the exact endpoints

cases.q: Linearized ALF should not be used beyond about:

parts.label: v
parts.explain: The defaults in the software are the oldest options; best practice has moved, and the right bias scheme depends on how many substituents the site has

problems.prompt: Result.txt gives {{gf}} kcal/mol in the folded ensemble with uncertainty {{sf}}, and {{gu}} with uncertainty {{su}} in the unfolded ensemble. What is the uncertainty of the folding ΔΔG (kcal/mol)?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: The folding ΔΔG subtracts the unfolded ensemble's value from the folded one, and the two legs are independent runs, so their uncertainties add in quadrature

cases.q: In alchemical_definitions.inp, the first substituent at a site is written as:
cases.o1: 0, standing for the native residue already in the non-alchemical structure file

cases.q: Subsequent substituents at a site are written as:
Histidine substituents need special codes because:
cases.o1: The three protonation states are separate substituents and need separate codes

cases.q: The terminal variables in that file usually have no effect unless:
cases.o1: The mutation site is near a chain terminus

cases.q: Mutating several sites in one simulation means:
cases.o1: Listing a second site resid and its own substituent sequence
cases.o4: Nothing: only one site is supported

parts.label: v
parts.explain: The file is the mutation set in machine-readable form; the native residue is always substituent zero, which is why nsubs is one more than the number of mutations

cases.q: system.inp is adapted from the production script by:
cases.o1: Stripping out the dynamics commands and adding the alchemical setup streams

cases.q: Why must the array-dimension line be removed from system.inp?
cases.o1: It only works in the first script CHARMM reads, and system.inp is streamed by another script

cases.q: A soft link to the topology directory is created because:
cases.o1: Everything must live under prep for ALF, but the stream file refers to the original names

cases.q: Of the three alchemical streams, which adds the extra atoms and their bonded terms?
What does the delete stream remove?
cases.o1: Angles and dihedrals the patching added by accident

cases.q: Which stream applies the lambda scaling to the right atom selections?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: The prep directory is a non-alchemical system plus four streams: patch, select, delete, then block setup

problems.prompt: Clustering {{nf}} frames at a {{cut}} angstrom RMSD cutoff puts {{n1}} frames in the largest cluster. What percentage of the trajectory does it hold?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: A cutoff that puts nearly everything in one cluster is too loose and one that makes every frame its own cluster is too tight; the representative structure is the member nearest the cluster centre, not the lowest-energy frame

cases.q: Why must the structure file be loaded before the trajectory?
cases.o1: The trajectory holds only numbers; without the structure file nothing says which atom each is

cases.q: A molecule appears split across the box edge. The cause:
cases.o1: Periodic wrapping: it must be unwrapped or re-centred before measuring

cases.q: Measuring an RMSD without first superposing gives:
cases.o1: A value dominated by overall translation and rotation

cases.q: A distance measured across a periodic boundary without the minimum image convention is:
cases.o1: Too large, because it uses the far copy

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Most trajectory analysis mistakes are bookkeeping: what the numbers mean, and which periodic copy they refer to

problems.prompt: A SLURM time limit is given as a single number, which slurm reads as minutes. How many minutes should be requested for a job expected to take {{hr}} hours, with a {{saf}}x safety factor?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: A bare number in the time option is minutes, so a full day is 1440; slurm uses the limit to schedule, and the lab is billed for the time actually used, not the limit

problems.prompt: A campaign needs {{ns}} ns of simulation and the system runs at {{rate}} ns/day on one GPU. At the paid GPU rate of 0.32 dollars per GPU-hour, what does it cost (dollars)?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: GPU-hours are the simulation length divided by the throughput; the free GPU partition costs nothing but a job there is killed when a paid job needs the node, so the usual plan is free for production and paid for debugging

cases.q: Which engine runs lambda dynamics fastest inside CHARMM?
cases.o2: The standard Fortran engine on CPUs

cases.q: Why can OpenMM not be used for the lambda-dynamics runs here, even though it is fast?
cases.o1: It does not yet run lambda dynamics from within CHARMM
cases.o2: It is slower than the standard engine

cases.q: The GPU domain-decomposition engine compares to BLaDE how?
cases.o1: Several times slower for these systems

cases.q: A quick energy evaluation of a small system is fine on:
cases.o1: The standard engine, since the setup cost dominates anyway

cases.q: CHARMM is preferred in this group over faster engines because:
cases.o1: Multisite lambda dynamics was developed in it and its features are there
cases.o3: It is the only one with a scripting language

parts.label: v
parts.explain: The engine choice is a speed decision except for lambda dynamics, where only some engines support it at all

cases.q: What distinguishes a constant-pressure BLaDE dynamics command from a constant-volume one?
cases.o1: The pressure-coupling keywords: the Monte Carlo barostat and its interval, reference pressure and volume move

cases.q: Before the dynamics command, the friction coefficient is set by:
cases.o1: A scalar assignment over the selected atoms
cases.o2: A keyword in the dynamics command

cases.q: The equilibration and production steps here differ in timestep by:
cases.o1: A factor of two: 1 fs for equilibration, 2 fs for production

cases.q: BLaDE is invoked for an energy or minimisation by:
cases.o1: Adding its keyword to that command

parts.label: v
parts.explain: The same keyword switches engine for energy, minimisation and dynamics; constant pressure only adds the barostat keywords

cases.q: Reproducing a CHARMM run in OpenMM from the same files requires matching:
cases.o1: The cutoff scheme, long-range method, constraints and thermostat parameters

cases.q: The commonest cause of a mismatch between two engines on the same system is:
cases.o1: Different nonbonded cutoff and switching conventions

cases.q: An engine comparison should be checked on:
cases.o1: The single-point energy of one configuration, before any dynamics

cases.q: Matching single-point energies between engines to within a small tolerance shows:
cases.o1: The system was set up the same way in both, which is what a cross-check is for
cases.o4: That the free energies will agree

parts.label: v
parts.explain: A cross-engine check is a setup check: agree on one configuration's energy first, and only then compare dynamics

cases.q: In a CHARMM script, how is a title ended?
cases.o1: A line containing only an asterisk

cases.q: Which character begins a comment?
How is the value of a script variable used?
cases.o1: With an at sign before its name

cases.q: What does a doubled at sign do?
cases.o1: Builds a variable name from another variable's value, giving array-like access

cases.q: How is a value that CHARMM itself computed, such as the atom count, referenced?
cases.o1: With a question mark before its name

cases.q: How are loops written in the CHARMM scripting language?
cases.o1: With a label, a counter, and an if test that jumps back to the label

cases.q: Why must a file path with capital letters be quoted?
cases.o1: CHARMM is case-insensitive but linux is not, so quoting preserves the case
cases.o4: To make it a stream file

parts.label: v
parts.explain: The language is small: titles, set and calc, at and doubled-at for variables, question mark for CHARMM's own values, stream, and if with goto for control flow

cases.q: Which of these is most often left out of a methods section and most often needed to reproduce a run?
cases.o1: The protonation states assigned to every titratable residue

cases.q: Recording the engine version matters because:
cases.o1: Defaults and algorithms change between versions, so the same input can give different runs
cases.o2: Versions are needed for citation only

cases.q: For an alchemical run, the record must also include:
cases.o1: The bias scheme, loss function and implicit constraint used, since the defaults are not best practice

cases.q: The box and ion composition belong in the record because:
cases.o1: They set the salt concentration and net charge the result depends on
cases.o2: They are needed for the figures

parts.label: v
parts.explain: A run is reproducible when someone else could rebuild the same system: the model, the states you chose, and the options that are not defaults

problems.prompt: A system has {{na}} atoms. Single-precision coordinates are written every {{iv}} steps of a {{ns}} ns run at a 2 fs timestep. How many gigabytes of trajectory is that, counting 12 bytes per atom per frame and 1 GB as 10^9 bytes?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: A nanosecond is 500000 steps at 2 fs, so the frame count is the step count over the save interval; raising the save interval is the lever that keeps a long production from filling the group's quota

cases.q: After a finished ALF project, which is safe to delete?
cases.o1: The per-cycle run directories and the intermediate analysis data
cases.o2: The alchemical trajectories of published work

cases.q: Which should essentially never be deleted for published work?
cases.o1: The alchemical trajectories, which are the data behind the numbers

cases.q: The spatial trajectories of a published project:
cases.o1: Can be deleted if space is desperate, after publication

cases.q: The cheapest way to generate less trajectory data in the first place is:
cases.o1: Raise the save interval on the production command

parts.label: v
parts.explain: The intermediates exist for debugging; what carries the result is the prep directory, the alchemical trajectories and the analysis output

cases.q: Intersite coupling biases are needed when:
cases.o1: Substituents at different sites interact, so one site's landscape depends on the other's state

cases.q: Without intersite flattening, a multi-site run tends to:
cases.o1: Sample some combinations of substituents and never others
cases.o3: Give a systematic shift in every answer

cases.q: The intersite setting is given:
cases.o1: Per site pair, as part of the flattening and postprocessing calls

cases.q: Two sites far apart in the structure:
cases.o1: Usually need no intersite biases, since they barely interact

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Coupling is a property of the structure: sites that touch need their joint landscape flattened, sites that do not can be treated independently

cases.q: The Potts-model estimator is preferred to counting end-state populations when:
cases.o1: The combinatorial space is too large for every combination to be visited

cases.q: The histogram estimator fails in a large space because:
cases.o1: Most combinations have zero counts, so their free energies are undefined

cases.q: The Potts model assumes the free energy is:
cases.o1: A sum of per-site terms plus pairwise couplings

cases.q: Pseudolikelihood is used instead of full likelihood because:
cases.o1: The full likelihood's normalisation is intractable for many sites

parts.label: v
parts.explain: A model estimator buys coverage of unvisited combinations at the price of its own assumption, so the assumption has to be checked

problems.prompt: A design needs {{tot}} substituents at one site, and a single simulation is held to at most {{cap}} substituents there. How many simulations does the site need, if one substituent must be the shared native in every one?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: The native has to appear in every batch so the batches can be referenced to each other, so each batch adds only cap minus one new substituents; the per-site cap depends on the bias scheme and implicit constraint chosen

cases.q: A charge-changing perturbation in a periodic box suffers from:
cases.o1: A finite-size error, because the neutralising background interacts with the solute

cases.q: The software's correction for this is applied by:
cases.o1: Declaring each substituent's charge so the discrete solvent correction can be computed

cases.q: The finite-size error shrinks with box size as:
cases.o1: Roughly the inverse of the box length, which is why it is slow to converge away
cases.o4: The inverse square of the atom count

cases.q: A relative calculation between two ligands of equal net charge:
cases.o1: Avoids the correction entirely, which is a reason to pair perturbations that way

parts.label: v
parts.explain: The correction is cheap and the box-size route is not, so declare the charges; better still, design the network so net charge does not change

cases.q: Which sites in the T4 lysozyme exercise needed replica exchange for converged free energies?
Biasing-potential replica exchange helps by:
cases.o1: Letting a replica stuck behind a spatial barrier swap into a differently biased landscape

cases.q: A site needs replica exchange when the slow coordinate is:
cases.o1: Spatial — the surrounding structure has to rearrange — rather than alchemical

cases.q: A symptom that flattening alone will not fix the sampling is:
cases.o1: Biases that converge but end-state populations that still depend on the starting structure
cases.o2: A nan in the first cycle

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Flattening handles alchemical barriers; a spatial barrier needs exchange, which is why four of the seven T4 lysozyme sites were enough for the exercise and three were not

cases.q: Why do proline mutations need a dedicated alchemical strategy?
cases.o1: Proline's ring closes the backbone, so the mutation changes backbone connectivity, not just a side chain

cases.q: Why is glycine a special case?
cases.o1: It removes the side chain entirely, including atoms the common core would otherwise share

cases.q: A standard side-chain-only perturbation scheme assumes:
cases.o1: A shared backbone that every substituent keeps unchanged

cases.q: The T4 lysozyme exercise is described as side-chain only, which means:
cases.o1: Proline and glycine substituents are outside its scope

parts.label: v
parts.explain: The common core is the backbone; proline and glycine break that assumption in opposite directions, so each needs its own treatment

cases.q: In an NVT simulation, which quantity fluctuates while the others are fixed?
cases.o4: The temperature parameter of the bath

cases.q: In an NPT simulation, the volume fluctuations measure what?
In NVT, the variance of the total energy gives what?
In which ensemble does the particle number fluctuate?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Each ensemble fixes some variables and lets their conjugates fluctuate; the size of the fluctuation is a response function

problems.prompt: A conformational barrier is ΔG‡ = {{dG}} kcal/mol at 298 K. With an attempt frequency of kT/h = 6.2 × 10¹² s⁻¹, about how many crossings does a {{L}} μs run see?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Fewer than about ten crossings means the run is quasi-nonergodic for that coordinate: its averages reflect where it started

problems.prompt: A system has {{n}} degrees of freedom at {{T}} K. What is its average kinetic energy, in kcal/mol? (R = 0.0019872 kcal/mol·K)

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Equipartition: ½kT per degree of freedom; the instantaneous temperature reads this backwards

problems.prompt: Two states are populated {{r}} : 1 at {{T}} K. What is their energy difference, in kcal/mol? (R = 0.0019872 kcal/mol·K)

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Each factor of ten in population is about 1.36 kcal/mol at room temperature

problems.prompt: Three states have free energies 0, {{g1}} and {{g2}} kcal/mol at 298 K. What fraction of the time is spent in the lowest state? (kT = 0.593 kcal/mol)

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Populations are Boltzmann weights normalised by the partition function over the states

cases.q: Which free energy does a potential of mean force W(ξ) become when integrated over the whole coordinate?
cases.o1: The free energy of the state: −kT ln of the integral of exp(−βW) over ξ
cases.o4: Nothing: it is only a relative curve

cases.q: Why is the Gibbs-vs-Helmholtz distinction small for binding in water?
cases.o1: PΔV is tiny for condensed-phase processes
cases.o2: Water is incompressible, so A = G exactly
cases.o4: It is not small: they differ by kT

cases.q: A PMF along a distance must be corrected by what to compare with a binding constant?
cases.o1: The Jacobian (2kT ln r) and a standard-state volume

cases.q: What does a flat PMF region mean?
cases.o1: No mean force: all positions there are equally likely

parts.label: v
parts.explain: A PMF is a free energy restricted to one coordinate; turning it into a standard binding free energy needs the volume element and a reference concentration

problems.prompt: In CHARMM, atom i has ε = {{ei}} and R_min/2 = {{ri}} Å; atom j has ε = {{ej}} and R_min/2 = {{rj}} Å. What is their LJ energy at r = {{r}} Å, in kcal/mol?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Lorentz–Berthelot in CHARMM form: R_min,ij = R_min,i/2 + R_min,j/2 and ε_ij = √(ε_iε_j); the energy is −ε at R_min

problems.prompt: A peptide carries {{nd}} ASP, {{ndp}} ASPP, {{ne}} GLU, {{nk}} LYS, {{nks}} LSN, {{nh}} HSP and {{nhd}} HSD residues, with charged termini (NTER, CTER). What is its net charge?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: ASPP, GLUP, LSN and HSD/HSE are neutral; HSP is +1. Charged termini cancel. The net charge sets the counterions

problems.prompt: The {{m}} water model puts {{qh}} e on each hydrogen at O–H = {{r}} Å and H–O–H = {{th}}°, with the balancing charge on oxygen. What is its dipole moment, in debye? (1 e·Å = 4.803 D)

parts.label: v
parts.explain: About 2.35 D against 1.85 D in the gas: fixed-charge models build in an average polarisation, which is part of why TIP3P diffuses too fast

problems.prompt: Velocity Verlet's energy fluctuation scales as Δt². By what factor does it shrink if the time step is cut from {{d1}} fs to {{d2}} fs?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Second-order accuracy: halving the step quarters the error but doubles the cost

problems.prompt: A particle of mass 1 has F = −{{k}}x. Leapfrog has x₀ = {{x0}} and v₋½ = {{v}}, with Δt = {{dt}}. What is x₁?

parts.label: r
parts.explain: v½ = v₋½ + a₀Δt, then x₁ = x₀ + v½Δt: the same trajectory as velocity Verlet, with velocities half a step out of phase

problems.prompt: A box holds a protein of {{N}} atoms with {{nh}} bonds to hydrogen constrained, plus {{w}} rigid waters. With centre-of-mass motion removed, how many degrees of freedom are left?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Each constraint removes one: a rigid water keeps 6 of its 9 (3 translations, 3 rotations). Get this wrong and the reported temperature is wrong

problems.prompt: Hydrogen mass repartitioning sets each H to 3.024 amu and takes the extra from its bonded heavy atom. What mass, in amu, does the carbon of a {{g}} group keep? (C 12.011, H 1.008)

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Total mass is conserved, so equilibrium properties are unchanged; only the fastest H motions slow down, allowing 4 fs

problems.prompt: The fastest vibration in a system is at {{nu}} cm⁻¹. Using the rule of about ten steps per period, what is the largest safe time step, in fs? (c = 2.998 × 10¹⁰ cm/s)

parts.label: v
parts.explain: O–H stretches at about 3400 cm⁻¹ have a 10 fs period: constraining X–H bonds is what makes 2 fs safe

problems.prompt: A Berendsen thermostat with τ = {{tau}} ps pulls a system from {{T0}} K toward {{Tb}} K. What is its temperature after {{t}} ps?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Exponential relaxation is fast and robust for equilibration, but it suppresses fluctuations, so Berendsen does not give the canonical ensemble

problems.prompt: A free particle of mass {{m}} g/mol undergoes Langevin dynamics with γ = {{g}} ps⁻¹ at 300 K. What is its diffusion coefficient D = kT/(mγ), in Å²/ps? (R = 8.314 J/mol·K)

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Friction slows diffusion: a large γ thermostats tightly but distorts transport, which is why production runs use small fbeta

problems.prompt: Water has κ_T = 4.5 × 10⁻⁵ bar⁻¹. A {{L}} Å cubic water box sees an instantaneous pressure swing of {{dP}} bar. By how many Å³ does its equilibrium volume change?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Liquids barely move under pressure, which is why instantaneous pressures swing by hundreds of bar while the density stays put

problems.prompt: A Monte Carlo barostat proposes V → V′ with ΔU = {{dU}} kT, PΔV = {{pv}} kT and N ln(V′/V) = {{nl}}. What is the acceptance probability, min(1, exp(−ΔU − PΔV + N ln(V′/V)))?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: The N ln(V′/V) term is the volume's entropy: it is what makes the sampled ensemble isobaric rather than isochoric

problems.prompt: A cubic box holds {{M}} × 10⁴ g/mol of material. What edge length, in Å, gives density {{rho}} g/cm³? (N_A = 6.022 × 10²³)

parts.label: v
parts.explain: 1 g/cm³ is 0.6022 amu/Å³: a 30 000 g/mol water box of density 1 is about 37 Å on a side

problems.prompt: In a cubic box of side {{L}} Å, two atoms are separated by raw differences Δx = {{dx}}, Δy = {{dy}}, Δz = {{dz}} Å. What is the minimum-image distance, in Å?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Wrap each component into [−L/2, L/2] separately before taking the length

problems.prompt: A solute spans {{d}} Å with {{e}} Å of water on every side. About how many waters does a truncated octahedron save over a cube with the same image distance? (water 0.0334 per Å³; the octahedron has 0.77 of the cube's volume)

parts.label: v
parts.explain: A rounder cell wastes less water in the corners: about 23% fewer atoms for the same distance between images

problems.prompt: With Ewald splitting parameter κ = {{k}} Å⁻¹, what fraction of a pair's Coulomb interaction is left in the real-space term at the cutoff r_c = {{rc}} Å, erfc(κr_c)?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: κ is chosen so the real-space part is negligible at the cutoff (about 10⁻⁵ or less); the rest goes to reciprocal space

problems.prompt: A {{L}} Å box needs a PME grid spacing of at most {{h}} Å. What is the smallest number of grid points along that edge?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Engines then round up to a size with small prime factors so the FFT is fast

problems.prompt: A pair has R_min = {{rm}} Å and ε = {{e}} kcal/mol. What is its LJ energy at the {{rc}} Å cutoff, as a fraction of the well depth (U/ε)?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: About −0.3% of the well depth at 12 Å: small per pair, but there are many pairs, so how the LJ is switched off matters

problems.prompt: A residue has pKa {{pKa}}. At what pH is it {{f}}% protonated?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: One pH unit from the pKa is 10/90; two units is 1/99: residues more than two units from the pKa are effectively one state

problems.prompt: A histidine has pKa {{pKa}}. What is its average charge at pH {{pH}}?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Histidine's pKa sits near physiological pH, so it is often partly charged: one fixed protonation state is a choice, not a fact

problems.prompt: A box has {{w}} waters and {{n}} added NaCl pairs (beyond neutralising ions). What salt concentration does that correspond to, in mM? (55.5 M water)

parts.label: v
parts.explain: About 1 ion pair per 370 waters makes 150 mM: small boxes give coarse salt steps

problems.prompt: Atoms of {{M}} g/mol have a 3-D rms speed of {{v}} Å/ps. What temperature, in K? (R = 8.314 J/mol·K; 1 Å/ps = 100 m/s)

parts.label: r
parts.explain: ⟨v²⟩ = 3kT/m: hydrogens move about 3.5 times faster than oxygens at the same temperature

problems.prompt: A quantity has integrated correlation time τ = {{tau}} ps and is saved every {{dt}} ps. What is its statistical inefficiency g = 1 + 2τ/Δt?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Saving more often than τ adds frames but not information: g counts how many frames make one independent sample

problems.prompt: A run gives N = {{N}} frames with standard deviation σ = {{s}} kcal/mol and statistical inefficiency g = {{g}}. What is the standard error of the mean, in kcal/mol?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: N/g effective samples: ignoring correlation understates error bars by √g

problems.prompt: Block averaging over a converged run gives a standard error of {{s}} kcal/mol. What standard error should a run {{f}} times longer give?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Error falls as 1/√(length) once blocks are independent: quartering the error costs 16 times the sampling

problems.prompt: Trials scatter with standard deviation {{s}} kcal/mol. About how many are needed for a 95% half-width of {{h}} kcal/mol? (Use 1.96 for large n.)

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Halving the interval costs four times as many trials; for small n the t factor makes it a few more

problems.prompt: A ratio K is measured as {{K}} with standard error {{sk}}. What is the propagated error in ΔG = −kT ln K at 298 K, in kcal/mol? (kT = 0.593)

parts.label: v
parts.explain: A 10% error in K is about 0.06 kcal/mol: free energies tolerate large relative errors in populations

problems.prompt: A perturbation has ΔA = {{dA}} kcal/mol at 298 K. What value of ⟨e^{−βΔU}⟩₀ must the sampling find? (kT = 0.593)

parts.label: v
parts.explain: A ΔA of 5 kcal/mol needs an average of about 2 × 10⁻⁴: dominated by rare low-ΔU samples, which is why big steps fail

problems.prompt: ΔU sampled in state 0 is Gaussian with standard deviation {{sd}} kcal/mol. By how much does the exact ΔA lie below the mean ⟨ΔU⟩, in kcal/mol, at 298 K? (kT = 0.593)

parts.label: v
parts.explain: For a Gaussian the cumulant series stops at second order, so σ²/2kT is exact; a σ of 2 kcal/mol already shifts ΔA by more than 3 kcal/mol

problems.prompt: Forward FEP gives ΔA(0→1) = {{f}} and reverse gives ΔA(1→0) = {{r}} kcal/mol. What is the hysteresis |ΔA_f + ΔA_r|?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Forward and reverse must be equal and opposite; a gap above about 1 kT means poor overlap

problems.prompt: ⟨∂U/∂λ⟩ is {{g0}}, {{g1}}, {{g2}}, {{g3}} and {{g4}} kcal/mol at λ = 0, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 1. Estimate ΔA with composite Simpson's rule, in kcal/mol.

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Simpson is Richardson extrapolation of two trapezoid estimates; where curvature is strong the two rules disagree, a hint to add windows

expect.v: (4*Rational(1, 4)*(nsimplify(g0)/2 + nsimplify(g1) + nsimplify(g2) + nsimplify(g3) + nsimplify(g4)/2) - Rational(1, 2)*(nsimplify(g0)/2 + nsimplify(g2) + nsimplify(g4)/2))/3

problems.prompt: A potential is mixed as U(λ) = U₀ + λ^{{n}}(U₁ − U₀). At a configuration with U₁ − U₀ = {{d}} kcal/mol, what is ∂U/∂λ at λ = {{l}}?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Powers of λ soften the start of the path; the integral of ⟨∂U/∂λ⟩ is the same, only its shape changes

problems.prompt: A relative binding ΔΔG of {{dd}} kcal/mol came from a complex leg of {{gc}} kcal/mol. What was the solvent leg?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: The two legs close a thermodynamic cycle; the unphysical mutation cancels

problems.prompt: A mutation has ΔΔG_fold = {{dd}} kcal/mol at 298 K. By what factor does it change the folding equilibrium constant? (kT = 0.593)

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Each 1.36 kcal/mol is a factor of ten; positive ΔΔG_fold means destabilising (smaller K)

problems.prompt: A three-edge cycle A→B→C→A has closure error {{e}} kcal/mol. Spreading it equally, by how much is each edge corrected?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Weighted least squares does better, giving uncertain edges more of the correction; an edge that carries a large share is suspect

problems.prompt: What restraint volume, in Å³, makes the standard-state correction −kT ln(V/1661 Å³) equal {{g}} kcal/mol at 298 K? (kT = 0.593)

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Tighter restraints cost more to release: a few Å³ costs about 3 kcal/mol

problems.prompt: A modification changes binding by ΔΔG = {{dd}} kcal/mol at 298 K. By what factor does K_d change? (kT = 0.593)

parts.label: v
parts.explain: A typical 1 kcal/mol prediction error is a fivefold error in K_d

problems.prompt: An MSλD run covers sites with {{n1}}, {{n2}} and {{n3}} substituents. How many pairwise FEP calculations would a star map from the native need to reach every end state?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: End states multiply across sites while λ variables only add: that combinatorial gain is MSλD's point

problems.prompt: Three substituents have θ = {{t1}}°, {{t2}}° and {{t3}}°. With fnex, λ_i = e^{c sin θ_i}/Σ_j e^{c sin θ_j} and c = 5.5. What is λ₁?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: A softmax over c sin θ: the λ values always sum to one and stay in (0, 1)

problems.prompt: With N = {{N}} substituents, what fnex constant c lets one λ reach 1 − {{d}} × 10⁻⁵? (λ_max = [1 + (N − 1)e^{−2c}]⁻¹)

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Larger c lets λ get closer to the endpoints but sharpens the landscape between them

problems.prompt: Substituents i and j have ΔG_i→j = {{dg}} kcal/mol and fixed biases differing by φ_j − φ_i = {{dphi}} kcal/mol at 298 K. What population ratio P_j/P_i should production show? (kT = 0.593)

parts.label: v
parts.explain: A well-flattened run has the biases cancel ΔG, so populations near 1:1 are the target

problems.prompt: Production starts at {{l0}} ns and each stage extends the length by a factor of {{f}}. How many stages until it reaches at least {{L}} ns?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Geometric ramps reach long runs in a few stages and give early checkpoints for convergence

problems.prompt: A mutation has ΔΔG_fold = {{dd}} kcal/mol from folded and unfolded legs with uncertainties {{sf}} and {{su}} kcal/mol. How many combined standard errors from zero is it?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Independent errors add in quadrature; below about 2 the sign of the effect is not established

problems.prompt: After superposition, four atoms are displaced by {{a}}, {{b}}, {{c}} and {{d}} Å. What is the RMSD, in Å?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Squares weight the large deviations: one flexible loop can dominate a protein's RMSD

problems.prompt: A residue has a crystallographic B-factor of {{B}} Å². What RMSF does that correspond to, in Å? (B = 8π²⟨u²⟩/3 with ⟨u²⟩ = RMSF²)

parts.label: v
parts.explain: B-factors also absorb static disorder and lattice motion, so simulated RMSF is usually lower

problems.prompt: A donor sits at (0, 0, 0) and an acceptor at ({{x1}}, {{y1}}, {{z1}}) Å. What is the donor–acceptor distance, in Å, and so does it pass a 3.5 Å criterion? Give the distance.

parts.label: v
parts.explain: A geometric criterion needs both the distance and the D–H···A angle; the cutoffs are conventions, so report which one you used

problems.prompt: A PMF has two minima {{dw}} kcal/mol apart at 298 K. In an unbiased histogram, what ratio of counts (shallower to deeper bin) should you expect? (kT = 0.593)

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Bins only a few kcal/mol up are already rarely visited, which is why barriers need biased sampling

problems.prompt: A campaign needs {{T}} μs of total sampling within {{d}} days on {{g}} GPUs. What throughput per GPU is needed, in ns/day?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Divide sampling by GPU-days; compare with benchmarked throughput before promising a date

problems.prompt: A trajectory of {{N}} atoms stored as single-precision xyz (12 bytes per atom per frame) must fit in {{G}} GB. How many frames can be saved?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Save interval sets storage: saving solvent only when needed, or every few ps instead of every step, is the lever

problems.prompt: A method scales as N^{{p}}. A calculation takes {{t}} times longer than one on a reference system. How many times larger is the system?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Steep scaling means modest growth in size costs orders of magnitude in time: CCSD(T) (N⁷) at twice the size is 128 times slower

cases.q: reproduce a binding measurement made on a bench at fixed temperature and pressure
test whether an integrator conserves energy
measure unperturbed dynamics, such as a diffusion coefficient, after equilibration
sample at fixed temperature in a box whose density is already set
let molecules enter and leave a region in contact with a reservoir

problems.prompt: Which ensemble fits this goal: {{q}}?

parts.label: a
parts.explain: Bench conditions are fixed T and P: NPT, whose free energy is G. NVT gives the Helmholtz energy A. NVE conserves the Hamiltonian, which is what an integrator test and unperturbed dynamics need. μVT fixes chemical potential and lets particle number vary

cases.q: What does the ergodic hypothesis claim?
A side chain has two rotamers separated by a barrier of many kT. What does that do to a short run?
A buried water never exchanges with bulk during the run. What is the consequence?
Two runs from different starts give different averages beyond their error bars. What is the likely cause?

parts.label: a
choice: A long time average equals the ensemble average
The run is quasi-nonergodic: it stays in one basin, so its averages describe only part of the ensemble
Neither run has visited all the relevant states
parts.explain: Time averages equal ensemble averages only if the trajectory visits every relevant state. Barriers of many kT (slow rotamers, buried waters, unfolding) make simulations nonergodic on accessible timescales

cases.q: An NVT simulation gives ratios of which partition function, and so which free energy?
An NPT simulation gives which free energy?
A histogram of a reaction coordinate gives what?
Why can a simulation not give an absolute free energy directly?

parts.label: a
choice: The canonical Q, so the Helmholtz energy A = −kT ln Q
The Gibbs energy G = −kT ln Δ
A potential of mean force, W(ξ) = −kT ln P(ξ) + const
The absolute partition function is intractable; only ratios of Q are ensemble averages
parts.explain: Simulations measure differences: a ratio of partition functions is an average you can sample, an absolute one is not. The PMF is a free energy along a chosen coordinate, defined up to a constant

cases.q: K_b(b − b₀)²
K_φ[1 + cos(nφ − δ)]
ε[(R_min/r)¹² − 2(R_min/r)⁶]
a correction map on pairs of backbone dihedrals
pairs of atoms one or two bonds apart
pairs of atoms three bonds apart

problems.prompt: In the CHARMM potential energy function, what is this? {{q}}

parts.label: a
choice: The Lennard-Jones term in CHARMM form
Excluded from nonbonded terms (1-2 and 1-3 pairs)
parts.explain: CHARMM: bonds, angles, Urey–Bradley, dihedrals, impropers and CMAP are bonded terms; Lennard-Jones and Coulomb act between nonbonded pairs, with 1-2 and 1-3 pairs excluded and 1-4 pairs using special LJ parameters

cases.q: atom names, types, charges, connectivity and patches for each residue
the numerical constants for bonds, angles, dihedrals and LJ
the generated list of atoms, bonds, angles and dihedrals for this particular system
the coordinates
a stream that reads in a whole topology and parameter set

problems.prompt: Which CHARMM file holds {{q}}?

parts.label: a
parts.explain: The RTF says which terms exist per residue; the PRM supplies their constants; the PSF is the system built from them; the CRD gives positions. Topology and parameters are read first, then the structure

cases.q: a protonated (neutral) aspartic acid
a protonated (neutral) glutamic acid
a doubly protonated, positive histidine
a neutral lysine
neutral caps on a peptide cut from a longer chain

problems.prompt: What CHARMM36 name or patch gives {{q}}?

parts.label: a
parts.explain: By default ASP and GLU are deprotonated and LYS protonated; histidine must always be specified (HSD, HSE or HSP). A whole protein gets charged NTER/CTER termini; a peptide cut from a chain gets neutral ACE/CT3 caps

cases.q: partial charges
dihedral parameters
Lennard-Jones parameters
cutoffs, constraints and the water model

problems.prompt: In CHARMM36 and CGenFF, how are the {{q}} set?

parts.label: a
choice: Fitted to quantum interaction energies with TIP3P water
Fitted to liquid densities and heats of vaporisation
They are part of the force field definition: use the settings it was fitted with
parts.explain: A force field is a package: change its water model, cutoff scheme or constraints and you are running a different, untested model

problems.prompt: CGenFF assigns a parameter with penalty score ${{pen}}$. What should you do?

parts.label: a
parts.explain: Below 10 the analogy is good; 10 to 50, check it; above 50 the assignment is a guess, so fit new parameters

choices.a: 0 if pen < 10 else (1 if pen <= 50 else 2)

cases.q: Which water model is CHARMM36 fitted with?
What does the CHARMM variant of TIP3P add?
What is TIP3P's best-known error?
What distinguishes TIP4P-type models?

parts.label: a
choice: It diffuses about twice too fast
A fourth, virtual M site carries the negative charge
parts.explain: A better water model is not automatically better with CHARMM36: the protein parameters were fitted alongside TIP3P, so swapping water breaks the balance

cases.q: In leapfrog, where are velocities stored?
Why does the energy of a symplectic integrator not drift?
Steady drift of total energy in NVE means what?

parts.label: a
choice: At half steps: v(t + ½Δt) = v(t − ½Δt) + a(t)Δt
It exactly conserves a nearby shadow Hamiltonian, so the true energy only fluctuates
The time step, constraint tolerance or cutoff treatment is too loose
parts.explain: Velocity Verlet and leapfrog are time-reversible and symplectic. Bounded fluctuation is healthy; a trend is a symptom

problems.prompt: A particle of mass 1 has force $F = -{{k}}x$. Take one velocity-Verlet step of $\Delta t = {{dt}}$ from $x_0 = {{x0}}$, $v_0 = {{v0}}$. What is $x_1$?

parts.label: r
parts.explain: $x_1 = x_0 + v_0\Delta t + \tfrac12a_0\Delta t^2$ with $a_0 = -{{k}}x_0$. Then compute $a_1$ at $x_1$ and finish with $v_1 = v_0 + \tfrac12(a_0 + a_1)\Delta t$

cases.q: You want 4 fs steps in a plain equilibrium simulation and care about thermodynamics, not kinetics.
A bond to an alchemical atom changes length between end states.
You need accurate dynamical rates.

problems.prompt: {{q}} What do you do?

parts.label: a
choice: Use hydrogen mass repartitioning: total mass and thermodynamics are kept
Drop the constraint on that bond and use 1 fs
Avoid mass repartitioning: it alters kinetics
parts.explain: HMR moves mass from heavy atoms to their hydrogens so the fastest motions slow down. Constraining a bond whose length differs between alchemical states biases single-topology results

cases.q: The run crashes in the first few steps with SHAKE failures.
The temperature spikes at once and the energy blows up after a fresh build.
A long NVE run shows a slow, steady energy drift.

problems.prompt: {{q}} What is the likely cause?

parts.label: a
choice: Unrelaxed contacts or too large a time step: minimise, or shorten the step
The time step, constraint tolerance or cutoff treatment is too loose
parts.explain: Early crashes point at the starting structure or a time step that cannot resolve the fastest motion; a slow drift points at accumulated error from settings

cases.q: a robust general-purpose canonical thermostat
canonical sampling of a small system that needs good ergodicity
a thermostat that also adds friction and noise, robust but damping dynamics
a thermostat that gives the wrong ensemble and can cause the flying ice cube

problems.prompt: Which thermostat is {{q}}?

parts.label: a
parts.explain: Berendsen suppresses kinetic-energy fluctuations and drains energy into slow modes; fine for a quick start, wrong for production

cases.q: What does raising the friction coefficient γ do?
What sets the size of the random force?
What does an fbeta of 0.1 ps⁻¹ mean?

problems.prompt: In Langevin dynamics, m dv/dt = F − γmv + R(t). {{q}}

parts.label: a
choice: Tighter temperature control but slower, less faithful dynamics
Weak coupling: dynamics stay close to Newtonian
parts.explain: The friction and the noise are tied together so the system samples the canonical ensemble at T. BLaDE uses a g-BAOAB Langevin integrator

cases.q: early equilibration only
NPT production for an isotropic solution
a membrane or a crystal

problems.prompt: Which pressure coupling suits {{q}}?

parts.label: a
choice: Monte Carlo barostat, Langevin piston or Parrinello–Rahman, isotropic
parts.explain: Berendsen relaxes the volume quickly but samples the wrong ensemble. A membrane needs its plane and its normal to respond separately

cases.q: iprs
pref
prdv
the N in the acceptance rule

problems.prompt: In BLaDE's Monte Carlo barostat, what does {{q}} set?

parts.label: a
choice: The standard deviation of the volume move in cubic ångström (100)
parts.explain: A volume move is accepted with probability min{1, exp[−β(ΔU + PΔV) + N ln(V′/V)]}

problems.prompt: A solute spans ${{d}}$ Å and needs ${{e}}$ Å of water on every side. Ignoring the solute's own volume, about how many waters fill a {{cell}} cell with the same image distance? (Water ≈ 0.0334 molecules per Å³; the cell's volume is ${{f}}$ times the cube's.)

parts.label: r
parts.explain: Image distance = solute extent + 2 × edge = ${{d + 2*e}}$ Å. A truncated octahedron needs 23% fewer atoms than a cube and a rhombic dodecahedron 29% fewer, for the same protection from images

cases.q: Why are periodic images better than a solvent droplet?
When do periodic artifacts grow?
Why do the unfolded-state pentapeptides use a fixed 40 Å box?

parts.label: a
choice: A droplet has a surface that distorts the solute; images have none
With a net charge, a small box, or a solute that expands
An unfolded chain can stretch, so it needs a larger box fixed in advance
parts.explain: Periodic boundaries trade a large surface artifact for a smaller image artifact; keep the image distance large compared with anything the solute can do

cases.q: Why does a plain Coulomb cutoff fail in a liquid?
What does the Ewald method do with 1/r?
How does PME scale?
How is a box with net charge handled?

parts.label: a
choice: 1/r falls off more slowly than the number of neighbours grows (as r²)
Splits it into a short-ranged erfc(κr)/r part summed in real space and a smooth part summed in reciprocal space
O(N log N), using a grid and fast Fourier transforms
A uniform neutralising background is added
parts.explain: Larger κ moves work from real space to reciprocal space; the split is exact, so only accuracy settings change the answer

cases.q: the real-space cutoff in a typical CHARMM36 setup
the Ewald splitting parameter κ
the reciprocal grid spacing
the interpolation orders BLaDE supports

problems.prompt: What is {{q}}?

parts.label: a
parts.explain: Cutoff, κ and grid are chosen together for a target accuracy; larger κ shifts work to reciprocal space

cases.q: the CHARMM36 Lennard-Jones treatment
the pair-list cutoff
what BLaDE accepts for electrostatics
when to add a long-range dispersion correction

problems.prompt: What is {{q}}?

parts.label: a
choice: 14 to 16 Å, a buffer beyond the cutoff
Only if the force field was fitted with one
parts.explain: Switched, shifted and force-switched cutoffs taper the energy or force differently; the cutoff scheme is part of the force field

problems.prompt: A residue has pKa ${{pKa}}$. What fraction of it is protonated at pH ${{pH}}$?

parts.label: r
parts.explain: $f = \dfrac{1}{1 + 10^{\mathrm{pH} - \mathrm{p}K_a}}$: below the pKa, mostly protonated. Use the predicted pKa for the folded state and the model pKa for an unfolded peptide, and record the choice for the methods section

cases.q: pH well below its pKa, so both nitrogens carry hydrogen
neutral, with an acceptor next to Nδ and a donor next to Nε
neutral, with an acceptor next to Nε and a donor next to Nδ
neutral, solvent-exposed, no clear hydrogen-bond partners

problems.prompt: Which histidine name fits: {{q}}?

parts.label: a
parts.explain: Put the hydrogen on the nitrogen that can donate it to a nearby acceptor. When exposed or unclear, HSE, which is marginally more stable in the unfolded state

cases.q: crystallographic waters for a folded protein
crystallisation additives such as BME or chloride
the temperature

problems.prompt: Building a box in CHARMM-GUI Solution Builder, what do you do with {{q}}?

parts.label: a
choice: Keep them: buried pockets refill slowly
Drop them unless they matter to the question
Set it to the experiment (often 298.15 K, not the 303.15 K default)
parts.explain: Match the simulated system to the experiment being reproduced, not to the crystal or the tool's defaults

cases.q: first
second, after velocities are assigned
third
last

problems.prompt: In the standard preparation, which stage comes {{q}}?

parts.label: a
choice: Restrained NVT, to relax the solvent at constant volume
NPT, to relax the volume at constant pressure
parts.explain: Each stage fixes what the next one assumes. NVT production at a set density needs an NPT equilibration first

problems.prompt: Velocities are drawn from a Maxwell–Boltzmann distribution at ${{T}}$ K. What is the standard deviation of one velocity component of {{atom}} (${{M}}$ g/mol), in Å/ps? ($R = 8.3145$ J/(mol·K); 1 Å/ps = 100 m/s.)

parts.label: r
parts.explain: $\sigma_v = \sqrt{k_BT/m}$ per Cartesian component, and $v_{rms} = \sqrt3\,\sigma_v$. Hydrogens move about $\sqrt{12}$ times faster than carbons

cases.q: Energy, temperature, pressure and density all fluctuate about stable means, and RMSD has plateaued
Density is still rising slowly
RMSD is small but still climbing

problems.prompt: {{q}}. Is equilibration complete?

parts.label: a
choice: Yes: discard the burn-in and analyse the rest
parts.explain: Look for no drift in several observables, not one small number. Apply the same burn-in cut to every run

problems.prompt: A time series has autocorrelation $C_j = {{r}}^j$. What is its statistical inefficiency $g = 1 + 2\sum_{j \ge 1} C_j$?

parts.label: r2
parts.explain: $\sum_{j\ge1} r^j = \dfrac{r}{1 - r}$, so $g = \dfrac{1 + r}{1 - r}$: about one independent sample every $g$ frames. Sum the measured $C_j$ until it converges, but stop before it starts integrating noise

problems.prompt: A trajectory is split into five equal blocks with means ${{b1}}$, ${{b2}}$, ${{b3}}$, ${{b4}}$ and ${{b5}}$. What is the standard error of the overall mean?

parts.label: r
parts.explain: Take the sample standard deviation of the block means (divide by $M - 1 = 4$), then divide by $\sqrt M$. Repeat with longer blocks: the right block size is where this estimate stops growing

expect.r: sqrt(((nsimplify(b1) - (nsimplify(b1) + nsimplify(b2) + nsimplify(b3) + nsimplify(b4) + nsimplify(b5))/5)**2 + (nsimplify(b2) - (nsimplify(b1) + nsimplify(b2) + nsimplify(b3) + nsimplify(b4) + nsimplify(b5))/5)**2 + (nsimplify(b3) - (nsimplify(b1) + nsimplify(b2) + nsimplify(b3) + nsimplify(b4) + nsimplify(b5))/5)**2 + (nsimplify(b4) - (nsimplify(b1) + nsimplify(b2) + nsimplify(b3) + nsimplify(b4) + nsimplify(b5))/5)**2 + (nsimplify(b5) - (nsimplify(b1) + nsimplify(b2) + nsimplify(b3) + nsimplify(b4) + nsimplify(b5))/5)**2)/4)/sqrt(5)

problems.prompt: ${{n}}$ independent trials give a standard deviation of ${{s}}$ kcal/mol across their means. What is the half-width of the 95% confidence interval, in kcal/mol? ($t = {{t}}$ for ${{n - 1}}$ degrees of freedom.)

parts.label: r
parts.explain: $SE = s/\sqrt n$, and the interval is $\bar x \pm t\,SE$. With so few trials $t$ is well above 1.96; and it only holds if the starting structures were independent

cases.q: What do you resample?
How is a 95% bootstrap interval read off?
A free energy is −4.3172 with an uncertainty of 0.4 kcal/mol. How should it be reported?

problems.prompt: Bootstrapping an uncertainty from correlated simulation data. {{q}}

parts.label: a
choice: Blocks or independent trials, never raw frames
The 2.5th to 97.5th percentiles of the resampled values
−4.3 ± 0.4 kcal/mol, with the confidence level stated
parts.explain: Resampling frames that are correlated shrinks the error bar; report only the digits the uncertainty supports

cases.q: Can convergence checks prove a simulation is well sampled?
Independent runs from different starts disagree beyond their error bars. What does it mean?
A property drifts throughout the run. What does it mean?

parts.label: a
choice: No: they can only rule good sampling out
Unvisited states: sampling error that no single error bar shows
The run has not reached the distribution it is sampling
parts.explain: Statistical uncertainty assumes the sampled distribution is the right one; sampling error is what happens when it is not

problems.prompt: Sampling state 0 gives $\langle e^{-\beta\Delta U}\rangle_0 = {{p}}$ at 298 K. What is $\Delta A_{0\to1}$, in kcal/mol? ($kT = 0.593$ kcal/mol.)

parts.label: r
parts.explain: Zwanzig: $\Delta A = -kT\ln\langle e^{-\beta\Delta U}\rangle_0$, exact in the limit because the average equals $Q_1/Q_0$. In practice the exponential average is dominated by rare low-$\Delta U$ samples

problems.prompt: $\Delta U$ sampled in state 0 has mean ${{mu}}$ and standard deviation ${{sd}}$ kcal/mol at 298 K. Estimate $\Delta A$ with the second-order cumulant expansion, in kcal/mol. ($kT = 0.593$.)

parts.label: r
parts.explain: $\Delta A \approx \langle\Delta U\rangle - \dfrac{\sigma^2}{2kT}$, exact for a Gaussian. The variance term grows fast: a σ much over 1–2 kT means the states barely overlap

cases.q: ΔU has a standard deviation of about 1 kT and forward and reverse agree
ΔU has a standard deviation of 5 kT
forward and reverse estimates differ by 2 kcal/mol

problems.prompt: An FEP step shows this: {{q}}. Is the estimate reliable?

parts.label: a
parts.explain: The exponential average is biased and noisy unless σ of ΔU is within about 1–2 kT; hysteresis between directions is the same warning

problems.prompt: $\langle\partial U/\partial\lambda\rangle$ is ${{g0}}$, ${{g1}}$, ${{g2}}$, ${{g3}}$ and ${{g4}}$ kcal/mol at $\lambda = 0, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 1$. Estimate $\Delta A$ with the trapezoid rule, in kcal/mol.

parts.label: r
parts.explain: Thermodynamic integration: $\Delta A = \int_0^1 \langle\partial U/\partial\lambda\rangle\,d\lambda$. Trapezoid: width × (half the ends + the middle points). Simpson needs an odd number of evenly spaced points

cases.q: For U = (1 − λ)U₀ + λU₁, what is ∂U/∂λ?
Why does ⟨∂U/∂λ⟩ misbehave near λ = 0 for an appearing atom under linear LJ scaling?

parts.label: a
choice: It diverges: other atoms can sit on the barely-present atom, so more windows or soft-core are needed
parts.explain: A linear path is simple to write but its integrand is badly curved at the ends when atoms appear or vanish

cases.q: What does BAR use that one-sided exponential averaging does not?

parts.label: a
choice: Samples from both directions, solved self-consistently: the minimum-variance two-state estimator

WHAM, which ALF uses for flattening
parts.explain: All three are the same idea at different scales: use every sample, from every state, to estimate every free energy

parts.label: a
choice: Their charges are switched off while the LJ cores are still on
Their LJ is transformed, with soft-core

parts.explain: Never change charges and LJ together on a linear path when sites appear or vanish: a charge without a core lets opposite charges collapse onto each other

problems.prompt: Mutating ligand A to B costs ${{gc}}$ kcal/mol in the complex and ${{gs}}$ kcal/mol in solvent. What is $\Delta\Delta G_{bind}$ for B relative to A, in kcal/mol?

parts.label: r
parts.explain: Close the cycle: $\Delta G_{bind}(B) - \Delta G_{bind}(A) = \Delta G_{complex} - \Delta G_{solvent}$. The physical binding legs are never simulated; negative means B binds better

problems.prompt: An alchemical mutation costs ${{gf}}$ kcal/mol in the folded protein and ${{gu}}$ kcal/mol in the unfolded-state pentapeptide. What is $\Delta\Delta G_{fold}$, in kcal/mol, and is the mutation stabilising?

parts.label: r
parts.explain: $\Delta\Delta G_{fold} = \Delta G_{alch}(\text{folded}) - \Delta G_{alch}(\text{unfolded})$; positive is destabilising. The capped pentapeptide models a locally solvated unfolded state and ignores nonlocal contacts

problems.prompt: In a perturbation network, A→B is ${{ab}}$, B→C is ${{bc}}$ and C→A is ${{ca}}$ kcal/mol. What is the cycle-closure error, in kcal/mol?

parts.label: r
parts.explain: Free energy is a state function, so the sum round a closed loop should be zero; what is left measures the error on those edges. Star maps are cheap but give no loops to check

Changes the barrier between pairs of substituents

Extra flexibility for systems with many substituents
parts.explain: Together the biases flatten the alchemical landscape so λ moves freely; the fixed biases are subtracted back out to get free energies

problems.prompt: A block setup has ${{nb}}$ blocks and uses ${{per}}$ potentials per pair ({{per == 5 ? "bcxs2018" : "bcxstu2026"}}). How many pairwise bias potentials must it allocate?

parts.explain: Pairs = nblocks(nblocks − 1)/2, times the potentials per pair. This is the ldbi count in the block setup

problems.prompt: In production, substituent i spends ${{Pi}}$ and substituent j ${{Pj}}$ of the frames at λ > 0.99. Their fixed biases differ by $\varphi_j - \varphi_i = {{dphi}}$ kcal/mol. What is $\Delta G_{i\to j}$, in kcal/mol? ($kT = 0.593$.)

parts.label: r
parts.explain: $\Delta G_{i\to j} = -kT\ln(P_j/P_i) - (\varphi_j - \varphi_i)$: the population ratio of the biased simulation, with the bias taken back out. Count only frames past the cutoff (0.99 in production)

problems.prompt: In your head: ${{a}} - {{b}}$. Slide both numbers up by ${{k}}$ so the second one ends in zero.

parts.explain: Adding ${{k}}$ to both numbers does not change the gap between them: ${{a}} - {{b}} = {{a + k}} - {{b + k}} = {{a - b}}$. No borrowing, because you are now taking away a number that ends in zero

problems.prompt: In your head: ${{a}} - {{b}}$. Slide both numbers up by ${{k}}$ first.

parts.label: r
parts.explain: ${{a}} - {{b}} = {{a + k}} - {{b + k}} = {{a - b}}$. Think of two marks on a number line: move both the same distance and they are still as far apart

problems.prompt: Fill the blank so the two subtractions have the same answer: ${{a}} - {{b}} = \;?\; - {{b + k}}$.

parts.label: r
parts.explain: The second number went up by ${{k}}$, so the first must go up by ${{k}}$ too: ${{a + k}} - {{b + k}}$. Both equal ${{a - b}}$. If only one of them moved, the answer would change

problems.prompt: In your head: ${{a}} - {{b}}$. Take away ${{100*h}}$, then fix it.

parts.label: r
parts.explain: ${{a}} - {{100*h}} = {{a - 100*h}}$, but that took away ${{k}}$ too many, so give ${{k}}$ back: ${{a - b}}$. Taking away too much means adding back, never subtracting again

problems.prompt: In your head: ${{100*H + up}} - {{100*H - dn}}$. The numbers are close, so count up from the smaller one.

parts.label: r
parts.explain: From ${{100*H - dn}}$ up to ${{100*H}}$ is ${{dn}}$; from ${{100*H}}$ up to ${{100*H + up}}$ is ${{up}}$. Together ${{up + dn}}$. Subtraction asks how far apart two numbers are, and when they are close it is quicker to walk the gap than to take one away from the other

problems.prompt: In your head: ${{T}} - {{b}}$. Count up from ${{b}}$: first to the next ten, then to ${{T}}$.

parts.label: r

problems.prompt: In your head: ${{a}} + {{b}}$. Move ${{k}}$ from the second number to the first.

problems.prompt: A gas-pair diffusivity is {{D1}} cm²/s at {{T1}} K and 1 atm. Ignoring the change in the collision integral, estimate it at {{T2}} K and {{P}} atm.

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Kinetic theory: faster molecules (√T) and a longer mean free path (T/P) give $T^{3/2}/P$. Gas diffusivities are about 0.1 cm²/s; liquids about 10⁻⁵

problems.prompt: A gas pair has D = {{D1}} cm²/s at {{T1}} K and 1 atm. At what temperature, in K, does D reach {{D2}} cm²/s at the same pressure? (Ignore the collision integral.)

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Invert D ∝ T^{3/2}: a 50% rise in D needs only about a 31% rise in absolute temperature

problems.prompt: A solute has $D = {{D1}}\times10^{-9}$ m²/s in water at {{T1}} K ($\mu = {{mu1}}$ mPa·s). Estimate $D$ at {{T2}} K, where $\mu = {{mu2}}$ mPa·s, in units of $10^{-9}$ m²/s.

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Heating a liquid helps twice: more thermal energy and a lower viscosity, which falls much faster than $T$ rises

problems.prompt: A protein has $D = {{D}}\times10^{-11}$ m²/s in water at 298 K ($\mu$ = 0.89 mPa·s). What hydrodynamic radius does Stokes–Einstein give, in nm? ($k_B = 1.381\times10^{-23}$ J/K)

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Run D = kT/(6πμa) backwards: diffusion measurements (DLS, NMR) report size this way

problems.prompt: Find the Knudsen diffusivity of a gas with $M = {{M}}$ g/mol in a pore {{d}} nm across at {{T}} K, in cm²/s.

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Molecules hit walls more often than each other, so the pore size replaces the mean free path. $D_K$ does not depend on pressure and goes as $\sqrt{T/M}$

problems.prompt: A gas (M = {{M}} g/mol) at {{T}} K has molecular diffusivity {{Dm}} cm²/s. Below what pore diameter, in nm, is the Knudsen diffusivity smaller than that? ($R = 8.314$)

parts.label: v
parts.explain: D_K grows linearly with pore size; where it equals the molecular value the transition region begins. Hydrogen's fast molecules push the crossover to larger pores

problems.prompt: A catalyst pellet has porosity {{e}} and tortuosity {{t}}; the pore diffusivity is {{D}} cm²/s. What is $D_{eff}$, in cm²/s?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Only the pore fraction carries flux, along paths longer than the pellet: divide by τ (typically 2–6)

problems.prompt: A pellet of porosity {{e}} shows $D_{eff}$ = {{De}} × 10⁻⁷ m²/s for a gas whose pore diffusivity is {{D}} × 10⁻⁶ m²/s. What tortuosity does that imply?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Measured D_eff fixes ε/τ together; values of τ from 2 to 6 are usual, and below 1 means the model is wrong

problems.prompt: Vapour A diffuses through {{L}} cm of stagnant air in a tube: $x_A = {{x1}}$ at the liquid surface and 0 at the top. With $c = 40.9$ mol/m³ and $D = {{D}}\times10^{-5}$ m²/s. Find $N_A$, in mmol/(m²·s).

parts.label: v
parts.explain: B is stagnant, so A carries B's share of the bulk flow: $N_A = -cD\,\frac{dx_A}{dz}/(1 - x_A)$. Integrating gives the log; for dilute A it reduces to Fick

problems.prompt: In a Stefan tube the liquid level falls from {{l1}} cm to {{l2}} cm below the top as it evaporates into stagnant air (c = 40.9 mol/m³, D = {{D}} × 10⁻⁵ m²/s, surface mole fraction {{xs}}, zero at the top). The liquid's molar density is {{rl}} kmol/m³. How long does that take, in hours?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Quasi-steady: the flux at each level is the stagnant-film flux over the current path length z, and ρ_L dz/dt equals it, so z² grows linearly in time. This is how D is measured

problems.prompt: Across a film, $x_A$ falls from {{x1}} to {{x2}}. By what factor is the flux through stagnant B larger than for equimolar counterdiffusion with the same $c$, $D$ and thickness?

parts.label: v

problems.prompt: Across a film, x_A is {{x1}} on one side and {{x2}} on the other, with B stagnant. What is the log-mean mole fraction of B?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: x_B,lm sits between the end values; when it is close to 1 the bulk-flow correction can be dropped

problems.prompt: A catalyst slab of half-thickness {{L}} mm runs a first-order reaction with $k = {{k}}$ s⁻¹ and $D_{eff} = {{D}}\times10^{-6}$ m²/s. Find the effectiveness factor.

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Solve $D c'' = kc$ with $c = c_s$ at the surface and no flux at the centre: $c = c_s\cosh(z\sqrt{k/D})/\cosh\phi$. η is the actual rate (the surface flux) over the rate if the whole slab saw $c_s$

problems.prompt: A first-order reaction in a catalyst slab has Thiele modulus φ = {{phi}}. If the slab is made {{f}} times thicker (same k and $D_{eff}$), by what factor does the rate per unit catalyst volume change?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Rate per volume ∝ η. Under strong diffusion control (φ > 3) η ≈ 1/φ, so a thicker slab wastes catalyst in proportion: the classic test for pore-diffusion limits

problems.prompt: A spherical pellet has Thiele modulus $\phi = R\sqrt{k/D_{eff}} = {{phi}}$. Find its effectiveness factor.

parts.label: v
parts.explain: The sphere's profile is $\sinh(\phi r)/(r\sinh\phi)$; η is $3/\phi^2$ times the dimensionless surface gradient. Large φ gives η ≈ 3/φ: only a thin shell works

problems.prompt: Pellets of radius {{R}} mm run a first-order reaction with k = {{k}} s⁻¹ and $D_{eff}$ = {{D}} × 10⁻⁷ m²/s at surface concentration {{c}} mol/m³. What is the observed rate per pellet volume, in mol/(m³·s)?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Same answer two ways: η k c, or the diffusive flux 4πR²D_e(dc/dr)_R through the surface divided by the volume

problems.prompt: A solute diffuses outward through a spherical shell from $r_1 = {{r1}}$ cm ($c = {{c1}}$ mol/m³) to $r_2 = {{r2}}$ cm ($c = 0$); $D = {{D}}\times10^{-9}$ m²/s. Find the rate, in nmol/s.

parts.label: v
parts.explain: The rate through every shell is the same, so $c$ falls as $1/r$. Letting $r_2 \to \infty$ gives Sh = 2 for an isolated sphere

problems.prompt: Diffusion through a spherical shell from $r_1$ = {{r1}} cm to $r_2$ = {{r2}} cm is estimated as a flat slab of the same thickness and the outer area. What is the ratio true rate / slab estimate?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Flux spreads outward, so the inner surface throttles the rate; the slab estimate with the outer area overstates it by r₂/r₁

problems.prompt: A water droplet of diameter {{d0}} µm evaporates into dry still air. With $D = 2.5\times10^{-5}$ m²/s, saturated vapour concentration {{cs}} kg/m³ at the surface and liquid density 1000 kg/m³, how long does it last, in s?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: The evaporation rate $4\pi rDc_s$ shrinks the droplet: $\rho\,r\,dr/dt = -Dc_s$, so $r^2$ falls linearly. Lifetime goes as $d_0^2$

problems.prompt: An evaporating droplet follows the d² law. What fraction of its total lifetime does it take to shrink to {{p}}% of its initial diameter?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: d² falls linearly in time, so shrinking to half the diameter uses three quarters of the life

problems.prompt: A gas is absorbed into a liquid film whose surface moves at {{v}} m/s over a length {{L}} cm. With $D = {{D}}\times10^{-9}$ m²/s, find the average mass-transfer coefficient, in µm/s.

parts.label: r
parts.explain: Each surface element is exposed for $t = L/v$ and absorbs like a semi-infinite liquid, local $k = \sqrt{D/\pi t}$. Averaging over the exposure doubles it

problems.prompt: In penetration theory, by what factor does the average coefficient change if the contact length grows {{f}}-fold and the surface speed {{g}}-fold?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: k ∝ √(D/t) with t = L/v, so k ∝ √(v/L): faster or shorter contact renews the surface more often

problems.prompt: Roughly how long does a solute with $D = {{D}}$ cm²/s take to diffuse {{L}} {{u}}, using $t \approx L^2/D$, in seconds?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Diffusion is fast over a cell (milliseconds) and hopelessly slow over centimetres in a liquid (hours). Stirring wins at large scales

problems.prompt: Roughly how far, in mm, does a solute with D = {{D}} × 10⁻⁹ m²/s spread in {{t}} using $L \approx \sqrt{Dt}$?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Diffusion distance grows as √t: a day only gets you about ten times further than fifteen minutes

problems.prompt: A surface held at $c_0 = {{c0}}$ mol/m³ contacts a deep, initially clean liquid ($D = {{D}}\times10^{-9}$ m²/s). How much solute enters per m² in {{t}} s, in mmol?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: The surface flux is $c_0\sqrt{D/\pi t}$, infinite at first and decaying; integrate in time. Uptake grows as $\sqrt t$

problems.prompt: A deep liquid with D = {{D}} × 10⁻⁹ m²/s takes up gas held at the surface at {{c0}} mol/m³. How long, in s, until {{m}} mmol/m² has been absorbed?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Uptake grows as √t, so absorbing twice as much takes four times as long

problems.prompt: A slab of half-thickness {{L}} mm ($D = {{D}}\times10^{-10}$ m²/s) is suddenly held at zero surface concentration. What is the time constant of the slowest mode, in hours?

parts.explain: Separation of variables gives modes $\cos(\lambda_n z)$ with $\lambda_n L = (n - \tfrac12)\pi$; the first, $\lambda_1 = \pi/2L$, decays slowest, with $\tau = 1/(D\lambda_1^2)$

problems.prompt: A slab dries by diffusion. If its thickness changes by a factor {{f}} and the diffusivity by {{g}}, by what factor does the time to reach the same average content change?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Every diffusion time scales with L²/D; that is the whole of the dimensional argument

problems.prompt: Gas-film $k_y = {{ky}}$ and liquid-film $k_x = {{kx}}$ mol/(m²·s); the equilibrium slope is $m = {{m}}$. Find $K_y$.

problems.prompt: An absorber has measured $K_y$ = {{K}} and gas-film $k_y$ = {{ky}} mol/(m²·s), with equilibrium slope m = {{m}}. What liquid-film $k_x$, in mol/(m²·s), does that imply?

parts.explain: Resistances add; subtract the gas film from the overall to find the liquid film

problems.prompt: With $k_y = {{ky}}$, $k_x = {{kx}}$ mol/(m²·s) and $m = {{m}}$, what fraction of the total resistance lies in the gas film?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Improve the controlling side: more gas turbulence helps only a gas-film-controlled system

problems.prompt: With $k_y$ = {{ky}}, $k_x$ = {{kx}} mol/(m²·s) and m = {{m}}, which film controls (holds over 80% of the resistance)?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Very soluble gases (small m, e.g. NH₃ in water) are gas-film controlled; sparingly soluble ones (large m, e.g. O₂) are liquid-film controlled

choices.v: 0 if (1/nsimplify(ky))/(1/nsimplify(ky) + nsimplify(m)/nsimplify(kx)) > Rational(8, 10) else (1 if (nsimplify(m)/nsimplify(kx))/(1/nsimplify(ky) + nsimplify(m)/nsimplify(kx)) > Rational(8, 10) else 2)

problems.prompt: A sphere in a flow has $Re = {{Re}}$ and $Sc = {{Sc}}$. Find the Sherwood number from Ranz–Marshall.

parts.label: v
parts.explain: The 2 is pure diffusion to a sphere in still fluid; the second term is convection. Liquids (Sc ~ 1000) gain much more from flow than gases

problems.prompt: A sphere {{d}} mm across dissolves in perfectly still water (D = {{D}} × 10⁻⁹ m²/s). What mass-transfer coefficient applies, in μm/s?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Sh = 2 is the pure-diffusion limit (Re → 0): steady diffusion from a sphere into an infinite medium, the floor that every sphere correlation starts from

problems.prompt: If the diffusivity rises by a factor of {{f}}, by what factor does $k$ rise according to {{mdl}}?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Experiments usually find exponents between ½ and ⅔, which is why film theory, though simple, is the least physical

problems.prompt: Changing the solute raises D by a factor {{f}} and the measured k by {{g}}. What exponent n in k ∝ Dⁿ does that give?

parts.explain: n ≈ 1 points to film theory, ½ to penetration or surface renewal, ⅔ to a laminar boundary layer

problems.prompt: A dilute absorber reduces $y$ from {{y1}} to {{y2}}; the driving forces $y - y^*$ are {{d1}} at the bottom and {{d2}} at the top. With $H_{OG} = {{H}}$ m, how tall must the packing be, in m?

parts.explain: A parabola is symmetric about the point halfway between its roots: $\dfrac{ {{p}} + {{p + d}} }{2} = {{p + d/2}}$. The vertex sits on that line, so the factored form gives the vertex almost for free

problems.prompt: Without solving: how many real solutions does ${{a}}x^2 + ({{b}})x + ({{c}}) = 0$ have?

parts.explain: Half the middle coefficient, squared: $({{2*h}}/2)^2 = {{h^2}}$, giving $(x + {{h}})^2$. This one move is completing the square

problems.prompt: A quadratic $x^2 + bx + c$ has roots ${{r1}}$ and ${{r2}}$. What is $c$?

parts.explain: $(x - r_1)(x - r_2) = x^2 - (r_1 + r_2)x + r_1r_2$: the constant is the product of the roots, ${{r1*r2}}$, and $b$ is minus their sum, ${{-(r1 + r2)}}$. Factoring is this run backwards

problems.prompt: A price goes up ${{p}}\%$ and then down ${{p}}\%$. What is the net percent change? (Negative for a decrease.)
