parts.explain: Percent changes multiply: $(1 + {{p/100}})(1 - {{p/100}}) = 1 - {{p/100}}^2 = {{1 - (p/100)^2}}$. Up then down never returns you to the start, because the second percent is taken of a bigger number

problems.prompt: Estimate with the rule of 72: about how many years does money take to double at ${{r}}\%$ a year, compounded annually?

parts.label: r2
parts.explain: $72 / {{r}} = {{72/r}}$ years; the exact answer is $\dfrac{\ln 2}{\ln(1 + {{r/100}})}$. The rule works because $\ln 2 \approx 0.69$ and $\ln(1 + r) \approx r$ for small $r$

problems.prompt: Using $\log 2 \approx 0.30$ and $\log 3 \approx 0.48$, estimate $\log_{10}({{m}} \times 10^{ {{k}} })$.

parts.label: r
parts.explain: A log splits a product: $\log {{m}} + {{k}}$. $\log 5 = \log(10/2) = 1 - 0.30 = 0.70$. The whole-number part of a log is just the power of ten

parts.label: r
parts.explain: Do not find a formula: $f^{-1}(c)$ asks which input gives $c$. Solve ${{a}}x + {{b}} = {{a*y + b}}$: undo the last step first, subtract ${{b}}$, then divide by ${{a}}$

problems.prompt: As $x \to -\infty$, what does $f(x) = {{a}}x^{ {{n}} } + 4x - 9$ do?

parts.label: a2
parts.explain: Only the leading term matters far from the origin. An even power makes $x^n$ positive on both sides; an odd power keeps the sign of $x$. Then apply the sign of the leading coefficient

problems.prompt: What is the average rate of change of $f(x) = x^2$ from $x = {{p}}$ to $x = {{p + d}}$?

problems.prompt: Every length of a solid is multiplied by ${{k}}$. By what factor does its {{dim == 2 ? "surface area" : "volume"}} change?

problems.prompt: Estimate $\sqrt{ {{a^2 + h}} }$ with a tangent line at ${{a^2}}$.

problems.prompt: Use geometry, not antiderivatives: $\displaystyle\int_0^{ {{L}} } ({{m}}x + {{b}})\,dx$

problems.prompt: Without integrating: what can you say about $\displaystyle\int_{- {{a}} }^{ {{a}} } {{f}}\,dx$?

choice: It is zero: the integrand is odd

problems.prompt: What is the average value of $f(x) = x^{ {{n}} }$ on $[0, {{b}}]$?

parts.explain: $\dfrac1b\displaystyle\int_0^b x^n\,dx = \dfrac{b^n}{n + 1}$: the end value divided by $n + 1$. A line averages half its end value, a parabola a third

problems.prompt: If $F(x) = \displaystyle\int_1^x \sqrt{t^2 + {{k^2*c^2 - c^2 + 0}} }\,dt$, what is $F'({{c}})$?

problems.prompt: Sum the series: ${{a}} + \dfrac{ {{a}} }{ {{d}} } + \dfrac{ {{a}} }{ {{d^2}} } + \dfrac{ {{a}} }{ {{d^3}} } + \dots$

parts.label: r2
parts.explain: $\dfrac{dV}{dt} = 4\pi r^2\dfrac{dr}{dt}$: the surface area times the speed of the surface. A thin shell of paint is the picture

problems.prompt: Use a double: ${{a}} + {{a + d}}$

parts.label: r
parts.explain: Double ${{a}}$ is ${{2*a}}$, and ${{a + d}}$ is ${{d}}$ more than ${{a}}$, so the sum is ${{2*a}} + {{d}} = {{2*a + d}}$

problems.prompt: Add in the easiest order: ${{a}} + {{b}} + {{10 - a}}$

parts.label: r
parts.explain: Numbers can be added in any order. ${{a}}$ and ${{10 - a}}$ make ten, so do them first: $10 + {{b}} = {{10 + b}}$

problems.prompt: Multiply by 9 as ten times minus once: $9 \times {{n}}$

parts.label: r
parts.explain: $9 \times {{n}} = 10 \times {{n}} - {{n}} = {{10*n}} - {{n}} = {{9*n}}$. The same move gives $\times 99$ and $\times 19$

problems.prompt: Multiply by doubling: ${{k}} \times {{n}}$

parts.label: r
parts.explain: Times 4 is double, double; times 8 is double three times. ${{n}} \to {{2*n}} \to {{4*n}}{{k == 8 ? " \\to " : ""}}{{k == 8 ? 8*n : ""}}$

problems.prompt: Think multiplication: ${{a*b}} \div {{a}}$ asks ${{a}} \times \;? = {{a*b}}$

parts.label: r
parts.explain: Division is finding the missing factor: ${{a}} \times {{b}} = {{a*b}}$, so ${{a*b}} \div {{a}} = {{b}}$. One multiplication fact answers two division questions

problems.prompt: In your head: ${{a}} \times {{b*z}}$

parts.label: r
parts.explain: ${{b*z}}$ is ${{b}}$ {{z == 10 ? "tens" : "hundreds"}}, so ${{a}} \times {{b}}$ {{z == 10 ? "tens" : "hundreds"}} is ${{a*b}}$ {{z == 10 ? "tens" : "hundreds"}}: ${{a*b*z}}$. Do the fact, then put the place value back

problems.prompt: Break ${{10*t + o}}$ into tens and ones: ${{a}} \times {{10*t + o}} = {{a*10*t}} + \;?$

parts.label: r
parts.explain: ${{a}} \times {{10*t + o}} = {{a}} \times {{10*t}} + {{a}} \times {{o}} = {{a*10*t}} + {{a*o}} = {{a*(10*t + o)}}$. This is the distributive property, and it is what each row of the written algorithm is doing

problems.prompt: Split the number into friendly parts: ${{d*(q1 + q2)}} \div {{d}} = ({{d*q1}} + {{d*q2}}) \div {{d}}$

parts.label: r
parts.explain: ${{d*q1}} \div {{d}} = {{q1}}$ and ${{d*q2}} \div {{d}} = {{q2}}$, so the answer is ${{q1}} + {{q2}} = {{q1 + q2}}$. Pull out the biggest multiple of ten you recognise, then deal with what is left

problems.prompt: Move a factor across: ${{f}} \times {{g*m}}$

parts.label: r
parts.explain: Take ${{g}}$ out of ${{g*m}}$ and give it to ${{f}}$: ${{f}} \times {{g*m}} = {{f*g}} \times {{m}} = {{f*g*m}}$. The product does not change when one factor is multiplied and the other divided by the same number

problems.prompt: Without a common denominator: is $\dfrac{ {{n}} }{ {{d}} }$ more or less than $\dfrac12$?

parts.label: a
parts.explain: Double the top and compare with the bottom: $2 \times {{n}} = {{2*n}}$ against ${{d}}$. Comparing two fractions is often easiest by placing each against a benchmark such as $\tfrac12$ or 1

problems.prompt: Without multiplying: is ${{N}} \times \dfrac{ {{n}} }{ {{d}} }$ bigger or smaller than ${{N}}$?

parts.label: a
parts.explain: Multiplying by a number greater than 1 stretches; by a number less than 1 it shrinks. $\dfrac{ {{n}} }{ {{d}} }$ is {{n > d ? "greater" : "less"}} than 1. "Multiplying makes bigger" is only true for factors above 1

problems.prompt: Treat the decimal as a fraction: ${{dec}} \times {{den*m}}$

parts.label: r
parts.explain: ${{dec}} = \dfrac{ {{num}} }{ {{den}} }$, so divide ${{den*m}}$ by ${{den}}$ to get ${{m}}${{num > 1 ? ", then multiply by " : ""}}{{num > 1 ? num : ""}}: ${{num*m}}$. Faster than lining up decimal points

problems.prompt: How many $\dfrac{1}{ {{d}} }$s are in ${{a}}$? That is ${{a}} \div \dfrac{1}{ {{d}} }$.

parts.label: r
parts.explain: Each whole holds ${{d}}$ pieces of size $\tfrac{1}{ {{d}} }$, so ${{a}}$ wholes hold ${{a}} \times {{d}} = {{a*d}}$. Dividing by a unit fraction is multiplying by its denominator

problems.prompt: In your head: ${{m}} {{up == 1 ? "\\times" : "\\div"}} {{10^k}}$

parts.label: r
parts.explain: Every digit moves ${{k}}$ place{{k > 1 ? "s" : ""}} to the {{up == 1 ? "left (the number gets bigger)" : "right (the number gets smaller)"}}. It is the digits that move, not the point: each place is worth ten times the one to its right

problems.prompt: Build it from 10%: ${{p}}\%$ of ${{N}}$
In your head: ${{a}} - ({{-b}})$

parts.label: r
parts.explain: Subtracting a number is adding its opposite, so ${{a}} - ({{-b}}) = {{a}} + {{b}} = {{a + b}}$. On a number line: how far, and which way, from ${{-b}}$ up to ${{a}}$?

problems.prompt: A calculator shows ${{a}} \times {{b}}$. Which answer is the right size?

parts.label: a2
parts.explain: Round each factor to one figure and multiply in your head; the exact product is ${{a*b|3}}$. An estimate will not give the digits, but it catches a slipped decimal point every time

choices.a2: 0 if a*b < 1 else (1 if a*b < 10 else (2 if a*b < 100 else 3))

problems.prompt: Scale both numbers by ${{k}}$ first: ${{d*q}} \div {{d}}$

parts.label: r
parts.explain: A quotient does not change when both numbers are multiplied by the same thing: ${{d*q}} \div {{d}} = {{d*q*k}} \div {{d*k}} = {{q}}$. Same idea as sliding both numbers in a subtraction, one level up

problems.prompt: A {{m}} kg crash-test dummy moving at {{v}} m/s is brought to rest. With no airbag it stops in {{t1}} s; an airbag stretches the stop to {{t2}} s. By what factor does the airbag reduce the average force?

parts.label: r
parts.explain: The momentum change is fixed by the crash; $\bar F = \Delta p/\Delta t$, so lengthening the stop is the whole design idea behind airbags, crumple zones and helmets

cases.q: Why is a cross-linked polymer (like vulcanised rubber) more rigid and heat-resistant than the same polymer without cross-links?
Why do metals conduct electricity and bend without shattering?
Why does a soap or detergent lift grease into water?
Why is diamond harder than graphite, though both are pure carbon?

parts.label: v
choice: Covalent bonds tie the chains together so they cannot slide past each other
Delocalised electrons move freely and the metal ions can slide while staying bonded
Each molecule has a nonpolar tail that dissolves in grease and a polar head that dissolves in water
Every atom is held by four covalent bonds in three dimensions, not in weakly stacked sheets
parts.explain: A designed material's job follows from its structure at the molecular scale: what holds the particles together and how they can move

problems.prompt: A student's small hydro generator is fed {{Q}} L/s of water falling {{h}} m and lights LEDs drawing {{P}} W. What is the device's efficiency? ($g = 9.81$, 1 L of water = 1 kg)

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Useful output over the energy supplied per second ($\dot m gh$). Designing a converter is choosing where the rest goes (friction, heat, sound) and how to cut it

problems.prompt: Audio is sampled {{f}} thousand times a second with {{b}}-bit samples in stereo (2 channels). How many megabytes does {{t}} minutes take, uncompressed (1 MB = 10⁶ bytes)?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Bits = samples per second × bits per sample × channels × seconds. Digital signals can be copied and sent without adding noise, at the cost of these large numbers (hence compression)

problems.prompt: A {{d}} uses electromagnetic waves at {{f}} GHz. What is the wavelength, in cm? ($c = 3.00\times10^8$ m/s)

parts.label: v
parts.explain: $\lambda = c/f$. Antennas are usually a quarter or half wavelength long, which is why higher-frequency devices can be smaller

problems.prompt: The species–area relation is $S = cA^{z}$ with $z = {{z}}$. If a habitat shrinks to {{f}} of its area, what fraction of its species is expected to be lost eventually?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Species fall more slowly than area ($z < 1$), but losing 90% of a habitat still costs about a third to a half of its species: the basis for protecting large, connected areas

problems.prompt: A fish stock of {{N}} thousand grows {{r}}% a year before harvest, and {{H}} thousand are caught each year. Simulate two years: what is the stock after year 2, in thousands?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Step the model a year at a time. Comparing catch limits this way is how a management rule is tested before it is used on a real population

problems.prompt: {{V}} cm³ of water seeps into a rock crack and freezes. Ice is less dense than water (917 vs 1000 kg/m³). What volume does the ice take up, in cm³?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Same mass, lower density: about 9% more volume. Repeated freezing wedges rock apart, one of the ways water's unusual properties shape the surface

cases.q: What first put large amounts of oxygen into Earth's atmosphere (the Great Oxidation Event, about 2.4 billion years ago)?
How did land plants change Earth's surface after they spread, about 400 million years ago?
What did the oxygen-rich atmosphere make possible high above the surface?
Where did most of the limestone in the crust come from?

parts.label: v
choice: Roots broke rock into soil and slowed erosion
An ozone layer that blocks ultraviolet light
Shells and skeletons of marine organisms
parts.explain: Life and the Earth system change each other: organisms alter the air, rocks and water, and those changes open or close niches for later life

problems.prompt: A {{P}} MW solar farm runs at a {{cf}}% capacity factor for {{y}} years and costs {{C}} million dollars in total. What is its cost per kWh of energy delivered, in cents?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Divide the lifetime cost by the lifetime energy. Comparing resources this way (and adding environmental and social costs) is the cost–benefit analysis the standard asks for

problems.prompt: A power plant emits {{E}} tonnes of SO₂ a year. A scrubber that removes {{eta}}% is installed. How many tonnes a year does it still emit?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: What remains is the fraction not captured. Going from 90% to 99% halves nothing but cuts the remainder tenfold, which is why the last few percent are worth arguing over

cases.s: it must cost less than 20 dollars per household
the more bacteria it removes the better
it must work with no electricity
a higher flow rate is preferred
it must use locally available materials
it should be as easy to clean as possible

problems.prompt: Designing a water filter for a village: is "{{s}}" a criterion or a constraint?

parts.label: v
choice: Criterion (a measure of how good a solution is)
Constraint (a limit every solution must meet)
parts.explain: Constraints rule solutions in or out; criteria rank the solutions that are left. Writing both down before designing is the first step of engineering design

problems.prompt: A device is broken into {{n}} subsystems in series, each working {{r}}% of the time, independently. What fraction of the time does the whole device work?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Breaking a problem into parts lets each be designed and tested, but the parts multiply: many good parts in series make a mediocre whole. Redundancy (parts in parallel) is the fix

problems.prompt: Two designs are scored 1–10 on cost (weight {{w1}}), safety (weight {{w2}}) and durability (weight {{w3}}). Design A scores {{a1}}, {{a2}}, {{a3}}. What is its weighted score?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: A decision matrix makes the trade-offs explicit: change the weights and see whether the winner changes. The weights are a value judgement, not a measurement

problems.prompt: A city's emissions are {{E}} kt/yr. A programme cuts them {{p}}% each year from the previous year's level. Simulate: what are they after {{n}} years, in kt/yr?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: A computational model steps the rule forward year by year; a steady percentage cut is a geometric decay, never quite reaching zero

problems.prompt: Bisection starts on an interval of length ${{L}}$. How many halvings are needed before the interval is no longer than $10^{-{{e}} }$?

parts.label: r
parts.explain: Each step halves the bracket: $L/2^n \le \varepsilon$ gives $n \ge \log_2(L/\varepsilon)$. About 3.3 steps per decimal digit, whatever the function; slow but it cannot fail once the root is bracketed

problems.prompt: Take one Newton step toward the cube root of ${{c}}$, solving $f(x) = x^3 - {{c}} = 0$ from $x_0 = {{x0}}$. What is $x_1$?

parts.label: r
parts.explain: $x_1 = x_0 - f(x_0)/f'(x_0)$, the root of the tangent line. Near a simple root the error squares each step: the number of correct digits roughly doubles

expect.r: solve(Eq((x0**3 - c) + diff(x**3 - c, x).subs(x, x0)*(x - x0), 0), x)[0]

problems.prompt: Solve $x^2 - {{c}} = 0$ by the secant method from $x_0 = {{x0}}$, $x_1 = {{x0 + d}}$. What is $x_2$?

parts.label: r
parts.explain: The secant replaces $f'$ by the slope through the last two points: $x_2 = x_1 - f(x_1)\dfrac{x_1 - x_0}{f(x_1) - f(x_0)}$. No derivative needed; convergence order about 1.6

problems.prompt: Does fixed-point iteration on ${{g}}$ converge to the root near ${{r0}}$ from a nearby start?

parts.label: a
parts.explain: Near the root the error is multiplied by $g'(r)$ each step: it converges when $|g'(r)| < 1$ and diverges when $|g'(r)| > 1$. The same equation rearranged can do either

problems.prompt: Solve ${{a}}x + ({{b}})y = {{e}}$, $({{c}})x + {{d}}y = {{f}}$ by Jacobi iteration from $(x, y) = ({{p}}, {{q}})$. What is $y$ after one step?

parts.label: r
parts.explain: Jacobi solves each equation for its own diagonal unknown using only the old values: $y_1 = (f - c\,x_0)/d$. Diagonal dominance (here $|a| > |b|$, $|d| > |c|$) guarantees convergence

problems.prompt: Solve ${{a}}x + ({{b}})y = {{e}}$, $({{c}})x + {{d}}y = {{f}}$ by Gauss–Seidel from $(x, y) = ({{p}}, {{q}})$, updating $x$ first. What is $y$ after one sweep?

parts.label: r
parts.explain: Gauss–Seidel uses each new value as soon as it has it: first $x_1 = (e - b\,y_0)/a$, then $y_1 = (f - c\,x_1)/d$. It usually converges about twice as fast as Jacobi

problems.prompt: Is $\begin{pmatrix} {{a}} & {{b}} & 1 \\ {{c}} & {{e}} & {{f}} \\ 1 & {{d}} & 6 \end{pmatrix}$ strictly diagonally dominant by rows (so Jacobi and Gauss–Seidel are guaranteed to converge)?

parts.label: a
parts.correct: (a > abs(b) + 1) and (e > abs(c) + abs(f)) and (6 > 1 + abs(d)) ? 0 : 1
parts.explain: Each row: the diagonal entry must beat the sum of the other entries' sizes. Row 1: ${{a}}$ vs ${{abs(b) + 1}}$; row 2: ${{e}}$ vs ${{abs(c) + abs(f)}}$; row 3: $6$ vs ${{1 + abs(d)}}$. Failing the test does not mean divergence, only that the guarantee is gone

choices.a: 0 if Min(a - Abs(b) - 1, e - Abs(c) - Abs(f), 6 - 1 - Abs(d)) > 0 else 1

problems.prompt: Fit the quadratic through $(0, {{y0}})$, $(1, {{y1}})$, $(2, {{y2}})$ and evaluate it at $x = {{t}}$.

parts.label: r
parts.explain: Lagrange form: $p(x) = \sum y_i L_i(x)$ with $L_0 = \tfrac{(x-1)(x-2)}{2}$, $L_1 = -x(x-2)$, $L_2 = \tfrac{x(x-1)}{2}$. At $x = 3$ it is extrapolating, where interpolants are least trustworthy

problems.prompt: Apply Simpson's rule with two panels ($h = 1$) to $\displaystyle\int_0^2 ({{a}}x^3 + ({{b}})x^2 + ({{c}})x + {{d}})\,dx$.

parts.label: r
parts.explain: $S = \tfrac h3\,(f_0 + 4f_1 + f_2)$. Simpson's rule is exact for cubics, so this equals the true integral: its error term involves $f^{(4)}$

problems.prompt: The composite trapezoid rule on a smooth integrand has error ${{E}}$. Roughly what is the error with ${{m}}$ times as many panels?

parts.label: r
parts.explain: Trapezoid error goes as $h^2$: ${{m}}$ times the panels, ${{m}}^2$ times smaller error. Simpson goes as $h^4$, so the same refinement would buy ${{m}}^4$

problems.prompt: A trapezoid estimate gives ${{I + k*s*4}}$ with step $h$ and ${{I + k*s}}$ with step $h/2$. What does Richardson extrapolation give?

parts.label: r
parts.explain: With error $\approx ch^2$, $T(h) = I + ch^2$ and $T(h/2) = I + ch^2/4$; eliminating $c$ gives $I \approx \dfrac{4T(h/2) - T(h)}{3}$. Repeated, this is Romberg integration

expect.r: solve([Eq(x + Symbol('C'), I + k*nsimplify(s)*4), Eq(x + Symbol('C')/4, I + k*nsimplify(s))], [x, Symbol('C')])[x]

problems.prompt: Use two-point Gauss–Legendre quadrature, $\int_{-1}^{1} f \approx f(-1/\sqrt3) + f(1/\sqrt3)$, on $f(x) = {{a}}x^3 + ({{b}})x^2 + ({{c}})$.

parts.label: r
parts.explain: The odd term cancels between the two points; $x^2 = 1/3$ at both. Two well-placed points integrate every cubic exactly, as Simpson does with three

problems.prompt: Take one Heun (improved Euler) step of size $h = {{h}}$ for $y' = {{k}}y + ({{b}})$, $y(0) = {{y0}}$. What is $y_1$?

parts.label: r
parts.explain: Predict with Euler, $y^* = y_0 + hf(y_0)$, then average the slopes at both ends: $y_1 = y_0 + \tfrac h2[f(y_0) + f(y^*)]$. Second order: it matches the Taylor series through $h^2$

problems.prompt: One classical RK4 step of size $h = {{h}}$ for $y' = {{k}}y$, $y(0) = {{y0}}$, multiplies $y$ by a factor. What is $y_1$?

parts.label: r
parts.explain: For $y' = \lambda y$ the four stages combine to $1 + z + z^2/2 + z^3/6 + z^4/24$ with $z = \lambda h$: the Taylor series of $e^z$ through fourth order. Error per step is $O(h^5)$

problems.prompt: Explicit Euler is used on $y' = -{{lam}}\,y$. What is the largest step size $h$ for which the numerical solution does not blow up?

parts.label: r
parts.explain: Each step multiplies $y$ by $1 - \lambda h$; stability needs $|1 - \lambda h| \le 1$, so $h \le 2/\lambda$. A stiff system with one fast mode forces this tiny step on the whole solution, which is why implicit methods exist

problems.prompt: Take one explicit Euler step of size ${{h}}$ for $u' = {{a}}u + ({{b}})w$, $w' = ({{c}})u + ({{d}})w$ from $(u, w) = ({{u}}, {{w}})$. What is the new $u$?

parts.label: r
parts.explain: A system steps exactly like a scalar equation, every component from the old values: $\mathbf y_1 = (I + hA)\mathbf y_0$

problems.prompt: Estimate $f'({{x0}})$ for $f(x) = {{a}}x^3 + ({{b}})x^2$ with the central difference $\dfrac{f(x+h) - f(x-h)}{2h}$, $h = {{h}}$. By how much does the estimate exceed the true derivative?

parts.label: r
parts.explain: The even Taylor terms cancel, leaving $\tfrac{h^2}{6}f'''(x) = \tfrac{h^2}{6}\cdot 6a$. Quadratics are differentiated exactly, so ${{b}}$ drops out; halving $h$ quarters the error

expect.r: ((a*(x0 + nsimplify(h))**3 + b*(x0 + nsimplify(h))**2) - (a*(x0 - nsimplify(h))**3 + b*(x0 - nsimplify(h))**2))/(2*nsimplify(h)) - diff(a*x**3 + b*x**2, x).subs(x, x0)

problems.prompt: Bisection starts on [{{a}}, {{b}}]. After {{n}} halvings, what is the largest possible error of the midpoint of the last bracket?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Each halving shrinks the bracket by 2; the midpoint is at most half a bracket from the root

problems.prompt: Newton's method on f(x) = 1/x − {{a}} computes 1/{{a}} without division. From $x_0$ = {{x0}}, what is $x_1$?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: x − f/f′ simplifies to x(2 − ax): only multiplications, which is how early hardware divided. It converges for 0 < x₀ < 2/a

expect.v: nsimplify(x0) - (1/Symbol('t') - a).subs(Symbol('t'), nsimplify(x0))/diff(1/Symbol('t') - a, Symbol('t')).subs(Symbol('t'), nsimplify(x0))

problems.prompt: Apply one step of false position to f(x) = x² − {{c}} on the bracket [{{a}}, {{b}}]. Where does the chord cross zero?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Like the secant step, but it keeps a bracket with a sign change, so it cannot diverge; one end can stall, though

problems.prompt: Fixed-point iteration converges linearly with |g′(root)| = {{L}}. About how many iterations reduce the error by a factor of 10^{{k}}?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Each step multiplies the error by about |g′|: L = 0.9 needs over 130 steps for six digits, which is why Newton is preferred

problems.prompt: For A = [[{{a}}, {{b}}], [{{c}}, {{d}}]], what is the spectral radius of the Jacobi iteration matrix?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Jacobi converges for every start exactly when ρ < 1; the error shrinks by about ρ each sweep

expect.v: Max(*[Abs(v) for v in (-Matrix([[a, 0], [0, d]]).inv()*Matrix([[0, b], [c, 0]])).eigenvals()])

problems.prompt: For A = [[{{a}}, {{b}}], [{{c}}, {{d}}]], what is the spectral radius of the Gauss–Seidel iteration matrix?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: For 2×2 (and consistently ordered) systems ρ_GS = ρ_J²: Gauss–Seidel needs about half as many sweeps

expect.v: Max(*[Abs(v) for v in (-Matrix([[a, 0], [c, d]]).inv()*Matrix([[0, b], [0, 0]])).eigenvals()])

problems.prompt: What is the smallest integer k that makes [[k, {{p}}, {{q}}], [{{r}}, k, {{s}}], [{{t}}, {{u}}, k]] strictly diagonally dominant by rows?

parts.label: v
parts.value: max(abs(p) + abs(q), abs(r) + abs(s), abs(t) + abs(u)) + 1
parts.explain: Each diagonal must beat the sum of its row's other magnitudes; the worst row sets k

expect.v: Max(Abs(p) + Abs(q), Abs(r) + Abs(s), Abs(t) + Abs(u)) + 1

problems.prompt: Data: f({{x0}}) = {{f0}}, f({{x1}}) = {{f1}}, f({{x2}}) = {{f2}}. What is the second divided difference f[x₀, x₁, x₂]?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: The second divided difference is the leading coefficient of the interpolating quadratic, which the Vandermonde solve confirms

problems.prompt: Simpson's rule (one panel) is applied to $\int_0^{{b}} x^4\,dx$. What is its error (Simpson minus exact)?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Simpson is exact for cubics, so a quartic shows its leading error, (b − a)⁵f⁗/2880 = b⁵·24/2880

problems.prompt: The composite trapezoid rule on [0, {{L}}] has error (b − a)³|f″|/(12n²). With |f″| = {{f2}} everywhere, how many panels keep the error below {{tol}}?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Error ∝ 1/n²: ten times tighter needs about three times the panels

problems.prompt: For $\int_0^{{b}} ({{c3}}x^3 + {{c1}}x)\,dx$, take the trapezoid rule with one and two panels and apply Richardson extrapolation (4T₂ − T₁)/3. What value results?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: One Richardson step on the trapezoid rule is Simpson's rule, exact for cubics; the value equals the integral

problems.prompt: Three-point Gauss–Legendre uses nodes 0, ±√(3/5) with weights 8/9, 5/9. Apply it to $\int_{-1}^{1} ({{a}}x^4 + {{c}})\,dx$.

parts.label: v
parts.explain: n Gauss points integrate polynomials up to degree 2n − 1 exactly: three points handle a quintic

problems.prompt: Take one midpoint (RK2) step of size h = {{h}} for y′ = t + y from t₀ = {{t0}}, y₀ = {{y0}}.

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Second-order methods match the Taylor series through h²: for this linear ODE the midpoint step equals that truncated series exactly

expect.v: nsimplify(y0) + nsimplify(h)*(t0 + y0) + nsimplify(h)**2/2*(1 + t0 + y0)

problems.prompt: Classical RK4 on y′ = λy has amplification R(z) = 1 + z + z²/2 + z³/6 + z⁴/24 with z = λh. For λh = {{z}}, is the step stable (|R| ≤ 1)?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: R(z) is the Taylor polynomial of e^z; on the real axis RK4 stays stable to about λh = −2.785

problems.prompt: Take one backward (implicit) Euler step for y′ = {{lam}}y with h = {{h}} from y₀ = {{y0}}.

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Implicit Euler damps any negative λ for any h: stable where explicit Euler (needing h < 2/|λ|) would blow up

problems.prompt: What is the stiffness ratio (largest over smallest |eigenvalue|) of y′ = Ay with A = [[{{a}}, {{b}}], [0, {{d}}]]?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: An explicit method must resolve the fastest mode for stability while the slowest sets how long you integrate: a ratio in the hundreds calls for an implicit method

expect.v: Max(*[Abs(v) for v in Matrix([[a, b], [0, d]]).eigenvals()])/Min(*[Abs(v) for v in Matrix([[a, b], [0, d]]).eigenvals()])

problems.prompt: Estimate f′({{x0}}) for f(x) = x³ with a forward difference, step h = {{h}}. What is the error of the estimate (estimate minus exact)?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Forward differences are first order: the error ≈ (h/2)f″ falls only tenfold when h does; central differences fall a hundredfold

problems.prompt: The order is ${{n*H}}$ mg by mouth. Tablets on hand are ${{H}}$ mg each. How many tablets do you give?

parts.label: tabs
parts.explain: Desired over have: ${{n*H}} \div {{H}} = {{n}}$. A half tablet is fine only if it is scored

problems.prompt: The order is ${{ml*H/V}}$ mg. The suspension is ${{H}}$ mg per ${{V}}$ mL. How many mL do you give?

parts.label: vol
parts.explain: $\dfrac{D}{H}\times V = \dfrac{ {{ml*H/V}} }{ {{H}} }\times {{V}} = {{ml}}$ mL

problems.prompt: A client weighs ${{kg*2.2}}$ lb. What is the weight in kilograms?

parts.label: w
parts.explain: Divide pounds by 2.2: ${{kg*2.2}} \div 2.2 = {{kg}}$ kg. Weight-based doses always use kilograms

problems.prompt: The order is ${{d}}$ mg/kg per dose. The child weighs ${{w}}$ kg. How many mg is one dose?

parts.label: mg
parts.explain: ${{d}}\ \text{mg/kg} \times {{w}}\ \text{kg} = {{d*w}}$ mg

cases.q: An odd prime p is a sum of two squares exactly when:
No integer that is 3 mod 4 is a sum of two squares because squares modulo 4 are only:
In the Gaussian integers, the prime 5 factorises as:
In the Gaussian integers, the prime 7:

parts.label: v
parts.explain: A prime splits in the Gaussian integers exactly when it is a sum of two squares, which is how the theorem is proved

problems.prompt: Use the prime number theorem to estimate how many primes are below 10^{{kk}}.

parts.label: v
parts.explain: π(x) ≈ x/ln x, and ln 10^k = k ln 10 ≈ 2.303k. The estimate runs about 10% low at these sizes: there are 78,498 primes below a million

problems.prompt: Compute 2^{{km}} modulo {{kn}} (note {{km}} = {{kn}} − 1). A result other than 1 proves {{kn}} is composite.

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Square repeatedly and reduce. A prime would give 1 by Fermat's little theorem; the test never needs a factor to convict a composite

problems.prompt: Find the remainder r (with 0 ≤ r < {{kn}}) when −{{ka}} is divided by {{kn}}.

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Go down to the multiple of n just below −a and measure up from there: the remainder is never negative

problems.prompt: {{ka}} = q · {{kn}} + r with 0 ≤ r < {{kn}}. Find q + r.

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Divide, keep the whole part as q and what is left over as r

problems.prompt: What is the highest power of {{kp}} that divides {{kn}}!? Give the exponent.

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Count the multiples of p up to n, then the multiples of p² again, then p³, and add

problems.prompt: How many zeros does {{kn}}! end in?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Each trailing zero needs a factor 2 and a factor 5, and fives are the scarce ones: count ⌊n/5⌋ + ⌊n/25⌋ + ⌊n/125⌋ + …

problems.prompt: Find the lowest common multiple of 2^{{a1}} · 3^{{b1}} and 2^{{a2}} · 3^{{b2}} · 5.

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Take the larger exponent of each prime that appears in either number

problems.prompt: Two positive integers have gcd {{kg}} and lcm {{kl}}, and one of them is {{ka}}. Find the other.

parts.label: v
parts.explain: gcd × lcm equals the product of the two numbers

problems.prompt: Find the remainder when {{ka}} · {{kb}} + {{kc}} is divided by {{kn}}.

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Reduce each number modulo n first, then multiply and add the small residues

problems.prompt: What is the last digit of {{ka}}^{{kk}}?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Last digits of powers repeat with period at most 4, so reduce the exponent modulo the period

problems.prompt: Find the remainder when {{kn}} is divided by 9.

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Add the digits (and again if needed): a number and its digit sum leave the same remainder modulo 9

problems.prompt: Find the remainder (between 0 and 10) when {{kn}} is divided by 11.

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Take the alternating sum of the digits starting from the units digit with a plus sign, then reduce modulo 11

problems.prompt: How many solutions modulo {{kn}} has {{ka}}x ≡ {{kb}} (mod {{kn}})?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Let d = gcd(a, n). If d does not divide b there are none; if it does there are exactly d

problems.prompt: Find the least non-negative solution of {{ka}}x ≡ {{kb}} (mod {{kn}}).

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Multiply both sides by the inverse of a modulo n, which exists because a and n are coprime

problems.prompt: φ({{kn}}) = {{kf}}. Use Euler's theorem to find {{ka}}^{{kk}} modulo {{kn}}.

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Reduce the exponent modulo φ(n), then compute the small power that remains

problems.prompt: Modulo the prime {{kp}}, the inverse of {{ka}} is {{ka}}^{{kq}}. Compute it.

parts.label: v
parts.explain: a^(p−1) ≡ 1, so a · a^(p−2) ≡ 1: the power a^(p−2) is the inverse

problems.prompt: How many solutions modulo {{kp}} has x² ≡ {{ka}} (mod {{kp}})?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Square 1, 2, …, (p − 1)/2 to list the non-zero squares. A value on the list is hit twice, by x and by −x

problems.prompt: How many of the numbers 1, 2, …, {{kq}} are squares modulo the prime {{kp}}?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: The map x ↦ x² is two-to-one on the non-zero residues, since x and −x have the same square, so exactly half are squares

problems.prompt: Compute {{ka}}^{{ke}} modulo {{kp}} (note {{ke}} = ({{kp}} − 1)/2). The answer is 1 or {{km}}.

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Euler's criterion: the result is 1 when a is a square modulo p and p − 1 (that is, −1) when it is not

cases.q: Modulo 13, 5⁶ ≡ −1. Therefore 5 is:
If a and b are both non-squares modulo an odd prime p, then ab is:
Modulo an odd prime p, (−1)^((p−1)/2) = 1 exactly when:
A primitive root modulo an odd prime is always:

parts.label: v
parts.explain: The squares form a subgroup of index 2 in the units, so the Legendre symbol multiplies: non-square times non-square is a square

problems.prompt: How many primes are there from {{ka}} to {{kb}} inclusive?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Cross out multiples of 2, 3, 5 and 7 (enough for anything below 121) and count what is left

problems.prompt: To show {{kn}} is prime by trial division, what is the largest prime you need to try?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: A composite number has a prime factor no larger than its square root, so stop at the largest prime below √n

problems.prompt: 2^{{kp}} − 1 = {{km}} is prime. Find the even perfect number it gives.

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Euclid: if 2ᵖ − 1 is prime, 2ᵖ⁻¹(2ᵖ − 1) equals the sum of its proper divisors

cases.q: 2¹¹ − 1 = 2047 = 23 · 89. This shows that:
cases.o1: p prime does not make 2ᵖ − 1 prime

cases.q: If n is composite, 2ⁿ − 1 is:
Every even perfect number has the form:
Whether an odd perfect number exists is:

parts.label: v
parts.explain: If n = ab then 2ᵃ − 1 divides 2ⁿ − 1, so only prime exponents can give Mersenne primes, and not all of them do

problems.prompt: Find the hypotenuse of the Pythagorean triple generated by m = {{km}}, n = {{kn}}.

parts.label: v
parts.explain: The triple is (m² − n², 2mn, m² + n²); the identity (m² − n²)² + (2mn)² = (m² + n²)² is why it works

problems.prompt: Is the Pythagorean triple generated by m = {{km}}, n = {{kn}} primitive (no common factor)?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Primitive exactly when m and n are coprime and one is even, one odd. If both are odd, all three numbers are even

problems.prompt: How many neutrons are in a nucleus of {{nm}} ($Z = {{Zn}}$)?

parts.label: r
parts.explain: The number after the name is the mass number $A$, protons plus neutrons: $N = A - Z = {{A}} - {{Zn}}$

problems.prompt: {{nm}} ($Z = {{Zn}}$) undergoes {{mode}}. What is the atomic number of the daughter?

parts.label: r
parts.explain: Charge is conserved. The emitted particle carries charge ${{q}}$ (alpha $+2$, beta-minus $-1$, positron $+1$), so the daughter has $Z = {{Zn}} - ({{q}})$. The mass number changes by ${{dA}}$: only an alpha takes nucleons away

problems.prompt: The mass defect of {{nm}} is ${{dm|7}}$ u. What is its binding energy per nucleon, in MeV? Use 1 u = 931.5 MeV.

parts.label: r
parts.explain: Binding energy is the mass defect as energy: ${{dm|7}} \times 931.5$ MeV, shared among ${{A}}$ nucleons. The curve peaks near iron at about 8.8 MeV; heavy nuclei sit near 7.6, which is why splitting them releases energy

problems.prompt: {{nm}} has a half-life of ${{T}}$ {{u}}. What percent of a sample is left after ${{t}}$ {{u}}?

parts.label: r
parts.explain: ${{t}}/{{T}} = {{t/T}}$ half-lives, so the fraction left is $\left(\tfrac12\right)^{ {{t/T}} }$. Ten half-lives leaves about a thousandth

problems.prompt: {{nm}} has a half-life of ${{T}}$ {{u}}. How long until its activity has fallen to $1/{{k}}$ of the starting value, in {{u}}?

parts.label: r
parts.explain: Activity falls with the number of atoms: $\left(\tfrac12\right)^{t/T} = \dfrac{1}{ {{k}} }$, so $t = T\log_2 {{k}}$. A factor of 1000 takes about ten half-lives

problems.prompt: A nuclide has a half-life of ${{T}}$ years. What is its decay constant, in per year?

parts.label: r
parts.explain: $\lambda = \dfrac{\ln 2}{T_{1/2}} = \dfrac{0.693}{ {{T}} }$. Activity is $\lambda N$: a short half-life means a hot source that does not last

problems.prompt: The dose rate ${{r1}}$ m from a point source is ${{D1}}$ mSv/h. What is it at ${{r2}}$ m, in mSv/h?

parts.label: r
parts.explain: A point source spreads over a sphere, so intensity goes as $1/r^2$: $\dot D_2 = \dot D_1\left(\dfrac{r_1}{r_2}\right)^2$. Doubling the distance quarters the dose. Distance is the cheapest shield

problems.prompt: A shield material has a half-value layer of ${{hvl}}$ cm for a gamma beam. What thickness cuts the beam to $1/{{k}}$ of its intensity, in cm? Ignore build-up.

parts.label: r
parts.explain: Each half-value layer halves the beam, so you need $\log_2 {{k}}$ of them. A tenth-value layer is 3.32 half-value layers

problems.prompt: A narrow gamma beam passes through ${{x}}$ cm of a material with linear attenuation coefficient $\mu = {{mu}}$ cm⁻¹. What percent gets through unscattered?

parts.label: r
parts.explain: $I = I_0e^{-\mu x}$ with $\mu x = {{mu*x}}$. The half-value layer is $\ln 2/\mu = {{log(2)/mu}}$ cm

problems.prompt: Tissue absorbs ${{D}}$ mGy from {{rad}} (radiation weighting factor ${{w}}$). What is the equivalent dose, in mSv?

parts.label: r
parts.explain: The gray measures energy deposited; the sievert weights it by how damaging the radiation is: $H = w_R D$. Alphas deposit their energy in a few cell widths, hence 20. (Also: 1 Sv = 100 rem, 1 Gy = 100 rad)

cases.q: Alpha particles
Beta particles
Gamma rays
Fast neutrons

problems.prompt: What is the appropriate shield? {{q}}.

parts.label: a
choice: A sheet of paper or the dead layer of skin
A few millimetres of plastic or aluminium
Thick dense material: lead, steel or concrete
Hydrogen-rich material: water, polyethylene or concrete
parts.explain: Alphas are heavy and doubly charged: they stop in a few centimetres of air, and matter only if taken into the body. Betas need a few millimetres of low-Z material (dense metal makes X-rays from them). Gammas are only attenuated, exponentially, best by high density. Neutrons lose energy fastest in collisions with nuclei their own mass, which means hydrogen

problems.prompt: A material has ${{N}} \times 10^{24}$ atoms/cm³ and a microscopic cross section of ${{sig}}$ barns (1 b = $10^{-24}$ cm²). What is the macroscopic cross section, in cm⁻¹?

parts.label: r
parts.explain: $\Sigma = N\sigma$: the powers of ten cancel when $N$ is in $10^{24}$/cm³ and $\sigma$ in barns. It is the probability of an interaction per centimetre travelled; its reciprocal, ${{1/(N*sig)}}$ cm, is the mean free path

problems.prompt: A neutron moves through a material with total macroscopic cross section $\Sigma = {{Sg}}$ cm⁻¹. What is its mean free path, in cm?

parts.label: r
parts.explain: The mean distance between interactions is $1/\Sigma$

problems.prompt: What is the characteristic energy $kT$ of thermal neutrons in a moderator at ${{T}}$ °C, in eV? ($k = 8.617 \times 10^{-5}$ eV/K.)

parts.label: r
parts.explain: $kT = 8.617 \times 10^{-5} \times {{T + 273.15}}$ eV. At room temperature it is 0.025 eV, a neutron speed of 2200 m/s: the reference point for tabulated thermal cross sections

cases.q: Where do delayed neutrons come from?
About what fraction of the neutrons from uranium-235 fission are delayed?
Why does a reactor depend on delayed neutrons?
What makes a good moderator?

parts.label: a
choice: From the decay of certain fission products (precursors), seconds after the fission
They stretch the average neutron generation time from microseconds to about a tenth of a second, slow enough to control
Light nuclei that scatter well and absorb little: hydrogen in water, deuterium, carbon
parts.explain: Prompt neutrons appear within about $10^{-14}$ s of fission. A small fraction $\beta$ (0.0065 for U-235, about 0.0021 for Pu-239) come later from precursor decay, with an average delay of roughly 13 s. As long as the reactor is not critical on prompt neutrons alone, those few set the pace

problems.prompt: A core has fast fission factor ${{eps}}$, fast non-leakage ${{Lf}}$, resonance escape ${{p}}$, thermal non-leakage ${{Lt}}$, thermal utilization ${{f}}$ and reproduction factor ${{eta}}$. What is $k_{eff}$?

parts.label: r
parts.explain: Follow one generation: $k_{eff} = \varepsilon\,L_f\,p\,L_t\,f\,\eta$, each factor the fraction of neutrons that survives one hazard (or, for $\varepsilon$ and $\eta$, the multiplication gained). Without the two leakage terms it is the four-factor $k_\infty$

problems.prompt: A reactor has $k_{eff} = {{k}}$ and a delayed neutron fraction of $0.0065$. What is its state?

parts.label: a
parts.explain: Reactivity $\rho = \dfrac{k - 1}{k} = {{(k - 1)/k}}$. Negative: subcritical. Zero: critical. Positive but less than $\beta = 0.0065$: power rises on the slow delayed-neutron timescale. Equal to or above $\beta$: critical on prompt neutrons alone

choices.a: 0 if k < 1 else (1 if k == 1 else (2 if (k - 1)/k < Rational(65, 10000) else 3))

problems.prompt: What is the reactivity of a core with $k_{eff} = {{k}}$, in pcm ($10^{-5}\,\Delta k/k$)?

parts.label: r
parts.explain: $\rho = \dfrac{k_{eff} - 1}{k_{eff}}$, then $\times 10^5$ for pcm. Negative means subcritical. One dollar of reactivity is $\rho = \beta$, about 650 pcm for U-235

problems.prompt: A subcritical core with $k_{eff} = {{k}}$ contains a steady neutron source. By what factor does the core multiply the source neutrons?

parts.label: r
parts.explain: Each source neutron starts a chain: $1 + k + k^2 + \dots = \dfrac{1}{1 - k}$. As $k \to 1$ the count rate climbs without limit, which is how an approach to criticality is monitored: plot $1/M$ and watch it head for zero

problems.prompt: A reactivity of ${{rho}}$ pcm is added to a critical reactor ($\beta = 650$ pcm, effective precursor decay constant $\lambda = 0.1$ s⁻¹). Estimate the stable period, in seconds.

parts.label: r
parts.explain: For reactivity well below $\beta$: $\tau \approx \dfrac{\beta - \rho}{\lambda\rho} = \dfrac{650 - {{rho}} }{0.1 \times {{rho}} }$. Power then grows as $e^{t/\tau}$. As $\rho$ approaches $\beta$ the period collapses toward the prompt timescale

problems.prompt: Reactor power is rising on a stable period of ${{tau}}$ s. By what factor does it increase in ${{t}}$ s?

parts.label: r
parts.explain: $P = P_0e^{t/\tau}$. One period multiplies power by $e$; the doubling time is $0.693\tau = {{log(2)*tau}}$ s

cases.q: Fuel temperature rises (Doppler broadening of the U-238 resonances)
Moderator temperature rises in an under-moderated water reactor
Xenon-135 builds up
Fuel is depleted over the cycle
A control rod is withdrawn
The boron concentration in the coolant is diluted
A burnable poison burns out

problems.prompt: What does this do to core reactivity? {{q}}.

parts.label: a
parts.explain: Anything that absorbs more neutrons outside fission, or removes fuel, is negative; removing an absorber is positive. The two temperature effects are what make a power reactor self-limiting: more power, hotter fuel and moderator, less reactivity

cases.q: Where does most xenon-135 in an operating core come from?
How is xenon-135 removed while the reactor is at power?
What happens to xenon-135 in the hours after a shutdown from high power?
How does samarium-149 differ from xenon-135?

parts.label: a
choice: From the decay of iodine-135 (half-life about 6.6 h), itself a fission product
By absorbing a neutron (burnup) and by its own decay (half-life about 9.1 h)
It rises to a peak about 10 hours later, because iodine keeps feeding it while burnup has stopped, then decays away
It is stable: it does not decay away, and is removed only by neutron absorption
parts.explain: Xenon-135 has an enormous thermal absorption cross section, so a little of it matters. At power its production and removal balance; after a shutdown the balance breaks and it peaks before decaying, which can delay a restart

problems.prompt: A reactor produces ${{P}}$ MW of heat. About how many grams of uranium-235 does it fission per day? Take 200 MeV per fission, 1 MeV = $1.602 \times 10^{-13}$ J, $N_A = 6.022 \times 10^{23}$.

parts.label: r
parts.explain: Energy per day is ${{P}}$ MW $\times$ 86 400 s. Divide by the energy of one fission ($3.2 \times 10^{-11}$ J) for the number of fissions, then by $N_A$ and multiply by 235 g/mol. Worth carrying: about 1 g fissioned per megawatt-day

cases.q: immediately after shutdown
about one hour after shutdown
about one day after shutdown

problems.prompt: A reactor has run at full power for a long time. Roughly what fraction of full power is still produced as decay heat {{q}}?

parts.label: a
parts.explain: Fission stops in seconds but the fission products keep decaying. The heat starts at 6–7% of full power and falls quickly at first, then slowly. For a 3000 MW core that is still tens of megawatts hours later, which is why cooling must continue after shutdown

problems.prompt: A cost function is $C(q) = {{F}} + {{b}}q + {{c}}q^2$ dollars. What is the marginal cost at $q = {{q0}}$, in dollars per unit?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Marginal cost is $C'(q) = {{b}} + 2({{c}})q$. The fixed cost ${{F}}$ does not affect it

problems.prompt: Revenue from selling q units is R(q) = {{ka}}q − {{kb}}q² dollars. At what q is the marginal revenue zero?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Marginal revenue is R′(q) = a − 2bq. Past the point where it reaches zero, selling one more unit lowers total revenue

problems.prompt: Items sell for ${{p}}$ dollars each, and making $q$ of them costs $C(q) = {{F}} + {{c}}q + {{d}}q^2$ dollars. How many items maximise profit?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: $P(q) = {{p}}q - C(q)$. Setting $P'(q) = 0$ gives ${{p}} = {{c}} + 2({{d}})q$: marginal revenue equals marginal cost. $P'' < 0$, so it is a maximum

problems.prompt: Items sell for {{kp}} dollars each, and making q of them costs C(q) = {{kf}} + {{kc}}q + {{kd}}q² dollars. What is the largest possible profit, in dollars?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Find q where marginal revenue equals marginal cost, q = (p − c)/(2d), then put it back into the profit

expect.v: (kp*x - kf - kc*x - nsimplify(kd)*x**2).subs(x, solve(diff(kp*x - kf - kc*x - nsimplify(kd)*x**2, x), x)[0])

problems.prompt: After a dose, a drug's blood concentration is $C(t) = {{A}}\,t\,e^{-{{k}}t}$ (t in hours). When is the concentration highest, in hours?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: $C'(t) = Ae^{-kt}(1 - kt) = 0$ at $t = 1/k$. The same shape (rise, then exponential decay) describes many absorption–elimination models

problems.prompt: After a dose, a drug's blood concentration is C(t) = {{ka}}·t·e^(−{{kk}}t) mg/L (t in hours). What is the highest concentration reached?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: C′ = A e^(−kt)(1 − kt) vanishes at t = 1/k, where C = A/(ke)

problems.prompt: Demand is $q = {{a}} - {{b}}p$. What is the price elasticity of demand $E = -\dfrac{p}{q}\dfrac{dq}{dp}$ at $p = {{p0}}$?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: $E = \dfrac{bp}{a - bp}$. Where $E > 1$ demand is elastic and raising the price lowers revenue; where $E < 1$ it raises revenue

problems.prompt: Demand is q = {{ka}} − {{kb}}p. At what price is demand unit elastic (E = 1)?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: E = bp/(a − bp) = 1 at p = a/(2b), the midpoint of a linear demand curve, which is also where revenue peaks

problems.prompt: Demand is $p = {{a}} - {{b}}q$ and the market price is ${{p0}}$. What is the consumer surplus?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Buyers who would have paid more than ${{p0}}$ save the difference. Integrate from 0 to the quantity sold, $q_0 = (a - p_0)/b$: a triangle

problems.prompt: Supply is p = {{kc}} + {{kd}}q and the market price is {{kp}}. What is the producer surplus?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Producer surplus is the area between the market price and the supply curve, out to the quantity supplied: a triangle here

problems.prompt: {{A}} mg of dye is injected and its concentration leaving the heart is $c(t) = {{k}}\,t({{T}} - t)$ mg/L for $0 \le t \le {{T}}$ s. What is the cardiac output, in L/s?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: All the dye passes through: $A = F\int_0^T c\,dt$. The integral of the parabola is $kT^3/6$

problems.prompt: A heart pumps {{kf}} L/s. Dye injected upstream leaves with concentration c(t) = {{kk}}·t({{kt}} − t) mg/L for 0 ≤ t ≤ {{kt}} s. How much dye was injected, in mg?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: All the dye passes the sensor, so the amount is flow × ∫ c dt; the same relation read the other way gives the cardiac output

problems.prompt: $f(x) = k\,x^{ {{n}} }$ on $[0, {{L}}]$ (and 0 elsewhere) is a probability density. What is $k$?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Total probability is 1: $k\dfrac{L^{n+1}}{n + 1} = 1$. Then $P(a < X < b) = \int_a^b f$

problems.prompt: f(x) = k·x^{{kn}} on [0, {{kl}}] (and 0 elsewhere) is a probability density. What is its mean?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Normalise first (k = (n + 1)/L^(n+1)), then μ = ∫ x f(x) dx. The mean sits past the midpoint because the density rises

problems.prompt: Evaluate $\displaystyle\int_0^{\pi/2} \sin^{ {{m}} }x\,\cos^{ {{n}} }x\,dx$.

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Odd power of sine: keep one $\sin x$ for $du$ with $u = \cos x$ and write the rest with $\sin^2 = 1 - \cos^2$ (and the same with sine and cosine swapped). Both even: $\sin^2 x = \tfrac12(1 - \cos 2x)$

cases.q: sin³x cos²x
sin²x cos³x
sin²x cos²x
sin⁵x cos⁴x
sin⁴x cos x
sin⁴x
cos³x

problems.prompt: To integrate {{q}}, the most direct first move is:

parts.label: v
choice: Save one sin x and substitute u = cos x
Save one cos x and substitute u = sin x
parts.explain: An odd power lends one factor to du and the rest converts with sin² + cos² = 1. Only when both powers are even do you need the half-angle identities

problems.prompt: Evaluate $\displaystyle\int_0^{ {{a}} } \frac{x^2}{\sqrt{ {{a^2}} - x^2}}\,dx$.

parts.label: v
parts.explain: $x = {{a}}\sin\theta$ turns $\sqrt{a^2 - x^2}$ into $a\cos\theta$ and $dx$ into $a\cos\theta\,d\theta$; the integral becomes $a^2\int_0^{\pi/2}\sin^2\theta\,d\theta = \pi a^2/4$

problems.prompt: Which substitution removes the root in an integral containing {{q}}?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Match the Pythagorean identity: a² − a² sin² = a² cos², a² + a² tan² = a² sec², a² sec² − a² = a² tan²

problems.prompt: A table gives $\displaystyle\int \frac{dx}{x(a + bx)} = \frac1a\ln\left|\frac{x}{a + bx}\right| + C$. Evaluate $\displaystyle\int_1^2 \frac{dx}{x({{a}} + {{b}}x)}$.

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Here $a = {{a}}$, $b = {{b}}$: $\frac{1}{ {{a}} }\left[\ln\frac{2}{ {{a + 2*b}} } - \ln\frac{1}{ {{a + b}} }\right]$. Partial fractions gives the same thing

problems.prompt: A table gives ∫ dx/(a² + x²) = (1/a) arctan(x/a) + C. Evaluate ∫ from 0 to {{ka}} of dx/({{ks}} + x²).

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Read a from the constant (a² = the number, so a is its square root), then arctan(1) − arctan(0) = π/4, divided by a

problems.prompt: A computer algebra system returns $\displaystyle\int x e^{ {{a}}x}\,dx = e^{ {{a}}x}\left(\frac{x}{ {{a}} } - \frac{1}{ {{a^2}} }\right) + C$. Use it to evaluate $\displaystyle\int_0^1 x e^{ {{a}}x}\,dx$.

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Evaluate at 1 and subtract the value at 0, which is $-1/a^2$. Differentiating the CAS answer gives back $xe^{ax}$, which is the check worth doing before trusting it

problems.prompt: A computer algebra system returns F(x) = e^({{ka}}x)(x/{{ka}} − 1/{{ks}}) for ∫ x e^({{ka}}x) dx. To check it, differentiate: what should F′({{kx}}) equal?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: If F is right, F′ is the integrand, x e^(ax). The product rule on F cancels everything else

problems.prompt: The region under $y = {{k}}x - x^2$ (above the $x$-axis) is spun about the $y$-axis. Find the volume.

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Shells of radius $x$ and height ${{k}}x - x^2$: $V = \int_0^{ {{k}} } 2\pi x({{k}}x - x^2)\,dx$. Washers would need $x$ as a function of $y$, which here means two branches

problems.prompt: The region under y = x^{{kn}} for 0 ≤ x ≤ 1 is spun about the y-axis. Find the volume by shells.

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Shells: ∫ 2πx·xⁿ dx = 2π/(n + 2). The check is the cylinder of volume π minus the washers' hole, ∫ π y^(2/n) dy

problems.prompt: The region between $y = x^2$, the $x$-axis and $x = {{a}}$ is spun about the $y$-axis. Find the volume.

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Shells: $\int_0^a 2\pi x\cdot x^2\,dx$. Washers in $y$: outer radius $a$, inner $\sqrt y$: $\int_0^{a^2} \pi(a^2 - y)\,dy$. Both give $\pi a^4/2$

problems.prompt: The region between y = x², the x-axis and x = {{ka}} is spun about the x-axis. Find the volume.

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Discs in x: ∫ π x⁴ dx. Shells in y give the same number: radius y, height a − √y

problems.prompt: The line $y = {{m}}x$, $0 \le x \le {{L}}$, is spun about the $x$-axis to make a cone. What is the cone's lateral surface area?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: $S = \int_0^L 2\pi(mx)\sqrt{1 + m^2}\,dx = \pi mL^2\sqrt{1 + m^2}$: the familiar $\pi r\ell$ with $r = mL$ and slant $\ell = L\sqrt{1 + m^2}$

problems.prompt: The line y = {{km}}x for {{ka}} ≤ x ≤ {{kb}} is spun about the x-axis. Find the area of the surface it sweeps.

parts.label: v
parts.explain: ∫ 2π y √(1 + y′²) dx = 2π m √(1 + m²) ∫ x dx. It agrees with the frustum formula π(r₁ + r₂) × slant length

problems.prompt: A triangular plate with its {{b}} m base at the water surface and its apex {{h}} m below hangs vertically in water ($\rho g = 9810$ N/m³). What is the force on one side, in kN?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: At depth $y$ the width is ${{b}}(1 - y/{{h}})$; $F = \int_0^h \rho g\,y\,b(1 - y/h)\,dy = \rho g b h^2/6$. Pressure, not area alone, decides the force: the wide part is shallow

problems.prompt: A vertical rectangular gate {{kw}} m wide and {{kh}} m tall has its top edge {{kd}} m below the water surface (ρg = 9810 N/m³). Find the force on it, in N.

parts.label: v
parts.explain: ∫ ρg·depth·width d(depth) from d to d + h. It equals the pressure at the gate's centroid times its area

problems.prompt: Find $\displaystyle\lim_{n\to\infty} \frac{ {{p}}n^2 + {{q}} }{ {{r}}n^2 + {{s}}n}$.

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Divide top and bottom by $n^2$: everything else goes to 0. A sequence converges when its terms settle; a series converges when its partial sums do

problems.prompt: Find the limit of (1 + {{ka}}/n)^n as n → ∞.

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Take logs: n ln(1 + a/n) → a, so the limit is e^a

problems.prompt: For $\displaystyle\sum_{n=1}^\infty \left(\frac{ {{a}}n}{ {{b}}n + 1}\right)^n$, find the root-test limit $\lim |a_n|^{1/n}$.

parts.label: v
parts.explain: The $n$th root strips the outer power: $\frac{ {{a}}n}{ {{b}}n + 1} \to {{a}}/{{b}}$. Below 1 converges, above 1 diverges; equal to 1 says nothing

problems.prompt: For the series with terms ({{q}})^n, the root test says it:

parts.label: v
parts.explain: The nth root is an/(bn + 1) → a/b. Below 1 converges, above 1 diverges, exactly 1 tells you nothing (here the terms do not even tend to 0, so the series diverges by the nth-term test)

problems.prompt: Which test settles $\displaystyle\sum {{s}}$ most directly?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Factorials → ratio. A whole expression to the nth power → root. Alternating signs with terms shrinking to 0 → alternating series test. Looks like a p-series or geometric series → compare. Terms that do not go to 0 → divergence

cases.q: 1/(n ln n)

problems.prompt: The series with terms {{q}} (n from 2 upward):

parts.label: v
parts.explain: p-series need p > 1; terms that do not tend to 0 diverge at once; factorials beat exponentials; 1/(n ln n) diverges by the integral test

problems.prompt: A curve is $x = t + {{h}}$, $y = {{b}}t^2 + {{c}}$. Eliminate $t$ and find $y$ when $x = {{x1}}$.

parts.label: v
parts.explain: $t = x - {{h}}$, so $y = {{b}}(x - {{h}})^2 + {{c}}$: a parabola. Eliminating the parameter loses the direction and speed of travel

problems.prompt: A curve is x = e^t, y = e^(2t) + {{kc}}. Eliminate t and find y when x = {{kx}}.

parts.label: v
parts.explain: e^(2t) = (e^t)² = x², so y = x² + c (for x > 0 only, since e^t is positive)

problems.prompt: Find the area under $x = t^2$, $y = t^3$ for $0 \le t \le {{T}}$ (between the curve and the $x$-axis).

parts.label: v
parts.explain: $\int y\,dx = \int_0^T t^3\cdot 2t\,dt = \tfrac25T^5$. Eliminating $t$ gives $y = x^{3/2}$, which integrates to the same

problems.prompt: Find the area enclosed by x = {{ka}} cos t, y = {{kb}} sin t.

parts.label: v
parts.explain: A = ∮ y dx taken clockwise = ∫ b sin t · a sin t dt over a full turn = πab

problems.prompt: The upper half of $x = {{r}}\cos t$, $y = {{r}}\sin t$ ($0 \le t \le \pi$) is spun about the $x$-axis. Find the volume.

parts.label: v
parts.explain: $V = \int \pi y^2\,dx = \int_\pi^0 \pi r^2\sin^2 t\,(-r\sin t)\,dt = \tfrac43\pi r^3$, the sphere

problems.prompt: The upper half of x = {{ka}} cos t, y = {{kb}} sin t (0 ≤ t ≤ π) is spun about the x-axis. Find the volume.

parts.label: v
parts.explain: V = ∫ π y² dx with dx = −a sin t dt, taken so that x runs left to right: an ellipsoid of semi-axes a, b, b

problems.prompt: The upper half of $x = {{r}}\cos t$, $y = {{r}}\sin t$ is spun about the $x$-axis. Find the surface area.

parts.label: v
parts.explain: $\sqrt{x'^2 + y'^2} = r$, so $S = \int_0^\pi 2\pi r\sin t\cdot r\,dt = 4\pi r^2$

problems.prompt: The arc x = {{kr}} cos t, y = {{kr}} sin t for 0 ≤ t ≤ {{kd}}° is spun about the x-axis. Find the area of the cap it sweeps.

parts.label: v
parts.explain: S = ∫ 2π y √(x′² + y′²) dt, and the speed on a circle is r. The result is 2πr × the cap's height, Archimedes' hat-box theorem

problems.prompt: Find the length of the cardioid $r = {{a}}(1 + \cos\theta)$.

parts.label: v
parts.explain: $r^2 + r'^2 = 2a^2(1 + \cos\theta) = 4a^2\cos^2(\theta/2)$, so $L = \int_0^{2\pi} 2a|\cos(\theta/2)|\,d\theta = 8a$. Watch the absolute value past $\theta = \pi$

problems.prompt: Find the length of the spiral r = e^θ for 0 ≤ θ ≤ {{kt}}.

parts.label: v
parts.explain: r and dr/dθ are both e^θ, so the integrand is √2 e^θ

problems.prompt: Find the second component of $\displaystyle\lim_{t\to0}\left\langle \frac{\sin {{a}}t}{t},\; \frac{e^{ {{b}}t} - 1}{t},\; \cos t\right\rangle$.

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Componentwise: the first is ${{a}}$, the second is the derivative of $e^{bt}$ at 0, which is ${{b}}$, the third is 1

problems.prompt: Find the length of the limit as t → 0 of ⟨sin({{ka}}t)/t, (1 − cos t)/t, {{kb}}⟩.

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Component by component: sin(at)/t → a, (1 − cos t)/t → 0, and the constant stays

problems.prompt: An RC circuit ($R = {{R}}\,\Omega$, $C = {{C}}$ F) is switched onto a ${{E}}$ V battery with the capacitor uncharged. What is the current, in A, at $t = {{t}}$ s?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: $q(t) = CE(1 - e^{-t/RC})$, and $i = dq/dt = \dfrac ER e^{-t/RC}$. The time constant here is $RC = {{R*C}}$ s; after five of them the capacitor is essentially full

problems.prompt: A capacitor of {{kcp}} µF charges through {{kr}} kΩ from zero. After how many ms has it reached {{kf}} of its final voltage?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: v/V = 1 − e^(−t/RC), and kΩ × µF = ms

problems.prompt: For $y' = y^2 - {{2*a}}y + r$, at what value of $r$ do the two equilibria merge and disappear?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Equilibria solve $y^2 - 2ay + r = 0$: two when $r < a^2$, one (half-stable) at $r = a^2$, none beyond. At a saddle-node bifurcation the phase line changes its count of equilibria

problems.prompt: y′ = {{kr}} − y². Find the stable equilibrium.

parts.label: v
parts.explain: The equilibria ±√r appear at r = 0. The upper one is stable because f′(y) = −2y is negative there

problems.prompt: Let $L = D^2 + ({{a}})D + ({{b}})$ with $D = d/dx$. Then $L[e^{ {{k}}x}] = c\,e^{ {{k}}x}$. Find $c$.

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Each $D$ brings down a factor ${{k}}$: $L[e^{kx}] = (k^2 + ak + b)e^{kx}$, the characteristic polynomial. That is why $e^{rx}$ solves $L[y] = 0$ exactly at its roots

problems.prompt: Apply (D² + {{ka}}D + {{kb}}) to e^({{kr}}x) and evaluate the result at x = 0.

parts.label: v
parts.explain: P(D)e^(rx) = P(r)e^(rx): an exponential turns a differential operator into its characteristic polynomial

problems.prompt: $y'' + \dfrac{1}{x - {{a}}}y' + \dfrac{1}{x + {{c}}}y = 0$ with $y({{x0}}) = 1$, $y'({{x0}}) = 0$. How long is the largest interval on which a unique solution is guaranteed?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: The coefficients break down at $x = {{a}}$ and $x = {{-c}}$; the initial point ${{x0}}$ lies between them, so the guarantee holds on $({{-c}}, {{a}})$. The solution may well extend further; the theorem just does not promise it

problems.prompt: (x − {{ka}})(x − {{kb}})y″ + y′ + y = 0 with y({{k0}}) = 1, y′({{k0}}) = 0. The solution is guaranteed on an interval a < x < b. Find b.

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Divide by the leading coefficient; the coefficients are continuous between its zeros, and the interval is the one containing the initial point

parts.label: v

parts.label: v
parts.explain: $z = \dfrac{c + di}{a + bi}\cdot\dfrac{a - bi}{a - bi} = \dfrac{(ac + bd) + (ad - bc)i}{a^2 + b^2}$

problems.prompt: Solve ({{ka}} + i)z = {{kb}} + {{kg}}i and give the imaginary part of z.

parts.label: v

problems.prompt: Solve $z^2 = {{a^2 - b^2}} + {{2*a*b}}i$. What is the real part of the root with positive real part?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Try $z = p + qi$: $p^2 - q^2 = {{a^2 - b^2}}$ and $2pq = {{2*a*b}}$, giving $p = {{a}}$, $q = {{b}}$. The other root is its negative

parts.label: v
parts.explain: The pole at ${{p}}$ lies inside $|z| = {{R}}$, so the integral is $2\pi i\,e^{ {{a}}\cdot{{p}} }$. A pole outside the contour would give 0 (Cauchy's theorem)

parts.label: v

parts.label: v

problems.prompt: Find the coefficient of $z^{ {{k}} }$ in the Maclaurin series of $e^{ {{a}}z}$.

parts.label: v
parts.explain: $e^w = \sum w^k/k!$ with $w = {{a}}z$. Complex Taylor series converge in the largest disc that avoids every singularity

problems.prompt: Find the coefficient of z^{{kn}} in the Taylor series of 1/({{ka}} − z) about 0.

parts.label: v
parts.explain: 1/(a − z) = (1/a)·1/(1 − z/a) = Σ zⁿ/a^(n+1), valid for |z| < a

problems.prompt: Find the coefficient of $1/z$ in the Laurent series of $\dfrac{e^{ {{a}}z}}{z^{ {{n}} }}$ about 0.

parts.explain: Divide the series of $e^{az}$ by $z^n$: the $z^{n-1}$ term becomes $1/z$. That coefficient is the residue, and $\oint f\,dz = 2\pi i$ times it

problems.prompt: A quarter-circle gate of radius {{R}} m and width {{w}} m holds water ($\rho g = 9810$ N/m³) above it, the water surface level with the top of the arc. What is the vertical force on the gate, in kN?

problems.prompt: A quarter-circle gate of radius {{R}} m and width {{w}} m has its top at the water surface. What horizontal force does the water exert on it, in kN?

parts.label: v

problems.prompt: A tank holds {{h1}} m of oil (SG {{s1}}) floating on {{h2}} m of water. What is the gauge pressure at the bottom, in kPa? ($g = 9.81$)

parts.label: v

problems.prompt: A mercury manometer (SG 13.6) across an orifice in a water line shows a {{h}} mm difference in levels. What is the pressure difference, in kPa?

problems.prompt: A cylinder of water with radius {{R}} m spins at {{w}} rad/s. How much higher is the surface at the wall than at the centre, in m? ($g = 9.81$)

parts.label: v

problems.prompt: An open cylinder of radius {{R}} cm holds water {{h0}} cm deep at rest. At what spin rate, in rad/s, does the free surface just touch the bottom at the centre? (g = 9.81)

problems.prompt: In the stagnation flow u = {{a}}x, v = −{{a}}y (s⁻¹, m), how long does a particle take to move from x = {{x0}} to {{x1}} m along a streamline?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: dx/dt = ax gives exponential motion: particles near the stagnation point take forever to leave

problems.prompt: A steady 1-D flow speeds up through a nozzle as $u = {{U}}(1 + x/{{Lz}})$ m/s. What is the fluid's acceleration at $x = {{xp}}$ m, in m/s²?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Nothing changes in time at a fixed point, but a particle moving downstream finds faster fluid: $a = u\,\partial u/\partial x$

problems.prompt: For the steady flow u = {{a}}x, v = −{{a}}y, what is the magnitude of the fluid acceleration at ({{px}} m, {{py}} m), in m/s²?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Steady flow can still accelerate particles: (u·∇)u is nonzero wherever speed changes along the path

problems.prompt: A flow has stream function $\psi = {{a}}x^2y - {{b}}y^3$. Find $v$ at $(x, y) = ({{x0}}, {{y0}})$.

problems.prompt: A flow has stream function ψ = {{a}}xy (m²/s). What volume flow per metre depth passes between the points ({{x1}}, {{y1}}) and ({{x2}}, {{y2}})?

problems.prompt: Fluid rotates as a solid body at {{Om}} rad/s. What is the circulation around a circle of radius {{R}} m centred on the axis, in m²/s?

parts.label: v

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Integrated dissipation equals Q·ΔP/L: all the pumping work becomes heat

problems.prompt: A ship {{L}} m long moves at {{V}} m/s. What is its Froude number? ($g = 9.81$)

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Nondimensionalising the momentum equation leaves Re, Fr, Ma and others; which ones matter depends on which forces act

problems.prompt: Water in a channel moves at {{V}} m/s. At what depth, in m, would the flow be critical (Fr = 1)?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Shallower than this the flow is supercritical: disturbances cannot travel upstream

problems.prompt: A lawn sprinkler's two arms of radius {{r}} m each discharge {{m}} kg/s tangentially at {{V}} m/s relative to the ground. What torque holds it still, in N·m?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Angular momentum leaves at $rV$ per kilogram from each arm; held still, the sprinkler must supply that torque

problems.prompt: A frictionless lawn sprinkler has arms of radius {{R}} cm with tangential nozzles ejecting water at {{V}} m/s relative to the arm. At what steady spin rate, in rad/s, is the torque zero?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: With no friction it spins up until the jets leave with no absolute tangential velocity, so they carry away no angular momentum

problems.prompt: A diffuser has area ratio $A_2/A_1 = {{ar}}$. What is the ideal pressure-recovery coefficient $C_p = \Delta p/(\tfrac12\rho V_1^2)$?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Continuity slows the flow by the area ratio and Bernoulli turns the lost velocity head into pressure. Real diffusers recover less; too steep a wall separates

problems.prompt: Air (1.2 kg/m³) enters an ideal diffuser at {{V}} m/s with area ratio A₂/A₁ = {{r}}. What static pressure rise, in Pa, does Bernoulli give?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Slowing the flow converts dynamic pressure into static; real diffusers recover 60–80% of this before the boundary layer separates

problems.prompt: Air ($\nu = 1.5\times10^{-5}$ m²/s) flows at {{U}} m/s over a flat plate. Using $\delta = 5x/\sqrt{Re_x}$, how thick is the boundary layer {{xp}} m from the leading edge, in mm?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: δ grows as $\sqrt x$. A momentum-integral estimate with a parabolic profile gives a slightly different constant (5.48)

problems.prompt: Air ($\nu = 1.5\times10^{-5}$ m²/s) at {{U}} m/s flows over a plate with a turbulent boundary layer from the leading edge. Estimate δ at x = {{xx}} m with δ = 0.37x/Re_x^{1/5}, in mm.

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Turbulent layers grow as x^{4/5}, much faster than laminar x^{1/2}, because eddies carry momentum across them

cases.q: What happens to a boundary layer in a strong adverse pressure gradient (pressure rising downstream)?
What does a favourable pressure gradient (pressure falling downstream) do to a boundary layer?
Where on a cylinder in cross-flow does the pressure gradient become adverse?

parts.label: v
choice: It thickens and may separate, with reversed flow near the wall
It thins and stays attached, delaying transition
Past the shoulder, on the rear half
parts.explain: The near-wall fluid has little momentum; pushing against rising pressure stops it first. Separation is why bluff bodies have large pressure drag

problems.prompt: Outside a boundary layer the speed varies as U(x) = {{a}} + {{b}}x. Is the pressure gradient along the wall favourable or adverse?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Euler at the edge: dp/dx = −ρU dU/dx. Decelerating outer flow raises pressure downstream and slows the near-wall fluid

problems.prompt: A 2-D line source discharges {{m}} m²/s. What is the radial speed {{r}} m away, in m/s?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: All the flow crosses a circle of circumference $2\pi r$; sources, sinks, vortices and uniform flow are the building blocks

problems.prompt: A 2-D source produces a radial speed of {{V}} m/s at r = {{r}} m. What is its strength (volume flow per unit depth), in m²/s?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: All the flow crosses every circle around the source

problems.prompt: A uniform stream of {{U}} m/s meets a 2-D source of strength {{m}} m²/s at the origin. How far upstream is the stagnation point, in m?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Superposition works because potential flow is linear; the dividing streamline through the stagnation point is the Rankine half-body's surface

problems.prompt: A uniform stream of {{U}} m/s meets a 2-D source of strength {{q}} m²/s. How wide, in m, does the Rankine half-body become far downstream?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Far downstream the source's whole output travels at U inside the body's outline, so q = U × width

problems.prompt: In ideal flow past a circular cylinder, what is the pressure coefficient on the surface at $\theta = {{t}}°$ from the front stagnation point?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Bernoulli with surface speed $2U\sin\theta$; the minimum $C_p = -3$ sits at the shoulders. Ideal flow predicts zero drag, which real flow (with separation) breaks

problems.prompt: A rotating cylinder in a {{U}} m/s air stream (1.2 kg/m³) carries circulation {{G}} m²/s. What lift per metre span, in N/m?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Kutta–Joukowski: lift per span = ρUΓ, whatever the body's shape

problems.prompt: The Joukowski map $z = \zeta + {{a}}^2/\zeta$ sends the circle $|\zeta| = {{a}}$ to a straight segment. How long is it?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: On the circle $\zeta = ae^{i\theta}$, so $z = 2a\cos\theta$. Shifted circles map to airfoil shapes

problems.prompt: The Joukowski map ζ = z + c²/z takes the circle |z| = c to a flat plate. With c = {{c}} m, how long is the plate, in m?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Points on the circle map to ζ = 2c cos θ: the circle collapses onto a segment from −2c to 2c

problems.prompt: A thin symmetric airfoil is at {{a}}° angle of attack. What lift coefficient does thin-airfoil theory predict?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Lift grows linearly with angle until the flow separates (stall, typically 12–16°)

problems.prompt: By thin-airfoil theory, what angle of attack, in degrees, gives a symmetric airfoil a lift coefficient of {{cl}}?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: C_L = 2πα in radians: about 0.11 per degree, until stall

problems.prompt: In ideal flow past a sphere with free-stream speed {{U}} m/s, what is the fastest speed on the surface, in m/s?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: A sphere disturbs the flow less than a cylinder (3D lets fluid go around in two directions): $1.5U$ against the cylinder's $2U$

problems.prompt: In potential flow past a sphere, what is the pressure coefficient at {{th}}° from the front stagnation point?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: The surface speed is 1.5U sinθ, less than the cylinder's 2U because flow can pass on all sides

problems.prompt: Air ($k = 1.4$) flows at Mach {{M}} with static temperature {{T}} K. What is its stagnation temperature, in K?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Bring the flow to rest adiabatically: $c_pT_0 = c_pT + V^2/2$. Re-entry heating is this effect at large Mach

problems.prompt: Air (γ = 1.4) has stagnation temperature {{T0}} K and static temperature {{T}} K. What is its Mach number?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: T₀/T = 1 + (γ − 1)M²/2: kinetic energy shows up as the gap between the two temperatures

problems.prompt: Air ($k = 1.4$) flows isentropically. What area ratio $A/A^*$ gives Mach {{M}}?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Subsonic flow speeds up in a converging duct, supersonic in a diverging one; both meet $A/A^* = 1$ at the throat

problems.prompt: Air (γ = 1.4, R = 287 J/(kg·K)) flows from a reservoir at {{p0}} kPa and {{T0}} K. What throat area, in cm², passes {{m}} kg/s when choked?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Choked mass flux depends only on stagnation conditions; to pass more mass, raise p₀ or the throat area

problems.prompt: A converging nozzle fed from a tank at {{P0}} kPa discharges air ($k = 1.4$). Below what back pressure is it choked, in kPa?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: At the throat $M = 1$; lowering the back pressure further cannot raise the mass flow

problems.prompt: Air (γ = 1.4) at {{p0}} kPa stagnation discharges through a converging nozzle into {{pb}} kPa. Is the nozzle choked?

parts.label: v
choice: Yes: p_b/p₀ is below the critical 0.528
parts.explain: Once choked, lowering the back pressure further does not raise the flow

problems.prompt: A normal shock stands in air ($k = 1.4$) with upstream Mach {{M}}. What is the downstream Mach number?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: A normal shock always leaves subsonic flow, with a jump in pressure and a loss of stagnation pressure

problems.prompt: A normal shock stands in air (γ = 1.4) with upstream Mach {{M}}. What is the static pressure ratio p₂/p₁?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Momentum across the shock gives p₂/p₁ = (1 + γM₁²)/(1 + γM₂²); with the M₂ relation it simplifies to the familiar form

problems.prompt: A supersonic projectile flies at Mach {{M}}. What is the half-angle of its Mach cone, in degrees?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Disturbances spread at the speed of sound while the source outruns them; oblique shocks lie at steeper angles than μ

problems.prompt: A Mach wave makes {{mu}}° with the flow direction. What is the Mach number?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: sin μ = 1/M: the faster the flow, the narrower the Mach cone

problems.prompt: For air ($k = 1.4$), what is the Prandtl–Meyer angle $\nu$ at Mach {{M}}, in degrees?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Turning a supersonic flow away from itself by an angle θ raises ν by θ; read the new Mach number from ν

problems.prompt: Supersonic air (γ = 1.4) expands from M = {{M1}} to M = {{M2}}. Through what angle, in degrees, does it turn?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: ν(M) is the integral of √(M² − 1)/(1 + (γ − 1)M²/2) dM/M; the turn is the difference between end values

problems.prompt: Air ($k = 1.4$) enters an adiabatic duct at Mach {{M}}. Find $\bar f L^*/D$ (Darcy $\bar f$), the friction length to choke.

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Friction drives both subsonic and supersonic Fanno flow toward Mach 1; a longer duct than $L^*$ reduces the flow rate instead

problems.prompt: In Fanno flow of air (γ = 1.4), what is T/T* at Mach {{M}}?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Fanno flow is adiabatic, so T₀ is fixed and T follows from T₀/T at each Mach number

problems.prompt: Air ($k = 1.4$) flows at Mach {{M}} in a frictionless duct. What is $T_0/T_0^*$, the fraction of the stagnation temperature at which heating would choke it?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Adding heat drives the flow toward Mach 1 from either side; the most heat that can be added without choking raises $T_0$ to $T_0^*$

problems.prompt: In Rayleigh flow of air (γ = 1.4), what is p/p* at Mach {{M}}?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Frictionless constant-area flow keeps p + ρV² = p(1 + γM²) fixed

problems.prompt: A rectangular channel carries {{q}} m²/s per metre of width. What is the critical depth, in m? ($g = 9.81$)

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Critical depth minimises the specific energy $E = y + q^2/2gy^2$; there $Fr = 1$

problems.prompt: A rectangular channel carries {{q}} m²/s per metre width. What is the minimum specific energy, in m? (g = 9.81)

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Minimising E = y + q²/(2gy²) gives critical depth, where E = 1.5y_c

expect.v: (Symbol('yp', positive=True) + nsimplify(q)**2/(2*Rational(981, 100)*Symbol('yp', positive=True)**2)).subs(Symbol('yp', positive=True), solve(diff(Symbol('yp', positive=True) + nsimplify(q)**2/(2*Rational(981, 100)*Symbol('yp', positive=True)**2), Symbol('yp', positive=True)), Symbol('yp', positive=True))[0])

problems.prompt: A concrete channel ($n = 0.013$) has hydraulic radius {{R}} m and slope {{S}}. What is the uniform-flow velocity, in m/s?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Gravity along the slope balances wall friction; Manning's $n$ is an empirical roughness

problems.prompt: A concrete channel (n = 0.013) with hydraulic radius {{Rh}} m must carry water at {{V}} m/s in uniform flow. What bed slope is needed?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Velocity goes as √S, so doubling speed needs four times the slope

problems.prompt: A rectangular channel must carry flow area {{A}} m². For the smallest wetted perimeter, what depth should it have, in m?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Minimise $P = b + 2y$ with $b = A/y$: $b = 2y$. The least perimeter means the least friction and lining

problems.prompt: The most efficient rectangular section for a flow area of {{A}} m² has width twice its depth. What is its hydraulic radius, in m?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Minimising the wetted perimeter at fixed area gives b = 2y and R_h = y/2

problems.prompt: In a gradually varied flow, $S_0 = {{S0}}$, the friction slope is $S_f = {{Sf}}$ and $Fr = {{Fr}}$. What is $dy/dx$?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: The sign tells whether the depth grows or falls downstream; it flips between subcritical and supercritical flow

problems.prompt: On a mild slope (normal depth {{yn}} m, critical depth {{yc}} m) the flow depth is {{y}} m. Which profile type?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Zones are set by where y sits relative to y_n and y_c; M1 backwater curves form behind dams

choices.v: 0 if nsimplify(y) > nsimplify(yn) else (1 if nsimplify(y) > nsimplify(yc) else 2)

problems.prompt: Supercritical flow {{y1}} m deep with $Fr_1 = {{Fr}}$ jumps to subcritical. What is the depth after the jump, in m?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Momentum, not energy, is conserved across the jump; the turbulence dissipates the difference

problems.prompt: A hydraulic jump goes from {{y1}} m to {{y2}} m depth. How much head does it dissipate, in m?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Specific energies before and after, with q² from the momentum balance (q²/g = y₁y₂(y₁ + y₂)/2), differ by (y₂ − y₁)³/(4y₁y₂)

problems.prompt: A hydro plant passes {{Q}} m³/s through a head of {{H}} m at overall efficiency {{eta}}. What is the power, in MW? ($\rho g = 9810$ N/m³)

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Water power $\rho gQH$ times efficiency. High head and low flow suit Pelton wheels; low head and high flow suit Kaplan turbines

problems.prompt: A turbine produces {{P}} MW from {{Q}} m³/s of water with efficiency {{eta}}%. What net head, in m, is it working with?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Shaft power = η ρgQH; turbines lose to the efficiency, pumps divide by it

cases.q: the polynomials of degree at most 3
the polynomials of degree exactly 3
the 2 × 2 symmetric matrices
the invertible 2 × 2 matrices
the functions on [0, 1] with f(0) = 0
the functions on [0, 1] with f(0) = 1
the solutions of y″ + y = 0
the solutions of y″ + y = 1
the 2 × 2 matrices with trace 0
the positive real numbers

problems.prompt: Is {{q}} a vector space under the usual addition and scalar multiplication?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Ask whether the zero element is in the set and whether sums and multiples stay in it. Degree exactly 3 fails (the sum of x³ and −x³ is 0); invertible matrices miss the zero matrix; a nonhomogeneous condition (f(0) = 1, y″ + y = 1) fails closure.

cases.q: ℝ² with ordinary addition but c(x, y) = (cx, 0). Which axiom fails?
The positive reals with x ⊕ y = xy and c ⊙ x = xᶜ. Is it a vector space?
cases.o2: No: there is no zero vector
cases.o3: No: it is not closed under scaling

cases.q: The polynomials with integer coefficients, over the reals. Which fails?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Check each axiom against the operations actually given, not the usual ones

parts.label: v
