problems.prompt: In a HAZOP study, what does the guide word {{k}} mean?

parts.label: y
parts.explain: Guide words are applied to each process parameter at each node (NO flow, MORE pressure, REVERSE flow…) to generate deviations; the team then lists causes, consequences and safeguards for each

cases.task: How long (min) until the output reaches 63.2% of its final change?
How long (min) until the output reaches 95% of its final change?
How long (min) until the output reaches 99% of its final change?
What fraction of the final change has occurred after 4 min?
What fraction of the final change has occurred after 9 min?
What fraction of the final change has occurred after 5 min?

problems.prompt: A first-order process (time constant {{tau}} min, no dead time) gets a step in its input. {{task}}

parts.label: y
parts.explain: τ dy/dt + y = K·Δu gives y = KΔu(1 − e^(−t/τ)): 63.2% at t = τ, 95% at 3τ, 99% at 4.6τ. The time constant is read off a step test at 63.2%

cases.q: Which mean diameter carries a powder's surface area per unit volume?
A catalyst's reaction rate depends on external surface area. Which mean describes the charge?
Reporting a single diameter for a powder is defensible only when:
cases.o1: The distribution is narrow, or the mean chosen is the one the application depends on

cases.q: Two powders have the same arithmetic mean but different Sauter means. This means:
cases.o1: Their distributions differ in shape, so their surface areas per unit volume differ

parts.label: v
parts.explain: A distribution needs a stated kind of average: the Sauter mean is the one tied to surface area, and it is the one catalysis, drying and dissolution follow

problems.prompt: A sieve analysis gives mass fractions {{f1}}, {{f2}}, {{f3}} and {{f4}} on four screens with the remainder in the pan. What percentage of the charge reaches the pan?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: A sieve stack's fractions must close to one, so the pan fraction is what the screens did not retain; a stack that does not close has lost material or been overloaded

problems.prompt: A powder has {{n1}} particles of {{d1}} micrometres, {{n2}} of {{d2}} and {{n3}} of {{d3}}. What is the Sauter mean diameter (micrometres)?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: A few large particles dominate the numerator, so the Sauter mean sits far above the arithmetic mean whenever the distribution has a coarse tail

problems.prompt: For a powder of {{n1}} particles at {{d1}} micrometres and {{n2}} at {{d2}}, by what factor does the Sauter mean exceed the arithmetic mean?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: The ratio is a measure of how wide the distribution is: for a monosized powder it is one, and it grows with every coarse particle added

problems.prompt: A powder of particle density {{rp}} kg/m3 has a bulk density of {{rb}} kg/m3. What is its voidage?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Voidage is the fraction of the bed that is gas; a poured powder usually sits near 0.4 and vibration can take it to 0.35, which is why bulk density is reported with how it was measured

problems.prompt: A particle density of {{rp}} kg/m3 and a voidage of {{ep}} give what bulk density (kg/m3)?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: The reverse calculation, which is how a silo's holding capacity is worked out from a material's particle density and the packing it is expected to reach

cases.q: A 200 mesh screen compared with a 100 mesh screen has:
cases.o1: A smaller aperture, because mesh counts wires per inch

cases.q: Material described as minus 100 mesh is:
cases.o1: The fraction that passed a 100 mesh screen

cases.q: A sieve analysis reports:
Sieving is unreliable below roughly a few tens of micrometres because:
cases.o1: Fine powder agglomerates and will not pass, so another method is needed
cases.o3: The mass is too small to weigh

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Mesh and aperture run in opposite directions, and plus and minus say retained or passed

problems.prompt: On a stack, {{r1}} per cent is retained on the coarse screen and {{r2}} per cent passes the fine one. What percentage lies between the two?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: The cut between two screens is what neither the coarse retention nor the fine pass took, which is how a specification on a size band is checked

problems.prompt: A mill takes feed from {{f80}} micrometres to a product of {{p80}} micrometres, eighty per cent passing. With a Bond work index of {{wi}} kWh/ton, what is the energy per ton (kWh), using E = 10*Wi*(1/sqrt(p80) - 1/sqrt(f80))?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Grinding energy rises steeply as the product gets finer, because the term in the product size dominates once it is much smaller than the feed: the last halving costs more than all the earlier ones

problems.prompt: Holding the feed size, by what factor does Bond energy rise when the product passes from {{p1}} to {{p2}} micrometres, if the feed term is negligible?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Energy goes as the reciprocal square root of product size, so halving the product costs about 1.41 times the energy and quartering it twice that: the scaling is the reason fine grinding dominates a plant's power bill

cases.q: Which law suits fine grinding, where new surface is what is created?
Which law suits coarse crushing, where energy follows the size ratio?
Which law is used for mill duties in the intermediate range?
cases.o1: Bond's law, through a measured work index

cases.q: The Bond work index is the energy needed to take a very large feed to:
A material with a high work index is:
cases.o1: Hard to grind, so it needs more energy per ton for the same size change

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Three laws for three ranges, and the work index is a measured material property that makes mills comparable

problems.prompt: {{m0}} kg of solution saturated at {{t1}} degrees Celsius, holding {{s1}} kg solute per 100 kg water, is cooled to where solubility is {{s2}} kg per 100 kg water. With no evaporation, what mass of anhydrous crystals forms (kg)?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: The water is conserved, so the yield is the water mass times the drop in solubility; working in kilograms of water rather than of solution is what keeps the balance straight

problems.prompt: The same cooling also evaporates {{ev}} per cent of the water. By what factor does that raise the yield over the no-evaporation case, if the final solubility is {{s2}} kg per 100 kg water and the initial is {{s1}}?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Evaporating water removes the solvent that was still holding solute, so a little evaporation buys a lot of yield when the final solubility is high

cases.q: Raising supersaturation in a crystallizer tends to give:
cases.o1: Many small crystals, because nucleation rises faster with it than growth does

cases.q: To grow large crystals a crystallizer is run:
cases.o1: At a low, steady supersaturation, with seed present

cases.q: The metastable zone is the region where:
cases.o1: The solution is supersaturated but has not yet nucleated, which is where seeded growth is done

cases.q: Crystal size in a given system is:
cases.o1: A control decision, set by the supersaturation profile

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Nucleation and growth compete for the same driving force, and which one wins decides the product size

problems.prompt: A belt carries a cross-section of {{ar}} square metres at {{vb}} m/s of material of bulk density {{rb}} kg/m3. What is the capacity (tonnes per hour)?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: A conveyor is set volumetrically, so the mass rate follows bulk density: the same setting on a lighter powder delivers proportionally fewer tonnes

problems.prompt: A conveyor is set for a bulk density of {{r1}} kg/m3 and the material is changed to one of {{r2}}. What percentage change in tonnes per hour results at the same setting?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: The reverse of the capacity calculation, and the reason a volumetric feeder has to be recalibrated whenever the material changes

cases.q: In a mass-flow hopper:
cases.o1: All the contents move whenever any is withdrawn
cases.o2: A central channel empties and the rest stays

cases.q: Funnel flow is a problem for a material that:
cases.o1: Cakes or degrades with time, since some of it stays indefinitely

cases.q: A hopper wall shallower than the material's flow requirement gives:
The angle of repose is:
cases.o1: The slope at which a poured heap of the material stands
cases.o2: The hopper wall angle required for mass flow

cases.q: Arching across an outlet is prevented by:
cases.o1: Making the outlet large enough for the material's cohesive strength

parts.label: v
parts.explain: A hopper is designed from the material's own flow properties, and the wall angle decides whether everything moves or only a channel

problems.prompt: A duct carries {{md}} kg/h of dust in {{qg}} m3/h of air. What is the dust concentration (g/m3), and does it exceed a minimum explosible concentration printed as {{mec}} g/m3? Give the concentration.

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Keeping a duct's loading well below the minimum explosible concentration is one layer; the others are removing ignition sources and relieving or suppressing what still ignites. The threshold is printed because the standard's own table was not read

problems.prompt: To hold {{md}} kg/h of dust below {{tc}} g/m3, what air flow is needed (m3/h)?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: The reverse: dilution is sized from the target concentration, and a target well under the explosible limit is what gives the design its margin

cases.q: Which document shows every line with its size and material, every valve and every instrument?
Which document carries the stream table of flows, compositions and conditions?
Which is the document the plant is built and operated from?
A block flow diagram is the right level for:
cases.o1: Showing the sequence of operations and the streams between them

cases.q: Utilities and minor lines usually appear on:

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Three levels of detail for three purposes; the P&ID is the one with legal and construction weight

problems.prompt: A mixer takes {{s1}} and {{s2}} kg/h in and sends {{s3}} kg/h out of one outlet. At steady state with no accumulation, what does the second outlet carry (kg/h)?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: A stream table is a material balance written out, so a blank follows from closing the balance; a table that will not close is an error in the table

problems.prompt: Two streams mix: {{m1}} kg/h at {{x1}} mass fraction solute and {{m2}} kg/h at {{x2}}. What is the outlet mass fraction?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: The component balance beside the total balance; both have to close, and a stream table gives enough entries to check that they do

cases.q: What does the tag FIC denote?
What does LT denote?
In an instrument tag, the first letter gives:
A control loop on a drawing consists of:
cases.o1: A transmitter, a controller and a final control element sharing one loop number

cases.q: PSV on a drawing denotes:

parts.label: v
parts.explain: The tag is a sentence: variable, then function, then loop number, which is how a loop is traced across drawings

problems.prompt: Equipment of capacity {{c1}} cost {{k1}} dollars. What does capacity {{c2}} cost, with an exponent of {{ex}}?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: An exponent below one is the economy of scale: doubling capacity on a 0.6 exponent costs about 1.5 times, not twice, which is the whole argument for a single large train

problems.prompt: A cost of {{k1}} dollars dates from a year whose cost index was {{i1}}. What is it worth at an index of {{i2}}?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Capacity scaling and index escalation are independent corrections and a cost quoted from a handbook needs both; applying only one is the commonest estimating error

problems.prompt: Purchased equipment comes to {{pe}} dollars. With a bare-module factor of {{bm}}, what is the installed cost (dollars)?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: The factor covers piping, instruments, electrical, structures, erection and the indirects, so an equipment quotation is a fraction of the capital the project needs

problems.prompt: A project's installed cost is {{tc}} dollars on purchased equipment of {{pe}}. What factor does that imply?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Backing the factor out of a finished project is how a company builds its own factors; a factor well outside the usual range for that kind of plant means the scope was not what it looked like

problems.prompt: An estimate of {{be}} dollars claims an accuracy of plus or minus {{ac}} per cent. What is the top of its range (dollars)?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: A class of estimate claims both a design definition and an accuracy band; the band is printed here because the classification standard's own table was not read. Contingency covers what is known to be missing at that definition, never undecided scope

cases.q: An estimate's accuracy band widens as:
cases.o1: The design definition behind it falls

cases.q: Contingency is money for:
cases.o1: What is known to be missing at this level of definition
cases.o2: Scope that has not been decided yet

cases.q: A screening estimate made from a block flow diagram is:
cases.o1: The least defined and the widest in claimed accuracy

cases.q: Carrying an estimate's number without its class is a problem because:
cases.o1: The number implies a precision the definition does not support
cases.o3: The number would be too high

parts.label: v
parts.explain: The class is the claim; a number quoted without it has lost the only thing that said how much to trust it

cases.q: A pressure-vessel code adopted into law by a jurisdiction fixes:
cases.o1: Minimum design, fabrication, inspection and stamping requirements

cases.q: A dimensional standard for flanges exists so that:
A vessel's wall thickness is:
cases.o1: Set by the code's rules for the design pressure and temperature, not purely by the designer

cases.q: A recognised and generally accepted good engineering practice matters because:
cases.o1: A regulator may hold a plant to it even where no code is adopted into law
cases.o4: It applies only to new plants

parts.label: v
parts.explain: A code is law where it is adopted and a standard is interchange; both take choices out of the designer's hands

problems.prompt: A vessel has a maximum allowable working pressure of {{mawp}} psig. What accumulated pressure is allowed for a non-fire case at 110 per cent (psig)?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Set pressure at or below the rating and accumulation to 110 per cent for a single device on a non-fire case; 116 per cent applies with multiple devices and 121 per cent for fire

cases.q: Which case allows the highest accumulation above the rating?
cases.o1: The external fire case, at 121 per cent
cases.o2: A single non-fire device, at 110 per cent

cases.q: A relief device's set pressure is:
cases.o1: At or below the maximum allowable working pressure

cases.q: Accumulation is:
cases.o1: The pressure reached while the device relieves, above the set pressure

cases.q: Operating too close to the set pressure causes:
cases.o1: Simmering and seat leakage, so a margin below set is designed in

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Four pressures in order: operating, set, accumulated, and the vessel's own limit

problems.prompt: Using A = W/(C*Kd*P1*Kb*Kc) * sqrt(T*Z/M), size the area for W = {{wf}} lb/h, C = {{cc}}, Kd = {{kd}}, P1 = {{p1}} psia, T = {{tt}} degrees Rankine, Z = {{zz}}, M = {{mm}}, with Kb and Kc equal to 1. Give the area in square inches.

parts.label: v
parts.explain: The equation and its coefficients are printed because the sizing standard's own tables were not read. Area falls with relieving pressure and rises with the square root of temperature over molecular weight, so a valve sized for one service does not transfer to another

problems.prompt: Holding everything else, by what factor does the required vapour relief area change when the relieving pressure goes from {{pa}} to {{pb}} psia?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Area is inversely proportional to relieving pressure, so raising a set pressure within the vessel's rating is often the cheapest way to shrink a relief device and its downstream header

problems.prompt: With Q = 21000*F*A^0.82 Btu/h for a wetted area A of {{aw}} square feet and an environment factor F of {{ff}}, and a latent heat of {{lh}} Btu/lb, what relief rate results (lb/h)?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: The correlation is printed because the standard's own text was not read. The environment factor is the credit for insulation or drainage, and it is the one term a designer can change: insulation can cut a fire relief load by an order of magnitude

problems.prompt: By what factor does the fire relief load fall when an environment factor of 1.0 is replaced by {{ff}}?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Insulation, water spray or drainage earn a credit, and the factor enters linearly, so the relief device and the whole flare header shrink with it

cases.q: Which device recloses after relieving and can be bench tested?
Which suits a corrosive or polymerising service that would foul a valve seat?
cases.o1: A rupture disc, often with a valve behind it

cases.q: A disc upstream of a relief valve is used to:
cases.o1: Isolate the valve from the fluid while still allowing full relief

cases.q: A rupture disc's burst pressure carries:
cases.o1: A manufacturing tolerance the set pressure must allow for
cases.o3: A tolerance only above the rating
cases.o4: A tolerance set by the user

cases.q: A pilot-operated valve is chosen when:
cases.o1: The operating pressure must sit close to the set pressure without leaking
cases.o2: The fluid is clean and cold

parts.label: v
parts.explain: The choice follows the service and how close operation runs to set, not the relief load alone

problems.prompt: A sealed vessel of gas at {{t1}} degrees Celsius and 101.3 kPa cools to {{t2}}. What absolute pressure results (kPa), and so what external pressure must the wall take?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Cooling a closed vessel pulls a vacuum, and a shell designed only for internal pressure buckles well below one atmosphere of external pressure: the usual answers are a vacuum breaker or designing for full vacuum

cases.q: A vessel emptied by pump against a closed vent will:
cases.o1: Pull a vacuum and can collapse

cases.q: A shell designed for internal pressure only:
cases.o1: Buckles under external pressure far below its internal rating, because buckling is a stability failure

cases.q: The simplest protection against underpressure is:
cases.o1: A vacuum breaker that admits air or inert gas

cases.q: Steaming out a vessel and then closing it causes:
cases.o1: A vacuum as the steam condenses

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Underpressure is the failure mode that gets forgotten, and it is a stability failure rather than a strength one

cases.q: A relieved stream may discharge to atmosphere only when:
cases.o1: It is safe at grade and in the plume, for everyone who could be there

cases.q: A two-phase relief stream is usually routed to:
cases.o1: A knockout drum, so liquid is separated before the vapour goes to flare

cases.q: A flare is chosen for a relief stream that is:
cases.o1: Flammable, so it is burned rather than released

cases.q: A catch tank downstream of a relief device exists to:
cases.o1: Contain the liquid so it is not released, and to let it be recovered or treated

parts.label: v
parts.explain: The relief device solves the vessel's problem and creates a disposal one; what leaves still has to go somewhere safe

problems.prompt: A charge has a heat of reaction of {{dh}} kJ/kg and a specific heat of {{cp}} kJ/(kg K). What adiabatic temperature rise does complete reaction give (K)?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: The adiabatic rise is a property of the charge, not of the vessel, so a reaction whose rise exceeds the margin to the vessel's limit cannot be made safe by cooling alone: the inventory or the chemistry has to change

problems.prompt: A charge at {{t0}} degrees Celsius has an adiabatic rise of {{dt}} K. By how much does the final temperature exceed a vessel limit of {{tl}} degrees Celsius (K)?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: A positive margin means the runaway ends above what the vessel can take, which is the calculation that decides whether a reaction needs a relief device, a quench or a smaller batch

cases.q: A strong acid and a cyanide salt sharing a drain creates:
cases.o1: A route to generating a toxic gas, so the drains are segregated

cases.q: Hypochlorite and acid must be kept apart because:
A water-reactive material argues for:
cases.o1: Keeping it away from water, water-based firefighting and humid air, and bunding separately
cases.o4: A water deluge system over it

cases.q: Two materials may share a vent header only when:
cases.o1: Their mixture is known to be safe at the conditions the header can reach

cases.q: A compatibility chart is consulted before:
cases.o1: Sharing a drain, a vent or a transfer line

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Reactivity hazards are created by the layout as much as by the chemistry: shared drains and headers are where incompatible materials meet

problems.prompt: A stream of {{qq}} m3/h carries {{cc2}} mg/L of a contaminant against a limit of {{lm}} mg/L. What mass per hour must be removed (kg/h)?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Meeting a concentration limit is removing the excess load, and diluting to meet it is generally not allowed; the cheapest route is not generating the contaminant, since a treated stream is paid for twice

problems.prompt: Changing the process cuts a contaminant load from {{l1}} to {{l2}} kg/h. What percentage reduction is that, and what fraction of the treatment duty disappears?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Source reduction removes the treatment duty rather than paying for it, which is why the waste hierarchy puts prevention above treatment and treatment above disposal

cases.q: A client asks an engineer to omit a finding that would delay the project and that bears on public safety. The governing duty:
cases.o1: Hold the public's safety, health and welfare paramount, so the finding stands
cases.o2: Act as a faithful agent for the client, so the finding is omitted

cases.q: An engineer's judgment on a safety matter is overridden by a supervisor. The Code's route is to:
cases.o1: Notify the employer and, where the danger persists, such other authority as may be appropriate
cases.o2: Comply, since the supervisor is senior
cases.o4: Say nothing until an incident occurs

cases.q: Confidentiality is overridden when:
cases.o1: The law or the Code requires disclosure, including a danger to the public

cases.q: The canons are ordered, which means:
cases.o1: Where duties conflict, the public's safety outranks loyalty to a client or employer
cases.o2: They are alternatives to choose between

parts.label: v
parts.explain: The ordering is the substance of the Code: it tells you what to do when two real obligations conflict

cases.q: An engineer who learns of an apparent Code violation by another is expected to:
cases.o1: Report it to the appropriate professional body and, where relevant, the public authorities
cases.o2: Keep it private to avoid harming a colleague
cases.o4: Address it only within the firm

cases.q: Signing off a document prepared by someone outside one's own competence is:
cases.o1: Not permitted: the seal is a claim of professional responsibility
cases.o2: Acceptable if the preparer is qualified

cases.q: Aiding the unlicensed practice of engineering is:
An engineer who discovers an error in work already issued should:
cases.o1: Acknowledge it and correct it, accepting responsibility
cases.o2: Wait to see whether it matters
cases.o4: Leave it to the next reviewer

parts.label: v
parts.explain: The duties are active: report, correct, refuse — not merely abstain

cases.q: An engineer is offered work in a field they have not practised. The Code allows accepting it only if:
cases.o1: They become qualified, or the unfamiliar parts are done by or under qualified people

cases.q: On a multidiscipline project, an engineer seals:
cases.o1: Only the technical segments they prepared or directly supervised

cases.q: Competence under the Code is:
cases.o1: A matter of actual qualification in the field, not of licence class alone

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Competence is per segment and per field, which is why a stamp is a claim about what the signer actually did

cases.q: An engineer specifying equipment is offered a supplier's gift. The Code's position:
cases.o1: Refuse it: the test is influence, not whether the decision in fact changed
cases.o3: Accept if its value is small
cases.o4: Accept if the supplier is best anyway

cases.q: Being paid by two parties for the same service requires:
cases.o1: The informed consent of everyone concerned
cases.o4: A written waiver from one party

cases.q: A conflict of interest is handled by:
cases.o1: Disclosing it to all affected parties

cases.q: An engineer on a public board decides on a matter involving their own firm. They should:
cases.o3: Vote and record the interest afterwards

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Disclosure first, and recusal where disclosure is not enough; the standard is appearance as well as effect

cases.q: Knowledge of a client's process gained on a project may be used to:
cases.o1: Nothing beyond that engagement without the client's consent
cases.o2: Win work from a competitor in the same field
cases.o4: Act against the client in a dispute

cases.q: The confidentiality duty after leaving an employer:
Disclosing confidential information is permitted when:
cases.o1: Consent is given, or law or the Code requires it

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Confidentiality is a continuing duty with narrow exceptions, and the law or a danger to the public is one of them

cases.q: An enforceable agreement needs:
cases.o1: An offer, acceptance and consideration, between competent parties for a lawful purpose

cases.q: Which clause decides whether extra work is a change order?
A standard-of-care clause that promises the highest standard rather than ordinary professional care is a problem because:
cases.o1: It can exceed what professional liability insurance covers

cases.q: An indemnity clause allocates:
cases.o1: Who bears the cost of a stated kind of loss

parts.label: v
parts.explain: The engineering risk sits in scope, standard of care, indemnity and limitation of liability, not in the fee

cases.q: A new catalyst formulation the firm intends to license is best protected by:
cases.o1: A utility patent, which grants exclusivity for twenty years from filing in exchange for publication
cases.o2: A trade secret, since it will be licensed

cases.q: A manufacturing know-how that cannot be reverse engineered is often kept as:
cases.o1: A trade secret, which lasts only while it stays secret

cases.q: A utility patent's term runs:
cases.o1: Twenty years from the filing date
cases.o2: Twenty years from the grant date
cases.o3: For the life of the inventor

cases.q: Publishing an invention before filing:
cases.o1: Can destroy patentability, and certainly destroys trade-secret protection

cases.q: A trademark lasts:
cases.o1: Indefinitely, while the mark remains in use and is defended

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Four protections with different bargains: publish for a term, keep secret for as long as it holds, or protect a mark or an expression

cases.q: Designs an engineer prepares as an employee generally belong to:
A client's own drawings supplied for a project:
cases.o1: Remain the client's, and are used only for that project

cases.q: Ownership of work product on a collaboration should be:
cases.o1: Settled in writing before the work starts

cases.q: Credit for engineering work is owed to:
cases.o1: Those who did it, which is a duty separate from who owns it

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Ownership and credit are separate duties, and both are settled in advance rather than argued afterwards

problems.prompt: A result is computed from measurements of {{a1}}, {{a2}} and {{a3}} significant figures. To how many significant figures should the product be reported?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: A product carries the significant figures of its least precise factor, so measuring one quantity to six figures buys nothing while another is known to two; rounding is done once, at the end

problems.prompt: Three measurements are known to {{d1}}, {{d2}} and {{d3}} decimal places. To how many decimal places should their sum be reported?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: A sum is limited by decimal place rather than by significant figures, which is the rule most often applied the wrong way round

problems.prompt: Two measurements carry absolute uncertainties of {{u1}} and {{u2}}. What is the uncertainty of their sum?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Absolute uncertainties add in quadrature through a sum, so the largest one dominates: with a 0.1 and a 1.5, improving the 0.1 changes almost nothing

problems.prompt: A product of two quantities known to {{r1}} and {{r2}} per cent carries what relative uncertainty (per cent)?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Relative uncertainties add in quadrature through a product or quotient, which is why a flow measured to five per cent fixes the accuracy of anything computed from it

cases.q: Five repeated readings agree closely but all sit well above the true value. The set is:
cases.o1: Precise but inaccurate, which points at a calibration error

cases.q: Precision is improved by:
Accuracy is improved by:
A systematic error:
cases.o1: Shifts every reading the same way, so averaging does not remove it
cases.o4: Is the same as random error

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Spread and offset are different problems with different fixes, and repeating only helps with one of them

problems.prompt: An option yields {{v1}} dollars with probability {{p1}} and {{v2}} dollars otherwise. What is its expected value (dollars)?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: The expected value ranks repeated decisions and says nothing about spread, so an option with a positive expectation and a branch the firm could not survive is still not taken

problems.prompt: What success probability makes an option with payoffs {{v1}} and {{v2}} dollars break even?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Inverting the expected value gives the probability the decision rests on, which is usually easier to argue about than the expectation itself

problems.prompt: A project's net present value is {{n1}} dollars at a product price of {{pr}} dollars per ton. A {{dp}} per cent price fall cuts revenue, whose present value is {{rv}} dollars. What net present value results (dollars)?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: A sensitivity run varies one input at a time; because revenue is usually the largest present value in the sum, a few per cent off the price moves the answer further than a large capital overrun

problems.prompt: By what percentage can the price fall before a net present value of {{n1}} dollars reaches zero, if revenue's present value is {{rv}} dollars?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: The breakeven swing is the margin the project has in its most important assumption, and it is the number a board asks for

cases.q: Two projects differ greatly in size. Which criterion answers the firm's question about value created?
Payback period is a poor ranking criterion because it:
cases.o1: Ignores everything after the payback date, and so prefers quick small projects

cases.q: Internal rate of return can mislead because it:
cases.o1: Is dimensionless, so it ignores how much money the project makes
cases.o3: Is always lower than the discount rate

cases.q: Where net present value and internal rate of return disagree on ranking:
cases.o1: Net present value is the one to follow for a firm maximising value

cases.q: A project with a positive net present value at the firm's discount rate:
cases.o1: Creates value at that cost of capital
cases.o2: Is profitable only if payback is short
cases.o3: Has a rate of return below the discount rate

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Three criteria answer three different questions; only one of them is the firm's

problems.prompt: Five readings are {{x1}}, {{x2}}, {{x3}}, {{x4}} and {{x5}}. By how much does the mean exceed the median?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: The gap between mean and median measures how far one reading is pulling the average: a large gap on five readings usually means an outlier to investigate rather than a skewed process

expect.v: (nsimplify(x1) + nsimplify(x2) + nsimplify(x3) + nsimplify(x4) + nsimplify(x5))/5 - sorted([nsimplify(x1), nsimplify(x2), nsimplify(x3), nsimplify(x4), nsimplify(x5)])[2]

problems.prompt: Four readings are {{x1}}, {{x2}}, {{x3}} and {{x4}}. What is the sample standard deviation?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Dividing by one less than the count corrects for having estimated the mean from the same data; with four readings the difference from dividing by four is about fifteen per cent

problems.prompt: A sample of {{nn}} gives a mean of {{xb}} against a claimed {{mu}}, with sample standard deviation {{sd}}. What is the t statistic?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: The statistic is the difference in units of its own standard error, so the same difference becomes significant with a larger sample: significance is about detectability, not about size mattering

cases.q: Failing to reject a claim at the five per cent level means:
cases.o1: The data were not surprising enough to rule it out, which is not evidence it holds

cases.q: A difference significant at one per cent on 10000 readings:
cases.o1: May still be far too small to matter in the plant

cases.q: A p-value is:
cases.o1: How probable data this extreme would be if the claim were true
cases.o2: The probability the claim is true

cases.q: Raising the sample size:
cases.o1: Narrows the standard error, so smaller real differences become detectable

parts.label: v
parts.explain: A test answers whether the data could have arisen by chance, never whether the difference is worth acting on

problems.prompt: Four points give sums: n = 4, sum x = {{sx}}, sum y = {{sy}}, sum xy = {{sxy}}, sum x squared = {{sxx}}. What is the least-squares slope?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: The slope is the covariance over the predictor's variance; a fitted line says nothing about whether the relationship is causal or whether a straight line was the right shape

problems.prompt: A fit has a coefficient of determination of {{r2}}. What percentage of the variation in the response does the line leave unaccounted for?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: The residual fraction is where the physics the model left out lives, and a high coefficient on a short range of the predictor often collapses as soon as the range is extended

problems.prompt: A unit fails with probability {{p1}} costing {{c1}} dollars, needs rework with probability {{p2}} costing {{c2}}, and is otherwise fine. What is the expected cost per unit (dollars)?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: The probability-weighted sum is the right basis for a cost repeated over many units, and it is what an inspection or a redesign has to beat to pay for itself

problems.prompt: Inspection would catch the failure mode costing {{c1}} dollars at probability {{p1}}. What is the most it is worth paying per unit (dollars)?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: A perfect inspection is worth the expected loss it removes, so the ceiling on its cost follows from the probability and the consequence together: a rare but ruinous mode justifies far more than a common cheap one

problems.prompt: A process has a standard deviation of {{sg}} and is charted in subgroups of {{ng}} about a centre line of {{cl}}. What is the upper control limit?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Control limits are three standard errors from the centre line, so they narrow with the square root of subgroup size; they are not the specification limits, and a process can sit inside them and still make scrap

problems.prompt: By what factor do an X-bar chart's control limits narrow when the subgroup size goes from {{n1}} to {{n2}}?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Larger subgroups make the chart more sensitive to a shift in the mean, which is why subgroup size is a design choice about what size of shift must be caught

problems.prompt: Specifications run from {{lsl}} to {{usl}}; the process sits at {{mu}} with a standard deviation of {{sg}}. What is the centred capability index?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: The centred index charges the process for sitting off target, so it is the smaller of the two one-sided margins; a capable but off-centre process has a high uncentred index and a low centred one

problems.prompt: For the same specifications {{lsl}} to {{usl}} and standard deviation {{sg}}, what is the uncentred capability index?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: The uncentred index is the best the process could do if it were perfectly centred, so the gap between the two indices is exactly what re-centring would recover, and re-centring is usually cheaper than reducing variation

cases.q: Eight consecutive points on one side of the centre line indicate:
cases.o1: A shift in the process mean, even with no point outside the limits

cases.q: A steady upward trend over several points suggests:
cases.o1: A drifting cause such as tool wear or fouling

cases.q: A single point beyond three sigma means:
cases.o1: Something changed, and the cause is looked for before more product is made

cases.q: The purpose of the run rules is to:
cases.o1: Catch a shift before product goes out of specification, rather than after

cases.q: Points hugging the centre line unusually closely can indicate:
cases.o1: That the subgroups are not what they are assumed to be, for instance stratified sampling

parts.label: v
parts.explain: The rules exist because a shift shows as a pattern long before it shows as a violation

problems.prompt: A mill drew {{en}} kWh/ton taking feed from {{f80}} to {{p80}} micrometres. What Bond work index does that imply (kWh/ton)?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Running Bond's law backwards from a measured duty is how a work index is obtained for a material that has not been tested, and how an existing mill's performance is checked against the test value

problems.prompt: Nucleation rate goes as supersaturation to the power {{bn}} and growth as the power {{gn}}. By what factor does the ratio of nucleation to growth change when supersaturation is multiplied by {{fs}}?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Nucleation's higher order is the whole reason a crystallizer run hard makes fines: doubling the driving force can multiply the nucleation-to-growth ratio several-fold

problems.prompt: A conical stockpile of base diameter {{dd}} m stands at an angle of repose of {{ang}} degrees. How tall is it (m)?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: The angle of repose fixes a stockpile's height for a given footprint, so it sets both the storage a yard can hold and the reclaim equipment's reach

problems.prompt: A unit has {{ne}} major items of equipment, each with {{nv}} valves and {{ni}} instruments. How many tagged items must the P&ID carry that the process flow diagram need not?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: The count is why the two drawings exist: the detail that makes a plant buildable would make the process unreadable, so the flow diagram carries the process and the P&ID carries the hardware

problems.prompt: A unit has {{nl}} control loops, each with a transmitter, a controller and a valve. How many tagged devices is that?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Every loop is three devices sharing one number, which is how a loop is traced from the drawing to the cabinet to the field

problems.prompt: A code's thin-wall rule gives t = P*R/(S*E - 0.6*P). For P = {{pp}} psi, R = {{rr}} in, S = {{ss}} psi and E = {{ee}}, what thickness results (in)?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: The equation is printed because the code's own text was not read. The joint efficiency term is the point: a vessel whose welds are not fully examined needs a thicker wall for the same duty, so inspection and steel trade against each other

problems.prompt: A rupture disc is specified at a burst pressure of {{bp}} psig with a tolerance of plus or minus {{tl}} per cent. What is the highest pressure at which it may still be intact (psig)?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: The top of the tolerance band, not the nameplate, is the pressure the vessel must survive, which is why a disc's specified burst sits below the rating by at least its tolerance

problems.prompt: A two-phase relief discharges {{wt}} lb/h of which {{lq}} per cent is liquid. What liquid rate must the knockout drum handle (lb/h)?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: The flare can only take vapour, so the liquid fraction sizes the knockout drum and the catch tank behind it; a relief treated as all vapour sends liquid to the flare tip

problems.prompt: A store holds {{ng}} incompatibility groups that must each be kept apart from every other. How many pairwise separations does that require?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: The pair count grows as the square, which is why a store is laid out by groups with bunds and separate drains rather than by checking each new drum against every other material present

problems.prompt: A submission has {{nt}} technical segments, of which this engineer prepared or directly supervised {{no}}. How many may they seal?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: The seal is a claim about what the signer did, so the count is exactly the segments they prepared or supervised: the remaining segments are sealed by the engineers who prepared them

cases.q: An engineer's spouse owns shares in a bidder on a project the engineer is evaluating. The required step is:
cases.o1: Disclose the interest to all affected parties before taking part
cases.o2: Nothing, since the interest is the spouse's
cases.o3: Evaluate the bid and mention it afterwards

cases.q: A consultant is paid a retainer by a client and a commission by the equipment supplier they recommend. This is:
cases.o1: Permitted only with the informed consent of everyone concerned, and the commission alone would not be
cases.o3: Permitted if the equipment is genuinely best

cases.q: An engineer reviewing a competitor's design for a client may:
cases.o1: Do it, keeping the review objective and the information confidential
cases.o2: Not do it under any circumstance
cases.o3: Do it and contact the competitor's client
cases.o4: Do it only with the competitor's consent

parts.label: v
parts.explain: The question is always what a reasonable affected party would want to know before relying on the engineer's judgment

cases.q: An engineer leaves a firm and is asked by a new employer about the former client's process. They may disclose:
cases.o1: Only general knowledge and skill, not the former client's confidential information

cases.q: An engineer notices, from confidential project data, a safety defect in a product already sold. The duty is:
cases.o1: The public's safety governs, so the matter is escalated, confidentiality notwithstanding
cases.o2: Confidentiality governs, so nothing is said

cases.q: Using a client's process knowledge to bid work for a competitor in the same field is:
cases.o1: Not permitted without the client's consent
cases.o2: Permitted, since knowledge cannot be returned

parts.label: v
parts.explain: The duty continues after the engagement, and the one thing that overrides it is a danger to the public

problems.prompt: A contract's scope covers {{ns}} deliverables at {{rt}} dollars each. The client requests {{nx}} more of the same kind. What is the change order worth (dollars)?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: A signed scope is what makes extra work a change order rather than an argument, which is why the scope clause carries more engineering risk than the fee does

problems.prompt: A utility patent is filed in {{yf}} and granted in {{yg}}. In what year does its twenty-year term end?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: The term runs from filing, not from grant, so a long examination eats into the exclusivity rather than extending it: that is the structural reason to file early and prosecute fast

cases.q: An engineer develops a tool on their own time that is used at work on company projects. Ownership:
cases.o1: Depends on the employment agreement and what the tool was developed from, so it is settled in writing in advance

cases.q: A client asks to reuse a design the engineer prepared for them on a second site. Reuse is:
cases.o1: A matter of what the agreement says about reuse and liability, settled rather than assumed
cases.o4: Permitted if the engineer is credited

cases.q: A paper is written up from a project. Authorship goes to:
cases.o1: Those who did the work, which is a duty separate from who owns it

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Each case turns on an agreement that should exist before the work, not on a default anyone can assume

problems.prompt: Five readings average {{xb}} against a standard of {{st}}. What is the systematic offset, and what percentage of the standard is it?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: A systematic offset is found only by comparison with a standard, and averaging more readings never removes it: it is the part of the error that repeating cannot help

problems.prompt: A project costs {{k0}} dollars and returns {{cf}} dollars a year for {{ny}} years. What is its simple payback period (years), and how much of the life does it ignore?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Payback ignores every cash flow after the date it reports and discounts nothing, so it ranks a short cheap project above a long valuable one; it is a liquidity screen, not a value measure

problems.prompt: On a centred, in-control process, what is the probability that {{nr}} consecutive points all fall on the same side of the centre line (either side)?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: The run rules are set where the chance under a stable process becomes comparable to a three-sigma point, which is why eight in a row is treated as a signal rather than a coincidence

problems.prompt: What nominal annual rate, compounded {{per}} ({{m}} times a year), gives an effective annual rate of {{e}}%?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Invert $(1 + r/m)^m - 1$; the nominal rate is always a little below the effective one

problems.prompt: A {{P}} thousand dollar plant must earn back its cost at {{i}}% over {{n}} years. What equal annual net cash flow, in thousand dollars, makes NPV zero (no salvage)?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: The capital-recovery factor (A/P, i, n) turns a present cost into an equivalent annual charge

problems.prompt: A {{P}} thousand dollar project returns {{cf}} thousand dollars a year in cash for {{n}} years and is depreciated straight-line to zero. What is its average return on investment, in % per year (profit after depreciation over investment)?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: ROI ignores the time value of money; it ranks projects quickly but NPV decides between them

problems.prompt: A {{S1}} m³ vessel cost {{C1}} thousand dollars when the cost index was {{I1}}. With the index now {{I2}} and the six-tenths rule, what capacity, in m³, can {{C2}} thousand dollars buy?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Invert the power law: doubling the budget at constant index buys about 3.2 times the capacity

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Year j takes (n − j + 1)/Σ of the depreciable amount: front-loaded like declining balance, but it lands exactly on the salvage value

problems.prompt: A fuel blend is {{a}}% methane (LFL 5.0%) and {{b}}% propane (LFL 2.1%) by volume. Air contains {{c}}% of this blend. Is the mixture below the lower flammable limit?

parts.label: v
choice: Below the LFL (too lean to burn)
parts.explain: Le Chatelier's rule gives the blend's LFL; compare the concentration in air with it (and with the UFL, for the rich side)

problems.prompt: A workplace has {{c1}} ppm of a solvent (TLV {{t1}} ppm) and {{c2}} ppm of another (TLV {{t2}} ppm), with additive effects. How high, in ppm, may a third (TLV {{t3}} ppm) go before the mixture limit is exceeded?

parts.explain: The fractions of each limit add; whatever is left of 1 is the third component's share

problems.prompt: Laplace's equation $u_{xx} + u_{yy} = 0$ on a rectangle, with {{say}}. After writing $u = X(x)Y(y)$, which factor gets the oscillating solutions (sines and cosines)?

parts.label: v
choice: X(x): sines or cosines in x, hyperbolic or exponential in y
Y(y): sines or cosines in y, hyperbolic or exponential in x
parts.explain: The direction with homogeneous conditions on both of its sides gets the eigenfunctions, because only an oscillating solution can satisfy two homogeneous conditions. The other direction carries the one nonhomogeneous condition and gets sinh, cosh or a decaying exponential. This fixes the sign of the separation constant

cases.why: sinh vanishes at y = 0, so that condition is met mode by mode

cases.say: u_y(x, 0) = 0 (insulated bottom), with the data on y = b
cases.why: cosh has zero slope at y = 0

problems.prompt: Laplace's equation with eigenfunctions $\sin(n\pi x/a)$ in $x$. The $y$-conditions are: {{say}}. The $y$-factor of mode $n$ is…

parts.label: v
parts.explain: {{why}}. Y solves Y″ = (nπ/a)²Y, whose solutions are sinh and cosh (or the two exponentials); pick the combination that satisfies the homogeneous condition

problems.prompt: A rod $0 < x < {{L}}$ has both ends held at 0 and obeys $u_t = {{al}}\,u_{xx}$. Mode ${{n}}$ is $e^{-t/\tau}\sin({{n}}\pi x/{{L}})$.

parts.label: tau
parts.explain: Substitute the mode into the PDE: $-1/\tau = -\alpha(n\pi/L)^2$, so $\tau = L^2/(\alpha n^2\pi^2)$. Mode $n$ dies $n^2$ times faster than mode 1, which is why the first term soon dominates

problems.prompt: Expand $f(x) = {{T0}}$ on $0 < x < {{L}}$ in the sine series $\sum b_n\sin(n\pi x/{{L}})$.

parts.label: b
parts.explain: $b_n = \tfrac{2}{L}\int_0^L f\sin(n\pi x/L)\,dx = \tfrac{2T_0}{n\pi}(1 - \cos n\pi)$: zero for even $n$ and $\tfrac{4T_0}{n\pi}$ for odd $n$. The length $L$ cancels

problems.prompt: Expand $f(x) = x$ on $0 < x < {{L}}$ in the sine series $\sum b_n\sin(n\pi x/{{L}})$.

parts.label: b
parts.explain: Integrate by parts: $b_n = \tfrac{2}{L}\int_0^L x\sin(n\pi x/L)\,dx = \tfrac{2L}{n\pi}(-1)^{n+1}$. The signs alternate and the size falls like $1/n$

problems.prompt: Solve $u_t = {{al}}\,u_{xx}$ on $0 < x < {{L}}$, $u = 0$ at both ends, with $u(x, 0) = {{A0}}\sin(\pi x/{{L}}) {{B0}}\sin(3\pi x/{{L}})$.

parts.ask: Coefficient $b_3$ of $\sin(3\pi x/{{L}})$ in the solution
parts.label: b3
parts.explain: The initial condition is already a sine series, so read the coefficients off. No integral is needed: orthogonality would just return them

parts.ask: Decay rate $k_3$ in that term's factor $e^{-k_3 t}$
parts.label: k3
parts.explain: $k_n = \alpha(n\pi/L)^2$ with $n = 3$. The solution is ${{A0}}e^{-k_1t}\sin(\pi x/L) {{B0}}e^{-k_3t}\sin(3\pi x/L)$

problems.prompt: A rod $0 < x < {{L}}$ is insulated at both ends and along its length. Initially $T(x, 0) = {{T1}} + {{dT/L}}\,x$.

parts.label: Ts
parts.explain: No heat can leave, so the rod settles to the average of its initial temperature: $\tfrac1L\int_0^L T(x,0)\,dx$. In the cosine series this is the $n = 0$ term, the only one that does not decay

problems.prompt: A string of length ${{L}}$ m fixed at both ends obeys $u_{tt} = c^2u_{xx}$ with $c = {{cc}}$ m/s.

parts.label: f
parts.explain: Mode $n$ is $\sin(n\pi x/L)\cos(\omega_n t)$ with $\omega_n = n\pi c/L$, so $f_n = \omega_n/2\pi = nc/(2L)$

problems.prompt: A string fixed at both ends is {{say}}. Each mode's time factor is…

parts.label: v
parts.explain: {{why}}. The wave equation is second order in time, so each mode has both cos and sin and needs two initial conditions; the heat equation is first order and gets one decaying exponential

problems.prompt: A semi-infinite cylinder of radius ${{a0}}$ cm has its wall at 0 and a hot base at $z = 0$. Far from the base, $T \approx A_1J_0(\alpha_1 r/a)\,e^{-z/\ell}$ with $\alpha_1 = 2.405$.

parts.label: ell

problems.prompt: The functions ${{fam}}$ are orthogonal on ${{dom}}$ with which weight inside the integral?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: The weight is read from the Sturm–Liouville form $(pX')' + (q + \lambda w)X = 0$. Bessel's equation is $(rR')' + \lambda^2 rR = 0$, so $w = r$: every Fourier–Bessel coefficient integral carries an extra $r$. For $X'' + \lambda^2X = 0$ the weight is 1

problems.prompt: With $h = {{h0}}$: $f(x - h) = {{fm}}$, $f(x) = {{f0}}$, $f(x + h) = {{fp}}$. Estimate $f''(x)$ with the central difference.

parts.label: d2
parts.explain: $\dfrac{f(x+h) - 2f(x) + f(x-h)}{h^2}$. Adding the two Taylor series cancels the odd terms, leaving an error of order $h^2$

expect.d2: diff(interpolate([(-h0, fm), (0, f0), (h0, fp)], x), x, 2)

cases.why: One Taylor series; the first neglected term is (h/2)f″
One Taylor series; the first neglected term is (h/2)f″
Subtracting the two series cancels the f″ term; the error starts at (h²/6)f‴
Adding the two series cancels the odd terms; the error starts at (h²/12)f⁗

problems.prompt: The approximation $\displaystyle {{fd}}$ for ${{of}}$ has truncation error of order…

parts.label: v
parts.explain: {{why}}. To find an order on the exam: Taylor-expand every sampled value about x, collect, and read the lowest power of h that survives

problems.prompt: Explicit scheme for $u_t = u_{xx}$ with $r = k/h^2 = {{r0}}$. At time level $j$: $u_{i-1} = {{um}}$, $u_i = {{ui}}$, $u_{i+1} = {{up}}$.

parts.label: un

problems.prompt: The explicit scheme is used for $u_t = {{al}}\,u_{xx}$ with $h = {{h0}}$.

parts.label: k
parts.explain: Stability needs $r = \alpha k/h^2 \le \tfrac12$. Halving $h$ forces four times as many time steps. Crank–Nicolson has no such limit

problems.prompt: For $u_t = u_{xx}$ with $r = k/h^2 = {{r0}}$, the {{sch}} scheme multiplies the most oscillatory grid mode (the sawtooth, $\sin^2(n\pi h/2) = 1$) by a factor $G$ each step.

parts.label: g
parts.explain: Explicit: $G = 1 - 4r\sin^2(n\pi h/2)$. Crank–Nicolson: $G = \dfrac{1 - 2r\sin^2(n\pi h/2)}{1 + 2r\sin^2(n\pi h/2)}$

parts.label: s
choice: No: |G| > 1, so it grows every step
parts.explain: A mode is stable when $|G| \le 1$. The explicit scheme needs $r \le \tfrac12$; for Crank–Nicolson the numerator is always smaller in size than the denominator, so it is stable for every $r$

problems.prompt: $u_t = {{k}}\,u_{xx}$ on $0 < x < {{L}}$ with $u(0,t) = 0$ and $u({{L}},t) = {{gtex}}$. Shift by $w = x\,g(t)/{{L}}$, so $v = u - w$ has zero ends and obeys $v_t = {{k}}v_{xx} + F(x,t)$. What is $F$ at $x = {{xp}}$, $t = 0$?

parts.explain: Steady state: $k u_s'' = -Q$, a parabola. Both ends zero: $u_s = \dfrac{Q}{2k}x(L - x)$, peak $QL^2/8k$ in the middle. Insulated at $L$: $u_s = \dfrac{Q}{k}\left(Lx - \dfrac{x^2}{2}\right)$, peak at the insulated end. Then $v = u - u_s$ is the source-free problem

problems.prompt: $u_t = u_{xx} + q(x)$ on $0 < x < {{L}}$, ends at 0, with $q(x) = {{ftex}}$. Expanding $u = \sum T_n(t)\sin(n\pi x/{{L}})$ gives $T_n' + (n\pi/{{L}})^2 T_n = q_n$. What is $q_{ {{n}} }$?

problems.prompt: $u_t = {{k}}\left(u_{rr} + \tfrac{2}{r}u_r\right)$ in a sphere of radius ${{a}}$, surface held at 0, initially ${{U0}}$ everywhere. At $t = {{t}}$, find {{wt}}.

parts.label: y
parts.explain: Put $v = ru$: the equation becomes $v_t = kv_{rr}$, a rod with $v(0) = 0$ (u finite) and $v(a) = 0$. So $v = \sum B_n\sin(n\pi r/a)e^{-k(n\pi/a)^2t}$ with $B_n = \dfrac{2}{a}\int_0^a rU_0\sin\dfrac{n\pi r}{a}dr = \dfrac{2aU_0(-1)^{n+1}}{n\pi}$, and $u = v/r$; at the centre $\sin(\lambda r)/r \to \lambda$

expect.y: [sphere_coef(U0, a, n), sphere_centre(U0, a, k, t), k*(pi/nsimplify(a))**2][w]

problems.prompt: $u_t = u_{xx}$, $u(0,t) = 0$, $u({{L}},t) = 1$, $u(x,0) = 0$ gives $U(x,s) = \dfrac{\sinh(\sqrt s\,x)}{s\sinh(\sqrt s\,{{L}})}$. Invert by residues. At $x = {{xp}}$, what is the coefficient of $e^{-({{n}}\pi/{{L}})^2 t}$?

parts.label: y
parts.explain: Poles: $s = 0$ (residue $x/L$, the steady state) and $\sqrt s = in\pi/L$, i.e. $s_n = -(n\pi/L)^2$, where $\sinh(\sqrt sL) = 0$. Each residue is $\dfrac{2(-1)^n}{n\pi}\sin\dfrac{n\pi x}{L}e^{s_nt}$. Summing all residues rebuilds the separation-of-variables series: the poles are the eigenvalues

problems.prompt: Explicit scheme for $u_t = u_{xx}$, $r = k/h^2 = {{r}}$, $h = {{h}}$, with the flux condition $u_x(0,t) = {{g}}$. Now $u_0 = {{u0}}$ and $u_1 = {{u1}}$. Using a ghost node, what is $u_0$ one step later?

parts.label: y
parts.explain: Central difference at the boundary: $(u_1 - u_{-1})/2h = g$, so the ghost value is $u_{-1} = u_1 - 2hg$. Put it in the usual update: $u_0^{new} = u_0 + r(2u_1 - 2u_0 - 2hg)$. Insulated ($g = 0$) mirrors the first interior node

problems.prompt: $u_t = u_{xx}$ with ends held at 0 and three interior nodes at ${{a}}, {{b}}, {{c}}$. Take one {{sch}} step with $r = {{r}}$. What is the new middle value?

parts.label: y
parts.explain: Implicit: $-r\theta u_{i-1}^{new} + (1 + 2r\theta)u_i^{new} - r\theta u_{i+1}^{new} = u_i + r(1 - \theta)(u_{i-1} - 2u_i + u_{i+1})$, with θ = 1 (backward Euler) or ½ (Crank–Nicolson). That is a tridiagonal system, solved by elimination (Thomas). Both are stable for any r; explicit needs r ≤ ½

cases.q: A rod has $u(0,t) = T_1$ and $u(L,t) = T_2$, both nonzero. What is the first move?
After writing $u = u_{ss}(x) + v(x,t)$, what boundary conditions does $v$ satisfy?
What equation and conditions define the steady state $u_{ss}(x)$ of the heat equation with fixed end temperatures?
Why can $u = X(x)G(t)$ not be used directly when $u(0,t) = T_1 \ne 0$?
After the shift, what initial condition does $v$ get if $u(x,0) = f(x)$?

parts.label: a
choice: Subtract the steady state: u = w(x) + v(x,t), with w the steady state
w″ = 0 with w(0) = T1 and w(L) = T2: a straight line
X(0)G(t) = T1 for all t forces G to be constant, so nothing could change in time
v(x,0) = f(x) − w(x), with w the steady state
parts.explain: Separation needs homogeneous boundary conditions. The steady state carries the nonzero ends; what is left, $v$, has zero ends and is solved exactly as before, but with the initial condition $f - u_{ss}$. As $t \to \infty$, $v \to 0$ and $u \to u_{ss}$

problems.prompt: A rod $0 < x < {{L}}$ has its ends held at $u(0,t) = {{T1}}$ and $u({{L}},t) = {{T2}}$. What is the steady-state temperature at $x = {{a}}$?

parts.label: r
parts.explain: At steady state $u_t = 0$, so $u_{ss}'' = 0$: a straight line through the two end values, $u_{ss}(x) = {{T1}} + \dfrac{ {{T2 - T1}} }{ {{L}} }x$

problems.prompt: A rod $0 < x < {{L}}$ starts at the uniform temperature ${{T0}}$; then its ends are held at ${{T1}}$ (at $x = 0$) and ${{T2}}$ (at $x = {{L}}$). With $u = u_{ss} + v$, what is $v$ at $x = {{a}}$, $t = 0$?

parts.label: r
parts.explain: $v(x,0) = u(x,0) - u_{ss}(x) = {{T0}} - \left({{T1}} + \dfrac{ {{T2 - T1}} }{ {{L}} }x\right)$. This, not ${{T0}}$, is what gets expanded in sines

problems.prompt: A rod $0 < x < L$ starts at ${{T0}}$; its ends are then held at ${{T1}}$ ($x = 0$) and ${{T2}}$ ($x = L$). The solution is $u = u_{ss}(x) + \sum b_n \sin\dfrac{n\pi x}{L}\,e^{-\alpha(n\pi/L)^2 t}$. Find $b_{ {{n}} }$.

parts.label: r
parts.explain: Expand $v(x,0) = {{T0}} - u_{ss}(x) = ({{T0 - T1}}) - ({{T2 - T1}})\dfrac{x}{L}$ in sines: $b_n = \dfrac2L\displaystyle\int_0^L v(x,0)\sin\dfrac{n\pi x}{L}\,dx$. The constant part gives $\dfrac{2({{T0 - T1}})}{n\pi}(1 - \cos n\pi)$ and the ramp gives $\dfrac{2({{T2 - T1}})}{n\pi}\cos n\pi$

problems.prompt: A slab $0 < x < {{L}}$ m ($k = {{k}}$ W/(m·K)) receives a steady heat flux of ${{q}}$ W/m² at $x = 0$ while $x = {{L}}$ is held at ${{T2}}$ °C. What is the steady temperature at $x = 0$?

parts.label: r
parts.explain: Steady state is still a straight line, but now one end fixes the slope: $-k\,u_{ss}'(0) = {{q}}$, so the slope is $-{{q/k}}$ K/m and the hot face sits ${{q*L/k}}$ K above the held face

problems.prompt: For $X'' + \omega^2 X = 0$ with {{bc}}, which condition fixes the eigenvalues $\omega_n$?

parts.label: a
parts.explain: Apply the condition at $x = 0$ first: it leaves a sine ($X(0) = 0$) or a cosine ($X'(0) = 0$). Put that into the condition at $x = L$. A convection (Robin) end mixes $X$ and $X'$, so the eigenvalues come from a transcendental equation and are not evenly spaced

cases.q: Laplace's equation on a rectangle has nonzero values on two different sides. How do you solve it?
In Laplace's equation on a rectangle with one nonzero side, which direction gets the sines (the eigenfunctions)?
In Laplace's equation on a rectangle with one nonzero side, what carries the solution across to that side?

parts.label: a
choice: Split it into two problems, each with one nonzero side, and add the solutions
The direction whose two sides are both zero
sinh (or cosh) in the other direction
parts.explain: The equation is linear, so solutions add. Each sub-problem has homogeneous conditions on three sides: the pair of zero sides sets the eigenfunctions, and the hyperbolic function grows from the remaining zero side up to the nonzero one

cases.q: Transforming in $t$, what does $u_t$ become?
Transforming in $t$, what does $u_{xx}$ become?
After transforming $u_t = \alpha u_{xx}$ in $t$, what kind of equation is left?

problems.prompt: Heat equation by Laplace transform, $U(x,s) = \mathcal L\{u(x,t)\}$. {{q}}

parts.label: a
choice: An ODE in x, with s as a parameter
parts.explain: The transform removes $t$: $u_t \to sU - u(x,0)$, and $x$-derivatives are untouched. What is left is the ordinary differential equation $\alpha U'' - sU = -u(x,0)$ in $x$, with transformed boundary conditions. Solve it, then invert

problems.prompt: A semi-infinite solid starts at zero temperature. The transformed heat equation is $\alpha U'' - sU = 0$, with bounded solution $U = A\,e^{-qx}$. For $\alpha = {{al}}$ and $s = {{s}}$, what is $q$?

parts.label: r
parts.explain: Try $e^{mx}$: $\alpha m^2 = s$, so $m = \pm\sqrt{s/\alpha}$. Boundedness as $x \to \infty$ keeps the minus sign: $q = \sqrt{s/\alpha}$

problems.prompt: A semi-infinite solid at zero has its surface suddenly held at $T_0$. Inverting $U = \dfrac{T_0}{s}e^{-x\sqrt{s/\alpha}}$ gives $u = T_0\,\operatorname{erfc}\!\left(\dfrac{x}{2\sqrt{\alpha t}}\right)$. What is $u/T_0$ at $x = {{xx}}$, $\alpha = {{al}}$, $t = {{t}}$?

parts.label: r
parts.explain: The argument is $\dfrac{ {{xx}} }{2\sqrt{ {{al*t}} }} = {{xx/(2*sqrt(al*t))}}$. Worth carrying: $\operatorname{erfc}(0.5) \approx 0.48$, $\operatorname{erfc}(1) \approx 0.16$, $\operatorname{erfc}(1.5) \approx 0.034$

problems.prompt: A rod $0 < x < \pi$ with zero ends starts at $u(x,0) = \sin x$. Transforming gives $\alpha U'' - sU = -\sin x$ with $U(0) = U(\pi) = 0$, solved by $U = A(s)\sin x$. For $\alpha = {{al}}$, what is $A$ at $s = {{s}}$?

parts.label: r
parts.explain: Put $U = A\sin x$ in: $-\alpha A - sA = -1$, so $A = \dfrac{1}{s + \alpha}$. Inverting gives $u = e^{-\alpha t}\sin x$, the same answer separation of variables gives

problems.prompt: A rod $0 < x < {{L}}\pi$ with zero ends: after transforming in $t$, the homogeneous problem $\alpha U'' - sU = 0$, $U(0) = U({{L}}\pi) = 0$ has a nonzero solution only for special values of $s$. For $\alpha = {{al}}$, what is the value of $s$ belonging to the mode $\sin\dfrac{ {{n}}x}{ {{L}} }$?

parts.label: r
parts.explain: Put $U = \sin(nx/L)$ in: $-\alpha(n/L)^2 = s$. These special values are the Sturm–Liouville eigenvalues of the $x$-problem; they are the poles of $U(x,s)$, and each pole $s_n$ inverts to a term $e^{s_n t}$: the same decaying modes as separation of variables

problems.prompt: Which approach fits best? {{q}}.

parts.label: a
choice: Subtract the steady state, then separate
parts.explain: Separation needs a finite interval with homogeneous conditions at both ends. Nonzero constant ends: shift first. No second end to quantise against, or a boundary value that changes in time: transform in $t$

problems.prompt: A {{m}} kg person stands on a scale in an elevator that is {{mot}} at {{a}} m/s². What does the scale read, in newtons? (g = 9.8 m/s²)

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Newton's second law on the person: N − mg = ma (up positive). Speeding up upward or slowing down downward both mean a points up

cases.q: Astronauts on the space station float. Why?

problems.prompt: At what height above Earth's surface, as a fraction of Earth's radius R, does g fall to {{f}} of its surface value?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: g ∝ 1/r², so (R/(R + h))² = f; g drops 1% only at h ≈ 0.005R (about 32 km), which is why g is taken as constant near the surface

problems.prompt: Treat a planet as a uniform sphere with surface gravity {{gs}} m/s². What is g at {{fr}} of the way from the centre to the surface?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Only the mass inside r pulls (shell theorem): M(r) = M r³/R³, so g = GM(r)/r² = g_s · r/R

problems.prompt: Springs of {{k1}} N/m and {{k2}} N/m are joined in {{how}}. What is the equivalent spring constant, in N/m?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Parallel springs share the load and add; series springs carry the same force and their stretches add, so compliances add

problems.prompt: A spring of constant {{k}} N/m is cut into {{n}} equal pieces. What is the spring constant of one piece, in N/m?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: The whole spring is n pieces in series: 1/k = n/k′, so each piece is n times stiffer

cases.q: A switch in a single loop is opened. What happens to the current?
cases.o1: It stops everywhere in the loop

problems.prompt: A {{emf}} V battery with internal resistance {{r}} Ω is connected to a {{R}} Ω resistor. What current flows, in A, and how much if a wire shorts the resistor? Give the current {{case}}.

parts.label: v
parts.explain: I = ε/(R + r); shorting removes R, so only the small internal resistance limits the current, which is why shorts heat batteries

problems.prompt: A particle moves as $x(t) = {{a}}t^3 + ({{b}})t^2 + {{c}}t$ m. What is its velocity at $t = {{t}}$ s, in m/s?

parts.label: r
parts.explain: $v = dx/dt = 3at^2 + 2bt + c$; differentiate again for $a(t) = 6at + 2b$. Velocity is the slope of position, acceleration the slope of velocity

problems.prompt: An object has $a(t) = {{k}}t$ m/s² and starts at ${{v0}}$ m/s. What is its velocity at $t = {{t}}$ s, in m/s?

parts.label: r
parts.explain: $v(t) = v_0 + \displaystyle\int_0^t a\,dt = v_0 + \tfrac12kt^2$. The constant of integration is the initial condition; integrate again, with $x_0$, for position

problems.prompt: A boat coasting through water has $a = -{{k}}v$ (per second). It starts at ${{v0}}$ m/s. How fast is it moving after ${{X}}$ m, in m/s?

parts.label: r
parts.explain: When the acceleration depends on speed and you want position, use $a = v\,\dfrac{dv}{dx}$: here $v\,dv/dx = -kv$, so $dv/dx = -k$ and the speed falls linearly with distance, even though it decays exponentially in time

problems.prompt: A particle moves as $\vec r(t) = ({{a}}t^2)\hat\imath + ({{b}}t)\hat\jmath$ m. What is its speed at $t = {{t}}$ s, in m/s?

parts.label: r
parts.explain: Differentiate each component: $\vec v = (2at)\hat\imath + b\hat\jmath$, then take the magnitude. Vector calculus is ordinary calculus done one component at a time

problems.prompt: A rod of length ${{L}}$ m has density $\lambda = cx^{ {{n}} }$, with $x$ measured from one end. Where is its centre of mass, in m from that end?

parts.label: r
parts.explain: $x_{cm} = \dfrac{\int x\lambda\,dx}{\int \lambda\,dx} = \dfrac{n + 1}{n + 2}L$. A uniform rod ($n = 0$) gives $L/2$; the heavier end pulls the balance point toward it

problems.prompt: A force $F = {{c}}t$ N acts on a ${{m}}$ kg mass at rest. What is its velocity at $t = {{t}}$ s, in m/s?

parts.label: r
parts.explain: $a = F/m = ct/m$, so $v = \dfrac{ct^2}{2m}$. When the force changes with time, integrate the acceleration rather than using the constant-acceleration equations

problems.prompt: A car on a curve of radius ${{r}}$ m is going ${{v}}$ m/s and speeding up at ${{at}}$ m/s². What is the magnitude of its total acceleration, in m/s²?

parts.label: r2
parts.explain: The tangential part, $dv/dt$, changes the speed; the radial part, $v^2/r$, changes the direction. They are perpendicular, so add them as a right triangle

problems.prompt: A force $F(x) = {{k}}x^{ {{n}} }$ N acts along $x$. How much work does it do from $x = 0$ to $x = {{L}}$ m, in J?

parts.label: r
parts.explain: $W = \displaystyle\int F\,dx$: the area under the force–position curve, which for a changing force is an integral, not $F \times d$

problems.prompt: A conservative force is $F(x) = -{{k}}x^3$ N. Taking $U(0) = 0$, what is the potential energy at $x = {{X}}$ m, in J?

parts.label: r
parts.explain: $U(x) = -\displaystyle\int_0^x F\,dx = \tfrac14kx^4$. The minus sign makes $U$ rise where the force pushes back toward the origin

problems.prompt: A particle has $U(x) = {{a}}x^2 - {{b}}x$ J. Where is its equilibrium point, in m? (It is stable: $U$ has a minimum there.)

parts.label: r
parts.explain: $F = -dU/dx = -(2ax - b)$ vanishes at $x = b/2a$. A minimum of $U$ is stable, a maximum unstable: the force always points downhill on the U(x) graph

problems.prompt: A motor delivers power $P(t) = {{c}}t$ W. How much work does it do in the first ${{T}}$ s, in J?

parts.label: r
parts.explain: Power is the rate of work, $P = dW/dt$, so $W = \displaystyle\int P\,dt$. Instantaneous power from a force is $\vec F\cdot\vec v$

problems.prompt: A kick exerts $F = {{F0}}\sin(\pi t/{{T}})$ N for $0 \le t \le {{T}}$ s on a ${{m}}$ kg ball at rest. How fast does the ball leave, in m/s?

parts.label: r
parts.explain: Impulse is the area under F–t: $\displaystyle\int_0^T F_0\sin(\pi t/T)\,dt = \dfrac{2F_0T}{\pi}$. Divide by the mass for the change in velocity

problems.prompt: A wheel turns as $\theta(t) = {{a}}t^3 + {{b}}t$ rad. What is its angular acceleration at $t = {{t}}$ s, in rad/s²?

parts.label: r
parts.explain: $\omega = d\theta/dt$ and $\alpha = d\omega/dt$: here $\alpha = 6at$. Exactly the linear rules with new letters

problems.prompt: A force $\vec F = ({{Fx}}, {{Fy}}, 0)$ N acts at $\vec r = ({{rx}}, {{ry}}, 0)$ m from an axis along $z$. What is the $z$ component of the torque, in N·m?

parts.label: r
parts.explain: $\tau_z = r_xF_y - r_yF_x$. Positive means counterclockwise seen from $+z$; the cross product gives the size and the sense at once

problems.prompt: Derive by integration the rotational inertia of {{shape}}, with mass ${{M}}$ kg and {{kind == 2 ? "radius" : "length"}} ${{L}}$ m. Give it in kg·m².

parts.label: r
parts.explain: $I = \displaystyle\int r^2\,dm$. For a rod $dm = (M/L)dx$; for a disk use rings, $dm = (M/\pi R^2)2\pi r\,dr$. That gives $ML^2/3$, $ML^2/12$ and $MR^2/2$

problems.prompt: A flywheel's angular momentum grows as $L(t) = {{c}}t^{ {{n}} }$ kg·m²/s. What net torque acts at $t = {{t}}$ s, in N·m?

parts.label: r
parts.explain: $\tau_{net} = dL/dt$, the rotational form of $F = dp/dt$. For a point mass $\vec L = \vec r \times \vec p$

problems.prompt: {{shape}} of mass ${{m}}$ kg rolls without slipping down a ${{th}}^\circ$ incline ($I = cMR^2$, $c = {{c}}$). What static friction force acts on it, in N?

parts.label: r
parts.explain: Translation: $mg\sin\theta - f = ma$. Rotation about the centre: $fR = cmR^2(a/R)$, so $f = cma$. Together $a = \dfrac{g\sin\theta}{1 + c}$ and $f = \dfrac{c}{1 + c}mg\sin\theta$: friction does no work, it only sets the spin

problems.prompt: A uniform rod ${{L}}$ m long swings from one end. What is its small-angle period, in s?

parts.label: r
parts.explain: $I\ddot\theta = -mgd\theta$ gives $\omega = \sqrt{mgd/I}$. With $I = mL^2/3$ and $d = L/2$: $T = 2\pi\sqrt{2L/3g}$, shorter than a simple pendulum of the same length

problems.prompt: A ring of radius ${{a}}$ m carries ${{Q}}$ nC spread evenly. What is the field on its axis ${{z}}$ m from the centre, in N/C? ($k = 8.99 \times 10^9$.)

parts.label: r
parts.explain: By symmetry the sideways parts cancel; each piece contributes $k\,dq\,z/(z^2 + a^2)^{3/2}$ along the axis, and they all have the same distance, so the integral is easy. Far away it becomes $kQ/z^2$

problems.prompt: A uniform field of ${{E}}$ N/C crosses a flat square of side ${{s}}$ m at ${{th}}^\circ$ to the square's normal. What is the flux, in N·m²/C?

parts.label: r2
parts.explain: $\Phi = \vec E \cdot \vec A = EA\cos\theta$. Through a closed surface with no charge inside, a uniform field gives zero net flux: what goes in comes out

problems.prompt: A solid sphere of radius ${{R}}$ m carries ${{Q}}$ nC spread uniformly through it. What is the field at ${{f*R}}$ m from the centre, in N/C?

parts.label: r2
parts.explain: Draw a spherical Gaussian surface through the point: $E\,4\pi r^2 = Q_{enc}/\varepsilon_0$. Outside, all of $Q$ is enclosed and $E = kQ/r^2$; inside, only $Q(r/R)^3$, so $E = kQr/R^3$, rising linearly from zero

problems.prompt: A sphere has charge density $\rho = c\,r^{ {{n}} }$. How much charge lies within radius ${{r}}$ (in units with $c = 1$)? The field there then follows from Gauss's law.

parts.label: r2
parts.explain: $Q_{enc} = \displaystyle\int_0^r \rho\,4\pi r'^2\,dr' = \dfrac{4\pi c\,r^{n + 3}}{n + 3}$, then $E = Q_{enc}/(4\pi\varepsilon_0r^2)$. Shells, not slices, because the density depends only on radius

problems.prompt: A field along $x$ is $E_x = {{c}}x$ V/m. What is $V(0) - V({{L}})$, in V?

parts.label: r
parts.explain: $V(b) - V(a) = -\displaystyle\int_a^b \vec E\cdot d\vec l$, so $V(0) - V(L) = \displaystyle\int_0^L cx\,dx = cL^2/2$. Potential falls in the direction the field points

problems.prompt: A ring of radius ${{a}}$ m carries ${{Q}}$ nC. What is the potential on its axis ${{z}}$ m from the centre, in V?

parts.label: r2
parts.explain: Potential is a scalar, so just add $k\,dq/r$; every bit of the ring is the same distance $\sqrt{z^2 + a^2}$ away. Differentiate along $z$ to recover the field

problems.prompt: The potential is $V(x) = {{a}}x^2 + {{b}}x$ V. What is $E_x$ at $x = {{X}}$ m, in V/m?

parts.label: r
parts.explain: $E_x = -dV/dx$: the field points down the potential slope, so here it is negative

problems.prompt: A ${{q}}$ nC point charge sits at the centre of a conducting shell carrying a net ${{Qs}}$ nC. What charge sits on the shell's outer surface, in nC?

parts.label: r
parts.explain: The field inside the metal is zero, so a Gaussian surface in it encloses no net charge: the inner surface carries $-q$. The rest of the shell's charge, $Q_s + q$, goes to the outside, and the field outside is as if it all sat at the centre

problems.prompt: Metal spheres of radii ${{R1}}$ cm and ${{R2}}$ cm, far apart, are joined by a thin wire and share ${{Q}}$ nC. How much charge ends up on the smaller one, in nC?

parts.label: r
parts.explain: Joined conductors reach the same potential: $kQ_1/R_1 = kQ_2/R_2$, so charge divides in proportion to radius. The smaller sphere then has the stronger surface field, which is why charge leaks from sharp points

expect.r: solve([Eq(x/R1, Symbol('q')/R2), Eq(x + Symbol('q'), Q)], [x, Symbol('q')], dict=True)[0][x]

problems.prompt: A {{shape}} capacitor has inner radius ${{a}}$ cm and outer radius ${{b}}$ cm. What is its capacitance, in pF{{kind == 1 ? " per metre" : ""}}? ($\varepsilon_0 = 8.854 \times 10^{-12}$ F/m.)

parts.label: r
parts.explain: Put $\pm Q$ on the conductors, find $E$ between them with Gauss, integrate for $\Delta V$, then $C = Q/\Delta V$. Sphere: $4\pi\varepsilon_0\dfrac{ab}{b - a}$. Cylinder: $\dfrac{2\pi\varepsilon_0L}{\ln(b/a)}$

problems.prompt: A region of ${{V}}$ cm³ holds a uniform field of ${{E}}$ MV/m. How much energy is stored in the field, in mJ? ($\varepsilon_0 = 8.854 \times 10^{-12}$.)

parts.label: r
parts.explain: The energy lives in the field itself: $u = \tfrac12\varepsilon_0E^2$ per unit volume. For a parallel-plate capacitor this reproduces $\tfrac12CV^2$ exactly

problems.prompt: A slab with dielectric constant ${{k}}$ fills a parallel-plate capacitor while the battery is {{conn == 1 ? "still connected" : "disconnected"}}. By what factor does {{q}} change?

parts.label: r
parts.explain: $C$ always rises by $\kappa$. With the battery connected $V$ is held fixed, so $Q = CV$ and $U = \tfrac12CV^2$ rise by $\kappa$. Disconnected, $Q$ is fixed, so $V = Q/C$, $E = V/d$ and $U = Q^2/2C$ all fall by $\kappa$

problems.prompt: The charge that has passed a point is $q(t) = {{a}}t^2 + {{b}}t$ C. What is the current at $t = {{t}}$ s, in A?

parts.label: r
parts.explain: $I = dq/dt$. In a wire $I = nqv_dA$: the drift speed of electrons is only about a tenth of a millimetre per second, even though the signal travels near light speed

problems.prompt: A proton moves with $\vec v = ({{vx}}, {{vy}}, 0) \times 10^6$ m/s through $\vec B = (0, 0, {{Bz}})$ T. What is the $y$ component of the force, in $10^{-13}$ N? ($e = 1.602 \times 10^{-19}$ C.)

parts.label: r
parts.explain: $\vec F = q\vec v \times \vec B$, and $(\vec v \times \vec B)_y = v_zB_x - v_xB_z = -v_xB_z$. A velocity component along $\vec B$ feels nothing

cases.arc: a semicircular arc (the straight leads point at the centre)
a quarter-circle arc (the straight leads point at the centre)

problems.prompt: A current of ${{I}}$ A flows round {{arc}} of radius ${{R}}$ cm. What is the field at the centre, in µT?

parts.label: r2
parts.explain: Biot–Savart: every element of the arc is the same distance $R$ away and perpendicular to the radius, so $B = \dfrac{\mu_0I}{4\pi R^2}\times(\text{arc length})$: $\mu_0I/2R$ for a full loop. Straight leads aimed at the centre add nothing

cases.where: inside a long straight wire of radius 2 cm, 1 cm from its axis
inside a long straight wire of radius 2 cm, at its surface
inside a toroid of 500 turns, 10 cm from its centre

problems.prompt: A current of ${{I}}$ A flows. Using Ampère's law, find $B$ {{where}}, in µT (current spread evenly over the wire's cross-section).

parts.label: r2
parts.explain: Take a circle where $B$ has one value: $B\,2\pi r = \mu_0I_{enc}$. Inside a wire $I_{enc} = I r^2/R^2$, so $B$ grows linearly with $r$; in a toroid $I_{enc} = NI$

problems.prompt: A rectangular loop ${{L}}$ cm long lies beside a long wire carrying ${{I}}$ A, its near and far sides ${{a}}$ cm and ${{b}}$ cm from the wire. What flux passes through it, in µWb?

parts.label: r
parts.explain: The field changes across the loop, so slice it into strips of width $dr$: $\Phi = \displaystyle\int_a^b \dfrac{\mu_0I}{2\pi r}L\,dr = \dfrac{\mu_0IL}{2\pi}\ln\dfrac ba$

problems.prompt: A ${{N}}$-turn coil of area ${{A}}$ cm² spins at ${{f}}$ rev/s in a ${{B}}$ T field. What is the peak emf, in V?

parts.label: r2
parts.explain: $\Phi = BA\cos\omega t$, so $\mathcal{E} = -N\,d\Phi/dt = NBA\omega\sin\omega t$, peaking at $NBA\omega$ with $\omega = 2\pi f$. Faster spinning or more turns means more voltage

problems.prompt: A rod of length ${{L}}$ m on rails in a ${{B}}$ T field is pulled by a constant ${{F}}$ N force; the circuit has resistance ${{R}}$ Ω. What terminal speed does it reach, in m/s?

parts.label: r2
parts.explain: The induced current $BLv/R$ feels a backward force $B^2L^2v/R$. It grows with speed until it equals $F$: $v_t = FR/B^2L^2$. The approach is exponential, like a falling object with drag

problems.prompt: A solenoid has ${{N}}$ turns, cross-section ${{A}}$ cm² and length ${{l}}$ cm. What is its self-inductance, in mH?

parts.label: r2
parts.explain: $B = \mu_0NI/l$ inside, each turn links $BA$, so $L = N\Phi/I = \mu_0N^2A/l$. The emf across it is $-L\,dI/dt$ and the energy it stores is $\tfrac12LI^2$

problems.prompt: A ${{C}}$ µF capacitor charged to ${{V}}$ V is connected across a ${{L}}$ mH inductor. What is the peak current, in mA?

parts.label: r2
