parts.explain: Energy sloshes between the fields: $\tfrac12CV_0^2 = \tfrac12LI_0^2$. The charge obeys $\ddot q = -q/LC$, an oscillator with $\omega = 1/\sqrt{LC}$

problems.prompt: An oil drop of mass ${{m}} \times 10^{-15}$ kg carries ${{n}}$ extra electron{{n > 1 ? "s" : ""}}. What upward field holds it still, in kV/m? ($e = 1.60 \times 10^{-19}$ C.)

parts.label: r
parts.explain: Balance the forces: $qE = mg$, so $E = mg/(ne)$. Millikan found that the charge always came in whole multiples of one value, $e$

problems.prompt: Two charges attract with ${{F}}$ N in vacuum. With the same separation in {{med}} (dielectric constant ${{k}}$), what is the force, in N?

parts.label: r
parts.explain: A medium screens the charges: $F = \dfrac{1}{4\pi\kappa\varepsilon_0}\dfrac{q_1q_2}{r^2}$, so the force falls by $\kappa$. Water's 80 is why salts dissolve in it

problems.prompt: A ${{q}}$ µC charge sits on a line between two other ${{q}}$ µC charges, ${{a}}$ m from one and ${{b}}$ m from the other. What is the magnitude of the net force on it, in N? ($k = 8.99 \times 10^9$.)

parts.label: r
parts.explain: Each neighbour pushes it away, in opposite directions, so subtract: $kq^2\left(\dfrac1{a^2} - \dfrac1{b^2}\right)$, pointing away from the nearer one. Forces add as vectors, never as plain magnitudes

problems.prompt: Two identical metal spheres carry ${{q1}}$ nC and ${{q2}}$ nC. They are touched together and separated. What charge does each carry, in nC?

parts.label: r
parts.explain: Charge is conserved and identical conductors share it equally: $\tfrac12(q_1 + q_2)$, signs included

problems.prompt: An electron sits in a uniform field of ${{E}}$ kN/C. What is the size of its acceleration, in $10^{14}$ m/s²? ($e/m_e = 1.759 \times 10^{11}$ C/kg.)

parts.label: r
parts.explain: $a = eE/m_e$, opposite to the field for a negative charge. Charges in a uniform field follow parabolas, just like projectiles

cases.q: the electric field inside a conductor in equilibrium
where the excess charge on a conductor sits
the direction of the field just outside a conductor
the field between two large, oppositely charged parallel plates

problems.prompt: What is true of {{q}}?

parts.label: a
choice: Uniform, pointing from the positive plate to the negative
parts.explain: Free charges move until they feel no force, so the field inside vanishes and any excess charge pushes itself to the surface. A field component along the surface would move charge, so the field leaves perpendicular to it

cases.q: Where do field lines start and end?
What does the spacing of field lines show?
Can two field lines cross?
A charge has twice as many lines leaving it as another. What does that mean?

parts.label: a
choice: They start on positive charges and end on negative ones
Closer lines mean a stronger field
No: the field has one direction at each point
parts.explain: A field line points the way a positive test charge would be pushed. Lines are a picture of direction and strength; a charge is never pushed along a line once it is moving, unless the line is straight

problems.prompt: What is the electric potential energy of charges of ${{q1}}$ µC and ${{q2}}$ µC that are ${{r}}$ m apart, in J? ($k = 8.99 \times 10^9$.)

parts.label: r2
parts.explain: $U = \dfrac{kq_1q_2}{r}$, with signs. Negative means the pair is bound: it takes work to pull them apart

problems.prompt: A capacitor has plates of area ${{A}}$ cm² separated by ${{d}}$ mm of air. What charge does it hold at ${{V}}$ V, in pC? ($\varepsilon_0 = 8.85 \times 10^{-12}$ F/m.)

parts.label: r
parts.explain: $C = \varepsilon_0A/d$, then $Q = CV$. Bigger plates or a narrower gap store more charge at the same voltage

problems.prompt: An electron starts from rest and is accelerated through ${{V}}$ V. How fast is it then moving, in $10^6$ m/s?

parts.label: r
parts.explain: The field does work $qV$, which all becomes kinetic energy: $eV = \tfrac12m_ev^2$. That energy is $V$ electronvolts, which is where the unit comes from

problems.prompt: A current of ${{I}}$ A flows in a wire. How many electrons pass a point each second, in units of $10^{18}$?

parts.label: r
parts.explain: $I = \Delta Q/\Delta t$, and each electron carries $e$: $N = I/e$. Conventional current points the way positive charge would flow, opposite to the electrons

problems.prompt: What is the resistance of ${{L}}$ m of copper wire ${{d}}$ mm across, in Ω? ($\rho = 1.68 \times 10^{-8}$ Ω·m.)

parts.label: r
parts.explain: $R = \rho L/A$ with $A = \pi d^2/4$. Doubling the length doubles $R$; doubling the diameter divides it by four

problems.prompt: What current flows through a ${{R}}$ Ω resistor with ${{V}}$ V across it, in A?

parts.label: r2
parts.explain: $I = V/R$. A component whose current is proportional to the voltage across it is ohmic; a bulb filament is not, because its resistance rises as it heats

problems.prompt: A battery with emf ${{em}}$ V and internal resistance ${{r}}$ Ω drives a ${{R}}$ Ω load. What voltage appears across its terminals, in V?

parts.label: r2
parts.explain: The current is $\varepsilon/(R + r)$, and $Ir$ is lost inside the battery: $V = \varepsilon - Ir$. A heavy load drags the terminal voltage down

problems.prompt: A ${{em}}$ V battery drives ${{R1}}$ Ω and ${{R2}}$ Ω resistors in series. What is the voltage across the ${{R2}}$ Ω resistor, in V?

parts.label: r
parts.explain: Round the loop the rises equal the drops: $\varepsilon = IR_1 + IR_2$. The voltage divides in proportion to the resistances

problems.prompt: Currents of ${{I1}}$ A and ${{I2}}$ A flow into a junction and ${{I3}}$ A flows out along one wire. How much flows out along the other wire, in A?

parts.label: r
parts.explain: Charge does not pile up at a junction: current in equals current out. A negative answer would mean that wire carries current in

problems.prompt: Batteries of ${{e1}}$ V (in series with ${{R1}}$ Ω) and ${{e2}}$ V (in series with ${{R2}}$ Ω) are connected in parallel, positive terminals together, across a ${{R3}}$ Ω load. What current flows through the load, in A?

parts.label: r
parts.explain: Call the load voltage $V$. Each branch delivers $(\varepsilon_i - V)/R_i$, and by the junction rule they add to $V/R_3$. One unknown, one equation

expect.r: solve([Eq(Symbol('a') + Symbol('b'), x), Eq(e1 - Symbol('a')*R1, x*R3), Eq(e2 - Symbol('b')*R2, x*R3)], [Symbol('a'), Symbol('b'), x], dict=True)[0][x]

problems.prompt: A ${{em}}$ V battery, a switch and a ${{R1}}$ Ω resistor are in series with a ${{R2}}$ Ω resistor that has an uncharged capacitor across it. What current does the battery supply {{late == 0 ? "just after the switch closes" : "a long time later"}}, in A?

parts.label: r
parts.explain: An uncharged capacitor acts as a wire at first, shorting out ${{R2}}$ Ω; a fully charged one carries no current, as if it were cut out. Between the two the change is exponential, with time constant set by the resistance the capacitor sees

expect.r: Rational(em, R1) if late == 0 else Rational(em, R1 + R2)

cases.q: Outside a bar magnet, which way do field lines run?
The Earth's geographic north pole is which kind of magnetic pole?
Which way does the north end of a compass needle point?
A bar magnet is cut in half. What do you get?

parts.label: a
choice: From the north pole round to the south pole
A magnetic south pole: it attracts compass north ends
Two smaller magnets, each with a north and a south pole
parts.explain: Magnetic poles always come in pairs: there is no magnetic charge, so field lines close on themselves, running inside the magnet from south to north

problems.prompt: Crossed fields of ${{E}}$ kV/m and ${{B}}$ T let one speed of charged particle pass straight through. What speed, in km/s?

parts.label: r2
parts.explain: The electric and magnetic forces cancel when $qE = qvB$, so $v = E/B$, independent of charge and mass

problems.prompt: Two long parallel wires ${{d}}$ cm apart carry ${{I1}}$ A and ${{I2}}$ A in the same direction. What force acts on each metre of wire, in µN, and is it attractive?

parts.label: r2
parts.explain: One wire's field, $\mu_0I_1/2\pi d$, acts on the other's current: $F/L = \dfrac{\mu_0I_1I_2}{2\pi d}$. Same direction attract, opposite directions repel; this once defined the ampere

problems.prompt: A ${{B}}$ T field passes through a ${{A}}$ cm² loop at ${{th}}^\circ$ to the loop's normal. What is the flux, in mWb?

parts.label: r2
parts.explain: $\Phi = BA\cos\theta$, with $\theta$ measured from the normal. A field lying in the plane of the loop gives no flux at all

problems.prompt: A ${{L}}$ m rod slides at ${{v}}$ m/s along rails through a ${{B}}$ T field, closing a circuit of resistance ${{R}}$ Ω. What current flows, in A?

parts.label: r2
parts.explain: The rod sweeps out area, so the flux changes at $BLv$: that is the emf, and $I = BLv/R$. The current feels a force $BIL$ opposing the motion, so something must keep pushing

problems.prompt: A person stands ${{d}}$ m in front of a plane mirror. How far is she from her image, in m?

parts.label: r
parts.explain: The image is as far behind the mirror as the object is in front, upright and the same size: ${{d}} + {{d}}$. Each ray reflects at the angle it came in, measured from the normal

cases.q: a concave mirror, object beyond twice the focal length
a concave mirror, object between one and two focal lengths
a concave mirror, object inside the focal length
a convex mirror, object anywhere in front

problems.prompt: Describe the image formed by {{q}}.

parts.label: a
parts.explain: Trace two rays: one parallel to the axis that reflects through the focus, one through the focus that reflects parallel. Where they meet is the image. Inside the focal length they diverge, so the image is behind the mirror: a make-up mirror. A convex mirror always gives a small upright image: a shop mirror

choices.a: (lambda m: 0 if -1 < m < 0 else (1 if m < -1 else (2 if m > 1 else 3)))(Rational(f, f - o))

problems.prompt: An object is ${{o}}$ cm in front of a concave mirror of focal length ${{f}}$ cm. Where is the image, in cm (positive in front of the mirror)?

parts.label: r
parts.explain: $\dfrac1{d_o} + \dfrac1{d_i} = \dfrac1f$. A negative $d_i$ is a virtual image behind the mirror. Magnification $m = -d_i/d_o$

problems.prompt: Light in air strikes {{med}} ($n = {{n}}$) at ${{th}}^\circ$ from the normal. At what angle from the normal does it travel inside, in degrees?

parts.label: r
parts.explain: $n_1\sin\theta_1 = n_2\sin\theta_2$. Entering a slower medium (larger $n = c/v$) bends the ray toward the normal

problems.prompt: What is the critical angle for light going from {{med}} ($n = {{n}}$) into air, in degrees?

parts.label: r
parts.explain: $\sin\theta_c = n_2/n_1$: past this angle no light escapes and all of it reflects. It only happens going from a higher to a lower index. Diamond's small critical angle traps light, which is why it sparkles

cases.q: a converging lens, object beyond twice the focal length (a camera)
a converging lens, object between one and two focal lengths (a projector)
a converging lens, object inside the focal length (a magnifier)
a diverging lens, object anywhere

problems.prompt: Describe the image formed by {{q}}.

parts.label: a
parts.explain: Three rays: parallel in, out through the far focus; through the centre, undeflected; through the near focus, out parallel. Real images form on the far side and can be projected; virtual ones are seen by looking through the lens

choices.a: (lambda m: 0 if -1 < m < 0 else (1 if m < -1 else (2 if m > 1 else 3)))(Rational(f, f - o))

problems.prompt: An object is ${{o}}$ cm from a converging lens of focal length ${{f}}$ cm. What is the magnification?

parts.label: r
parts.explain: Find $d_i$ from $\dfrac1{d_o} + \dfrac1{d_i} = \dfrac1f$, then $m = -d_i/d_o$. Negative means inverted; a size above 1 means enlarged

cases.q: sound in air
light
a wave on a guitar string
a seismic P wave
a seismic S wave
a compression pulse along a Slinky

problems.prompt: Is {{q}} transverse or longitudinal?

parts.label: a
choice: Transverse: the medium moves across the direction of travel
Longitudinal: the medium moves along the direction of travel
parts.explain: A wave carries energy and momentum, not matter: each bit of the medium only oscillates about where it was. Only transverse waves can be polarised, and fluids carry only longitudinal waves, which is how S waves revealed the liquid outer core

problems.prompt: Sound travels at 343 m/s. What is the wavelength of a ${{f}}$ Hz tone, in m?

parts.label: r
parts.explain: $v = f\lambda$. The medium sets the speed; the source sets the frequency; the wavelength follows. Frequency does not change when a wave crosses into a new medium

problems.prompt: A string under ${{T}}$ N of tension has a mass of ${{mu}}$ g per metre. How fast do waves travel on it, in m/s?

parts.label: r
parts.explain: $v = \sqrt{T/\mu}$: tighter is faster, heavier is slower. Tuning a guitar string up raises the tension and so the pitch

cases.q: a pulse reaches a fixed end
a pulse reaches a free end
a pulse goes from a light string into a heavy one
a pulse goes from a heavy string into a light one

problems.prompt: What happens when {{q}}?

parts.label: a
choice: Part reflects inverted, part goes on upright
Part reflects upright, part goes on upright
parts.explain: Going into a slower, heavier medium acts like a fixed end: inverted reflection. Going into a faster, lighter one acts like a free end. The transmitted pulse is never inverted. Light reflecting off a higher-index surface flips the same way

problems.prompt: Unpolarised light passes through two polarisers whose axes are ${{th}}^\circ$ apart. What fraction of the original intensity gets through?

parts.label: r
parts.explain: The first polariser passes half of unpolarised light. Each later one passes $\cos^2\theta$ of what reaches it (Malus's law). Crossed polarisers pass nothing

problems.prompt: What is the frequency of {{band}}, wavelength ${{lam}}$ m, in Hz? Give the power of ten: $\log_{10} f$. ($c = 3.00 \times 10^8$ m/s.)

parts.label: r
parts.explain: $f = c/\lambda$. Radio (metres, ~$10^8$ Hz), microwaves (cm), infrared, visible (400–700 nm, ~$10^{14.7}$ Hz), ultraviolet, X-rays (~0.1 nm), gamma rays: all the same thing at different wavelengths

problems.prompt: A ${{f}}$ Hz siren moves {{dir == 1 ? "toward" : "away from"}} you at ${{vs}}$ m/s. What frequency do you hear, in Hz? (Sound at 343 m/s.)

parts.label: r
parts.explain: $f' = f\dfrac{v}{v \mp v_s}$: an approaching source bunches its wavefronts, raising the pitch; a receding one spreads them out

problems.prompt: Two speakers emit the same ${{lam}}$ m wavelength in phase. A point is ${{k*lam/2}}$ m farther from one speaker than from the other. What happens there?

parts.label: a
parts.explain: Divide the path difference by the wavelength. A whole number of wavelengths puts crests on crests; an odd number of half wavelengths puts crests on troughs

cases.kind: a string fixed at both ends
a pipe open at both ends
a pipe closed at one end

problems.prompt: What is the fundamental frequency of {{kind}}, ${{L}}$ m long, with wave speed ${{v}}$ m/s, in Hz?

parts.label: r
parts.explain: Fit the standing wave: same type of end at both ends gives half a wavelength, $f_n = nv/2L$ for every $n$. A closed pipe has a node at one end and an antinode at the other, a quarter wavelength, $f_n = nv/4L$ for odd $n$ only

problems.prompt: Two tones of ${{f1}}$ Hz and ${{f1 + d}}$ Hz sound together. How many beats per second do you hear?

parts.label: r
parts.explain: The loudness swells and fades at the difference of the frequencies. Tuners listen for the beats to slow and vanish

problems.prompt: Light of wavelength ${{lam}}$ nm passes through a slit ${{a}}$ µm wide. At what angle is the first dark fringe, in degrees?

parts.label: r
parts.explain: $a\sin\theta = \lambda$ for the first minimum. A narrower opening spreads light more: diffraction matters when the opening is not much bigger than the wavelength

problems.prompt: Light of ${{lam}}$ nm falls on two slits ${{d}}$ mm apart. How far apart are the bright fringes on a screen ${{L}}$ m away, in mm?

parts.label: r
parts.explain: Bright where $d\sin\theta = m\lambda$; for small angles the fringes are evenly spaced by $\lambda L/d$. A grating has many slits and the same rule, but much sharper bright lines

problems.prompt: A soap film ($n = 1.33$) in air looks bright in reflected light of ${{lam}}$ nm. What is its smallest possible thickness, in nm?

parts.label: r
parts.explain: The front reflection flips phase (air to soap) and the back one does not, so the film is bright when $2nt = \tfrac12\lambda$, the thinnest at $t = \lambda/4n$. Count the phase flips before choosing the condition

problems.prompt: What is the energy of a ${{lam}}$ nm photon, in eV?

parts.label: r
parts.explain: $E = hc/\lambda$, and $hc = 1240$ eV·nm: carry that number. Visible light is about 1.8 to 3.1 eV, the size of a chemical bond

problems.prompt: What is the de Broglie wavelength of an electron accelerated from rest through ${{V}}$ V, in nm?

parts.label: r
parts.explain: $\lambda = h/p$ with $p = \sqrt{2m_eeV}$: about $1.23/\sqrt V$ nm. At 150 V it is 0.1 nm, the spacing of atoms in a crystal, which is how electron diffraction was found

problems.prompt: In the Bohr model, what is the energy of hydrogen's $n = {{n}}$ level, in eV?

parts.label: r
parts.explain: $E_n = -13.6\text{ eV}/n^2$. Negative means bound; 13.6 eV ionises the atom from the ground state

problems.prompt: Hydrogen drops from $n = {{hi}}$ to $n = {{lo}}$. What wavelength does it emit, in nm?

parts.label: r
parts.explain: The photon carries the energy difference, $13.6\left(\dfrac1{n_l^2} - \dfrac1{n_h^2}\right)$ eV, then $\lambda = 1240/E$. Drops to $n = 2$ are the visible Balmer lines: 3→2 is the red 656 nm line

problems.prompt: Light of ${{lam}}$ nm falls on {{met}}, work function ${{phi}}$ eV. What is the maximum kinetic energy of the ejected electrons, in eV?

parts.label: r
parts.explain: One photon frees one electron: $K_{max} = hf - \phi$. The stopping potential is the same number in volts. Below the threshold frequency nothing is ejected, however bright the light

problems.prompt: An X-ray photon scatters off a free electron through ${{th}}^\circ$. By how much does its wavelength increase, in pm?

parts.label: r
parts.explain: $\Delta\lambda = \dfrac{h}{m_ec}(1 - \cos\theta)$ with $h/m_ec = 2.43$ pm. It treats light as a particle with momentum, and it is only noticeable for short wavelengths

cases.q: speed
velocity
mass
displacement
acceleration
kinetic energy
force
distance travelled
momentum
temperature

problems.prompt: Is {{q}} a scalar or a vector?

parts.label: a
choice: Vector: a size and a direction
parts.explain: Ask whether "which way?" has an answer. Speed and distance have none; velocity and displacement do. Energy is a scalar even though the motion that carries it has a direction

problems.prompt: A cart moves ${{a}}$ m east, then ${{b}}$ m west. Taking east as positive, what is its displacement, in m?

parts.label: r
parts.explain: Give each step a sign and add: $+{{a}} + (-{{b}}) = {{a - b}}$ m. A negative answer means the cart ended west of where it started

problems.prompt: A runner goes ${{a}}$ m forward and then ${{b}}$ m back. What distance did she travel, in m? (Her displacement is ${{a - b}}$ m.)

parts.label: r
parts.explain: Distance adds every step as positive: ${{a}} + {{b}} = {{a + b}}$ m. Displacement only cares where she ended up. Average speed uses distance; average velocity uses displacement

problems.prompt: A car goes from ${{v1}}$ m/s to ${{v2}}$ m/s in ${{t}}$ s. What is its average acceleration, in m/s²?

parts.label: r
parts.explain: $\bar a = \dfrac{\Delta v}{\Delta t} = \dfrac{ {{v2}} - {{v1}} }{ {{t}} }$. Acceleration is how fast the velocity changes, not how fast the car is going

problems.prompt: A velocity–time graph is a straight line from ${{v0}}$ m/s at $t = 0$ to ${{v1}}$ m/s at $t = {{t}}$ s. How far does the object travel, in m?

parts.label: r
parts.explain: Displacement is the area under a v–t graph: here a trapezoid, the average velocity times the time. The slope of the same line, ${{(v1 - v0)/t}}$ m/s², is the acceleration

problems.prompt: An object starts at ${{v0}}$ m/s and accelerates at ${{a}}$ m/s² over ${{d}}$ m. How fast is it then going, in m/s?

parts.label: r
parts.explain: No time is given or asked, so use $v^2 = v_0^2 + 2a\Delta x$. Choose the kinematic equation that leaves out the quantity you neither know nor want

problems.prompt: A stone is dropped from rest ${{h}}$ m above the ground. How long does it take to land, in s? (No air resistance.)

parts.label: r
parts.explain: $h = \tfrac12gt^2$, so $t = \sqrt{2h/g}$. Mass does not appear: everything falls with the same acceleration

cases.q: moves at constant velocity away from the origin
speeds up at a steady rate from rest
slows down steadily and stops
stands still
is thrown straight up and falls back (upward positive)

problems.prompt: An object {{q}}. What does its velocity–time graph look like?

parts.label: a
choice: A straight line rising from zero
A straight line falling to zero
A straight line falling through zero
parts.explain: On a v–t graph the height is the velocity and the slope is the acceleration. Steady speeding up or slowing down is a straight sloped line; a thrown ball has the same downward slope, g, all the way, crossing zero at the top

problems.prompt: A train moves at ${{u}}$ m/s. A passenger walks {{dir == 1 ? "toward the front" : "toward the back"}} at ${{w}}$ m/s relative to the train. What is her speed relative to the ground, in m/s?

parts.label: r
parts.explain: Velocities in the same line add with signs: $v_{PG} = v_{PT} + v_{TG}$. Walking backward subtracts

problems.prompt: A velocity of ${{v}}$ m/s points ${{th}}^\circ$ above the horizontal. What is its {{comp == 0 ? "horizontal" : "vertical"}} component, in m/s?

parts.label: r
parts.explain: The side next to the angle gets cosine, the side opposite gets sine. A 37°–53°–90° triangle is very nearly 3–4–5

problems.prompt: A ball rolls off a table ${{h}}$ m high at ${{v}}$ m/s. How far from the table does it land, in m?

parts.label: r
parts.explain: The fall time is set by the vertical motion alone, $t = \sqrt{2h/g}$; the horizontal speed does not change, so $x = vt$. A ball dropped at the same moment lands at the same time

problems.prompt: A ball is launched at ${{v}}$ m/s, ${{th}}^\circ$ above level ground. How far away does it land, in m?

parts.label: r
parts.explain: $R = \dfrac{v^2\sin 2\theta}{g}$: largest at 45°, and equal for angles that add to 90° (30° and 60°). Time of flight is $2v\sin\theta/g$ and peak height $v^2\sin^2\theta/2g$

problems.prompt: A boat heads straight across a river ${{w}}$ m wide at ${{b}}$ m/s relative to the water. The current flows at ${{c}}$ m/s. How far downstream does it land, in m?

parts.label: r
parts.explain: The crossing time depends only on the across-stream speed: $t = w/b$. In that time the current carries the boat $c\,t$ downstream. Perpendicular velocities do not affect each other

cases.q: the tension in the string joining the two blocks
the weight of the front block
a hand pushing the back block
the normal force from the floor on the front block
the contact force of one block on the other

problems.prompt: The system is two blocks joined by a string on a floor. Is {{q}} internal or external to the system?

parts.label: a
choice: Internal: both objects in the pair are inside the system
External: one object is outside the system
parts.explain: A force is internal when both the object exerting it and the object feeling it are in the system; such forces cancel in pairs and cannot change the motion of the centre of mass. Choosing the system wisely removes forces you do not know

problems.prompt: A ${{m1}}$ kg mass sits at $x = 0$ and a ${{m2}}$ kg mass at $x = {{d}}$ m. Where is their centre of mass, in m?

parts.label: r
parts.explain: $x_{cm} = \dfrac{\sum m_ix_i}{\sum m_i}$. It sits closer to the heavier mass; equal masses put it at the midpoint

cases.q: the upward force on a book resting on a table
the downward force on a book resting on a table
the upward force on a lamp hanging from a cord
the backward force on a box sliding across a floor
the force that keeps the Moon in orbit

problems.prompt: Which object exerts {{q}}?

parts.label: a
choice: The surface it touches (a contact force)
parts.explain: Every force is one object pushing or pulling another. Name the other object. If you cannot name it, the force is not real: "the force of motion" has no agent

cases.q: a ball in flight, ignoring air
a book resting on a table
a lamp hanging from one cord
a block sliding down a rough incline
a box pulled by a rope across a rough floor
a block resting on a frictionless incline, held by a string parallel to the slope

problems.prompt: How many forces belong on the free-body diagram of {{q}}?

parts.label: r
parts.explain: One arrow for gravity, then one for each thing touching the object: a surface gives a normal force and, if rough and slipping or about to, a friction force; a rope gives tension. Velocity is never a force

cases.q: The Earth pulls down on an apple. What is the third-law partner?
A table pushes up on a book. What is the third-law partner?
A book's weight and the table's normal force on it are equal and opposite. Are they a third-law pair?
A truck hits a fly. Which force is larger?

parts.label: a
choice: The apple pulls up on the Earth
The book pushes down on the table
No: both act on the book, so they are a balanced pair
Neither: the two forces are equal in size
parts.explain: A third-law pair is the same interaction seen from both ends: the forces act on different objects, are of the same type, and are always equal and opposite. Forces that balance on one object are a different thing

problems.prompt: A ${{m}}$ kg sign hangs from two cords, each at ${{th}}^\circ$ to the vertical. What is the tension in each cord, in N?

parts.label: r
parts.explain: Vertical components hold the weight: $2T\cos\theta = mg$. The flatter the cords, the larger the tension, without limit

problems.prompt: A ${{m}}$ kg box is pushed with ${{F}}$ N while friction pulls back with ${{f}}$ N. What is its acceleration, in m/s²?

parts.label: r
parts.explain: Use the net force: $a = \dfrac{F - f}{m}$. Draw the diagram first so no force is missed or counted twice

problems.prompt: Masses of ${{m1}}$ kg and ${{m2}}$ kg hang over a light frictionless pulley. What is their acceleration, in m/s²?

parts.label: r
parts.explain: Treat the two masses as one system: the net force is the difference of the weights and the mass moved is the total. The tension, $\dfrac{2m_1m_2g}{m_1 + m_2}$, lies between the two weights

expect.r: solve([Eq(m1*Rational(98, 10) - Symbol('T'), m1*x), Eq(Symbol('T') - m2*Rational(98, 10), m2*x)], [x, Symbol('T')], dict=True)[0][x]

problems.prompt: A block slides down a frictionless incline at ${{th}}^\circ$. What is its acceleration, in m/s²?

parts.label: r
parts.explain: Tilt the axes along the slope: the component of gravity down the slope is $mg\sin\theta$, and the normal force cancels $mg\cos\theta$. Check the limits: flat gives zero, vertical gives $g$

problems.prompt: What is the gravitational force between ${{m1}}$ kg and ${{m2}}$ kg ${{r}}$ m apart, in µN? ($G = 6.674 \times 10^{-11}$ N·m²/kg².)

parts.label: r2
parts.explain: $F = \dfrac{Gm_1m_2}{r^2}$. Between people it is a few tenths of a micronewton, which is why gravity only matters when one of the masses is a planet

problems.prompt: At ${{k}}$ times the Earth's radius from its centre, what is the gravitational field strength, in m/s²? (9.8 m/s² at the surface.)

parts.label: r
parts.explain: $g = GM/r^2$, so it falls as the square of the distance from the centre, not from the surface. At the height of the International Space Station it is still about 90% of its surface value

problems.prompt: A puck slides at ${{v}}$ m/s on a surface with $\mu_k = {{mu}}$. How far does it slide before stopping, in m?

parts.label: r
parts.explain: Friction $\mu_kmg$ gives a deceleration $\mu_kg$, independent of mass. Then $v^2 = 2ad$ gives the stopping distance; doubling the speed quadruples it

problems.prompt: A block rests on an incline at ${{th}}^\circ$ with $\mu_s = {{mu}}$. Does it stay put?

parts.label: a
choice: It stays: static friction can supply what is needed
It slides: the slope is steeper than friction can hold
parts.explain: The block holds while $\tan\theta \le \mu_s$; here $\tan {{th}}^\circ = {{tan(th*pi/180)|3}}$. Static friction is only as large as it needs to be, up to $\mu_sN$

problems.prompt: A spring with $k = {{k}}$ N/m is stretched ${{ext}}$ cm. What force does it exert, in N?

parts.label: r
parts.explain: $F = kx$ with $x$ in metres. On a force–extension graph $k$ is the slope; the spring pulls back toward its natural length

problems.prompt: A car takes a curve of radius ${{r}}$ m at ${{v}}$ m/s. What is its centripetal acceleration, in m/s²?

parts.label: r2
parts.explain: $a_c = v^2/r$, toward the centre. Something real must supply it: on a flat road, static friction between the tyres and the road

problems.prompt: What is the fastest a car can take a flat curve of radius ${{r}}$ m if $\mu_s = {{mu}}$, in m/s?

parts.label: r2
parts.explain: Static friction supplies the centripetal force: $\mu_smg = mv^2/r$, so $v = \sqrt{\mu_sgr}$, independent of mass. Wet roads lower $\mu_s$ and so the safe speed

problems.prompt: Find the period of a circular orbit of radius ${{r}}$ m around the Earth (as for {{orbit}}), in hours. ($GM_E = 3.986 \times 10^{14}$ m³/s².)

parts.label: r2
parts.explain: Gravity supplies the centripetal force: $GMm/r^2 = mv^2/r$, so $v = \sqrt{GM/r}$ and $T = 2\pi r/v = 2\pi\sqrt{r^3/GM}$. That is Kepler's third law, $T^2 \propto r^3$

problems.prompt: An object's speed is multiplied by ${{fv}}$ and its mass by ${{fm}}$. By what factor does its kinetic energy change?

parts.label: r
parts.explain: $K = \tfrac12mv^2$: linear in mass, quadratic in speed. A car at twice the speed needs four times the braking distance

problems.prompt: A ${{F}}$ N force acts at ${{th}}^\circ$ to an object's ${{d}}$ m displacement. How much work does it do, in J?

parts.label: r
parts.explain: $W = Fd\cos\theta$: only the component along the motion does work. Past 90° the work is negative; at exactly 90°, as for the normal force on a level road, it is zero

problems.prompt: How much work does it take to stretch a spring with $k = {{k}}$ N/m by ${{ext}}$ cm from its natural length, in J?

parts.label: r
parts.explain: The force grows from 0 to $kx$, so the work is the triangular area under the F–x graph: $\tfrac12kx^2$. Not $kx \times x$

problems.prompt: A net force of ${{F}}$ N pushes a ${{m}}$ kg cart from rest through ${{d}}$ m. How fast is it then moving, in m/s?

parts.label: r
parts.explain: Net work equals the change in kinetic energy: $Fd = \tfrac12mv^2$. No acceleration or time needed

problems.prompt: How much gravitational potential energy does a ${{m}}$ kg object gain when raised ${{h}}$ m, in J?

parts.label: r
parts.explain: $\Delta U = mg\Delta h$. Only the change in height matters, not the path, and the energy belongs to the object–Earth system

problems.prompt: A ${{m}}$ kg satellite is ${{k}}$ Earth radii from the Earth's centre. What is the gravitational potential energy of the satellite–Earth system, in GJ? ($GM_E = 3.986 \times 10^{14}$ m³/s², $R_E = 6.371 \times 10^6$ m.)

parts.label: r
parts.explain: $U = -\dfrac{GMm}{r}$, zero far away and negative everywhere else: the satellite is bound. $mgh$ is only the small-change version of this near the surface

problems.prompt: A sled starts from rest ${{h}}$ m above the bottom of a frictionless hill. How fast is it going at the bottom, in m/s?

parts.label: r
parts.explain: $mgh = \tfrac12mv^2$, so $v = \sqrt{2gh}$, whatever the shape of the hill and whatever the mass

problems.prompt: A ${{m}}$ kg box slides from rest down a ramp ${{h}}$ m high and reaches the bottom at ${{v}}$ m/s. How much energy went to friction, in J?

parts.label: r
parts.explain: Energy in = energy out: $mgh = \tfrac12mv^2 + E_{friction}$. The missing mechanical energy became thermal energy in the box and ramp

problems.prompt: What is the escape speed from the surface of {{body}}, in km/s? ($GM = {{GM}}$ m³/s², $R = {{R}}$ m.)

parts.label: r
parts.explain: Kinetic energy must cover the whole well: $\tfrac12mv^2 = GMm/R$. It is $\sqrt2$ times the speed of a grazing circular orbit, and does not depend on the direction of launch

problems.prompt: A ${{m}}$ kg person climbs ${{h}}$ m of stairs in ${{t}}$ s. What average power does that take, in W?

parts.label: r
parts.explain: Power is work per time: $P = mgh/t$. A brisk stair climb is several hundred watts; instantaneous power is $P = Fv$

problems.prompt: A ${{m1}}$ kg cart moves right at ${{v1}}$ m/s and a ${{m2}}$ kg cart moves left at ${{v2}}$ m/s. What is the velocity of their centre of mass, in m/s (right positive)?

parts.label: r
parts.explain: Total momentum divided by total mass: $v_{cm} = \dfrac{p_{total}}{M}$. Whatever the carts do to each other, this does not change unless an outside force acts

problems.prompt: A bat exerts an average force of ${{F}}$ N for ${{t}}$ s on a ${{m}}$ kg ball. By how much does the ball's velocity change, in m/s?

parts.label: r
parts.explain: Impulse $F\Delta t$ equals the change in momentum $m\Delta v$. Airbags and padding work by stretching $\Delta t$ to lower $F$

problems.prompt: A ${{M}}$ kg rifle fires a ${{m}}$ kg bullet at ${{v}}$ m/s. What is the rifle's recoil speed, in m/s?

parts.label: r
parts.explain: The system starts at rest, so the total momentum stays zero: $mv = MV$. Equal and opposite momenta, very unequal kinetic energies

problems.prompt: A ${{m1}}$ kg car heading east at ${{v1}}$ m/s collides with a ${{m2}}$ kg car heading north at ${{v2}}$ m/s, and they stick. How fast is the wreck moving, in m/s?

parts.label: r
parts.explain: Conserve momentum separately east and north, then combine: $v = \dfrac{\sqrt{(m_1v_1)^2 + (m_2v_2)^2}}{m_1 + m_2}$

expect.r: sqrt(solve(Eq((m1 + m2)*x, m1*v1), x)[0]**2 + solve(Eq((m1 + m2)*x, m2*v2), x)[0]**2)

problems.prompt: A ${{m}}$ kg cart at ${{u}}$ m/s hits an identical cart at rest. Afterwards {{kind == 0 ? "the first cart stops and the second moves at the first one's speed" : (kind == 1 ? "they move off together at half the speed" : "the first moves at a quarter and the second at three quarters of the original speed")}}. What kind of collision is it?

parts.label: a
choice: Inelastic: some kinetic energy is lost
Perfectly inelastic: they stick, losing the most
parts.explain: Momentum is conserved in all three. Compare $\sum\tfrac12mv^2$ before and after: equal means elastic. Objects moving off together lose the most kinetic energy that momentum conservation allows

choices.a: 0 if kind == 0 else (2 if kind == 1 else 1)

problems.prompt: A ${{m1}}$ kg cart hits a ${{m2}}$ kg cart at rest and they stick. What fraction of the kinetic energy is lost?

parts.label: r
parts.explain: The common speed is $\dfrac{m_1}{m_1 + m_2}v$, so the kinetic energy kept is $\dfrac{m_1}{m_1 + m_2}$ of the original. Hitting a heavy target at rest loses almost everything

problems.prompt: A ${{m1}}$ kg ball at ${{v}}$ m/s collides elastically head-on with a ${{m2}}$ kg ball at rest. How fast does the second ball move afterwards, in m/s?

parts.label: r
parts.explain: $v_2' = \dfrac{2m_1}{m_1 + m_2}v$. Equal masses swap velocities; a light ball bouncing off a heavy one reverses; a heavy ball hitting a light one sends it off at up to twice its own speed

expect.r: [s for s in solve([Eq(m1*v, m1*Symbol('u') + m2*x), Eq(m1*v**2, m1*Symbol('u')**2 + m2*x**2)], [Symbol('u'), x], dict=True) if s[x] != 0][0][x]

problems.prompt: A ${{m}}$ kg bullet at ${{v}}$ m/s embeds in a ${{M}}$ kg block hanging on a string. How high does the block swing, in cm?

parts.label: r
parts.explain: Two stages. The collision conserves momentum (not energy): $V = \dfrac{mv}{m + M}$. The swing conserves energy (not momentum): $h = V^2/2g$

problems.prompt: A wheel starts from rest with angular acceleration ${{al}}$ rad/s². Through what angle does it turn in ${{t}}$ s, in rad?

parts.label: r
parts.explain: The rotational equations are the linear ones with $x \to \theta$, $v \to \omega$, $a \to \alpha$: $\theta = \tfrac12\alpha t^2$. Divide by $2\pi$ for revolutions

problems.prompt: A wheel of radius ${{r}}$ m spins at ${{N}}$ revolutions per minute. How fast does a point on the rim move, in m/s?

parts.label: r2
parts.explain: Convert to rad/s first, $\omega = 2\pi N/60$, then $v = \omega r$. Every point has the same $\omega$; the rim moves fastest

problems.prompt: A ${{F}}$ N force is applied ${{r}}$ m from a hinge at ${{th}}^\circ$ to the door. What torque does it produce, in N·m?

parts.label: r2
parts.explain: $\tau = rF\sin\theta$: only the component perpendicular to the lever arm turns. Pushing at the hinge or straight toward it does nothing

problems.prompt: Masses of ${{m1}}$ kg at ${{r1}}$ m and ${{m2}}$ kg at ${{r2}}$ m from an axis are joined by a light rod. What is the rotational inertia, in kg·m²?

parts.label: r
parts.explain: $I = \sum mr^2$: mass far from the axis counts for much more than mass near it

cases.shape: a uniform rod about one end
a uniform disk about a point on its rim
a solid sphere about a tangent line

problems.prompt: Using the parallel-axis theorem, find the rotational inertia of {{shape}}, with mass ${{M}}$ kg and {{h == 0.5 ? "length" : "radius"}} ${{L}}$ m, in kg·m².

parts.label: r
parts.explain: $I = I_{cm} + Md^2$: start from the inertia about the centre of mass and add the mass times the square of the shift. The centre-of-mass axis always gives the smallest inertia

problems.prompt: A ${{L}}$ m plank of mass ${{M}}$ kg rests on supports at both ends. A ${{m}}$ kg person stands ${{d}}$ m from the left end. What force does the right support exert, in N?

parts.label: r
parts.explain: Take torques about the left support so its unknown force drops out: $F_RL = Mg\tfrac L2 + mgd$. Then forces up equal forces down gives the left support

problems.prompt: A net torque of ${{tau}}$ N·m acts on a wheel with rotational inertia ${{I}}$ kg·m². What is its angular acceleration, in rad/s²?

parts.label: r
parts.explain: $\tau = I\alpha$, the rotational form of $F = ma$, with rotational inertia in the place of mass

problems.prompt: A ${{m}}$ kg mass hangs from a rope wrapped around a uniform disk pulley of mass ${{M}}$ kg that is free to turn. What is the acceleration of the mass, in m/s²?

parts.label: r
parts.explain: Mass: $mg - T = ma$. Pulley: $TR = \tfrac12MR^2\alpha$ with $a = \alpha R$, so $T = \tfrac12Ma$. Together $a = \dfrac{mg}{m + M/2}$: the pulley acts like extra mass of half its own

expect.r: solve([Eq(m*Rational(98, 10) - Symbol('T'), m*x), Eq(Symbol('T'), Rational(M, 2)*x)], [x, Symbol('T')], dict=True)[0][x]

problems.prompt: A uniform disk of mass ${{M}}$ kg and radius ${{R}}$ m spins at ${{w}}$ rad/s. What is its rotational kinetic energy, in J?

parts.label: r
parts.explain: $K = \tfrac12I\omega^2$ with $I = \tfrac12MR^2$ for a disk. A flywheel stores energy this way

problems.prompt: A constant torque of ${{tau}}$ N·m turns a shaft through ${{n}}$ revolution{{n > 1 ? "s" : ""}}. How much work does it do, in J?

parts.label: r
parts.explain: $W = \tau\Delta\theta$ with the angle in radians: one revolution is $2\pi$. That work becomes rotational kinetic energy if nothing else acts

problems.prompt: A ${{m}}$ kg ball moves in a straight line at ${{v}}$ m/s, passing ${{d}}$ m from a pivot at its closest. What is its angular momentum about the pivot, in kg·m²/s?

parts.label: r
parts.explain: $L = mvd_\perp$: a particle moving in a straight line still has angular momentum about any point it does not head straight at, and it stays constant

problems.prompt: A torque of ${{tau}}$ N·m acts for ${{t}}$ s on a wheel at rest with $I = {{I}}$ kg·m². What angular speed does it reach, in rad/s?

parts.label: r
parts.explain: Angular impulse equals the change in angular momentum: $\tau\Delta t = I\Delta\omega$

problems.prompt: A skater spinning at ${{w}}$ rev/s pulls in her arms, cutting her rotational inertia to $1/{{k}}$ of its value. How fast does she now spin, in rev/s?

parts.label: r
parts.explain: No outside torque, so $I\omega$ stays the same: smaller $I$, faster spin. Her kinetic energy goes up by the same factor ${{k}}$: she does work pulling her arms in

problems.prompt: {{shape}} rolls without slipping from rest down a ramp ${{h}}$ m high. How fast is it moving at the bottom, in m/s? ($I = c\,MR^2$ with $c = {{c|4}}$.)

parts.label: r
parts.explain: $Mgh = \tfrac12Mv^2(1 + c)$: some of the energy goes into spinning. Smaller $c$ wins the race, so a solid sphere beats a cylinder, which beats a hoop, whatever their sizes or masses

problems.prompt: A satellite moves at ${{vp}}$ km/s at its closest point, ${{rp}}$ units from the planet's centre. Its farthest point is ${{ra}}$ units away. How fast does it move there, in km/s?

parts.label: r
parts.explain: Gravity points at the planet, so it exerts no torque about it and angular momentum is conserved: $r_pv_p = r_av_a$ at the two ends, where the velocity is perpendicular to the radius. That is Kepler's equal-areas law

problems.prompt: A satellite in a circular orbit has kinetic energy ${{K}}$ GJ. What is the {{ask2 == 0 ? "gravitational potential" : "total"}} energy of the system, in GJ?

parts.label: r
parts.explain: For a circular orbit $K = \dfrac{GMm}{2r}$ and $U = -\dfrac{GMm}{r}$, so $U = -2K$ and $E = -K$. To climb to a higher orbit the satellite must gain total energy and yet end up moving slower

cases.q: a mass on a spring
a pendulum swinging through a few degrees
a ball bouncing on a floor
a pendulum swinging through 90 degrees
a block on a spring with a cubic force, F = −kx³
a floating cylinder bobbing up and down

problems.prompt: Is the motion of {{q}} simple harmonic?

parts.label: a
choice: Yes: the restoring force is proportional to the displacement
No: the restoring force is not proportional to the displacement
parts.explain: Simple harmonic motion needs $F = -kx$ about an equilibrium. A bouncing ball feels constant gravity, not a force growing with distance; a pendulum is only close to SHM while $\sin\theta \approx \theta$

problems.prompt: What is the period of a simple pendulum ${{L}}$ m long, swinging through a small angle, in s?

parts.label: r
parts.explain: $T = 2\pi\sqrt{L/g}$, independent of mass and of amplitude while the swing is small. A 1 m pendulum ticks about once a second each way

problems.prompt: An oscillator moves as $x = {{A}}\cos(2\pi t/{{T}})$ cm. What is its maximum speed, in cm/s, and where is it reached?

parts.label: r
parts.explain: $v_{max} = A\omega = 2\pi A/T$, reached passing through equilibrium. The acceleration is largest at the turning points, where the speed is zero

expect.r: Max(*[Abs(diff(A*cos(2*pi*x/nsimplify(T)), x).subs(x, nsimplify(T)*Rational(k, 4))) for k in range(4)])

problems.prompt: A ${{m}}$ kg mass on a spring with $k = {{k}}$ N/m oscillates with amplitude ${{A}}$ m. How fast is it moving at $x = {{f*A}}$ m, in m/s?

parts.label: r
parts.explain: Energy: $\tfrac12kA^2 = \tfrac12kx^2 + \tfrac12mv^2$, so $v = \sqrt{\tfrac km(A^2 - x^2)}$. At equilibrium all the energy is kinetic

problems.prompt: A material has density ${{rho}}$ kg/m³. What is the mass of ${{V}}$ cm³ of it, in g?

parts.label: r
parts.explain: $m = \rho V$. Handy: 1000 kg/m³ is exactly 1 g/cm³, so divide by 1000 to work in grams and cubic centimetres. Water 1, aluminium 2.7, steel 7.9, gold 19.3

problems.prompt: A tyre's absolute pressure is ${{p}}$ kPa and the atmosphere is at 101 kPa. What does a tyre gauge read, in kPa?

parts.label: r
parts.explain: A gauge measures pressure above the atmosphere: $P_{gauge} = P_{abs} - P_{atm}$. A flat tyre reads zero, not 101

problems.prompt: What is the gauge pressure ${{h}}$ m below the surface of fresh water, in kPa?

parts.label: r2
parts.explain: $P = \rho gh$: about 10 kPa per metre, so 10 m of water adds one atmosphere. Only depth matters, not the shape of the container

problems.prompt: What fraction of a block of {{obj}} (${{r1}}$ kg/m³) floats below the surface of {{fl}} (${{r2}}$ kg/m³)?

parts.label: r
parts.explain: Floating means buoyancy equals weight: $\rho_fgV_{sub} = \rho_ogV$, so the submerged fraction is the density ratio. If the ratio is above 1 the object sinks

problems.prompt: A hydraulic lift has pistons ${{d1}}$ cm and ${{d2}}$ cm across. A ${{F}}$ N push on the small piston lifts how much on the large one, in N?

parts.label: r
parts.explain: The pressure is the same throughout: $F_1/A_1 = F_2/A_2$. Areas go as diameter squared. The small piston moves farther by the same factor, so no energy is created

problems.prompt: Water flows at ${{v}}$ m/s through a pipe ${{d1}}$ cm across, which narrows to ${{d2}}$ cm. How fast does it flow in the narrow part, in m/s?

parts.label: r
parts.explain: An incompressible fluid has the same volume flow everywhere: $A_1v_1 = A_2v_2$. Halving the diameter quarters the area and quadruples the speed: a thumb over a hose

problems.prompt: Water speeds up from ${{v1}}$ m/s to ${{v2}}$ m/s in a level pipe. By how much does its pressure drop, in kPa?

parts.label: r
parts.explain: Bernoulli at constant height: $P + \tfrac12\rho v^2$ is constant along a streamline, so faster flow means lower pressure. It is energy conservation per unit volume

problems.prompt: In a box of gas, the molecules' speed is multiplied by ${{fv}}$ and their number by ${{fn}}$. By what factor does the pressure change?

parts.label: r
parts.explain: Each collision delivers momentum $\propto v$, and faster molecules hit more often, also $\propto v$: pressure $\propto Nv^2$. That is why pressure is proportional to temperature

problems.prompt: What is the rms speed of {{gas}} molecules ($M = {{M}}$ kg/mol) at ${{T}}$ K, in m/s? ($R = 8.314$.)

parts.label: r
parts.explain: $\tfrac12mv_{rms}^2 = \tfrac32k_BT$, so $v_{rms} = \sqrt{3RT/M}$ with $M$ in kg/mol. Air molecules at room temperature move at about 500 m/s, faster than sound

problems.prompt: A gas at ${{P1}}$ kPa and ${{T1}}$ K is heated to ${{T2}}$ K while its volume is multiplied by ${{fV}}$. What is its new pressure, in kPa?

parts.label: r
parts.explain: With the amount of gas fixed, $PV/T$ is constant: $P_2 = P_1\dfrac{T_2}{T_1}\dfrac{V_1}{V_2}$. Temperatures must be in kelvin

cases.q: A small hot nail touches a large cool block. Which way does energy flow?
A large warm pool and a small cold ice cube touch. Which way does energy flow?
Two blocks at the same temperature but different sizes touch. What happens?
Metal and wood in the same room feel different. Are they at different temperatures?

parts.label: a
choice: From the hotter object to the colder, whatever their sizes
No net flow: they are in thermal equilibrium
No: metal conducts energy from your hand faster, so it feels colder
parts.explain: Temperature, not internal energy, decides the direction of heat. Objects at the same temperature exchange no net energy; that is the zeroth law and the reason thermometers work

problems.prompt: By how much does the internal energy of ${{n}}$ mol of a monatomic ideal gas rise when it warms by ${{dT}}$ K, in J? ($R = 8.314$.)

parts.label: r
parts.explain: $U = \tfrac32nRT$ for a monatomic gas: three translational degrees of freedom, each $\tfrac12RT$ per mole. It depends on temperature alone, whatever the process

problems.prompt: A gas goes round a rectangular clockwise cycle on a P–V diagram between ${{P1}}$ and ${{P2}}$ kPa and between ${{V1}}$ and ${{V2}}$ L. What net work does it do per cycle, in J?

parts.label: r
parts.explain: The net work is the area enclosed: $(P_2 - P_1)(V_2 - V_1)$, and kPa × L is exactly J. Clockwise means the gas does net work, so over one cycle it must take in that much net heat, since $\Delta U = 0$

problems.prompt: A ${{mm}}$ g block of aluminium ($c = 0.90$ J/(g·K)) at ${{Tm}}$ °C is dropped into ${{mw}}$ g of water ($c = 4.18$) at 20 °C. What is the final temperature, in °C?

parts.label: r
parts.explain: Heat lost by the metal equals heat gained by the water: $m_mc_m(T_m - T_f) = m_wc_w(T_f - 20)$. Water's large heat capacity keeps the final temperature close to where the water started

cases.q: the system, as ice melts
the system, as a gas is compressed slowly at constant temperature
the universe, as heat flows from a hot block to a cold one
the universe, in a perfectly reversible process
the system, as water vapour condenses
the system, as a gas expands freely into a vacuum

problems.prompt: Does the entropy of {{q}} increase, decrease or stay the same?

parts.label: a
parts.explain: More ways to arrange the energy means more entropy: melting, boiling and expanding raise it. A system's entropy can fall, but only if the surroundings gain at least as much; the total never decreases

problems.prompt: An engine takes in ${{Qh}}$ J from a ${{Th}}$ K source and does ${{W}}$ J of work per cycle, exhausting to ${{Tc}}$ K. What is its efficiency? (The Carnot limit here is ${{1 - Tc/Th|3}}$.)

parts.label: r
parts.explain: $e = W/Q_h$, and the rest, $Q_h - W$, must go out as waste heat. No engine between these temperatures can beat $1 - T_c/T_h$; a claimed efficiency above it breaks the second law

problems.prompt: A clock moves at {{beta}}c. It ticks every {{tau}} μs in its own frame. How long between ticks in the lab (μs)?

parts.label: y
parts.explain: Δt = γΔτ, γ = 1/√(1 − β²). Muons with a 2.2 μs proper lifetime reach the ground because the lab sees them live ten times longer (and they see the atmosphere contracted)

problems.prompt: A rod of rest length {{L0}} m moves along its length at {{beta}}c. How long is it in the lab (m)?

parts.label: y
parts.explain: L = L₀/γ, only along the motion. Both ends must be marked at the same lab time, which is why contraction and dilation come together

problems.prompt: A ship moving at {{u}}c fires a probe forward at {{v}}c relative to the ship. How fast is the probe in the original frame (in units of c)?

parts.label: y
parts.explain: $w = \dfrac{u + v}{1 + uv/c^2}$; it never exceeds c. Rapidities (artanh β) simply add, which is the same rule

problems.prompt: {{name}} (mc² = {{m}} MeV) moves at {{beta}}c. What is its {{wt}}?

parts.label: y
parts.explain: E = γmc², K = (γ − 1)mc², p = γmv; check with E² = (pc)² + (mc²)². ½mv² underestimates K badly above ~0.3c

problems.prompt: A source emitting at {{f}} Hz approaches at {{beta}}c. What frequency is received?

parts.label: y
parts.explain: $f = f_0\sqrt{\dfrac{1+\beta}{1-\beta}}$ approaching (swap signs receding). Unlike sound, only the relative speed matters

cases.text: An Atwood machine holds 3 kg and 2 kg on a massless pulley. Find the acceleration (m/s²).
An Atwood machine holds 5 kg and 1 kg. Find the acceleration (m/s²).
A solid cylinder (I = ½mr²) rolls without slipping down a 30° incline. Find its acceleration (m/s²).
A solid sphere (I = ⅖mr²) rolls without slipping down a 20° incline. Find its acceleration (m/s²).
A thin hoop (I = mr²) rolls without slipping down a 15° incline. Find its acceleration (m/s²).
A simple pendulum is 2.0 m long. Find its small-oscillation angular frequency (rad/s).
A uniform rod 1.5 m long swings from one end. Find its small-oscillation angular frequency (rad/s).
A 2 kg mass sits between two springs (10 and 30 N/m) fixed to opposite walls. Find ω (rad/s).
A 2 kg mass hangs on springs of 10 and 30 N/m joined end to end. Find ω (rad/s).

problems.prompt: Use g = 9.81 m/s². {{text}}

parts.label: y
parts.explain: Write L = T − V in one generalised coordinate, apply d/dt(∂L/∂q̇) = ∂L/∂q, and read off q̈ (or, linearised, ω² = −∂q̈/∂q). Constraint forces never appear, which is the point

problems.prompt: The absolute temperature of a gas is multiplied by ${{f}}$. By what factor does the rms speed of its molecules change?

parts.label: y
parts.explain: $\tfrac12mv_{rms}^2 = \tfrac32k_BT$, so $v_{rms} \propto \sqrt T$. Quadrupling the temperature only doubles the speed

expect.y: sqrt(3*Symbol('k', positive=True)*f*Symbol('T', positive=True)/Symbol('m', positive=True))/sqrt(3*Symbol('k', positive=True)*Symbol('T', positive=True)/Symbol('m', positive=True))

problems.prompt: A tank holds ${{V}}$ L of gas at ${{P}}$ kPa and ${{T}}$ K. How many moles does it contain? ($R = 8.314$ J/(mol·K).)

parts.label: y
parts.explain: $n = \dfrac{PV}{RT}$ in SI units: kPa × L is J, conveniently, since $10^3 \times 10^{-3} = 1$

problems.prompt: You mix ${{m1}}$ g of water at ${{T1}}$ °C with ${{m2}}$ g of water at ${{T2}}$ °C in an insulated cup. What is the final temperature, in °C?

parts.label: y
parts.explain: Heat lost by the hot water equals heat gained by the cold: $m_1c(T_1 - T_f) = m_2c(T_f - T_2)$. With one substance, $c$ cancels and $T_f$ is the mass-weighted average

problems.prompt: A sample of monatomic ideal gas is replaced by ${{fn}}$ times as many moles at ${{fT}}$ times the absolute temperature. By what factor does its internal energy change?

parts.label: y
parts.explain: $U = \tfrac32nRT$: proportional to both the amount and the absolute temperature, and nothing else

problems.prompt: A gas at a constant ${{P}}$ kPa changes volume from ${{V1}}$ L to ${{V1 + dV}}$ L. How much work does the gas do on its surroundings, in J?

parts.label: y
parts.explain: At constant pressure the area under the P–V line is a rectangle: $W = P\Delta V$ (kPa × L = J). A gas that is compressed does negative work; the surroundings do work on it

problems.prompt: A gas does ${{W}}$ J of work on its surroundings while its internal energy changes by ${{dU}}$ J. How much heat flowed into it, in J (negative if heat left)?

parts.label: y
parts.explain: First law with $W$ as work done by the gas: $\Delta U = Q - W$, so $Q = \Delta U + W$. Check the sign convention your course uses: AP Physics writes $\Delta U = Q + W$ with $W$ done on the gas

problems.prompt: In each cycle an engine takes in ${{Qh}}$ J of heat and rejects ${{Qc}}$ J. What is its efficiency, as a fraction?

parts.label: y
parts.explain: Over a cycle $\Delta U = 0$, so the net work is $Q_h - Q_c$, the area enclosed on the P–V diagram. Efficiency is work out over heat in

problems.prompt: It takes ${{Q}}$ J to warm ${{m}}$ g of a metal by ${{dT}}$ K. What is its specific heat, in J/(g·K)?

parts.label: y
parts.explain: $Q = mc\Delta T$, so $c = Q/(m\Delta T)$. Water's 4.18 is unusually high; most metals are under 1

problems.prompt: A wall's area is multiplied by ${{fA}}$ and its thickness by ${{fL}}$, same material and same temperatures. By what factor does the rate of heat conduction change?

parts.label: y
parts.explain: $\dfrac{Q}{t} = \dfrac{kA\Delta T}{L}$: more area, more flow; thicker, less. Doubling insulation thickness halves the loss

problems.prompt: ${{Q}}$ J of heat flows from a reservoir at ${{Th}}$ K to one at ${{Tc}}$ K. What is the total entropy change of the two reservoirs, in J/K?

parts.label: y
parts.explain: The hot reservoir loses $Q/T_h$, the cold one gains the larger $Q/T_c$. The total is positive whenever heat flows from hot to cold, the second law

problems.prompt: Each of two charges is multiplied by ${{fq}}$ and their separation by ${{fr}}$. By what factor does the force between them change?

parts.label: y
parts.explain: $F = kq_1q_2/r^2$: both charges scale, so $f_q^2$; the distance enters squared in the denominator

problems.prompt: An oil drop of mass ${{m}} \times 10^{-15}$ kg hangs still in an upward field of ${{E}}$ kV/m. How many extra electrons does it carry? ($e = 1.60 \times 10^{-19}$ C.)

parts.label: y
parts.explain: Balance: $neE = mg$, so $n = \dfrac{mg}{eE}$. Millikan found the charges always came in whole multiples of $e$

problems.prompt: Two charges are moved from vacuum into a liquid of dielectric constant ${{k}}$. By what factor must their separation change to keep the force the same?

parts.label: y
parts.explain: In the medium $F = \dfrac{q_1q_2}{4\pi\kappa\varepsilon_0r^2}$. To undo the factor $\kappa$, $r^2$ must shrink by $\kappa$, so $r$ by $\sqrt\kappa$

problems.prompt: Positive charges of ${{q1}}$ µC and ${{q2}}$ µC are ${{d}}$ m apart. How far from the ${{q1}}$ µC charge, on the line between them, is the net field zero, in m?

parts.label: y
parts.explain: Between two like charges their fields point opposite ways; they cancel where $q_1/x^2 = q_2/(d - x)^2$, nearer the smaller charge

expect.y: Max(*solve(Eq(q1*(d - x)**2, q2*x**2), x)) if q1 < q2 else Min(*solve(Eq(q1*(d - x)**2, q2*x**2), x))

problems.prompt: Identical metal spheres with ${{q1}}$ nC and ${{q2}}$ nC are touched, then returned to their original separation. By what factor does the magnitude of the force between them change?

parts.label: y
parts.explain: Touching shares the total charge equally: each gets $(q_1 + q_2)/2$. The force goes from $|q_1q_2|$ to $\left(\frac{q_1 + q_2}{2}\right)^2$, always repulsive afterwards

problems.prompt: A point charge is multiplied by ${{fq}}$ and you move to ${{fr}}$ times the distance from it. By what factor does the electric field change?

parts.label: y
parts.explain: $E = kq/r^2$: linear in charge, inverse square in distance

problems.prompt: A proton starts from rest in a uniform ${{E}}$ N/C field and moves ${{d}}$ m along it. How fast is it then moving, in km/s? ($e = 1.60 \times 10^{-19}$ C, $m_p = 1.67 \times 10^{-27}$ kg.)

parts.label: y
parts.explain: Constant force $eE$, so constant acceleration $eE/m$, and $v^2 = 2ad$. Equivalently the work $eEd$ becomes kinetic energy

problems.prompt: A thin metal shell of radius ${{R}}$ m carries ${{Q}}$ nC. What is the field at ${{k2}}$ times its radius from the centre, in N/C? (Inside the shell it would be zero. $k = 8.99 \times 10^9$.)

parts.label: y
parts.explain: Outside a charged shell the field is that of a point charge at the centre, $kQ/r^2$; inside it is zero, because the charge sits on the surface and its pulls cancel (Gauss's law)

problems.prompt: On a field-line drawing, the lines are twice as close together at point A as at point B. How do the fields compare?

parts.label: a
choice: The same: line spacing shows only direction
parts.explain: Line density shows field strength; the tangent shows direction. Lines never cross, start on positive charges and end on negative ones

problems.prompt: How much work does it take to bring three ${{q}}$ µC charges from far apart to the corners of an equilateral triangle of side ${{a}}$ m, in J? ($k = 8.99 \times 10^9$.)

parts.label: y
parts.explain: Add the energy of every pair once: three pairs, each $kq^2/a$. The first charge is free; the second costs one pair; the third costs two

problems.prompt: Charges of ${{q1}}$ nC and ${{q2}}$ nC are ${{d}}$ m apart. What is the electric potential at the midpoint between them, in V? ($k = 8.99 \times 10^9$.)

parts.label: y
parts.explain: Potential is a scalar: add $kq/r$ with signs, no components. Equal and opposite charges give zero potential at the midpoint, though the field there is not zero

problems.prompt: Plates are held at ${{V}}$ V apart. How close must they be for a field of ${{E}}$ V/m between them, in mm?

parts.label: y
parts.explain: In a uniform field $\Delta V = Ed$. Air breaks down at about $3 \times 10^6$ V/m, which limits how close high-voltage plates can be

problems.prompt: A parallel-plate capacitor's plate area is multiplied by ${{fA}}$, its gap by ${{fd}}$, and the gap is filled with a dielectric of constant ${{k}}$ (it was air). By what factor does its capacitance change?

parts.label: y
parts.explain: $C = \kappa\varepsilon_0A/d$: up with area and dielectric, down with gap

problems.prompt: A charged capacitor is disconnected from its battery, then its plate gap is multiplied by ${{f}}$. By what factor does its stored energy change?

parts.label: y
parts.explain: Disconnected, the charge is fixed. $C \propto 1/d$ and $U = Q^2/2C$, so $U \propto d$. Pulling the plates apart takes work, which is where the extra energy comes from

problems.prompt: A proton and an alpha particle (twice the charge, four times the mass) are accelerated from rest through the same potential difference. What is the ratio of the alpha's final speed to the proton's?

parts.label: y
parts.explain: $qV = \tfrac12mv^2$, so $v \propto \sqrt{q/m}$: the alpha has $\sqrt{2/4}$ of the proton's speed, though twice its kinetic energy

problems.prompt: A steady ${{I}}$ A current flows for ${{t}}$ s. How much charge passes, in C?

parts.label: y
parts.explain: Current is charge per time, $I = \Delta Q/\Delta t$. One amp-hour is 3600 C, the unit on phone batteries

problems.prompt: A wire's length is multiplied by ${{fL}}$ and its diameter by ${{fd}}$, same metal. By what factor does its resistance change?

parts.label: y
parts.explain: $R = \rho L/A$ and $A \propto d^2$. Stretching a wire to twice the length also thins it, which is a different problem: then $R$ goes up by four

problems.prompt: On a current–voltage graph for a resistor, the straight line passes through the origin and through ${{V}}$ V, ${{I}}$ A. What is the resistance, in Ω?

parts.label: y
parts.explain: An ohmic resistor gives a straight line through the origin. With $V$ on the x-axis and $I$ on the y-axis, the slope is $1/R$; read off one point and divide

problems.prompt: Bulbs of ${{R1}}$ Ω and ${{R2}}$ Ω are in series across a battery. What is the ratio of the power of the ${{R2}}$ Ω bulb to that of the ${{R1}}$ Ω bulb?

parts.label: y
parts.explain: In series the current is the same, so $P = I^2R \propto R$: the higher resistance glows brighter. In parallel the voltage is the same and $P = V^2/R$ reverses it

problems.prompt: ${{n}}$ identical ${{R}}$ Ω resistors are connected in parallel. What is the equivalent resistance, in Ω?

parts.label: y
parts.explain: $n$ equal paths in parallel: $\dfrac1{R_{eq}} = \dfrac{n}{R}$. Adding a branch always lowers the total, because it gives current another way through

problems.prompt: Capacitors of ${{C1}}$ µF and ${{C2}}$ µF in series are connected across ${{V}}$ V. What charge does each hold, in µC?

parts.label: y
parts.explain: In series every capacitor holds the same charge; the voltages, $Q/C$, add to the battery's: $Q/C_1 + Q/C_2 = V$

problems.prompt: A battery of emf ${{em}}$ V shows ${{Vt}}$ V across its terminals while driving a ${{R}}$ Ω load. What is its internal resistance, in Ω?

parts.label: y
parts.explain: The current is $V_t/R$; the missing $\varepsilon - V_t$ is dropped inside the battery across $r$, so $r = \dfrac{\varepsilon - V_t}{I}$

problems.prompt: A ${{V}}$ V supply drives ${{R1}}$ kΩ in series with a second resistor. What must the second resistor be for ${{Vout}}$ V across it, in kΩ?

parts.label: y
parts.explain: Same current through both, so voltages split in proportion to resistance: $\dfrac{V_{out}}{V} = \dfrac{R_2}{R_1 + R_2}$

problems.prompt: A total current of ${{I}}$ A splits between ${{R1}}$ Ω and ${{R2}}$ Ω resistors in parallel. How much goes through the ${{R1}}$ Ω resistor, in A?

parts.label: y
parts.explain: Same voltage across both, so currents split inversely to resistance: $I_1 = I\dfrac{R_2}{R_1 + R_2}$. More current takes the easier path

expect.y: solve([Eq(x + Symbol('b'), I), Eq(x*R1, Symbol('b')*R2)], [x, Symbol('b')])[x]

problems.prompt: A ${{e1}}$ V battery with ${{R1}}$ Ω in series is connected, positive to positive, to a ${{e2}}$ V battery with ${{R2}}$ Ω in series, forming one loop. What current flows, in A?

parts.label: y
parts.explain: Going round the loop the emfs oppose: $\varepsilon_1 - IR_1 - IR_2 - \varepsilon_2 = 0$. The stronger battery charges the weaker one

problems.prompt: A ${{C}}$ µF capacitor charges through ${{R}}$ kΩ from a battery. How long until it reaches ${{f}}$ of the battery voltage, in s?

parts.label: y
parts.explain: $V = \varepsilon(1 - e^{-t/RC})$, so $t = -RC\ln(1 - f)$. Half charge takes $0.69RC$; 99% takes $4.6RC$

problems.prompt: A long wire runs north–south above a compass and carries current toward the north. Which way does the compass's north pole swing, viewed from above?

parts.label: a
parts.explain: Right-hand rule: thumb north, fingers curl down past the wire's underside toward the west. The compass sits below the wire, so the field there points west (Ørsted's 1820 experiment)

problems.prompt: A charge moving through a uniform field feels ${{f}}$ of the largest magnetic force it could feel at that speed. What angle does its velocity make with the field, in degrees (between 0 and 90)?

parts.label: y
parts.explain: $F = qvB\sin\theta$ is largest at 90° and zero along the field. Only the perpendicular part of the velocity counts

problems.prompt: A proton circles in a ${{B}}$ T field. How long does one revolution take, in ns? ($e = 1.60 \times 10^{-19}$ C, $m_p = 1.67 \times 10^{-27}$ kg.)

parts.label: y
parts.explain: $r = mv/qB$, so the time round, $2\pi r/v = 2\pi m/qB$, does not depend on speed. A cyclotron uses that: one fixed frequency keeps up as the particles speed up

problems.prompt: A velocity selector must pass ions at ${{v}}$ km/s with a ${{B}}$ T magnetic field. What electric field does it need, in kV/m?

parts.label: y
parts.explain: Undeflected means $qE = qvB$, so $E = vB$; the charge and mass cancel. Faster ions are bent one way, slower ones the other

problems.prompt: At what distance from a long straight wire carrying ${{I}}$ A is the magnetic field ${{B}}$ µT, in cm? ($\mu_0 = 4\pi \times 10^{-7}$ T·m/A.)

parts.label: y
parts.explain: $B = \dfrac{\mu_0I}{2\pi r}$, falling as $1/r$ (not $1/r^2$: the wire is a line, not a point)

problems.prompt: A ${{L}}$ m length of wire carrying ${{I}}$ A lies at ${{th}}^\circ$ to a ${{B}}$ T field. What force acts on it, in N?

parts.label: y
parts.explain: $F = ILB\sin\theta$: the force on all the moving charges in the wire. Along the field there is none

problems.prompt: A ${{A}}$ cm² loop starts face-on to a ${{B}}$ T field and is turned a quarter turn so the field lies in its plane. By how much does the flux through it change, in mWb?

parts.label: y
parts.explain: $\Phi = BA\cos\theta$ with $\theta$ measured from the loop's normal: from $BA$ at 0° to zero at 90°

problems.prompt: A coil's number of turns is multiplied by ${{fN}}$ and the same change in field happens in ${{ft}}$ times the time. By what factor does the average emf change?

parts.label: y
parts.explain: $\varepsilon = N\dfrac{\Delta\Phi}{\Delta t}$: more turns or a faster change both raise it

cases.q: the north pole of a magnet is pushed toward the coil
the north pole of a magnet is pulled away from the coil
a magnet is held still inside the coil

problems.prompt: Viewed from the magnet's side, the coil's face behaves like a magnetic pole when {{q}}. Which?

parts.label: a
choice: A north pole, repelling the approach
A south pole, attracting it back
parts.explain: Lenz: the induced current opposes the change in flux. An approaching north is repelled by a north face; a retreating one is held back by a south. No change, no current

problems.prompt: A ${{L}}$ m rod slides at ${{v}}$ m/s on rails through a ${{B}}$ T field, closing a ${{R}}$ Ω circuit. What force must push it to keep its speed constant, in N?

parts.label: y
parts.explain: The emf $BLv$ drives $I = BLv/R$, and the field pushes back on that current with $ILB$. Pushing faster costs more: $F \propto v$, and the power $Fv$ appears as heat in $R$

problems.prompt: How tall must a flat wall mirror be for a ${{h}}$ m person to see their whole body in it, in m?

parts.label: y
parts.explain: Rays from your feet reflect halfway up to your eyes, and from the top of your head halfway down. The mirror needs half your height, whatever your distance from it

problems.prompt: An object is ${{o}}$ cm in front of a convex mirror with a focal length of ${{f}}$ cm (that is, $f = -{{f}}$ cm). Where is the image, in cm (negative behind the mirror)?

parts.label: y
parts.explain: $\dfrac1{d_o} + \dfrac1{d_i} = \dfrac1f$ with $f < 0$ always gives $d_i < 0$: a virtual, upright, smaller image behind the mirror. That is why shop and car mirrors are convex

problems.prompt: An object is ${{k}}$ focal lengths from a concave mirror with $f = {{f}}$ cm. What is the magnification?

parts.label: y
parts.explain: $m = -d_i/d_o$. Beyond $2f$ the image is real, inverted and smaller; between $f$ and $2f$, real, inverted and larger; inside $f$, virtual, upright and larger

problems.prompt: Light travels at ${{v}} \times 10^8$ m/s in a material. What is its index of refraction? ($c = 3.00 \times 10^8$ m/s.)

parts.label: y
parts.explain: $n = c/v$, always at least 1. Light bends toward the normal going into the slower medium

problems.prompt: Light in glass ($n = {{n1}}$) meets a boundary with a material of $n = {{n2}}$. What is the critical angle, in degrees?

parts.label: y
parts.explain: Snell with 90° refraction: $n_1\sin\theta_c = n_2$. The closer the indices, the larger the critical angle; optical fibre cladding is chosen to keep it workable

problems.prompt: An object is held ${{k}}$ of a focal length from a converging lens with $f = {{f}}$ cm. Where is the image, in cm (negative on the object's side)?

parts.label: y
parts.explain: Inside the focal length a converging lens cannot form a real image: $d_i < 0$, a virtual, upright, enlarged image on the object's side. That is a magnifying glass

problems.prompt: An object is ${{o}}$ cm from a converging lens of focal length ${{f}}$ cm. How far from the lens does the image form, in cm?

parts.label: y
parts.explain: $\dfrac1{d_o} + \dfrac1{d_i} = \dfrac1f$. A real image forms on the far side; at $d_o = 2f$ it is also at $2f$ and the same size

problems.prompt: A wave passes along a rope. What does the wave carry from one end to the other?

parts.label: a
choice: Energy, but not the rope itself
The rope's material, moving along with the wave
Nothing: a wave is only a pattern
parts.explain: Each bit of rope moves up and down about its own rest position and stays put on average. The disturbance, and the energy with it, travels

problems.prompt: A ${{f}}$ Hz sound passes from air (${{v1}}$ m/s) into a medium where sound moves at ${{v2}}$ m/s. What is its wavelength there, in m?

parts.label: y
parts.explain: The frequency is set by the source and does not change at a boundary; the speed does, so the wavelength changes in proportion

problems.prompt: The tension in a guitar string is multiplied by ${{f}}$. By what factor does the wave speed on it change?

parts.label: y
parts.explain: $v = \sqrt{T/\mu}$. Tightening a string raises its pitch, but four times the tension only doubles the speed and the frequency

cases.q: a fixed end
a free end
a heavier rope joined to it
a lighter rope joined to it

problems.prompt: An upward pulse on a rope reaches {{q}}. Is the reflected pulse upright or inverted?

parts.label: a
parts.explain: Reflection off something harder to move (a fixed end, a denser medium) inverts the pulse; off something easier to move (a free end, a lighter medium) keeps it upright. The transmitted pulse is always upright

problems.prompt: Unpolarised light passes through two polarisers and ${{f}}$ of it gets through. What angle is there between their axes, in degrees?

parts.label: y
parts.explain: The first polariser passes half; the second passes $\cos^2\theta$ of that: $f = \tfrac12\cos^2\theta$

problems.prompt: You drive {{dir == 1 ? "toward" : "away from"}} a stationary ${{f}}$ Hz siren at ${{vo}}$ m/s. What frequency do you hear, in Hz? (Sound at 343 m/s.)

parts.label: y
parts.explain: A moving observer meets wavefronts at $v \pm v_o$; the wavelength is unchanged. $f' = f\dfrac{v \pm v_o}{v}$. A moving source instead squeezes the wavelength: $f\dfrac{v}{v \mp v_s}$

problems.prompt: Two speakers play the same ${{f}}$ Hz tone in phase. What is the smallest path difference that gives a quiet spot, in m? (Sound at 343 m/s.)

parts.label: y
parts.explain: Destructive when the paths differ by half a wavelength (or 3/2, 5/2, …); constructive at whole wavelengths

problems.prompt: How long must a pipe closed at one end be for its fundamental to be ${{f}}$ Hz, in cm? (Sound at 343 m/s.)

parts.label: y
parts.explain: A closed pipe has a node at the closed end and an antinode at the open end: a quarter wavelength fits, $f_1 = v/4L$. It plays only odd harmonics

problems.prompt: A string and a ${{f0}}$ Hz tuning fork give ${{b}}$ beats per second. Tightening the string slightly makes the beats faster. What was the string's frequency, in Hz?

parts.label: y
parts.explain: Beats give only the difference, $|f - f_0|$, so the string is $f_0 \pm b$. Tightening raises $f$; if that widens the gap, $f$ was already above $f_0$

problems.prompt: The first dark fringe of ${{lam}}$ nm light through a single slit is at ${{th}}^\circ$. How wide is the slit, in µm?

parts.label: y
parts.explain: First minimum: $a\sin\theta = \lambda$. A narrower slit spreads the light more

problems.prompt: Light of ${{lam}}$ nm falls on a grating with ${{N}}$ lines per mm. At what angle is the order-${{m}}$ bright line, in degrees?

parts.label: y
parts.explain: Line spacing $d = 1/N$; bright where $d\sin\theta = m\lambda$. More lines per mm spread the colours farther

problems.prompt: A non-reflective coating ($n = {{n}}$) on glass ($n = 1.5$) is designed to cancel reflected ${{lam}}$ nm light. What is its smallest thickness, in nm?

parts.label: y
parts.explain: Both reflections (air to coating, coating to glass) flip phase, so they cancel; the round trip must add half a wavelength in the film: $2t = \lambda/2n$. A quarter-wave coating

problems.prompt: A photon carries ${{E}}$ eV. What is its wavelength, in nm? ($hc = 1240$ eV·nm.)

parts.label: y
parts.explain: $E = hc/\lambda$ with $hc \approx 1240$ eV·nm: visible light runs from about 1.8 eV (red) to 3.1 eV (violet)

problems.prompt: An electron's kinetic energy is multiplied by ${{f}}$ (non-relativistic). By what factor does its de Broglie wavelength change?

parts.label: y
parts.explain: $\lambda = h/p$ and $p = \sqrt{2mK}$, so $\lambda \propto 1/\sqrt K$. Electron microscopes use high voltages to get short wavelengths

problems.prompt: How much energy does it take to ionise a hydrogen atom from its $n = {{n}}$ level, in eV?

parts.label: y
parts.explain: $E_n = -13.6/n^2$ eV and ionised means $E = 0$, so it takes $13.6/n^2$ eV. Excited atoms are much easier to ionise

problems.prompt: A hydrogen atom drops from $n = {{hi}}$ to $n = {{lo}}$. What energy does the emitted photon carry, in eV?

parts.label: y
parts.explain: The photon carries the difference of the levels. Drops to $n = 1$ (Lyman) are ultraviolet; drops to $n = 2$ (Balmer) are visible

problems.prompt: A star's surface temperature is multiplied by ${{f}}$. By what factor does its total radiated power per unit area change?

parts.label: y
parts.explain: Stefan–Boltzmann: $P/A = \sigma T^4$. Twice as hot, sixteen times the power, and the peak shifts to half the wavelength (Wien)

problems.prompt: A metal has a work function of ${{phi}}$ eV. What is the longest wavelength that can eject electrons from it, in nm? ($hc = 1240$ eV·nm.)

parts.label: y
parts.explain: At threshold the photon has just enough energy: $hc/\lambda_0 = \phi$. Longer wavelengths eject nothing however bright the light, the clue that light comes in photons

problems.prompt: What is the largest possible Compton shift in wavelength for a photon scattered by a free electron, in pm? ($h/m_ec = 2.426$ pm.)

parts.label: y
parts.explain: $\Delta\lambda = \dfrac{h}{m_ec}(1 - \cos\theta)$ is largest at $\theta = 180°$: twice the Compton wavelength

problems.prompt: A sample has ${{N0}}$ undecayed nuclei with a half-life of ${{th}}$ days. How many are left after ${{k*th}}$ days?

parts.label: y
parts.explain: Each half-life halves what is left: $N = N_0(1/2)^{t/t_{1/2}}$. After $k$ half-lives, $N_0/2^k$

problems.prompt: A star's emission peaks at {{l}} nm. What is its surface temperature, in K? (b = 2.898 × 10⁻³ m·K)

parts.label: v
parts.explain: T = b/λ_max: the Sun peaks near 500 nm at about 5800 K; a red giant near 1000 nm is about 2900 K

problems.prompt: A particle moves as x(t) = {{a}}t³ + ({{b}})t² + {{c}}t m. What is its acceleration at t = {{T}} s, in m/s²?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Differentiate twice: the cubic term gives a linearly growing acceleration

problems.prompt: An object starts at x = 0 with velocity {{v0}} m/s and has a(t) = {{k}}t m/s². Where is it at t = {{T}} s, in m?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Integrate twice, adding the initial velocity after the first integral

problems.prompt: A boat coasting with a = −{{k}}v (per second) starts at {{v0}} m/s. How far does it travel before its speed halves, in m?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: With a = v dv/dx = −kv, speed falls linearly with distance: v = v₀ − kx. It never stops in finite time but stops within v₀/k

problems.prompt: A particle moves as r(t) = ({{a}}t³) î + ({{b}}t²) ĵ m. What is the magnitude of its acceleration at t = {{T}} s, in m/s²?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Differentiate each component separately, then take the length

problems.prompt: A rod of length {{L}} m has linear density λ = {{c}}x^{{n}} kg/m. What is its total mass, in kg?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: M = ∫λ dx; the centre of mass then divides ∫xλ dx by this

problems.prompt: A force F = {{c}}t N acts on a {{m}} kg mass that starts at rest at the origin. Where is it at t = {{T}} s, in m?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: a = F/m = ct/m; integrate twice from rest

problems.prompt: An object falls from rest with linear drag (b = {{b}} kg/s, m = {{m}} kg). How long until it reaches {{f}}% of terminal speed, in s?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: v = v_t(1 − e^{−bt/m}): about 2.3 time constants to 90%, 4.6 to 99%

problems.prompt: A car on a curve of radius {{r}} m moves at {{v}} m/s and speeds up at {{at}} m/s². What angle does its total acceleration make with the radial (inward) direction, in degrees?

parts.label: y
parts.explain: The radial part v²/r turns the velocity; the tangential part changes the speed

problems.prompt: An attractive force F = −{{k}}/x² N acts along x. How much work does it do as the object moves from x = {{a}} to x = {{b}} m, in J?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Moving away against an attraction, the force does negative work

problems.prompt: A conservative force is F(x) = −{{k}}x + {{c}} N. Taking U(0) = 0, what is U at x = {{X}} m, in J?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: U(x) = −∫F dx: a spring plus a constant force is a shifted parabola

problems.prompt: A particle has U(x) = {{a}}x³ − {{b}}x J. At what positive x is its stable equilibrium, in m?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: F = −dU/dx = 0 at ±√(b/3a); U'' > 0 at the positive root, so that one is stable

problems.prompt: The work a motor has done grows as W(t) = {{c}}t³ J. What power does it deliver at t = {{T}} s, in W?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: P = dW/dt: the reverse of integrating power to get work

problems.prompt: A kick exerts F = {{F0}} sin(πt/{{T}}) N for 0 ≤ t ≤ {{T}} s. What is the average force over the kick, in N?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: F̄ = J/Δt; for a half-sine the average is 2/π of the peak

problems.prompt: A wheel starts from rest with α = {{k}}t rad/s². Through what angle has it turned at t = {{T}} s, in rad?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: The same calculus as linear motion: integrate α twice
