problems.prompt: A force F = ({{Fx}}, {{Fy}}, {{Fz}}) N acts at r = ({{rx}}, {{ry}}, {{rz}}) m from a pivot. What is the magnitude of the torque, in N·m?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: τ = r × F: compute all three components, then the length

problems.prompt: A uniform rod of mass {{M}} kg and length {{L}} m turns about an axis {{d}} m from its centre, perpendicular to it. What is its rotational inertia, in kg·m²?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: The parallel-axis theorem, here derived by integrating directly about the shifted axis

problems.prompt: A {{m}} kg particle at r = ({{rx}}, {{ry}}, 0) m moves with v = ({{vx}}, {{vy}}, 0) m/s. What is the z component of its angular momentum about the origin, in kg·m²/s?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: L = r × p: a particle in a straight line still has angular momentum about a point off that line

problems.prompt: {{shape}} rolls without slipping down a {{th}}° incline. What is its acceleration, in m/s²? (g = 9.81, I = cMR², c = {{c}})

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Friction supplies the torque; the more mass far from the axis (larger c), the slower the roll

problems.prompt: A {{m}} kg mass on a spring of constant {{k}} N/m oscillates. What is its period, in s?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Any potential minimum oscillates with ω² = U''/m: a spring's U'' is k

problems.prompt: A uniform rod {{L}} m long swings about a pivot {{d}} m from its centre. What is its small-angle period, in s? (g = 9.81)

parts.label: v
parts.explain: T = 2π√(I/mgd): the period is longest near the centre and has a minimum at d = L/√12

problems.prompt: A rod {{L}} m long carries {{Q}} nC spread evenly. What is the field {{d}} m from its midpoint along the perpendicular bisector, in N/C? (k = 8.99 × 10⁹)

parts.label: v
parts.explain: By symmetry only the perpendicular components add; far away it looks like a point charge

problems.prompt: An infinite line carries {{lam}} nC/m. What is the field {{d}} m from it, in N/C? (ε₀ = 8.854 × 10⁻¹²)

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Gauss with a cylinder gives λ/2πε₀r directly; summing the line's pieces gives the same

problems.prompt: A long cylinder has charge density ρ = c r^{{n}}. How much charge per unit length lies within radius {{R}} (in units with c = 1)?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Shells of area 2πr per unit length; Gauss then gives E = λ_in/2πε₀r

problems.prompt: A point charge of {{Q}} nC sits at the origin. What is V({{a}} m) − V({{b}} m), in V? (k = 8.99 × 10⁹)

parts.label: v
parts.explain: V(a) − V(b) = ∫ₐᵇ E dr along the field line

problems.prompt: A disk of radius {{R}} m carries {{sig}} nC/m² uniformly. What is the potential on its axis {{z}} m from the centre, in V? (ε₀ = 8.854 × 10⁻¹²)

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Sum rings of charge σ2πr dr, each at the same distance from the axis point

problems.prompt: The potential is V(x, y) = {{a}}x²y + {{b}}y V. What is the magnitude of E at ({{X}}, {{Y}}) m, in V/m?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: E = −∇V: each component is a partial derivative

expect.v: Matrix([diff(a*Symbol('X1')**2*Symbol('Y1') + b*Symbol('Y1'), Symbol('X1')), diff(a*Symbol('X1')**2*Symbol('Y1') + b*Symbol('Y1'), Symbol('Y1'))]).subs({Symbol('X1'): X, Symbol('Y1'): Y}).norm()

problems.prompt: A {{q}} nC charge sits at the centre of a conducting shell carrying net {{Qs}} nC. What is the field {{d}} m from the centre, outside the shell, in N/C? (k = 8.99 × 10⁹)

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Outside, Gauss sees the total enclosed charge: q plus the shell's net charge

problems.prompt: Two far-apart metal spheres of radii {{R1}} and {{R2}} cm are joined by a wire. What is the ratio of surface charge densities σ₁/σ₂?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Equal potentials put charge in proportion to R, so σ ∝ 1/R: sharp points carry dense charge

problems.prompt: What is the capacitance of an isolated metal sphere of radius {{R}} cm, in pF? (ε₀ = 8.854 × 10⁻¹²)

parts.label: v
parts.explain: A spherical capacitor with the outer shell sent to infinity: even the Earth is only about 700 μF

problems.prompt: A metal sphere of radius {{R}} cm holds {{Q}} nC. How much energy is stored in its field, in μJ? (ε₀ = 8.854 × 10⁻¹²)

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Integrate ε₀E²/2 over all space outside: the same as Q²/2C

problems.prompt: A dielectric slab (κ = {{k}}) fills half the gap of a parallel-plate capacitor, covering the whole plate area. By what factor does the capacitance rise?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Two capacitors in series, each half the gap; the empty half limits the gain to at most 2

problems.prompt: A copper wire of cross-section {{A}} mm² carries {{I}} A. What is the electron drift speed, in mm/s? (n = 8.5 × 10²⁸ m⁻³, e = 1.602 × 10⁻¹⁹ C)

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Fractions of a millimetre per second: the signal travels fast, the electrons do not

problems.prompt: A {{C}} μF capacitor charges through {{R}} kΩ from a {{V}} V battery. What is the current {{t1}} ms after the switch closes, in mA?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: I = dQ/dt: the current starts at V/R and decays with τ = RC (here RC in ms is R[kΩ]·C[μF])

problems.prompt: A {{C}} μF capacitor charges fully from {{V}} V through any resistor. How much energy does the resistor dissipate, in mJ?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Exactly half the battery's energy, whatever R is; the other half is stored in the capacitor

problems.prompt: A proton moves at {{v}} × 10⁶ m/s perpendicular to a {{B}} T field. What is the radius of its circle, in cm? (m = 1.673 × 10⁻²⁷ kg, e = 1.602 × 10⁻¹⁹ C)

parts.label: r
parts.explain: qvB supplies the centripetal force mv²/r; the period 2πm/qB does not depend on speed

problems.prompt: A loop of radius {{R}} cm carries {{I}} A. What is the field on its axis {{z}} cm from the centre, in μT?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Biot–Savart: each element's contribution has the same axial part, so the integral is just 2π times one of them

problems.prompt: A square loop of side {{L}} m lies in the xy-plane with one corner at the origin, in a field B_z = {{B0}}x/{{L}} T. What is the flux through it, in Wb?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Integrate B·dA when the field varies across the loop; the average field here is B₀/2

problems.prompt: A {{N}}-turn coil of area {{A}} cm² sits in a field rising as B = {{B0}} + {{k}}t T. What emf is induced, in mV?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Only the changing part of the flux induces an emf; the constant B₀ does nothing

problems.prompt: A rod of mass {{m}} kg and length {{L}} m slides on rails in a {{B}} T field with total resistance {{R}} Ω. Released at {{v0}} m/s with no applied force, how fast is it moving after {{T}} s, in m/s?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: The induced current brakes the rod with force B²L²v/R: an exponential decay with τ = mR/B²L²

problems.prompt: A current I = {{I0}} sin({{w}}t) A flows in a {{L}} mH inductor. What is the peak emf across it, in V?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: ℰ = L dI/dt peaks where the current crosses zero, a quarter-cycle ahead

problems.prompt: An LR circuit has L = {{L}} mH and R = {{R}} Ω. How long after the switch closes does the current reach {{f}}% of its final value, in ms?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: I = (V/R)(1 − e^{−Rt/L}); τ = L/R, here in ms when L is in mH

problems.prompt: At what speed, as a fraction of c, does a moving clock run slow by a factor γ = {{g}}?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: γ = 2 needs 0.866c; γ = 10 needs 0.995c

problems.prompt: At what speed, as a fraction of c, does a rod appear {{f}}% of its rest length?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: L = L₀/γ: contraction only along the motion

problems.prompt: A ship moves at {{v}}c. A probe is seen in the original frame moving at {{u}}c in the same direction. How fast is it moving relative to the ship (in units of c)?

parts.label: r
parts.explain: Invert the addition law; it reduces to u − v only when both speeds are small

problems.prompt: A source approaching head-on is received at {{r}} times its emitted frequency. How fast is it moving, as a fraction of c?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: f/f₀ = √((1 + β)/(1 − β)) for approach; doubling the frequency needs 0.6c

problems.prompt: A particle has kinetic energy equal to {{k}} times its rest energy. How fast is it moving, as a fraction of c?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: K = (γ − 1)mc²: at K = mc² the particle moves at 0.866c, far below what ½mv² would suggest

problems.prompt: An Atwood machine has masses {{m1}} and {{m2}} kg on a massless pulley. Using L = T − V, what is the acceleration of the heavier mass, in m/s²? (g = 9.81)

parts.label: v
parts.explain: One coordinate: L = ½(m₁ + m₂)ẋ² + (m₁ − m₂)gx, so (m₁ + m₂)ẍ = (m₁ − m₂)g

expect.v: Abs(solve(Eq(diff(diff((m1 + m2)*Symbol('xd')**2/2, Symbol('xd')).subs(Symbol('xd'), x*Symbol('t')), Symbol('t')), (m1 - m2)*Rational(981, 100)), x)[0])

problems.prompt: Two forces of ${{a}}$ N and ${{b}}$ N act on one object, in directions you may choose. What is the {{k == 0 ? "largest" : "smallest"}} possible magnitude of their sum, in N?

parts.label: y
parts.explain: Vectors add by direction: parallel gives the sum of the sizes, opposite gives the difference, and every angle in between gives something between. A scalar sum would always be $a + b$

problems.prompt: Three forces act along one line: ${{a}}$ N to the right, ${{b}}$ N to the left, and an unknown third. The net force is ${{c}}$ N (positive to the right). What is the third force, in N (positive to the right)?

parts.label: y
parts.explain: Pick right as positive: $a - b + F_3 = F_{net}$, so $F_3 = F_{net} - a + b$. A negative answer points left

problems.prompt: A dog runs ${{d1}}$ m east, then ${{d2}}$ m west, taking ${{t}}$ s in all. What is the magnitude of its average velocity, in m/s?

parts.label: y
parts.explain: Average velocity is displacement over time: only the net $|d_1 - d_2|$ counts. Average speed would use the whole path, $(d_1 + d_2)/t$

problems.prompt: A car covers the first half of a trip's distance at ${{v1}}$ km/h and the second half at ${{v2}}$ km/h. What is its average speed for the trip, in km/h?

parts.label: y
parts.explain: Equal distances, not equal times: $\bar v = \dfrac{2D}{D/v_1 + D/v_2} = \dfrac{2v_1v_2}{v_1 + v_2}$, the harmonic mean. It is below the plain average because the slow half takes longer

problems.prompt: On a position–time graph, an object's line runs straight from ${{x0}}$ m at $t = 0$ to ${{x1}}$ m at $t = {{t}}$ s. What is its velocity, in m/s?

parts.label: y
parts.explain: Velocity is the slope of $x$ against $t$: rise over run. A line sloping down means motion in the negative direction; the area under an $x$–$t$ graph means nothing

problems.prompt: A car's speed is multiplied by ${{f}}$, and it brakes with the same constant deceleration. By what factor does its stopping distance change?

parts.label: y
parts.explain: $v^2 = 2ad$ gives $d = v^2/2a \propto v^2$. Twice the speed takes four times the distance, the reason speed limits near schools are low

problems.prompt: A stone dropped from rest off a bridge hits the water ${{t}}$ s later. How high is the bridge, in m? (No air resistance.)

parts.label: y
parts.explain: From rest, $h = \tfrac12gt^2$. The distance grows with the square of the time: the stone falls 4.9 m in the first second and 14.7 m in the next

problems.prompt: A ball is thrown straight up. At the very top of its path, what are its velocity and acceleration?

parts.label: a
parts.explain: Velocity is zero for an instant as it changes sign, but it is still changing, so the acceleration is $g$ downward the whole flight. On a $v$–$t$ graph the line crosses zero with the same slope

problems.prompt: Two cyclists ${{D}}$ m apart ride straight toward each other at ${{v1}}$ m/s and ${{v2}}$ m/s. How long until they meet, in s?

parts.label: y
parts.explain: In one rider's frame the other approaches at $v_1 + v_2$, so $t = D/(v_1 + v_2)$. Riding the same way, the gap closes at $v_1 - v_2$

problems.prompt: A displacement has components ${{a}}$ m east and ${{b}}$ m north. At what angle north of east does it point, in degrees?

parts.label: y
parts.explain: $\tan\theta = \dfrac{\text{north}}{\text{east}}$; the magnitude is $\sqrt{a^2 + b^2}$. Check the quadrant: atan alone cannot tell (3, 4) from (−3, −4)

problems.prompt: A ball rolls off a table at a fixed speed. The table is made ${{f}}$ times as high. By what factor does the horizontal distance to landing change?

parts.label: y
parts.explain: Fall time is $\sqrt{2h/g}$ and the horizontal distance is $v\,t$, so $x \propto \sqrt h$. Four times the height only doubles the distance

problems.prompt: A ball is launched at ${{v}}$ m/s, ${{th}}^\circ$ above the horizontal. How high does it rise above the launch point, in m?

parts.label: y
parts.explain: Only the vertical component $v\sin\theta$ fights gravity: $H = \dfrac{(v\sin\theta)^2}{2g}$. The horizontal component carries on unchanged and does not help it climb

problems.prompt: A boat moves at ${{vb}}$ m/s relative to the water, in a river flowing at ${{vc}}$ m/s. At what angle upstream of straight across must it head to land directly opposite, in degrees?

parts.label: y
parts.explain: The upstream part of the boat's velocity must cancel the current: $v_b\sin\theta = v_c$. If the current were faster than the boat, no heading would work

problems.prompt: The driver of a stalled car pushes forward on the dashboard with ${{F}}$ N, while a friend outside pushes the car forward with ${{Pf}}$ N. Taking the car and driver as the system, what is the net external horizontal force, in N? (Ignore friction.)

parts.label: y
parts.explain: The driver's push on the dashboard and the dashboard's push back on the driver are both inside the system and cancel. Only the friend is outside: you cannot push your own car from the inside

problems.prompt: A ${{m1}}$ kg mass sits at $x = 0$. Where must a ${{m2}}$ kg mass go so the centre of mass is at $x = {{xc}}$ m?

parts.label: y
parts.explain: $x_{cm} = \dfrac{m_1x_1 + m_2x_2}{m_1 + m_2}$; solve for $x_2$. A light mass has to go far out to pull the centre toward it

cases.f: the normal force on a book resting on a table
the friction on a box sliding across a floor
the buoyant force on a floating boat
the drag on a falling skydiver
the tension pulling a sled forward

problems.prompt: What object exerts {{f}}?

parts.label: a
parts.explain: Every force is a push or pull by one named object on another. If you cannot name the agent (motion, speed, momentum, "inertia"), it is not a force

problems.prompt: A crate has four forces on it: ${{a}}$ N right, ${{b}}$ N left, its ${{W}}$ N weight down, and a ${{N}}$ N push up from the floor. What is the magnitude of the net force, in N?

parts.label: y
parts.explain: Add by components: $F_x = a - b$, $F_y = N - W$, then $|F| = \sqrt{F_x^2 + F_y^2}$. If the floor pushes less than the weight, the crate presses into it no less: that only happens when something else holds it up

problems.prompt: A ${{M}}$ kg truck and a ${{m}}$ kg car collide. What is the ratio of the car's acceleration to the truck's during the collision?

parts.label: y
parts.explain: The forces are a third-law pair: equal in size. With equal forces, $a = F/m$, so the lighter car accelerates $M/m$ times as much. The forces are equal; the damage is not

problems.prompt: A ${{m}}$ kg block is held at rest on a frictionless ${{th}}^\circ$ incline by a rope parallel to the slope. What is the tension, in N?

parts.label: y
parts.explain: Along the slope only the component $mg\sin\theta$ pulls the block down; the rope balances it. The normal force takes $mg\cos\theta$ across the slope

problems.prompt: The net force on an object is multiplied by ${{fF}}$ and its mass by ${{fm}}$. By what factor does its acceleration change?

parts.label: y
parts.explain: $a = F_{net}/m$: proportional to force, inversely proportional to mass

problems.prompt: A ${{m1}}$ kg block on a frictionless table is tied over a light pulley at the edge to a hanging ${{m2}}$ kg mass. What is their acceleration, in m/s²?

parts.label: y
parts.explain: Only the hanging weight $m_2g$ drives the system, but it accelerates both masses: $a = \dfrac{m_2g}{m_1 + m_2}$. The tension, $m_1a$, is less than $m_2g$

expect.y: solve([Eq(Symbol('T'), m1*x), Eq(m2*Rational(98, 10) - Symbol('T'), m2*x)], [x, Symbol('T')])[x]

problems.prompt: A block slides down a frictionless incline with acceleration ${{a}}$ m/s². What is the angle of the incline, in degrees?

parts.label: y
parts.explain: Without friction $a = g\sin\theta$, independent of mass. So $\theta = \sin^{-1}(a/g)$

problems.prompt: The distance between two moons' centres is multiplied by ${{f}}$. By what factor does the gravitational force between them change?

parts.label: y
parts.explain: Inverse square: $F = Gm_1m_2/r^2$. Twice as far, a quarter of the force

problems.prompt: A planet has ${{fM}}$ times the Earth's mass and ${{fR}}$ times its radius. What is $g$ at its surface as a multiple of Earth's?

parts.label: y
parts.explain: $g = GM/R^2$: up with mass, down with the square of the radius. A planet twice as wide and eight times as massive has twice our gravity

problems.prompt: A car at ${{v}}$ m/s locks its brakes and skids to a stop on a road with $\mu_k = {{mu}}$. How far does it skid, in m?

parts.label: y
parts.explain: Friction $\mu mg$ gives deceleration $\mu g$, so $d = \dfrac{v^2}{2\mu g}$. The mass cancels: a loaded truck skids no farther than an empty one on the same tyres

problems.prompt: A board is tilted slowly with a block on it. The coefficient of static friction is ${{mu}}$. At what angle does the block start to slide, in degrees?

parts.label: y
parts.explain: It slips when $mg\sin\theta$ exceeds the maximum $\mu_s mg\cos\theta$: $\tan\theta = \mu_s$. Measuring this angle is a quick way to find $\mu_s$

problems.prompt: Two identical springs, each with $k = {{k}}$ N/m, are joined {{kind == 0 ? "end to end (in series)" : "side by side (in parallel)"}}. What is the spring constant of the pair, in N/m?

parts.label: y
parts.explain: In series each spring carries the whole force and stretches the full amount, so the total stretch doubles: $k/2$. In parallel they share the force: $2k$. The rules are the reverse of resistors

expect.y: solve(Eq(1/x, 1/k + 1/k), x)[0] if kind == 0 else k + k

problems.prompt: A car's speed around a curve is multiplied by ${{fv}}$ and the radius by ${{fr}}$. By what factor does the centripetal acceleration change?

parts.label: y
parts.explain: $a_c = v^2/r$. Doubling speed on the same curve needs four times the grip

problems.prompt: A curve of radius ${{r}}$ m is banked at ${{th}}^\circ$. At what speed can a car take it with no friction needed, in m/s?

parts.label: y
parts.explain: Vertically $N\cos\theta = mg$; horizontally $N\sin\theta = mv^2/r$. Dividing, $\tan\theta = \dfrac{v^2}{rg}$. Slower and friction must hold the car up the bank; faster and it must hold it down

problems.prompt: A satellite's circular orbit radius is multiplied by ${{f}}$. By what factor does its period change?

parts.label: y
parts.explain: Gravity supplies the centripetal force: $GM/r^2 = 4\pi^2r/T^2$, so $T^2 \propto r^3$ (Kepler's third law). Four times the radius, eight times the period

problems.prompt: A ${{m}}$ kg object has ${{K}}$ J of kinetic energy. How fast is it moving, in m/s?

parts.label: y
parts.explain: $K = \tfrac12mv^2$, so $v = \sqrt{2K/m}$

problems.prompt: A ${{m}}$ kg box slides ${{L}}$ m down a ${{th}}^\circ$ incline. How much work does gravity do on it, in J?

parts.label: y
parts.explain: Only the drop in height matters: $W_g = mgh = mgL\sin\theta$. Equivalently, the component $mg\sin\theta$ along the slope times $L$

problems.prompt: A spring with $k = {{k}}$ N/m is already stretched ${{x1}}$ m. How much work does it take to stretch it to ${{x2}}$ m, in J?

parts.label: y
parts.explain: The area under $F = kx$ between the two stretches: $\tfrac12k(x_2^2 - x_1^2)$, not $\tfrac12k(x_2 - x_1)^2$. The second centimetre costs more than the first

problems.prompt: A ${{m}}$ kg car at ${{v}}$ m/s stops in ${{d}}$ m. What average braking force acted, in N?

parts.label: y
parts.explain: Work–energy: the brakes remove all the kinetic energy, $Fd = \tfrac12mv^2$

problems.prompt: A spring's compression is multiplied by ${{f}}$. By what factor does its stored energy change?

parts.label: y
parts.explain: $U = \tfrac12kx^2$. Twice the compression stores four times the energy

problems.prompt: How much work does it take to lift a ${{m}}$ kg probe from the Earth's surface to a height of ${{k}}$ Earth radii (ignoring any speed it is given), in GJ? ($GM_E = 3.986 \times 10^{14}$ m³/s², $R_E = 6.371 \times 10^6$ m.)

parts.label: y
parts.explain: Far from the surface use $U = -GMm/r$: $W = GMm\left(\dfrac1{R} - \dfrac1{(k+1)R}\right)$. Using $mgh$ here overestimates, because $g$ weakens with height

problems.prompt: A pendulum ${{L}}$ m long is released from rest at ${{th}}^\circ$ from vertical. How fast is the bob moving at the bottom, in m/s?

parts.label: y
parts.explain: The bob drops $h = L(1 - \cos\theta)$; the string does no work, so $v = \sqrt{2gh}$

problems.prompt: A box slides from rest ${{L}}$ m down a ${{th}}^\circ$ ramp with $\mu_k = {{mu}}$. How fast is it moving at the bottom, in m/s?

parts.label: y
parts.explain: Energy in: $mgL\sin\theta$. Energy to friction: $\mu mg\cos\theta\cdot L$. What is left is $\tfrac12mv^2$; the mass cancels

problems.prompt: A planet has the Earth's density but ${{f}}$ times its radius. What is its escape speed as a multiple of Earth's?

parts.label: y
parts.explain: $v_{esc} = \sqrt{2GM/R}$ and at fixed density $M \propto R^3$, so $v_{esc} \propto R$

problems.prompt: A car's engine delivers ${{P}}$ W to the wheels against a total resistive force of ${{F}}$ N. How fast does it cruise, in m/s?

parts.label: y
parts.explain: At constant speed the drive force equals the resistance, and power is force times velocity: $P = Fv$

problems.prompt: A ${{m1}}$ kg cart moves at ${{v1}}$ m/s and a ${{m2}}$ kg cart at ${{v2}}$ m/s along the same track. What is the velocity of their centre of mass, in m/s?

parts.label: y
parts.explain: Total momentum over total mass. It is the one velocity a collision between them cannot change

problems.prompt: A kick's force rises steadily from zero to ${{F}}$ N and falls back to zero, a triangle lasting ${{t}}$ s on a force–time graph. What impulse does it deliver, in N·s?

parts.label: y
parts.explain: Impulse is the area under $F$–$t$: a triangle, $\tfrac12F_{max}\Delta t$. The average force is half the peak

expect.y: integrate(2*F*Symbol('s')/t, (Symbol('s'), 0, t/2)) + integrate(2*F*(t - Symbol('s'))/t, (Symbol('s'), t/2, t))

problems.prompt: A shell at rest bursts into two pieces of ${{m1}}$ kg and ${{m2}}$ kg. What is the ratio of the lighter piece's kinetic energy to the heavier one's?

parts.label: y
parts.explain: Equal and opposite momenta: $K = p^2/2m$, so with the same $p$ the lighter piece gets the larger share, in the ratio $m_2/m_1$. A rifle's bullet carries nearly all the energy

problems.prompt: A ${{m1}}$ kg car heading east at ${{v1}}$ m/s collides with a ${{m2}}$ kg car heading north at ${{v2}}$ m/s, and they stick. In what direction does the wreck move, in degrees north of east?

parts.label: y
parts.explain: Momentum is conserved in each direction separately: east $m_1v_1$, north $m_2v_2$. The wreck moves along the total, at $\tan\theta = \dfrac{m_2v_2}{m_1v_1}$; the shared mass cancels

problems.prompt: A ${{m1}}$ kg cart hits a ${{m2}}$ kg cart at rest and they stick. What fraction of the original kinetic energy is lost?

parts.label: y
parts.explain: The final speed is $\dfrac{m_1v}{m_1 + m_2}$, which leaves $\dfrac{m_1}{m_1 + m_2}$ of the kinetic energy; the rest, $\dfrac{m_2}{m_1 + m_2}$, goes to heat and deformation. Equal masses lose half

problems.prompt: A ${{m1}}$ kg cart hits a ${{m2}}$ kg cart at rest; they stick and move off at ${{vf}}$ m/s. How fast was the first cart moving, in m/s?

parts.label: y
parts.explain: Momentum: $m_1v = (m_1 + m_2)v_f$. Kinetic energy is not conserved, so it cannot be used here

problems.prompt: A ${{m1}}$ kg ball collides elastically head-on with a ${{m2}}$ kg ball at rest. What fraction of its kinetic energy does it hand over?

parts.label: y
parts.explain: The target leaves at $\dfrac{2m_1}{m_1 + m_2}v$, carrying $\dfrac{4m_1m_2}{(m_1 + m_2)^2}$ of the energy. Equal masses transfer all of it, which is why reactor moderators use light nuclei

expect.y: (Rational(1, 2)*m2*solve([Eq(m1*Symbol('v'), m1*Symbol('a') + m2*x), Eq(x - Symbol('a'), Symbol('v'))], [Symbol('a'), x])[x]**2)/(Rational(1, 2)*m1*Symbol('v')**2)

problems.prompt: A ${{m}}$ kg bullet embeds in a ${{M}}$ kg block hanging on a string, and the block swings up ${{h}}$ cm. How fast was the bullet moving, in m/s?

parts.label: y
parts.explain: Work backward: the swing gives the speed just after impact, $V = \sqrt{2gh}$ (energy). The collision conserves momentum, not energy: $mv = (m + M)V$

problems.prompt: A wheel spinning at ${{w}}$ rad/s slows steadily to rest in ${{t}}$ s. How many revolutions does it make while stopping?

parts.label: y
parts.explain: Average angular speed is $\omega_0/2$, so $\Delta\theta = \tfrac12\omega_0t$ radians; divide by $2\pi$ per revolution

problems.prompt: A bicycle moves at ${{v}}$ m/s on wheels of radius ${{r}}$ m without slipping. How many revolutions per minute do the wheels turn?

parts.label: y
parts.explain: Rolling without slipping means $v = \omega r$. Then $\omega$ in rad/s × 60 / $2\pi$ gives rpm

problems.prompt: A bolt needs ${{tau}}$ N·m of torque. You push on a wrench ${{L}}$ m from the bolt at ${{th}}^\circ$ to the handle. What force do you need, in N?

parts.label: y
parts.explain: $\tau = rF\sin\theta$: only the part of the force perpendicular to the handle turns it. Pushing at 90° and at the end of the handle takes the least force

problems.prompt: A flywheel is rebuilt with ${{fm}}$ times the mass and ${{fr}}$ times the radius, same shape. By what factor does its rotational inertia change?

parts.label: y
parts.explain: $I = cMR^2$ for any fixed shape: linear in mass, square in size. Mass far from the axis counts most

problems.prompt: A uniform disk (${{M}}$ kg, radius ${{R}}$ m) spins about an axis perpendicular to it through a point on its rim. What is its rotational inertia, in kg·m²?

parts.label: y
parts.explain: Parallel axis: $I = I_{cm} + Md^2 = \tfrac12MR^2 + MR^2 = \tfrac32MR^2$

problems.prompt: A ${{m1}}$ kg child sits ${{d1}}$ m from a seesaw's pivot. How far on the other side must a ${{m2}}$ kg child sit to balance it, in m?

parts.label: y
parts.explain: Balance means the torques cancel: $m_1gd_1 = m_2gd_2$. The heavier child sits closer

problems.prompt: The same torque is applied to a uniform disk and then to one of the same mass but ${{f}}$ times the radius. By what factor does the angular acceleration change?

parts.label: y
parts.explain: $\alpha = \tau/I$ and $I = \tfrac12MR^2$, so $\alpha \propto 1/R^2$

problems.prompt: A ${{m}}$ kg mass hangs from a rope wrapped around a uniform disk pulley of mass ${{M}}$ kg free to turn. What is the tension in the rope, in N?

parts.label: y
parts.explain: For the mass: $mg - T = ma$. For the disk: $TR = \tfrac12MR^2\,(a/R)$, so $T = \tfrac12Ma$. Together $T = \dfrac{mgM}{2m + M}$, less than $mg$ because the mass accelerates

expect.y: solve([Eq(m*Rational(98, 10) - x, m*Symbol('a')), Eq(x, M*Symbol('a')/2)], [x, Symbol('a')])[x]

problems.prompt: {{shape}} rolls without slipping ($I = c\,MR^2$, $c = {{c|4}}$). What fraction of its kinetic energy is rotational?

parts.label: y
parts.explain: With $\omega = v/R$, $K_{rot} = \tfrac12cMv^2$ and $K_{tr} = \tfrac12Mv^2$, so the rotational share is $\dfrac{c}{1 + c}$. A hoop splits evenly; a sphere keeps most in translation, which is why it wins the race

problems.prompt: A constant ${{tau}}$ N·m torque turns a flywheel ($I = {{Iw}}$ kg·m²) from rest through ${{n}}$ revolutions. How fast is it then spinning, in rad/s?

parts.label: y
parts.explain: Rotational work–energy: $W = \tau\,\Delta\theta = \tfrac12I\omega^2$, with $\Delta\theta = 2\pi n$ radians

problems.prompt: A uniform disk (${{M}}$ kg, radius ${{R}}$ m) spins at ${{w}}$ rad/s about its axis. What is its angular momentum, in kg·m²/s?

parts.label: y
parts.explain: $L = I\omega$ with $I = \tfrac12MR^2$ for a disk about its axis

problems.prompt: A ${{tau}}$ N·m braking torque acts on a wheel ($I = {{Iw}}$ kg·m²) spinning at ${{w}}$ rad/s. How long until it stops, in s?

parts.label: y
parts.explain: Angular impulse equals the change in angular momentum: $\tau\,\Delta t = I\omega$

problems.prompt: A spinning skater pulls in her arms, cutting her rotational inertia to $1/{{k}}$ of its value. By what factor does her rotational kinetic energy change?

parts.label: y
parts.explain: $L$ is conserved, so $\omega$ goes up by $k$; $K = \dfrac{L^2}{2I}$ goes up by $k$ too. The extra energy is the work her arms do pulling inward

problems.prompt: {{shape}} ($c = {{c}}$ in $I = cMR^2$) rolls from rest down a ramp; a block slides down an identical frictionless ramp. What is the ratio of the rolling object's speed at the bottom to the block's?

parts.label: y
parts.explain: The same $mgh$ must also pay for spin: $mgh = \tfrac12(1 + c)mv^2$ against $\tfrac12mv^2$. The ratio is $1/\sqrt{1 + c}$, whatever the height

problems.prompt: A body orbits the Sun with a semi-major axis of ${{a}}$ AU. What is its period, in years?

parts.label: y
parts.explain: Kepler's third law in solar units: $T^2 = a^3$ with $T$ in years and $a$ in AU, because the Earth gives 1 = 1

problems.prompt: A satellite moves to a circular orbit ${{f}}$ times the radius. By what factor does its kinetic energy change?

parts.label: y
parts.explain: $\dfrac{mv^2}{r} = \dfrac{GMm}{r^2}$ gives $K = \dfrac{GMm}{2r} \propto 1/r$. Higher orbits are slower, though their total energy is greater

cases.law: F = −k (a constant, always toward the centre)
F = −m g sin θ for a pendulum at large angles
F = −m g θ for a pendulum at small angles

problems.prompt: Does a restoring force {{law}} produce simple harmonic motion?

parts.label: a
choice: Yes: the force is proportional to the displacement
No: the period would depend on the amplitude
parts.explain: Simple harmonic means $F \propto -x$ exactly; then the period is the same for every amplitude. Any other force law still oscillates, but the period changes with amplitude

problems.prompt: A ${{m}}$ kg mass oscillates on a spring with $k = {{k}}$ N/m. What is the period, in s?

parts.label: y
parts.explain: $T = 2\pi\sqrt{m/k}$: heavier is slower, stiffer is faster. The amplitude and $g$ do not appear

problems.prompt: The mass on a spring is multiplied by ${{fm}}$ and the spring constant by ${{fk}}$. By what factor does the period change?

parts.label: y
parts.explain: $T \propto \sqrt{m/k}$. Four times the mass on the same spring doubles the period

problems.prompt: A pendulum clock is taken where $g$ is $1/{{f}}$ of Earth's. By what factor does its period change?

parts.label: y
parts.explain: $T = 2\pi\sqrt{L/g}$. Weaker gravity, slower swing: on the Moon ($g/6$) the period is $\sqrt6 \approx 2.45$ times longer

problems.prompt: An oscillator has amplitude ${{A}}$ m and period ${{T}}$ s. What is its maximum acceleration, in m/s²?

parts.label: y
parts.explain: $a = -\omega^2x$ is largest at the turning points: $a_{max} = A\omega^2$ with $\omega = 2\pi/T$. Speed is zero there

problems.prompt: An oscillator is at ${{r}}$ of its amplitude from equilibrium. What fraction of its energy is kinetic?

parts.label: y
parts.explain: Total energy is $\tfrac12kA^2$ and potential is $\tfrac12kx^2$, so $K/E = 1 - (x/A)^2$. At half amplitude three quarters of the energy is kinetic

problems.prompt: A solid cube is replaced by one of the same material with ${{f}}$ times the edge length. By what factor does its mass change?

parts.label: y
parts.explain: Same density, so mass goes with volume, $s^3$. Twice the size, eight times the mass, but only four times the area

problems.prompt: A ${{m}}$ kg person stands with all her weight on one heel of area ${{A}}$ cm². What pressure does the heel exert on the floor, in MPa?

parts.label: y
parts.explain: $P = F/A$ with $A$ in m² (1 cm² = $10^{-4}$ m²). A stiletto heel presses harder than an elephant's foot

problems.prompt: At what depth in {{fl}} (${{rho}}$ kg/m³) does the gauge pressure reach one atmosphere (101.3 kPa), in m?

parts.label: y
parts.explain: $P_{gauge} = \rho gh$. About 10 m of water equals one atmosphere; the same pressure takes only 0.76 m of mercury, which is why barometers use it

problems.prompt: A ${{V}}$ cm³ metal block (${{rho}}$ kg/m³) hangs from a spring scale, fully under water. What does the scale read, in N?

parts.label: y
parts.explain: Weight minus buoyancy: $(\rho - \rho_w)Vg$. The water pushes up with the weight of the water the block displaces

problems.prompt: The small piston (${{A1}}$ cm²) of a hydraulic lift is pushed down ${{d1}}$ cm. How far does the large piston (${{A2}}$ cm²) rise, in cm?

parts.label: y
parts.explain: The liquid's volume is fixed: $A_1d_1 = A_2d_2$. The force is multiplied by $A_2/A_1$ and the distance divided by it, so the work is the same: no free energy

problems.prompt: A hose nozzle narrows the outlet to $1/{{f}}$ of the hose's diameter. By what factor is the water faster at the outlet?

parts.label: y
parts.explain: Continuity: $A_1v_1 = A_2v_2$, and area goes as diameter squared. A third of the diameter, nine times the speed

problems.prompt: A hadron has quark content {{q}} (capital = antiquark). What kind is it?

parts.label: a
choice: A baryon: three quarks, baryon number +1
A meson: a quark and an antiquark, baryon number 0
An antibaryon: three antiquarks, baryon number -1
parts.explain: Each quark has baryon number $+\tfrac13$ and each antiquark $-\tfrac13$. Baryons are fermions; mesons are bosons. No free quark has ever been seen

problems.prompt: Do charge, baryon number and the lepton numbers all balance? {{rx}}

parts.label: a
choice: Yes: nothing forbids it on these grounds
No: baryon number does not balance
No: a lepton number does not balance
parts.explain: Check in order: charge, baryon number, then electron and muon lepton number separately. Beta decay needs an antineutrino exactly so that the electron's lepton number is cancelled. A reaction that passes may still be forbidden by energy

cases.q: Which particle carries the electromagnetic force?
Which particles carry the weak force?
Which particle carries the strong force between quarks?
Which interaction is responsible for beta decay?
Which interaction changes a quark's flavour?
Which interaction holds a proton together?
Which carrier has mass, giving its force a very short range?

parts.label: a
parts.explain: Photon: electromagnetic, massless, infinite range. W and Z: weak, about 80 and 91 GeV, so the range is tiny; only the weak force changes flavour. Gluons: strong, massless but confined. Gravity has no place in the Standard Model

problems.prompt: What is the rest energy of a particle of mass ${{m|6}}$ u, in MeV? (1 u = 931.494 MeV/c².)

parts.label: r
parts.explain: $E = mc^2$, and in these units the conversion is a single multiplication. Worth knowing: electron 0.511 MeV, muon 105.7 MeV, proton 938.3 MeV, neutron 939.6 MeV

problems.prompt: What is the least energy a photon needs to create {{pair}}, in MeV? (Rest energy ${{m}}$ MeV each.)

parts.label: r
parts.explain: Twice the rest energy: matter is made in particle-antiparticle pairs so that charge and lepton or baryon number stay zero. Annihilation runs it backward, giving two 0.511 MeV photons for an electron and positron at rest

problems.prompt: A particle moves at ${{b}}c$. What is its Lorentz factor $\gamma$?

parts.label: r
parts.explain: $\gamma = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{1 - v^2/c^2}}$. Its lifetime in the lab is $\gamma$ times its lifetime at rest and its total energy is $\gamma mc^2$. $0.6c$ gives 1.25 and $0.8c$ gives 1.67, the 3-4-5 triangle

problems.prompt: A muon lives $2.2$ µs at rest. How far does one travel on average at nearly the speed of light with $\gamma = {{g}}$, in km? ($c = 3.0 \times 10^5$ km/s.)

parts.label: r
parts.explain: Its lifetime in our frame is $\gamma \times 2.2$ µs. Without time dilation a muon would cover about 0.66 km; that cosmic-ray muons made 15 km up reach the ground is a direct test of relativity

problems.prompt: {{p}} ($Z = {{Zp}}$) undergoes ${{na}}$ alpha decay{{na > 1 ? "s" : ""}} and ${{nb}}$ beta-minus decay{{nb == 1 ? "" : "s"}}. What is the atomic number of the result?

parts.label: r
parts.explain: Each alpha takes away 2 protons and 4 nucleons; each beta-minus turns a neutron into a proton, adding 1 to $Z$ and leaving $A$ alone. The mass number here is ${{A - 4*na}}$. The order of the decays does not matter

problems.prompt: The decay series from {{p}} ($Z = {{Z1}}$) ends at {{d}} ($Z = {{Z2}}$). How many beta-minus decays does it contain?

parts.label: r
parts.explain: Only alphas change the mass number, so count them first: $({{A1}} - {{A2}})/4 = {{(A1 - A2)/4}}$. They lower $Z$ by ${{(A1 - A2)/2}}$; the betas must bring it back up to ${{Z2}}$

expect.r: solve([Eq(A1 - 4*x, A2), Eq(Z1 - 2*x + Symbol('b'), Z2)], [x, Symbol('b')], dict=True)[0][Symbol('b')]

problems.prompt: What is the activity of 1.0 µg of {{iso}} (half-life ${{T}}$ {{unit}}, which is ${{sec}}$ s), in MBq? ($N_A = 6.022 \times 10^{23}$.)

parts.label: r
parts.explain: $A = \lambda N$ with $\lambda = \dfrac{\ln 2}{T_{1/2}}$ in s⁻¹ and $N = \dfrac{m}{M}N_A$. A short half-life means a high specific activity: the same mass decays faster

problems.prompt: Convert ${{a}}$ mCi to MBq. (1 Ci = $3.7 \times 10^{10}$ Bq.)

parts.label: r
parts.explain: 1 mCi = 37 MBq. A becquerel is one decay per second, which is tiny; the curie is the activity of about a gram of radium

problems.prompt: A sample has ${{f*100}}\%$ of the carbon-14 activity of living material. How old is it, in years? (Half-life 5730 years.)

parts.label: r
parts.explain: $t = T_{1/2}\,\dfrac{\ln(1/f)}{\ln 2}$. Each halving is 5730 years; after about ten half-lives too little is left to measure, which sets the limit of the method near 50,000 years

problems.prompt: A radionuclide has a physical half-life of ${{Tp}}$ and is cleared from the body with a biological half-life of ${{Tb}}$ (same units). What is its effective half-life?

parts.label: r
parts.explain: The two removal rates add, so the half-lives combine like resistors in parallel: $\dfrac1{T_{eff}} = \dfrac1{T_p} + \dfrac1{T_b}$. The result is always shorter than either

cases.q: A long-lived parent has been sealed with its short-lived daughter for many daughter half-lives. How do their activities compare?

problems.prompt: What is the specific charge (charge ÷ mass) of {{p}}, in units of $10^{7}$ C/kg? (Mass ${{m}}$ u, 1 u = $1.6605 \times 10^{-27}$ kg, $e = 1.602 \times 10^{-19}$ C.)

cases.o1: A transition state, not a minimum

cases.o3: Equivalent to optimising in the large basis

parts.label: v
parts.explain: The Hessian and the imaginary mode are what turn a stationary point into a claim

problems.prompt: A bond scan gives energies {{e1}}, {{e2}}, {{e3}}, {{e4}} hartree at {{r1}}, {{r2}}, {{r3}}, {{r4}} angstrom. At which distance is the minimum?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: The lowest energy on the scan is the equilibrium value; a minimum at the edge of the scan means the range was too narrow

problems.prompt: A reaction with {{nel}} electrons has a free-energy change of {{dg}} kJ/mol. What is the standard potential (V), using F = 96485.33212 C/mol?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: E = -dG/(nF); a computed potential also needs a reference electrode to be comparable with experiment

problems.prompt: A CCSD(T) job on a {{k1}}-function basis took {{hr}} hours. Scaling as the seventh power, how many hours would a {{k2}}-function basis take?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: The arithmetic that decides a project: at N^7 a modest basis increase turns hours into weeks

cases.q: A paper reports 'DFT energies' with no functional named. The result is:
cases.o1: Not reproducible: the functional is the method
cases.o3: Fine if the basis is given
cases.o4: Only a problem for weak interactions

cases.q: A reported interaction energy with no mention of counterpoise or basis is:
cases.o1: Hard to compare with anything, because BSSE could account for much of it

cases.q: Two papers disagree on a barrier height by 5 kcal/mol. The first thing to compare:
cases.o1: The functional, basis and geometry each used

cases.q: Reporting a geometry as 'optimised' without the level is a problem because:
cases.o1: The energy was computed at a geometry nobody else can reproduce

parts.label: v
parts.explain: The same standard as the design pipeline: a number nobody can regenerate is not a result

problems.prompt: The function $f(x) = {{tex}}({{k}}x)$ is an eigenfunction of $\dfrac{d^2}{dx^2}$. What is its eigenvalue?

parts.label: r
parts.explain: Differentiate twice and compare with the original. An exponential $e^{\pm kx}$ returns $+k^2$ times itself; a sine or cosine returns $-k^2$ times itself. The eigenvalue is whatever constant multiplies the function you started with

problems.prompt: Normalise $\psi(x) = N\sin\dfrac{ {{n}}\pi x}{ {{L}} }$ on $0 \le x \le {{L}}$. What is $N$ (taken positive)?

parts.label: r
parts.explain: $\displaystyle\int_0^L \sin^2\dfrac{n\pi x}{L}\,dx = \dfrac L2$ for any whole number $n$ (sine squared averages one half), so $N^2\dfrac L2 = 1$ and $N = \sqrt{2/L}$

problems.prompt: A particle is in the state $\psi = c\,({{a}}\,\psi_1 + {{b}}\,\psi_2)$, where $\psi_1$ and $\psi_2$ are normalised eigenfunctions with energies $E_1$ and $E_2$. What is the probability that an energy measurement gives $E_2$?

parts.label: r
parts.explain: Probabilities are squared coefficients after normalising: $P_2 = \dfrac{ {{b}}^2}{ {{a}}^2 + {{b}}^2}$. The cross terms vanish because the eigenfunctions are orthogonal

expect.r: [s[x] for s in solve([Eq(Symbol('u') + x, 1), Eq(x*a**2, Symbol('u')*b**2)], [x, Symbol('u')], dict=True)][0]

problems.prompt: A particle in a box is in the state $c\,({{a}}\,\psi_1 + {{b}}\,\psi_{ {{m}} })$. What is the expectation value of its energy, in units of the ground-state energy $E_1$?

parts.label: r
parts.explain: Weight each energy by its probability: $E_n = n^2E_1$, so $\langle E\rangle = \dfrac{ {{a}}^2(1) + {{b}}^2({{m}}^2)}{ {{a}}^2 + {{b}}^2}\,E_1$. No single measurement returns this value; it is the average of many

cases.q: A particle is in a single energy eigenstate. Does its probability density change with time?
A particle is in a superposition of two eigenstates with different energies. Does its probability density change with time?
What multiplies each eigenfunction as time passes?

parts.label: a
choice: No: the phase factor cancels in |ψ|², which is why it is called a stationary state
Yes: it oscillates at the frequency (E₂ − E₁)/h
parts.explain: Each eigenfunction carries $e^{-iE_nt/\hbar}$. In one state it disappears from $|\psi|^2$. In a superposition the two phases beat against each other, so the density sloshes at the Bohr frequency $(E_2 - E_1)/h$

problems.prompt: Evaluate the commutator $\left[\dfrac{d}{dx},\, x^{ {{n}} }\right]$ acting on a function $f$. The result is $c\,x^{ {{n - 1}} }f$. What is $c$?

parts.label: r
parts.explain: $\dfrac{d}{dx}(x^nf) - x^n\dfrac{df}{dx} = nx^{n-1}f$: the product rule leaves one term standing. With $n = 1$ this is $[d/dx, x] = 1$, the root of $[\hat x, \hat p] = i\hbar$

cases.q: position $x$ and momentum $p_x$
position $x$ and momentum $p_y$
$L^2$ and $L_z$
$L_x$ and $L_y$
the energy and $L^2$ of a hydrogen atom

problems.prompt: Can these two observables be known exactly at the same time? {{q}}

parts.label: a
choice: No: their operators do not commute
parts.explain: Two observables share a complete set of eigenfunctions, and so can both be sharp, exactly when their operators commute. $[\hat x, \hat p_x] = i\hbar$ and $[\hat L_x, \hat L_y] = i\hbar\hat L_z$ do not vanish

problems.prompt: A particle in a one-dimensional box of length $L$ is in the state $n = {{n}}$. What is the probability of finding it between $x = 0$ and $x = \tfrac{ {{fn}} }{ {{fd}} }L$?

parts.label: r
parts.explain: $P = \dfrac2L\displaystyle\int_0^{fL}\sin^2\dfrac{n\pi x}{L}\,dx = f - \dfrac{\sin(2\pi nf)}{2\pi n}$ with $f = \tfrac{ {{fn}} }{ {{fd}} }$. The second term is the quantum correction to the classical answer $f$; it vanishes whenever the interval ends on a node or an antinode pair

problems.prompt: A particle in a box of length ${{L}}$ nm is in the state $n = {{n}}$. Where is the node nearest the left wall (not counting the wall itself), in nm?

parts.label: r
parts.explain: $\sin\dfrac{n\pi x}{L} = 0$ at $x = \dfrac{kL}{n}$. State $n$ has $n - 1$ interior nodes, evenly spaced; more nodes means more curvature and more kinetic energy

expect.r: Min(*[s for s in solve(Eq(sin(n*pi*x/L), 0), x) if s > 0])

problems.prompt: In a cubic box the energy is $E = (n_x^2 + n_y^2 + n_z^2)\,\dfrac{h^2}{8mL^2}$. How many states share the level with $n_x^2 + n_y^2 + n_z^2 = {{E}}$?

parts.label: r
parts.explain: Find the sets of three positive whole numbers whose squares add to ${{E}}$, then count the distinct orderings: all equal gives 1, two equal gives 3, all different gives 6. Degeneracy comes from the symmetry of the cube

problems.prompt: An electron meets a barrier ${{dE}}$ eV higher than its energy. Inside the barrier $\psi \propto e^{-\kappa x}$ with $\kappa = \dfrac{\sqrt{2m(V - E)}}{\hbar}$. What is $\kappa$, in nm⁻¹? ($m_e = 9.109 \times 10^{-31}$ kg, $\hbar = 1.0546 \times 10^{-34}$ J·s, 1 eV = $1.602 \times 10^{-19}$ J.)

parts.label: r
parts.explain: Worth carrying: for an electron, $\kappa \approx 5.1\sqrt{(V - E)/\text{eV}}$ nm⁻¹. A 1 eV barrier lets the wavefunction leak about 0.2 nm, the scale of an atom

problems.prompt: A particle tunnels through a barrier of width ${{a}}$ nm in which its wavefunction decays with $\kappa = {{kap}}$ nm⁻¹. Estimate the transmission probability as $T \approx e^{-2\kappa a}$.

parts.label: r
parts.explain: The amplitude falls by $e^{-\kappa a}$ across the barrier and the probability is its square: $e^{-2({{kap}})({{a}})}$. Because the width sits in the exponent, a slightly thinner barrier tunnels far more, which is how a scanning tunnelling microscope resolves atoms

cases.q: an electron or a proton, at the same energy below the same barrier
hydrogen or deuterium, in the same reaction
a barrier 0.5 nm wide or one 1 nm wide
a barrier 4 eV above the particle energy or one 1 eV above

problems.prompt: Which tunnels more readily: {{q}}?

parts.label: a
parts.explain: $T \approx \exp\!\left(-2a\sqrt{2m(V - E)}/\hbar\right)$: lighter, thinner and lower all help, and each sits inside the exponent. This is why tunnelling matters for electrons and hydrogen and almost never for heavier atoms

problems.prompt: A particle on a ring has energies $E_m = \dfrac{m^2\hbar^2}{2I}$. What is the energy needed to go from $|m| = {{m1}}$ to $|m| = {{m1 + d}}$, in units of $\dfrac{\hbar^2}{2I}$?

parts.label: r
parts.explain: $\Delta E = \left[({{m1 + d}})^2 - ({{m1}})^2\right]\dfrac{\hbar^2}{2I}$. Every level except $m = 0$ is doubly degenerate (clockwise and anticlockwise), and there is no zero-point energy because $m = 0$ is allowed

problems.prompt: What is the magnitude of the orbital angular momentum for $l = {{l}}$, in units of $\hbar$? And how many values of $m_l$ does it have? Answer the magnitude.

parts.label: r
parts.explain: $|L| = \sqrt{l(l + 1)}\,\hbar$, the square root of the $\hat L^2$ eigenvalue $l(l + 1)\hbar^2$. The $z$-component is $m_l\hbar$ with $m_l = -l \dots l$, which is $2l + 1 = {{2*l + 1}}$ values; since $\sqrt{l(l+1)} > l$, the vector can never lie exactly along $z$

cases.q: the vibration of N₂ in the infrared
the vibration of HCl in the infrared
the pure rotational (microwave) spectrum of CO
the pure rotational (microwave) spectrum of H₂
a harmonic-oscillator transition from v = 0 to v = 2
a rigid-rotor absorption from J = 1 to J = 2

problems.prompt: Is this allowed? {{q}}

parts.label: a
parts.explain: Rotation absorbs only if the molecule has a permanent dipole; vibration only if the dipole changes during it. Within those, the harmonic oscillator allows $\Delta v = \pm1$ and the rigid rotor $\Delta J = \pm1$. Overtones such as $0 \to 2$ appear weakly only because real bonds are anharmonic

cases.q: How do the Einstein coefficients for absorption and stimulated emission compare (non-degenerate levels)?
How does the ratio of spontaneous to stimulated emission, A/B, depend on frequency?
What does a laser need that thermal equilibrium never provides?

parts.label: a
choice: It rises as the cube of the frequency
A population inversion: more molecules in the upper level than the lower
parts.explain: Equal $B$ coefficients mean light is as likely to drive a molecule down as up, so net absorption only reflects the population difference. $A/B = 8\pi h\nu^3/c^3$: spontaneous emission dominates in the visible and ultraviolet and is negligible at radio frequencies

problems.prompt: A dye absorbs at ${{l1}}$ nm and fluoresces at ${{l1 + d}}$ nm. What is the Stokes shift, in cm⁻¹?

parts.label: r
parts.explain: Convert each wavelength to wavenumbers, $\tilde\nu = 10^7/\lambda(\text{nm})$, then subtract. Emission is always at lower energy: the excited molecule relaxes vibrationally before it emits, and lands in a vibrationally excited ground state

problems.prompt: How much energy removes the electron from the $n = {{n}}$ level of {{sp}}, in eV? (The hydrogen ground state lies at $-13.6$ eV.)

parts.label: r
parts.explain: $E_n = -13.6\,\dfrac{Z^2}{n^2}$ eV, so ionising from level $n$ costs $13.6 \times \dfrac{ {{Zn}}^2}{ {{n}}^2}$ eV. The energy depends on $n$ alone, which is special to one-electron atoms

problems.prompt: How many orbitals are there in the shell $n = {{n}}$?

parts.label: r
parts.explain: $l$ runs from $0$ to $n - 1$ and each $l$ has $2l + 1$ orbitals: $1 + 3 + 5 + \dots = n^2$. With two spins that is $2n^2 = {{2*n^2}}$ electrons

problems.prompt: For the {{orb}} orbital of a one-electron atom with $Z = {{Zn}}$, the radial part goes as $r^{ {{n - 1}} }e^{-Zr/{{n}}a_0}$. At what radius is the electron most likely to be found, in units of $a_0$?

parts.label: r
parts.explain: Maximise the radial distribution $r^2R^2 \propto r^{ {{2*n}} }e^{-2Zr/{{n}}a_0}$: set its derivative to zero to get $r = \dfrac{n^2a_0}{Z}$. For hydrogen 1s this is exactly the Bohr radius

problems.prompt: Use Slater's rules to estimate the effective nuclear charge felt by a {{orb}} electron in {{el}} ($Z = {{Zn}}$). It has ${{same}}$ other electrons in its own group, ${{n1}}$ in the shell below and ${{n2}}$ deeper.

parts.label: r
parts.explain: For an $s$ or $p$ electron: each other electron in the same group shields 0.35, each in the next shell down 0.85, each deeper one 1.00. Shielding $= 0.35({{same}}) + 0.85({{n1}}) + 1.00({{n2}}) = {{0.35*same + 0.85*n1 + n2}}$

expect.r: Zn - sum(w*c for w, c in [(Rational(35, 100), same), (Rational(85, 100), n1), (1, n2)])

cases.q: A trial wavefunction gives an energy below the true ground-state energy. What does that tell you?
Two trial wavefunctions give −2.75 and −2.85 hartree for helium. Which is better?
How is a parameter in a trial wavefunction chosen?

parts.label: a
choice: A mistake was made: a variational energy can never fall below the true ground-state energy
The lower one, −2.85: closer to the true energy from above
By minimising the energy with respect to it
parts.explain: For any acceptable trial function, $\dfrac{\langle\phi|\hat H|\phi\rangle}{\langle\phi|\phi\rangle} \ge E_0$. So lower is better, and you improve a guess by pushing its energy down

problems.prompt: Use Hund's rules to find the ground-state term of {{el}}.

parts.label: a
parts.explain: Fill the orbitals from the highest $m_l$ down, one electron each with parallel spins before pairing. The total spin gives the multiplicity $2S + 1$ and the sum of the $m_l$ values gives $L$ (S, P, D, F for 0, 1, 2, 3). A shell with $n$ holes has the same terms as one with $n$ electrons, which is why carbon and oxygen match

problems.prompt: The ground term of {{el}} is {{term}}. Its subshell is {{more == 1 ? "more" : "less"}} than half full. What is $J$ for the ground level?

parts.label: r
parts.explain: Hund's third rule: less than half full, the lowest level has $J = |L - S|$; more than half full, $J = L + S$. Here $L = {{Lq}}$ and $S = {{Sq}}$

problems.prompt: In a term split by spin–orbit coupling with constant $A = {{A}}$ cm⁻¹, how far apart are the levels $J = {{J}}$ and $J = {{J - 1}}$, in cm⁻¹?

parts.label: r
parts.explain: The spin–orbit energy is $\tfrac12A[J(J + 1) - L(L + 1) - S(S + 1)]$, so neighbouring levels differ by $A \times$ the larger $J$: the Landé interval rule

problems.prompt: For H₂⁺ in the LCAO approximation with $H_{aa} = {{al}}$ eV, $H_{ab} = {{be}}$ eV and overlap $S = {{Sv}}$, what is the energy of the bonding orbital, in eV?

parts.label: r
parts.explain: $E_\pm = \dfrac{H_{aa} \pm H_{ab}}{1 \pm S}$. The antibonding level, $\dfrac{ {{al}} - ({{be}}) }{1 - {{Sv}} } = {{(al - be)/(1 - Sv)}}$ eV, is pushed up further than the bonding level is pulled down, because it is divided by the smaller $1 - S$

problems.prompt: What is the bond order of {{sp}}? (It has ${{nb}}$ electrons in bonding and ${{na}}$ in antibonding molecular orbitals, counting the 1s pair.)

parts.label: r
parts.explain: Bond order $= \tfrac12(\text{bonding} - \text{antibonding})$. A higher bond order means a shorter, stronger bond: removing an antibonding electron (O₂ to O₂⁺) strengthens the bond, removing a bonding one (N₂ to N₂⁺) weakens it

problems.prompt: Is {{sp}} paramagnetic or diamagnetic?

parts.label: a
parts.explain: It has ${{unp}}$ unpaired electron{{unp == 1 ? "" : "s"}} in its molecular-orbital diagram. O₂ and B₂ each put two electrons, spins parallel, into a degenerate π pair: molecular-orbital theory predicts that; a Lewis structure does not

problems.prompt: What is the hybridisation of {{sp}}?

parts.label: a
parts.explain: Count electron domains on the atom (bonded atoms plus lone pairs): ${{dom}}$. Two, three, four, five and six domains go with sp, sp², sp³, sp³d and sp³d², and with linear, trigonal planar, tetrahedral, trigonal bipyramidal and octahedral arrangements

problems.prompt: In Hückel theory the π orbitals of a linear chain of $N$ carbons have energies $\alpha + x\beta$. For {{mol}} ($N = {{N}}$), what is $x$ for orbital number ${{k}}$, counting from the lowest?

parts.label: r
parts.explain: $x_k = 2\cos\dfrac{k\pi}{N + 1}$. Since $\beta$ is negative, the largest $x$ is the lowest orbital. Ethylene gives $\pm1$; butadiene $\pm1.618$ and $\pm0.618$

problems.prompt: A geometry optimisation stops where the gradient is zero and the Hessian has ${{nneg}}$ negative eigenvalue{{nneg == 1 ? "" : "s"}} (imaginary frequenc{{nneg == 1 ? "y" : "ies"}}). What kind of point is it?

parts.label: a
choice: A first-order saddle point: a transition state
A higher-order saddle point: not chemically meaningful, keep searching
parts.explain: Zero gradient only says the surface is flat there. All curvatures positive is a minimum; exactly one negative is a transition state, a maximum along the reaction coordinate and a minimum in every other direction. Always run a frequency calculation to check

choices.a: 0 if nneg == 0 else (1 if nneg == 1 else 2)

problems.prompt: A Hartree–Fock calculation at the basis-set limit gives ${{Ehf|8}}$ hartree and the exact non-relativistic energy is ${{Ehf - dc|8}}$ hartree. What is the correlation energy, in hartree?

parts.label: r
parts.explain: $E_{corr} = E_{exact} - E_{HF}$, always negative: Hartree–Fock lets each electron see only the average of the others. It is small next to the total energy but comparable to a bond energy (1 hartree is 2625 kJ/mol), which is why post-Hartree–Fock and density-functional methods exist

problems.prompt: Two electrons occupy one spatial orbital. The one-electron energy is $h = {{h}}$ hartree and the Coulomb integral is $J = {{J}}$ hartree. What is the Hartree–Fock electronic energy, in hartree?

parts.label: r
parts.explain: $E = 2h + J$: each electron contributes its kinetic and nuclear-attraction energy $h$, and the pair repels once. There is no exchange term here because the two electrons have opposite spins; counting $2\varepsilon$ instead would count the repulsion twice

problems.prompt: Find sup |f_n(x) − f(x)| on {{dm}} for f_n(x) = {{sh}} and its pointwise limit f, at n = {{kn}}.

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Find where |f_n − f| is largest: at an endpoint, or where its derivative vanishes. Convergence is uniform exactly when this supremum tends to 0

problems.prompt: On {{dm}}, the sequence f_n(x) = {{sh}} converges:

parts.label: v
parts.explain: xⁿ on [0, 1] has a discontinuous limit, so the convergence cannot be uniform. nx/(1 + n²x²) takes the value 1/2 at x = 1/n for every n, so its supremum never shrinks

problems.prompt: The M-test bounds Σ cos(nx)/n^{{kp}} (n from 1 to ∞) by Σ 1/n^{{kp}}. Evaluate that bounding sum.

parts.label: v
parts.explain: |cos(nx)/n^p| ≤ 1/n^p for every x, and Σ 1/n^p converges for p > 1, so the series converges uniformly on the whole real line and its sum is continuous

cases.q: f_n is n on (0, 1/n) and 0 elsewhere on [0, 1]. Then f_n → 0 pointwise, but ∫ f_n = 1 for every n. This is possible because the convergence is not:
A uniform limit of continuous functions is always:
f_n(x) = sin(nx)/√n converges uniformly to 0, yet f_n′ does not converge. So uniform convergence of f_n does not control:
A power series converges uniformly on:
cases.o1: Every closed disc strictly inside its disc of convergence
cases.o2: Its whole open disc of convergence, always

cases.q: If f_n → f uniformly on [a, b] and each f_n is Riemann integrable, then the integral of f_n tends to:

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Uniform convergence passes limits through integrals for free and through continuity for free; for derivatives you need the derivatives themselves to converge uniformly

problems.prompt: In R³, find the distance between ({{a1}}, {{a2}}, {{a3}}) and the origin in the {{nm}} norm.

parts.label: v
parts.explain: ℓ¹ adds the absolute values, ℓ² is the Euclidean length, ℓ∞ takes the largest absolute value

problems.prompt: What is the largest possible value of ‖x‖₁/‖x‖₂ for a non-zero vector x in R^{{kn}}?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: By Cauchy-Schwarz ‖x‖₁ ≤ √n ‖x‖₂, with equality when every coordinate has the same size. Constants like this are what Lipschitz equivalence of norms means

the integers with the usual distance
the polynomials on [0, 1] with the uniform norm

problems.prompt: Is this metric space complete: {{sp}}?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Find a Cauchy sequence whose limit has left the space: rationals approaching √2, 1/n in (0, 1), Taylor polynomials approaching eˣ, continuous ramps approaching a step in the integral norm. In the integers a Cauchy sequence is eventually constant

cases.q: A closed subset of a complete metric space is:
Completeness is not a topological property: (0, 1) and the real line are homeomorphic, but only one is complete. The complete one is:
A uniformly Cauchy sequence of continuous functions on [a, b] converges uniformly to a continuous function. This says C[a, b] is:
Which theorem needs completeness as a hypothesis?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Completeness is what lets you prove something exists by building a Cauchy sequence that approximates it

problems.prompt: A contraction with constant k = {{kk}} is iterated from x₀, and d(x₁, x₀) = {{kd}}. What is the least n for which the bound kⁿ d(x₁, x₀)/(1 − k) is below {{kt}}?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Solve kⁿ < tolerance × (1 − k)/d by taking logarithms, or tabulate the powers of k. The bound needs only the first step, not the fixed point

problems.prompt: f(x) = {{sh}} maps [{{ka}}, {{kb}}] into itself. Find its contraction constant, the largest value of |f′| on the interval.

parts.label: v
parts.explain: By the mean value theorem |f(x) − f(y)| ≤ sup|f′| · |x − y|, so f is a contraction when that supremum is below 1

problems.prompt: f(x, y) = {{sh}} has a critical point at the origin. Find the determinant of its Hessian there.

parts.label: v
parts.explain: The Hessian is the matrix of second partials; its determinant is f_xx f_yy − f_xy². Positive with f_xx > 0 is a minimum, positive with f_xx < 0 a maximum, negative a saddle

problems.prompt: f(x, y) = {{sh}} has a critical point at the origin. It is:

parts.label: v
choice: Not decided by the Hessian test
parts.explain: Compute f_xx f_yy − f_xy². Negative is a saddle; positive takes the sign of f_xx; zero (as for x⁴ + y⁴, whose Hessian vanishes) leaves the second-order test silent, whatever the point really is

problems.prompt: Find the supremum of the set {{st}}.

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Find a value the set approaches or reaches from below and check nothing smaller is still an upper bound

problems.prompt: Does the set {{st}} contain its supremum?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: A supremum that belongs to the set is a maximum. Sets that creep up to a bound without reaching it have a supremum but no maximum

problems.prompt: What is the least positive integer n with 1/n < {{ke}}?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: 1/n < ε exactly when n > 1/ε, so take the first integer strictly beyond 1/ε

cases.q: Which property distinguishes the real numbers from the rational numbers?
cases.o1: Every non-empty set bounded above has a least upper bound
cases.o2: Between any two elements lies another
cases.o3: Addition and multiplication obey the field axioms

cases.q: Between any two distinct real numbers there is:
cases.o1: Both a rational and an irrational number
cases.o2: A rational but not always an irrational

cases.q: The proof that √2 is irrational assumes √2 = a/b in lowest terms and shows:
cases.o1: Both a and b are even

cases.q: A bounded increasing sequence of real numbers must:

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Density and the field axioms hold in the rationals too; the least upper bound axiom is what fills in the gaps

problems.prompt: a_n = {{sh}} converges to {{kl}}. What is the least N such that |a_n − {{kl}}| < {{ke}} for every n ≥ N?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Write |a_n − L| as a simple expression in n and solve the inequality; the answer is the first integer that satisfies it

problems.prompt: Find the limit of a_n = {{sh}} as n → ∞.

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Divide through by the dominant term, or recognise a standard limit such as (1 + a/n)ⁿ → e^a and n^(1/n) → 1

problems.prompt: x₁ = 1 and x_(n+1) = √({{kk}} + x_n). The sequence is increasing and bounded. Find its limit.

parts.label: v
parts.explain: The limit L satisfies L = √(k + L), so L² − L − k = 0; take the positive root. The step that needs proof is that the limit exists at all

cases.q: Bolzano-Weierstrass says every bounded sequence of real numbers has:
A sequence is Cauchy when:
cases.o1: Its terms are eventually within ε of each other, for every ε

cases.q: a_n = 1 + 1/2 + … + 1/n has a_(n+1) − a_n → 0. The sequence:
In the real numbers, a sequence converges exactly when it is:
The sequence (−1)ⁿ is bounded and has:

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Consecutive terms closing up is weaker than Cauchy: the harmonic sums gain a full 1/2 between n and 2n however large n is

problems.prompt: The isothermal gas-phase reaction {{rx}}, $-r_A = kC_A^{ {{n}} }$ with $k = {{k}}$ {{ku}}, is fed as {{feed}} at $v_0 = {{v0}}$ L/min, $C_{A0} = {{CA0}}$ mol/L, no pressure drop. What PFR volume (L) reaches $X = {{X}}$?

parts.explain: $V = F_{A0}\int_0^X \dfrac{dX}{-r_A}$ with $C_A = C_{A0}\dfrac{1 - X}{1 + \varepsilon X}$. First order: $V = \dfrac{v_0}{k}\left[(1 + \varepsilon)\ln\dfrac1{1 - X} - \varepsilon X\right]$. Second order: $V = \dfrac{v_0}{kC_{A0}}\left[2\varepsilon(1 + \varepsilon)\ln(1 - X) + \varepsilon^2X + \dfrac{(1 + \varepsilon)^2X}{1 - X}\right]$. Expansion ($\varepsilon > 0$) speeds the gas through, so it needs more volume

problems.prompt: A CSTR full of solvent starts receiving feed. The reaction is first order with $k = {{k}}$ min⁻¹ and $\tau = {{tau}}$ min. How long (min) until the exit $C_A$ reaches {{pc}}% of its steady value?

problems.prompt: In a batch reactor A → B → C, both steps first order with $k_1 = {{k1}}$ and $k_2 = {{k2}}$ min⁻¹, starting from pure A at ${{CA0}}$ mol/L. What is the highest $C_B$ reached (mol/L)?

A PFR passes through every concentration, so $C_D = \int_{C_A}^{C_{A0}}\phi\,dC_A$. Whichever reaction has the higher order favours high concentration (PFR); the lower order favours the CSTR

problems.prompt: A surface reaction is rate-limiting, with {{mech}}. $k = {{k}}$ mol/(kg·s), $K_A = {{KA}}$ and $K_B = {{KB}}$ atm⁻¹; $P_A = {{PA}}$ and $P_B = {{PB}}$ atm. What is $-r'_A$ (mol/(kg·s))?

parts.label: y
parts.explain: Adsorption steps at equilibrium give $\theta_A = K_AP_A\theta_v$, $\theta_B = K_BP_B\theta_v$, and the site balance gives $\theta_v = \dfrac{1}{1 + K_AP_A + K_BP_B}$. Single site: $-r' = kK_AP_A\theta_v$. Dual site: $-r' = kK_AP_A\theta_v^2$, the squared denominator. Adsorbed product B only slows the rate

problems.prompt: For A ⇌ B on a catalyst (adsorb A, react on the surface, desorb B), the measured rate fits $-r'_A = {{law}}$. Which step limits the rate?

parts.label: y
parts.explain: Read the denominator: it holds a term for every species adsorbed in equilibrium. If adsorption of A is slow, A·S is not in equilibrium with gas A, so $P_A$ drops out of the denominator. If desorption of B is slow, B·S is set by A's equilibria and the denominator shows only $P_A$. A surface-reaction limit keeps both $K_AP_A$ and $K_BP_B$

problems.prompt: Gas A decomposes by A + A → A* + A ($k_1 = {{k1}}$), A* + A → A + A ($k_2 = {{k2}}$), A* → products ($k_3 = {{k3}}$), concentrations in mol/L and time in s. With the PSSH on A*, what is the rate of formation of products at $C_A = {{Cc}}$ mol/L?

parts.label: y
parts.explain: PSSH: $k_1C_A^2 - k_2C_AC_{A^*} - k_3C_{A^*} = 0$, so $C_{A^*} = \dfrac{k_1C_A^2}{k_2C_A + k_3}$ and $r_P = k_3C_{A^*} = \dfrac{k_1k_3C_A^2}{k_2C_A + k_3}$. The active intermediate never appears in the final law

problems.prompt: With $r = \dfrac{k_1k_3C_A^2}{k_2C_A + k_3}$, $k_2 = {{k2}}$ L/(mol·s), $k_3 = {{k3}}$ s⁻¹, what is the apparent order at $C_A = {{Cc}}$ mol/L?

parts.label: y
parts.explain: Compare $k_2C_A$ with $k_3$. High concentration ($k_2C_A \gg k_3$): deactivation by collision wins and $r \to (k_1k_3/k_2)C_A$, first order. Low concentration: $r \to k_1C_A^2$, second order. This is why unimolecular gas reactions fall off at low pressure

problems.prompt: E + S ⇌ E·S → E + P with $k_1 = {{k1}}$ L/(mol·s), $k_{-1} = {{km1}}$ s⁻¹, $k_2 = {{k2}}$ s⁻¹, total enzyme ${{Et}}$ M. What is the rate (M/s) at $S = {{Sc}}$ M?

parts.label: y
parts.explain: PSSH on E·S plus the enzyme balance give $r = \dfrac{V_{\max}S}{K_m + S}$ with $V_{\max} = k_2E_t$ and $K_m = \dfrac{k_{-1} + k_2}{k_1}$. At $S = K_m$ the rate is half of $V_{\max}$

problems.prompt: An enzyme gives rate ${{v1}}$ at $S = {{S1}}$ and ${{v2}}$ at $S = {{S2}}$ (consistent units). Assuming Michaelis–Menten kinetics, what is {{wt}}?

parts.label: y
parts.explain: Lineweaver–Burk: $\dfrac1r = \dfrac{K_m}{V_{\max}}\dfrac1S + \dfrac1{V_{\max}}$. Two points fix the line: intercept $1/V_{\max}$, slope $K_m/V_{\max}$. With real data, prefer a nonlinear fit, since the reciprocal plot magnifies low-S scatter

Uncompetitive: I binds only E·S ($K_m$ and $V_{\max}$ fall together; parallel lines). Noncompetitive: I binds E and E·S alike ($V_{\max}$ falls, same $K_m$; lines meet on the 1/S axis)

problems.prompt: A chemostat with Monod growth, $\mu_{\max} = {{mm}}$ h⁻¹, $K_s = {{Ks}}$ g/L, yield $Y_{X/S} = {{Yx}}$, is fed sterile substrate at ${{S0}}$ g/L with dilution rate $D = {{Dl}}$ h⁻¹. What is the {{wt}}?

parts.label: y
parts.explain: At steady state $\mu = D$, so $S = \dfrac{K_sD}{\mu_{\max} - D}$ (the feed strength does not enter), and $X = Y_{X/S}(S_0 - S)$. Washout happens when even feed-strength substrate cannot grow cells as fast as they leave: $D_{\max} = \dfrac{\mu_{\max}S_0}{K_s + S_0}$

problems.prompt: A reaction with $\Delta H_{\rm rx} = {{dH}}$ J/mol A (constant, $\Delta C_p = 0$) runs adiabatically. The feed enters at ${{T0}}$ K with $\sum\Theta_iC_{p,i} = {{cp}}$ J/(mol A·K). What is the {{wt}}?

parts.label: y
parts.explain: Adiabatic energy balance: $T = T_0 + \dfrac{(-\Delta H_{\rm rx})X}{\sum\Theta_iC_{p,i}}$, a straight line in the X–T plane for any adiabatic reactor, batch or flow. Endothermic reactions cool as they go

problems.prompt: The exothermic liquid reaction A ⇌ B has $K_C = {{K1}}$ at ${{T1}}$ K and $\Delta H_{\rm rx} = {{dH}}$ J/mol. Pure A enters an adiabatic reactor at ${{T0}}$ K with $\sum\Theta_iC_{p,i} = {{cp}}$ J/(mol·K). What is the adiabatic equilibrium conversion?

parts.label: y
parts.explain: Two curves: the energy balance $X_{EB} = \dfrac{\sum\Theta_iC_{p,i}(T - T_0)}{-\Delta H_{\rm rx}}$ and equilibrium $X_e = \dfrac{K}{1 + K}$ with $K(T) = K_1\exp\!\left[-\dfrac{\Delta H}{R}\left(\dfrac1T - \dfrac1{T_1}\right)\right]$. They cross once; iterate on T. Cooling between stages (or a colder feed) gets past it

problems.prompt: A first-order liquid reaction runs in an adiabatic CSTR: $\tau = {{tau}}$ min, $k = {{k1}}$ min⁻¹ at ${{T1}}$ K, $E = {{Ea}}$ J/mol, $\Delta H_{\rm rx} = {{dH}}$ J/mol, $\sum\Theta_iC_{p,i} = {{cp}}$ J/(mol·K), feed at ${{T0}}$ K. How many steady states are there?

parts.label: y
parts.explain: Steady states are where heat generated, $G(T) = (-\Delta H)\dfrac{\tau k}{1 + \tau k}$, meets heat removed, $R(T) = \sum\Theta_iC_{p,i}(T - T_0)$. The sigmoid G can cut the line R once (low or high) or three times; the middle one of three is unstable. Raising $T_0$ slides the line right and can ignite the reactor

choices.y: cstr_adiabatic(0, tau, k1, T1, Ea, dH, cp, T0)

problems.prompt: A first-order liquid reaction runs in an adiabatic CSTR: $\tau = {{tau}}$ min, $k = {{k1}}$ min⁻¹ at ${{T1}}$ K, $E = {{Ea}}$ J/mol, $\Delta H_{\rm rx} = {{dH}}$ J/mol, $\sum\Theta_iC_{p,i} = {{cp}}$ J/(mol·K), feed at ${{T0}}$ K. It has a single steady state. What is its temperature (K)?

parts.label: y
parts.explain: Solve $X_{MB}(T) = \dfrac{\tau k(T)}{1 + \tau k(T)}$ together with $X_{EB}(T) = \dfrac{\sum\Theta_iC_{p,i}(T - T_0)}{-\Delta H}$ by iterating on T. Check the answer sits between $T_0$ and the adiabatic limit $T_0 - \Delta H/\sum\Theta_iC_{p,i}$

problems.prompt: A first-order surface reaction ($k_r = {{kr}}$ m/s) sits behind a film with $k_c = {{kc}}$ m/s. The bulk concentration is ${{Cb}}$ mol/m³. What is the rate per area (mol/(m²·s))?

parts.label: y
parts.explain: Steady state: what crosses the film reacts, $k_c(C_b - C_s) = k_rC_s$. Eliminate $C_s$: $-r''_A = \dfrac{C_b}{1/k_c + 1/k_r}$, resistances in series. The smaller of $k_c$ and $k_r$ controls; if mass transfer controls, raising the temperature barely helps but raising the velocity does

problems.prompt: A fast reaction in a packed bed is limited entirely by external mass transfer: $k_c = {{kc}}$ m/s, $a_c = {{a}}$ m²/m³, bed length ${{Lb}}$ m, superficial velocity ${{U}}$ m/s. What is the conversion?

parts.explain: With $C_s \approx 0$, a balance on a slice gives $U\dfrac{dC}{dz} = -k_ca_cC$, so $X = 1 - \exp\!\left(-\dfrac{k_ca_cL}{U}\right)$. Doubling $U$ halves the exponent only partly, since $k_c$ grows roughly as $U^{1/2}$

problems.prompt: A first-order reaction ($k = {{k}}$ s⁻¹ per pellet volume) runs in a {{shape}} ${{Rp}}$ cm, effective diffusivity ${{De}}$ cm²/s. What is the internal effectiveness factor η?

parts.label: y
parts.explain: Thiele modulus $\phi = L\sqrt{k/D_e}$ (length = half-thickness or radius). Slab: $\eta = \dfrac{\tanh\phi}{\phi}$; sphere: $\eta = \dfrac{3}{\phi^2}(\phi\coth\phi - 1)$. Large φ: η → 1/φ (slab) or 3/φ (sphere), and the apparent activation energy is halved

problems.prompt: A spherical pellet (radius ${{Rp}}$ cm, $D_e = {{De}}$ cm²/s) runs a first-order reaction with intrinsic $k = {{k}}$ s⁻¹. What is the Weisz–Prater parameter $C_{WP}$?

problems.prompt: A first-order reaction ($k = {{k}}$ s⁻¹ per reactor volume, internal η = ${{et}}$) sits behind an external film, $k_c = {{kc}}$ m/s, $a_c = {{a}}$ m²/m³. Bulk $C_A = {{Cb}}$ mol/m³. What is the rate per reactor volume (mol/(m³·s))?

parts.label: y
parts.explain: In series: $k_ca_c(C_b - C_s) = \eta kC_s$, so the rate is $\dfrac{C_b}{1/(k_ca_c) + 1/(\eta k)}$, which is $\Omega kC_b$ with overall effectiveness $\Omega = \dfrac{\eta}{1 + \eta k/(k_ca_c)}$

problems.prompt: Which pathway dominates? {{q}}

parts.label: a
parts.explain: Ask two questions in order. Is the reagent a strong base or nucleophile? If not (water or an alcohol alone), only a carbocation route is open: SN1 with E1, and only on a secondary or tertiary carbon. If it is strong: a good nucleophile that is a weak base (I⁻, CN⁻, RS⁻, N₃⁻) does SN2 on methyl, primary and secondary carbons; a strong base does E2 on secondary and tertiary carbons, and on primary too when it is bulky. Tertiary carbons never do SN2

problems.prompt: A benzene ring carries {{g}}. Where does the next electrophile go, and is the ring faster or slower than benzene?

parts.explain: Look at the atom attached to the ring. A lone pair there, or an alkyl group, donates into the ring: ortho/para. A positive or partly positive atom (a carbonyl carbon, nitro nitrogen, CF₃) withdraws: meta, and slower. Halogens are the one mixed case: the lone pair directs ortho/para, but the electronegativity slows the ring

problems.prompt: A sample of liquid with light-key mole fraction {{xl}} is in equilibrium with vapour at {{yv}}. What relative volatility does that give?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: α = (y/x)/((1 − y)/(1 − x)): the ratio of the two components' K-values, nearly constant for similar molecules

problems.prompt: A column has the equivalent of {{n}} ideal stages at total reflux, α = {{al}}, and bottoms at $x_B$ = {{xb}}. What distillate purity $x_D$ can it reach?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: At total reflux each stage multiplies the separation ratio by α, so purity climbs steeply with stages once α is well above 1

problems.prompt: A saturated-vapour feed (z = {{z}}) enters a column with α = {{al}} and $x_D$ = {{xd}}. What is the minimum reflux ratio? (The pinch is where the horizontal q-line y = z meets the equilibrium curve.)

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Slope of the pinched rectifying line R/(R + 1) = (x_D − y*)/(x_D − x*); a vapour feed needs more reflux than a liquid feed for the same job

problems.prompt: An absorber has {{n}} ideal stages and absorption factor A = {{Af}}, with solute-free liquid. What fraction of the solute is absorbed?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: With A < 1 even infinite stages cannot absorb everything (the limit is A); with A > 1 complete absorption is possible in principle

problems.prompt: Air at {{P}} kPa total has absolute humidity {{H}} kg water/kg dry air; the vapour pressure of water at its temperature is {{ps}} kPa. What is the relative humidity, in %?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Back out the water partial pressure from H = 0.622 p/(P − p), then divide by the saturation pressure

problems.prompt: A single-effect evaporator concentrates {{F}} kg/h of feed from {{x1}}% to {{x2}}% solids, fed at its boiling point. Latent heat of the vapour is {{lv}} kJ/kg and of the steam {{ls}} kJ/kg. How much steam, in kg/h?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Solids balance gives the water evaporated; with no sensible heating and no boiling-point rise, roughly one kg of steam per kg of water (economy about 1). Multiple effects reuse the vapour

problems.prompt: An ideal binary liquid holds mole fraction {{xa}} of A. Pure-component vapour pressures are {{PA}} kPa (A) and {{PB}} kPa (B). What is A's mole fraction in the vapour?

parts.label: y
parts.explain: Relative volatility α = P_A*/P_B*, and $y = \dfrac{\alpha x}{1 + (\alpha - 1)x}$. The larger α, the easier the split; α near 1 means many stages

problems.prompt: A binary column with constant relative volatility α = {{alpha}} must make x_D = {{xD}} and x_B = {{xB}}. What is the minimum number of equilibrium stages (total reflux)?

parts.label: y
parts.explain: Fenske: $N_{\min} = \dfrac{\ln[(x_D/(1-x_D))((1-x_B)/x_B)]}{\ln\alpha}$, counting the reboiler as a stage. Halving α − 1 roughly doubles the stages

problems.prompt: A saturated-liquid feed with x_F = {{xF}} goes to a binary column (α = {{alpha}}) making x_D = {{xD}}. What is the minimum reflux ratio?

parts.label: y
parts.explain: For a saturated-liquid feed, Underwood reduces to $R_{\min} = \dfrac{1}{\alpha - 1}\left[\dfrac{x_D}{x_F} - \dfrac{\alpha(1 - x_D)}{1 - x_F}\right]$. Graphically, the top operating line pinches the equilibrium curve on the q-line. Columns usually run at 1.2–1.5 R_min

problems.prompt: An absorber with absorption factor A = L/(mV) = {{A}} and solute-free solvent must remove {{pct}}% of the solute. How many equilibrium stages?

parts.label: y
parts.explain: Kremser: fraction absorbed $= \dfrac{A^{N+1} - A}{A^{N+1} - 1}$, so $N = \dfrac{\ln[(A - f)/(1 - f)]}{\ln A} - 1$. With A < 1 the recovery is capped at A however many stages

problems.prompt: Air at {{P}} kPa has {{pc}}% relative humidity where water's vapour pressure is {{ps}} kPa. What is the absolute humidity (kg water per kg dry air)?

parts.label: y
parts.explain: p_w = RH × p*, then $H = \dfrac{p_w}{P - p_w}\dfrac{M_w}{M_{air}} = 0.622\dfrac{p_w}{P - p_w}$. Saturation is RH = 100%; cooling air at constant H raises RH until dew forms

problems.prompt: An evaporator concentrates {{F}} kg/h of a solution from {{p0}}% to {{p1}}% solids. How much water is evaporated (kg/h)?

parts.label: y
parts.explain: Solids pass through unchanged: F x₀ = L x₁, so L = F x₀/x₁ and V = F − L. A balance on the non-volatile component always comes first

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Writing the rep to a word count is how a pace target becomes practisable: the speaker is not judging pace by feel, they are fitting a known number of words into a minute
