problems.prompt: A 3-minute answer has {{nm}} main points and {{ns}} section boundaries, each getting a {{pl}}-second pause. What fraction of the answer is pause (per cent)?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Deliberate pauses are a few per cent of the time and they are what makes structure audible; speakers resist them because a two-second silence feels far longer from inside than from outside

cases.q: A one-second silence after the main point is:
cases.o1: A deliberate pause, which marks the structure

cases.q: A silence in the middle of a phrase while the speaker searches for a word is:
'Um' while thinking is:
cases.o1: A filled pause, which the listener hears as uncertainty

cases.q: The fix for a filled pause is:
cases.o1: To let the same gap be silent, which the listener reads as thought rather than uncertainty

cases.q: A fluency hiccup is best prevented by:
cases.o1: Planning the first sentence, so the search happens before the turn starts

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Three kinds of gap, one of them wanted; the filled pause and the hiccup have different fixes

problems.prompt: Over {{nq}} questions, a speaker who opens each with a {{pl}}-second silence instead of a {{rl}}-second restatement saves how long (seconds)?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Restating the question is the commonest way to fill the opening gap, and over a Q&A session it costs minutes while adding nothing: the silence does the same job in one or two seconds

problems.prompt: A transcript of {{ss}} seconds contains {{nf}} filler sounds and {{nc}} filler phrases. What is the total filler rate per minute?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Counting sounds and phrases separately matters because they have different causes: sounds fill a search for words, phrases fill a search for a point

problems.prompt: A 60-second rep allows at most {{mx}} filler sounds with a target of {{tg}}. By what percentage must a speaker at {{cu}} fillers improve to hit the target?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Expressing the target as a reduction rather than a count makes it a practice plan: going from sixteen to one is a different undertaking from going from three to one

cases.q: Awareness training means:
cases.o1: Catching the filler on the way out and marking it, before trying to stop it

cases.q: A competing response for a filler is:
cases.o1: A deliberate silent pause put in the place the filler occupied

cases.q: Trying to suppress a filler without a competing response usually:
cases.o1: Fails, because the gap it filled is still there

cases.q: Naming your own top two fillers matters because:
cases.o1: The habit is specific, and catching a word you are listening for is far easier

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Catch it, then replace it with silence: suppression alone leaves the pause unfilled and the habit intact

problems.prompt: A recording has {{ns}} claim sentences of which {{nf}} end on a falling pitch. What percentage rise or stay level?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: A claim that ends on a rise reads as a question, so the listener hears uncertainty the speaker did not intend: counting them on a playback is the measurement that makes it fixable

cases.q: A delivery with almost no pitch movement is:
cases.o1: Monotone, corrected by marking one key word a sentence to stress

cases.q: A delivery with a repeating melodic pattern regardless of meaning is:
cases.o1: Sing-song, corrected by letting the meaning choose the stress

cases.q: A delivery where statements end on a rising pitch is:
cases.o1: Upspeaking, corrected by dropping pitch on the last stressed syllable

cases.q: A delivery that sounds tight and effortful in the throat is:
cases.o1: Pressed, corrected by breath support and releasing the jaw rather than by pushing

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Four faults with four different corrections; pressed is the one that gets worse if the speaker simply tries harder

problems.prompt: A script of {{ns}} sentences is marked with one key word each. If {{nm}} are stressed on playback, what percentage were missed?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Marking one key word a sentence converts vocal variety from a vague instruction into a checkable list, which is why the drill is marking first and delivering second

cases.q: Between two deliveries of the same line, the stronger on vocal variety is the one that:
cases.o1: Moves pitch, volume and rate where the meaning changes

cases.q: Variety for its own sake, unrelated to meaning, reads as:
cases.o1: Performed rather than meant, which costs credibility

cases.q: The clearest single marker of a stressed word is:
cases.o1: A change on it relative to the words around it, in any of pitch, volume or length

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Variety is relative and tied to meaning; absolute loudness or slowness is not variety

problems.prompt: A 4-minute talk holds eye contact for one complete thought of about {{st}} seconds per listener. How many listeners can be reached?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Holding a whole thought with one person, rather than scanning, is what makes eye contact land; the arithmetic shows a four-minute talk can genuinely reach only a few dozen people

cases.q: A grounded stance has:
cases.o1: Feet planted, weight even, hands at rest unless gesturing on purpose

cases.q: Rocking or shifting weight reads to an audience as:
cases.o1: Nervousness, because the movement is not tied to anything being said

cases.q: A gesture is worth making when:
cases.o1: It shows something the words are describing

cases.q: Hands at rest is a skill because:
cases.o1: Stillness has to be chosen; under adrenaline the default is movement

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Stillness by default, movement on purpose: the audience reads unmotivated movement as nerves

problems.prompt: A pre-speaking routine is two breaths with the exhale {{rt}} times the inhale. With a {{ih}}-second inhale, how long do the two breaths take (seconds)?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: A longer exhale than inhale is what slows the heart rate, and the routine is short enough to run in the seconds before a turn: the planned first sentence is the other half of it

cases.q: 'Sorry, this might be wrong, but' before a point does what?
cases.o1: Tells the listener to discount the point before they have heard it

cases.q: 'I just think' differs from 'I think' by:
cases.o1: Shrinking the claim, which is almost never what the speaker intends

cases.q: Genuine uncertainty is better expressed as:
cases.o1: A statement of what is and is not known, which is information rather than apology

cases.q: Hedges cluster:
cases.o1: At the start of a turn, where the speaker is least settled

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Cut the hedge, keep the honesty: say what is uncertain rather than apologising for speaking

problems.prompt: A {{dur}}-second answer should give its point within the first {{fp}} seconds. What percentage of the answer is that?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: The point belongs in the first tenth or so, because a listener who does not know where an answer is going cannot tell which of the supporting details matter

cases.q: Between an answer-first and a context-first opening to a direct question, the stronger is usually:
cases.o1: Answer first, because the listener can then place the context
cases.o2: Context first, so the answer is understood

cases.q: Context-first openings fail because:
cases.o1: The listener spends the context wondering where it is going

cases.q: A context-first opening is defensible when:
cases.o1: The answer would be misunderstood or rejected without a specific fact first

cases.q: 'It depends' as a complete opening is weak because:
cases.o1: It defers the answer without saying what it depends on

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Answer first by default, context first only when the answer is unintelligible without a specific fact

problems.prompt: An answer announces {{nr}} parallel reasons in a {{dur}}-second turn. How many seconds does each reason get, after {{op}} seconds of opening and {{cl}} of closing?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Announcing the count commits the speaker to parallel support and lets the listener keep place; the arithmetic shows why three reasons in a minute leaves barely fifteen seconds each

problems.prompt: A 60-second PREP answer gives its four parts roughly equal time. How many seconds is each?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Point, Reason, Example, Point restated at about fifteen seconds each is why PREP works under pressure: the speaker never has to decide what comes next, only to keep each part short

cases.q: In SCQA, the Complication is:
cases.o1: What changed or went wrong that makes the question live

cases.q: The Question in SCQA is:
cases.o1: The decision the listener now faces, stated explicitly

cases.q: SCQA suits a proposal because:
cases.o1: It establishes why a decision is needed before asking for one

cases.q: An SCQA with no Complication produces:
cases.o1: A recommendation with no reason to act now

parts.label: v
parts.explain: The Complication is the part that makes the proposal urgent, and it is the part most often left out

cases.q: A prompt asking for your opinion suits:
A prompt asking for a decision or resource suits:
A prompt beginning 'tell me about a time' suits:
A persuasive turn aimed at action suits:
Using STAR for an opinion question produces:
cases.o1: A long anecdote where a claim was wanted

parts.label: v
parts.explain: The frame follows what the question asks for: a claim, a decision, an experience or an action

problems.prompt: A talk has {{np}} parts, each signposted on entry and summarised at the end, plus one preview and one final summary. How many structural markers is that?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Signposting feels repetitive to the speaker, who knows the structure, and is the only way the listener can keep place: the count is deliberately higher than feels natural

cases.q: An answer whose point arrives in the last sentence has:
cases.o1: A buried point, fixed by moving it first

cases.q: An answer that returns to the same idea three times has:
cases.o1: A circling problem, usually from not having decided the point before starting

cases.q: An answer that answers a related but different question has:
cases.o1: A tangent, fixed by returning to the question as asked

cases.q: An answer where the listener cannot tell when one reason ended has:
All four faults share one cause:
cases.o1: Starting to speak before deciding the point

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Four diagnoses, one root cause: the pause before the answer is where the point gets decided

cases.q: A deliberate ending is:
cases.o1: One sentence restating the point or giving the ask, then stopping
cases.o3: Thanks and an apology for overrunning

cases.q: Trailing off at the end costs:
cases.o1: The last thing the listener keeps, which is the most memorable position in the turn

cases.q: 'That's all I had' as an ending:
cases.o1: Wastes the strongest position in the turn

cases.q: Dropping pitch at the end does what?
cases.o1: Signals completion, so the listener knows the turn is over

parts.label: v
parts.explain: The last sentence is the one that is remembered, so it is the one most worth planning

problems.prompt: A table topic allows a pause of at most {{pm}} seconds before a {{dur}}-second answer. What fraction of the turn is the pause (per cent)?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: A few seconds is a tiny fraction of the turn and buys the decision about the point, which is what prevents the rambling the rest of the turn would otherwise contain

cases.q: The three parts of a good 'I don't know' are:
cases.o1: What you do know, what you would need to find out, and when you will come back
cases.o2: An apology, a guess, and a caveat

cases.q: Guessing when you do not know costs:
cases.o1: Credibility on everything else you said

cases.q: Promising a follow-up without a date:
cases.o1: Is heard as a polite refusal

cases.q: Saying what you do know first matters because:
cases.o1: It shows the boundary of your knowledge rather than its absence

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Three parts, and the date is the one that makes it a commitment rather than a deflection

problems.prompt: A Q&A of {{mn}} minutes handles questions with pause, answer, support and check taking {{qs}} seconds each. How many questions fit?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Budgeting the Q&A in advance is what keeps the first question from taking a third of it; the check at the end of each answer is what prevents a follow-up spending another slot

cases.q: 'Could you say more about the second step?' is:
cases.o1: A clarifying question, answered by expanding that step

cases.q: 'That won't work because of X' is:
cases.o1: A challenging question, answered by engaging X directly

cases.q: A long statement of the asker's own views ending without a question is:
cases.o1: A comment not a question, acknowledged and then redirected

cases.q: A question about something the talk did not cover is:
cases.o1: Off topic, answered briefly and taken offline if it needs more

cases.q: Misclassifying a challenge as a clarification produces:
cases.o1: An expansion the asker did not want, leaving the objection standing

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Four kinds with four moves; the expensive mistake is treating a challenge as a request for more detail

problems.prompt: A {{dur}}-second STAR answer spends about {{sp}} per cent on situation and task together. How many seconds remain for action and result?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Most of the answer belongs to what you did and what happened; the commonest STAR failure is spending half the time on context nobody needed

cases.q: A STAR answer that says 'we' throughout fails because:
cases.o1: The listener cannot tell what the speaker did

cases.q: A STAR answer with no result fails because:
cases.o1: The listener cannot tell whether the action worked

cases.q: A STAR answer with two minutes of context has:
cases.o1: Too much situation, leaving no time for action and result

cases.q: A STAR answer with no reflection leaves out:
cases.o1: What the speaker would do differently, which is what the question was often really asking

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Four faults, and 'we' is the one speakers defend as modesty while it costs them the answer

problems.prompt: A 30-second introduction leads with the current work in the first {{fp}} seconds. How long is left for the path to it?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Leading with what you do now, not with where you started, is what makes a thirty-second introduction land: the chronological version runs out of time before reaching the present

cases.q: Stating what the listener already knows before explaining does what?
cases.o1: Fixes the starting point, so the explanation neither repeats nor skips

cases.q: The commonest failure of a technical explanation is:
cases.o1: Starting above the listener's actual starting point

cases.q: The second commonest is:
cases.o1: Explaining what the listener already knows, which costs the attention the hard part needs

cases.q: The starting point is best established by:
cases.o1: Asking, or by stating it explicitly and inviting correction

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Two failures, one in each direction; both are avoided by saying the assumption out loud

problems.prompt: A three-sentence explanation at {{wp}} words a minute with {{nw}} words a sentence takes how long (seconds)?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: What it is, what it is for, and why it is hard fits in well under half a minute, which is why the three-sentence version is the one to have ready rather than the full account

cases.q: Re-pitching an explanation for a specialist changes:
cases.o1: The vocabulary and the depth, and usually drops the analogy

cases.q: For an adjacent expert, the useful move is:
cases.o1: Connecting to what they already know from their own field

cases.q: For a novice, the depth is set by:
cases.o1: What they need to decide or do, not by what is interesting

cases.q: An explanation that works at all three levels unchanged is:
cases.o1: Unlikely: the three audiences need different starting points

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Three audiences, three starting points; the analogy that helps a novice usually irritates a specialist

cases.q: Concrete to abstract means:
cases.o1: A specific case first, then the general rule it illustrates

cases.q: Starting with the abstract rule fails because:
cases.o1: The listener has nothing to attach it to, so they cannot tell what it rules out

cases.q: The bridge between the two is:
cases.o1: Naming what in the specific case corresponds to each part of the rule

cases.q: Two examples with no stated rule leaves:
cases.o1: The listener to guess the generalisation, which they will do differently from you

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Case, bridge, rule: the bridge is the part that gets skipped, and without it the example and the rule stay separate

cases.q: Stating where an analogy breaks matters because:
cases.o1: The listener will otherwise extend it to conclusions that are false

cases.q: An analogy is well chosen when:
cases.o1: Its familiar part maps onto the part the listener finds hard
cases.o4: It is from the listener's field

cases.q: An analogy that maps the easy part and not the hard part:
cases.o1: Gives the listener a feeling of understanding without the understanding

cases.q: The best moment to state the break is:
cases.o1: Immediately after the analogy, before any conclusion is drawn from it
cases.o2: At the end of the talk

parts.label: v
parts.explain: An analogy is a loan the listener will over-spend unless its limit is stated with it

cases.q: Between abstract-first and example-first versions of the same explanation, the stronger for a novice is:
cases.o4: Abstract first with more jargon defined

cases.q: Between two explanations, the one with more detail is better only if:
cases.o1: The extra detail is what the listener needed to decide or do something

cases.q: A complete and accurate explanation can still fail by:
cases.o1: Spending the listener's attention before reaching the part they needed

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Completeness is not the goal; the listener's attention is the budget, and it is spent in order

problems.prompt: A {{ns}}-step explanation pauses {{pl}} seconds after each step. How much of a {{dur}}-second explanation is pause (per cent)?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: One idea a step with a pause after each is how a listener is given time to attach it; the pauses are a small fraction of the time and they are what the speaker cuts first under pressure

cases.q: A check that requires the listener to use the idea is:
cases.o1: Asking them to predict or apply it to a new case

cases.q: 'Does that make sense?' is a weak check because:
cases.o1: Almost everyone says yes, whether or not it did

cases.q: A good check reveals:
cases.o1: Which part of the explanation did not land, so it can be redone differently
cases.o2: Whether the listener was paying attention

cases.q: The cost of a real check is:
cases.o1: Time, and the speaker finding out the explanation did not work

parts.label: v
parts.explain: A check is only a check if its answer could be wrong; 'does that make sense' cannot be

cases.q: When a listener's answer shows a misunderstanding, the right move is:
cases.o1: A different route, not the same explanation more slowly

cases.q: Repeating the same explanation louder or slower fails because:
cases.o1: The route, not the delivery, is what did not work

cases.q: Diagnosing from the listener's answer means:
cases.o1: Working out which step they took differently, and starting there

cases.q: The most useful second route is usually:
cases.o1: A concrete case where their understanding gives the wrong prediction

parts.label: v
parts.explain: The second attempt has to be a different route; a case where their version predicts wrongly is the strongest one

problems.prompt: A figure of {{nv}} out of {{nt}} is stated for the ear as about one in how many?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: A spoken number needs rounding and one comparison: 'about one in four' is kept and '23.4 out of 96' is not, however much precision is lost

cases.q: Talking a listener through a figure starts with:
cases.o1: What the axes are and what one point means

cases.q: After the axes, the next thing to say is:
Stating the conclusion before the axes fails because:
cases.o1: The listener is still working out what they are looking at

cases.q: A figure with no stated takeaway leaves:
cases.o1: Each listener to form a different one

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Axes, then where to look, then what it means: three sentences, in that order

problems.prompt: A speaker takes a breath every {{pw}} words at {{wp}} words a minute. How many breaths a minute is that?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Breathing at phrase boundaries gives roughly ten to twenty breaths a minute in speech; far more than that means breathing mid-phrase, and far fewer means running out of air at the end of each one

cases.q: A sustained exhale drill improves speech because:
cases.o1: It builds the steady airflow a long phrase needs without pushing
cases.o4: It slows the heart rate only

cases.q: Running out of air at the end of a phrase makes the voice:
cases.o1: Pressed and the pitch drop uncontrolled

cases.q: The drill builds gradually because:
cases.o1: Forcing a long exhale creates the tension the drill is meant to remove

parts.label: v
parts.explain: The target is steadiness rather than length: a long exhale with tension is worse than a short one without

cases.q: Setting volume to the room means:
cases.o1: Projecting to the back row, which is louder than feels natural from the front

cases.q: A speaker who sounds right to themselves in a large room is usually:
Projection is produced by:
cases.o1: Breath support and open resonance, not by pushing from the throat

cases.q: With a microphone, the correct adjustment is:
cases.o1: Speaking at conversational volume and letting the system project

parts.label: v
parts.explain: The room sets the level, the speaker's own ear is a poor guide, and a microphone changes the answer entirely

problems.prompt: A sentence has {{nw}} words of which {{nf}} end in a plosive. If {{nd}} are dropped, what percentage of the final plosives were dropped?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Counting dropped endings on a playback turns 'clearer diction' into a number; final plosives are the ones to count because they carry the least loudness and are dropped first

cases.q: A dense technical sentence needs every ending because:
cases.o1: The listener cannot recover a dropped plural or tense from context as easily as in ordinary speech

cases.q: Unstressed syllables are dropped when:
cases.o1: The speaker's rate outruns the articulation, usually under pressure

cases.q: Reading at a controlled rate rather than fast helps because:
cases.o1: Articulation is what fails first when rate rises, before pitch or volume

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Density raises the cost of a dropped ending, which is exactly when rate most needs holding down

cases.q: An answer in a meeting is best delivered at:
An explanation of a hard idea is best delivered at:
The reason the explanation band is slower is:
cases.o1: The listener is doing more work per word

cases.q: A speaker who holds one rate for both:
cases.o1: Is too fast for the explanation or too slow for the answer

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Two bands for two jobs; the gap between them is about fifteen per cent of rate

problems.prompt: A key claim is delivered at {{w1}} words a minute inside an answer otherwise at {{w2}}. What percentage slower is the claim?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: A fifteen to thirty per cent drop on the key sentence is audible without sounding laboured; the contrast, not the absolute rate, is what marks the claim

cases.q: A deliberate pause belongs:
cases.o1: After the main point, between sections, and before a key number

cases.q: A pause after the main point does what?
cases.o1: Gives the listener time to register it before support arrives

cases.q: A pause before a key number does what?
cases.o1: Marks it as worth attending to, so it is heard rather than passed over

cases.q: A two-second pause feels to the speaker:
cases.o1: Much longer than it does to the listener, which is why it gets cut
cases.o2: The same as to the listener

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Three places where a pause does work, and one perceptual fact that explains why speakers drop them

problems.prompt: A minute of speech contains {{nd}} deliberate pauses, {{nh}} hiccups and {{nf}} filled pauses. What percentage of the gaps were deliberate?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: The ratio is a better progress measure than the filler count alone, because it rises both when fillers fall and when deliberate pauses are added: the same silence used on purpose

cases.q: The best opening move on an unexpected question is:
cases.o1: A one to two second silence

cases.q: Restating the question costs:
cases.o1: Several seconds and signals that thinking has not started

cases.q: 'That's a great question' is weak because:
cases.o1: It is a filler with more syllables

cases.q: The silence works because:
cases.o1: It is read as thought, and the speaker uses it to choose the point

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Silence, then the point: the alternatives all cost time and signal the opposite of composure

cases.q: 'Um' and 'uh' are:
cases.o1: Filler sounds, which fill a search for words

cases.q: 'You know', 'sort of' and 'I mean' are:
cases.o1: Filler phrases, which fill a search for a point

cases.q: Counting the two separately matters because:
cases.o1: They have different causes and different fixes

cases.q: The fix for filler phrases is:
cases.o1: Deciding the point before speaking, since the phrase is covering its absence

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Sounds are a word search and phrases are a point search; conflating them means fixing the wrong thing

problems.prompt: A 60-second rep contains {{nf}} fillers. What is the rate per minute, and how many must go to reach a target of {{tg}}?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: At a minute's length the count and the rate are the same number, which is why the sixty-second rep is the unit: the target is a count the speaker can hold in mind while speaking

problems.prompt: A speaker goes from {{f1}} to {{f2}} fillers a minute over {{wk}} weeks. What is the reduction per week (fillers a minute)?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Filler reduction is fast once awareness is in place and then plateaus, so the useful target is the first large drop rather than a steady rate to zero

cases.q: A claim ending on a rising pitch is heard as:
cases.o1: A question or a request for approval

cases.q: The pitch drop belongs:
cases.o1: On the last stressed syllable of the sentence
cases.o4: Only at the end of a section

cases.q: A speaker who upspeaks on every claim:
cases.o1: Asks the audience to agree rather than telling them something

cases.q: Genuine questions should:
cases.o1: Rise, which is what makes the falling claims readable as claims

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Falling for claims and rising for questions; using one contour for both removes the distinction the listener relies on

problems.prompt: A monotone delivery spans {{s1}} semitones and a varied one {{s2}}. By what factor is the varied range larger?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Expressive speech spans about an octave and monotone a few semitones, so the difference is several-fold; hearing it on a playback is what makes the fault concrete rather than a comment

cases.q: A word can be stressed with:
cases.o1: Pitch, volume or length, and usually a combination

cases.q: Stressing every word in a sentence:
cases.o1: Stresses none of them, because stress is relative

cases.q: The key word in a sentence is:
cases.o1: The one that changes the meaning if replaced

cases.q: Marking the key word before delivering matters because:
cases.o1: Under pressure stress lands on whatever word the sentence happens to reach

parts.label: v
parts.explain: One key word, marked in advance, carried by any of three acoustic means

problems.prompt: Two deliveries score {{a1}} and {{a2}} on pitch movement and {{b1}} and {{b2}} on stress placement, each out of 5. Which total is higher, and by how much?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Scoring two components separately is what makes a comparison teachable: a delivery can win on pitch movement and lose on where the stress landed, and only the second is a meaning error

cases.q: Eye contact works best held for:
cases.o1: One complete thought with one person, about three to five seconds
cases.o2: A second with each person in turn
cases.o3: The whole talk with one person

cases.q: Scanning the room continuously reads as:
cases.o1: Not looking at anyone, which is how an audience experiences it

cases.q: Moving on at a thought boundary rather than mid-sentence matters because:
cases.o1: The listener gets a whole unit of meaning rather than a fragment

cases.q: In a large room, eye contact is managed by:
cases.o1: Choosing people in different parts and holding each for a thought

parts.label: v
parts.explain: One thought per person, moving at boundaries: the unit is the sentence, not the second

problems.prompt: A 5-minute talk has {{ng}} gestures of which {{np}} illustrate something being said. What percentage are unmotivated?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Counting motivated against total gestures on a playback is how 'too fidgety' becomes a number; the unmotivated ones are what an audience reads as nerves

cases.q: The pre-speaking routine's three parts are:
cases.o1: Two slow exhale-longer breaths, a planned first sentence, and shoulders down
cases.o2: A pep talk, a stretch and a smile
cases.o3: Reviewing notes, drinking water, deep breath

cases.q: The exhale is made longer than the inhale because:
cases.o1: A long exhale slows the heart rate, which a long inhale does not

cases.q: Planning the first sentence helps because:
cases.o1: The first seconds are when adrenaline is highest and improvisation hardest

cases.q: The routine is short because:
cases.o1: It has to run in the seconds actually available before a turn

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Breath, first sentence, shoulders: three things that fit in the gap before speaking

problems.prompt: A transcript of {{nw}} words contains {{nh}} hedges. What is the hedge rate per hundred words?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Hedges cluster at the start of turns, so the rate per hundred words understates their effect; the useful second measure is how many of the turns opened with one

cases.q: Giving the point first helps the listener because:
cases.o1: They can then tell which of the supporting details matter

cases.q: Burying the point costs most when:
cases.o1: The listener may stop listening or interrupt before it arrives

cases.q: A speaker who cannot state the point in one sentence:
cases.o1: Has not yet decided it, which is what the opening pause is for

cases.q: Point first does not mean:
cases.o1: Omitting the reasoning, which follows immediately

parts.label: v
parts.explain: The point first is about order, not length: everything else still gets said, in an order the listener can use

problems.prompt: Two openings to the same question reach the point at {{t1}} and {{t2}} seconds. How much sooner is the faster one (seconds)?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Measuring seconds-to-the-point on a recording is the single most useful number in this unit, because it is objective and it correlates with how the answer was received

cases.q: Announcing 'two reasons' before giving them does what?
cases.o1: Lets the listener allocate attention and know when the answer is complete

cases.q: Parallel reasons means:
cases.o1: Reasons at the same level of abstraction, not one reason and one example
cases.o2: An equal number of words each

cases.q: Announcing three and giving two:
cases.o1: Leaves the listener waiting for the third

cases.q: Why two or three rather than five?
cases.o1: More than three cannot be held while also following each one

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Announce the count, keep them parallel, and deliver the number you announced

cases.q: In PREP, the Reason is:
cases.o1: Why the point holds, stated before the example

cases.q: The final P exists to:
cases.o1: Return to the point, so the answer ends where it began rather than on the example

cases.q: PREP works under pressure because:
cases.o1: The speaker never has to decide what comes next

cases.q: The commonest PREP failure is:
cases.o1: The example growing until there is no time to restate the point

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Four parts, and the restatement is the one that gets squeezed out by a long example

problems.prompt: A {{dur}}-second SCQA update gives Situation and Complication {{sc}} per cent of the time. How long is left for Question and Answer (seconds)?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: The Answer is what the listener is there for, so the setup has to be held to a minority of the time; an SCQA where the situation takes half the slot has become a status report

problems.prompt: Of {{np}} prompts in a practice set, {{n1}} suit PREP, {{n2}} SCQA and {{n3}} STAR. What percentage suit none of the three?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: A practice set with many prompts fitting none of the frames is a sign the frames are being applied too narrowly: most real prompts fit one of them once the question behind the prompt is identified

cases.q: A preview at the start of a talk states:
A signpost on entering a part does what?
cases.o1: Tells the listener which part has started

cases.q: A summary at the end of a part does what?
cases.o1: Closes it, so the next part is not heard as a continuation

cases.q: Signposting feels repetitive to the speaker because:
cases.o1: They know the structure and the listener does not

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Preview, signpost, summarise, at every level: it is the only way a listener can keep place without a document

problems.prompt: An answer of {{dur}} seconds reaches its point at {{tp}} seconds. What percentage of the answer preceded the point?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: A point arriving past the halfway mark is a buried point by definition, whatever the speaker intended; the percentage is the diagnosis, and moving the point first is the fix

problems.prompt: An ending is one sentence of {{nw}} words at {{wp}} words a minute. How long is it (seconds)?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: A planned ending is five to ten seconds, which is a trivial cost for the most memorable position in the turn: the alternative is trailing off into whatever was said last

cases.q: The pause before an impromptu answer is used to:
cases.o1: Choose the point and the frame, not to begin composing sentences

cases.q: A 60-second impromptu answer is best structured as:
cases.o1: A frame the speaker already knows, usually PREP

cases.q: The commonest impromptu failure is:
cases.o1: Starting to speak before deciding the point

cases.q: Practising impromptu with random prompts builds:
cases.o1: The habit of choosing a point and a frame fast, which is the transferable part

parts.label: v
parts.explain: The pause chooses point and frame; everything else is the frame the speaker already has

problems.prompt: A speaker promises follow-ups on {{nq}} questions within {{dd}} days each. If {{nk}} are delivered on time, what percentage of promises were kept?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: The 'I don't know, I'll come back to you' move only works if the rate is high; a speaker who promises and does not deliver has spent the move's credibility for everyone else too

cases.q: The four parts of a good answer to an audience question are:
cases.o1: Pause, one-sentence answer, one support, check

cases.q: Giving one support rather than three does what?
cases.o1: Leaves room for the follow-up, which is where the asker's real question usually is

cases.q: The check at the end is:
cases.o1: Asking whether that answered what they asked

cases.q: Skipping the check costs:
cases.o1: Finding out the answer missed the question, so the next question is the same one

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Four parts, and the check is the one that stops a Q&A circling the same question

problems.prompt: A Q&A had {{nc}} clarifying, {{nh}} challenging, {{no}} off-topic questions and {{nm}} comments. What percentage needed a move other than expanding?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Most questions in a technical Q&A are not requests for more detail, which is why treating every one as a clarification leaves objections standing and comments unbounded

expect.v: 100*Rational(nh + no + nm, nc + nh + no + nm)

problems.prompt: In a {{dur}}-second STAR answer, action takes {{na}} seconds and result {{nr}}. What percentage is action and result together?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Action and result should be most of the answer; below about two-thirds the answer is mostly context, which is the fault the interviewer notices and the speaker does not

problems.prompt: A STAR answer uses 'I' {{ni}} times and 'we' {{nw}} times. What percentage of the agent references were first person singular?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Counting the pronouns on a transcript is the fastest diagnosis of the 'we' fault, and it is the one speakers most reliably deny until they see the count

cases.q: A 30-second introduction should lead with:
A chronological introduction fails because:
cases.o1: It spends the listener's attention before reaching the present

cases.q: The path to the current work belongs:
cases.o1: After it, and only the part that explains it

cases.q: The introduction should end:
cases.o1: Pointing at what the listener can do with the information

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Now, then the path that explains now: the chronological version never reaches the point

problems.prompt: An explanation has {{ns}} steps of which the listener already knows {{nk}}. What percentage of the explanation is new to them?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Establishing the starting point is what lets the known steps be compressed into a sentence, buying the attention the new ones need

cases.q: The three sentences of a short explanation are:
cases.o1: What it is, what it is for, and why it is hard

cases.q: Having the three-sentence version ready matters because:
cases.o1: Most occasions to explain are short and unplanned

cases.q: 'Why it is hard' is included because:
cases.o1: It tells the listener why the work exists, which is what they usually wanted

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Three sentences, and the third is the one that turns a definition into a reason to care

problems.prompt: An explanation uses {{nj}} technical terms for a specialist. Re-pitched for a novice, {{nk}} are kept. What percentage were replaced or dropped?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Re-pitching is mostly a vocabulary edit plus a depth decision; counting the terms kept is a quick check that the novice version really was re-pitched rather than just slowed down

problems.prompt: An explanation has one case, one bridge and one rule, in {{ns}} sentences total. If the case takes {{nc}} and the bridge {{nb}}, how many are left for the rule?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: The rule is usually the shortest part, which is the opposite of how explanations are written: most of the words belong to the case and the bridge

problems.prompt: An analogy maps {{nm}} of the idea's {{nt}} features. What percentage of the idea does it not cover, and so has to be stated as the break?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: An analogy usually covers a minority of the features, which is why the break has to be named: the listener assumes everything maps unless told otherwise

problems.prompt: A listener's attention allows about {{at}} seconds. An explanation spends {{sp}} seconds before the part they needed. What percentage of their attention was spent first?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Attention is a budget spent in order, so an explanation that is complete and correct can still fail by reaching the needed part after the budget is gone

cases.q: A step in an explanation should contain:
cases.o1: One idea, so a failed step can be identified
cases.o2: As much as fits in a sentence

cases.q: Pausing after a step does what?
cases.o1: Gives the listener time to attach it before the next arrives

cases.q: A step containing three ideas fails because:
cases.o1: When the listener loses it, neither of you knows which idea it was

cases.q: The number of steps is set by:
cases.o1: How many ideas the explanation actually contains

parts.label: v
parts.explain: One idea a step is what makes a failure locatable, which is the whole point of stepping an explanation

problems.prompt: An explanation of {{ns}} steps includes {{nc}} real checks. What percentage of steps were checked?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Checking every step is too slow and checking none means finding out at the end; checking at the steps where understanding is most likely to fail is the judgment the number prompts

problems.prompt: A concept took {{na}} attempts to land, each about {{dr}} seconds. How long was spent in total (seconds)?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Each re-explanation costs as much as the first, which is the argument for a real check early: finding the misunderstanding after three attempts has already spent the time three different routes would have

cases.q: A number stated for the ear should be:
cases.o1: Rounded, with one comparison and a stated unit

cases.q: 'About one in three' is better than '34.2 per cent' because:
cases.o1: The listener can hold it and picture it

cases.q: The comparison matters because:
cases.o1: A magnitude without a reference means nothing to a listener

cases.q: Giving three precise figures in a sentence:
cases.o1: Loses all three, since none can be held

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Round it, compare it, name the unit, and give one number at a time

problems.prompt: Talking through {{nf}} figures at three sentences each, at {{wp}} words a minute and {{nw}} words a sentence, takes how long (seconds)?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Three sentences a figure is the minimum that orients a listener, and the arithmetic shows why a talk with a dozen figures cannot explain any of them

cases.q: Monroe's motivated sequence runs:
The visualisation step does what?
cases.o1: Shows the listener what the world looks like once the proposal is adopted

cases.q: Skipping the need step produces:
cases.o1: A solution to a problem the listener has not accepted exists

cases.q: The action step must be:
cases.o1: Specific enough that the listener knows what to do next

cases.q: Monroe's sequence differs from SCQA by:
cases.o1: Ending in an ask for action rather than in an answer to a question

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Five steps, and the two most often dropped are need at the front and a specific action at the end

problems.prompt: A {{dur}}-second pitch gives attention {{a1}} and action {{a2}} seconds. How long is left for need, satisfaction and visualisation each (seconds)?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: The three middle steps carry the argument and get most of the time; a pitch that spends a third of itself on attention has no room to establish the need

cases.q: Naming the strongest objection before the listener raises it does what?
cases.o1: Shows you have considered it, and lets you answer it on your terms

cases.q: Waiting for the objection costs:
cases.o1: The chance to frame it, since the listener's version will be the hardest one

cases.q: The objection worth naming is:
cases.o1: The strongest one, not the easiest to answer

cases.q: Naming an objection and not answering it:
cases.o1: Leaves it standing with your endorsement

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Name the strongest, answer it, and do not raise one you cannot address

problems.prompt: An ask names who, what and by when. Of {{nq}} recorded asks, {{nc}} name all three. What percentage were incomplete?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: An ask missing any of who, what or by when is heard as a wish; counting the complete ones on a recording is how a vague close becomes visible

cases.q: The five parts of a short story are:
cases.o1: A person, a goal, an obstacle, a turn and a point
cases.o2: A beginning, a middle and an end

cases.q: A story with no obstacle is:
cases.o1: A report, which carries none of a story's hold on attention

cases.q: The turn is:
cases.o1: The moment the situation changes, which is what the listener remembers

cases.q: A story with no stated point:
cases.o1: Leaves each listener to draw their own, usually not yours

cases.q: A 90-second story spends most of its time on:

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Five parts, and the obstacle is what separates a story from an anecdote

problems.prompt: A 90-second story spends {{sp}} seconds on setup, {{ob}} on the obstacle and turn, and the rest on the point. How long is the point (seconds)?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: The point is one or two sentences at the end; a story that reaches ninety seconds with the point still to come has spent its setup budget

cases.q: A story opening a lesson must be:
cases.o1: Connected explicitly to the content that follows

cases.q: An unconnected opening story costs:
cases.o1: The attention it earned, because the listener files it separately

cases.q: The connection is best made:
cases.o1: Immediately after the story, in one sentence
cases.o2: At the end of the lesson

cases.q: A case rather than a personal story is preferable when:
cases.o1: The listener needs to see the idea working in their own setting

parts.label: v
parts.explain: The story buys attention; the sentence after it is what converts attention into the lesson

cases.q: A good paraphrase is:
cases.o1: One sentence naming their concern, offered for confirmation

cases.q: Confirming the paraphrase matters because:
cases.o1: If it is wrong you find out before answering the wrong question

cases.q: Repeating someone's words verbatim is weaker than paraphrasing because:
cases.o1: It does not show whether you understood them

cases.q: Paraphrasing their motive rather than their point:
cases.o1: Reads as an accusation, however accurate

parts.label: v
parts.explain: One sentence on their point, confirmed: not their words, and not their motive

problems.prompt: A {{nw}}-word contribution is paraphrased in one sentence of {{ps}} words. What compression is that (factor)?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: A paraphrase compresses by an order of magnitude, which is why it is a test of understanding: you cannot compress what you have not understood

cases.q: A follow-up that builds does what?
cases.o1: Takes their last point further rather than introducing yours

cases.q: The commonest failure in conversation is:
cases.o1: Waiting to say a prepared point rather than responding to what was said

cases.q: A question beginning 'what makes you say that' does what?
cases.o1: Asks for the reasoning behind the point, which is where the disagreement usually is

cases.q: A follow-up that introduces a new topic:
cases.o1: Ends the thread, whatever its merits

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Build on the last point: the test is whether your question could have been asked before they spoke

problems.prompt: A 30-second meeting contribution at {{wp}} words a minute holds how many words?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Seventy or eighty words is three or four sentences: connect, point, reason. Writing a contribution to that budget is what keeps a meeting turn from becoming a speech

cases.q: A short meeting contribution opens by:
cases.o1: Connecting to what was just said

cases.q: Thirty seconds is the budget because:
cases.o1: Beyond it a contribution becomes a speech and the discussion stops

cases.q: The connection at the start does what?
cases.o1: Shows the contribution belongs to this discussion rather than to your agenda

cases.q: A contribution with no reason:
cases.o1: Is a vote, not an argument, so it cannot persuade anyone
cases.o4: Is fine if the point is clear

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Connect, point, reason, in half a minute: the connection is what distinguishes a contribution from an interruption

cases.q: The four parts of disagreeing well are:
Acknowledging first does what?
cases.o1: Shows what you are disagreeing with, so the disagreement is about the substance

cases.q: Hedging the position:
cases.o1: Leaves everyone unsure whether you disagreed at all

cases.q: Ending with a proposal does what?
cases.o1: Turns a disagreement into a decision the group can make

cases.q: Acknowledging without agreeing means:
cases.o1: Stating their point accurately before giving yours

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Acknowledge, position, reason, proposal: the hedge belongs to none of the four parts

problems.prompt: A disagreement with four parts of {{ns}} sentences each at {{nw}} words a sentence, at {{wp}} words a minute, takes how long (seconds)?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: All four parts fit in well under a minute, which is the answer to the worry that disagreeing properly takes too long

problems.prompt: A 60-second rep gives {{nw}} words, {{nf}} fillers and reaches its point at {{tp}} seconds. What is the words-per-minute figure?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: At exactly a minute the word count is the rate, which is why the sixty-second rep is the measurement unit: four numbers come off one recording with no arithmetic

cases.q: The four numbers logged from a rep are:
cases.o1: Words per minute, fillers a minute, seconds to the point, and longest unbroken stretch

cases.q: Logging numbers rather than impressions matters because:
cases.o1: An impression of a recording changes with the speaker's mood; a number does not

cases.q: Seconds to the point is included because:
cases.o1: It is the structural measure that correlates most with how an answer was received

cases.q: The longest unbroken stretch measures:
cases.o1: Whether deliberate pauses are actually being taken

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Four numbers, two about delivery and two about structure, all readable off one transcript

problems.prompt: Eight competencies are each scored 1 to 3. A recording scores {{n1}} threes, {{n2}} twos and the rest ones. What is the total?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: The scale runs 8 to 24, so a middling recording scores around 16; the useful output is not the total but which competency scored lowest

cases.q: The purpose of scoring eight competencies is:
cases.o1: To find the lowest one, which is the next thing to practise
cases.o2: To track the total over time

cases.q: Working on the highest-scoring competency:
cases.o1: Buys the least improvement for the effort

cases.q: A total that rises while the lowest score does not:
cases.o1: Means the practice went to what was already strong

parts.label: v
parts.explain: The lowest score is the instruction; the total is just a record

problems.prompt: A practice block runs {{bl}} minutes with reps of {{rl}} seconds and {{gp}} seconds of review each. How many reps fit?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Review takes as long as the rep or longer, so a twenty-minute block holds fewer reps than it looks; one measurable target per block is what makes the few reps count

cases.q: A spoken evaluation gives:
cases.o1: One specific commend, one specific recommend, and one thing to try next time

cases.q: 'That was great' as a commend is weak because:
cases.o1: The speaker cannot repeat what they do not know they did

cases.q: A recommend should be:
cases.o1: One thing, specific and actionable in the next rep

cases.q: Giving five recommends:
cases.o1: Means none of them is acted on

parts.label: v
parts.explain: One of each, specific enough to be repeated or changed: the discipline is in the count as much as the content

cases.q: Rating a delivery on Vocal Variety looks at:
cases.o1: Whether pitch, volume and rate moved with the meaning

cases.q: Rating on Clarity looks at:
cases.o1: Whether words and endings were intelligible and the structure followable

cases.q: Rating on Body Language looks at:
cases.o1: Stance, gesture and whether movement was motivated

cases.q: Rating a criterion the recording does not show:
cases.o1: Is not done; the criterion is marked not assessable

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Each criterion has its own evidence, and a criterion with no evidence in the recording is not scored

problems.prompt: A {{mn}}-minute lecture is planned as segments of {{sl}} minutes, each with its own point, example and check. How many segments?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Segmenting at ten to fifteen minutes matches how long attention holds without a change; each segment needing its own check is what makes the count a design constraint rather than a guideline

cases.q: Each lecture segment needs:
cases.o1: Its own point, example and check

cases.q: Segmenting helps attention because:
cases.o1: A change of activity resets it, and the check is the change

cases.q: A 50-minute lecture delivered as one continuous explanation:
cases.o1: Loses most of the audience partway, whatever its quality

cases.q: The check at the end of a segment serves two purposes:
cases.o1: Resetting attention and finding out whether the segment worked

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Point, example, check, repeated: the check does double duty as the attention reset

cases.q: A keyword outline differs from a script by:
cases.o1: Holding the structure and the key phrases, not the sentences

cases.q: Delivering from a script costs:
cases.o1: Eye contact and the ability to respond to the room

cases.q: A keyword outline is riskiest for:
cases.o1: The exact wording of a definition or a quotation, which is written out in full

cases.q: Reading a script while trying to look up produces:
cases.o1: Lost place and broken sentences, worse than either alternative

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Keywords for structure, full text only for wording that must be exact

problems.prompt: A talk of {{nw}} words at a measured {{wp}} words a minute fits a {{sl}}-minute slot at what percentage of the slot, if 90 per cent is the target?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Fitting to ninety per cent of the slot leaves room for the questions and the overrun that always happens; a talk written to a hundred per cent is a talk that overruns

problems.prompt: A talk runs {{nw}} words at {{wp}} words a minute against a {{sl}}-minute slot targeted at 90 per cent. How many words must be cut?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Cutting to a word count is the only reliable way to fit a slot, because cutting by feel removes the parts the speaker is least attached to rather than the parts the talk needs least

cases.q: The camera should be:
cases.o1: At eye level, so the speaker looks at the listener rather than down at them

cases.q: The light should be:
cases.o1: In front of the speaker, not behind

cases.q: A microphone is best placed:
cases.o1: About 15 to 30 centimetres away, off the direct breath path

cases.q: A laptop microphone across a desk gives:
cases.o1: Room reverberation and keyboard noise, which cost intelligibility more than any delivery fault

cases.q: Looking at the camera rather than the faces on screen:
cases.o1: Is what the listener experiences as eye contact

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Lens at eye level, light in front, microphone close: the setup costs nothing per talk and outranks delivery

problems.prompt: Sound intensity falls with the square of distance. Moving a microphone from {{d1}} to {{d2}} cm changes the direct-sound level by what factor?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Direct sound falls with the square of distance while room reverberation does not, so moving the microphone away costs intelligibility twice: less signal and the same reflected noise

cases.q: A clear falling ending matters more on a remote call because:
cases.o1: The listener cannot read the visual cues that normally mark a finished turn

cases.q: A pause before answering on a remote call should be:
cases.o1: Long enough to let the lag resolve, so you do not speak over the other person

cases.q: Talking over someone on a laggy call usually means:
cases.o1: Both stop, and the turn has to be renegotiated

cases.q: Handing the turn over explicitly on a remote call:
cases.o1: Removes the ambiguity the lag creates

parts.label: v
parts.explain: The lag removes the cues that manage turns, so the endings and the hand-offs have to be explicit

problems.prompt: A round-trip lag of {{lg}} ms means waiting how long after the other person appears to stop, to be sure they have (seconds), allowing a safety factor of {{sf}}?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: A few hundred milliseconds doubled is still under a second, which is the practical answer: a deliberate short pause before answering costs almost nothing and prevents most collisions

problems.prompt: A {{dur}}-second recommendation spends {{ob}} seconds naming and answering the strongest objection. What percentage of the turn is that?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: A fifth of the turn spent on the strongest objection is usually well spent, because the alternative is spending the whole Q&A on it with the framing chosen by someone else

cases.q: A specific ask names:
'Let me know what you think' as an ask:
cases.o1: Names no action, so nothing happens

cases.q: The easiest ask is one that:
cases.o1: The listener can act on without needing anyone else's approval

cases.q: An ask with no date:
cases.o1: Is deferred indefinitely, since everything with a date outranks it

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Who, what, by when, and within the listener's own authority: four properties, all of them checkable

problems.prompt: A {{mn}}-minute lesson opens with a {{st}}-second story. What percentage of the lesson is the story?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: A story is worth a few per cent of a lesson, and the sentence connecting it to the content is what earns that: an unconnected story at five per cent is five per cent wasted

problems.prompt: In a conversation of {{nt}} turns, {{nb}} build on the previous point. What percentage changed the subject?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Counting building turns on a transcript is the measurement behind 'good listener': a conversation where most turns change the subject is two people waiting to speak

cases.q: One measurable target per practice block is used because:
cases.o1: Two targets at once means neither is attended to while speaking

cases.q: A good target is:
cases.o1: A number the speaker can check immediately after the rep

cases.q: 'Be clearer' as a target fails because:
cases.o1: Nothing in the recording settles whether it was met

cases.q: The target changes when:
cases.o1: It has been met in consecutive blocks, which is what the log is for

parts.label: v
parts.explain: One number, checkable off the recording, held until it is met twice

problems.prompt: A {{mn}}-minute evaluation gives a commend, a recommend and a thing to try. How long is each, with {{op}} seconds of framing (seconds)?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Thirty to fifty seconds each is enough to be specific about one thing, which is why the count is three rather than everything noticed

problems.prompt: Six criteria are rated 1 to 5, scoring {{a}}, {{b}}, {{c}}, {{d}}, {{e2}} and {{f}}. What is the gap between the highest and the lowest?

parts.label: v
parts.value: max(a, max(b, max(c, max(d, max(e2, f))))) - min(a, min(b, min(c, min(d, min(e2, f)))))
parts.explain: A wide spread says the practice has been uneven, and the lowest criterion is where the next block goes; a narrow spread at a low level is a different problem from a wide one

expect.v: Max(a, b, c, d, e2, f) - Min(a, b, c, d, e2, f)

problems.prompt: A {{mn}}-minute talk is outlined with {{nk}} keywords. How many seconds does each keyword cover?

parts.label: v
parts.explain: Twenty to forty seconds a keyword is about right: denser and it is a script, sparser and the speaker loses the thread between keywords

cases.q: SELECT COUNT(salary) FROM emp

cases.s: UPDATE emp SET salary = salary + 500 WHERE dept = 'Sales'
cases.q: SELECT SUM(salary) FROM emp

cases.s: DELETE FROM emp WHERE salary IS NULL OR salary < 4500
cases.q: SELECT COUNT(*) FROM emp

cases.q: SELECT COUNT(*) FROM emp WHERE mgr = 3

cases.s: INSERT INTO emp SELECT id + 10, name, dept, salary, mgr, hired FROM emp WHERE dept = 'IT'
cases.q: SELECT COUNT(*) FROM emp

cases.s: UPDATE emp SET salary = NULL WHERE dept = 'HR'

cases.s: UPDATE emp SET salary = 7000
cases.q: SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT salary) FROM emp

problems.prompt: After {{s}}, what does {{q}} return?

parts.label: a
parts.explain: Columns left out of an INSERT get their default, NULL unless one was declared. UPDATE and DELETE touch every row the WHERE clause keeps, and with no WHERE clause, every row. INSERT … SELECT copies as many rows as the query returns, with no VALUES keyword

cases.s: DELETE FROM emp WHERE id = 6; SAVEPOINT s1; DELETE FROM emp WHERE id = 5; ROLLBACK TO s1; COMMIT;
cases.vs: BEGIN; DELETE FROM emp WHERE id = 6; SAVEPOINT s1; DELETE FROM emp WHERE id = 5; ROLLBACK TO s1; COMMIT;
cases.q: SELECT COUNT(*) FROM emp

cases.s: DELETE FROM emp WHERE id = 6; ROLLBACK;
cases.vs: BEGIN; DELETE FROM emp WHERE id = 6; ROLLBACK;
cases.q: SELECT COUNT(*) FROM emp

cases.s: UPDATE emp SET salary = 1000 WHERE id = 1; COMMIT; ROLLBACK;
cases.vs: BEGIN; UPDATE emp SET salary = 1000 WHERE id = 1; COMMIT;
cases.q: SELECT salary FROM emp WHERE id = 1

cases.s: DELETE FROM emp WHERE dept = 'IT'; CREATE TABLE t (x NUMBER); ROLLBACK;
cases.vs: BEGIN; DELETE FROM emp WHERE dept = 'IT'; COMMIT;
cases.q: SELECT COUNT(*) FROM emp

cases.s: INSERT INTO emp (id, name) VALUES (7, 'Gus'); SAVEPOINT a; INSERT INTO emp (id, name) VALUES (8, 'Hal'); SAVEPOINT b; DELETE FROM emp WHERE id = 1; ROLLBACK TO a; COMMIT;
cases.vs: BEGIN; INSERT INTO emp (id, name) VALUES (7, 'Gus'); SAVEPOINT a; INSERT INTO emp (id, name) VALUES (8, 'Hal'); SAVEPOINT b; DELETE FROM emp WHERE id = 1; ROLLBACK TO a; COMMIT;
cases.q: SELECT COUNT(*) FROM emp

cases.s: UPDATE emp SET salary = 9000 WHERE id = 2; SAVEPOINT a; UPDATE emp SET salary = 8000 WHERE id = 2; ROLLBACK TO a; ROLLBACK;
cases.vs: BEGIN; UPDATE emp SET salary = 9000 WHERE id = 2; SAVEPOINT a; UPDATE emp SET salary = 8000 WHERE id = 2; ROLLBACK TO a; ROLLBACK;
cases.q: SELECT salary FROM emp WHERE id = 2

cases.s: DELETE FROM emp WHERE id = 1; TRUNCATE TABLE depts; ROLLBACK;
cases.vs: BEGIN; DELETE FROM emp WHERE id = 1; COMMIT;
cases.q: SELECT COUNT(*) FROM emp

problems.prompt: One Oracle session runs: {{s}} Then what does {{q}} return?

parts.label: a
parts.explain: A transaction starts with the first DML and ends at COMMIT or ROLLBACK. ROLLBACK TO a savepoint undoes only the work after it and leaves the transaction open; a plain ROLLBACK undoes all of it. Any DDL (CREATE, TRUNCATE…) commits what came before it, so a ROLLBACK afterward has nothing to undo

cases.s: MERGE INTO depts d USING (SELECT DISTINCT dept FROM emp) e ON (d.dept = e.dept) WHEN NOT MATCHED THEN INSERT (dept, city) VALUES (e.dept, 'TBD')
cases.vs: INSERT INTO depts SELECT DISTINCT dept, 'TBD' FROM emp WHERE dept NOT IN (SELECT dept FROM depts);
cases.q: SELECT COUNT(*) FROM depts

cases.s: MERGE INTO emp e USING (SELECT 5 id, 5200 sal FROM DUAL) n ON (e.id = n.id) WHEN MATCHED THEN UPDATE SET e.salary = n.sal WHEN NOT MATCHED THEN INSERT (id, salary) VALUES (n.id, n.sal)
cases.vs: UPDATE emp SET salary = 5200 WHERE id = 5;
cases.q: SELECT SUM(salary) FROM emp

cases.s: MERGE INTO emp e USING (SELECT 9 id, 5200 sal FROM DUAL) n ON (e.id = n.id) WHEN MATCHED THEN UPDATE SET e.salary = n.sal WHEN NOT MATCHED THEN INSERT (id, salary) VALUES (n.id, n.sal)
cases.q: SELECT COUNT(*) FROM emp

cases.s: MERGE INTO emp e USING depts d ON (e.dept = d.dept) WHEN MATCHED THEN UPDATE SET e.salary = NVL(e.salary, 0) + 100
cases.vs: UPDATE emp SET salary = NVL(salary, 0) + 100 WHERE dept IN (SELECT dept FROM depts);
cases.q: SELECT SUM(salary) FROM emp

problems.prompt: After {{s}}, what does {{q}} return?

parts.label: a
parts.explain: MERGE matches each source row to the target with the ON condition: matched rows take the WHEN MATCHED update, unmatched source rows the WHEN NOT MATCHED insert. Either branch may be left out. Target rows with no source row are untouched, and a target row matched twice is an error

cases.s: INSERT ALL WHEN salary >= 5000 THEN INTO hi VALUES (id) WHEN salary >= 4500 THEN INTO mid VALUES (id) SELECT id, salary FROM emp
cases.vs: CREATE TABLE hi (id NUMBER); CREATE TABLE mid (id NUMBER); INSERT INTO hi SELECT id FROM emp WHERE salary >= 5000; INSERT INTO mid SELECT id FROM emp WHERE salary >= 4500;

cases.s: INSERT FIRST WHEN salary >= 5000 THEN INTO hi VALUES (id) WHEN salary >= 4500 THEN INTO mid VALUES (id) SELECT id, salary FROM emp
cases.vs: CREATE TABLE hi (id NUMBER); CREATE TABLE mid (id NUMBER); INSERT INTO hi SELECT id FROM emp WHERE salary >= 5000; INSERT INTO mid SELECT id FROM emp WHERE salary >= 4500 AND salary < 5000;

cases.s: INSERT ALL WHEN salary >= 5000 THEN INTO hi VALUES (id) WHEN salary >= 4500 THEN INTO mid VALUES (id) SELECT id, salary FROM emp
cases.vs: CREATE TABLE hi (id NUMBER); CREATE TABLE mid (id NUMBER); INSERT INTO hi SELECT id FROM emp WHERE salary >= 5000; INSERT INTO mid SELECT id FROM emp WHERE salary >= 4500;
cases.vq: SELECT (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM hi) + (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM mid)

cases.s: INSERT FIRST WHEN salary >= 5000 THEN INTO hi VALUES (id) WHEN salary >= 4500 THEN INTO mid VALUES (id) SELECT id, salary FROM emp
cases.vs: CREATE TABLE hi (id NUMBER); CREATE TABLE mid (id NUMBER); INSERT INTO hi SELECT id FROM emp WHERE salary >= 5000; INSERT INTO mid SELECT id FROM emp WHERE salary >= 4500 AND salary < 5000;
cases.vq: SELECT (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM hi) + (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM mid)

cases.s: INSERT ALL INTO hi VALUES (id) INTO mid VALUES (id) SELECT id FROM emp WHERE dept = 'IT'
cases.vs: CREATE TABLE hi (id NUMBER); CREATE TABLE mid (id NUMBER); INSERT INTO hi SELECT id FROM emp WHERE dept = 'IT'; INSERT INTO mid SELECT id FROM emp WHERE dept = 'IT';
cases.vq: SELECT (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM hi) + (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM mid)

problems.prompt: Empty tables hi(id) and mid(id) exist. After {{s}}, how many {{w}}?

parts.label: a
parts.explain: INSERT ALL tests every WHEN clause for each source row and inserts into every table whose test passes. INSERT FIRST stops at the first passing WHEN, so a row lands in one table at most. Without WHEN, INSERT ALL puts every row into every listed table

parts.label: a

problems.prompt: On a {{fps}} fps clip one full stroke cycle takes {{fr}} frames. What is the stroke rate in cycles per minute?

Young or lightly trained swimmers may need:
In one group aiming at one meet, tapers are usually:
cases.o1: Different lengths by swimmer and event

problems.prompt: A distribution has mean ${{mu}}$ and standard deviation ${{sd}}$. What is the z-score of ${{mu + z*sd}}$?

parts.label: r
parts.explain: $z = \dfrac{x - \mu}{\sigma}$: how many standard deviations from the mean, and on which side. It lets values from different scales be compared

cases.q: within one standard deviation of the mean
within two standard deviations of the mean
within three standard deviations of the mean
above the mean
more than two standard deviations above the mean
more than one standard deviation below the mean
between the mean and one standard deviation above it
between one and two standard deviations above the mean

problems.prompt: In a normal distribution, about what percent of values lie {{q}}? Use the 68-95-99.7 rule.

parts.label: r
parts.explain: About 68% within one, 95% within two, 99.7% within three. Everything else comes from symmetry: split what is left over equally between the two tails

problems.prompt: Each of ${{n}}$ independent trials succeeds with probability ${{p}}$. What is the probability of exactly ${{k}}$ successes?

parts.label: r
parts.explain: $\dbinom{n}{k}p^k(1 - p)^{n - k}$: the probability of one particular arrangement of ${{k}}$ successes and ${{n - k}}$ failures, times the $\dbinom{ {{n}} }{ {{k}} } = {{factorial(n)/(factorial(k)*factorial(n - k))}}$ arrangements

problems.prompt: A binomial count has $n = {{n}}$ and $p = {{p}}$. What is its standard deviation?

parts.label: r
parts.explain: Mean $np = {{n*p}}$, variance $np(1 - p)$, so $\sigma = \sqrt{np(1 - p)}$. The spread is widest at $p = 0.5$ and grows only as $\sqrt n$

problems.prompt: Each attempt succeeds with probability $\dfrac{1}{ {{d}} }$. On average, how many attempts does the first success take?

parts.label: r
parts.explain: For a geometric wait, $E = 1/p$. A one-in-six event takes six tries on average, although the single most likely number of tries is one

problems.prompt: $X$ has standard deviation ${{s}}$. What is the standard deviation of $Y = {{a}} + ({{b}})X$?

parts.label: r
parts.explain: Adding a constant slides the distribution without changing its spread; multiplying stretches it by $|b|$. A standard deviation is never negative

problems.prompt: $X$ and $Y$ are independent with standard deviations ${{s1}}$ and ${{s2}}$. What is the standard deviation of $X {{sign == 0 ? "+" : "-"}} Y$?

parts.label: r
parts.explain: Variances add, standard deviations do not: $\sqrt{ {{s1}}^2 + {{s2}}^2}$. It is the same for a difference as for a sum, because subtracting a random quantity adds uncertainty too

problems.prompt: A population has standard deviation ${{s}}$. What is the standard deviation of the mean of a random sample of ${{n}}$?

parts.label: r
parts.explain: $\sigma_{\bar x} = \dfrac{\sigma}{\sqrt n}$. Averages vary less than individuals, but only by the square root of the sample size

problems.prompt: The true proportion is ${{p}}$. What is the standard deviation of the sample proportion for random samples of ${{n}}$?

parts.label: r
parts.explain: $\sigma_{\hat p} = \sqrt{\dfrac{p(1 - p)}{n}}$: the binomial standard deviation divided by $n$. Largest at $p = 0.5$, which is why polls quote a single margin of error

problems.prompt: A poll is repeated with ${{f}}$ times as many people. By what factor does its margin of error change?

parts.label: r
parts.explain: Margin of error goes as $1/\sqrt n$. Halving the margin takes four times the sample: precision gets expensive fast

problems.prompt: In a random sample of ${{n}}$, the sample proportion is ${{ph}}$. What is the margin of error of a 95% confidence interval? Use $z^* = 1.96$.

parts.label: r
parts.explain: $E = z^*\sqrt{\dfrac{\hat p(1 - \hat p)}{n}}$. Quick check: for $\hat p$ near 0.5 it is about $1/\sqrt n$

problems.prompt: How many people must a poll sample for a 95% margin of error of ${{E}}$, planning for the worst case $p = 0.5$? Use $z^* = 2$ and give the exact value before rounding up.

parts.label: r
parts.explain: $n = \left(\dfrac{z^*}{E}\right)^2p(1 - p) = \dfrac{4 \times 0.25}{E^2} = \dfrac{1}{E^2}$. With $z^* = 2$ the worst-case rule is simply one over the margin squared

problems.prompt: Test $H_0\!: p = {{p0}}$. A random sample of ${{n}}$ gives $\hat p = {{p0 + d}}$. What is the z statistic?

parts.label: r
parts.explain: $z = \dfrac{\hat p - p_0}{\sqrt{p_0(1 - p_0)/n}}$. The standard error uses the hypothesised $p_0$, because the test asks what would happen if $H_0$ were true

problems.prompt: Test $H_0\!: \mu = {{mu0}}$. A sample of ${{n}}$ has mean ${{mu0 + d}}$ and standard deviation ${{s}}$. What is the t statistic?

parts.label: r
parts.explain: $t = \dfrac{\bar x - \mu_0}{s/\sqrt n}$, with $n - 1 = {{n - 1}}$ degrees of freedom. It counts how many standard errors the sample mean sits from the claim

cases.q: a one-sample t test with 24 observations
a matched-pairs t test on 15 pairs
a chi-square goodness-of-fit test with 6 categories
a chi-square test on a table with 3 rows and 4 columns
a chi-square test on a 2 by 2 table
a t test for the slope of a regression line through 20 points

problems.prompt: How many degrees of freedom has {{q}}?

parts.label: r
parts.explain: Count the values free to vary once the totals are fixed: $n - 1$ for a mean, categories minus one for goodness of fit, $(r - 1)(c - 1)$ for a table, and $n - 2$ for a slope, which uses up two estimates

problems.prompt: A test gives a p-value of ${{pv}}$ at significance level $\alpha = {{al}}$. What is the conclusion?

parts.label: a2
choice: Reject the null hypothesis: the result is statistically significant
Fail to reject the null hypothesis: the evidence is not strong enough
parts.explain: Reject when $p < \alpha$. The p-value is the probability of data at least this extreme if the null hypothesis were true. It is not the probability that the null hypothesis is true, and failing to reject is not the same as accepting

cases.q: A test concludes a drug works when in fact it does not.
A test fails to detect a drug that really does work.
A fire alarm sounds with no fire (null: no fire).
A fire alarm stays silent during a fire (null: no fire).
Lowering α from 0.05 to 0.01, with nothing else changed, makes which error more likely?
The probability of which error equals the significance level α?

problems.prompt: {{q}} Which error is it?

parts.label: a2
choice: Type I: rejecting a true null hypothesis
Type II: failing to reject a false null hypothesis
parts.explain: Type I is a false alarm, with probability $\alpha$. Type II is a miss, with probability $\beta$; power is $1 - \beta$. For a fixed sample size, making one rarer makes the other more common

problems.prompt: In a two-way table of ${{N}}$ people, one row totals ${{rt}}$ and one column totals ${{ct}}$. What count is expected in their cell if the two variables are independent?

parts.label: r
parts.explain: Row total times column total over the grand total. It is the multiplication rule for independent events, $P(A)P(B)$, turned into a count

problems.prompt: A cell has observed count ${{E + d}}$ and expected count ${{E}}$. What does it contribute to the chi-square statistic?

parts.label: r
parts.explain: $\dfrac{(O - E)^2}{E}$: the squared miss, measured against what was expected. A miss of 5 matters much more when 10 were expected than when 50 were

cases.q: What does "95% confident" refer to?
A 95% interval for a mean is 12 to 18. Is there a 95% chance the next observation falls in it?
With the same data, how does a 99% interval compare with a 95% one?
A 95% interval for a difference in means contains 0. What follows at the 5% level?

parts.label: a2
choice: The method: 95 in 100 intervals built this way capture the true value
No: the interval is about the population mean, not individual values
It is wider: more confidence costs precision
The difference is not statistically significant
parts.explain: A confidence level describes how often the procedure works over many samples. Any one interval either contains the parameter or does not

cases.q: A website asks visitors to click to answer a poll.
A phone survey reaches only landlines.
Half the people selected for a survey do not reply.
A researcher surveys the first 50 people leaving a gym about exercise.
A survey asks: do you agree that wasteful spending should be cut?

problems.prompt: {{q}} What is the main problem?

parts.label: a2
parts.explain: Ask who had no chance of being chosen (undercoverage), who chose themselves (voluntary response), who was chosen but is missing (nonresponse), who was merely easy to reach (convenience), and whether the question pushed an answer. A bigger sample cures none of them

cases.q: Why are subjects assigned to treatments at random?
Why can an observational study not show cause and effect?
Why is a placebo group used?
Why are subjects grouped into blocks before assignment?

parts.label: a2
choice: So the groups are alike on average in everything except the treatment
A confounding variable may explain both the treatment and the outcome
To separate the effect of the treatment from the effect of being treated at all
To remove variation from a known source so the treatment effect is easier to see
parts.explain: Random sampling lets you generalise to a population; random assignment lets you conclude cause. They are different randomisations doing different jobs

problems.prompt: The correlation between two variables is $r = {{r}}$. What percent of the variation in $y$ does the regression line explain?

parts.label: r2
parts.explain: $r^2$, as a percent. A correlation of 0.5 sounds moderate but explains only a quarter of the variation; the sign of $r$ does not matter here

problems.prompt: Two variables have correlation ${{r}}$, with $s_x = {{sx}}$ and $s_y = {{sy}}$. What is the slope of the least-squares line?

parts.label: r2
parts.explain: $b = r\,\dfrac{s_y}{s_x}$. One standard deviation along $x$ predicts only $r$ standard deviations in $y$: that shrinkage is regression to the mean

problems.prompt: Use Stirling's approximation to estimate $\ln N!$ for $N = {{N}}$.

parts.label: y
parts.explain: $\ln N! \approx N\ln N - N$, from $\ln N! = \sum\ln k \approx \int_1^N \ln x\,dx$. Already within 1% at N = 100; for a mole of particles it is exact for all purposes, which is why entropy formulas use it

problems.prompt: With Stirling's approximation, what is $\ln W$ for $W = \binom{ {{N}} }{ {{n}} }$ (choosing {{n}} of {{N}} sites)?

parts.label: y
parts.explain: $\ln W \approx N\ln N - n\ln n - (N - n)\ln(N - n) = -N[x\ln x + (1 - x)\ln(1 - x)]$ with $x = n/N$: the mixing-entropy form

problems.prompt: A variable takes the values {{xs}} with probabilities {{ps}}. What is its {{wt}}?

parts.label: y
parts.explain: $\langle x\rangle = \sum p_ix_i$; $\sigma^2 = \langle x^2\rangle - \langle x\rangle^2$. The variance is the mean-square fluctuation, the quantity behind heat capacities and compressibilities

problems.prompt: Two subsystems can exchange {{what}}. Maximising the total entropy makes which quantity equal on both sides?

parts.label: y
parts.explain: Set dS_total = 0 for the exchange: energy gives 1/T₁ = 1/T₂; volume gives P₁/T₁ = P₂/T₂; particles give μ₁/T₁ = μ₂/T₂. Each conserved quantity that can move pairs with an intensive variable that equalises

cases.s: At fixed S, V and N, an equilibrium state minimises U.
At fixed U, V and N, an equilibrium state minimises S.
Maximum entropy at fixed energy and minimum energy at fixed entropy pick out the same state.
The energy minimum principle needs (∂S/∂U) to be negative.

parts.label: y
parts.explain: The entropy maximum principle at fixed U and the energy minimum principle at fixed S describe the same equilibrium: because (∂S/∂U) = 1/T > 0, a state that is not an energy minimum at fixed S can lower U and return the energy as heat, raising S at fixed U

problems.prompt: A system is held at fixed {{c}}. Which function is minimised at equilibrium?

parts.label: y
parts.explain: Each potential is minimised when its natural variables are fixed: U(S,V,N), H(S,P,N), A(T,V,N), G(T,P,N), Ω(T,V,μ). A bath fixes T; a piston at constant external pressure fixes P; a reservoir of particles fixes μ

a single-phase mixture of ethanol and water

problems.prompt: How many intensive variables can be changed independently in {{sys}}?

parts.label: y
parts.explain: Gibbs phase rule: $F = C - P + 2$ (C components, P phases, no reactions). A pure substance has F = 1 along a coexistence line (T fixes P) and 0 at the triple point

cases.s: Boiling water at 1 atm, with a latent heat
A ferromagnet losing its magnetisation smoothly at the Curie point, with a diverging susceptibility
Melting ice: the volume jumps
A liquid–gas system exactly at its critical point
