MK-1.1.A.t: Count to 100 by ones and by tens.

MK-1.1.B.t: Count forward beginning from a given number within the known sequence (instead of having to begin at 1).

MK-1.1.C.t: Write numbers from 0 to 20 and represent a number of objects with a written numeral 0–20 (0 = no objects).

MK-1.1.D.t: Count objects by saying the number names in standard order, pairing each object with one and only one number name.

MK-1.1.E.t: Count to answer "how many?" for up to 20 objects in a line, array or circle (10 scattered), and count out that many objects given a number 1–20.

MK-1.1.F.t: Identify whether the number of objects in one group is greater than, less than, or equal to the number in another group (up to 10).

MK-1.1.G.t: Compare two numbers between 1 and 10 presented as written numerals.

MK-1.2.A.t: Represent addition and subtraction with objects, fingers, drawings, sounds, acting out situations, expressions or equations.

MK-1.2.B.t: Solve addition and subtraction word problems, and add and subtract within 10 (e.g. 1 + 1), using objects or drawings.

MK-1.2.C.t: Decompose numbers less than or equal to 10 into pairs in more than one way (5 = 2 + 3 = 4 + 1).

MK-1.2.D.t: For any number 1 to 9, find the number that makes 10 when added to it.

MK-1.3.A.t: Compose and decompose numbers from 11 to 19 into ten ones and some further ones (18 = 10 + 8).

MK-1.4.A.t: Describe measurable attributes of objects, such as length or weight, and several attributes of one object.

MK-1.4.B.t: Directly compare two objects with a measurable attribute in common and say which has more or less of it.

MK-1.4.C.t: Classify objects into given categories, count the objects in each category, and sort the categories by count (counts ≤ 10).

MK-1.5.A.t: Describe objects in the environment using names of shapes and their relative positions (above, below, beside, in front of, behind, next to).

MK-1.5.B.t: Name shapes correctly regardless of their orientation or overall size.

MK-1.5.C.t: Identify shapes as two-dimensional (flat) or three-dimensional (solid).

MK-1.5.D.t: Analyze and compare two- and three-dimensional shapes by their parts and attributes (number of sides, vertices, equal sides).

MK-1.5.E.t: Model shapes by building them from components (sticks, clay) and drawing them.

MK-1.5.F.t: Compose simple shapes to form larger shapes (two triangles make a rectangle).

MK-2.1.A.t: Use addition and subtraction within 20 to solve word problems (adding to, taking from, putting together, taking apart, comparing) with unknowns in all positions.

MK-2.1.B.t: Solve word problems that call for adding three whole numbers whose sum is ≤ 20.

MK-2.1.C.t: Apply the commutative and associative properties of addition as strategies (8+3 = 3+8; 2+6+4 = 2+10).

MK-2.1.D.t: Understand subtraction as an unknown-addend problem (10 − 8 as 8 + ? = 10).

MK-2.1.E.t: Relate counting to addition and subtraction (counting on 2 to add 2).

MK-2.1.F.t: Add and subtract within 20, fluently within 10, using strategies such as making ten, decomposing to ten, and known sums (8+6 = 8+2+4).

MK-2.1.G.t: Understand the meaning of the equal sign and decide whether equations like 6 = 6, 7 = 8 − 1, 5 + 2 = 2 + 5 are true or false.

MK-2.1.H.t: Determine the unknown whole number in an addition or subtraction equation relating three whole numbers (8 + ? = 11).

MK-2.2.A.t: Count to 120 starting at any number less than 120; read and write numerals in this range.

MK-2.2.B.t: Understand that the two digits of a two-digit number represent amounts of tens and ones (10 is a bundle of ten ones; 11–19 are a ten and some ones; 10, 20 … 90 are tens and 0 ones).

MK-2.2.C.t: Compare two two-digit numbers based on the meanings of the tens and ones digits, recording with >, =, <.

MK-2.2.D.t: Add within 100 (two-digit + one-digit, two-digit + a multiple of 10) using models and place-value strategies, composing a ten when needed.

MK-2.2.E.t: Given a two-digit number, mentally find 10 more or 10 less without counting.

MK-2.2.F.t: Subtract multiples of 10 in the range 10–90 from multiples of 10 in the same range.

MK-2.3.A.t: Order three objects by length, and compare the lengths of two objects indirectly by using a third object.

MK-2.3.B.t: Express the length of an object as a whole number of length units by laying copies of a shorter unit end to end with no gaps or overlaps.

MK-2.3.C.t: Tell and write time in hours and half-hours using analog and digital clocks.

MK-2.3.D.t: Organize, represent and interpret data with up to three categories; ask and answer how many in each and how many more or less.

MK-2.4.A.t: Distinguish defining attributes (triangles are closed and three-sided) from non-defining ones (color, orientation, size); build and draw shapes with given attributes.

MK-2.4.B.t: Compose two- or three-dimensional shapes into a composite shape, and compose new shapes from it.

MK-2.4.C.t: Partition circles and rectangles into two and four equal shares, using halves, fourths and quarters; more equal shares make smaller shares.

MK-3.1.A.t: Use addition and subtraction within 100 to solve one- and two-step word problems with unknowns in all positions.

MK-3.1.B.t: Fluently add and subtract within 20 using mental strategies; know from memory all sums of two one-digit numbers.

MK-3.1.C.t: Determine whether a group of up to 20 objects has an odd or even number of members (pairing, counting by 2s); write an even number as a sum of two equal addends.

MK-3.1.D.t: Use addition to find the total in a rectangular array with up to 5 rows and 5 columns; write an equation as a sum of equal addends.

MK-3.2.A.t: Understand that the three digits of a three-digit number represent hundreds, tens and ones; 100 is a bundle of ten tens.

MK-3.2.C.t: Read and write numbers to 1000 using base-ten numerals, number names and expanded form.

MK-3.2.D.t: Compare two three-digit numbers based on the meanings of the digits, using >, =, <.

MK-3.2.E.t: Fluently add and subtract within 100 using strategies based on place value, properties of operations, and the relationship between addition and subtraction.

MK-3.2.F.t: Add up to four two-digit numbers using strategies based on place value and properties of operations.

MK-3.2.G.t: Add and subtract within 1000 using models, drawings and place-value strategies, composing or decomposing tens and hundreds as needed.

MK-3.2.I.t: Explain why addition and subtraction strategies work, using place value and the properties of operations.

MK-3.2.H.t: Mentally add or subtract 10 or 100 to or from a number 100–900.

MK-3.3.A.t: Measure the length of an object by selecting and using an appropriate tool (ruler, yardstick, meter stick, measuring tape).

MK-3.3.B.t: Measure an object twice using units of different lengths and describe how the measurements relate to the unit size.

MK-3.3.C.t: Estimate lengths using units of inches, feet, centimeters and meters.

MK-3.3.D.t: Measure to determine how much longer one object is than another, in a standard length unit.

MK-3.3.E.t: Use addition and subtraction within 100 to solve word problems involving lengths in the same units.

MK-3.3.F.t: Represent whole numbers as lengths from 0 on a number line with equally spaced points, and represent sums and differences within 100 on it.

MK-3.3.G.t: Tell and write time from analog and digital clocks to the nearest five minutes, using a.m. and p.m.

MK-3.3.H.t: Solve word problems involving dollar bills, quarters, dimes, nickels and pennies, using $ and ¢ symbols.

MK-3.3.I.t: Generate length data by measuring several objects to the nearest whole unit and show it on a line plot.

MK-3.3.J.t: Draw a picture graph and a bar graph (single-unit scale) for up to four categories, and solve put-together, take-apart and compare problems from it.

MK-3.4.A.t: Recognize and draw shapes with specified attributes (number of angles or faces); identify triangles, quadrilaterals, pentagons, hexagons and cubes.

MK-3.4.B.t: Partition a rectangle into rows and columns of same-size squares and count to find the total number of them.

MK-3.4.C.t: Partition circles and rectangles into two, three or four equal shares, described as halves, thirds, fourths; recognize equal shares need not have the same shape.

MK-4.1.A.t: Interpret products of whole numbers (5 × 7 as the total in 5 groups of 7 objects).

MK-4.1.B.t: Interpret whole-number quotients (56 ÷ 8 as the number in each share, or the number of shares).

MK-4.1.C.t: Use multiplication and division within 100 to solve word problems with equal groups, arrays and measurement quantities.

MK-4.1.D.t: Determine the unknown whole number in a multiplication or division equation relating three whole numbers (8 × ? = 48).

MK-4.1.E.t: Apply the commutative, associative and distributive properties as strategies to multiply and divide.

MK-4.1.F.t: Understand division as an unknown-factor problem (32 ÷ 8 is the number that makes 32 when multiplied by 8).

MK-4.1.G.t: Fluently multiply and divide within 100; know from memory all products of two one-digit numbers.

MK-4.1.H.t: Solve two-step word problems using the four operations, representing them with equations with a letter for the unknown, and check answers by mental computation and estimation.

MK-4.1.I.t: Identify arithmetic patterns (including in the addition and multiplication tables) and explain them using properties of operations.

MK-4.2.A.t: Use place value understanding to round whole numbers to the nearest 10 or 100.

MK-4.2.B.t: Fluently add and subtract within 1000 using strategies and algorithms based on place value, properties, and the add–subtract relationship.

MK-4.2.C.t: Multiply one-digit whole numbers by multiples of 10 in the range 10–90 (9 × 80, 5 × 60).

MK-4.3.A.t: Understand a fraction 1/b as one part when a whole is partitioned into b equal parts, and a/b as a parts of size 1/b.

MK-4.3.B.t: Represent 1/b on a number line by partitioning 0 to 1 into b equal parts; each part has size 1/b and its endpoint locates 1/b.

MK-4.3.C.t: Represent a/b on a number line by marking off a lengths of 1/b from 0.

MK-4.3.D.t: Explain equivalence of fractions as being the same size or the same point on a number line; recognize and generate simple equivalent fractions (1/2 = 2/4, 4/6 = 2/3) with a visual model.

MK-4.3.E.t: Express whole numbers as fractions and recognize fractions equivalent to whole numbers (3 = 3/1; 4/4 = 1).

MK-4.3.F.t: Compare two fractions with the same numerator or the same denominator by reasoning about their size, recording with >, =, <; comparisons are valid only for the same whole.

MK-4.4.A.t: Tell and write time to the nearest minute; measure time intervals in minutes and solve elapsed-time word problems (e.g. on a number line).

MK-4.4.B.t: Measure and estimate liquid volumes and masses in g, kg and L; solve one-step word problems with them using the four operations.

MK-4.4.C.t: Draw a scaled picture graph and scaled bar graph for several categories, and solve one- and two-step "how many more/less" problems from them.

MK-4.4.D.t: Measure lengths with rulers marked in halves and fourths of an inch and show the data on a line plot in whole numbers, halves or quarters.

MK-4.4.E.t: Recognize area as an attribute of plane figures: a unit square has one square unit of area, and a figure covered by n unit squares without gaps or overlaps has area n.

MK-4.4.F.t: Measure areas by counting unit squares (square cm, square m, square in, square ft, and improvised units).

MK-4.4.G.t: Find the area of a rectangle with whole-number sides by tiling it and show it equals the product of the side lengths; multiply side lengths to solve area problems.

MK-4.4.H.t: Use tiling to show that a rectangle with sides a and b + c has area a × b + a × c (area models for the distributive property).

MK-4.4.I.t: Find areas of rectilinear figures by decomposing them into non-overlapping rectangles and adding the areas.

MK-4.4.J.t: Solve perimeter problems: find the perimeter from side lengths, find an unknown side, and show rectangles with the same perimeter and different areas or the same area and different perimeters.

MK-4.5.A.t: Understand that shapes in different categories may share attributes that define a larger category; recognize rhombuses, rectangles and squares as quadrilaterals and draw quadrilaterals that are none of these.

MK-4.5.B.t: Partition shapes into parts with equal areas and express the area of each part as a unit fraction of the whole.

MK-5.1.A.t: Interpret a multiplication equation as a comparison (35 = 5 × 7 as 35 is 5 times as many as 7) and write comparisons as equations.

MK-5.1.B.t: Multiply or divide to solve word problems involving multiplicative comparison, distinguishing it from additive comparison.

MK-5.1.C.t: Solve multistep word problems with whole numbers and the four operations, including problems where remainders must be interpreted; check with estimation.

MK-5.1.D.t: Find all factor pairs of a whole number 1–100, recognize it as a multiple of each factor, and determine whether it is prime or composite.

MK-5.1.E.t: Generate a number or shape pattern that follows a given rule and identify features of the pattern not explicit in the rule.

MK-5.2.A.t: Recognize that in a multi-digit whole number a digit in one place represents ten times what it represents in the place to its right (700 ÷ 70 = 10).

MK-5.2.B.t: Read and write multi-digit whole numbers using base-ten numerals, number names and expanded form; compare two multi-digit numbers with >, =, <.

MK-5.2.C.t: Use place value understanding to round multi-digit whole numbers to any place.

MK-5.2.D.t: Fluently add and subtract multi-digit whole numbers using the standard algorithm.

MK-5.2.E.t: Multiply a whole number of up to four digits by a one-digit number, and two two-digit numbers, using place-value strategies and properties; illustrate with equations, arrays and area models.

MK-5.2.F.t: Find whole-number quotients and remainders with up to four-digit dividends and one-digit divisors using place-value strategies and the multiplication–division relationship.

MK-5.3.A.t: Explain why a/b = (n × a)/(n × b) using visual fraction models, and use this to recognize and generate equivalent fractions.

MK-5.3.B.t: Compare two fractions with different numerators and different denominators by creating common denominators or numerators or comparing to a benchmark like 1/2.

MK-5.3.C.t: Understand addition and subtraction of fractions as joining and separating parts referring to the same whole.

MK-5.3.D.t: Decompose a fraction into a sum of fractions with the same denominator in more than one way (3/8 = 1/8 + 2/8; 2 1/8 = 1 + 1 + 1/8 = 8/8 + 8/8 + 1/8).

MK-5.3.E.t: Add and subtract mixed numbers with like denominators by replacing each with an equivalent fraction or using properties of operations.

MK-5.3.F.t: Solve word problems involving addition and subtraction of fractions referring to the same whole and having like denominators.

MK-5.3.G.t: Understand a/b as a multiple of 1/b and multiply a fraction by a whole number: n × (a/b) = (n × a)/b.

MK-5.3.H.t: Solve word problems involving multiplication of a fraction by a whole number.

MK-5.3.I.t: Express a fraction with denominator 10 as an equivalent fraction with denominator 100, and add two fractions with denominators 10 and 100 (3/10 + 4/100 = 34/100).

MK-5.3.J.t: Use decimal notation for fractions with denominators 10 or 100 (0.62 = 62/100) and locate them on a number line.

MK-5.3.K.t: Compare two decimals to hundredths by reasoning about their size, recording with >, =, <; comparisons are valid only for the same whole.

MK-5.4.A.t: Know relative sizes of units in one system (km, m, cm; kg, g; lb, oz; l, ml; hr, min, sec) and express a larger-unit measurement in a smaller unit, recording equivalents in a two-column table.

MK-5.4.B.t: Use the four operations to solve word problems involving distances, time intervals, liquid volumes, masses and money, including simple fractions or decimals; represent quantities on number line diagrams.

MK-5.4.C.t: Apply the area and perimeter formulas for rectangles in real-world and mathematical problems, including finding an unknown side.

MK-5.4.D.t: Make a line plot of measurements in fractions of a unit (1/2, 1/4, 1/8) and solve addition and subtraction of fractions using it.

MK-5.4.E.t: Recognize an angle as two rays sharing an endpoint and measure it against a circle: a one-degree angle turns through 1/360 of a circle; n one-degree angles make n degrees.

MK-5.4.F.t: Measure angles in whole-number degrees with a protractor and sketch angles of a specified measure.

MK-5.4.G.t: Recognize angle measure as additive and solve addition and subtraction problems to find unknown angles on a diagram.

MK-5.5.A.t: Draw points, lines, segments, rays, angles (right, acute, obtuse), and perpendicular and parallel lines, and identify them in figures.

MK-5.5.B.t: Classify two-dimensional figures by parallel or perpendicular lines and by angles of a specified size; recognize right triangles.

MK-5.5.C.t: Recognize a line of symmetry for a two-dimensional figure, identify line-symmetric figures and draw lines of symmetry.

MK-6.1.A.t: Use parentheses, brackets or braces in numerical expressions and evaluate expressions with these symbols.

MK-6.1.B.t: Write simple expressions that record calculations with numbers and interpret them without evaluating (3 × (18932 + 921) is three times as large as 18932 + 921).

MK-6.1.C.t: Generate two numerical patterns from two given rules, form ordered pairs from corresponding terms, graph them, and identify relationships between corresponding terms.

MK-6.2.A.t: Recognize that in a multi-digit number a digit represents 10 times as much as in the place to its right and 1/10 of what it represents in the place to its left.

MK-6.2.B.t: Explain patterns in the number of zeros of a product when multiplying by a power of 10 and in decimal-point placement when multiplying or dividing by a power of 10; use whole-number exponents for powers of 10.

MK-6.2.C.t: Read and write decimals to thousandths using base-ten numerals, number names and expanded form (347.392 = 3×100 + 4×10 + 7×1 + 3×(1/10) + 9×(1/100) + 2×(1/1000)).

MK-6.2.D.t: Compare two decimals to thousandths based on the meanings of the digits, using >, =, <.

MK-6.2.E.t: Use place value understanding to round decimals to any place.

MK-6.2.F.t: Fluently multiply multi-digit whole numbers using the standard algorithm.

MK-6.2.G.t: Find whole-number quotients of whole numbers with up to four-digit dividends and two-digit divisors using place-value strategies and the multiplication–division relationship.

MK-6.2.H.t: Add, subtract, multiply and divide decimals to hundredths using models, place-value strategies and properties of operations, and explain the reasoning.

MK-6.3.A.t: Add and subtract fractions with unlike denominators (including mixed numbers) by replacing them with equivalent fractions that have like denominators.

MK-6.3.B.t: Solve word problems involving addition and subtraction of fractions referring to the same whole, including unlike denominators, and use benchmark fractions to check reasonableness.

MK-6.3.C.t: Interpret a fraction as division of the numerator by the denominator (a/b = a ÷ b) and solve word problems where whole-number division gives a fraction or mixed number.

MK-6.3.D.t: Interpret (a/b) × q as a parts of a partition of q into b equal parts, and multiply a fraction by a fraction: (a/b) × (c/d) = ac/bd.

MK-6.3.E.t: Find the area of a rectangle with fractional side lengths by tiling with unit squares of the appropriate unit-fraction side, and show it equals the product of the side lengths.

MK-6.3.F.t: Interpret multiplication as scaling: compare the size of a product to one factor from the other factor, without multiplying.

MK-6.3.G.t: Solve real-world problems involving multiplication of fractions and mixed numbers using visual fraction models or equations.

MK-6.3.H.t: Divide a unit fraction by a non-zero whole number and a whole number by a unit fraction (1/3 ÷ 4 = 1/12; 4 ÷ 1/5 = 20), using the multiplication–division relationship.

MK-6.3.I.t: Solve real-world problems involving division of unit fractions by whole numbers and of whole numbers by unit fractions.

MK-6.4.A.t: Convert among different-sized standard measurement units within one system (5 cm to 0.05 m) and use the conversions in multi-step real-world problems.

MK-6.4.B.t: Make a line plot of measurements in fractions of a unit (1/2, 1/4, 1/8) and use operations on fractions to solve problems from it (redistribute amounts equally).

MK-6.4.C.t: Recognize volume as an attribute of solid figures: a unit cube has one cubic unit of volume, and a solid packed by n unit cubes without gaps or overlaps has volume n.

MK-6.4.D.t: Measure volumes by counting unit cubes (cubic cm, cubic in, cubic ft, improvised units).

MK-6.4.E.t: Find the volume of a right rectangular prism with whole-number edges by packing it with unit cubes, show it equals the product of the edge lengths, and apply V = l × w × h and V = b × h.

MK-6.4.F.t: Recognize volume as additive and find volumes of solids made of two non-overlapping right rectangular prisms.

MK-6.5.A.t: Use a pair of perpendicular number lines (axes) meeting at the origin to define a coordinate system, and locate a point with an ordered pair (x-coordinate, y-coordinate).

MK-6.5.B.t: Represent real-world and mathematical problems by graphing points in the first quadrant and interpret coordinate values in context.

MK-6.5.C.t: Understand that attributes of a category of two-dimensional figures belong to all its subcategories (all rectangles have four right angles, and squares are rectangles).

MK-6.5.D.t: Classify two-dimensional figures in a hierarchy based on properties.

MK-7.1.A.t: Use ratio language to describe a ratio relationship between two quantities ("for every 2 wings there was 1 beak").

MK-7.1.B.t: Describe the unit rate a/b associated with a ratio a:b (b ≠ 0) using rate language ("$5 for 4 burgers is $1.25 per burger").

MK-7.1.C.t: Make tables of equivalent ratios with whole-number measurements, find missing values, plot the pairs on the coordinate plane, and use tables to compare ratios.

MK-7.1.D.t: Solve unit rate problems, including unit pricing and constant speed.

MK-7.1.E.t: Find a percent of a quantity as a rate per 100 (30% of a quantity is 30/100 times it) and find the whole given a part and the percent.

MK-7.1.F.t: Use ratio reasoning to convert measurement units, multiplying or dividing quantities appropriately.

MK-7.2.A.t: Interpret and compute quotients of fractions and solve word problems involving division of fractions by fractions ((2/3) ÷ (3/4) = 8/9).

MK-7.2.B.t: Fluently divide multi-digit numbers using the standard algorithm.

MK-7.2.C.t: Fluently add, subtract, multiply and divide multi-digit decimals using the standard algorithm for each operation.

MK-7.2.D.t: Find the greatest common factor of two whole numbers ≤ 100 and the least common multiple of two whole numbers ≤ 12; use the distributive property to factor out a common factor (36 + 8 = 4(9 + 2)).

MK-7.2.E.t: Use positive and negative numbers to represent quantities with opposite directions or values (temperature, elevation, credits/debits), explaining the meaning of 0 in context.

MK-7.2.F.t: Recognize a rational number as a point on the number line; opposite signs indicate locations on opposite sides of 0, and −(−3) = 3.

MK-7.2.G.t: Interpret signs of ordered pairs as quadrants and reflections across the axes; find and position integers and other rationals on number lines and the coordinate plane.

MK-7.2.H.t: Interpret statements of inequality as relative position on a number line, and write and explain statements of order for rational numbers in context (−3 °C > −7 °C).

MK-7.2.I.t: Understand the absolute value of a rational number as its distance from 0, and distinguish comparisons of absolute value from statements about order (balance < −30 means debt > $30).

MK-7.2.J.t: Solve problems by graphing points in all four quadrants, including distances between points that share a first or second coordinate, using absolute value.

MK-7.3.A.t: Write and evaluate numerical expressions involving whole-number exponents.

MK-7.3.B.t: Write expressions in which letters stand for numbers ("subtract y from 5" as 5 − y) and identify their parts using sum, term, product, factor, quotient, coefficient.

MK-7.3.C.t: Evaluate expressions at specific values of their variables, including formulas (V = s³, A = 6s²), using the order of operations.

MK-7.3.D.t: Apply the properties of operations to generate equivalent expressions (3(2 + x) = 6 + 3x; 24x + 18y = 6(4x + 3y); y + y + y = 3y).

MK-7.3.E.t: Identify when two expressions are equivalent — they name the same number for every value substituted.

MK-7.3.F.t: Understand solving an equation or inequality as finding which values from a set make it true, and use substitution to check.

MK-7.3.G.t: Use variables to represent numbers and write expressions when solving a real-world or mathematical problem.

MK-7.3.H.t: Write and solve equations of the form x + p = q and px = q for nonnegative rational x, p, q in real-world and mathematical problems.

MK-7.3.I.t: Write an inequality x > c or x < c for a constraint, recognize that it has infinitely many solutions, and show them on a number line.

MK-7.3.J.t: Use variables for two quantities that change together; write an equation expressing the dependent variable in terms of the independent one, and relate it to graphs and tables (d = 65t).

MK-7.4.A.t: Find the area of right triangles, other triangles, special quadrilaterals and polygons by composing into rectangles or decomposing into triangles and other shapes.

MK-7.4.B.t: Find the volume of a right rectangular prism with fractional edge lengths by packing it with unit cubes of unit-fraction edge, and show it matches V = lwh and V = bh.

MK-7.4.C.t: Draw polygons in the coordinate plane given vertex coordinates, and use coordinates to find side lengths that share a first or second coordinate.

MK-7.4.D.t: Represent three-dimensional figures using nets made of rectangles and triangles and use the nets to find surface area.

MK-7.5.A.t: Recognize a statistical question as one that anticipates variability in the data ("How old are the students in my school?").

MK-7.5.B.t: Understand that a distribution of data collected to answer a statistical question can be described by its center, spread and overall shape.

MK-7.5.C.t: Recognize that a measure of center summarizes all values with one number, while a measure of variation describes how the values vary with one number.

MK-7.5.D.t: Display numerical data in plots on a number line: dot plots, histograms and box plots.

MK-7.5.E.t: Summarize a numerical data set by reporting the number of observations and describing the attribute under investigation, how it was measured and its units.

MK-7.5.F.t: Give quantitative measures of center (median, mean) and variability (interquartile range, mean absolute deviation), describe the pattern and striking deviations, and relate the choice of measures to the shape of the data.

MK-8.1.A.t: Compute unit rates associated with ratios of fractions, including ratios of lengths, areas and other quantities in like or different units (1/2 mile per 1/4 hour = 2 miles per hour).

MK-8.1.B.t: Decide whether two quantities are in a proportional relationship by testing for equivalent ratios in a table or a straight-line graph through the origin.

MK-8.1.C.t: Identify the constant of proportionality (unit rate) in tables, graphs, equations, diagrams and verbal descriptions.

MK-8.1.D.t: Represent proportional relationships by equations (t = pn) and explain what a point (x, y) on the graph means, especially (0, 0) and (1, r) where r is the unit rate.

MK-8.1.E.t: Use proportional relationships to solve multistep ratio and percent problems: simple interest, tax, markups and markdowns, gratuities, commissions, fees, percent increase and decrease, percent error.

MK-8.2.A.t: Add rational numbers on a number line: opposite quantities combine to 0, and p + q is |q| from p in the positive or negative direction depending on the sign of q.

MK-8.2.B.t: Understand subtraction of rationals as adding the additive inverse (p − q = p + (−q)), show that the distance between two rationals is the absolute value of their difference, and apply properties to add and subtract.

MK-8.2.C.t: Multiply and divide rational numbers by extending the properties of operations, giving (−1)(−1) = 1 and −(p/q) = (−p)/q = p/(−q).

MK-8.2.D.t: Apply properties of operations to multiply and divide rationals, and convert a rational number to a decimal by long division, knowing the decimal terminates or repeats.

MK-8.2.E.t: Solve real-world and mathematical problems involving the four operations with rational numbers.

MK-8.3.A.t: Apply properties of operations to add, subtract, factor and expand linear expressions with rational coefficients.

MK-8.3.B.t: Rewrite an expression in different forms to show how the quantities in it are related (a + 0.05a = 1.05a: "increase by 5%" means "multiply by 1.05").

MK-8.3.C.t: Solve multi-step real-life problems with positive and negative rational numbers in any form, converting between forms, and assess reasonableness with mental computation and estimation.

MK-8.3.D.t: Solve word problems leading to equations px + q = r and p(x + q) = r fluently, and compare the algebraic solution to an arithmetic one.

MK-8.3.E.t: Solve word problems leading to inequalities px + q > r or px + q < r, graph the solution set and interpret it in context.

MK-8.4.A.t: Solve problems involving scale drawings, including computing actual lengths and areas from a scale drawing and reproducing it at a different scale.

MK-8.4.B.t: Draw geometric shapes with given conditions (freehand, ruler and protractor, technology), especially triangles from three measures of angles or sides, noting when the conditions give a unique triangle, more than one, or none.

MK-8.4.C.t: Describe the two-dimensional figures that result from slicing three-dimensional figures, as in plane sections of right rectangular prisms and pyramids.

MK-8.4.D.t: Know the formulas for the area and circumference of a circle, use them to solve problems, and give an informal derivation of the relationship between them.

MK-8.4.E.t: Use facts about supplementary, complementary, vertical and adjacent angles in multi-step problems to write and solve simple equations for an unknown angle.

MK-8.4.F.t: Solve real-world problems involving area, volume and surface area of two- and three-dimensional objects composed of triangles, quadrilaterals, polygons, cubes and right prisms.

MK-8.5.A.t: Understand that statistics gain information about a population by examining a sample, that generalizations are valid only if the sample is representative, and that random sampling tends to produce representative samples.

MK-8.5.B.t: Use data from a random sample to draw inferences about a population with an unknown characteristic, and generate multiple samples to gauge the variation in estimates.

MK-8.5.C.t: Informally assess the visual overlap of two numerical distributions with similar variabilities, measuring the difference between centers as a multiple of a measure of variability.

MK-8.5.D.t: Use measures of center and variability for numerical data from random samples to draw informal comparative inferences about two populations.

MK-8.5.E.t: Understand the probability of a chance event as a number between 0 and 1 expressing its likelihood: near 0 unlikely, 1/2 neither, near 1 likely.

MK-8.5.F.t: Approximate a probability by collecting data on a chance process and observing its long-run relative frequency, and predict the approximate relative frequency given the probability.

MK-8.5.G.t: Develop a probability model (uniform, or from observed frequencies), use it to find probabilities, and compare them to observed frequencies, explaining discrepancies.

MK-8.5.H.t: Find probabilities of compound events as the fraction of outcomes in the sample space, representing the sample space with organized lists, tables and tree diagrams.

MK-8.5.I.t: Design and use a simulation to generate frequencies for compound events.

MK-9.1.A.t: Know that numbers that are not rational are irrational; every number has a decimal expansion; rational numbers' expansions eventually repeat; convert a repeating decimal into a rational number.

MK-9.1.B.t: Use rational approximations of irrational numbers to compare their size, locate them on a number line and estimate expressions (π²; √2 between 1.4 and 1.5).

MK-9.2.A.t: Know and apply the properties of integer exponents to generate equivalent numerical expressions (3² × 3⁻⁵ = 3⁻³ = 1/27).

MK-9.2.B.t: Use square root and cube root symbols for solutions of x² = p and x³ = p (p a positive rational); evaluate roots of small perfect squares and cubes; know √2 is irrational.

MK-9.2.C.t: Use numbers of the form (single digit) × 10ⁿ to estimate very large or very small quantities and to say how many times as much one is as another.

MK-9.2.D.t: Perform operations with numbers in scientific notation, choose units of appropriate size, and interpret scientific notation generated by technology.

MK-9.2.E.t: Graph proportional relationships, interpreting the unit rate as the slope, and compare two proportional relationships represented in different ways.

MK-9.2.F.t: Use similar triangles to explain why the slope m is the same between any two distinct points on a non-vertical line, and derive y = mx and y = mx + b.

MK-9.2.G.t: Give examples of linear equations in one variable with one solution, infinitely many solutions, or no solutions, by transforming them to x = a, a = a, or a = b.

MK-9.2.H.t: Solve linear equations with rational coefficients, including ones that need the distributive property and collecting like terms.

MK-9.2.I.t: Understand that solutions of a system of two linear equations in two variables correspond to the intersection points of their graphs.

MK-9.2.J.t: Solve systems of two linear equations algebraically, estimate solutions by graphing, and solve simple cases by inspection (3x + 2y = 5 and 3x + 2y = 6 have no solution).

MK-9.2.K.t: Solve real-world and mathematical problems leading to two linear equations in two variables.

MK-9.3.A.t: Understand that a function is a rule assigning to each input exactly one output, and that its graph is the set of ordered pairs (input, corresponding output).

MK-9.3.B.t: Compare properties of two functions each represented differently (algebraically, graphically, in a table, or verbally).

MK-9.3.C.t: Interpret y = mx + b as defining a linear function whose graph is a straight line, and give examples of functions that are not linear (A = s²).

MK-9.3.D.t: Construct a function to model a linear relationship, determine its rate of change and initial value from a description or two (x, y) values, and interpret them in context.

MK-9.3.E.t: Describe a functional relationship qualitatively from a graph (increasing, decreasing, linear, nonlinear) and sketch a graph from a verbal description.

MK-9.4.A.t: Verify experimentally the properties of rotations, reflections and translations: they take lines to lines, segments to equal segments, angles to equal angles, parallel lines to parallel lines.

MK-9.4.B.t: Understand that a figure is congruent to another if a sequence of rotations, reflections and translations maps one onto the other, and describe such a sequence.

MK-9.4.C.t: Describe the effect of dilations, translations, rotations and reflections on two-dimensional figures using coordinates.

MK-9.4.D.t: Understand that a figure is similar to another if a sequence of rotations, reflections, translations and dilations maps one onto the other, and describe such a sequence.

MK-9.4.E.t: Use informal arguments to establish the triangle angle sum and exterior angle facts, the angles formed when parallel lines are cut by a transversal, and the angle-angle criterion for similar triangles.

MK-9.4.F.t: Explain a proof of the Pythagorean Theorem and its converse.

MK-9.4.G.t: Apply the Pythagorean Theorem to find unknown side lengths in right triangles in two and three dimensions.

MK-9.4.H.t: Apply the Pythagorean Theorem to find the distance between two points in a coordinate system.

MK-9.4.I.t: Know the formulas for the volumes of cones, cylinders and spheres and use them to solve problems.

MK-9.5.A.t: Construct and interpret scatter plots for bivariate measurement data and describe patterns: clustering, outliers, positive or negative association, linear or nonlinear association.

MK-9.5.B.t: Know that straight lines model linear association between two quantitative variables; informally fit a line to a scatter plot and judge the fit by closeness of the points.

MK-9.5.C.t: Use the equation of a linear model to solve problems with bivariate measurement data, interpreting the slope and intercept.

MK-9.5.D.t: Understand patterns of association in bivariate categorical data from frequencies and relative frequencies in a two-way table, and use relative frequencies by row or column to describe possible association.

MM-1.1.B.t: Take a fraction of a whole number by dividing first.

MM-1.1.A.t: Add and subtract multi-digit numbers left to right, and subtract from a power of ten by complements.

MM-1.2.A.t: Evaluate a short expression with mixed operations in the right order.

MM-1.3.A.t: Spot a common factor and add before multiplying.

MM-1.5.A.t: Multiply by 11, 25, 5, 99 and 101 by rewriting the multiplier.

MM-1.5.B.t: Multiply two numbers just under 100 from their shortfalls.

MM-1.5.C.t: Multiply two-digit numbers that share a tens digit and whose ones digits sum to 10, or that sit evenly around a round number.

MM-1.5.D.t: Double one factor and halve the other to make a round number.

MM-1.5.E.t: Divide by 5 and 25 by rewriting the divisor, and by a two-digit number in stages.

MM-1.5.F.t: Divide by a decimal by moving both decimal points until the divisor is whole.

MM-1.6.A.t: Square a number ending in 5, or near 50 or 100, from its pattern.

MM-1.6.B.t: Square any two-digit number by sliding to a multiple of ten.

MM-1.7.A.t: Recall the percent form of the common fractions, and use it to take a percent of a number.

MM-1.7.B.t: Convert between common units of length, capacity, weight and time, including square and cubic units.

MM-1.8.A.t: Find the GCD and LCM of two numbers under 100.

MM-1.9.A.t: Take a percent of a number by swapping or building from 10%, and apply a percent increase or decrease.

MM-1.10.A.t: Find a mean with a focus number and the median of a short unsorted list.

MM-1.11.A.t: Sum the first n integers, the first n odd numbers, or a short arithmetic series.

MM-1.12.A.t: Find a remainder on division by 3, 4, 9 or 11 from the digits.

MM-1.13.A.t: Find a sale price or similar everyday percent amount.

MM-1.14.A.t: Count the divisors of a number, and sum them, from its prime factorisation.

MM-1.15.A.t: Estimate a product, a quotient or a square root to within 5 percent.

MM-2.1.A.t: Recall the powers of 2 to 2¹² and the cubes to 12³.

MM-2.2.A.t: Evaluate an expression at given values without writing it out.

MM-2.3.A.t: Solve a one-step word problem (ages, rates, coins) mentally.

MM-2.4.A.t: Give the additive or multiplicative inverse of an integer, fraction or mixed number.

MM-2.5.A.t: Evaluate an expression with absolute values.

MM-2.6.A.t: Solve a proportion by scaling or cross-multiplying.

MM-2.7.A.t: Find the root of a perfect square or cube from its size and last digit.

MM-2.8.A.t: Count subsets, and elements of unions and intersections.

MM-2.9.A.t: Convert a short numeral from another base to base 10.

MM-2.10.A.t: Solve a one- or two-step linear equation mentally.

MM-2.11.A.t: Find x + y or x − y from a 2 × 2 system by adding or subtracting the equations.

MM-2.12.A.t: Write a repeating decimal as a fraction.

MM-2.13.A.t: Find the remainder of a sum or product from the remainders of its parts.

MM-2.14.A.t: Find the perimeter or area of a rectangle, triangle, trapezoid or circle from its dimensions.

MM-2.15.A.t: Find the next or the n-th term of an arithmetic or geometric sequence.

MM-2.16.A.t: Give the sum or product of the roots of a quadratic or cubic from its coefficients.

MM-3.1.A.t: Simplify a product or quotient of powers by moving to a common base.

MM-3.2.A.t: Complete a Pythagorean triple or a 30-60-90 or 45-45-90 triangle.

MM-3.3.A.t: Find a slope, midpoint, distance or intercept from two points or an equation.

MM-3.4.A.t: Find an interior or exterior angle, or the number of diagonals, of a regular polygon.

MM-3.5.A.t: Solve a linear inequality or count its integer solutions.

MM-3.6.A.t: Use an angle, chord, tangent or similarity fact to find a length or angle.

MM-3.7.A.t: Find a value from a direct or inverse variation.

MM-3.9.A.t: Multiply two complex numbers or find a modulus or a power of i.

MM-3.10.A.t: Evaluate a logarithm of an exact power.

MM-3.11.A.t: Evaluate a small combination, permutation or factorial ratio.

MM-3.12.A.t: Give the probability or odds of a simple event with dice, coins or cards.

MM-3.13.A.t: Read a centre, vertex, focus or axis length from a conic in standard form.

MM-3.14.A.t: Give a coefficient or the sum of coefficients of a binomial expansion.

MM-3.15.A.t: Add, subtract or multiply two short numerals in another base.

MM-3.16.A.t: Use Vieta's relations to find symmetric expressions in the roots.

MM-3.17.A.t: Find the n-th triangular, pentagonal or hexagonal number.

MM-4.1.A.t: Find the volume or surface area of a prism, cylinder, cone or sphere, in terms of π where needed.

MM-4.2.A.t: Evaluate a floor expression, including of negative numbers.

MM-4.3.A.t: Find the remainder of a polynomial on division by x − a.

MM-4.4.A.t: Recall exact trig values at the special angles and use basic identities.

MM-4.6.A.t: Find an entry of a matrix sum, product or inverse.

MM-4.7.A.t: Find a dot product or a magnitude.

MM-4.8.A.t: Evaluate f(g(a)) for simple f and g.

MM-4.9.A.t: Convert a fraction to or from a numeral with digits after the point in another base.

MM-4.10.A.t: Convert a point between polar and rectangular form at a special angle.

MM-5.1.A.t: State the excluded value or the range of a simple rational, radical or quadratic function.

MM-5.2.A.t: Evaluate a sum, product or power modulo m.

MM-5.3.A.t: Evaluate a limit of a rational function at a point or at infinity by inspection.

MM-5.4.A.t: Evaluate the derivative of a polynomial or basic function at a point.

MM-5.5.A.t: Give the slope of the tangent to a curve at a point.

MM-5.6.A.t: Read the asymptotes of a rational function from its formula.

MM-5.7.A.t: Find where a polynomial's derivative is zero.

MM-5.8.A.t: Find the maximum or minimum value of a quadratic or a simple cubic on an interval.

MM-5.9.A.t: Evaluate a definite integral of a polynomial with easy limits.

MM-5.10.A.t: Evaluate f⁻¹(a) for a linear or simple rational f without finding the inverse formula.

MM-6.1.A.t: Read off one coefficient of a partial-fraction decomposition with distinct linear factors by covering up.

MM-6.1.B.t: Use cover-up where it still works: the top power of a repeated factor, and a linear factor beside an irreducible quadratic.

MM-6.2.A.t: Integrate a basic function of a linear inside (cos kx, sin kx, e^kx, (kx + b)^n, 1/(kx + b)) by guessing the shape and fixing the constant.

MM-6.2.B.t: Spot an integrand of the form f(g(x))·g′(x) up to a constant and write its antiderivative.

MM-6.3.A.t: Write the derivative of a one-layer composite or a power-times-exponential product without intermediate steps.

MM-6.4.A.t: Find the eigenvalues of a 2 × 2 matrix from its trace and determinant.

MM-6.4.B.t: Classify y″ + by′ + cy = 0 by comparing b² with 4c, and choose the trial form for an exponential forcing term.

MH-1.1.A.t: Use units to choose and check the solution path of a multi-step problem, converting units and choosing scales for graphs.

MH-1.1.B.t: Define the quantities and variables needed to describe a situation.

MH-1.1.C.t: Report a computed quantity to a level of accuracy that matches the limitations of the measurements it came from.

MH-1.2.A.t: Identify the terms, factors and coefficients of an expression and say what each means in context.

MH-1.2.B.t: Interpret a complicated expression by viewing one or more of its parts as a single entity, e.g. P(1 + r)^n as the product of P and a factor not depending on P.

MH-1.3.A.t: Explain each step in solving a simple equation as following from the equality asserted in the previous step, and justify the method.

MH-1.3.B.t: Solve a linear equation in one variable, including equations with coefficients represented by letters.

MH-1.3.C.t: Solve a linear inequality in one variable and write the solution set.

MH-1.4.A.t: Write and solve a one-variable linear equation or inequality that represents a word problem.

MH-1.4.B.t: Write an equation in two variables that relates two quantities and graph it on coordinate axes with labels and scales.

MH-1.4.C.t: Represent constraints by equations or inequalities, or by systems of them, and decide whether a solution is viable in context.

MH-1.4.D.t: Rearrange a formula to highlight a quantity of interest, e.g. Ohm's law V = IR for R.

MH-2.1.A.t: Decide whether a relation given by a table, graph, mapping or rule is a function, and state its domain and range.

MH-2.1.B.t: Evaluate a function written in function notation for given inputs and interpret f(a) in context.

MH-2.1.C.t: Recognise a sequence as a function whose domain is a subset of the integers, and generate terms from a recursive definition.

MH-2.2.A.t: Interpret key features of a graph or table in context (intercepts, intervals of increase and decrease, where positive or negative, maxima and minima), and sketch a graph from a verbal description.

MH-2.2.B.t: Relate the domain of a function to its graph and to the quantity it describes.

MH-2.2.C.t: Calculate and interpret the average rate of change of a function over an interval from a formula, a table or a graph.

MH-2.3.A.t: Explain that the graph of an equation in two variables is the set of all its solutions plotted in the coordinate plane.

MH-2.3.B.t: Graph a linear function from its equation, showing the intercepts and the slope.

MH-2.4.A.t: Prove that linear functions grow by equal differences over equal intervals and exponential functions grow by equal factors over equal intervals.

MH-2.4.B.t: Recognise a situation in which one quantity changes at a constant rate per unit interval relative to another.

MH-2.4.C.t: Recognise a situation in which a quantity grows or decays by a constant percent rate per unit interval.

MH-2.5.A.t: Construct a linear or exponential function, including arithmetic and geometric sequences, from a graph, a description of a relationship, or two input–output pairs.

MH-2.5.B.t: Write an arithmetic or geometric sequence both recursively and with an explicit formula, and translate between the two forms.

MH-2.5.C.t: Determine an explicit expression, a recursive process, or steps for calculation from a context.

MH-2.5.D.t: Interpret the parameters of a linear or exponential function in terms of a context.

MH-2.6.A.t: Explain how the meaning of rational exponents follows from extending the properties of integer exponents, e.g. why 5^(1/3) is the cube root of 5.

MH-2.6.B.t: Rewrite expressions involving radicals and rational exponents using the properties of exponents.

MH-2.6.C.t: Graph an exponential function y = a·b^x, showing the intercept and end behaviour.

MH-2.6.D.t: Show with graphs and tables that a quantity increasing exponentially eventually exceeds one increasing linearly.

MH-2.6.E.t: Compare properties of two functions each represented in a different way (algebraically, graphically, numerically in a table, or by a verbal description).

MH-2.7.A.t: Solve a system of two linear equations approximately by graphing.

MH-2.7.B.t: Solve a system of two linear equations exactly by substitution or elimination.

MH-2.7.C.t: Prove that replacing one equation of a system by the sum of that equation and a multiple of the other gives a system with the same solutions.

MH-2.7.D.t: Explain why the x-coordinates of the intersections of y = f(x) and y = g(x) solve f(x) = g(x), and approximate them with graphs or tables (linear and exponential f, g).

MH-2.7.E.t: Graph the solutions of a linear inequality in two variables as a half-plane, and of a system of linear inequalities as the intersection of half-planes.

MH-3.1.A.t: Represent data with plots on the real number line: dot plots, histograms and box plots.

MH-3.1.B.t: Compare the center (median, mean) and spread (interquartile range, standard deviation) of two or more data sets, using statistics suited to their shape.

MH-3.1.C.t: Interpret differences in shape, center and spread in context, accounting for possible effects of extreme data points (outliers).

MH-3.2.A.t: Summarise categorical data for two categories in two-way frequency tables and interpret joint, marginal and conditional relative frequencies.

MH-3.2.B.t: Fit a function (linear, quadratic or exponential) to data on two quantitative variables in a scatter plot and use it to solve problems in the context of the data.

MH-3.2.C.t: Informally assess the fit of a function by plotting and analysing residuals.

MH-3.2.D.t: Fit a linear function to a scatter plot that suggests a linear association.

MH-3.3.A.t: Interpret the slope (rate of change) and intercept (constant term) of a linear model in the context of the data.

MH-3.3.B.t: Compute (using technology) and interpret the correlation coefficient of a linear fit.

MH-4.1.A.t: Add, subtract and multiply polynomials, and explain why the result is again a polynomial.

MH-4.1.B.t: Use the structure of an expression to rewrite it, e.g. x⁴ − y⁴ as (x²)² − (y²)² = (x² − y²)(x² + y²).

MH-4.2.A.t: Factor a quadratic expression to reveal the zeros of the function it defines.

MH-4.2.B.t: Complete the square in a quadratic expression to reveal the maximum or minimum value of the function it defines.

MH-4.2.C.t: Use the properties of exponents to transform an exponential expression, e.g. 1.15^t ≈ 1.012^(12t), to reveal an equivalent monthly rate.

MH-4.3.A.t: Solve a quadratic equation by inspection, by taking square roots, or by factoring.

MH-4.3.B.t: Complete the square to transform a quadratic equation into the form (x − p)² = q, and derive the quadratic formula from that form.

MH-4.3.C.t: Solve a quadratic equation with the quadratic formula, choosing the method that fits its form, and use the discriminant to recognise when it has no real solutions.

MH-4.3.D.t: Write and solve a quadratic equation that models a word problem, rejecting solutions that do not fit the context.

MH-4.4.A.t: Solve a system of one linear and one quadratic equation in two variables algebraically and graphically, e.g. find where y = −3x meets x² + y² = 3.

MH-5.1.A.t: Explain why the sum or product of two rational numbers is rational, the sum of a rational and an irrational number is irrational, and the product of a nonzero rational and an irrational number is irrational.

MH-5.2.A.t: Rewrite a quadratic function by factoring and completing the square to show its zeros, extreme value and symmetry, and interpret them in context.

MH-5.2.B.t: Graph a quadratic function, showing intercepts, the vertex (maximum or minimum) and the axis of symmetry.

MH-5.2.C.t: Interpret the key features of a quadratic model in context, e.g. the maximum height and landing time of a projectile.

MH-5.2.D.t: Graph square-root, cube-root and piecewise-defined functions, including step functions and absolute-value functions.

MH-5.2.E.t: Use the properties of exponents to classify an exponential function as growth or decay and find its percent rate, e.g. y = (0.97)^t, y = (1.01)^(12t), y = (1.2)^(t/10).

MH-5.2.F.t: Compare a quadratic with a function represented differently, e.g. decide which of an algebraic quadratic and a graphed one has the larger maximum.

MH-5.3.A.t: Combine standard function types using arithmetic operations, e.g. a decaying exponential plus a constant for a cooling body.

MH-5.3.B.t: Identify the effect on the graph of replacing f(x) by f(x) + k, k·f(x), f(kx) and f(x + k), and find k from a graph.

MH-5.3.C.t: Recognise even and odd functions from their graphs and from their algebraic expressions.

MH-5.3.D.t: Solve f(x) = c for a simple invertible function f and write an expression for the inverse, e.g. f(x) = 2x³ or f(x) = (x + 1)/(x − 1).

MH-5.3.E.t: Show with tables and graphs that an increasing exponential function eventually exceeds any quadratic or polynomial function.

MH-6.1.A.t: State precise definitions of angle, circle, perpendicular line, parallel line and line segment, based on the undefined notions of point, line, distance along a line and distance around a circular arc.

MH-6.1.B.t: Represent transformations as functions that take points in the plane to other points, and compare those that preserve distance and angle (rigid motions) with those that do not (e.g. a horizontal stretch).

MH-6.1.C.t: Describe the rotations and reflections that carry a rectangle, parallelogram, trapezoid or regular polygon onto itself.

MH-6.1.D.t: Define rotations, reflections and translations in terms of angles, circles, perpendicular lines, parallel lines and line segments.

MH-6.1.E.t: Draw the image of a figure under a given rotation, reflection or translation, and specify a sequence of transformations that carries one figure onto another.

MH-6.2.A.t: Predict the effect of a rigid motion on a figure, and decide whether two figures are congruent by whether a rigid motion carries one onto the other.

MH-6.2.B.t: Show, using the rigid-motion definition, that two triangles are congruent if and only if corresponding sides and corresponding angles are congruent.

MH-6.2.C.t: Explain how the ASA, SAS and SSS criteria for triangle congruence follow from the definition of congruence in terms of rigid motions.

MH-6.3.A.t: Prove theorems about lines and angles: vertical angles are congruent; a transversal of parallel lines makes congruent alternate interior and corresponding angles; points on a perpendicular bisector are equidistant from the segment's endpoints.

MH-6.3.B.t: Prove theorems about triangles: interior angles sum to 180°, base angles of an isosceles triangle are congruent, the midsegment is parallel to the third side and half its length, the medians meet at a point.

MH-6.3.C.t: Prove theorems about parallelograms: opposite sides and opposite angles are congruent, the diagonals bisect each other, and a rectangle is a parallelogram with congruent diagonals.

MH-6.4.A.t: Construct with compass and straightedge a copy of a segment and of an angle, an angle bisector, a perpendicular bisector, a perpendicular to a line, and a parallel to a line through a point not on it.

MH-6.4.B.t: Construct an equilateral triangle, a square and a regular hexagon inscribed in a circle.

MH-7.1.A.t: Verify experimentally that a dilation takes a line not through the center to a parallel line, and leaves a line through the center unchanged.

MH-7.1.B.t: Verify experimentally that a dilation multiplies the length of every segment by the scale factor.

MH-7.1.C.t: Decide whether two figures are similar using similarity transformations, and explain triangle similarity as equal corresponding angles and proportional corresponding sides.

MH-7.1.D.t: Establish the AA criterion for triangle similarity from the properties of similarity transformations.

MH-7.2.A.t: Prove that a line parallel to one side of a triangle divides the other two proportionally, and prove the Pythagorean theorem using triangle similarity.

MH-7.2.B.t: Use congruence and similarity criteria for triangles to solve problems and prove relationships in figures.

MH-7.3.A.t: Explain that by similarity the side ratios of a right triangle depend only on its acute angle, which defines sine, cosine and tangent.

MH-7.3.B.t: Explain and use the relationship between the sine and cosine of complementary angles.

MH-7.3.C.t: Use trigonometric ratios and the Pythagorean theorem to solve right triangles in applied problems.

MH-7.4.A.t: Use geometric shapes, their measures and their properties to describe objects, e.g. a tree trunk or a human torso as a cylinder.

MH-7.4.B.t: Apply concepts of density based on area and volume, e.g. persons per square mile or BTUs per cubic foot.

MH-7.4.C.t: Apply geometric methods to design problems, e.g. design an object to satisfy physical constraints or minimise cost.

MH-7.5.A.t: Derive the formula A = ½ab sin C for the area of a triangle by drawing an auxiliary line from a vertex perpendicular to the opposite side.

MH-7.5.B.t: Prove the Laws of Sines and Cosines.

MH-7.5.C.t: Use the Laws of Sines and Cosines to find unknown measurements in right and non-right triangles, including the ambiguous SSA case.

MH-8.1.A.t: Give an informal argument for the circumference and area of a circle and the volume of a cylinder, pyramid and cone (dissection, Cavalieri's principle, limits).

MH-8.1.B.t: Use the volume formulas for cylinders, pyramids, cones and spheres to solve problems.

MH-8.2.A.t: Identify the shapes of two-dimensional cross-sections of three-dimensional objects, and the three-dimensional objects generated by rotating two-dimensional objects.

MH-8.2.B.t: Model a real object as a combination of solids and estimate its volume.

MH-9.1.A.t: Use coordinates to prove simple geometric theorems algebraically, e.g. that a given quadrilateral is a rectangle.

MH-9.1.B.t: Prove the slope criteria for parallel and perpendicular lines and use them to write the equation of a line parallel or perpendicular to a given line through a given point.

MH-9.1.C.t: Find the point on a directed line segment between two given points that partitions it in a given ratio.

MH-9.1.D.t: Use coordinates and the distance formula to compute perimeters of polygons and areas of triangles and rectangles.

MH-9.2.A.t: Derive the equation of a parabola given a focus and directrix.

MH-10.1.A.t: Prove that all circles are similar.

MH-10.1.B.t: Identify and describe relationships among inscribed angles, radii and chords, including central, inscribed and circumscribed angles.

MH-10.1.C.t: Construct the inscribed and circumscribed circles of a triangle, and prove that opposite angles of a quadrilateral inscribed in a circle are supplementary.

MH-10.1.D.t: (+) Construct a tangent line from a point outside a given circle to the circle.

MH-10.2.A.t: Derive using similarity that the arc length intercepted by an angle is proportional to the radius, define radian measure as the constant of proportionality, and derive the formula for the area of a sector.

MH-10.3.A.t: Derive the equation of a circle of given center and radius using the Pythagorean theorem, and complete the square to find the center and radius of a circle given by an equation.

MH-10.3.B.t: Prove or disprove that a given point lies on a circle centered at a given point through another given point.

MH-11.1.A.t: Describe events as subsets of a sample space using characteristics of the outcomes, or as unions, intersections or complements of other events.

MH-11.1.B.t: Decide whether two events are independent using the fact that A and B are independent exactly when P(A and B) = P(A)·P(B).

MH-11.1.C.t: Interpret the conditional probability of A given B as P(A and B)/P(B), and independence as P(A|B) = P(A).

MH-11.1.D.t: Construct and interpret a two-way frequency table, using it to decide whether events are independent and to approximate conditional probabilities.

MH-11.1.E.t: Recognise and explain conditional probability and independence in everyday language and situations.

MH-11.2.A.t: Find the conditional probability of A given B as the fraction of B's outcomes that also belong to A, and interpret it in terms of the model.

MH-11.2.B.t: Apply the Addition Rule, P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B) − P(A and B), and interpret the answer in terms of the model.

MH-11.2.C.t: (+) Apply the general Multiplication Rule in a uniform probability model, P(A and B) = P(A)P(B|A) = P(B)P(A|B).

MH-11.2.D.t: (+) Use permutations and combinations to compute probabilities of compound events and solve problems.

MH-11.3.A.t: (+) Use probabilities to make fair decisions, e.g. drawing by lots or using a random number generator.

MH-11.3.B.t: (+) Analyse decisions and strategies using probability concepts, e.g. product testing, medical testing, pulling a hockey goalie at the end of a game.

MH-12.1.A.t: Know there is a complex number i with i² = −1, and write every complex number in the form a + bi with a and b real.

MH-12.1.B.t: Add, subtract and multiply complex numbers using i² = −1 and the commutative, associative and distributive properties.

MH-12.1.C.t: Solve a quadratic equation with real coefficients that has complex solutions.

MH-12.1.D.t: (+) Extend polynomial identities to the complex numbers, e.g. rewrite x² + 4 as (x + 2i)(x − 2i).

MH-12.2.A.t: Use the structure of a polynomial to factor it, e.g. x³ − 8 as a difference of cubes, or x⁴ − 5x² + 4 as a quadratic in x².

MH-12.2.B.t: Prove polynomial identities and use them to describe numerical relationships, e.g. (x² + y²)² = (x² − y²)² + (2xy)² generates Pythagorean triples.

MH-12.2.C.t: (+) Expand (x + y)^n with the Binomial Theorem, the coefficients given by Pascal's triangle.

MH-12.3.A.t: Apply the Remainder Theorem: the remainder on division of p(x) by x − a is p(a), so p(a) = 0 exactly when x − a is a factor.

MH-12.3.B.t: Identify the zeros of a polynomial from a suitable factorization and use them to sketch a rough graph.

MH-12.3.C.t: Graph a polynomial function, identifying zeros when suitable factorizations are available and showing end behaviour.

MH-12.3.D.t: (+) Know the Fundamental Theorem of Algebra and show that it is true for quadratic polynomials.

MH-12.4.A.t: Derive the formula for the sum of a finite geometric series (common ratio not 1) and use it to solve problems, e.g. mortgage payments.

MH-12.5.A.t: Rewrite a rational expression a(x)/b(x) as q(x) + r(x)/b(x) by inspection or long division.

MH-12.5.B.t: (+) Add, subtract, multiply and divide rational expressions, and explain why they form a system closed under these operations (division by a nonzero expression).

MH-12.5.C.t: Solve a simple rational or radical equation in one variable, and give examples of extraneous solutions.

MH-12.5.D.t: Find approximate solutions of f(x) = g(x) where f and g are polynomial, rational, absolute-value, exponential or logarithmic, with technology, tables or successive approximations.

MH-13.1.A.t: Understand radian measure of an angle as the length of the arc on the unit circle it subtends, and convert between degrees and radians.

MH-13.1.B.t: Explain how the unit circle extends sine and cosine to all real numbers, read as radian measures of angles traversed counterclockwise.

MH-13.2.A.t: Choose a trigonometric function y = A sin(B(x − h)) + k to model a periodic phenomenon with given amplitude, frequency and midline.

MH-13.3.A.t: Prove the Pythagorean identity sin²θ + cos²θ = 1 and use it to find sin θ, cos θ or tan θ from one of them and the quadrant.

MH-14.1.A.t: Express the solution of ab^(ct) = d as a logarithm (base 2, 10 or e) and evaluate it with technology.

MH-14.1.B.t: Graph a logarithmic function, showing the intercept, the vertical asymptote and end behaviour, as the reflection of an exponential across y = x.

MH-14.2.A.t: Create equations in two or more variables, including exponential and rational relationships, that model a situation.

MH-14.2.B.t: Build a model by combining function families arithmetically, e.g. a damped oscillation y = A·e^(−kt)·cos(ωt).

MH-14.2.C.t: Interpret the key features of polynomial, exponential, logarithmic and periodic models in context (intercepts, extrema, end behaviour, periodicity).

MH-14.2.D.t: Compare properties of two functions from different families, each given in a different representation.

MH-15.1.A.t: Use the mean and standard deviation of a data set to fit it to a normal distribution and estimate population percentages, recognising when that is not appropriate.

MH-15.2.A.t: Explain statistics as a process for making inferences about population parameters from a random sample of that population.

MH-15.2.B.t: Decide whether a specified model is consistent with results from a data-generating process, e.g. by simulation.

MH-15.3.A.t: Recognise the purposes of and differences among sample surveys, experiments and observational studies, and explain how randomisation relates to each.

MH-15.3.B.t: Use data from a sample survey to estimate a population mean or proportion, and develop a margin of error through simulation models for random sampling.

MH-15.3.C.t: Use data from a randomised experiment to compare two treatments, and use simulation to decide whether differences between parameters are significant.

MH-16.1.A.t: (+) Compose functions, e.g. T(h(t)) for the temperature at the location of a weather balloon at time t.

MH-16.1.D.t: (+) Produce an invertible function from a non-invertible function by restricting the domain.

MH-16.2.A.t: (+) Use the inverse relationship between exponents and logarithms to derive and apply the product, quotient, power and change-of-base rules.

MH-16.2.B.t: (+) Solve exponential and logarithmic equations, rejecting solutions outside the logarithm's domain.

MH-16.3.A.t: (+) Graph a rational function, identifying zeros, vertical asymptotes, holes and end behaviour.

MH-17.1.A.t: (+) Use 30-60-90 and 45-45-90 triangles to find exact sine, cosine and tangent of π/6, π/4, π/3, and the unit circle to extend them to π − x, π + x and 2π − x.

MH-17.1.C.t: Graph sine, cosine and tangent functions, showing period, midline, amplitude and (for tangent) asymptotes.

MH-17.2.A.t: (+) Restrict a trigonometric function to a domain on which it is always increasing or always decreasing so that its inverse can be constructed.

MH-17.2.B.t: (+) Use inverse functions to solve trigonometric equations that arise in modeling contexts, evaluate the solutions with technology, and interpret them.

MH-17.3.A.t: (+) Prove the addition and subtraction formulas for sine, cosine and tangent.

MH-17.3.B.t: (+) Use the addition formulas, and the double-angle formulas they give, to find exact values and simplify expressions.

MH-18.1.A.t: (+) Find the conjugate of a complex number, and use conjugates to find moduli and quotients.

MH-18.1.B.t: (+) Represent complex numbers on the complex plane in rectangular and polar form, and convert between the two forms.

MH-18.1.D.t: (+) Calculate the distance between numbers in the complex plane as the modulus of the difference, and the midpoint of a segment as the average of its endpoints.

MH-19.1.A.t: (+) Recognise vector quantities as having both magnitude and direction, represent them by directed line segments, and use notation such as v, |v| and ‖v‖.

MH-19.1.B.t: (+) Find the components of a vector by subtracting the coordinates of its initial point from those of its terminal point.

MH-19.2.B.t: (+) Given two vectors in magnitude-and-direction form, find the magnitude and direction of their sum.

MH-19.2.D.t: (+) Multiply a vector by a scalar graphically and component-wise.

MH-19.2.E.t: (+) Compute the magnitude of a scalar multiple cv as |c|·‖v‖ and give its direction.

MH-19.3.A.t: (+) Solve problems involving velocity and other quantities that can be represented by vectors, e.g. a plane's ground velocity in a crosswind.

MH-19.4.A.t: (+) Use matrices to represent and manipulate data, e.g. payoffs or incidence relationships in a network.

MH-19.4.C.t: (+) Add, subtract and multiply matrices of appropriate dimensions.

MH-19.4.D.t: (+) Show that multiplication of square matrices is not commutative but is associative and distributive.

MH-19.4.F.t: (+) Multiply a vector (as a one-column matrix) by a matrix of suitable dimensions to produce another vector.

MH-19.5.A.t: (+) Represent a system of linear equations as a single matrix equation Ax = b in a vector variable.

MH-19.5.B.t: (+) Find the inverse of a matrix if it exists and use it to solve a system of linear equations (technology for 3×3 or larger).

MH-20.1.A.t: (+) Derive the equations of ellipses and hyperbolas given the foci, using the fact that the sum or difference of distances from the foci is constant.

MH-20.1.B.t: (+) Give an informal argument using Cavalieri's principle for the formulas for the volume of a sphere and other solid figures.

MH-21.1.A.t: (+) Define a random variable for a quantity of interest by assigning a numerical value to each event in a sample space, and graph its probability distribution.

MH-21.1.C.t: (+) Develop a theoretical probability distribution and find the expected value, e.g. the number of correct answers from guessing on a multiple-choice test.

MH-21.1.D.t: (+) Develop an empirical probability distribution from observed frequencies and find the expected value.

MH-21.2.A.t: (+) Find the expected payoff for a game of chance, e.g. a state lottery ticket or a fast-food prize game.

MH-21.2.B.t: (+) Evaluate and compare strategies on the basis of expected values, e.g. a high-deductible versus a low-deductible insurance policy.

SPK-1.1.A.t: Breathe low and silently between phrases — ribs and abdomen expand, shoulders stay down — while reading a passage aloud, with no audible gasps.

SPK-1.2.A.t: Set volume to the room: in a timed rep, deliver the same 30-second passage at conversational, small-room (~25 people) and large-room levels without pitch rising or the throat tightening.

SPK-1.3.A.t: Classify a consonant by manner (plosive, fricative, nasal, lateral, affricate) and voicing, and name the articulators that make it.

SPK-1.3.B.t: In a timed rep, read a dense technical sentence at 150 wpm with every final consonant and unstressed syllable audible on playback.

SPK-1.4.A.t: Rewrite a written sentence for the ear: shorter clauses, the subject and verb early, acronyms spelled out on first use.

SPK-2.1.A.t: Compute wpm from a transcript and its duration, and classify the result as slow, presentation-range, conversational or fast.

SPK-2.1.B.t: In a timed 60-second rep, hold 140–160 wpm on an answer and 125–150 wpm on an explanation, checked from the transcript.

SPK-2.1.C.t: Vary rate on purpose within one answer — slow for the key claim or a hard step, faster for context — and point to where on playback.

SPK-2.2.A.t: Place deliberate 1–2 second pauses after the main point, between sections and before a key number, and mark them with '/' or '//' on a script before delivering it.

SPK-2.2.B.t: Classify a described pause as a deliberate pause, a fluency hiccup, or a filled pause, and say whether it helped or hurt.

SPK-2.2.C.t: Start every on-the-spot answer with a silent 1–2 second pause instead of a filler or a restatement of the question.

SPK-2.3.A.t: Count fillers per minute in a recording or transcript, separating filler sounds (um, uh, er) from filler words (like, you know, so, basically, right?).

SPK-2.3.B.t: In a timed 60-second rep on a random prompt, deliver with ≤ 3 filler sounds (target ≤ 1), measured from the transcript.

SPK-2.3.C.t: Apply awareness training and a competing response: name your top two fillers, catch them on playback, then replace each with a closed-mouth silent pause or breath in the next rep.

SPK-3.1.A.t: End declarative sentences with a falling pitch, and in a recorded rep make every claim sentence of a 60-second answer fall rather than rise.

SPK-3.1.B.t: Diagnose a described voice as monotone, sing-song, upspeaking or pressed, and choose the correction.

SPK-3.2.A.t: Mark the one key word per sentence in a script and, on playback, stress it with pitch, volume or a pause before it — and change the meaning by moving the stress.

SPK-3.2.B.t: Pick the stronger of two recorded or described deliveries of the same line on vocal variety, and name what made the difference.

SPK-3.3.A.t: Hold eye contact for one complete thought per listener (about 3–5 seconds) and move across the room; on video, look at the lens for whole sentences.

SPK-3.3.B.t: Stand or sit grounded — feet planted, hands still at rest, gestures only on purpose — and on video count distracting movements (sway, fidget, touch face) per minute.

SPK-3.4.A.t: Use a pre-speaking routine — two slow exhale-longer breaths, a planned first sentence, shoulders down — before class, a meeting turn or an interview answer.

SPK-3.4.B.t: Cut hedges and apologies from an answer — 'sorry, this might be wrong, but', 'I just think', 'kind of' — and in a rep state the claim plainly with its real confidence level once.

SPK-4.1.A.t: In a timed rep, give the answer or recommendation in the first sentence (within ~10 seconds) of a 60-second response to a random question.

SPK-4.1.B.t: Pick the stronger of two openings to the same question — answer-first or context-first — and say what the weaker one makes the listener wait for.

SPK-4.1.C.t: Group support into two or three parallel reasons and announce the count ('two reasons: cost and risk').

SPK-4.2.A.t: In a timed 60-second rep, deliver a PREP answer: Point, Reason, Example, Point restated — each element identifiable in the transcript.

SPK-4.2.B.t: Frame a meeting update or proposal as SCQA — Situation, Complication, Question, Answer — in four sentences.

SPK-4.2.C.t: Choose the right frame for a described prompt — PREP (opinion), SCQA (proposal), STAR (behavioural), past–present–future (trend), problem–solution — and justify it.

SPK-4.3.B.t: Diagnose a described rambling answer — buried point, tangent, no transitions, circling back — and name the restructure.

SPK-4.4.A.t: End on purpose: restate the point or give the ask in one sentence, drop pitch, then stop — no trailing 'so, yeah, that's it'.

SPK-5.2.B.t: Classify a described question as clarifying, challenging, off-topic or a comment-not-a-question, and choose the response move for each.

SPK-6.3.C.t: Diagnose a described misunderstanding from a listener's answer and re-explain with a different example, not the same words louder.

SPK-6.4.A.t: State a number for the ear: round it, give one comparison ('about a third — one in three'), and say the unit.

SPK-6.4.B.t: Talk a listener through a figure or board diagram: say what the axes are, where to look, and the one takeaway, before the details.
