los.do: Use the Archimedean property and say where the rationals fail to be complete.
los.ek: For any real ε > 0 there is a natural number n with 1/n < ε. The rationals are dense but not complete: {x : x² < 2} has no rational least upper bound.

los.do: Turn an absolute-value inequality into an interval and use the triangle inequality.
los.ek: |x − a| < r means a − r < x < a + r. The triangle inequality |x + y| ≤ |x| + |y| and its reverse ||x| − |y|| ≤ |x − y| are the two tools nearly every estimate in analysis uses.

los.do: Find upper and lower bounds of a set and say whether it is bounded.
los.ek: An upper bound is any number at least as large as every element; the infimum is the greatest lower bound. A set is bounded when it has both kinds.

los.do: Use the AM-GM and Bernoulli inequalities to bound an expression.
los.ek: For positive numbers the arithmetic mean is at least the geometric mean, with equality only when they are equal; so x + k/x ≥ 2√k. Bernoulli: (1 + x)ⁿ ≥ 1 + nx for x ≥ −1.

los.do: Produce the N that the definition of a limit asks for.
los.ek: a_n → L means: for every ε > 0 there is an N with |a_n − L| < ε for all n ≥ N. Solving the inequality for n gives N as a function of ε.

los.do: Find the limit of a bounded monotone recursive sequence and know what guarantees it exists.
los.ek: A bounded monotone sequence converges. Once the limit is known to exist, it must satisfy the recurrence as a fixed-point equation. Bolzano-Weierstrass: every bounded sequence has a convergent subsequence.

los.do: Find the limit superior and limit inferior of a bounded sequence.
los.ek: lim sup is the largest limit of any subsequence and lim inf the smallest. The sequence converges exactly when the two agree.

los.do: Find a limit with the algebra of limits and the squeeze rule.
los.ek: Limits respect sums, products and quotients (non-zero denominator). If a_n ≤ b_n ≤ c_n and the outer two share a limit, so does b_n: bounded × null is null.

los.do: Rank the growth of standard sequences.
los.ek: For large n: logarithms ≪ powers of n ≪ exponentials cⁿ (c > 1) ≪ n! ≪ nⁿ. The ratio of a slower to a faster one tends to 0.

los.do: Use subsequences to show a sequence diverges and count its subsequential limits.
los.ek: Every subsequence of a convergent sequence has the same limit, so two subsequences with different limits prove divergence.

los.do: Test a sequence against the Cauchy criterion.
los.ek: A sequence is Cauchy when |a_m − a_n| can be made small for all large m and n together, not just neighbours. The harmonic sums fail: s_2n − s_n ≥ 1/2 for every n.

los.do: Classify a series as absolutely convergent, conditionally convergent or divergent.
los.ek: Absolute convergence implies convergence. The alternating series test gives convergence for decreasing terms tending to 0; Σ 1/n^p converges exactly when p > 1.

los.do: Sum a geometric or telescoping series exactly.
los.ek: Σ r^n from n = 0 is 1/(1 − r) for |r| < 1. A telescoping series is summed from its partial sums, which collapse to the first and last terms.

los.do: Find the radius of convergence of a power series and test its endpoints.
los.ek: Σ a_n x^n converges absolutely for |x| < R and diverges for |x| > R, with 1/R = lim |a_(n+1)/a_n| when that exists. Behaviour at |x| = R must be tested separately.

los.do: Compute partial sums and apply the nth-term test.
los.ek: A series converges when its partial sums do. If the terms do not tend to 0 the series diverges; if they do, the test says nothing.

los.do: Decide convergence by comparison with a p-series.
los.ek: For positive terms, a series behaves like Σ 1/nᵖ when its terms are comparable to 1/nᵖ, and that converges exactly when p > 1. For a ratio of polynomials, p is the degree gap.

los.do: Say what absolute convergence allows that conditional convergence does not.
los.ek: An absolutely convergent series can be rearranged freely with the same sum. A conditionally convergent one can be rearranged to converge to any number, or to diverge (Riemann).

los.do: Bound the error of an alternating series and of a p-series tail.
los.ek: For an alternating series with terms decreasing to 0, the error after n terms is at most the next term. For Σ 1/kᵖ the tail after n terms is at most ∫ₙ^∞ x⁻ᵖ dx = 1/((p − 1)nᵖ⁻¹).

los.do: Produce the δ that the definition of continuity asks for.
los.ek: f is continuous at a when for every ε > 0 there is a δ > 0 with |f(x) − f(a)| < ε whenever |x − a| < δ. For a linear f, δ = ε/|slope|; for x², restrict to δ ≤ 1 and bound the other factor.

los.do: Apply the intermediate and extreme value theorems and say which hypothesis each needs.
los.ek: A continuous function on a closed bounded interval takes every value between its end values, is bounded, and attains its bounds. Each conclusion fails on an open or unbounded interval, or for a discontinuous function.

los.do: Decide whether a function is uniformly continuous and find a Lipschitz constant.
los.ek: Uniform continuity means one δ works at every point. A continuous function on a closed bounded interval is uniformly continuous; a bounded derivative gives a Lipschitz constant sup|f′|, hence uniform continuity.

los.do: Find one-sided limits and classify a discontinuity.
los.ek: A limit exists when both one-sided limits exist and agree. Agree but differ from the value: removable. Exist but differ: jump. One fails to exist as a finite number: essential.

los.do: Evaluate standard limits of functions and use sequences to show a limit fails.
los.ek: sin x / x → 1, (1 − cos x)/x² → 1/2 and (eˣ − 1)/x → 1 as x → 0. f(x) → L exactly when f(x_n) → L for every sequence x_n → a; two sequences with different outcomes show there is no limit.

los.do: Locate the points where a function is continuous.
los.ek: Sums, products, quotients (non-zero denominator) and compositions of continuous functions are continuous. Step functions jump at their break points; a function can even be continuous at exactly one point.

los.do: Find the point the mean value theorem promises and say what Rolle's theorem needs.
los.ek: If f is continuous on [a, b] and differentiable inside, some c has f′(c) = (f(b) − f(a))/(b − a). Rolle is the case f(a) = f(b).

los.do: Bound a Taylor remainder with Lagrange's form.
los.ek: f(x) = Taylor polynomial of degree n + R_n, with R_n = f⁽ⁿ⁺¹⁾(c) x^(n+1)/(n + 1)! for some c between 0 and x. For e^x at x = 1, |R_n| < 3/(n + 1)!.

los.do: Compute upper and lower Riemann sums and say which functions are integrable.
los.ek: For an increasing f on n equal pieces, the upper sum uses right endpoints and the lower sum left endpoints, and U − L = (f(b) − f(a))(b − a)/n → 0. Monotone and continuous functions are integrable; the indicator of the rationals is not.

los.do: Decide whether an improper integral converges and evaluate it.
los.ek: ∫₁^∞ x^(−p) dx converges exactly when p > 1, to 1/(p − 1); ∫₀¹ x^(−p) dx converges exactly when p < 1, to 1/(1 − p). Comparison with these settles most cases.

los.do: Compute a derivative from the difference quotient and decide differentiability at a point.
los.ek: f′(a) = lim (f(a + h) − f(a))/h. Differentiable implies continuous but not conversely: |x| has a corner and ∛x a vertical tangent at 0.

los.do: Evaluate an indeterminate limit by L'Hôpital's rule or a Taylor expansion.
los.ek: For 0/0 or ∞/∞ forms, lim f/g = lim f′/g′ when the latter exists. Expanding numerator and denominator to the first non-vanishing order gives the same answer and shows why.

los.do: Differentiate an inverse function.
los.ek: If f is differentiable with f′(a) ≠ 0 and b = f(a), then (f⁻¹)′(b) = 1/f′(a): the graph is reflected in the diagonal, so slopes are reciprocated.

los.do: Measure how far a sequence of functions is from its limit in the uniform norm and decide whether convergence is uniform.
los.ek: f_n → f uniformly when sup |f_n − f| → 0. Pointwise convergence lets the worst point move with n; uniform convergence does not. A uniform limit of continuous functions is continuous.

los.do: Apply the Weierstrass M-test and say what uniform convergence lets you exchange.
los.ek: If |f_n(x)| ≤ M_n for all x and Σ M_n converges, then Σ f_n converges uniformly. Uniform convergence allows a limit to pass through an integral, and through a derivative when the derivatives converge uniformly.

los.do: Compute distances in the standard norms on Rⁿ and compare the norms.
los.ek: ‖x‖₁ = Σ|x_i|, ‖x‖₂ = √Σx_i², ‖x‖∞ = max|x_i|, with ‖x‖∞ ≤ ‖x‖₂ ≤ ‖x‖₁ ≤ n‖x‖∞. All norms on a finite-dimensional space are Lipschitz equivalent, so they give the same open sets.

los.do: Decide whether a metric space is complete and say what completeness buys.
los.ek: A space is complete when every Cauchy sequence converges in it. Rⁿ and C[a, b] with the uniform norm are complete; the rationals and an open interval are not. A closed subset of a complete space is complete.

los.do: Apply the contraction mapping theorem: find the contraction constant and bound the error of the iteration.
los.ek: If d(f(x), f(y)) ≤ k d(x, y) with k < 1 on a complete space, f has exactly one fixed point, and the iterates satisfy d(x_n, x*) ≤ kⁿ d(x₁, x₀)/(1 − k). Picard's theorem for ODEs is this theorem in C[a, b].

los.do: Classify a critical point of a function of two variables from its Hessian.
los.ek: At a critical point, a positive-definite Hessian is a local minimum, negative-definite a local maximum, indefinite a saddle; a zero determinant leaves the test undecided. Mixed partials agree when they are continuous.

los.do: Compute n-step transition probabilities and push a distribution forward one step.
los.ek: The n-step probabilities are the entries of Pⁿ (Chapman-Kolmogorov), and a row vector of probabilities evolves by μ ↦ μP.

los.do: Find the communicating classes of a chain, say which are closed, and find the period of a state.
los.ek: States communicate when each can reach the other. A class is closed if the chain cannot leave it; a chain with one class is irreducible. The period of a state is the gcd of its possible return times.

los.do: Find an absorption probability and a mean hitting time by first-step analysis.
los.ek: h(i), the probability of hitting A from i, satisfies h = 1 on A and h(i) = Σ p(i, j) h(j) elsewhere. k(i), the mean time to hit A, satisfies k = 0 on A and k(i) = 1 + Σ p(i, j) k(j).

los.do: Read and complete a transition matrix.
los.ek: Entry (i, j) is the probability of moving from state i to state j in one step. Every row is a probability distribution, so each row sums to 1; columns need not.

los.do: Classify a state as absorbing, transient or recurrent from the diagram.
los.ek: A state is absorbing if the chain can never leave it. In a finite chain a state is recurrent if it lies in a closed class and transient if the chain can leave its class for good.

los.do: Find the probability of a particular path.
los.ek: By the Markov property the probability of a path is the product of its one-step transition probabilities: the future depends on the past only through the present state.

los.do: Evolve a starting distribution for one or two steps.
los.ek: If the chain starts with distribution μ (a row vector), after n steps its distribution is μPⁿ: multiply on the left, one step at a time.

los.do: Solve the gambler's ruin problem for the chance of winning and the expected duration.
los.ek: On 0…N with up-probability p and q = 1 − p: from i the chance of reaching N first is i/N if p = 1/2 and (1 − (q/p)^i)/(1 − (q/p)^N) otherwise. The fair game lasts i(N − i) steps on average.

los.do: Say whether a random walk is recurrent or transient and find a biased walk's return probability.
los.ek: A state is recurrent if return is certain, equivalently if Σ pⁿ(i, i) diverges. The simple symmetric walk is recurrent in one and two dimensions and transient in three (Pólya). On the integers with p ≠ 1/2 the return probability is 1 − |p − q|.

los.do: Find the distribution of a simple random walk after n steps by counting paths.
los.ek: A walk of n steps ends at k when it takes (n + k)/2 steps up, so P(S_n = k) = C(n, (n + k)/2) p^((n+k)/2) q^((n−k)/2), and zero unless n and k have the same parity.

los.do: Find the mean and variance of a random walk's position.
los.ek: Each step has mean p − q and variance 4pq, and steps are independent, so S_n has mean n(p − q) and variance 4npq. A symmetric walk is typically about √n from its start.

los.do: Compute return probabilities of the symmetric walk.
los.ek: The walk is at 0 after 2n steps with probability C(2n, n)/4ⁿ, about 1/√(πn). It first returns at step 2n with probability C(2n, n)/((2n − 1)4ⁿ).

los.do: Find the invariant distribution of a small chain.
los.ek: π is invariant when πP = π with entries summing to 1. For two states with p(0, 1) = a and p(1, 0) = b, π = (b, a)/(a + b).

los.do: Relate the invariant distribution to mean return times and long-run proportions.
los.ek: In an irreducible positive-recurrent chain the mean return time to i is 1/π_i, and the long-run proportion of time spent in i is π_i whatever the start.

los.do: Use detailed balance, including for a random walk on a graph.
los.ek: If π_i p(i, j) = π_j p(j, i) for all pairs then π is invariant and the chain is reversible. A random walk on a graph has π_v = deg(v)/(2E).

los.do: Say when a chain converges to equilibrium and how fast.
los.ek: An irreducible aperiodic positive-recurrent chain has pⁿ(i, j) → π_j. For two states, pⁿ(0, 0) − π₀ = π₁ λⁿ with λ = 1 − a − b, the second eigenvalue.

los.do: Check whether a given distribution is invariant.
los.ek: π is invariant when πP = π: for each state, the probability flowing in over one step equals the probability already there.

los.do: Use symmetry to find an invariant distribution without solving.
los.ek: If the columns of P also sum to 1 (a doubly stochastic matrix), the uniform distribution is invariant. A symmetric transition matrix is doubly stochastic.

los.do: Compute a long-run average from the invariant distribution.
los.ek: For an irreducible positive-recurrent chain the long-run average of f(X_n) is Σ π_i f(i), whatever the starting state (the ergodic theorem).

los.do: Compute probabilities and waiting times for a Poisson process.
los.ek: With rate λ, the number of arrivals in time t is Poisson with mean λt, the gaps are independent exponentials of mean 1/λ, and the kth arrival comes at mean time k/λ.

los.do: Combine and split Poisson processes.
los.ek: Independent Poisson processes of rates λ and μ superpose to rate λ + μ, and the next event is from the first with probability λ/(λ + μ). Keeping each event with probability p gives a Poisson process of rate pλ.

los.do: Find the equilibrium of a birth-death chain and of the M/M/1 queue.
los.ek: Balance across each cut: π_n λ_n = π_(n+1) μ_(n+1). For M/M/1 with ρ = λ/μ < 1, π_n = (1 − ρ)ρⁿ and the mean number in the system is ρ/(1 − ρ).

los.do: Compute with the exponential distribution and its memoryless property.
los.ek: An exponential time with rate λ has P(T > t) = e^(−λt) and mean 1/λ. Memoryless: given T > s, the remaining time is again exponential with rate λ.

los.do: Find the time until the first of several independent exponential events.
los.ek: The minimum of independent exponentials with rates λ₁, …, λ_n is exponential with rate λ₁ + … + λ_n. With n identical clocks of rate λ the first rings after mean time 1/(nλ).

los.do: Find the idle probability and the mean time in an M/M/1 queue.
los.ek: With ρ = λ/μ < 1 the server is idle a fraction 1 − ρ of the time, and a customer spends on average 1/(μ − λ) in the system (Little's formula L = λW).

topics.title: Fair games in discrete and continuous time

los.do: Compute a conditional expectation and decide whether a process is a martingale.
los.ek: M is a martingale when E[M_(n+1) | past] = M_n: a fair game. For a simple symmetric walk S_n, both S_n and S_n² − n are martingales; for a biased walk, (q/p)^S_n is.

los.do: Use the optional stopping theorem to find exit probabilities and expected exit times.
los.ek: For a martingale and a bounded stopping time (or bounded increments and finite mean time), E[M_T] = M₀. Applied to S_n it gives P(hit b before −a) = a/(a + b); applied to S_n² − n it gives E[T] = ab.

los.do: Price a claim in the one-period binomial model by the risk-neutral probability.
los.ek: If the stock moves from S to uS or dS and the bank pays 1 + r, with d < 1 + r < u, the risk-neutral up-probability is q = (1 + r − d)/(u − d), and any claim costs its discounted q-expectation: the price of the portfolio that replicates it.

los.do: Compute variances, covariances and hitting probabilities for Brownian motion.
los.ek: B_t − B_s is normal with mean 0 and variance t − s, independent of the past, so Cov(B_s, B_t) = min(s, t). Reflection principle: P(max over [0, t] ≥ a) = 2 P(B_t ≥ a).

los.do: Check the axioms of a topology on a small set and generate a topology from given sets.
los.ek: A topology contains the empty set and the whole space and is closed under arbitrary unions and finite intersections.

los.do: Find the closure and interior of a subset.
los.ek: The closure is the smallest closed set containing A (closed means the complement is open); the interior is the largest open set inside A.

los.do: Recognise continuity, homeomorphism and topological properties, including the Hausdorff property.
los.ek: f is continuous when preimages of open sets are open. A homeomorphism is a continuous bijection with continuous inverse; properties it preserves are topological. In a Hausdorff space distinct points have disjoint open neighbourhoods, so limits are unique.

los.do: Describe subspace, product and quotient topologies and identify a quotient of an interval or square.
los.ek: A subspace takes the intersections of open sets with it; a product is generated by products of open sets; a quotient makes a set open when its preimage is. Gluing the ends of an interval gives a circle; gluing opposite sides of a square gives a torus.

topics.title: Distances and open sets on the line

los.do: Check the axioms of a metric and compute distances in different metrics.
los.ek: A metric is non-negative, zero only between equal points, symmetric, and satisfies the triangle inequality. The Euclidean, taxicab and maximum metrics on the plane give different distances but the same open sets.

los.do: Decide whether a subset of the real line is open, closed, both or neither.
los.ek: A set is open if every point has a small interval around it inside the set, and closed if its complement is open. Only the empty set and the whole line are both; a half-open interval is neither.

los.do: Find the boundary, interior and closure of a union of intervals.
los.ek: The interior drops every endpoint, the closure adds every endpoint, and the boundary is the closure minus the interior: the endpoints and isolated points.

los.do: Identify the limit points of a set and relate them to closedness.
los.ek: x is a limit point of A if every neighbourhood of x meets A in a point other than x. A set is closed exactly when it contains all its limit points.

los.do: Decide whether a space is connected and count its components.
los.ek: A space is connected when it is not the union of two disjoint non-empty open sets. Removing a point disconnects the line but not the plane, which is one way to tell them apart.

los.do: Relate connectedness, path-connectedness and continuous images.
los.ek: A continuous image of a connected space is connected (the intermediate value theorem is the case of an interval). Path-connected implies connected; the converse holds for open subsets of Euclidean space but fails for the topologist's sine curve.

los.do: Test a map between finite spaces for continuity by pulling back open sets.
los.ek: f is continuous when the preimage of every open set is open. Into the two-point Sierpinski space, a continuous map is the same thing as a choice of open set.

los.do: Generate a topology from a basis or subbasis.
los.ek: A subbasis generates the topology whose open sets are unions of finite intersections of its members; it is the smallest topology in which those sets are open.

los.do: Decide whether a space is compact.
los.ek: Compact means every open cover has a finite subcover. Heine-Borel: a subset of Euclidean space is compact exactly when it is closed and bounded.

los.do: Use what compactness guarantees.
los.ek: Closed subsets of compact spaces are compact; compact subsets of Hausdorff spaces are closed; continuous images of compact spaces are compact; a continuous bijection from a compact space to a Hausdorff space is a homeomorphism.

los.do: Extract a smallest subcover from a cover.
los.ek: A subcover keeps some of the cover's sets and still covers the space. Compactness says a finite one always exists; finding the smallest is a counting problem.

los.do: Count the connected components of a graph or a union of intervals.
los.ek: Components are the maximal connected pieces. For a graph, V − E + (number of independent cycles) counts them; for intervals on a line, pieces that overlap or touch merge.

los.do: Compute an Euler characteristic and the genus it implies.
los.ek: χ = V − E + F for any triangulation or polygonal division. A closed orientable surface of genus g has χ = 2 − 2g: sphere 2, torus 0, double torus −2.

los.do: Read a polygon with sides identified: count its vertices and name the surface.
los.ek: Follow each corner round the gluing to see which corners become one point. With one face and n edge pairs, χ = V − n + 1. Standard words: a a⁻¹ sphere, a a projective plane, a b a⁻¹ b⁻¹ torus, a b a b⁻¹ Klein bottle.

los.do: Use orientability and the Euler characteristic to classify a closed surface.
los.ek: Every closed surface is a sphere with g handles (χ = 2 − 2g) or a sphere with k crosscaps (χ = 2 − k). Orientability and χ together determine the surface. A connected sum has χ(A # B) = χ(A) + χ(B) − 2.

los.do: Use Euler's formula on the sphere and on other surfaces.
los.ek: A division of a surface into faces satisfies V − E + F = χ: 2 on a sphere, 0 on a torus. So a map on a torus has two fewer faces than the same vertex and edge counts would give on a sphere.

los.do: Count handles or crosscaps from the Euler characteristic.
los.ek: An orientable closed surface has g = (2 − χ)/2 handles; a non-orientable one has k = 2 − χ crosscaps. One crosscap is the projective plane, two the Klein bottle.

los.do: Name a closed surface from its orientability and Euler characteristic.
los.ek: The pair (orientable or not, χ) determines a closed surface: orientable χ = 2 sphere, 0 torus, −2 double torus; non-orientable χ = 1 projective plane, 0 Klein bottle.

los.do: Recognise homotopy equivalence and say what a space deformation-retracts to.
los.ek: Two spaces are homotopy equivalent when each maps to the other with both composites homotopic to the identity. A deformation retraction shrinks a space onto a subspace: an annulus or a Möbius band onto a circle, a disc onto a point.

los.do: Name the fundamental group of a standard space and find the rank of the fundamental group of a graph.
los.ek: π₁ is trivial for a sphere (dimension ≥ 2) or a disc, Z for the circle, Z² for the torus, Z/2 for the projective plane, and free on n generators for a wedge of n circles. A connected graph has free fundamental group of rank E − V + 1.

los.do: Count sheets of a covering and use the multiplicativity of Euler characteristic.
los.ek: An n-sheeted covering has χ(cover) = n χ(base) and corresponds to a subgroup of index n in the fundamental group of the base. The real line covers the circle with infinitely many sheets; the sphere covers the projective plane twice.

los.do: Read Betti numbers and Euler characteristic and use the fixed-point theorems they give.
los.ek: χ = b₀ − b₁ + b₂ − … . A closed orientable surface of genus g has Betti numbers 1, 2g, 1; the sphere Sⁿ has homology only in degrees 0 and n. Brouwer: every continuous map of a closed ball to itself has a fixed point.

los.do: Classify a sample as an element, compound, homogeneous mixture or heterogeneous mixture from a description or particle diagram.
los.ek: A pure substance has fixed composition; a mixture's composition can vary and it can be separated by physical means.

los.do: Sort properties and changes into physical and chemical.
los.ek: A chemical change makes new substances (bonds broken and formed); a physical change alters state or form only.

los.do: Count significant figures in a measurement and round a calculated result correctly for × ÷ and for + −.
los.ek: × ÷: keep the fewest significant figures; + −: keep the fewest decimal places; exact counts and defined constants don't limit.

los.do: Calculate density, mass or volume from the other two, including volume by water displacement.
los.ek: ρ = m/V; 1 mL = 1 cm³; water ≈ 1.00 g/mL near room temperature.

los.do: Write quantities in scientific notation and convert between SI prefixes (p, n, μ, m, c, k, M, G).
los.ek: Each prefix is a power of ten; moving the decimal changes the exponent by the same count.

los.do: Distinguish accuracy from precision and calculate percent error.
los.ek: Accuracy = closeness to the true value; precision = agreement among repeats; % error = |measured − true|/true × 100.

los.do: Convert temperatures among °C, K and °F.
los.ek: K = °C + 273.15; °F = 1.8·°C + 32; gas laws and thermodynamics need kelvin.

los.do: Convert a quantity through a chain of conversion factors, including squared and cubed units.
los.ek: Multiply by factors equal to one, arranged so unwanted units cancel; cube the factor for volume (1 m³ = 10⁶ cm³).

topics.title: Atoms, ions, the periodic table and naming

los.do: Count protons, neutrons and electrons from a nuclide symbol for an atom or ion.
los.ek: Z = protons; A = protons + neutrons; electrons = Z − charge.

los.do: Use periodic-table position (group, metal or nonmetal) to name, and write formulas for, binary ionic, polyatomic ionic, binary molecular compounds and common acids.
los.ek: Metals left of the staircase form cations, nonmetals anions. Ionic: cation then anion, charges balance, Roman numeral for variable-charge metals; molecular: Greek prefixes; -ate → -ic acid, -ite → -ous acid.

topics.title: The mole as a counting unit

los.do: Use the picometre size of atoms to see why a mole is so large.
los.ek: Atoms are about 100–300 pm across; a millimetre holds millions of them in a row, so a visible sample holds ~10²³.

los.do: Explain the mole as a count of particles and compute a compound's molar mass from its formula.
los.ek: 1 mol = 6.022 × 10²³ particles; molar mass in g/mol = sum of atomic masses × subscripts.

los.do: Classify an error as random or systematic, predict its direction, and choose a procedure that limits it.
los.ek: Systematic errors push every result one way (a mis-zeroed balance, a wet sample); random errors scatter both ways and shrink with replicates; blanks and calibration remove systematic ones.

los.do: Keep a laboratory record that others can verify.
los.ek: Write directly in a bound notebook in ink, date every entry, cross out mistakes with one line instead of erasing, and record conditions and raw data.

los.do: Choose the safety equipment and handling for a hazard, reading GHS pictograms and safety data sheets.
los.ek: Goggles always; fume hood for volatile or toxic substances; know the eyewash, shower and extinguisher; GHS pictograms and SDS sections name the hazard and the response.

los.do: Dispose of laboratory waste by category.
los.ek: Separate halogenated from non-halogenated solvents, keep oxidisers apart from organics, neutralise or collect acids and bases, never pour heavy metals or organics down the drain.

los.do: Reduce radiation dose with time, distance and shielding.
los.ek: Dose rate falls with the square of the distance from a point source; each half-value layer of shielding halves it; dose = rate × time.

los.do: Convert among mass, moles and number of particles of a compound or of one element inside it.
los.ek: n = m/M; N = n·N_A; route every conversion through moles; subscripts are mole ratios (1 mol Fe₂O₃ holds 2 mol Fe).

los.do: Calculate an element's average atomic mass from its isotopes' masses and abundances.
los.ek: Average mass = Σ (fractional abundance × isotope mass).

los.do: Read isotopes and relative abundances off a mass spectrum, or find two isotopes' abundances from the average mass.
los.ek: Peak position = isotope mass; peak height ∝ abundance; with two isotopes, x·m₁ + (1 − x)·m₂ = average.

los.do: Calculate the mass percent of each element in a compound from its formula.
los.ek: % X = (subscript × M_X)/M_compound × 100.

los.do: Determine an empirical formula from mass-percent or mass data.
los.ek: Assume 100 g, convert each to moles, divide by the smallest, clear fractions to whole numbers.

los.do: Find a molecular formula from the empirical formula and the molar mass.
los.ek: Molecular formula = (empirical formula)ₙ with n = M/M_empirical.

los.do: Find an empirical formula from combustion-analysis masses of CO₂ and H₂O.
los.ek: All C ends in CO₂ and all H in H₂O; O is found by difference from the sample mass.

los.do: Calculate the mass percent of a component in an impure sample or mixture from elemental analysis.
los.ek: Mass of analyte element → mass of the compound containing it → percent of the sample.

los.do: Write full and noble-gas ground-state electron configurations for atoms and ions.
los.ek: Fill by Aufbau order (1s 2s 2p 3s 3p 4s 3d 4p …), two electrons per orbital; cations of transition metals lose ns before (n−1)d.

los.do: Compare the attraction of an electron to the nucleus using Coulomb's law with nuclear charge, shielding and distance.
los.ek: F ∝ q₁q₂/r²; Z_eff ≈ Z − core electrons; outer, well-shielded electrons are held least tightly.

los.do: Draw an orbital (box) diagram, count unpaired electrons, and predict paramagnetism or diamagnetism.
los.ek: Hund: fill degenerate orbitals singly with parallel spins first; any unpaired electron ⇒ paramagnetic.

los.do: Assign each peak of a photoelectron spectrum to a subshell, read its electron count, and identify the element.
los.ek: Position = binding energy (core electrons far left/high); relative peak height = number of electrons in that subshell.

los.do: Rank atoms by radius, first ionization energy, electron affinity and electronegativity, and justify with Z_eff and shell number.
los.ek: Across a period Z_eff rises (smaller, higher IE, higher EN); down a group n rises (larger, lower IE, lower EN); IE dips at groups 13 and 16 (p electron, first p pairing).

los.do: Identify an element's group from a jump in successive ionization energies.
los.ek: The big jump comes after the valence electrons are gone, when a core electron is removed.

los.do: Compare ion sizes with their parent atoms and rank an isoelectronic series.
los.ek: Cations shrink, anions grow; in an isoelectronic series, more protons ⇒ smaller.

los.do: Predict an element's common ion charge and the formula of the ionic compound two elements form.
los.ek: Main-group atoms gain or lose electrons to reach a noble-gas configuration; total charge sums to zero.

los.do: Predict the formula or reactivity of an unfamiliar compound from an analogous compound of a same-group element.
los.ek: Same group ⇒ same valence configuration ⇒ analogous formulas (Na₂O → K₂O); reactivity trends follow IE and EN.

los.do: Assign quantum numbers n, l, m_l, m_s, decide whether a set is allowed, and count the orbitals and electrons in a subshell or shell.
los.ek: l = 0…n−1; m_l = −l…+l; m_s = ±½; no two electrons share all four (Pauli); subshell holds 2(2l + 1) e⁻, shell 2n².
los.std: DAT-GC Atomic and Molecular Structure (quantum theory), acs-accm-general:I.B.2, acs-accm-inorganic:I.B.1, acs-accm-inorganic:I.B.2

los.do: Balance a nuclear equation for alpha, beta-minus, positron, electron-capture and gamma processes.
los.ek: Mass numbers and atomic numbers each sum equally on both sides; α = ⁴₂He, β⁻ = ⁰₋₁e, β⁺ = ⁰₊₁e.
los.std: DAT-GC Nuclear Reactions, acs-accm-general:I.F.2, acs-accm-organic:I.F, acs-accm-inorganic:I.F.1, acs-accm-analytical:I.F.1

los.do: Calculate the amount remaining, or the elapsed time, after a whole number of half-lives.
los.ek: Remaining = initial × (½)^(t/t½).

los.do: Calculate a nucleus's mass defect and binding energy per nucleon.
los.ek: Δm = (mass of separate nucleons) − (nucleus mass); E = Δm c², 1 u ↔ 931.5 MeV.
los.std: DAT-GC Nuclear Reactions, acs-accm-general:VI.I.1, acs-accm-organic:VI.I, acs-accm-inorganic:VI.I.1

units.title: Molecular and ionic compound structure and properties

los.do: Classify a bond as nonpolar covalent, polar covalent, ionic or metallic from the elements and their electronegativity difference, and mark partial charges.
los.ek: Metal + nonmetal ⇒ ionic; nonmetals ⇒ covalent; ΔEN ≈ 0 nonpolar, larger ΔEN more polar; metals ⇒ metallic.

los.do: Read bond length and bond energy from a potential-energy vs internuclear-distance curve, and compare curves for different bonds.
los.ek: The well's minimum gives bond length (x) and bond energy (depth); higher bond order and smaller atoms ⇒ deeper, shorter well.

los.do: Rank ionic compounds by lattice energy using Coulomb's law.
los.ek: Lattice energy ∝ q₁q₂/(r₁ + r₂): charge dominates, then ion size.

los.do: Represent an ionic solid as a lattice and use it to explain high melting point, brittleness and conductivity only when molten or dissolved.
los.ek: Alternating ions maximise attraction; shifting a layer brings like charges together and it shatters; ions must be mobile to conduct.

los.do: Explain metallic conductivity, malleability and luster with the electron-sea model, and classify an alloy as interstitial or substitutional from atomic radii.
los.ek: Delocalised valence electrons move freely; similar radii ⇒ substitutional (brass), much smaller atom ⇒ interstitial (steel), which is stiffer.

los.do: Draw the Lewis structure of a molecule or polyatomic ion that obeys the octet rule.
los.ek: Count valence electrons (adjust for charge), connect atoms, complete outer octets, move lone pairs into multiple bonds if the centre is short.

los.do: Draw Lewis structures for octet exceptions: incomplete octets, expanded octets and odd-electron species.
los.ek: B and Be can be electron-deficient; period-3+ central atoms can exceed eight; an odd electron count leaves a radical.

los.do: Calculate formal charges and use them to pick the best of several Lewis structures.
los.ek: FC = valence e⁻ − lone-pair e⁻ − ½ bonding e⁻; prefer FCs near zero, with negatives on more electronegative atoms.

los.do: Draw all resonance structures of a species and calculate the average bond order.
los.ek: Resonance forms differ only in electron placement; the real structure is the average, e.g. bond order 4/3 in NO₃⁻; higher bond order ⇒ shorter, stronger bond.

los.do: Predict electron-domain geometry, molecular shape and approximate bond angles with VSEPR.
los.ek: 2–6 domains ⇒ linear, trigonal planar, tetrahedral, trigonal bipyramidal, octahedral; lone pairs squeeze angles (109.5° → 107° → 104.5°).

los.do: Assign the hybridization of a central atom and count σ and π bonds.
los.ek: 2, 3, 4, 5, 6 domains ⇒ sp, sp², sp³, sp³d, sp³d²; a single bond is σ, a double σ + π, a triple σ + 2π.
los.std: SAP-4.C, acs-accm-general:II.C.3, acs-accm-general:II.F.1, acs-accm-organic:II.E.1, acs-accm-inorganic:II.C.1, acs-accm-inorganic:II.F.2

los.do: Decide whether a molecule is polar from its shape and bond dipoles.
los.ek: Polar bonds in a symmetric shape cancel (CO₂, CCl₄); lone pairs or unlike atoms usually break the symmetry.

los.do: Fill a molecular-orbital diagram for a period-2 diatomic or ion and find its bond order and magnetism.
los.ek: Bond order = ½(bonding − antibonding e⁻); O₂ has two unpaired π* electrons (paramagnetic); σ2p/π2p order flips after N₂.
los.std: DAT-GC Atomic and Molecular Structure (quantum theory), acs-accm-general:II.E.1, acs-accm-organic:II.E.3, acs-accm-inorganic:II.B.1, acs-accm-inorganic:II.E.1, acs-accm-inorganic:II.E.2, acs-accm-inorganic:X.D.2

los.do: Identify every intermolecular force present between particles: London dispersion, dipole–dipole, hydrogen bonding, ion–dipole.
los.ek: All molecules have dispersion; polar ⇒ dipole–dipole; H on N, O or F next to a lone pair on N, O or F ⇒ hydrogen bond.

los.do: Rank substances by boiling point, vapor pressure, viscosity or surface tension from their intermolecular forces.
los.ek: Stronger IMF ⇒ higher bp, lower vapor pressure; dispersion grows with electron count and contact area and can outweigh dipoles.

los.do: Classify a solid as ionic, molecular, covalent-network or metallic and predict its melting point, hardness and conductivity.
los.ek: Network (diamond, SiO₂) highest mp and non-conducting; molecular low mp; metallic conducts as a solid; ionic conducts only molten or dissolved.

los.do: Explain vapor pressure and boiling as an IMF-versus-kinetic-energy balance, and why boiling point changes with external pressure.
los.ek: Boiling occurs when vapor pressure = external pressure; normal bp is at 1 atm.

los.do: Read a phase diagram: identify phases, the triple point, the critical point and normal melting and boiling points, and trace a path.
los.ek: Lines are coexistence curves; water's solid–liquid line slopes left because ice is less dense than liquid water.

los.do: Solve PV = nRT for any variable with consistent units and the matching value of R.
los.ek: R = 0.08206 L·atm/(mol·K) = 8.314 J/(mol·K); T in kelvin; 1 atm = 760 torr = 101.325 kPa.

los.do: Predict a new P, V, T or n when conditions change, using the combined gas law and Boyle's, Charles's, Gay-Lussac's and Avogadro's laws.
los.ek: P₁V₁/(n₁T₁) = P₂V₂/(n₂T₂); cancel whatever is held constant.

los.do: Calculate a gas's density or molar mass from P, V, T and mass.
los.ek: M = ρRT/P; at STP one mole occupies 22.4 L.

los.do: Calculate partial pressures and mole fractions with Dalton's law, including a gas collected over water.
los.ek: P_total = Σ P_i; P_i = χ_i P_total; subtract water's vapor pressure from the collected gas pressure.

los.do: State the postulates of kinetic molecular theory and interpret Maxwell–Boltzmann speed distributions at different temperatures and molar masses.
los.ek: Average KE ∝ T only; higher T or lower M spreads the curve to higher speeds.

los.do: Compare rms speeds and rates of effusion of two gases with Graham's law.
los.ek: u_rms = √(3RT/M); rate₁/rate₂ = √(M₂/M₁).

topics.title: Deviation from the ideal gas law

los.do: Predict when and in which direction a real gas deviates from ideal behavior, and explain the van der Waals a and b terms.
los.ek: High P: particle volume matters (b, V larger than ideal); low T: attractions matter (a, P lower than ideal); polar or large gases deviate most.

los.do: Calculate molarity, moles of solute or solution volume from the other two.
los.ek: M = mol solute / L solution.

los.do: Calculate the result of a dilution and describe how to prepare a solution of given concentration.
los.ek: Moles of solute are unchanged by adding solvent: M₁V₁ = M₂V₂; dissolve, then fill to the mark in a volumetric flask.

los.do: Calculate each ion's concentration in a solution of a strong electrolyte.
los.ek: 0.10 M CaCl₂ ⇒ 0.10 M Ca²⁺ and 0.20 M Cl⁻.

los.do: Convert among molarity, molality, mass percent, mole fraction and ppm.
los.ek: m = mol solute / kg solvent; converting molarity ↔ molality needs the solution's density.

los.do: Draw a particle diagram of a solution with correct solute ratios and solvent orientation around ions.
los.ek: Water's O (δ⁻) faces cations; its H (δ⁺) faces anions; ion counts follow the formula.

los.do: Explain a chromatography or distillation separation, and compute R_f, from differences in intermolecular forces.
los.ek: A component that interacts more with the stationary phase travels less (lower R_f); distillation separates by volatility.

los.do: Predict relative solubility in polar and nonpolar solvents from solute–solvent interactions.
los.ek: 'Like dissolves like': dissolving is favored when solute–solvent attractions rival solute–solute and solvent–solvent ones.

los.do: Predict how temperature and pressure change solubility, and use Henry's law for a dissolved gas.
los.ek: Gas solubility falls as T rises and rises with its partial pressure: C = k_H P; most solids dissolve better when hot.

los.do: Match a region of the electromagnetic spectrum to the molecular or electronic transition it causes.
los.ek: Microwave → rotation; infrared → vibration; UV–visible → electronic transitions.

los.do: Calculate a photon's energy, frequency or wavelength, per photon or per mole.
los.ek: E = hν = hc/λ; c = λν; h = 6.626 × 10⁻³⁴ J·s; multiply by N_A for per-mole energy.

los.do: Calculate the energy and wavelength of a hydrogen-atom transition, and relate emission lines to energy levels.
los.ek: E_n = −2.18 × 10⁻¹⁸ J / n²; ΔE = photon energy; emission drops to lower n.
los.std: SAP-8.B, DAT-GC Atomic and Molecular Structure (quantum theory), acs-accm-general:IX.E.3, acs-accm-inorganic:I.D.1

los.do: Calculate a concentration from absorbance, directly or from a calibration curve.
los.ek: A = εbc; at fixed λ and path, A ∝ c, so the calibration line's slope is εb.

los.do: Calculate the vapor pressure of a solution with Raoult's law.
los.ek: P_solution = χ_solvent P°_solvent for a nonvolatile solute.

los.do: Calculate a boiling-point elevation or freezing-point depression with the van 't Hoff factor, and rank solutions by it.
los.ek: ΔT = i·K·m; i counts particles per formula unit (NaCl ≈ 2, glucose 1).

los.do: Calculate osmotic pressure, or a solute's molar mass from colligative data.
los.ek: Π = iMRT; measured ΔT or Π → moles of solute → M = mass/moles.

los.do: Identify evidence of a chemical reaction and balance a chemical equation by inspection.
los.ek: Gas, precipitate, color or temperature change can signal reaction; balance atoms with coefficients, never by changing subscripts.

los.do: Predict whether a precipitate forms on mixing two ionic solutions, using solubility rules.
los.ek: Always soluble: Group 1, NH₄⁺, NO₃⁻ (AP's minimum); DAT adds halides (except Ag⁺, Pb²⁺, Hg₂²⁺), sulfates (except Ba, Sr, Pb, Ca), mostly insoluble carbonates, phosphates, hydroxides.

los.do: Write the molecular, complete ionic and net ionic equations for a reaction in solution.
los.ek: Split only strong electrolytes in solution; cancel spectator ions; keep solids, liquids, gases and weak electrolytes whole.

los.do: Translate between a particle diagram of a reaction and its balanced equation, including which reactant is left over.
los.ek: Count particles before and after; the coefficient ratio is the ratio of particles that react.

los.do: Classify a process (dissolving, melting, ionization, combustion) as physical or chemical from whether bonds or interparticle forces change.
los.ek: Breaking only IMFs is physical; breaking and forming intramolecular bonds is chemical; dissolving an ionic salt is a borderline case.

los.do: Find the mass of an element that can be recovered from an ore or mineral sample.
los.ek: Mass of element = mass of ore × fraction of mineral × (mass of element in one formula unit ÷ formula mass).

los.do: Calculate the mass of a product or reactant from the mass of another, through the mole ratio.
los.ek: grams A → mol A → (coefficient ratio) → mol B → grams B.

los.do: Identify the limiting reactant, the theoretical yield and the amount of excess reactant left.
los.ek: The limiting reactant is the one that makes less product; leftover = initial − consumed.

los.do: Calculate percent yield from actual and theoretical yield.
los.ek: % yield = actual/theoretical × 100; it can't exceed 100% for a dry, pure product.
los.std: SPQ-4.A, acs-accm-general:V.F.2, acs-accm-general:IX.E.1, acs-accm-organic:I.E.1, acs-accm-organic:V.A.2, acs-accm-organic:X.B.1, acs-accm-inorganic:I.E.1

los.do: Solve solution stoichiometry: volumes and molarities in, mass or concentration out.
los.ek: mol = M·V for each solution; mix volumes add for the final concentration.

los.do: Solve gas stoichiometry with the ideal gas law or molar volume.
los.ek: Convert gas P, V, T to moles with n = PV/RT, then use the mole ratio; equal volumes of gases at the same T, P ⇒ equal moles.

los.do: Calculate an unknown concentration or sample purity from titration data at the equivalence point.
los.ek: At equivalence, moles titrant × (ratio) = moles analyte; endpoint is where the indicator changes.

los.do: Classify a reaction as precipitation, acid–base or redox (including synthesis, decomposition, combustion, single and double replacement).
los.ek: Electron transfer ⇒ redox; proton transfer ⇒ acid–base; insoluble product from ions ⇒ precipitation.

los.do: Predict the products of combustion, synthesis, decomposition and double-replacement reactions.
los.ek: Hydrocarbon + O₂ → CO₂ + H₂O; double replacement swaps partners; metal carbonates decompose to oxide + CO₂.

los.do: Identify Brønsted–Lowry acids, bases and conjugate pairs, and write the proton-transfer equation.
los.ek: Acid donates H⁺, base accepts it; conjugates differ by exactly one H⁺; water is amphoteric.

los.do: Assign oxidation numbers to every atom in a species.
los.ek: Elements 0; monatomic ions = charge; O usually −2, H +1 (−1 in hydrides), F −1; sum = overall charge.

los.do: Identify the species oxidized and reduced and the oxidizing and reducing agents.
los.ek: Oxidation = loss of e⁻ (number rises); the oxidizing agent is the species reduced.

los.do: Balance a redox equation by half-reactions in acidic or basic solution.
los.ek: Balance atoms, O with H₂O, H with H⁺, charge with e⁻; equalize electrons; in base add OH⁻ to neutralize H⁺.

los.do: Predict whether a single-replacement reaction occurs from an activity series.
los.ek: A metal displaces ions of any metal below it; metals above H displace H₂ from acids.

los.do: Express a reaction's rate from the rate of change of any reactant or product, using the coefficients.
los.ek: rate = −(1/a)d[A]/dt = (1/c)d[C]/dt for aA → cC.

los.do: Determine reaction orders and the rate constant, with its units, from initial-rates data.
los.ek: Compare two runs where only one concentration changes: rate ratio = (conc ratio)^order; k has units M^(1−n)·s⁻¹ for overall order n.

los.do: Predict the change in rate when one or more concentrations change.
los.ek: Second order in A: doubling [A] quadruples the rate; zero order: no change.

los.do: Use the zero-, first- or second-order integrated rate law to find a concentration at time t, or the time to reach one.
los.ek: [A] = [A]₀ − kt; ln[A] = ln[A]₀ − kt; 1/[A] = 1/[A]₀ + kt.

los.do: Identify reaction order from which plot ([A], ln[A] or 1/[A] vs t) is linear, and read k from its slope.
los.ek: Linear [A] ⇒ zero; linear ln[A] ⇒ first (slope −k); linear 1/[A] ⇒ second (slope +k).

los.do: Calculate a half-life, and use the constancy of first-order half-life to solve decay problems.
los.ek: First order t½ = 0.693/k, independent of [A]₀; radioactive decay is first order.

los.do: Write the rate law of an elementary step directly from its molecularity.
los.ek: Only for elementary steps do the exponents equal the coefficients: A + B → products ⇒ rate = k[A][B].

los.do: Explain and quantify how dividing a solid raises its surface area and its reaction rate.
los.ek: Cutting a cube into n³ smaller cubes multiplies the exposed area by n; a surface reaction speeds up in proportion.

los.do: Explain rate in terms of collision frequency, orientation and the fraction of collisions with energy above E_a.
los.ek: Raising T shifts the Maxwell–Boltzmann tail past E_a, so a small T rise greatly increases the effective collisions.

los.do: Label a reaction energy profile with the transition state, forward and reverse E_a, and ΔH.
los.ek: E_a,rev = E_a,fwd − ΔH; the transition state is the maximum, not an isolable species.

los.do: Find the activation energy from rate constants at two temperatures (Arrhenius).
los.ek: ln(k₂/k₁) = −(E_a/R)(1/T₂ − 1/T₁).
los.std: TRA-4.C, DAT-GC Chemical Kinetics (activation energy), acs-accm-general:VII.B.2, acs-accm-inorganic:VI.B.1

los.do: Predict a rate constant at a new temperature, or the factor a rate rises by, from E_a.
los.ek: k₂ = k₁ exp[−(E_a/R)(1/T₂ − 1/T₁)]; bigger E_a ⇒ more temperature-sensitive.

los.do: Check that a proposed mechanism sums to the overall equation, and identify intermediates and catalysts in it.
los.ek: Intermediates are made then used up; catalysts are used up then remade.

los.do: Derive the rate law predicted by a mechanism whose first step is slow, and test it against an observed rate law.
los.ek: The slow (rate-determining) step's rate law is the overall rate law when it contains no intermediates.

los.do: Derive a rate law when a fast reversible step precedes the slow step, eliminating the intermediate.
los.ek: Fast equilibrium: k₁[A][B] = k₋₁[I] ⇒ [I] = (k₁/k₋₁)[A][B]; substitute into the slow step's rate law.

los.do: Read a multistep energy profile: count steps, locate intermediates, and pick the rate-determining step.
los.ek: Each hump is a transition state, each valley between them an intermediate; the highest barrier controls the rate.

los.do: Explain how a catalyst (homogeneous, heterogeneous or enzyme) speeds a reaction, and what it leaves unchanged.
los.ek: It provides a new mechanism with lower E_a; ΔH, ΔG and K are unchanged, and forward and reverse rates rise together.

los.do: Classify a process as endothermic or exothermic from the temperature change of its surroundings, and give q its sign.
los.ek: Surroundings warm ⇒ the system released heat ⇒ exothermic, q < 0, ΔH < 0.

los.do: Draw and read an energy diagram that shows reactants and products relative to each other and ΔH.
los.ek: Products below reactants ⇒ exothermic; the vertical gap is ΔH.

los.do: Explain heat flow between objects at the particle level until thermal equilibrium.
los.ek: Collisions pass kinetic energy from hotter to colder particles until average KE (T) is equal.

los.do: Calculate heat, mass, specific heat or temperature change with q = mcΔT.
los.ek: Water's c = 4.18 J/(g·°C); ΔT in °C equals ΔT in K.

los.do: Find the final temperature when two bodies at different temperatures reach equilibrium.
los.ek: Isolated system: q_lost + q_gained = 0, so m₁c₁(T_f − T₁) + m₂c₂(T_f − T₂) = 0.

los.do: Calculate ΔH per mole of reaction from coffee-cup calorimetry data.
los.ek: q_rxn = −q_solution; ΔH = q_rxn / mol of limiting reactant.

los.do: Calculate the heat for a phase change at constant temperature.
los.ek: q = n·ΔH_fus or n·ΔH_vap; temperature stays constant while the phase changes; ΔH_vap ≫ ΔH_fus.

los.do: Calculate the total heat along a heating curve that crosses one or more phase changes.
los.ek: Sum the sloped segments (mcΔT, each phase's own c) and the flat segments (nΔH).

los.do: Scale a reaction's ΔH to a given amount of reactant or product, and change its sign for the reverse reaction.
los.ek: ΔH is per mole of reaction as written: heat = ΔH × (mol / coefficient).

los.do: Estimate ΔH of reaction from average bond enthalpies.
los.ek: ΔH ≈ Σ(bonds broken) − Σ(bonds formed); breaking costs energy, forming releases it.
los.std: ENE-3.A, acs-accm-general:II.D.1, acs-accm-general:VI.D.1, acs-accm-organic:V.B.1, acs-accm-organic:VI.D.1, acs-accm-organic:VI.G.1, acs-accm-inorganic:VI.D.2, acs-accm-inorganic:VI.G.1

los.do: Write the formation reaction of a compound from its elements in their standard states.
los.ek: One mole of product from elements in standard states (O₂(g), C(graphite), Br₂(l)); ΔH_f° of an element in its standard state is 0.

los.do: Calculate ΔH°_rxn from standard enthalpies of formation.
los.ek: ΔH°_rxn = Σ n ΔH_f°(products) − Σ n ΔH_f°(reactants).

los.do: Combine given reactions (reversing and scaling them) to find ΔH of a target reaction.
los.ek: Enthalpy is a state function: reverse ⇒ −ΔH, multiply by n ⇒ nΔH, add reactions ⇒ add ΔH.

topics.title: The first law, work and internal energy

los.do: Calculate ΔU from heat and work with correct sign conventions, including pressure–volume work.
los.ek: ΔU = q + w; w = −P_ext ΔV (work done on the system is positive); 1 L·atm = 101.3 J.
los.std: DAT-GC Thermodynamics and Thermochemistry (laws of thermodynamics), acs-accm-general:VI.A.2, acs-accm-general:VI.F.1

los.do: Convert between ΔH and ΔU for a reaction that changes the moles of gas.
los.ek: ΔH = ΔU + Δn_gas RT; equal only when Δn_gas = 0.
los.std: DAT-GC Thermodynamics and Thermochemistry (laws of thermodynamics), acs-accm-general:VI.A.4

los.do: Estimate a vapor pressure at a new temperature, or ΔH_vap from two points, with the Clausius–Clapeyron equation.
los.ek: ln(P₂/P₁) = −(ΔH_vap/R)(1/T₂ − 1/T₁).

los.do: Explain dynamic equilibrium and identify when it is reached on a concentration-vs-time graph.
los.ek: At equilibrium forward rate = reverse rate; concentrations stop changing but need not be equal.
los.std: TRA-6.A, acs-accm-general:VIII.A.1, acs-accm-general:VIII.B.1, acs-accm-organic:VIII.B.1, acs-accm-inorganic:VIII.B.1, acs-accm-analytical:VIII.B.1

los.do: Predict the direction of net change from the relative forward and reverse rates.
los.ek: Forward rate > reverse rate ⇒ net reaction to the right, until the rates equalize.

los.do: Write the K_c and K_p expressions for a reaction, including heterogeneous ones.
los.ek: Products over reactants, each raised to its coefficient; pure solids and liquids are left out.

los.do: Calculate Q from given concentrations or pressures and compare it with K to predict the direction of shift.
los.ek: Q < K ⇒ forward; Q > K ⇒ reverse; Q = K ⇒ at equilibrium.

los.do: Calculate K from equilibrium concentrations or partial pressures.
los.ek: Substitute equilibrium (not initial) values into the K expression.

los.do: Use an ICE table with initial amounts and one equilibrium amount to find K.
los.ek: Changes follow the coefficients: −ax, −bx, +cx; one known equilibrium value fixes x.

los.do: Convert between K_c and K_p.
los.ek: K_p = K_c(RT)^Δn with R = 0.08206 and Δn = moles gas products − reactants.

los.do: Find the fraction of a protein bound to its ligand from the dissociation constant.
los.ek: P + L ⇌ PL with K_d = [P][L]/[PL]; with ligand in excess, the fraction bound is [L]/(K_d + [L]): half bound when [L] = K_d.

los.do: Judge from the size of K whether reactants or products are favored at equilibrium.
los.ek: K ≫ 1 ⇒ products favored; K ≪ 1 ⇒ reactants favored.

los.do: Find K for a reversed, scaled or summed reaction.
los.ek: Reverse ⇒ 1/K; multiply by n ⇒ Kⁿ; add reactions ⇒ multiply their K's.

los.do: Find equilibrium concentrations from K and initial amounts with an ICE table and the small-x approximation, and check the approximation.
los.ek: If K is small, x ≪ initial: drop x where it is subtracted; valid if x is under 5% of the initial value.

los.do: Solve for equilibrium concentrations with the quadratic formula when the small-x approximation fails.
los.ek: Rearrange to ax² + bx + c = 0 and keep the physically meaningful root (no negative concentrations).

los.do: Draw or interpret a particle diagram of an equilibrium mixture consistent with a given K.
los.ek: Particle counts stand in for concentrations; plug them into the K expression to check.

los.do: Predict the shift caused by adding or removing a species, changing volume or pressure, changing temperature, adding an inert gas, or adding a catalyst.
los.ek: The system shifts to counteract the stress; smaller volume favors fewer gas moles; heat acts as a reactant (endothermic) or product (exothermic); inert gas at constant V and catalysts cause no shift.

topics.title: Reaction quotient and Le Châtelier's principle

los.do: Explain a Le Châtelier shift by how the stress changes Q relative to K, and identify temperature as the only stress that changes K.
los.ek: Concentration and pressure changes move Q away from an unchanged K; temperature changes K itself.

los.do: Write a K_sp expression and calculate K_sp from molar solubility.
los.ek: MₐXᵦ(s) ⇌ aM + bX: K_sp = (as)ᵃ(bs)ᵇ; for AB₂, K_sp = 4s³.

los.do: Calculate molar solubility in g/L or mol/L from K_sp, and compare solubilities of salts with different ion ratios.
los.ek: Compare K_sp directly only for salts with the same ion ratio; otherwise compare s.

los.do: Predict whether a precipitate forms on mixing solutions by comparing Q_sp with K_sp.
los.ek: Use concentrations after mixing (diluted); Q_sp > K_sp ⇒ precipitate forms.

los.do: Calculate the solubility of a salt in a solution that already contains one of its ions.
los.ek: Put the common ion's concentration into the ICE table; solubility falls (Le Châtelier).

los.do: Convert among pH, pOH, [H₃O⁺] and [OH⁻] at 25 °C.
los.ek: pH = −log[H₃O⁺]; K_w = [H₃O⁺][OH⁻] = 1.0 × 10⁻¹⁴; pH + pOH = 14.

topics.title: pH and pOH of strong acids and bases

los.do: Identify the strong acids and bases, and calculate the pH of their solutions.
los.ek: Strong acids: HCl, HBr, HI, HNO₃, H₂SO₄ (first H), HClO₄; strong bases: Group 1 and heavy Group 2 hydroxides; they ionize completely.

los.do: Calculate the pH and percent ionization of a weak acid from K_a and its concentration.
los.ek: [H₃O⁺] ≈ √(K_a·C) when ionization < 5%; % ionization = [H₃O⁺]/C × 100, and it rises on dilution.

los.do: Calculate the pH of a weak base solution from K_b.
los.ek: [OH⁻] ≈ √(K_b·C); then pOH → pH.

los.do: Find K_a or K_b from a measured pH and the initial concentration.
los.ek: [H₃O⁺] = 10^(−pH) is x in the ICE table; K_a = x²/(C − x).

los.do: Convert between K_a of an acid and K_b of its conjugate base.
los.ek: K_a·K_b = K_w; pK_a + pK_b = 14 at 25 °C; stronger acid ⇒ weaker conjugate base.

los.do: Calculate the pH after mixing a strong acid with a strong base.
los.ek: Neutralize mole for mole; the excess, divided by total volume, sets the pH.

los.do: Identify what remains after mixing a weak acid or base with a strong one, and classify the result as a buffer, a salt solution or excess strong reagent.
los.ek: React to completion first; weak acid + its conjugate base both present ⇒ buffer.

los.do: Predict whether a salt solution is acidic, basic or neutral and calculate its pH.
los.ek: Conjugate bases of weak acids raise pH; conjugates of weak bases (NH₄⁺) lower it; ions of strong acids and bases are neutral.

los.do: Calculate the pH at the start, before, at and past the equivalence point of a weak acid–strong base (or weak base–strong acid) titration.
los.ek: Start: weak acid; before: buffer; half-equivalence: pH = pK_a; equivalence: conjugate base only; after: excess strong base.

los.do: Read a titration curve to find the equivalence volume, pK_a and the analyte's strength, and choose a suitable indicator.
los.ek: Weak acid–strong base equivalence pH > 7; pick an indicator whose pK_a (color change) brackets the equivalence pH.

los.do: Interpret the titration curve of a polyprotic acid.
los.ek: One equivalence point per acidic proton (if K_a's differ enough); pK_a1 and pK_a2 at the half-equivalence points.

topics.title: Molecular structure of acids and bases

los.do: Rank acid strength from molecular structure: H–X bond strength and polarity, oxyacid O count, electronegativity of the central atom, and conjugate-base resonance.
los.ek: Down a group, weaker H–X bonds ⇒ stronger acid (HI > HF); more O's and higher EN stabilize the conjugate base ⇒ stronger oxyacid.

los.do: Identify Lewis acids and bases, including metal ions and electron-deficient molecules.
los.ek: Lewis acid accepts an electron pair (BF₃, Al³⁺); Lewis base donates one (NH₃, OH⁻).
los.std: SAP-9.F, DAT-GC Acids and Bases (strength), acs-accm-general:V.D.3, acs-accm-inorganic:II.B.2, acs-accm-inorganic:III.A.1, acs-accm-inorganic:V.D.1

los.do: Predict the predominant protonation form of an acid at a given pH from its pK_a.
los.ek: pH < pK_a ⇒ protonated form dominates; pH > pK_a ⇒ deprotonated; pH = pK_a ⇒ 1:1.

los.do: Explain how a buffer resists pH change, writing the net ionic reaction with an added strong acid or base.
los.ek: Added H₃O⁺ is consumed by A⁻; added OH⁻ is consumed by HA; the ratio [A⁻]/[HA] barely changes.

los.do: Calculate a buffer's pH with the Henderson–Hasselbalch equation.
los.ek: pH = pK_a + log([A⁻]/[HA]); mole ratio works as well as concentration ratio.

los.do: Calculate a buffer's new pH after adding a strong acid or base.
los.ek: Do the stoichiometry in moles first (HA ↔ A⁻), then apply Henderson–Hasselbalch.

los.do: Design a buffer: choose a conjugate pair and the base-to-acid ratio for a target pH.
los.ek: Pick pK_a within ±1 of the target pH; ratio = 10^(pH − pK_a).

los.do: Compare buffer capacities from component amounts and ratio.
los.ek: More moles of HA and A⁻ ⇒ more capacity; capacity against acid depends on A⁻, against base on HA; best at a 1:1 ratio.

los.do: Predict how pH changes the solubility of a salt whose anion is a weak base (or whose cation forms a hydroxide).
los.ek: Acid removes basic anions (F⁻, CO₃²⁻, OH⁻) and pulls the dissolution forward; salts of strong-acid anions (Cl⁻) are unaffected.

los.do: Predict the sign of ΔS for a process from changes in phase, moles of gas, mixing, dissolution and temperature.
los.ek: Energy and matter more dispersed ⇒ ΔS > 0: s → l → g, more gas moles, mixing, heating.

los.do: Calculate ΔS°_rxn from standard molar entropies.
los.ek: ΔS° = Σ n S°(products) − Σ n S°(reactants); S° of an element is not zero (third law: S = 0 only for a perfect crystal at 0 K).

topics.title: Gibbs free energy and thermodynamic favorability

los.do: Calculate ΔG° from ΔH° and ΔS°, or from standard free energies of formation.
los.ek: ΔG° = ΔH° − TΔS° (convert ΔS° to kJ); ΔG° = Σ n ΔG_f°(products) − Σ n ΔG_f°(reactants).

los.do: Decide from the signs of ΔH and ΔS at which temperatures a process is favorable, and find the crossover temperature.
los.ek: −ΔH, +ΔS always; +ΔH, −ΔS never; mixed signs switch at T = ΔH/ΔS.

los.do: Explain why a thermodynamically favorable process can be too slow to observe.
los.ek: ΔG < 0 says it can go; a large E_a can keep it from going at a measurable rate (diamond → graphite).

los.do: Calculate K from ΔG°.
los.ek: K = exp(−ΔG°/RT); ΔG° < 0 ⇔ K > 1.

los.do: Calculate ΔG° from K.
los.ek: ΔG° = −RT ln K, with R = 8.314 J/(mol·K).

los.do: Calculate ΔG under nonstandard conditions and predict the direction of reaction.
los.ek: ΔG = ΔG° + RT ln Q = RT ln(Q/K); ΔG < 0 ⇒ forward.

los.do: Explain whether a salt dissolves from the enthalpy (lattice vs hydration) and entropy changes of dissolution.
los.ek: ΔH_soln = lattice breaking (+) + hydration (−); ordering of water around small, highly charged ions can make ΔS_soln negative.

los.do: Calculate ΔG° for coupled reactions and explain how a favorable reaction drives an unfavorable one.
los.ek: Add the reactions and their ΔG°'s; a shared intermediate links them (ATP hydrolysis in biology); light or current can also supply the free energy.

los.do: Label a galvanic cell's anode and cathode, electron and ion flow, salt bridge, and write its cell notation.
los.ek: Oxidation at the anode, reduction at the cathode; electrons flow anode → cathode through the wire; anode ‖ cathode in notation.

los.do: Distinguish galvanic from electrolytic cells by the sign of ΔG and the electrode charges.
los.ek: Galvanic: spontaneous, anode (−); electrolytic: driven by an external source, anode (+); oxidation is always at the anode.

los.do: Calculate E°_cell from standard reduction potentials and predict whether a redox reaction is spontaneous.
los.ek: E°_cell = E°_cathode − E°_anode; don't multiply E° by coefficients; E° > 0 ⇒ spontaneous.

los.do: Convert among E°_cell, ΔG° and K.
los.ek: ΔG° = −nFE°; F = 96 485 C/mol e⁻; E° = (RT/nF) ln K.
los.std: ENE-6.B, acs-accm-general:VIII.F.2, acs-accm-inorganic:VI.E.1, acs-accm-inorganic:VIII.F.1, acs-accm-analytical:VIII.F.2, acs-accm-analytical:VIII.F.4

los.do: Predict qualitatively whether changing concentrations raises or lowers the cell potential, and why a battery dies.
los.ek: Q < 1 ⇒ E > E°; as the cell runs Q → K and E → 0.

los.do: Calculate a cell potential with the Nernst equation, including a concentration cell.
los.ek: E = E° − (RT/nF) ln Q = E° − (0.0592/n) log Q at 25 °C; a concentration cell has E° = 0.

los.do: Calculate the mass deposited, current or time in electrolysis with Faraday's law.
los.ek: charge = I·t; mol e⁻ = charge/F; half-reaction gives mol e⁻ per mol product.

los.do: Find ΔH° from K at two temperatures, or K at a new temperature, with the van 't Hoff equation.
los.ek: ln(K₂/K₁) = −(ΔH°/R)(1/T₂ − 1/T₁): endothermic ⇒ K rises with T.

los.do: Give the atomic number of any main-group element.
los.ek: Noble gases at 2, 10, 18, 36, 54, 86, 118 anchor each row.

los.do: Write the heavy p-block row from memory.
los.ek: Tl Pb Bi Po At Rn, 81 to 86.

los.do: Give the atomic number of any transition metal.
Give the group of any transition metal.
los.ek: Group number = s + d valence electrons.

los.do: Name the element below a given transition metal, and write a triad.
los.ek: Add 18, then 32; the lanthanoids sit between the 4d and 5d rows.

los.do: Write each d row from memory, in order.
los.ek: Sc Ti V Cr Mn Fe Co Ni Cu Zn; Y Zr Nb Mo Tc Ru Rh Pd Ag Cd; Hf Ta W Re Os Ir Pt Au Hg.

los.do: Give the d-electron count of a metal in a stated oxidation state.
los.ek: d count = group − oxidation state.

los.do: Give the atomic number of any lanthanoid or actinoid.
los.ek: La 57 to Lu 71; Ac 89 to Lr 103.

los.do: Write the lanthanoids and the actinoids from memory, in order.
los.ek: La Ce Pr Nd Pm Sm Eu Gd Tb Dy Ho Er Tm Yb Lu; Ac Th Pa U Np Pu Am Cm Bk Cf Es Fm Md No Lr.

los.do: Give the 4f count of a trivalent lanthanoid ion.
los.ek: Ln³⁺ is [Xe]4fⁿ with n = Z − 57.

los.do: Give the d and s electron counts of any 3d, 4d or 5d atom.
los.ek: Regular: ns² (n−1)dⁿ. Exceptions: Cr, Cu; Nb, Mo, Ru, Rh, Pd, Ag; Pt, Au.

los.do: Say whether an atom follows the filling order or is an exception.
los.ek: Ten exceptions in three rows; W is regular, Pd is 4d¹⁰ 5s⁰.

los.do: Write the full configuration of a transition-metal atom with its noble-gas core.
los.ek: The 5d metals carry 4f¹⁴ in the core.

los.do: Give the f-electron count of a lanthanoid or actinoid atom.
los.ek: Most are fⁿ s²; La, Ce, Gd, Lu and Ac to Np, Cm keep d electrons.

los.do: Write the full configuration of a lanthanoid or actinoid atom.
los.ek: Gd is 4f⁷ 5d¹ 6s²; Th is 6d² 7s² with no 5f electron.

topics.title: Scalars and vectors in one dimension

los.do: Classify a quantity as a scalar or a vector and state a vector's magnitude and direction.
los.ek: A vector has magnitude and direction (displacement, velocity, force); a scalar has magnitude only (distance, speed, mass, energy).

los.do: Add collinear vectors using a sign convention for direction.
los.ek: In 1-D, pick a positive direction; opposite vectors carry opposite signs and add algebraically.

los.do: Calculate displacement and distinguish it from distance travelled.
los.ek: Δx = x_f − x_i depends only on start and end points; distance is the total path length.

los.do: Calculate average velocity and average acceleration over a time interval.
los.ek: v_avg = Δx/Δt; a_avg = Δv/Δt; acceleration opposite to velocity means slowing down.

los.do: Read instantaneous velocity and acceleration from slopes, and displacement and Δv from areas, on motion graphs.
los.ek: Slope of x–t is v; slope of v–t is a; area under v–t is Δx; area under a–t is Δv.

los.do: Solve a constant-acceleration problem with the kinematic equations.
los.ek: v = v₀ + at; x = x₀ + v₀t + ½at²; v² = v₀² + 2aΔx; pick the one missing the unknown you don't need.

los.do: Analyze vertical free fall as motion with constant acceleration g downward.
los.ek: Near Earth's surface a = −9.8 m/s² (up positive) throughout the flight, including at the top where v = 0.

los.do: Translate between a narrative, a motion diagram and consistent x–t, v–t and a–t sketches.
los.ek: The three graphs must agree: where v–t crosses zero, x–t has a turning point; constant a gives a straight v–t and a parabolic x–t.

los.do: Calculate an object's velocity as measured by observers in different inertial frames moving along one line.
los.ek: v_A rel C = v_A rel B + v_B rel C; all inertial observers measure the same acceleration.

topics.title: Vectors and motion in two dimensions

los.do: Resolve a vector into perpendicular components and rebuild a vector from its components.
los.ek: A_x = A cos θ, A_y = A sin θ (θ from +x); |A| = √(A_x² + A_y²), θ = tan⁻¹(A_y/A_x) with quadrant check.

los.do: Analyze a horizontally launched projectile by treating horizontal and vertical motion independently.
los.ek: Ignoring air: a_x = 0, a_y = −g; the two directions share only the time.

los.do: Calculate time of flight, maximum height and range of a projectile launched at an angle.
los.ek: v_y = 0 at the top; on level ground R = v₀² sin 2θ / g, maximal at 45°.

los.do: Add relative velocities in two dimensions (boat crossing a river, plane in a crosswind).
los.ek: Relative velocities add as vectors; add components, then find magnitude and heading.

los.do: Choose a system and sort the forces on it into internal and external.
los.ek: Internal forces cancel in pairs; only external forces change the motion of the system's center of mass.

los.do: Calculate the center of mass of a system of point masses.
los.ek: x_cm = Σm_i x_i / Σm_i (each axis separately); it lies closer to the heavier parts.

los.do: Identify each force on an object as an interaction with a named other object, contact or at a distance.
los.ek: Every force has an agent; no agent, no force ("force of motion" is not a force).

los.do: Draw a free-body diagram with every force on the object, from its point of action, in the correct direction.
los.ek: Normal force is perpendicular to the surface, tension along the string away from the object, gravity toward Earth's center.

los.do: Identify third-law force pairs and distinguish them from balanced forces on one object.
los.ek: A third-law pair is equal and opposite, acts on two different objects and is the same type of force.

los.do: Find an unknown force (tension, normal, applied) on an object in translational equilibrium.
los.ek: Constant velocity (including rest) ⇔ ΣF = 0; write ΣF_x = 0 and ΣF_y = 0 separately.

los.do: Apply ΣF = ma to one object to find its acceleration or an unknown force.
los.ek: a = ΣF/m points along the net force; the kinematics then follows from Unit 1.

los.do: Find the acceleration and string tension of connected objects (Atwood machine, blocks joined by a string).
los.ek: Treat the whole as one system for a, then isolate one object for the tension; an ideal string has one tension and one |a|.

los.do: Analyze an object on an incline by resolving gravity along and perpendicular to the surface.
los.ek: Along the incline mg sin θ, into it mg cos θ; on a frictionless incline a = g sin θ.

los.do: Find apparent weight in an accelerating frame and tell inertial from gravitational mass.
los.ek: A scale reads the normal force: N = m(g + a) with a positive upward; in free fall N = 0 (weightless) though gravity still acts; inertial and gravitational mass are equal to high precision.

los.do: Decide when g is constant and find g above a planet or inside a uniform sphere.
los.ek: Outside: g = GM/r², nearly constant when the height is small next to the radius; inside a uniform sphere g = GMr/R³, growing linearly from zero at the centre.

los.do: Calculate the gravitational force between two masses with Newton's law of gravitation.
los.ek: F = Gm₁m₂/r², r center to center; doubling r quarters F.

los.do: Calculate the gravitational field strength g at a planet's surface or at altitude.
los.ek: g = GM/r²; weight mg is the gravitational force, and g is also the free-fall acceleration.

los.do: Calculate kinetic friction on a sliding object and the acceleration it produces.
los.ek: f_k = μ_k N, opposite to the relative sliding velocity; N is found from the perpendicular force balance, not assumed to be mg.

los.do: Decide whether static friction can hold an object and find the friction force actually acting.
los.ek: f_s ≤ μ_s N: static friction is whatever the balance needs, up to the maximum; slipping starts when the need exceeds μ_s N.

los.do: Combine springs in series and in parallel.
los.ek: Parallel: k = k₁ + k₂ (same stretch); series: 1/k = 1/k₁ + 1/k₂ (same force).

los.do: Apply Hooke's law to find a spring force, stretch or spring constant, including k from a force–extension graph.
los.ek: F_s = −kΔx, restoring toward equilibrium; k is the slope of F vs Δx.

los.do: Calculate centripetal acceleration and identify which real force supplies the net inward force.
los.ek: a_c = v²/r toward the center; centripetal is a role (tension, friction, gravity, normal), never an extra force on the FBD.

los.do: Apply ΣF_r = mv²/r to a car on a flat curve, a vertical loop or a conical pendulum.
los.ek: Flat curve: μ_s mg ≥ mv²/r; top of a loop: N + mg = mv²/r, minimum speed √(gr).

los.do: Derive the speed and period of a circular orbit from gravity as the centripetal force.
los.ek: GMm/r² = mv²/r ⇒ v = √(GM/r), T² = 4π²r³/(GM); orbital speed is independent of the satellite's mass.

los.do: Calculate translational kinetic energy and predict how it scales with speed and mass.
los.ek: K = ½mv² is a scalar, never negative; doubling v quadruples K.

los.do: Calculate the work done by a constant force over a straight displacement.
los.ek: W = Fd cos θ; a force perpendicular to the motion (normal, centripetal) does no work; friction on a sliding object does negative work.

los.do: Find work as the area under a force–position graph, including the work to stretch a spring.
los.ek: W = area under F–x; for a spring from 0 to x, W = ½kx².

los.do: Apply the work–energy theorem to find a speed or a force.
los.ek: W_net = ΔK; the net work is the sum of the work done by each force.

los.do: Calculate gravitational potential energy near Earth and elastic potential energy of a spring for a system.
los.ek: U_g = mgh (reference level is a choice; only ΔU matters); U_s = ½kx²; potential energy belongs to a system of interacting objects.

los.do: Calculate the gravitational potential energy of two widely separated masses.
los.ek: U_G = −Gm₁m₂/r with U = 0 at infinite separation; it rises toward zero as r grows.

los.do: Apply conservation of mechanical energy to find a speed, height or spring compression.
los.ek: With only conservative forces doing work inside the system, K_i + U_i = K_f + U_f.

los.do: Account for friction and external work in an energy balance.
los.ek: ΔK + ΔU + ΔE_th = W_ext; sliding friction converts f_k d into thermal energy.

los.do: Calculate the escape speed from a planet's surface.
los.ek: ½mv_esc² − GMm/R = 0 ⇒ v_esc = √(2GM/R), √2 times the circular orbital speed at the same r.

los.do: Calculate average power and the instantaneous power delivered by a force.
los.ek: P_avg = W/Δt = ΔE/Δt; P = Fv cos θ; 1 W = 1 J/s.

los.do: Calculate the momentum of an object and of a system, and relate system momentum to the center-of-mass velocity.
los.ek: p = mv is a vector; p_sys = Σm_i v_i = M v_cm.

los.do: Calculate impulse as average force times time or as the area under F–t, and equate it to the change in momentum.
los.ek: J = F_avg Δt = Δp; the same Δp over a longer time needs a smaller force (airbags, bent knees).

los.do: Apply conservation of momentum in one dimension, including explosions and recoil.
los.ek: If the net external impulse on the system is zero, p_sys before = p_sys after; an explosion from rest gives m₁v₁ = −m₂v₂.

los.do: Apply conservation of momentum in two dimensions by components.
los.ek: Momentum is conserved separately along x and along y.

los.do: Classify a collision as elastic or inelastic by comparing kinetic energy before and after.
los.ek: Momentum is conserved in every isolated collision; kinetic energy only in elastic ones.

los.do: Find the final velocity and the kinetic energy lost in a perfectly inelastic collision.
los.ek: Objects stick: v_f = (m₁v₁ + m₂v₂)/(m₁ + m₂); the lost K becomes thermal energy and deformation.

los.do: Find both final velocities in a one-dimensional elastic collision.
los.ek: Conserve p and K; equivalently the relative speed reverses: v₁ − v₂ = −(v₁′ − v₂′).

los.do: Solve a two-stage problem (ballistic pendulum) with momentum for the collision and energy afterward.
los.ek: Energy is not conserved through the inelastic collision, momentum is not conserved during the swing; use each only where it holds.

los.do: Solve constant-angular-acceleration problems with the rotational kinematic equations.
los.ek: ω = ω₀ + αt; θ = ω₀t + ½αt²; ω² = ω₀² + 2αΔθ — the linear equations with θ, ω, α.

los.do: Convert between angular and linear quantities for a point on a rotating object.
los.ek: s = rθ, v = rω, a_t = rα (θ in radians); every point shares ω, speed grows with r.

los.do: Calculate the torque of a force about an axis and its sense of rotation.
los.ek: τ = rF sin θ = r⊥F (lever arm); counterclockwise positive by convention.

los.do: Calculate the rotational inertia of point masses and combine given inertias of rigid shapes.
los.ek: I = Σm_i r_i²; inertias about the same axis add; mass far from the axis costs the most.

los.do: Shift a rotational inertia to a parallel axis.
los.ek: I = I_cm + Md²; I is smallest about an axis through the center of mass.

los.do: Find unknown forces on a beam, ladder or sign in static equilibrium.
los.ek: ΣF = 0 and Στ = 0 about any axis; choose the axis through an unknown force to drop it.

topics.title: Newton's second law in rotational form

los.do: Apply Στ = Iα to find the angular acceleration of a rigid object.
los.ek: α = Στ/I about a fixed axis or the center of mass.

los.do: Solve a massive-pulley problem by coupling the translational and rotational equations.
los.ek: Each hanging mass: ΣF = ma; pulley: (T₁ − T₂)R = Iα; no-slip: a = Rα. Tensions differ when the pulley has mass.

units.title: Energy and momentum of rotating systems

los.do: Calculate the rotational kinetic energy of a rigid object.
los.ek: K_rot = ½Iω².

los.do: Calculate the work done by a torque and apply the rotational work–energy theorem.
los.ek: W = τΔθ for constant τ; W_net = ΔK_rot.

los.do: Calculate the angular momentum of a rigid object and of a point mass moving past an axis.
los.ek: L = Iω for a rigid object; L = mvr⊥ for a point mass (r⊥ = perpendicular distance from the axis to the line of motion).

los.do: Relate angular impulse to the change in angular momentum.
los.ek: τ_avg Δt = ΔL; area under τ–t is ΔL.

los.do: Apply conservation of angular momentum to a spinning skater, a merry-go-round or a mass striking a rod.
los.ek: Zero net external torque ⇒ I_iω_i = I_fω_f; K_rot can change (it rises when I drops).

los.do: Find the speed of an object rolling without slipping down an incline, and rank shapes by speed.
los.ek: v = Rω; K = ½Mv² + ½Iω²; with I = βMR², v = √(2gh/(1 + β)) — smaller β wins.

los.do: Compare a satellite's speed at different points of an elliptical orbit using angular momentum and energy.
los.ek: Gravity exerts no torque about the planet: mv_1r_1 = mv_2r_2 at perigee and apogee; total K + U_G is constant.

los.do: Calculate the kinetic, potential and total energy of a circular orbit.
los.ek: K = GMm/2r, U = −GMm/r, E = −GMm/2r; a lower orbit is faster but has less total energy.

los.do: Identify simple harmonic motion from a restoring force proportional to displacement and locate the equilibrium position.
