los.ek: U = (1 − λ)U₀ + λU₁ ⇒ ∂U/∂λ = U₁ − U₀; for appearing atoms ⟨∂U/∂λ⟩ diverges as λ → 0 under linear LJ scaling.

los.do: Explain how BAR combines forward and reverse ΔU samples and why it beats one-sided exponential averaging.
los.ek: BAR solves a self-consistent equation for ΔA using both directions; it is the minimum-variance two-state estimator and much less biased than Zwanzig.

los.do: Explain MBAR as reweighting all samples to all states, and relate it to BAR and WHAM.
los.ek: MBAR solves for every state's free energy simultaneously from all samples; with two states it reduces to BAR; binned, it is WHAM (used in ALF flattening).

los.do: Read an MBAR overlap matrix and decide where to add λ states — choice rep.
los.ek: Each state should share substantial overlap with its neighbours (off-diagonal elements not near zero); a weak link between two neighbours is where to insert a state. 20–40 states are typical.

los.do: Design an alchemical λ schedule for inserting or deleting atoms: order of electrostatic and LJ changes, soft-core, and number of states.
los.ek: Remove charges while LJ cores are on, then transform LJ with soft-core, then restore charges on inserted atoms; never change both at once on linear paths when sites appear or vanish.

los.do: Explain the endpoint catastrophe and how soft-core potentials remove it.
los.ek: As an atom's LJ is scaled to zero, other atoms can overlap it and r⁻¹² diverges; soft-core remaps short distances so the energy stays finite (in MSλD, distances inside a λ-dependent cutoff, r₀ = 2 Å).

los.do: Distinguish single, dual and multiple topology and decoupling vs annihilation, and identify the topology MSλD uses — choice rep.
los.ek: MSλD uses a shared core plus one complete substituent group per alternative; substituents at the same site never interact with each other; decoupling turns off only intermolecular terms.

los.do: Close a thermodynamic cycle to compute a relative binding ΔΔG from alchemical legs in complex and solvent — numeric rep.
los.ek: ΔΔG_bind = ΔG_bind(B) − ΔG_bind(A) = ΔG_complex(A→B) − ΔG_solvent(A→B); the physical binding legs are never simulated.

los.do: Compute a mutational folding ΔΔG from alchemical legs in the folded protein and an unfolded-state peptide model, and state its sign convention — numeric rep.
los.ek: ΔΔG_fold = ΔG_alch(folded) − ΔG_alch(unfolded); positive = destabilizing. The capped pentapeptide (mutating residue ± 2) models a locally solvated unfolded state and ignores nonlocal contacts.

los.do: Compute cycle-closure errors in a perturbation network and use them to flag unreliable edges — numeric rep.
los.ek: ΔG summed around any closed loop should be 0; nonzero closure measures error. Star maps are cheap; redundant, connected maps allow error analysis.

los.do: Lay out the double-decoupling cycle with restraints and identify every term in ΔG°_bind, including the standard-state correction.
los.ek: Decouple the ligand in solvent and in the restrained site; add the restraint free energy (analytic for Boresch's six-DOF restraints) and the standard-state term; remove charges before LJ.

los.do: Calculate the standard-state correction for confining a ligand to a given restraint volume — numeric rep.
los.ek: ΔG = −k_BT ln(V_site/V°), V° = 1661 Å³ per molecule at 1 M.

los.do: Choose a relative or absolute calculation for a described project — choice rep.
los.ek: Relative: congeneric series with a shared core and a reliable bound pose. Absolute: no common substructure, uncertain site, or comparing sites or poses.

los.do: Convert between K_d and ΔG° and between fold-changes and ΔΔG, and judge a prediction against expected accuracy — numeric rep.
los.ek: ΔG° = RT ln(K_d/1 M); a 10× change in K_d is 1.36 kcal/mol at 298 K; ~1–2 kcal/mol RMS error is typical in favourable cases.

los.do: Match simulation conditions (pH, salt, temperature, construct, protonation) to the experiment being reproduced.
los.ek: The T4 lysozyme sites were measured at pH 3.0 (L99, M106, F153) and 5.4 (V149), so two folded-state setups are needed.

units.title: Free-energy practice: protocol, convergence and reporting

los.do: Apply the pathway rules: soft-core for Lennard-Jones, never charges without LJ, fewest insertions, and electrostatics off before LJ.
los.ek: Use soft-core when LJ is removed (α = 0.5 unless there is a reason not to); remove charges before LJ or soften Coulomb faster; prefer mutating atoms to inserting them.

los.do: Make the relative-calculation choices: topology, atom mapping, constraints on transformed bonds and perturbation size.
los.ek: Single, dual or hybrid topology; keep transformations to about 1–5 heavy atoms; don't constrain bonds to transforming atoms (use about a 1 fs step); ring breaking is hard.

los.do: Make the absolute-calculation choices: restraint type, the standard state, weak binders and net charge changes.
los.ek: Harmonic, flat-bottom (does not restrain rotation) or Boresch (all six rigid-body degrees of freedom); correct to 1 M; net charge changes need co-alchemical ions or corrections.

los.do: Choose a sampling scheme and equilibrate correctly at every λ.
los.ek: Independent fixed-λ runs, Hamiltonian replica exchange (recommended), single-replica λ moves, or nonequilibrium switching; equilibrate each λ separately and for equal lengths.

los.do: Choose and cross-check estimators and read the diagnostics: overlap, forward–reverse drift and estimator disagreement.
los.ek: Prefer TI, BAR or MBAR; EXP is biased; first off-diagonal overlap at least 0.03; estimators disagreeing by more than 1 kcal/mol, or forward–reverse by more than 1 kT, means not converged.

los.do: Detect equilibration and decorrelate data: count effectively uncorrelated samples per state.
los.ek: Discard the early part; N_eff = (T − t₀)/g; aim for at least about 50 per state; if T is not about 20 times t₀, the run is short.

los.do: Plan what to save: the energies each estimator needs and how often to write them.
los.ek: TI needs dU/dλ, EXP one-direction ΔU, BAR both neighbours, MBAR every state; write roughly every 50–100 steps; set the target uncertainty before running.

los.do: Compute an uncertainty from independent repeats and combine the uncertainties of independent legs.
los.ek: The gold standard is independent copies and their standard error; an estimator's own error assumes uncorrelated data and usually underestimates; independent legs add in quadrature.

los.do: Diagnose common failures from their symptoms.
los.ek: Ligand leaving the site, inconsistent estimators, poor replica mixing, slow torsions, rough ΔG(λ), drift, and starting-pose dependence; wrong binding modes are common.

los.do: Verify a result: alternate cycles, cycle closure, repeat spread against the error bar, and the checklist's red flags.
los.ek: Results from different cycles should agree; repeats should differ by about what their error bars allow; standard error above 1 kcal/mol or |ΔΔG| above about 15 kcal/mol is suspect.

los.do: Report a benchmark the way the field expects: replicates, MUE and RMSE, correlation and ranking statistics, and honest plots.
los.ek: At least three replicates; RMSE and MUE for relative results (correlation depends on sign convention); bootstrap statistics; equal axes with 1 and 2 kcal/mol bands.

units.title: λ dynamics and multisite λ dynamics

los.do: Write the λ-dynamics extended Hamiltonian and explain how treating λ as a particle samples several alchemical states in one simulation.
los.ek: H = K(x) + ½ m_λ λ̇² + U(x, λ); λ moves under −∂U/∂λ with a fictitious mass, so its population over time reflects relative free energies.

los.do: Write the MSλD potential for several sites and substituents and identify which terms scale with λ.
los.ek: U = U₀ + Σ_s Σ_i λ_si U_si + Σ λ_si λ_tj U_si,tj (s ≠ t); Σ_i λ_si = 1 and λ_si ≥ 0 at each site; the environment U₀ is unscaled; substituents at one site don't see each other.

los.do: Calculate the number of λ variables and chemical end states for a multisite system from its nsubs list — numeric rep.
los.ek: nsubs counts native + each mutant per site (V149 with 5 mutants ⇒ 6); nblocks = Σ nsubs; end states = Π nsubs (15 sites × 2 ⇒ 32 768).

los.do: Compute λ values from θ coordinates with the fnex implicit constraint and verify they sum to one — numeric rep.
los.ek: λ_i = exp(c sin θ_i) / Σ_j exp(c sin θ_j), c = 5.5 (fnex); θ is unbounded, λ stays in (0, 1) and sums to 1 automatically.

los.do: Calculate the λ bounds an fnex constraint can reach for a given number of substituents and explain the endpoint error it causes — numeric rep.
los.ek: Bounds = [1 + (N − 1)e^{±2c}]⁻¹, so exact endpoints are never sampled (≈ 0.1–0.2 kcal/mol error) and sampling weakens past 8–9 substituents; piecewise constraints (fnpwise2026) reach the exact endpoints.

los.do: Identify the role of each ALF bias term — fixed φ (b), quadratic ψ (c), endpoint χ (x) and ω (s), and the newer t and u terms — on the alchemical landscape.
los.ek: φ offsets each substituent's free energy (≈ −ΔG) so all endpoints are equally populated; ψ_ij/4 changes the barrier between substituents; χ/ω shape the region near endpoints; bcxstu2026 adds t and u terms for many substituents.

los.do: Calculate the number of pairwise bias potentials a block setup must allocate for a given nblocks and bias scheme — numeric rep.
los.ek: Pairs = nblocks(nblocks − 1)/2; bcxs2018 uses 5 potentials per pair, bcxstu2026 uses 9 (ldbi count).

los.do: Calculate the free-energy difference between two substituents from their end-state populations (λ > 0.99) and fixed biases — numeric rep.
los.ek: ΔG_i→j = −k_BT ln(P_j/P_i) − (φ_j − φ_i), with P counted only where λ > λ_c (0.99 in production; 0.8 in older work).

los.do: Interpret nan or very noisy entries in Result.txt as unsampled substituents and decide whether to refine biases before extending production.
los.ek: A histogram estimator needs every end state visited; unvisited substituents mean biases are not yet converged — run another production of the same length first.

los.do: Describe one ALF cycle — run MD, reweight recent runs, compute 1-D and 2-D free-energy profiles, fit bias changes, write the next variables file — and why changes are capped.
los.ek: WHAM/MBAR combine several recent runs at different biases; a linear model of profile response feeds a quadratic penalty on deviations from flat. Only the bottom few kcal/mol of a basin is sampled, so updates are limited to a few kcal/mol.

los.do: Judge from PlotFreeEnergy5 profiles whether flattening has converged enough to start production.
los.ek: Sampling should extend across every profile with no large unsampled gaps; perfect flatness isn't required, thermodynamic accessibility is.

los.do: Plan the flattening schedule and convert it to step counts at a given timestep — numeric rep.
los.ek: initialize; ~100 runflat cycles of 100 ps (200 for arginine), equilibration = ¼ of each run (25 ps + 75 ps, so the sampling-steps argument is 3× the equilibration one); then ~10 cycles of 1 ns. At 2 fs, 25 ps = 12 500 steps.

los.do: Plan a production ramp of independent trials extended by factors of 4–5 to a target length, and total its simulation time — numeric rep.
los.ek: 5 trials (a–e) each round, e.g. 5 → 20 → 100 ns. Typical totals: solvation 10–20 ns; well-behaved protein point mutations 40 ns; hard or multiple mutations 100 ns; massive spaces 400 ns.

los.do: Write alf_info.py for a system: name, nsubs, nblocks, temp, enginepath, nreps, and optional q, loss, bias and impcons keys.
los.ek: name must match prep/name.inp; nblocks = Σ nsubs; nreps = 1 without replica exchange; q lists each substituent's net charge.

los.do: Choose loss function, bias scheme and implicit constraint for a described system — choice rep.
los.ek: Defaults linear2018 / bcxs2018 / fnex2011 are no longer best practice: use nonlinear2024 loss and fnpwise2026; bcxs2018 for ~2 substituents, bcxstu2026 for ~20 (with matching blocksetup.inp edits).

los.do: Compute ΔΔG_fold with its uncertainty from Result.txt values in the folded and unfolded ensembles — numeric rep.
los.ek: ΔΔG = dG(folded) − dG(unfolded) per mutant relative to native; combine the two legs' errors in quadrature.

topics.title: Building the alchemical system in CHARMM

los.do: Edit alchemical_definitions.inp for a mutation set: site resids, substituent sequence codes, segids and terminal variables.
los.ek: s1seq1 = 0 is the native residue; further entries are one-letter codes (h/b/j = HSD/HSE/HSP); nterres/cterres = first and last resid of the chain (1–162 folded, site ± 2 unfolded).

los.do: Assemble a prep directory — system.inp adapted from step5_production.inp, toppar soft link, aa_stream patch/select/delete/blocksetup streams, nbond.str, alf_info.py — and test it with RunSetup.
los.ek: DIMENS must be in the first script CHARMM reads, so it is removed from system.inp; patchloop adds alchemical atoms, selectloop names them, deleteloop removes spurious angles/dihedrals, blocksetup applies λ scaling and biases.

los.do: Compute the RMSD between two small coordinate sets after optimal superposition, and use RMSD vs time to judge stability before free-energy runs — numeric rep.
los.ek: RMSD = √[(1/N) Σ |r_i − r_i^ref|²] after Kabsch alignment on a chosen atom set (Cα or backbone); a plateau, not a small number, is the stability signal.

los.do: Compute per-residue RMSF and convert it to a crystallographic B-factor for comparison with experiment — numeric rep.
los.ek: RMSF_i = √⟨|r_i − ⟨r_i⟩|²⟩ after alignment; B = (8π²/3) RMSF².

los.do: Classify a contact as a hydrogen bond from donor–acceptor distance and angle under a stated criterion — choice rep.
los.ek: Common criterion: D···A ≤ 3.5 Å and D–H···A angle ≥ 120–150°; report occupancy as fraction of frames, and state the criterion used.

los.do: Cluster conformations by RMSD and report cluster populations and representative structures.
los.ek: Cutoff-based or hierarchical clustering on pairwise RMSD; combined clustering of independent runs tests whether they sample the same states.

los.do: Compute a potential of mean force from a histogram of a coordinate — numeric rep.
los.ek: W(ξ) = −k_BT ln P(ξ) + const; bins with no counts carry no information.

los.do: Load a trajectory correctly (PSF before DCD in VMD) and re-centre or unwrap periodic coordinates before measuring.
los.ek: A DCD holds only coordinates; the PSF supplies atom identities. Molecules split across box faces corrupt RMSD and distances until imaged.

los.do: Write a SLURM script for a GPU CHARMM job with partition, account, time limit, GPU request and memory, and submit or debug it without using the login node.
los.ek: -p free-gpu or gpu; -A rhayes1_lab_gpu on paid partitions only; --time in minutes; --gres=gpu:1 (a GPU partition alone gives no GPU); --mem only after an OOM; srun --pty for interactive debugging; --array=1-4%1 runs chained segments one at a time.

los.do: Estimate GPU-hours and cost for a simulation campaign from throughput in ns/day, and choose free vs paid partitions — numeric rep.
los.ek: GPU-h = 24 × total ns / (ns/day); paid gpu is $0.32 per GPU-hour; free-gpu costs nothing but jobs are preempted (ALF tolerates restarts).

los.do: Choose an engine — CHARMM standard, DOMDEC, BLaDE, OpenMM — for a described job — choice rep.
los.ek: Standard CHARMM is CPU and slow; DOMDEC GPU is ~5× slower than BLaDE; BLaDE runs MSλD 5–8× faster than DOMDEC; OpenMM is fast for plain MD but does not run λ dynamics within CHARMM.

los.do: Write BLaDE NVT and NPT dynamics commands and state BLaDE's restrictions.
los.ek: Add 'blade' to ENER/MINI/DYNA; NPT adds 'prmc iprs 100 pref 1 prdv 100'; set friction with 'scalar fbeta set 0.1 sele all end'. Langevin or NVE only, MC barostat only, H-bond constraints only, one GPU per OpenMP thread, no MPI.

los.do: Run an equivalent plain-MD simulation through OpenMM's Python API from CHARMM files.
los.ek: Load PSF + parameter set, build the System with PME and H-bond constraints, LangevinMiddleIntegrator at T, MonteCarloBarostat at 1 bar; CHARMM-GUI can emit OpenMM inputs directly.

los.do: Read and write CHARMM scripts using titles, set/calc, @ and @@ variables, ? system values, stream, if/goto loops, bomlev and stop, and find the right documentation section.
los.ek: Titles start with * and end at a lone *; ! starts comments; CHARMM is case-insensitive but file paths aren't (quote them). Key docs: BLOCK, CONSTRAINTS (SHAKE, restraints), Ewald, nonbonded, CRYSTAL and IMAGE.

los.do: Record everything needed to reproduce a run: force-field and engine versions, protonation states, box and ions, seeds, all scripts under version control, and unprocessed data.
los.ek: A result without its inputs and analysis scripts can't be checked; document the full uncertainty procedure too.

los.do: Estimate trajectory storage from atom count, save interval and simulation length — numeric rep.
los.ek: DCD stores single-precision x, y, z: 12 bytes per atom per frame; frames = steps / nsavc.

los.do: Clean up a finished ALF project, separating disposable intermediates from data that must be kept.
los.ek: run*/output, analysis*/data, Energy, Lambda and slurm logs are disposable; keep alchemical trajectories (run*/res) of published work; spatial DCDs may go after publication.

los.do: Decide whether intersite coupling biases are needed and set ntersite for flattening and postprocessing.
los.ek: Default [0,0] ignores coupling; with significant coupling use [0,1] in short runflat cycles and [2,1] in postprocess (adjusting only c intersite biases).

los.do: Choose between the histogram estimator and the Potts-model estimator (likelihood vs pseudolikelihood) for a given chemical-space size — choice rep.
los.ek: Histograms need every end state visited (~100–500 states max); Potts keeps one- and two-site terms only; LM below ~10⁶ end states, PLM above.

los.do: Partition a mutation set across sites and systems to respect substituent-per-site limits — choice rep.
los.ek: The ALF README advises ≤ 6 substituents per site (9 the tested ceiling); split larger sets across systems sharing a reference substituent. Newer constraints and biases (2024–2026) extend this to dozens.

los.do: Correct a charge-changing perturbation: explain its PME finite-size errors and apply ALF's discrete solvent correction with the q key.
los.ek: Net-charge changes in a neutral PME box introduce artifacts; the discrete solvent correction is the largest computable term; alternatives include co-alchemical ions.

los.do: Explain when a site needs replica exchange (e.g. A42, A98, M102 in T4 lysozyme) and how biasing-potential replica exchange helps.
los.ek: Some sites have slow coupled conformational and alchemical barriers; replicas with offset biases exchange to cross them. Replica runs need nreps > 1 and working MPI on the cluster.

los.do: Explain why proline and glycine mutations need a dedicated alchemical strategy.
los.ek: Proline bonds its side chain back to the backbone N and glycine lacks Cβ, so backbone terms (CMAP, ring closure) differ between substituents; Hayes & Brooks 2021 give the workaround.

los.do: Count basis functions for a molecule in a named Pople basis.
los.ek: 6-31G(d): 1 function per H, 15 per first-row atom (9 + 6 Cartesian d).

los.do: Scale the cost of a method with system size from its formal power law.
los.ek: HF ~N⁴, MP2 ~N⁵, CCSD(T) ~N⁷: doubling N costs 2^p.

los.do: Convert between hartree, kcal/mol, kJ/mol and cm⁻¹, and compute a vibrational zero-point energy.
los.ek: 1 hartree = 627.51 kcal/mol; ZPE = ½hcν̃ per mode.

los.do: Place a density functional on Jacob's ladder and pick the first fix for a known failure such as missing dispersion.
los.ek: LDA → GGA → meta-GGA → hybrid → double hybrid; add a dispersion correction (D3) for stacking.

los.do: Read a method and basis label and say what each part fixes.
los.ek: A label such as CCSD(T)/cc-pVTZ names the correlation treatment and the basis separately; neither alone defines the calculation, and the geometry it was run at is a third choice.

los.do: Count electrons, occupied and virtual orbitals, and determinants for a closed-shell molecule in a given basis.
los.ek: A closed-shell molecule with N electrons fills N/2 spatial orbitals; a basis of K functions gives K spatial orbitals, so K - N/2 are virtual. Excitation counts come from choosing occupied and virtual pairs.

los.do: Distinguish restricted, unrestricted and restricted open-shell references and say when each is used.
los.ek: RHF pairs spatial orbitals for closed shells; UHF lets alpha and beta differ, which allows spin contamination; ROHF keeps a pure spin state at the cost of flexibility.

los.do: Compute the expected value of S squared for a given multiplicity and judge spin contamination from a reported value.
los.ek: For a pure state, S squared equals S(S+1) with S = (multiplicity - 1)/2: 0 for a singlet, 0.75 for a doublet, 2 for a triplet. A UHF value well above that is contaminated.

los.do: Put the steps of an SCF cycle in order and say what makes it self-consistent.
los.ek: Build the core Hamiltonian and overlap, guess a density, build the Fock matrix from it, solve the generalised eigenvalue problem, form a new density, repeat until the density and energy stop changing.

los.do: Compute the Hartree-Fock energy from its one- and two-electron pieces and the nuclear repulsion.
los.ek: The electronic energy is a trace over the density with the core and Fock matrices; the total adds the nuclear repulsion, which is a pure geometry term.

los.do: Define correlation energy and say which correlation Hartree-Fock already includes.
los.ek: Correlation energy is the exact non-relativistic energy minus the Hartree-Fock energy, always negative. Hartree-Fock includes exchange, and so same-spin (Fermi) correlation, but no opposite-spin (Coulomb) correlation.

los.do: Compute a correlation energy or a percentage recovered from reported total energies.
los.ek: E_corr = E_method - E_HF; the fraction recovered compares a method's correlation energy with a reference such as a complete-basis coupled-cluster value.

los.do: Diagnose an SCF that will not converge and name the usual remedies.
los.ek: Oscillation points at near-degenerate orbitals or a poor guess: DIIS acceleration, level shifting, damping, a better initial guess, or converging a simpler basis or method first.

los.do: Count the two-electron integrals a basis implies and say why screening and density fitting matter.
los.ek: There are about K^4/8 unique two-electron integrals for K basis functions once permutational symmetry is used; screening discards negligible ones and density fitting replaces the four-index set with a smaller three-index one.

los.do: Read a basis-set name and say what it adds: split valence, polarisation, diffuse functions, and the correlation-consistent series.
los.ek: A split-valence set gives valence orbitals more than one function; polarisation functions add higher angular momentum for bonding flexibility; diffuse functions matter for anions and weak interactions; cc-pVXZ is a series designed to converge smoothly.

los.do: Count basis functions for a molecule in a stated basis.
los.ek: Count per atom and sum: a minimal basis gives one function per occupied atomic orbital, and each added shell contributes its own degeneracy (3 for p, 5 or 6 for d).

los.do: Judge from a series of results whether a property has converged in the basis.
los.ek: A property is converged when successive members of a systematic series change by less than the accuracy wanted; geometries converge faster than energies, and interaction energies slowest.

los.do: Compute a counterpoise-corrected interaction energy and explain basis-set superposition error.
los.ek: In a small basis each monomer borrows functions from its partner, over-binding the complex; the counterpoise correction recomputes each monomer in the full dimer basis and subtracts the difference.

los.do: State what MP2 adds and when perturbation theory is the wrong tool.
los.ek: MP2 adds the leading double-excitation correction from the Hartree-Fock reference. It fails where the reference is poor: small gaps, bond breaking, diradicals, and transition metals.

los.do: Compute an MP2 correlation contribution from given orbital energies and integrals for one excitation.
los.ek: Each doubly-excited amplitude contributes a term whose numerator is the integral squared and whose denominator is the sum of occupied minus virtual orbital energies, so small gaps make large contributions.

los.do: Order the common correlation methods by cost and accuracy, and say what CCSD(T) means.
los.ek: MP2, then CCSD, then CCSD(T), which adds a perturbative triples correction and is the usual accuracy reference for single-reference molecules.

los.do: Compute how much longer a calculation takes when the system grows, from a method's formal scaling.
los.ek: Formal cost scales as a power of basis size: about the fourth power for Hartree-Fock, the fifth for MP2, the sixth for CCSD and the seventh for CCSD(T). The ratio of two sizes raised to that power is the slowdown.

los.do: Say what a symmetry-adapted perturbation theory decomposition gives that a total interaction energy does not.
los.ek: It splits the interaction into electrostatics, exchange, induction and dispersion, so two complexes with the same binding energy can be told apart by what binds them.

los.do: Attribute a described interaction to the dominant SAPT component.
los.ek: A hydrogen bond is electrostatics-dominated; two nonpolar rings stacking is dispersion-dominated; a polar molecule beside a polarisable one gains induction.

los.do: Place a functional on the rungs from local density through generalised gradient to hybrid and double hybrid, and say what each rung adds.
los.ek: LDA uses the density; GGA adds its gradient; meta-GGA adds the kinetic-energy density; a hybrid mixes in exact exchange; a double hybrid adds perturbative correlation.

los.do: Compute the exchange mixture a hybrid applies from its stated fraction of exact exchange.
los.ek: A hybrid replaces a stated fraction of the functional's exchange with Hartree-Fock exchange; range-separated hybrids make that fraction depend on distance.

los.do: Name what DFT handles poorly and the correction usually applied.
los.ek: Plain functionals miss long-range dispersion, so an empirical correction is added; self-interaction error distorts charge-transfer states and barriers, which range-separated hybrids reduce.

los.do: Compute an integration-grid or a dispersion-corrected energy from stated components.
los.ek: The total is the functional's energy plus the dispersion correction, which is a sum of damped pairwise terms; a grid too coarse adds noise that looks like a real energy difference.

los.do: State what an optimiser converges on and how a minimum is told from a saddle point.
los.ek: The gradient goes to zero at any stationary point; the Hessian's eigenvalues decide which it is, and a frequency calculation reports one imaginary frequency for a transition state.

los.do: Read a potential energy surface scan for a bond length, angle or intermolecular distance and extract the minimum and the well depth.
los.ek: Scanning one coordinate while relaxing or fixing the rest gives a curve whose minimum is the equilibrium value and whose depth below the separated limit is the binding energy.

los.do: Compute a zero-point vibrational energy from a set of harmonic frequencies.
los.ek: ZPE is half the sum of h times each harmonic frequency; a nonlinear molecule of n atoms has 3n - 6 modes and a linear one 3n - 5.

los.do: Compute a reaction energy or a standard potential from computed energies and say what corrections it needs.
los.ek: A reaction energy is the sum of products minus reactants, corrected for zero-point energy and thermal terms; an electrode potential divides the free-energy change by minus the electrons times the Faraday constant and needs a reference.

los.do: State what a reported result must include to be reproducible.
los.ek: Method, basis, geometry (or that it was optimised at the same level), any dispersion correction and solvation model, the program and its version, and for a transition state the imaginary frequency.

los.do: Choose a method and basis for a stated problem and defend both choices.
los.ek: Match the treatment to the chemistry and the basis to the property: geometries tolerate small bases, interaction energies do not; a multireference problem rules out single-reference methods whatever the basis.

units.title: Protein geometry and the rotamer picture

topics.title: Backbone and side-chain degrees of freedom

los.do: Name the backbone and side-chain dihedrals and say which are free, which are nearly fixed, and which regions of the Ramachandran plot the common secondary structures occupy.
los.ek: φ (C−N−Cα−C), ψ (N−Cα−C−N) and ω (nearly planar, about 180° trans); side-chain χ1, χ2…; right-handed α-helix near φ ≈ −60°, ψ ≈ −45°, β-sheet near φ ≈ −120°, ψ ≈ +130°; glycine is permissive and proline restricted.

los.do: Count the conformational degrees of freedom of a chain and show why enumeration is hopeless.
los.ek: Two free backbone dihedrals per residue; discretising each into a few states gives states^(2n) conformations, which is Levinthal's paradox in numbers.

los.do: Explain what a rotamer library is and why side-chain conformations are treated as a discrete, backbone-dependent set.
los.ek: Side-chain χ angles cluster in a few favoured combinations; the Dunbrack library gives their probabilities as a function of φ/ψ, and fa_dun scores the chosen rotamer's internal energy.

los.do: Count the rotamer combinations of a set of designable positions and convert a rotamer probability into an energy.
los.ek: Combinations multiply: Π k_i over positions. A probability p maps to an energy −kT ln p, so a rotamer ten times less likely costs about 1.4 kcal/mol at 298 K.

los.do: Describe what a Pose holds and how residues are addressed, and distinguish pose numbering from PDB numbering.
los.ek: A Pose carries the sequence, the conformation as internal coordinates, the fold tree and the energies; pose numbering is 1…N over all residues, while PDB numbering carries chains, gaps and insertion codes.

los.do: Convert between pose and PDB numbering across chains of known length.
los.ek: Pose index of residue j in chain c is j plus the lengths of the preceding chains, so gaps in PDB numbering do not shift pose indices.

los.do: Contrast the centroid and full-atom representations and say which stage of a protocol uses each.
los.ek: Centroid replaces each side chain with one pseudo-atom and a simple score for fast global search; full atom restores every atom for local refinement and final ranking. Multi-resolution modelling is the standard pattern.

los.do: Compute how many atoms a representation tracks and the speed-up a coarse-grained model buys.
los.ek: Pairwise interaction work scales with the square of the number of interacting centres, so a fourfold cut in centres is about a sixteenfold cut in pair work.

los.do: Name the main energy terms and classify each as physics-based or knowledge-based.
los.ek: Physics-based: fa_atr and fa_rep (Lennard-Jones split at its minimum), fa_sol (Lazaridis–Karplus desolvation), lk_ball_wtd (anisotropic polar solvation), fa_elec (distance-dependent dielectric). Knowledge-based: fa_dun (rotamer), rama_prepro (backbone φ/ψ), p_aa_pp (residue given φ/ψ), the hydrogen-bond and disulfide terms fit to structures.

los.do: Compute a total score as the weighted sum of its terms.
los.ek: Total = Σ w_i E_i. Physics-based terms carry weight 1.0; fa_rep is 0.55, fa_dun 0.7, rama_prepro 0.45, p_aa_pp 0.4, omega 0.6, dslf_fa13 1.25, fa_intra_rep 0.005.

los.do: Explain what the reference energy does and why design, not scoring, needs it.
los.ek: ref adds a constant per amino-acid type standing for the unfolded state, fitted to maximise native sequence recovery. For a fixed sequence it is a constant offset; when sequences are compared it removes the composition bias the other terms would impose.

los.do: Compute a stability difference between two candidate sequences including their reference energies.
los.ek: ΔΔG ≈ (E_folded − Σ ref) for one sequence minus the same for the other; a design that scores better only because of composition bias loses that advantage once ref is included.

los.do: State what the energy's units mean and how far to trust a computed ΔΔG.
los.ek: The current function is parameterised in kcal/mol rather than arbitrary Rosetta Energy Units, but the paper's own worked mutation gave −4.95 kcal/mol against −1.11 kcal/mol measured: the sign and the ranking are more reliable than the magnitude.

los.do: Decompose a score change into terms and name the interaction responsible.
los.ek: Subtract term by term between two states; per-residue and atom-pair tables locate the contact that changed. A buried polar group shows up in solvation, a clash in fa_rep.

los.do: State the Metropolis rule and explain why uphill moves are accepted at all.
los.ek: A move raising the score by ΔE is accepted with probability exp(−ΔE/kT); uphill steps let the search leave local minima, which gradient descent cannot do.

los.do: Compute a Metropolis acceptance probability and show how annealing changes it.
los.ek: P = exp(−ΔE/kT) for ΔE > 0, P = 1 otherwise; lowering the temperature during a run makes the same uphill move far less likely, which is simulated annealing.

los.do: Describe what the packer does, and how packing, minimisation and relax differ.
los.ek: The packer runs simulated annealing over discrete rotamers at the positions a task allows; minimisation moves continuous degrees of freedom downhill; relax alternates the two so a structure settles without drifting far.

los.do: Count the entries of a rotamer pair-energy table and explain the cost of precomputing it.
los.ek: With n positions and k rotamers each, there are n·k one-body terms and k² entries for each of the n(n−1)/2 position pairs, so the table grows as the square of both.

los.do: Read and write a design specification: which positions repack, which design, and to what alphabet.
los.ek: A resfile or task operation sets per-position behaviour — repack only, design to all residues, or design to a restricted set; everything else stays fixed. Getting this wrong is the usual cause of a nonsense design.

los.do: Count the sequence space a design specification opens.
los.ek: Π a_i over designable positions, where a_i is the alphabet allowed at position i; 20^n for unrestricted design, which is why the space is sampled and never enumerated.

los.do: Plan a point-mutation scan and read its output.
los.ek: A saturation scan tries 19 substitutions at each chosen position, scoring each after local repacking; the result is a ranked ΔΔG list, not a verdict.

los.do: Count the jobs and compute the ΔΔG values a scan produces.
los.ek: 19 substitutions per position times the positions, times the independent trials each is run with; ΔΔG = E_mutant − E_wild-type, with a positive value destabilising.

los.do: Match a sequence-optimisation method to its guarantee: dead-end elimination, mean field, annealing, genetic algorithms.
los.ek: Dead-end elimination prunes provably non-optimal rotamers and can return the true optimum; annealing and genetic algorithms are stochastic and return good solutions without a proof.

los.do: Use native sequence recovery to judge an energy function or protocol.
los.ek: Redesign a natural protein's positions and count how often the native residue comes back; random choice recovers about 5%, buried positions recover best, and surface positions worst.

los.do: Describe the two stages of docking and what a funnel plot shows.
los.ek: A global rigid-body search (often Fourier-based) is followed by local high-resolution refinement; plotting score against RMSD to a reference should funnel toward low RMSD if the function discriminates.

los.do: Compute a binding or interface energy from component scores.
los.ek: ΔE_interface = E_complex − E_partner A alone − E_partner B alone, each scored in the same function; near-native models gain in van der Waals, electrostatics and side-chain hydrogen bonds.

los.do: Lay out how a ligand-binding pocket is designed and why designed enzymes fall short of natural ones.
los.ek: Place the ligand, design the shell around it, then repack and minimise. Pocket shape and binding are achievable; transition-state stabilisation, and so catalytic efficiency, is not yet.

los.do: Choose one-sided or two-sided interface design for a stated problem and say what makes it hard.
los.ek: Two-sided design redesigns both partners and is easier; a binder against a fixed natural surface is one-sided and much harder, which is also why antibody design remains difficult.

los.do: Contrast the routes to a de novo backbone: fragment assembly, distance constraints and parametric equations.
los.ek: Fragments splice pieces of known structures; constraints specify the contacts wanted; parametric equations generate ideal folds such as coiled coils and β-barrels from a handful of numbers.

los.do: Compute the geometry of a parametric helical bundle from its parameters.
los.ek: A coiled-coil's superhelical radius, pitch and the number of residues per repeat fix the backbone; the rise along the axis per residue follows from the pitch and the residues per turn.

los.do: Say why buried hydrogen-bond networks are designed before the rest of the sequence.
los.ek: A network of buried polar residues is rare and easily broken by later repacking, so it is found first and then held fixed while the surrounding core is designed.

los.do: Explain negative and multi-state design and compute the energy gap that must be opened.
los.ek: Favour the target state by scoring it against competing states and maximising the gap; a conformational switch is a multi-state design where each state's gap is tuned, and a gap of a few kT sets the population ratio.

units.title: Deep learning for structure and design

los.do: Name the inputs a modern structure predictor takes and read its confidence metrics.
los.ek: Sequence, a multiple-sequence alignment and optional templates go in; pLDDT scores per-residue local confidence (higher is better, with roughly 70 and 90 as useful marks) and PAE scores the expected error between residue pairs, which is what judges domain placement.

los.do: Explain why alignment depth limits prediction and coevolution-based contacts.
los.ek: Coevolution separates direct couplings from indirect ones only when the alignment is deep; shallow families, including many eukaryote-specific ones, lose that signal, and MSA coverage plots are read for exactly this.

los.do: Match a representation to its architecture: sequence tokens for language models, residue or atom graphs for message passing.
los.ek: A protein language model is trained on sequences alone and its embeddings transfer to downstream tasks; a graph network passes messages between residues or atoms, where invariance and equivariance to rotation matter.

los.do: Describe the diffusion design pipeline and what each stage contributes.
los.ek: A diffusion model denoises a backbone (unconditionally, scaffolding a motif, or against a target), an inverse-folding model assigns a sequence to that backbone, and a structure predictor checks that the sequence folds back to it.

los.do: Say what a self-consistency check does and does not establish.
los.ek: Designing a sequence for a backbone and recovering that backbone from the sequence shows the two models agree; it is not experimental evidence, since both may share the same blind spots.

los.do: Compute the yield of a filtered design funnel.
los.ek: Multiply the pass fractions of the stages: backbones generated, sequences per backbone, and the fraction whose predicted structure falls within the RMSD and confidence cut-offs.

units.title: Validation and the bridge to simulation

los.do: Plan the experiments that test a design and say how many candidates to make.
los.ek: Expression and solubility, then thermal or chemical denaturation for stability, oligomeric state, a high-resolution structure, and a function assay. A stabilisation project may test a handful; a new binder may need thousands, screened by display and sequencing.

los.do: Compute the number of designs to order for a target number of successes at an expected hit rate.
los.ek: Expected successes = N × hit rate, so N = target/hit rate; low rates are why display libraries, not individual clones, are used for binders.

topics.title: Where a score is not enough

los.do: Decide when a score-function ΔΔG is enough and when an alchemical free-energy calculation is warranted.
los.ek: A score-function scan ranks many mutations cheaply and is right about signs more often than magnitudes; when a few candidates must be quantitative, or when a result must survive review, λ dynamics or another alchemical method gives a statistical-mechanics estimate with an error bar.

los.do: Name what current energy functions handle worst and relate it to a failed design.
los.ek: Balancing polar against nonpolar energetics, solvation, flexible loops and backbone flexibility are the open problems; a design that expresses but is unstructured usually points at one of them.

los.do: Say what fitting a model into electron density adds to a purely computational score, and what it cannot fix.
los.ek: Density is experimental evidence that restrains the model, scored alongside the energy function; it cannot rescue a region the map does not resolve, where confidence stays low whatever the score says.

los.do: Order the stages of a refinement protocol and say what each stage is allowed to move.
los.ek: Refinement alternates small backbone perturbations, side-chain repacking and minimisation under the all-atom function, usually with the repulsive weight ramped, so the structure settles without escaping the starting fold.

los.do: Say what a loop-closure method must guarantee and why loops are modelled separately from the rest of a structure.
los.ek: A rebuilt loop must still join the fixed flanking residues, so closure is a constraint, not a preference; kinematic closure solves for the dihedrals that close the gap, and loops are irregular and flexible, which is why they are rebuilt rather than threaded.

los.do: Describe what a symmetric model fixes and count the independent degrees of freedom symmetry removes.
los.ek: One asymmetric unit plus a symmetry definition generates the rest, so the energy and the moves apply to the unit and are replicated; n copies of an m-residue chain under exact symmetry leave one chain's degrees of freedom instead of n.

los.do: Say what antibody design optimises and why it is a one-sided problem.
los.ek: Design chooses CDR sequence and length against a chosen epitope on a target that cannot be changed, so it combines one-sided interface design with flexible-loop modelling: the two hardest cases in the field at once.

los.do: Describe how an antibody structure is modelled from its framework and loops, and which loop is the hard one.
los.ek: The variable domains' frameworks are conserved enough to graft from templates by canonical class; the six complementarity-determining loops are modelled on top, and CDR H3 is the longest, most variable and least predictable.

los.do: Set up a membrane protein in a bilayer and say what the energy function must change.
los.ek: The protein is embedded with its hydrophobic span across the membrane and its orientation and depth fixed relative to the bilayer; the solvation term must treat the membrane interior as nonpolar, so a water-based function would misscore buried polar residues.

los.do: Distinguish the three ways a design campaign is parallelised and match each to its job.
los.ek: Independent decoys of one protocol (embarrassingly parallel), one protocol distributed across workers, and many protocols over many inputs; a scan is the first, a large generative pipeline the third.

los.do: State what a run must record for a design to be reproducible, and compute the decoy count a campaign needs.
los.ek: The random seed, the protocol version, the input structure and every option, kept with the output; decoys scale as inputs × protocols × decoys per input, and the lowest-scoring decoy of too small a set is just noise.

los.do: Apply Kirchhoff's current and voltage laws.
los.ek: KCL: the currents entering a node equal the currents leaving it. KVL: the voltage rises and drops round any closed loop sum to zero.

los.do: Reduce series and parallel resistors and use the divider rules.
los.ek: Series resistances add. For two in parallel, R = R1 R2 ÷ (R1 + R2). A voltage divider gives V2 = V × R2 ÷ (R1 + R2); a current divider sends the larger current through the smaller resistance.

los.do: Find a Thevenin equivalent and the maximum power it can deliver.
los.ek: Any linear two-terminal network is equivalent to a source Vth (the open-circuit voltage) in series with Rth (the resistance seen with sources switched off). A load draws maximum power when it equals Rth, and that power is Vth² ÷ (4 Rth).

los.do: Solve a single-node circuit by node analysis and by superposition.
los.ek: Write KCL at the unknown node with each branch current as a voltage difference over a resistance. With several sources, superposition gives the same answer: find the response to each source with the others switched off, then add.

los.do: Convert between peak, RMS, frequency and period.
los.ek: For a sinusoid the RMS value is the peak divided by √2; it is the DC value that would heat a resistor equally. Frequency is the reciprocal of the period, and angular frequency is 2πf.

los.do: Compute the reactance of an inductor and a capacitor.
los.ek: An inductor's reactance is ωL and rises with frequency; a capacitor's is 1 ÷ (ωC) and falls with frequency. As impedances they are jωL and 1 ÷ (jωC): current lags voltage in an inductor and leads it in a capacitor.

los.do: Combine resistance and reactance into an impedance magnitude and phase.
los.ek: In a series circuit Z = R + j(X_L − X_C), so |Z| = √(R² + X²) and the phase angle is arctan(X ÷ R): positive (current lags) when the circuit is inductive.

los.do: Compute real, reactive and apparent power and the power factor.
los.ek: Apparent power S = V_rms I_rms (VA). Real power P = S cos φ (W); reactive power Q = S sin φ (var); S² = P² + Q². The power factor is cos φ = P ÷ S.

los.do: Find a first-order time constant and the response at a given time.
los.ek: An RC circuit has time constant τ = RC and an RL circuit τ = L ÷ R. A step response rises as V(1 − e^(−t/τ)): 63% after one time constant, effectively complete after five.

los.do: Find the resonant frequency and quality factor of an RLC circuit.
los.ek: Resonance is where the inductive and capacitive reactances are equal: ω0 = 1 ÷ √(LC). For a series RLC circuit Q = ω0 L ÷ R, and the bandwidth is the resonant frequency divided by Q.

los.do: Read a transfer function for DC gain, time constant and stability.
los.ek: For H(s) = K ÷ (s + a) the pole is at s = −a, the time constant is 1 ÷ a and the DC gain is H(0) = K ÷ a. A system is stable when every pole has a negative real part.

los.do: Find a first-order cutoff frequency and express a gain in decibels.
los.ek: An RC low-pass filter has H = 1 ÷ (1 + jωRC), cutoff frequency fc = 1 ÷ (2πRC) and gain 1/√2 (−3 dB) there. A voltage gain in decibels is 20 log10 of the ratio.

los.do: Apply the Nyquist criterion and find an alias frequency.
los.ek: A signal must be sampled at more than twice its highest frequency. A component above half the sampling rate appears at the distance to the nearest multiple of the sampling rate: f_alias = |f − k fs|.

los.do: Name filter types and compute a first-order filter's gain.
los.ek: Low-pass, high-pass, band-pass and band-stop filters are named for what they let through. A first-order low-pass filter has gain 1 ÷ √(1 + (f/fc)²) and rolls off at 20 dB per decade above cutoff.

los.do: Run a difference equation and find a digital filter's DC gain.
los.ek: A digital filter computes each output from present and past samples. FIR filters use inputs only; IIR filters also feed back past outputs. The DC gain is the transfer function H(z) at z = 1.

los.do: Use the constant-drop diode model and the transistor current gain.
los.ek: A forward-biased silicon diode is modelled as a 0.7 V drop; reverse-biased, it is an open circuit. In the active region a bipolar transistor's collector current is β times its base current.

los.do: Find the gain of ideal op-amp circuits.
los.ek: An ideal op-amp with negative feedback holds its two inputs at the same voltage and draws no input current. Inverting amplifier: gain −Rf ÷ Rin. Non-inverting amplifier: gain 1 + Rf ÷ R1.

los.do: Compute converter resolution and a rectifier's average output.
los.ek: An n-bit converter divides its range into 2^n steps, so one step is the range ÷ 2^n. The average (DC) value of an ideal full-wave rectified sine is 2Vp ÷ π; half-wave gives Vp ÷ π.

los.do: Relate line and phase quantities and compute three-phase power.
los.ek: In a balanced wye connection the line voltage is √3 times the phase voltage and line current equals phase current; in delta the roles swap. Total real power is √3 × V_line × I_line × power factor.

los.do: Use the turns ratio of an ideal transformer.
los.ek: For an ideal transformer V1 ÷ V2 = N1 ÷ N2 and I1 ÷ I2 = N2 ÷ N1, so power is conserved. A load Z on the secondary looks like (N1 ÷ N2)² Z from the primary.

los.do: Compute synchronous speed and slip.
los.ek: Synchronous speed in rev/min is 120 f ÷ P for P poles. An induction motor runs slightly slower; slip = (synchronous speed − rotor speed) ÷ synchronous speed.

los.do: Reduce a feedback loop and find its steady-state error.
los.ek: With forward gain G and feedback gain H, negative feedback gives a closed-loop gain of G ÷ (1 + GH). For unity feedback and a step input, a system with DC loop gain K has a steady-state error of 1 ÷ (1 + K); an integrator in the loop makes it zero.

los.do: Predict overshoot, settling time and damping type from ζ and ωn.
los.ek: A second-order system is underdamped for ζ < 1, critically damped at ζ = 1 and overdamped above. For ζ < 1 the percent overshoot is 100 e^(−πζ/√(1−ζ²)), and the 2% settling time is about 4 ÷ (ζ ωn).

los.do: Read Bode slopes and judge stability from margins.
los.ek: Each pole adds −20 dB per decade above its corner frequency and each zero adds +20 dB per decade. A closed loop is stable when the open loop has positive gain and phase margins; phase margin is 180° plus the open-loop phase at the gain-crossover frequency.

los.do: Find the resultant of two forces and the moment of a force.
los.ek: Two forces at angle θ have a resultant of magnitude √(A² + B² + 2AB cos θ). The moment of a force about a point is the force times its perpendicular distance: M = F d sin θ.

los.do: Solve a concurrent force system in equilibrium.
los.ek: For a particle in equilibrium the forces sum to zero in each direction. A weight hung from two identical cables at angle θ above the horizontal gives 2T sin θ = W.

los.do: Find support reactions on a beam.
los.ek: Sum moments about one support to get the other reaction, then sum vertical forces. A uniform load acts at the middle of its length.

los.do: Find member forces in a simple truss and state the truss assumptions.
los.ek: Truss members are two-force members joined by pins and loaded only at joints, so each carries pure tension or compression. At a joint the forces balance: in a symmetric triangular truss with a load P at the apex, each inclined member carries P ÷ (2 sin θ) in compression.

los.do: Locate a centroid and compute an area moment of inertia.
los.ek: The centroid of a composite area is the area-weighted average of its parts' centroids. A rectangle has I = b h³ ÷ 12 about its own centroidal axis; the parallel-axis theorem moves it: I = I_c + A d².

los.do: Apply the laws of static friction.
los.ek: Static friction takes whatever value equilibrium needs up to μs N. A block on an incline is on the point of sliding when tan θ = μs.

los.do: Find velocity by integrating acceleration and the normal acceleration on a curve.
los.ek: Velocity is the integral of acceleration over time. On a curved path the acceleration has a tangential part dv/dt and a normal part v² ÷ ρ directed toward the centre of curvature.

los.do: Apply Newton's second law with kinetic friction.
los.ek: On an incline at angle θ a sliding block accelerates at g (sin θ − μk cos θ) down the slope. On level ground a pushed block accelerates at (F − μk m g) ÷ m.

los.do: Use work-energy and impulse-momentum for a particle.
los.ek: The work done by all forces equals the change in kinetic energy. The impulse (force × time) equals the change in momentum.

los.do: Relate angular and linear motion and use rolling without slipping.
los.ek: A point at radius r on a body turning at ω moves at v = ω r. A wheel rolling without slipping has v = ω r at its centre; the contact point is momentarily at rest and the top moves at 2v.

los.do: Apply Newton's second law to rotation and to rolling bodies.
los.ek: Torque = I α. A solid disc has I = ½ m r², a hoop m r², a solid sphere ⅖ m r². A body with I = k m r² rolling without slipping down an incline accelerates at g sin θ ÷ (1 + k).

los.do: Find the natural frequency and damping ratio of a spring-mass system.
los.ek: Undamped natural frequency ωn = √(k ÷ m), so f = ωn ÷ 2π. Damping ratio ζ = c ÷ (2 √(k m)): below 1 the system oscillates, at 1 it is critically damped. A forcing frequency near the natural frequency gives resonance.

los.do: Compute axial stress and elongation.
los.ek: Normal stress σ = P ÷ A. Within the elastic range the elongation is δ = P L ÷ (A E).

los.do: Compute thermal expansion and the stress in a constrained bar.
los.ek: A free bar changes length by δ = α ΔT L. If both ends are fixed the bar cannot expand, and the stress is σ = E α ΔT (compressive on heating), whatever its length or area.

los.do: Compute torsional shear stress and angle of twist in a solid shaft.
los.ek: Maximum shear stress τ = T c ÷ J with J = π d⁴ ÷ 32 for a solid circular shaft, so τ = 16 T ÷ (π d³). Angle of twist φ = T L ÷ (G J).

los.do: Find the maximum shear and bending moment in standard beams.
los.ek: Simply supported beam with a central point load P: maximum shear P ÷ 2, maximum moment P L ÷ 4. With a uniform load w: maximum shear w L ÷ 2, maximum moment w L² ÷ 8. A cantilever with an end load P: maximum moment P L at the wall.

los.do: Compute bending stress and a standard beam deflection.
los.ek: Bending stress σ = M c ÷ I; for a rectangle b × h this is 6M ÷ (b h²). A simply supported beam with a central load deflects P L³ ÷ (48 E I) at midspan.

los.do: Find principal stresses and the maximum in-plane shear stress.
los.ek: For plane stress the centre of Mohr's circle is (σx + σy) ÷ 2 and its radius is √(((σx − σy) ÷ 2)² + τxy²). The principal stresses are centre ± radius and the maximum in-plane shear stress is the radius.

los.do: Compute pressure-vessel stresses and combine axial and bending stress.
los.ek: A thin-walled cylinder under pressure p has hoop stress p r ÷ t and longitudinal stress p r ÷ (2t). Axial load and bending on the same section superpose: σ = P ÷ A ± M c ÷ I.

los.do: Compute an Euler buckling load and choose the effective length factor.
los.ek: Critical load P = π² E I ÷ (K L)². K is 1 for pinned-pinned ends, 0.5 for fixed-fixed, about 0.7 for fixed-pinned and 2 for fixed-free. Buckling depends on stiffness and slenderness, not on strength.

los.do: Count the atoms in a cubic unit cell and state its coordination number.
los.ek: A corner atom is shared by 8 cells, a face atom by 2, a body atom by 1. FCC holds 4 atoms with 12 nearest neighbours; BCC holds 2 with 8; simple cubic holds 1 with 6.

los.do: Relate the cell edge to the atomic radius in FCC and BCC.
los.ek: Atoms touch along the face diagonal in FCC, so a√2 = 4r; along the body diagonal in BCC, so a√3 = 4r.

los.do: Compute an atomic packing factor.
los.ek: APF is the volume of the atoms in the cell over the cell volume: 0.74 for FCC and HCP, 0.68 for BCC, 0.52 for simple cubic.

los.do: Compute a theoretical density from the unit cell.
los.ek: ρ = nA ÷ (V_cell N_A): atoms per cell times molar mass, over cell volume times Avogadro's number. With a in nm, a³ in cm³ is (a × 10⁻⁷)³.

los.do: Write the Miller indices of a plane from its intercepts and test whether a direction lies in a plane.
los.ek: Take the intercepts in units of the cell edges, invert, and clear fractions; a plane parallel to an axis has index 0 for it. In a cubic crystal [uvw] lies in (hkl) when hu + kv + lw = 0.

los.do: Write a direction's indices and find the angle between two directions.
los.ek: A direction is the vector between two lattice points reduced to smallest integers. In a cubic crystal the angle between [u₁v₁w₁] and [u₂v₂w₂] comes from the dot product.

los.do: Compute the spacing of (hkl) planes in a cubic crystal.
los.ek: d = a ÷ √(h² + k² + l²). Low-index planes are the most widely spaced and the most densely packed.

los.do: Use Bragg's law.
los.ek: nλ = 2d sin θ. A diffractometer reports 2θ, the angle between the incident and diffracted beams.

los.do: Decide which reflections a cubic structure allows.
los.ek: BCC reflects only when h + k + l is even; FCC only when h, k and l are all odd or all even; simple cubic reflects for every plane.

los.do: Compute a linear and a planar density.
los.ek: Linear density is atom centres per length along a direction; planar density is atoms per area on a plane. Slip prefers the densest directions on the densest planes.

los.do: Compute an equilibrium vacancy concentration.
los.ek: N_v ÷ N = exp(−Q_v ÷ kT), with k = 8.617 × 10⁻⁵ eV/K. Near melting about one site in ten thousand is vacant.

los.do: Tell substitutional from interstitial solid solutions and apply the size rule.
los.ek: A solute sits on host sites when its radius is within about 15% of the host's and the structures, valences and electronegativities are alike; a much smaller atom (C, N, H) sits between host atoms.

los.do: Convert a composition between weight percent and atom percent.
los.ek: Divide each weight percent by its molar mass to get moles, then normalise; multiply atom percents by molar mass and normalise to go back.

los.do: Identify Schottky and Frenkel defects and the vacancies a dopant forces in an ionic crystal.
los.ek: A Schottky defect is a cation vacancy with an anion vacancy; a Frenkel defect is a cation moved to an interstitial site. Both keep the crystal neutral, and an impurity of different charge brings compensating vacancies.

los.do: Tell edge, screw and mixed dislocations apart by the Burgers vector and the line.
los.ek: The Burgers vector b is the lattice displacement a dislocation carries. Edge: b perpendicular to the line (an extra half-plane). Screw: b parallel to the line (a spiral ramp). Anything between is mixed.

los.do: Find a Burgers vector from a Burgers circuit.
los.ek: Walk a closed loop of lattice steps around the line, equal steps in opposite directions. In perfect crystal the loop closes; around a dislocation it does not, and the vector needed to close it is b.

los.do: Compute the magnitude of a Burgers vector from its indices.
los.ek: A perfect dislocation's b joins nearest neighbours: (a/2)⟨110⟩ in FCC, (a/2)⟨111⟩ in BCC. Its length is (a/2)√(h² + k² + l²), which equals two atomic radii.

los.do: Use the b² rule for a dislocation's energy and for dislocation reactions.
los.ek: The elastic energy per length of a dislocation is about ½Gb². A reaction b₁ → b₂ + b₃ is favourable when b₁² > b₂² + b₃² (Frank's rule), which is why dislocations take the shortest lattice vector.

los.do: Work with a dislocation density.
los.ek: Density ρ is line length per volume, in m⁻²: about 10¹⁰ in an annealed metal, 10¹⁴ to 10¹⁶ after heavy cold work. The mean spacing between dislocations is about 1 ÷ √ρ.

los.do: Convert between ASTM grain size number and grain count.
los.ek: N = 2^(G − 1): N grains per square inch at 100× magnification for ASTM grain size number G. A larger G means finer grains.

los.do: Identify low-angle boundaries, twins and stacking faults.
los.ek: A low-angle tilt boundary is a wall of edge dislocations of spacing D with misorientation θ ≈ b ÷ D. A twin boundary is a mirror plane; a stacking fault is a mistake in the ABCABC sequence.

los.do: Name the slip systems of FCC, BCC and HCP metals.
los.ek: Slip runs on the most densely packed planes along the closest-packed directions: (111) planes and 110-type directions in FCC (12 systems), 111-type directions in BCC, the basal plane in HCP (3 systems).

los.do: Apply Schmid's law.
los.ek: τ_R = σ cos φ cos λ, with φ between the load axis and the slip-plane normal and λ between the load axis and the slip direction. Slip starts when τ_R reaches the critical resolved shear stress; the factor cannot exceed 0.5.

los.do: Compare theoretical and observed shear strength.
los.ek: Shearing a whole plane at once would take about G ÷ 2π. Real crystals yield at a thousandth of that because a dislocation moves the slip one row at a time.

los.do: Use the Hall-Petch relation.
los.ek: σ_y = σ₀ + k_y d^(−1/2): a grain boundary stops a dislocation, so finer grains give higher yield strength.

los.do: Compute percent cold work and the strength from dislocation density.
los.ek: %CW = (A₀ − A_d) ÷ A₀ × 100. Work hardening follows τ = αGb√ρ with α about 0.5: flow stress rises as the square root of dislocation density.

los.do: Explain solid-solution and precipitation strengthening and use the Orowan stress.
los.ek: Solute atoms strain the lattice and drag on dislocations. Fine coherent precipitates are cut; larger ones are bypassed by bowing between them at τ = Gb ÷ L, so strength peaks at an intermediate ageing time and falls on overageing.

los.do: Order recovery, recrystallization and grain growth.
los.ek: On annealing a cold-worked metal: recovery rearranges dislocations and relieves stress with little change in strength; recrystallization replaces the worked grains with new strain-free ones and restores ductility; grain growth then coarsens them.

los.do: Read ductility and plastic strain from a tensile test.
los.ek: Percent elongation is (l_f − l₀) ÷ l₀ × 100. On unloading, the elastic strain σ ÷ E is recovered along a line parallel to the elastic slope, leaving the plastic strain.

los.do: Convert engineering stress and strain to true stress and strain.
los.ek: σ_T = σ(1 + ε) and ε_T = ln(1 + ε) = ln(l ÷ l₀), valid up to necking. True strain adds up the increments dl ÷ l.

los.do: Use the strain-hardening law.
los.ek: In the plastic range σ_T = K ε_T^n. The exponent n runs from about 0.1 to 0.5, and necking begins when the true strain equals n.

los.do: Compute the modulus of resilience and tell it from toughness.
los.ek: Resilience is the elastic energy per volume up to yield, U_r = σ_y² ÷ 2E; toughness is the whole area under the stress-strain curve to fracture.

los.do: Relate hardness to strength and name the hardness tests.
los.ek: Hardness is resistance to local plastic indentation. For steels, tensile strength in MPa is about 3.45 times the Brinell number.

los.do: Apply Fick's first law to steady diffusion through a plate.
los.ek: J = −D dC/dx: flux runs down the concentration gradient. For a linear profile J = D ΔC ÷ Δx.

los.do: Use the Arrhenius law for a diffusion coefficient.
los.ek: D = D₀ exp(−Q_d ÷ RT). A plot of ln D against 1 ÷ T is a line of slope −Q_d ÷ R.

los.do: Scale a diffusion depth with time and temperature.
los.ek: For a fixed surface concentration, a given composition is reached at a depth proportional to √(Dt). The same profile results whenever the product Dt is the same.

los.do: Compare diffusion mechanisms and paths.
los.ek: Interstitial atoms diffuse faster than substitutional ones, which must wait for a vacancy. Grain boundaries and surfaces are faster paths than the lattice; open structures and low melting points give faster diffusion.

los.do: Apply the Gibbs phase rule at constant pressure.
los.ek: F = C − P + 1 when pressure is fixed. In a binary system a two-phase field has one degree of freedom and a three-phase reaction (eutectic, eutectoid, peritectic) has none: it happens at one temperature.

los.do: Use the lever rule.
los.ek: In a two-phase field the phase compositions are the ends of the tie line, and the fraction of one phase is the opposite lever arm over the whole tie line.

los.do: Split a hypoeutectic alloy into primary phase and eutectic.
los.ek: Just above the eutectic temperature the liquid has the eutectic composition; all of it becomes eutectic microconstituent. The primary phase fraction is a lever between the solubility limit and the eutectic point.

los.do: Name the invariant reactions.
los.ek: On cooling: eutectic, liquid → two solids; eutectoid, one solid → two solids; peritectic, liquid + solid → a different solid.

los.do: Identify the phases and landmarks of the iron-carbon diagram.
los.ek: Ferrite (α) is BCC and holds at most 0.022 wt% C; austenite (γ) is FCC and holds up to 2.14; cementite Fe₃C is 6.70 wt% C. The eutectoid is 0.76 wt% C at 727 °C; steels lie below 2.14 wt% C, cast irons above.

los.do: Compute the microconstituents of a slowly cooled steel.
los.ek: In a hypoeutectoid steel the austenite left at 727 °C has 0.76 wt% C and becomes pearlite, so pearlite is a lever between 0.022 and 0.76. Total cementite is a lever between 0.022 and 6.70.

los.do: Predict the product of an isothermal or quench treatment from a TTT diagram.
los.ek: Austenite held just below 727 °C gives coarse pearlite, lower gives fine pearlite, below the nose (about 550 to 250 °C) bainite; quenched fast enough to miss the nose it shears to martensite, which is hard, brittle and not on the equilibrium diagram.

los.do: Choose a heat treatment for steel and explain hardenability.
los.ek: Full annealing (furnace cool) gives the softest structure; normalizing (air cool) a finer, stronger one; quench and temper gives the best strength with toughness. Hardenability is the depth to which a steel forms martensite, measured by the Jominy end-quench test and raised by alloying.

los.do: Use the Avrami equation for the fraction transformed.
los.ek: y = 1 − exp(−k tⁿ): the S-shaped curve of nucleation and growth. The rate is often quoted as 1 ÷ t at half transformation.

los.do: Compute a critical nucleus radius and scale the nucleation barrier.
los.ek: A solid nucleus gains volume free energy and pays surface energy: r* = 2γT_m ÷ (ΔH_f ΔT) and ΔG* varies as 1 ÷ ΔT². Larger undercooling means smaller nuclei and a lower barrier.

los.do: Tell a glass transition from melting.
los.ek: A crystal melts sharply at T_m. An amorphous solid has no T_m: it softens over the glass transition T_g, where the slope of volume against temperature changes. A semicrystalline polymer shows both.

los.do: Use fracture toughness to find a critical stress or flaw size.
los.ek: K = Yσ√(πa); fracture when K reaches K_IC. For a surface crack a is the depth, for an internal crack half the length.

los.do: Apply the Griffith criterion and tell ductile from brittle fracture.
los.ek: A brittle crack grows when the elastic energy released pays for the new surface: σ_c = √(2Eγ_s ÷ πa). Ductile fracture absorbs far more energy through plastic flow (cup and cone); BCC metals turn brittle below a transition temperature.

los.do: Compute the stress at the tip of a flaw.
los.ek: σ_m = 2σ₀√(a ÷ ρ_t): the maximum stress at a crack of length a and tip radius ρ_t. Sharp cracks concentrate stress; drilling a hole at the tip blunts it.

los.do: Describe a fatigue cycle and read an S-N curve.
los.ek: σ_m = (σ_max + σ_min) ÷ 2, σ_a = (σ_max − σ_min) ÷ 2, R = σ_min ÷ σ_max. Steels and titanium alloys have a fatigue limit below which life is unlimited; aluminium, copper and magnesium do not.

los.do: Use the Paris law for fatigue crack growth.
los.ek: da/dN = A(ΔK)^m with ΔK = YΔσ√(πa) and m about 2 to 4 for metals. Life is the integral of dN from the initial to the critical crack length.

los.do: Work with steady-state creep and the Larson-Miller parameter.
los.ek: Steady creep rate goes as σⁿ exp(−Q_c ÷ RT); creep matters above about 0.4 of the absolute melting temperature. The Larson-Miller parameter T(C + log t_r), with C about 20 and t_r in hours, trades temperature against rupture life.

los.do: Predict a ceramic's coordination from the radius ratio and name the common structures.
los.ek: The cation takes as many anion neighbours as can touch it: r_C ÷ r_A of 0.225 to 0.414 gives tetrahedral (4), 0.414 to 0.732 octahedral (6), 0.732 to 1.0 cubic (8).

los.do: Compute a ceramic's density and cell edge from its ions.
los.ek: ρ = n′(ΣA_C + ΣA_A) ÷ (V_cell N_A), with n′ formula units per cell. In rock salt the ions touch along the cell edge, so a = 2(r_C + r_A).

los.do: Compute a flexural strength from a three-point bend test.
los.ek: Ceramics are tested in bending because they are hard to grip in tension. For a rectangular bar σ_fs = 3FL ÷ 2bd², with L the support span.

los.do: Compute a thermal stress and a thermal shock limit.
los.ek: A constrained body heated or cooled by ΔT carries σ = EαΔT. A brittle solid survives a sudden temperature change of about σ_f ÷ Eα, so low expansion and high conductivity resist thermal shock.

los.do: Compute a continuous-fibre composite's modulus along the fibres.
los.ek: Loaded along the fibres, fibre and matrix strain equally (isostrain): E_c = E_m V_m + E_f V_f, the upper bound.

los.do: Compute the transverse modulus and say which loading gives which bound.
los.ek: Loaded across the fibres, fibre and matrix carry equal stress (isostress): 1 ÷ E_c = V_m ÷ E_m + V_f ÷ E_f, the lower bound, dominated by the soft matrix.

los.do: Compute the load carried by the fibres and the critical fibre length.
los.ek: Under isostrain F_f ÷ F_m = E_f V_f ÷ E_m V_m. A fibre reaches its full strength only if it is longer than l_c = σ_f d ÷ 2τ_c, with τ_c the fibre-matrix bond strength.

los.do: Compute a conductivity from carrier density and mobility.
los.ek: σ = n|e|μ, with e = 1.602 × 10⁻¹⁹ C. Metals have about one free electron per atom or more; their mobility, not their carrier count, falls on heating or alloying.

los.do: Classify a solid by its band gap and compute an intrinsic conductivity.
los.ek: Metals have a partly filled band or overlapping bands; semiconductors a gap under about 2 eV; insulators a wider one. An intrinsic semiconductor has equal electrons and holes: σ = n_i|e|(μ_e + μ_h).

los.do: Predict the carrier type a dopant gives.
los.ek: In silicon or germanium a group 15 atom (P, As, Sb) donates an electron: n-type. A group 13 atom (B, Al, Ga, In) accepts one and leaves a hole: p-type.

los.do: Classify magnetic behaviour and state what a superconductor does.
los.ek: Diamagnets weakly oppose a field; paramagnets weakly align with it; ferromagnets (Fe, Co, Ni) align strongly and stay magnetised below the Curie temperature. Below T_c a superconductor has zero resistance and expels magnetic flux.

los.do: Read a steel designation and tell the classes of ferrous alloy apart.
los.ek: In AISI/SAE four-digit steels the last two digits are carbon in hundredths of a weight percent: 1040 is plain carbon with 0.40% C. Stainless steels need at least about 11% Cr. Gray iron has graphite flakes, ductile iron spheroids.

los.do: Identify the common nonferrous alloys and how they are strengthened.
los.ek: Brass is Cu-Zn, bronze Cu-Sn. Aluminium tempers: T means solution treated and aged, H strain hardened, O annealed. Titanium alloys give the best strength to weight; nickel superalloys keep strength hot.

los.do: Match a manufacturing process to what it does to the metal.
los.ek: Casting fills a mould with liquid; forging, rolling, extrusion and drawing shape the solid, hot (above recrystallization, no hardening) or cold (strain hardened, better finish); powder metallurgy presses and sinters powder; welding leaves a heat-affected zone.

los.do: Choose between XRD, EDS and XPS.
los.ek: X-ray diffraction gives crystal structure, phases and lattice parameters. EDS in an electron microscope gives elemental composition from characteristic X-rays. XPS gives the composition and chemical state of the top few nanometres.

los.do: Choose between optical, scanning and transmission electron microscopy.
los.ek: Optical microscopes resolve about 0.2 µm and show grains on a polished, etched surface. SEM resolves nanometres with great depth of field on bulk samples. TEM passes electrons through a thin foil and images dislocations and lattice planes.

los.do: Choose between DSC and TGA and read what each shows.
los.ek: DSC (and DTA) record heat flow against temperature: glass transitions, melting, crystallisation, heats of reaction. TGA records mass against temperature: drying, decomposition, oxidation, filler content.

los.do: Run a heat balance for heating and melting a charge.
los.ek: Q = m[c_p(T_m − T₀) + L_f]: sensible heat to the melting point plus latent heat. Furnace energy is this divided by the thermal efficiency.

los.do: Compute a standard free energy of oxidation and where it changes sign.
los.ek: ΔG° = ΔH° − TΔS°. On an Ellingham diagram this is a line of slope −ΔS°; an oxide decomposes on heating above the temperature where its line crosses zero.

los.do: Decide from free energies of formation whether one metal reduces another's oxide.
los.ek: Compare the oxides per mole of O₂: the element whose oxide has the more negative ΔG° takes the oxygen. Carbon's line to CO slopes downward, so carbon reduces more oxides the hotter it gets.

los.do: Compute the entropy and enthalpy of mixing of a binary solution.
los.ek: Ideal mixing: ΔS = −R(x ln x + (1 − x) ln(1 − x)), largest at x = 0.5. A regular solution adds ΔH = Ωx(1 − x): positive Ω means like atoms prefer each other.

los.do: Link a solution model to the shape of the phase diagram.
los.ek: Phases in equilibrium share a common tangent to their free-energy curves. A regular solution with Ω > 2RT has a double-welled curve and separates into two phases; the miscibility gap closes at T_c = Ω ÷ 2R.

los.do: Estimate a casting's solidification time with Chvorinov's rule.
los.ek: t = B(V ÷ A)²: freezing time goes as the square of the volume-to-surface ratio (the casting modulus). A riser must have a larger modulus than the section it feeds.

los.do: Compute radiant heat loss from a hot surface.
los.ek: q = εσA(T⁴ − T_s⁴), with σ = 5.670 × 10⁻⁸ W/m²·K⁴. Because of the fourth power, radiation dominates the heat loss of hot metal.

los.do: Use residence time for a ladle or tundish.
los.ek: Mean residence time τ = V ÷ Q. In a well-mixed vessel a step change washes out as exp(−t ÷ τ); plug flow would deliver it all at once after τ.

los.do: Use the Biot number to choose a quench model.
los.ek: Bi = hL_c ÷ k compares surface convection with conduction inside. Below about 0.1 the part is nearly uniform and a lumped model works; above it, the inside lags and a conduction solution is needed.

los.do: Choose and compute a material index for a light, stiff or strong part.
los.ek: Translate the design: function, constraint, objective, free variable. A light stiff tie maximises E ÷ ρ, a beam E^½ ÷ ρ, a panel E^⅓ ÷ ρ; a light strong tie σ_y ÷ ρ.

los.do: Compare two materials by index and read a selection chart.
los.ek: For a tie of fixed stiffness the mass goes as ρ ÷ E. On a log-log property chart, materials on a line of slope set by the index perform equally; those above it are better.

los.do: Compute a shape factor and say what limits it.
los.ek: Shape puts material far from the neutral axis. The elastic bending shape factor φ = 4πI ÷ A² is 1 for a solid round bar; for a tube it is (r_o² + r_i²) ÷ (r_o² − r_i²).

los.do: Compute an embodied energy and name the stages of a life cycle assessment.
los.ek: Embodied energy is mass times the energy to make a kilogram, less with recycled content. An LCA sets a functional unit, then counts material production, manufacture, use and end of life.

los.do: Find the cell voltage of a galvanic couple and which metal corrodes.
los.ek: The metal with the lower (more negative) potential is the anode and corrodes; the emf is E_cathode − E_anode. A small anode joined to a large cathode corrodes fastest.

los.do: Apply the Nernst equation to a metal electrode.
los.ek: E = E° + (0.0592 ÷ n) log[Mⁿ⁺] at 25 °C: a metal in a dilute solution of its ions is more active, which is what drives a concentration cell.

los.do: Compute a corrosion rate from weight loss and from current density.
los.ek: Penetration in mm/yr = 87.6W ÷ (ρAt), with W in mg, ρ in g/cm³, A in cm², t in hours. By Faraday's law a corrosion current density i removes iM ÷ (nFρ) of depth per second.

los.do: Read the active, passive and transpassive regions of a polarization curve.
los.ek: A passive metal (stainless steel, aluminium, titanium) forms a thin oxide film and its corrosion current falls by orders of magnitude as the potential rises; at higher potential still the film breaks down. Chlorides break the film locally and cause pitting.

los.do: Compute a Pilling-Bedworth ratio and judge the oxide scale.
los.ek: P-B ratio = volume of oxide formed ÷ volume of metal consumed = (M_oxide ρ_metal) ÷ (n M_metal ρ_oxide). Under 1 the scale is porous; 1 to 2 protective; well above 2 it cracks and spalls. A protective scale grows parabolically.

los.do: Tell stress-corrosion cracking, hydrogen embrittlement and corrosion fatigue apart.
los.ek: SCC needs a tensile stress, a susceptible alloy and a specific environment together. Hydrogen embrittlement comes from atomic hydrogen entering high-strength steel. Corrosion fatigue removes the fatigue limit.

los.do: Choose a protection method and size a sacrificial anode.
los.ek: Cathodic protection makes the structure the cathode, by a sacrificial anode (Zn, Mg, Al) or an impressed current. Anodic protection holds a passivating alloy in its passive range. Coatings are barriers; inhibitors slow the anodic or cathodic reaction. Anode mass consumed is ItM ÷ nF.

los.do: Describe how polymers and ceramics degrade.
los.ek: Polymers swell or dissolve in chemically similar liquids, and their chains are cut by UV, heat, oxygen and hydrolysis. Ceramics are already oxides and resist corrosion, but dissolve in molten slags and, for silicates, in hydrofluoric acid and strong alkali.

los.do: Compute wear volume with Archard's law and name the wear modes.
los.ek: V = KFs ÷ H: wear volume grows with load and sliding distance and falls with hardness; K is a dimensionless wear coefficient found by test.

los.do: Compute the size of a random-coil chain.
los.ek: A freely jointed chain of n links of length l has root-mean-square end-to-end distance l√n, far shorter than its contour length nl. That gap is why rubber can stretch several hundred percent.

los.do: Match a molar-mass method to the average it gives and use the Mark-Houwink relation.
los.ek: Colligative methods (osmometry, end-group analysis) count molecules and give M_n; light scattering weights by size and gives M_w; viscometry gives M_v through [η] = K Mᵃ; gel permeation chromatography gives the whole distribution.

los.do: Use the Flory-Huggins parameter to judge solvent quality.
los.ek: χ measures polymer-solvent contact energy. Below 0.5 the solvent is good and coils swell; at 0.5 (the theta condition) they are ideal; above it the polymer separates. For a chain of N segments the critical value is ½(1 + 1 ÷ √N)².

los.do: Estimate a glass transition temperature and say what moves it.
