PF: High/Critical, Capabilities + Safeguards Reports, SAG advises, Leadership decides. FSF: CCLs with alert thresholds and response plans, safety case reviews.

los.do: Evaluate a framework on threshold specificity, external verification, enforceability and how it can be revised, and find who can actually say no (drill: spot the flaw).
los.ek: Most frameworks are voluntary and revisable by the company; triggers vary widely across companies (IASR 2026); SAG cannot block leadership.

los.do: Identify which RSP threshold or obligation a described result triggers — CBRN, AI R&D-4 affirmative misalignment-risk case, sabotage risk report (drill: map to framework).
los.ek: Crossing AI R&D-4 requires an affirmative case naming the most immediate misalignment risks and mitigations; models clearly beyond Opus 4.5 get sabotage risk reports. v2 tied ASL-3 deployment and security standards to thresholds; v3 (Feb 2026) rewrote the policy around Risk Reports and Roadmaps.

los.do: Explain the RSP's accountability machinery — Risk Reports with coverage dates and marked redactions, LTBT-requested external review, noncompliance reporting — and what each makes verifiable.
los.ek: v3.4: unredacted Risk Reports to ≥200 staff; multiple external reviewers may split sections if all are covered.

los.do: Decide whether a described result reaches High or Critical in a tracked category and what is then required, and before when (drill: map to framework).
los.ek: Tracked: Bio/Chem, Cyber, AI Self-improvement. High: safeguards must sufficiently minimise risk before deployment. Critical: also during development. Thresholds are holistic calls; scalable evals carry only indicative thresholds.

los.do: Map a safeguard to the threat it answers — robustness, usage monitoring, trust-based access (malicious users) vs autonomy limits, value/instruction alignment, oversight, system architecture (misaligned model) (drill: classify).
los.ek: Misuse safeguards assume a benign model and a hostile user; misalignment safeguards assume the model itself may act against you.

los.do: Evaluate the marginal-risk clause: when it lets OpenAI relax safeguards and what it does to race dynamics.
los.ek: Allowed only if overall risk doesn't meaningfully rise, it is publicly acknowledged, and OpenAI stays more protective than the other developer.

los.do: Identify which CCL a described capability approaches and the FSF response — alert threshold, response plan, safety case review, internal-deployment scope (drill: map to framework).
los.ek: Early-warning evals fire alert thresholds before a CCL; reaching a CCL needs a safety case review before external launch, and for advanced ML R&D CCLs before large internal deployments too. v3 added a harmful-manipulation CCL; TCLs flag lesser risks sooner.

los.do: Structure a safety case as claims, arguments and evidence, and classify its argument as inability, control or trustworthiness (drill: classify).
los.ek: Inability: the model can't. Control: it can't cause harm even if it tries, given the protocol. Trustworthiness: it won't.

los.do: Find the weakest premise in a described safety case (drill: spot the flaw).
los.ek: A case is as strong as its least-supported premise; inability arguments rest on elicitation, control arguments on red-team strength, trustworthiness arguments on evidence we mostly don't have yet.

los.do: Decide from training compute whether a model is GPAI and whether it is presumed to carry systemic risk (drill: compute).
los.ek: Indicative GPAI criterion: > 10²³ FLOP and generates language. Systemic risk presumed above 10²⁵ FLOP (under review); the Commission can also designate.

los.do: Identify which GPAI obligation a described provider has missed, separating all-provider duties from systemic-risk duties (drill: map to framework).
los.ek: All providers: technical documentation, information for downstream providers, copyright policy, public training-content summary. Systemic risk: notify the Commission, evaluate incl. adversarial testing, assess and mitigate risk, report serious incidents, ensure cybersecurity.

los.do: State the GPAI timeline, the open-source carve-out, and the role of the Code of Practice.
los.ek: Obligations apply from 2 Aug 2025; Commission enforcement from 2 Aug 2026; models placed earlier comply by 2 Aug 2027. Free open-source models skip some documentation duties unless systemic-risk. The Code (Transparency, Copyright, Safety & Security) is a voluntary route to show compliance.

los.do: Sort described risk-management activities into Govern, Map, Measure and Manage (drill: classify).
los.ek: Govern: culture, roles, policy (cuts across). Map: context and risks of a use. Measure: assess and track. Manage: prioritise, act, monitor over time.

los.do: Map a Generative AI Profile risk (e.g. CBRN information or capabilities, confabulation, information security) to the Measure actions an eval team would own, and explain how voluntary standards become binding.
los.ek: AI 600-1 lists 12 GAI risks with actions keyed to the four functions. Standards bind through procurement, contracts and, in the EU, harmonised standards that give a presumption of conformity.

los.do: Explain why compute is a governance lever — detectable, excludable, quantifiable, with a concentrated supply chain — and list the tools it enables (export controls, cloud KYC, reporting thresholds, on-chip mechanisms).
los.ek: A handful of firms control fabrication, lithography and leading chips; frontier runs need clusters visible to the cloud providers that host them.

los.do: Estimate a run's training compute from cluster size, chip throughput, utilisation and duration, and compare it to regulatory thresholds (drill: compute).
los.ek: C = N_chips × FLOP/s × MFU × seconds; 10⁴ chips × 10¹⁵ FLOP/s × 0.4 × 90 days ≈ 3 × 10²⁵ FLOP.

los.do: Evaluate the weaknesses of fixed compute thresholds: algorithmic efficiency, post-training and inference compute, distillation.
los.ek: A fixed FLOP line falls behind as efficiency improves 2–6×/yr; capability can be reached below it, or added after pretraining.

topics.title: International coordination and the evidence dilemma

los.do: Identify the coordination problem in a described scenario — race to the bottom, verification gap, free-riding, non-credible commitment (drill: classify).
los.ek: Without verification, mutual restraint is unstable: each side fears the other defects.

los.do: Trace the summit-and-institute track — Bletchley 2023, Seoul commitments 2024, Paris 2025, India 2026; the AISI/CAISI network; the International AI Safety Report — and what each actually produced.
los.ek: Seoul: companies committed to publish safety frameworks. Institutes test pre-deployment under voluntary agreements, can't block release, and publish findings unevenly (UK AISI more, CAISI less).

los.do: Explain the evidence dilemma and how if-then commitments and transparency requirements respond to it.
los.ek: IASR 2026: evidence about risk arrives slower than capability; acting early risks bad policy, waiting risks exposure. If-then rules commit now to act on evidence later.

los.do: Map who can act on a given frontier-AI decision — labs, compute providers, governments, standards bodies, investors — and where each depends on the others.
los.ek: Leverage sits at chokepoints: chips, cloud, capital, talent, market access; policy windows open when one of them shifts.

los.do: Argue both sides of the open-weights question using marginal risk, irreversibility and the closed–open capability gap, and name your crux.
los.ek: Open models trail the closed frontier by under a year (IASR) / 4–8 months (AISI); benefits to research and access; safeguards removable, weights unrecallable.

los.do: Build a simple timeline forecast from compute growth, algorithmic progress and a benchmark trend, and name the bottleneck most likely to break it (drill: compute).
los.ek: IASR 2026 bottlenecks: data, chips, capital, energy. Capability is 'jagged' — strong on some hard tasks, weak on some easy ones — so one trend line rarely means 'AGI'.

los.do: Make probabilistic forecasts on AI questions and score them with the Brier score (drill: compute).
los.ek: Brier = mean (p − o)²; 0 is perfect, 0.25 is always saying 50 %.

los.do: Explain the AI-R&D feedback loop behind fast takeoff, what limits it, and why AI R&D thresholds are the frameworks' early warning for it.
los.ek: If AI multiplies research output, progress compounds (software intelligence explosion), limited by experiment compute. PF Critical: generational gains in 1/5 the 2024 time; RSP AI R&D-4; FSF ML R&D CCLs extend reviews to internal deployment.

los.do: Classify a described scenario as misuse, malfunction/loss of control or systemic risk, and name the mitigation layer that does most against it (drill: classify).
los.ek: IASR 2026 taxonomy: malicious use (content, influence, cyber, bio/chem); malfunctions (reliability, loss of control); systemic (labour, autonomy).

los.do: Compare loss-of-control, misuse and power-concentration threat models on what drives their likelihood and which interventions help each.
los.ek: Misuse: access and uplift → safeguards, security. Loss of control: misalignment + autonomy → alignment, control. Power concentration: AI replacing the cooperation that checks power → governance, distribution.

los.do: Compare strategies for the transition — safe-lead racing, coordinated pause, defensive acceleration, frameworks-plus-regulation — by their assumptions and failure modes, and stress-test one against accelerating capability and competition.
los.ek: Each strategy bets on something: verification, a lead, defence outpacing offence, or institutions keeping pace.

los.do: Prioritise safety interventions by importance, tractability and neglectedness and your comparative advantage, and state a theory of change with its crux.
los.ek: Theory of change: action → intermediate outcome → risk reduction. A crux is a belief whose change would flip the decision.

los.do: Split an attention head into its QK and OV circuits and say what each decides.
los.ek: W_QK = W_Qᵀ W_K decides where to attend; W_OV = W_V W_O decides what gets moved.

los.do: Compute a component's direct logit attribution for a correct-vs-wrong token pair (drill: compute).
los.ek: DLA = (component output, scaled by the final LayerNorm) · (W_U[:, correct] − W_U[:, wrong]).

los.do: Identify the prompt-injection pathways in a described agent deployment and the least-privilege or containment control for each (drill: classify).
los.ek: Untrusted data in the context is an instruction channel; limit tools, permissions and egress so a hijacked agent can do little.

los.do: Explain why per-instance monitors miss distributed attacks across many agent instances.
los.ek: Each instance's actions can look benign; the harm lies in the combination, so monitoring must aggregate across instances.

los.do: Relate the reproduction number, growth rate, generation interval and doubling time.
los.ek: T_d = ln 2 / r; with a fixed generation interval T_g, R = e^{rT_g}.

los.do: Compute the herd-immunity threshold from R₀, and R₀ from it.
los.ek: Threshold = 1 − 1/R₀.

los.do: Distinguish case and infection fatality ratios and correct for under-ascertainment.
los.ek: CFR = deaths/confirmed cases; IFR = deaths/infections; infections ≈ cases ÷ ascertainment.

los.do: Place landmark events in the history of pandemics and biological weapons.
los.ek: 1918 influenza; smallpox eradication certified 1980; BWC 1972; Sverdlovsk 1979; the 2001 anthrax letters.

los.do: Distinguish natural, accidental and deliberate biological risks and say what makes a risk catastrophic.
los.ek: Spillover, lab accident, misuse; transmissibility, severity and our ability to respond set the scale.

los.do: Name the links in the chain of infection and the stages of natural history, and say which measure breaks which link.
los.ek: Reservoir, portal of exit, transmission, portal of entry, susceptible host; incubation, latent and infectious periods.

los.do: Read an epidemic curve: point source, continuous or propagated, and the likely exposure time.
los.ek: Point source: one peak about one incubation period wide; exposure ≈ peak − median incubation.

los.do: Compute attack rates and secondary attack rates.
los.ek: Attack rate = cases ÷ population at risk; secondary attack rate counts contacts of primary cases only.

los.do: Distinguish incidence from prevalence and relate them through duration.
los.ek: Prevalence ≈ incidence rate × mean duration (steady state).

los.do: Compute a risk ratio or an odds ratio from a 2 × 2 table and say which design gives which.
los.ek: Cohort: RR = (a/(a+b))/(c/(c+d)); case-control: OR = ad/bc.

los.do: Compute attributable risk and the population attributable fraction.
los.ek: AR% among exposed = (RR − 1)/RR; PAF = p(RR − 1)/(1 + p(RR − 1)).

los.do: Order the steps of an outbreak investigation and apply case definitions.
los.ek: Prepare, confirm the outbreak, verify the diagnosis, define and find cases, describe by time, place and person, hypothesise, test, control, communicate.

los.do: Evaluate a surveillance system by sensitivity, predictive value and timeliness.
los.ek: Sensitivity = cases detected ÷ true cases; PVP = true cases ÷ cases reported.

los.do: Compute the final size of an epidemic and the effective reproduction number as susceptibles fall.
los.ek: Final size z solves z = 1 − e^{−R₀z}; R_eff = R₀ × susceptible fraction.

los.do: Explain superspreading with the dispersion parameter and compute the chance a case transmits to no one.
los.ek: Negative binomial offspring: P(0) = (1 + R/k)^{−k}; small k means most cases infect no one and a few infect many.

los.do: State what the BWC prohibits, how it is implemented and reviewed, and what it lacks.
los.ek: Article I: never develop, produce, stockpile or acquire; no verification regime; confidence-building measures; a small Implementation Support Unit.

los.do: Match export controls and other regimes (Australia Group, UNSCR 1540) to what they do.
los.ek: Australia Group harmonises national export lists; UNSCR 1540 obliges states to keep WMD from non-state actors.

los.do: Explain DNA synthesis screening: what is screened and why both sequence and customer matter.
los.ek: Screen orders against sequences of concern and verify customers; benchtop synthesisers move the checkpoint.

los.do: Recognise dual-use research of concern and the oversight and publication choices around it.
los.ek: Research reasonably expected to give knowledge or products that could be misapplied; review before funding and before publishing.

los.do: Describe layered AI model safeguards and compute the residual risk through independent layers.
los.ek: Refusal training, input/output classifiers, evaluations, access controls; residual = product of each layer's miss rate.

los.do: Use the WHO risk-based approach: inherent versus residual risk, core requirements, heightened control and maximum containment.
los.ek: Risk assessment decides the controls; core requirements apply everywhere.

los.do: Choose primary containment (biosafety cabinet class) and compute filter penetration.
los.ek: Class I protects worker and environment, II also the sample, III is gas-tight; HEPA ≥ 99.97% at the most penetrating size.

los.do: Compute decontamination by log reduction and D-values.
los.ek: N = N₀·10^{−t/D}; a 6-log kill takes six D-values.

los.do: Place a national capacity in its JEE technical area and pillar.
los.ek: Prevent P1–P8, Detect D1–D3, Respond R1–R5, plus points of entry, chemical and radiation events.

los.do: Match surveillance systems to what they see and name the IHR's notification duties.
los.ek: Syndromic, wastewater, metagenomic, clinical; IHR (2005) PHEIC and, since 2025, the pandemic emergency.

los.do: Compute how detection delay translates into cases.
los.ek: Cases at time t = initial × 2^{t/T_d}.

los.do: Compute the sequencing depth needed to see a target at a given relative abundance.
los.ek: Expected target reads = total reads × relative abundance.

los.do: Compute the probability that sequencing sees at least one target read.
los.ek: Reads are Poisson: P(≥ 1) = 1 − e^{−λ}; 95% needs λ ≈ 3.

los.do: Compute predictive values of a test from sensitivity, specificity and prevalence.
los.ek: PPV falls as prevalence falls; a second independent positive raises it.

los.do: Estimate airborne infection risk with the Wells–Riley model and combine air-cleaning rates.
los.ek: P = 1 − exp(−Iqpt/Q); equivalent air changes add.

los.do: Explain far-UVC, filtration and ventilation and compute clearance times.
los.ek: 222 nm barely penetrates the skin's dead layer; 99% removal takes ln 100 / ACH hours.

los.do: Check a room against an equivalent clean airflow per person target.
los.ek: Total clean air = outdoor air + filtered recirculation × efficiency + air cleaners; ECA per person = total ÷ occupants.

los.do: Compare respirator classes by filtration and assigned protection factor, and compute the effect of masking on R.
los.ek: N95 filters ≥ 95%; APF 10 half-mask, 50 full-face, 25 loose PAPR; R_eff = R(1 − ce).

los.do: Compute the effect of testing, isolation and contact tracing on R, and match measures to transmission routes.
los.ek: Removing a fraction f of onward transmission multiplies R by 1 − f.

los.do: Describe rapid countermeasure programmes: platforms, the 100 Days Mission, financing and trials.
los.ek: CEPI's goal: vaccines within 100 days of a threat; platform technologies; advance commitments.

los.do: Compute the vaccination coverage needed for herd protection given vaccine efficacy.
los.ek: V_c = (1 − 1/R₀)/E; above 100% means vaccination alone cannot stop spread.

los.do: Compute vaccine efficacy from trial attack rates.
los.ek: VE = 1 − AR_vaccinated / AR_unvaccinated.

los.do: Compute the number needed to vaccinate and the expected cases averted.
los.ek: NNV = 1/(AR_unvaccinated × VE).

los.do: Name the global health governance instruments and who decides what.
los.ek: IHR (2005) and its 2024 amendments; the WHO Pandemic Agreement (2025); the Director-General declares a PHEIC on Emergency Committee advice.

los.do: Compute manufacturing and delivery rates needed to cover a population in time.
los.ek: Doses per day = population × doses per person ÷ days.

topics.title: Working responsibly and choosing a focus

los.do: Apply information-hazard norms in discussion and writing.
los.ek: Don't brainstorm new ways to cause harm; discuss defences, not attack details; ask before sharing.

los.do: Map an intervention to its layer and compute the combined protection of independent layers.
los.ek: P(all layers fail) = product of each layer's failure probability.

los.do: State what the legal-instruments and financing capacities require of a country
los.ek: A country needs the laws and regulations that let it act in an emergency, assessed before the emergency rather than drafted during it, and a financing route that releases money fast enough to matter; both are capacities that look like paperwork and fail only when they are needed.

los.do: State what the National IHR Focal Point is for and what it must be able to do
los.ek: Every State Party names a focal point reachable at all times that notifies the WHO of events and relays information inside the country, so the capacity being assessed is a channel and the authority to use it, not an office.

los.do: Compute antimicrobial consumption in defined daily doses per 1000 inhabitants per day
los.ek: Consumption is reported in defined daily doses per thousand inhabitants per day so that countries and years can be compared, and it is the denominator against which a resistance trend is read: rising resistance with flat consumption points somewhere other than prescribing.

los.do: Compute a resistance proportion and what a stated change means for empirical therapy
los.ek: A resistance proportion is isolates resistant over isolates tested, and once it passes the threshold a guideline sets, the empirical first choice has to change: the number is surveillance, the threshold is policy.

los.do: State what zoonotic-disease and food-safety capacities each require and where they meet
los.ek: Zoonotic capacity is joint human, animal and environmental surveillance with a route for one sector to act on another's signal; food safety is the ability to trace a contaminated product and recall it. Both are One Health capacities, and most emerging human pathogens arrive through them.

los.do: Compute an attack rate and the food-specific risk ratio in a stated outbreak investigation
los.ek: A food-specific attack rate among those who ate an item, against those who did not, gives the risk ratio that identifies the vehicle; the investigation is a case-control or cohort calculation done against the clock.

los.do: Compute the immunization coverage a stated reproduction number needs, and the effective coverage a vaccine's efficacy gives
los.ek: The herd-immunity threshold is one minus the reciprocal of the reproduction number, and because no vaccine is perfectly effective the coverage needed is that threshold divided by the efficacy, which is why a highly transmissible pathogen can need coverage above what any real programme reaches.

los.do: State what a national laboratory system must provide and what tiering it
los.ek: The capacity is reliable testing for the priority diseases, a specimen referral and transport system that reaches it, and a quality system that makes the results trustworthy; tiering puts screening near the patient and confirmation in reference laboratories.

los.do: Compute specimen turnaround time and what a stated referral delay costs an outbreak response
los.ek: Turnaround is collection to result, and every day of it is a day of transmission the response cannot act on: a test that is accurate but slow has the epidemiological value of a test that is not done.

los.do: Compute a public-health workforce density and the field-epidemiology output a stated target needs
los.ek: Workforce capacity is measured as staff per unit population, and a trained field epidemiologist is the scarcest part: a programme graduating a fixed cohort a year takes a predictable number of years to reach a density target.

los.do: State what health emergency management requires beyond a written plan
los.ek: The capacity is an emergency operations centre that can be activated within hours with named people, a plan that has been exercised, and the legal authority to direct resources; a plan that has never been exercised is evidence of intent rather than of capacity.

los.do: Compute the surge demand a stated caseload puts on beds and oxygen
los.ek: Surge demand is incident cases times the fraction needing that level of care times the length of stay, which converts an epidemic curve into beds and oxygen: the peak, not the total, is what decides whether the system holds.

los.do: Compute a healthcare-associated infection rate and the effect of a stated compliance change
los.ek: Infection rates are reported per thousand patient-days or per device-day so that a busier ward is comparable with a quieter one, and the interventions that move them are hand hygiene, device care and isolation rather than new agents.

los.do: State what risk communication and community engagement must achieve and how it fails
los.ek: The capacity is a channel to the public that is in place before the emergency and trusted when it arrives, with messages that say what is known, what is not, and what to do; it fails by silence, by over-reassurance later contradicted, and by addressing a population that does not use that channel.

los.do: Compute the detections a stated border screening programme can expect, and its positive predictive value
los.ek: Entry screening detects the fraction of infected travellers who are symptomatic at that moment, so for a pathogen with a long incubation it finds very few; the arithmetic is why border measures delay rather than prevent introduction.

los.do: Compute the dilution or distance a stated chemical release requires to reach an exposure guideline
los.ek: Chemical-event capacity is an inventory of what is held where, guideline exposure levels for each, and the ability to model a release well enough to decide who shelters and who evacuates.

los.do: Compute dose rate against distance, time and shielding for a stated radiation source
los.ek: Dose rate falls with the square of distance, rises with time and falls by half for each half-value layer of shielding, which is the whole of protective practice: distance first because it is free, then time, then shielding.

los.do: Compute the activity left after a stated decay time and when a source reaches a release level
los.ek: Activity falls by half each half-life, so a short-lived isotope is managed by waiting and a long-lived one by containment; which it is decides whether an incident is an evacuation or a cordon.

los.do: State what Articles II and III of the Convention require and of whom
los.ek: Article II requires existing stocks to be destroyed or diverted to peaceful purposes, and Article III forbids transferring the agents or assisting anyone to acquire them, which is what makes export controls and screening a treaty obligation rather than a courtesy.

los.do: State the routes the Convention gives for dealing with a suspected breach
los.ek: Article V provides for consultation and cooperation among the Parties, and Article VI allows a complaint to the Security Council, which may investigate; the Convention has no verification organisation of its own, which is the structural weakness every review conference returns to.

los.do: State what Article VII provides and what triggers it
los.ek: A Party exposed to danger as a result of a violation may request assistance, and the other Parties undertake to provide it if the Security Council decides the Party has been exposed; the obligation is to help a victim, not to deter an attacker.

los.do: State what Article X protects and the tension it creates with Article III
los.ek: Article X protects the right to exchange equipment, materials and information for peaceful purposes and to participate in that exchange, so every control measure under Article III has to be justified against it: the Convention's bargain is non-proliferation without blocking public-health and industrial biology.

los.do: Breathe low and silently between phrases — ribs and abdomen expand, shoulders stay down — while reading a passage aloud, with no audible gasps.
los.ek: Expansion belongs in the lower ribs, abdomen and back; a 'big breath' raises the shoulders and tightens the throat. Outflow is regulated by slow, even abdominal contraction — 'less is more', don't fill to capacity.

los.do: In a timed rep, sustain a steady exhale on [s] for a target count (build 4 → 8 → 16) and then speak a full sentence on one breath without trailing off.
los.ek: Rosine's 4-in / 2-hold / 4-out pattern, extended to 8 and 16 on [s] or [v], trains even outflow. Sentences that fade at the end usually ran out of air, not volume — mark breath points with a slash.

los.do: Set volume to the room: in a timed rep, deliver the same 30-second passage at conversational, small-room (~25 people) and large-room levels without pitch rising or the throat tightening.
los.ek: Small classroom or office: a few steps above conversational volume; larger rooms need projection or a microphone; beginners usually err too quiet. Projection comes from breath pressure and open resonance (pharynx first, then mouth; nose only for m n ŋ), not from pushing the larynx — strain shows up as rising pitch and hoarseness.

los.do: Classify a consonant by manner (plosive, fricative, nasal, lateral, affricate) and voicing, and name the articulators that make it.
los.ek: Plosives p b t d k g stop then release; fricatives f v s z ʃ ʒ θ ð partly block; nasals m n ŋ route through the nose; l is lateral; tʃ dʒ are affricates. Voiced/unvoiced pairs: b/p, d/t, g/k, z/s, v/f, ʒ/ʃ, dʒ/tʃ.

los.do: In a timed rep, read a dense technical sentence at 150 wpm with every final consonant and unstressed syllable audible on playback.
los.ek: Dropped and merged sounds — 'gonna', 'dinnt', 'hunnerd', 'probly' — are the common faults; low volume makes them worse. Slowing slightly and using lips, tongue tip and teeth fully restores them; mumbling = small jaw and lip movement, slurring = rate outrunning the articulators.

topics.title: Pronunciation and word choice for the ear

los.do: Rewrite a written sentence for the ear: shorter clauses, the subject and verb early, acronyms spelled out on first use.
los.ek: Listeners can't re-read; long noun stacks and late verbs overload working memory. NCA competency 5: language clear, vivid, free of unexplained jargon for this audience. Check unfamiliar names and terms against dictionary audio or someone who knows; pick one accepted pronunciation, rehearse it aloud, use it consistently (NCA 7).

los.do: Compute wpm from a transcript and its duration, and classify the result as slow, presentation-range, conversational or fast.
los.ek: wpm = words ÷ minutes; conversation ≈ 150 (NCVS), comfortable presentation ≈ 125–150, audiobooks 150–160. Below ~100 reads as hesitant or unprepared; sustained >180 overwhelms after a minute or two.

los.do: In a timed 60-second rep, hold 140–160 wpm on an answer and 125–150 wpm on an explanation, checked from the transcript.
los.ek: Top-scored practice talks in VirtualSpeech's data had a median of 138 wpm. Fast is the more common fault; nerves push rate up.

los.do: Vary rate on purpose within one answer — slow for the key claim or a hard step, faster for context — and point to where on playback.
los.ek: Rate is a signal: slowing marks importance or difficulty, speeding adds momentum; one steady rate for minutes reads as monotone. RiseGuide scores both rate and how much it varies.

los.do: Place deliberate 1–2 second pauses after the main point, between sections and before a key number, and mark them with '/' or '//' on a script before delivering it.
los.ek: Intended pauses add emphasis and signal transitions; the speaker feels them as longer than the listener does. Mark breath and pause points on the outline; a pause after a question gives the room time to think.

los.do: Classify a described pause as a deliberate pause, a fluency hiccup, or a filled pause, and say whether it helped or hurt.
los.ek: Fluency hiccups come from losing your place or thread; a brief silent hiccup often goes unnoticed or reads as deliberate. A filled pause (um, uh) spends the same time and announces the trouble.

los.do: Start every on-the-spot answer with a silent 1–2 second pause instead of a filler or a restatement of the question.
los.ek: Silent pausers are rated surer than filler users (Brennan & Williams 1995, in Clark & Fox Tree 2002). The opening pause is where the structure gets chosen.

los.do: Count fillers per minute in a recording or transcript, separating filler sounds (um, uh, er) from filler words (like, you know, so, basically, right?).
los.ek: Fillers/min = count ÷ minutes; a student logged ~30 'um's in 3 minutes (10/min). Filler sounds hurt perceived effectiveness more than filler words (Laske et al. 2024).

los.do: In a timed 60-second rep on a random prompt, deliver with ≤ 3 filler sounds (target ≤ 1), measured from the transcript.
los.ek: 12 fillers/min clearly lowered listener ratings; ≤5/min was not significantly harmful — 'acceptable' is the floor, not the goal. Um announces a long delay, uh a short one: frequent ums mean the thinking is happening mid-sentence.

los.do: Apply awareness training and a competing response: name your top two fillers, catch them on playback, then replace each with a closed-mouth silent pause or breath in the next rep.
los.ek: Awareness training (identify, record, count) alone has reduced filled pauses in JABA studies; habit reversal adds a competing response — a silent pause where the filler would go. Fillers cluster at sentence starts and transitions; 'so' and 'and' chaining sentences is the same leak.

los.do: End declarative sentences with a falling pitch, and in a recorded rep make every claim sentence of a 60-second answer fall rather than rise.
los.ek: Rising terminals on statements (upspeak) sound like questions and invite doubt; a slight drop marks completion, serious points and the ending. A lower pitch at the close cues the room that you're done.

los.do: Diagnose a described voice as monotone, sing-song, upspeaking or pressed, and choose the correction.
los.ek: Speakers believe they vary pitch more than listeners hear — recording is the check. Range exercise: slide from your highest to lowest comfortable note and back; use more of that range for key words.

los.do: Mark the one key word per sentence in a script and, on playback, stress it with pitch, volume or a pause before it — and change the meaning by moving the stress.
los.ek: 'I didn't say she took it' has seven meanings by stressed word; emphasis tells the listener where the information is. Stressing everything stresses nothing.

los.do: Pick the stronger of two recorded or described deliveries of the same line on vocal variety, and name what made the difference.
los.ek: NCA 'excellent' vocal variety: exceptionally varied yet conversational, controlled pace, clearly heard, pitch that enhances the message. Variety serves meaning — random variation is as distracting as none.

los.do: Hold eye contact for one complete thought per listener (about 3–5 seconds) and move across the room; on video, look at the lens for whole sentences.
los.ek: Eye contact gauges reaction and engages; darting or reading notes breaks it. On a call the lens is the listener's eyes.

los.do: Stand or sit grounded — feet planted, hands still at rest, gestures only on purpose — and on video count distracting movements (sway, fidget, touch face) per minute.
los.ek: NCA: posture, gesture, movement, facial expression and eye contact consistently reinforce the message; Toastmasters rates distracting or absent gestures 'Emerging'. Stillness reads as confidence; a gesture that matches a word (size, sequence, contrast) reinforces it.

los.do: Use a pre-speaking routine — two slow exhale-longer breaths, a planned first sentence, shoulders down — before class, a meeting turn or an interview answer.
los.ek: Nerves speed rate, raise pitch and shorten breath; a long exhale and a known first line counter all three. Comfort Level is its own Toastmasters criterion: the audience reads ease from voice and body.

los.do: Cut hedges and apologies from an answer — 'sorry, this might be wrong, but', 'I just think', 'kind of' — and in a rep state the claim plainly with its real confidence level once.
los.ek: Never apologise for an impromptu answer; hedging every clause signals less certainty than you have. Calibrated confidence: say 'I'm fairly sure' once, where it applies, not on every sentence.

los.do: In a timed rep, give the answer or recommendation in the first sentence (within ~10 seconds) of a 60-second response to a random question.
los.ek: Pyramid: the top line first, then the reasons that support it; any point that doesn't support the top gets cut. NCA 'excellent' thesis: every listener can state it within the opening few sentences.

los.do: Pick the stronger of two openings to the same question — answer-first or context-first — and say what the weaker one makes the listener wait for.
los.ek: Context-first ('So, background…') makes the listener hold details with no frame to hang them on. Busy listeners (committees, managers, interviewers) decide in the first sentence whether to keep listening.

los.do: Group support into two or three parallel reasons and announce the count ('two reasons: cost and risk').
los.ek: Reasons at one level should be the same kind of thing and not overlap; three is the most a listener reliably holds without notes.

los.do: In a timed 60-second rep, deliver a PREP answer: Point, Reason, Example, Point restated — each element identifiable in the transcript.
los.ek: PREP = state the point, give a reason, support with one specific example, restate the point. One concrete example beats three vague ones.

los.do: Frame a meeting update or proposal as SCQA — Situation, Complication, Question, Answer — in four sentences.
los.ek: Situation = agreed current state; Complication = what changed or went wrong; Question = the one problem to solve; Answer = the recommendation the rest supports. Close by restating the answer and the ask.

los.do: Choose the right frame for a described prompt — PREP (opinion), SCQA (proposal), STAR (behavioural), past–present–future (trend), problem–solution — and justify it.
los.ek: The frame follows the question type; forcing STAR on an opinion question or PREP on a story wastes the structure.

los.do: Preview, signpost and summarise for the ear: announce the parts, mark each move ('first… the second reason… so'), and recap before closing; in a 2-minute rep, a listener can list your parts afterwards.
los.ek: Spoken structure must be audible — headings don't exist out loud. Tell them what you'll say, say it, tell them what you said: redundant on paper, necessary by ear.

los.do: Diagnose a described rambling answer — buried point, tangent, no transitions, circling back — and name the restructure.
los.ek: Rambling is usually a missing top line: the speaker is searching for the point while talking. The fix is choosing the point in the opening pause, not talking faster.

los.do: End on purpose: restate the point or give the ask in one sentence, drop pitch, then stop — no trailing 'so, yeah, that's it'.
los.ek: NCA 'excellent' conclusion reflects the content and leaves a strong message or call to action. The last sentence is the one remembered; trailing off spends it.

units.title: Impromptu speaking — table topics, Q&A, interviews

los.do: In a timed rep, take a random prompt, pause ≤ 3 seconds, and deliver a 60-second structured answer that lands within ±5 seconds of time.
los.ek: Impromptu = 1–3 minutes' notice or none; the pause is for choosing the point and the frame. Hitting time is a skill: plan point, one example, close — then stop.

los.do: When you don't know the answer, say what you do know, what you'd need to find out, and when — in under 20 seconds, without fillers or apology.
los.ek: Bluffing costs more credibility than a clear 'I don't know, here's how I'd find out'. A partial answer stated plainly is still an answer.

los.do: Answer an audience question with pause → one-sentence answer → one support → check ('does that get at it?'), in under 45 seconds in a rep.
los.ek: Q&A answers should be shorter than the talk's sections; the questioner wanted one thing. Repeat or rephrase the question only when the room didn't hear it — not as a stall. To return to your message, answer first, then bridge ('…and the bigger point is'); bridging without answering reads as evasion.

los.do: Classify a described question as clarifying, challenging, off-topic or a comment-not-a-question, and choose the response move for each.
los.ek: Challenge: acknowledge the point, give your reason, don't concede what you don't believe; off-topic: brief answer, offer to follow up; comment: thank and bridge.

los.do: In a timed 90–120-second rep, answer a 'tell me about a time' question in STAR with roughly 20 / 10 / 60 / 10 time split and a quantified result.
los.ek: Situation ~20%, Task ~10%, Action ~60% (what *you* did, even on a team), Result ~10% with numbers. Most weak STAR answers over-spend on Situation.

los.do: Diagnose a described STAR answer — too much context, 'we' instead of 'I', missing result, no lesson — and fix it.
los.ek: Use 'I' for your actions; state the outcome with a number and, if asked, what you'd do differently.

los.do: Deliver a 30-second answer to 'tell me about yourself' or 'what do you work on' that leads with the role and one through-line, then two proof points, tailored to the listener.
los.ek: Present → past → why-this: start with what you do now and the thread connecting teacher, chemist and AI-safety work, not a chronological biography.

los.do: Before explaining, state in one sentence what the listener already knows and what they need to be able to do afterwards, and cut anything that doesn't serve it.
los.ek: NCA 'excellent' topic: suited to purpose, time limit and audience, from real audience analysis. The expert's blind spot: once you know a thing it is hard to imagine not knowing it — name the prerequisite explicitly.

los.do: In a timed rep, explain a concept from your field in three sentences to a novice — what it is, a concrete example, why it matters — with no undefined jargon.
los.ek: Three sentences force the top line; every technical term is either defined in plain words or removed. Test: could the listener repeat the gist in their own words?

los.do: Re-pitch the same explanation at three levels — novice, adjacent expert, specialist — changing vocabulary, depth and examples while the top line stays the same.
los.ek: Depth and jargon change with the audience; the claim doesn't. Explaining a CBRN eval to a policy lawyer vs an ML engineer is the same idea with different handholds.

los.do: Order an explanation concrete → bridge → abstract: a specific case first, then the general rule or symbol.
los.ek: Concreteness fading (McNeil & Fyfe 2012): concrete, then intermediate, then abstract beat either alone on transfer at 1 and 3 weeks (70% vs 38% at ceiling). Lead with the example the listener can picture; name the rule once they've seen it work.

los.do: Build an analogy for a technical idea, then state explicitly where the analogy breaks.
los.ek: A good analogy maps the structure (what causes what), not surface features. Saying where it breaks prevents the listener from over-extending it.

los.do: Pick the stronger of two explanations of the same idea — abstract-first vs example-first, or jargon-dense vs plain — and say why.
los.ek: Example-first wins for novices; experts tolerate abstract-first but still benefit from a worked case.

los.do: Break a multi-step explanation into steps of one idea each, and pause after each step for the listener to try or restate it before moving on.
los.ek: Rosenshine: present new material in small steps with practice after each; aim for a high success rate before moving on.

los.do: Check understanding with a question that requires the listener to use the idea (predict, apply, explain back) instead of 'any questions?' or 'make sense?'.
los.ek: Effective teachers ask many questions and check every student's response, not just volunteers'. 'Make sense?' gets a nod; 'what would happen if we doubled it?' gets evidence.

los.do: Diagnose a described misunderstanding from a listener's answer and re-explain with a different example, not the same words louder.
los.ek: A wrong answer reveals the listener's model; repair the model, don't repeat the script.

topics.title: Numbers, precision and visuals out loud

los.do: State a number for the ear: round it, give one comparison ('about a third — one in three'), and say the unit.
los.ek: Listeners can't hold 3.847 × 10⁻⁴; give the order of magnitude and what it means. One well-chosen number beats a list of five.

los.do: Talk a listener through a figure or board diagram: say what the axes are, where to look, and the one takeaway, before the details.
los.ek: Supporting material should be clearly tied to the thesis and add clarity; a slide the speaker doesn't narrate is noise.

los.do: Outline a 2-minute pitch in Monroe's Motivated Sequence — attention, need, satisfaction, visualisation, action — one or two sentences each.
los.ek: Need = the problem, who it hurts and how much; Satisfaction = a concrete step-by-step plan; Visualisation = life once solved (and answering objections); Action = one easy, immediate ask.

los.do: Make a recommendation that names the strongest objection and answers it before the listener raises it.
los.ek: Pre-empting the obvious objection builds credibility with a sceptical audience; ignoring it invites it in Q&A. Back the answer with one piece of evidence and its source in a sentence — NCA: support tied to the thesis enhances credibility.

los.do: End a persuasive turn with one specific, easy ask (who does what, by when), and pick the stronger of two given asks.
los.ek: 'Let's think about it' is not an ask; 'can we pilot it on two evals by Friday?' is.

los.do: In a timed 90-second rep, tell a story with a person, a goal, an obstacle, a turn and a point, and say the point in the last sentence.
los.ek: A story needs someone wanting something and something in the way; the point is what changed. Specific details (a time, a place, a line of dialogue) make it vivid; background beyond that is cut.

los.do: Choose a short story or case to open a lesson or argument and connect it explicitly to the claim it illustrates.
los.ek: A story that isn't tied back is an anecdote; the bridge sentence ('that's why…') makes it evidence.

los.do: Paraphrase what someone said in one sentence and confirm it ('so your concern is X — right?') before responding.
los.ek: Paraphrase checks you heard the point, not just the words; it also slows a heated exchange. Answer the question they asked, not the one you prepared for.

los.do: Ask a follow-up question that builds on the speaker's last point rather than changing the subject, and classify given questions as open, closed or leading.
los.ek: Open questions ('what led you to…') invite elaboration; closed ones confirm facts; leading ones push an answer.

los.do: Make a meeting contribution in ≤ 30 seconds: connect to what was just said, give your point first, one reason, and the decision or next step you want.
los.ek: Short, point-first turns get heard; long preambles get interrupted. Linking ('building on Maria's point…') shows you listened and frames your turn.

los.do: Disagree in a meeting with acknowledge → position → reason → proposal, without hedging the position away.
los.ek: Separate the idea from the person; state your view at its real confidence level and propose what would resolve it.

los.do: Record a 60-second rep, get a transcript, and log four numbers: wpm, fillers/min, seconds to the main point, and longest silent pause.
los.ek: These four map onto the app scores: Pace, Pauses/fillers, Structure; Confidence needs listening for pitch and volume. Speakers misjudge their own pace, variety and fillers until they hear and count them.

los.do: Score a recording against the NCA eight competencies (1–3 each, 8–24 total) and name the lowest one as the next target.
los.ek: NCA competencies: topic, thesis, support, organisation, language, vocal variety, pronunciation/grammar/articulation, physical behaviours.

los.do: Set one measurable target per practice block (e.g. ≤ 2 fillers in 60 s, answer in first sentence), run 3–5 reps, and stop when it holds on 3 in a row.
los.ek: One target per rep: trying to fix pace, fillers and structure at once fixes none. Track the number across sessions; the trend, not one take, is the evidence.

los.do: Give a 2–3 minute spoken evaluation of someone's speech: one specific commend, one specific recommend with the moment it happened, one challenge.
los.ek: Toastmasters: what they excelled at, what they may want to work on, a stretch goal; feedback must be tactful, constructive and timed. Specific beats general: 'your pause before the 70% landed' not 'good pausing'. Receiving it: thank, ask one clarifying question, turn it into the next rep's target.

los.do: Rate a described delivery on a Toastmasters criterion (Clarity, Vocal Variety, Eye Contact, Gestures, Audience Awareness, Comfort, Interest, Well Supported) on the 1–5 scale and justify the rating.
los.ek: 5 Exemplary · 4 Excels · 3 Accomplished · 2 Emerging · 1 Developing; e.g. gestures 'distracting or limited' = 2.

los.do: Plan a 50-minute lecture as 10–15-minute segments, each with its own point, example and check for understanding, opened by a short review.
los.ek: Begin with a review of prior learning; attention and working memory reset between segments; each segment gets an answer-first top line.

los.do: Deliver from a keyword outline instead of a script, and on playback show eye contact and conversational rate held throughout.
los.ek: Reading drops eye contact, flattens pitch and speeds rate; a keyword outline keeps you talking to people. Mark 'SLOW DOWN', breath slashes and stressed words on the outline.

los.do: Fit a talk to its time slot: estimate length from word count at your measured wpm, cut to 90% of the slot, and finish within ±30 s in rehearsal.
los.ek: Minutes ≈ words ÷ wpm; at 130 wpm a 10-minute slot holds ~1 300 words — plan ~1 150 to leave room for pauses and questions.

los.do: Set up for a video call or recording — lens at eye level, light in front, mic 15–30 cm away — and keep energy one notch above in-person to compensate for compression.
los.ek: Video flattens vocal variety and facial expression; slightly more energy and pitch range reads as normal on screen. With a mic, keep a constant distance; don't project into it.

los.do: Handle a remote Q&A or interview turn with the lag in mind: finish with a clear falling ending and a handoff ('happy to go deeper on any of that') so no one talks over you.
los.ek: Latency of a few hundred ms causes collisions; clear endings and explicit handoffs replace the visual turn-taking cues lost on calls.

los.do: Given a 5-out, 4-out-1-in or 3-out-2-in alignment and a drive, choose which defender must help and which offensive player is left open.
los.ek: The nearest helper to the drive's path helps; whoever he left, and the rotation behind him, is the open man.

los.do: Identify spacing errors in a described or diagrammed half-court set (two players in one help zone, empty corner, crowded lane) and name the fix.
los.ek: Spacing sets help distance; teaching starts at ~12 ft apart (a lane width) and widens to 15–18 ft and the three-point line as range grows. A filled corner forces the low helper to choose between the rim and a corner three.

los.do: Choose the correct spacing move for each off-ball player on a drive — fill, lift, drift, or dive.
los.ek: Baseline drive: corner lifts to the wing or drifts behind; middle drive: wings drift to the corner, opposite shooters stay one pass away, the big dunker-spots.

los.do: Given a described catch, choose the triple-threat read: shoot if the closeout is late, drive the high foot if the defender is close, pass if help has arrived.
los.ek: The defender's distance and feet decide: space ⇒ shot, momentum toward you ⇒ drive past it, help shown ⇒ move it.

los.do: Name the ways an offense creates an advantage (ball screen, post touch, isolation, off-ball screen, transition, offensive rebound) and pick which fits a given personnel group.
los.ek: Advantage = a defender out of position or a numbers edge; it is created on-ball, off-ball or in the open floor.

los.do: Recognise a mismatch in a described lineup (size, speed, a poor defender) and choose how to attack it — post, isolate, or force it into the action.
los.ek: Attack the mismatch quickly, before the defense scrambles back; involve the weak defender as screener or screened.

topics.title: Keeping the advantage — the advantage chain

los.do: Given a described drive-and-kick sequence, choose the next action for the receiver (shoot, attack the closeout, swing, or extra pass).
los.ek: Decide on the catch (~0.5 s): an advantage held too long dies as the defense recovers. The extra pass beats a two-on-one closeout; driving a hard closeout beats a scrambled rotation.

los.do: Distinguish a good shot from a quick shot in a described possession by naming the advantage it came from.
los.ek: A good shot is an open, in-range attempt from a created advantage; a contested early shot with no advantage wastes the possession.

los.do: Given how a defender plays an off-ball screen (trails, goes under, cheats over, top-locks), choose the cut: curl, pop/fade, flare, or backdoor.
los.ek: Trail ⇒ curl; under or sagging ⇒ pop or fade; top-locked or overplayed ⇒ backdoor; defender shoots the gap ⇒ flare or re-screen.

los.do: Read a described post-entry: choose the entry angle and the post player's read against a double from the top, the baseline or no double.
los.ek: Enter from the wing at a 45° angle; a double from the top leaves the passer; from the baseline it leaves the opposite block or corner.

los.do: Choose when to backdoor, basket-cut or relocate when a defender denies or turns his head.
los.ek: Denial or ball-watching opens the backdoor; a cut must create a passing lane, not fill one already used.

los.do: Assign transition lanes and roles (ball, wings sprinting to corners, rim-runner, trailer) for a given rebound or turnover.
los.ek: Wide lanes stretch the retreat; the rim-runner forces the deepest defender to pick him up; the trailer arrives for a late three or a drag screen.

los.do: Given a 2-on-1, 3-on-2 or 4-on-3 break, choose who shoots or receives the pass.
los.ek: Make the last defender commit before passing; in a 3-on-2 the first pass usually goes to the wing the top defender didn't take.

los.do: Decide whether to push for an early-offense shot or flow into half-court, given numbers, score and clock.
los.ek: Push when numbers or mismatches exist before the defense sets; a leading team late may flow into half-court to burn clock.

los.do: Identify the ball-screen type (high, side, drag, step-up, spain, pick-and-pop) and its spacing in a described possession.
los.ek: Screen angle and location decide which way the ball goes and which helpers are involved.

los.do: Choose the ball-handler's set-up: reject, use, or re-screen, given how the on-ball defender is positioned.
los.ek: A defender jumping to take away the screen opens the reject; the ball-handler sets up his man before using the screen, shoulder to hip.

los.do: Given a described drop coverage, choose the read: pull-up, floater in the pocket, pop, or lob over a big who is too high.
los.ek: Drop concedes the pull-up and the pick-and-pop three; a deep drop takes away the roll.

los.do: Given a hedge/show or a blitz, choose the read: escape dribble, pass to the short roll, or skip to the open shooter.
los.ek: Two on the ball means 4-on-3 behind it; the short-roller is the decision-maker in that 4-on-3.

los.do: Given a switch, choose how to attack: slip before the switch, post the smaller defender, or isolate against the big.
los.ek: Switching gives up mismatches; slipping punishes an early switch.

los.do: Given ice/blue or weak coverage, choose the counter: reject, pop, or attack downhill to the weak hand.
los.ek: Ice forces the ball sideline and concedes the pop and long two; rejecting beats a defense that pre-rotates for the screen.

los.do: Choose the screener's action — roll, short-roll, pop, slip or ghost — given his skills and the coverage.
los.ek: Roll vs level/hedge, pop vs drop, slip vs switch or hard hedge, short-roll vs blitz.

los.do: Given which defender tags the roller, choose the pass: lob, pocket, kick to the tagger's man, or skip to the opposite corner.
los.ek: If the tag comes from the corner, the corner is open; if it comes from the wing, the skip or the lift is.

los.do: Choose the direction to force the ball (baseline, middle, weak hand) for a given scheme and scouting report, and justify it.
los.ek: Forcing baseline needs a low helper waiting; forcing middle relies on bodies in the gaps. Either way, take away the strength.

los.do: Place each defender correctly given where the ball is — on-ball, one pass away (deny or gap), two passes away (help side).
los.ek: Ball–you–man: see both; one pass away up the line, two passes away on the line (in the paint), nail help on middle drives. On-ball: between the man and the basket, about an arm's length, eyes on the waist.

los.do: Identify the low man on a described possession and his job when the ball is driven or a roller dives.
los.ek: Low man = deepest weak-side defender; he protects the rim or tags the roller, and the help behind him zones the two weak-side shooters.

los.do: Given a described drive or post touch, name who helps, who rotates to the helper's man, and who is left (the X-out or sink-and-fill).
los.ek: Help comes from the closest gap; rotation goes toward the basket first; the last defender splits two shooters.

los.do: Choose whether to stunt, dig or fully help on a drive given the driver and the shooter being left.
los.ek: Stunt and recover vs a non-shooter's teammate; never fully help off an elite shooter one pass away.

los.do: Choose the closeout type (high-hands shot contest, short closeout to take away the drive, run-by) for a described shooter and game situation.
los.ek: Sprint, then chop the last steps with hands high; close out short on a driver, high on a shooter; late in the game vs a must-make three, run him off the line.

los.do: Assign box-out responsibilities on a described shot, including the shooter and the weak side, where misses go long.
los.ek: Hit first, then pursue; long shots bounce long, often to the weak side.

los.do: Given a described live-ball turnover or long rebound, choose the transition defense priorities in order: stop the ball, protect the rim, find shooters, match up.
los.ek: First back takes the rim, the next stops the ball; matching up comes after the paint and the ball are safe.

los.do: Identify the coverage (drop, deep drop, at the level, hedge/show, blitz, ice, weak, switch) from a described position of the screener's defender and the on-ball defender.
los.ek: Drop: big several feet below the screen; level: at the screen; hedge: above it, then retreats; blitz: above and stays to trap; ice: ball forced sideline, big sitting below; switch: assignments trade.

los.do: State what each coverage takes away and what it concedes.
los.ek: Drop concedes pull-ups and pops; hedge/blitz concede the short roll and 4-on-3; switch concedes mismatches; ice concedes the pop and long two.

los.do: Choose the over/under/through route for the on-ball defender given the ball-handler's shooting range.
los.ek: Under a non-shooter, over a shooter; going under a pull-up shooter concedes the three.

los.do: Given a described ball-handler, screener and your two defenders, choose the coverage and justify it (an auto-checked pick).
los.ek: Non-shooting ball-handler ⇒ go under / drop; elite shooter ⇒ level, hedge or blitz; non-shooting screener ⇒ ice or drop is cheap; like-sized pair ⇒ switch. Mobile bigs can hedge and recover; slow bigs can't.

los.do: Assign the weak-side help (tagger, low man, X-out) behind a given coverage.
los.ek: Every coverage that sends two to the ball needs a tag on the roller and a rotation to the tagger's man.

los.do: Identify a zone (2-3, 3-2, 1-3-1, matchup) from a described alignment and response to the first pass.
los.ek: A zone guards areas, a man defense follows cutters; a matchup zone looks like man until a cutter crosses zones.

los.do: Name the weak spots of each standard zone.
los.ek: 2-3: high post, short corner, skip to corners; 1-3-1: corners and baseline; 3-2: the low blocks.

los.do: Choose man or a zone for a described opponent and justify it with their shooting, size and depth.
los.ek: Zones protect foul trouble and size mismatches and concede threes and offensive rebounds; man suits good individual defenders against motion teams.

los.do: Given a described zone and ball position, choose the attack: gap dribble, high-post entry, short-corner feed, skip pass, or overload.
los.ek: Make two defenders guard one; zones shift on the pass, so skips and quick ball reversal beat them. Line up in the gaps (odd front vs even, even front vs odd).

los.do: Identify a press (2-2-1, 1-2-1-1, 1-3-1) and its trap locations from a description.
los.ek: Presses trap near the sideline and the half-court corners, using the line as an extra defender.

los.do: Given a described trap, choose the outlet: middle, reversal, or the long pass over the top.
los.ek: Don't dribble into the corner trap; the middle and the ball-side flash beat it; the trap leaves someone open behind it.

los.do: Given the game clock, shot clock length and score, compute whether a 2-for-1 is available and when to shoot.
los.ek: Shoot when game clock ≈ shot clock + 6–10 s: the opponent can't run out the clock, and you still get the last possession.

los.do: Given score, game clock and shot clock, decide whether the leading team can run the clock out, and when the trailing team must foul.
los.ek: If the game clock is below the shot clock, the leader with the ball can drain it unless fouled; trailing by more than one possession late means foul to stop the clock.

los.do: Choose when to start the attack for a last shot of a quarter or game (hold for one, leave time for a rebound).
los.ek: Start the action at ~8–6 s so a miss leaves no time for the opponent but a tip remains possible.

los.do: Given a lead of 3, seconds left and the opponent's shooters, decide whether to foul or defend, citing the evidence.
los.ek: kenpom's college sample: defend ≈ 93.5% vs foul ≈ 92.0% wins, noisy and selection-biased. Fouling is worth it mainly against several good shooters and with confidence in the defensive rebound. A foul in the act of a three, or a missed FT the trailing team rebounds, is the main risk.

los.do: Trailing by 2 with one possession left, compute the win probability of going for 3 vs going for 2 and overtime, and choose.
los.ek: P(win | go for 3) = P(make 3); P(win | go for 2) = P(make 2) × P(win OT) — OT is roughly a coin flip unless one side is clearly better.

los.do: Trailing late, choose whom to foul and compute the expected points conceded given the bonus rule for the level.
los.ek: Two-shot foul ⇒ expected points = 2 × FT%; under a one-and-one ⇒ p + p² (NCAA men's 7th–9th foul). NFHS: two shots from the 5th team foul in a quarter; FIBA: two shots after 4 team fouls in a quarter; NCAA women: two from the 5th per quarter.

los.do: Choose whether to use a foul to give when leading late, given the opponent's team fouls and time left.
los.ek: Below the bonus, a non-shooting foul costs only a throw-in and seconds, and breaks up a set play.

los.do: Decide whether to call a timeout or play on after a defensive rebound or made basket late, given timeouts left, the league rule and the defense's state.
los.ek: Calling a timeout lets a scrambled defense set; FIBA's last-2-minutes option to throw in from the frontcourt throw-in line can make it worth it.

los.do: Apply the timeout allotment and restrictions for a level to a described late-game sequence (FIBA: 2 in the first half, 3 in the second with at most 2 in the last 2:00, 1 per OT).
los.ek: FIBA: unused timeouts don't carry; the scoring team can't take one after a goal in the last 2:00 unless play was interrupted.

topics.title: Special situations — BLOB, SLOB, last-second plays

los.do: Choose a baseline or sideline out-of-bounds set for a described need (quick two, a three, a safe inbound) and identify the primary and the safety.
los.ek: Every inbound set has a scoring option and a safety; the 5-s count starts when the inbounder has the ball.

los.do: Given time on the clock for a last inbound, choose a feasible action (catch-and-shoot, tip, full-court pass, quick hit).
los.ek: The clock starts on the touch inbounds, not the throw; with fractions of a second only a tip or a quick catch-and-release is realistic.

los.do: Defend a described last-second inbound: choose whether to guard the inbounder, switch everything, or deny the shooter.
los.ek: Leaving the inbounder adds a defender; switching everything stops screens from freeing the shooter; up 3, take the three away first.

los.do: Given a described sequence, state the shot-clock reset for the level (FIBA 24 / 14; NCAA men 30 / 20 off the rim in the frontcourt).
los.ek: FIBA: frontcourt throw-in after a stoppage resets to 14 if 13 or fewer remain. NCAA men: ball hits the rim and the offense keeps it in the frontcourt ⇒ 20; in the backcourt ⇒ 30.

los.do: Identify the violation in a described play — 3 s, 5 s closely guarded, 5 s throw-in, 8 s backcourt, backcourt, travel — and its penalty.
los.ek: FIBA: 3 s in the restricted area; 5 s closely guarded or to release a throw-in; 8 s to cross half-court.

los.do: Given a level and a team-foul count, state the free throws awarded on a non-shooting foul.
los.ek: NFHS: two shots from the 5th team foul per quarter, reset each quarter. NCAA men: 1-and-1 from the 7th, two from the 10th per half. NCAA women: two from the 5th per quarter. FIBA: two after 4 per quarter; OT fouls count to the 4th quarter.

los.do: State the free throws for a shooting foul (made two, missed two, missed three) and for an unsportsmanlike foul.
los.ek: Made: count + 1; missed 2-pt: 2; missed 3-pt: 3. FIBA unsportsmanlike: free throws plus a frontcourt throw-in; two unsportsmanlike (or technical) fouls disqualify.

los.do: Judge whether a described late-game foul is a common foul or unsportsmanlike under FIBA criteria.
los.ek: Unsportsmanlike: no legitimate attempt to play the ball, excessive contact, stopping a fast break, or contact from behind with no defender between the player and the basket.

los.do: Call a described block/charge play using the legal-guarding-position standard.
los.ek: NCAA (2023-24): the defender must be in legal guarding position before the offensive player's plant foot lands to go airborne.

los.do: Call goaltending or basket interference in a described play and state the result.
los.ek: Goaltending: touching a shot completely above the ring on its downward flight or after it hits the board. Defense ⇒ points awarded; offense ⇒ no points, throw-in to the opponent.

los.do: Use knowledge of officiating mechanics (crew positions, primary coverage areas) to predict which calls are likely missed and adjust tactics.
los.ek: Each official covers a primary area; action outside it, or screened by bodies, is called less often.

los.do: Compute a team's possessions from a box score.
los.ek: Poss ≈ FGA − ORB + TOV + 0.44·FTA; average the two teams' estimates for one game.

los.do: Compute points per possession, offensive and defensive rating (per 100), and net rating from a box score.
los.ek: ORtg = 100·PTS/Poss; DRtg = 100·Opp PTS/Poss; net = ORtg − DRtg. Pace = possessions per 40 or 48 minutes.

los.do: Explain why per-possession numbers beat per-game numbers when comparing a fast team and a slow team, using a worked comparison.
los.ek: Points per game mixes pace with efficiency; per-100 isolates efficiency.

los.do: Compute eFG% from FGM, 3PM and FGA, and explain why it exceeds FG% for three-point shooters.
los.ek: eFG% = (FGM + 0.5·3PM)/FGA: a three counts as 1.5 makes.

los.do: Compute TS% and true shot attempts from PTS, FGA and FTA.
los.ek: TS% = PTS / (2·(FGA + 0.44·FTA)); 0.44 reflects the mix of 2-shot, 3-shot and and-one trips (0.5 if all were 2-shot) and differs by league.

los.do: Compare two players' efficiency with FG%, eFG% and TS%, and say which measure fits the question.
los.ek: FG% ignores threes and FTs; eFG% adds threes; TS% adds free throws.

los.do: Compute all four factors for both teams from a box score.
los.ek: eFG%; TOV% = TOV/(FGA + 0.44·FTA + TOV); ORB% = ORB/(ORB + Opp DRB); FT rate = FT/FGA (bbref) or FTA/FGA (kenpom).

los.do: Given two teams' four factors, identify which factor decided the game and weigh it.
los.ek: Oliver's approximate weights: shooting 40%, turnovers 25%, rebounding 20%, free throws 15%.

los.do: Translate a four-factors deficit into a coaching emphasis (shot selection, ball security, crashing, attacking the rim).
los.ek: Each factor maps to a controllable habit; fix the largest weighted gap first.

topics.title: Expected value of shots and decisions

los.do: Compute the expected points of a shot from its make probability and value, and compare shot types (corner three, above-the-break three, mid-range, rim).
los.ek: EV = p × points: 36% from three ≈ 1.08; 50% at two = 1.00; 40% mid-range = 0.80. Shooting fouls add value: fold in P(foul) × expected FT points.

los.do: Compute the break-even make percentage at which a three equals a given two, and use it to judge a shot choice.
los.ek: Break-even p₃ = (2·p₂)/3; a 50% two equals a 33.3% three.

los.do: Include offensive rebounding in a shot's expected value and compare a quick shot with working for a better one.
los.ek: EV ≈ p·v + (1 − p)·ORB%·PPP_second-chance; passing up a shot costs some turnover risk and clock.

los.do: Judge whether a described stat (a shooter's 3P%, a lineup's net rating, a late-game study) has enough sample to act on.
los.ek: Three-point percentage and small-lineup ratings are noisy over a few hundred attempts or possessions; late-game samples are tiny and coaches choose when to foul.

los.do: Identify selection bias or role confounding in a described analytic claim (e.g. 'defensive stops are higher when X is on the floor').
los.ek: Who plays, against whom and when is chosen, not random; on/off numbers carry teammates and opponents with them.

los.do: From a described player profile (shot chart, hand, tendencies), write the defensive key: force direction, closeout type, ball-screen coverage.
los.ek: A personnel key states what to take away and what to concede, in a few words players can use in the game.

los.do: Classify an opponent's players as shooter, driver, post or non-threat and set help rules from it.
los.ek: Help off non-shooters, stay home on shooters; label each player so help rules follow.

los.do: Identify an opponent's base offense, main sets and ATO tendencies from described film clips.
los.ek: Tag first action, entry, and the shot it creates; repeated actions are the scout.

los.do: Identify an opponent's ball-screen coverage and help rules from described clips, and pick the counter you would run.
los.ek: Read the screener's defender first; the coverage plus the tagger tells you the open pass.

los.do: Self-scout: from your own tagged possessions, find the action with the lowest points per possession and say what to change.
los.ek: Rank actions by PPP with sample size; small samples flag where to look, not what to conclude.

los.do: Place a described player on the USA Basketball level (Introductory, Foundational, Advanced, Performance) by skill mastery, not age, and name the matching LTAD stage.
los.ek: Levels are by mastery; LTAD stages run Active Start (0–6), Fundamentals (6–9), Learning to Train (8–12), Training to Train (12–15), Training to Compete (14–17), Training to Win (17+).

los.do: Set the training-to-competition balance and position policy for a level.
los.ek: Foundational 70:30; Advanced 60:40 shifting to 50:50; Performance 25:75. Foundational: teach position concepts but don't assign positions.

los.do: Sequence team concepts by level: what to teach before 5-on-5, when help-side defense enters, when positions are assigned.
los.ek: Introductory: team principles only, no 5-on-5 yet, no on-ball defending; help-side comes later; positions may be assigned late in Advanced.

los.do: Convert a principle (e.g. drive-and-kick reads) into a small-sided, competitive drill with live defenders and a scoring rule that rewards the right decision.
los.ek: Decisions transfer from representative reps: live defense, game spacing, time pressure; scoring rewards the read, not just the make.

los.do: Build a practice plan with progression (1-on-1 → 2-on-2 → 3-on-3 → 5-on-5), time blocks and stated objectives for a given week.
los.ek: Add players to add reads; every block names the objective it serves.

los.do: Write a short teaching cue for a skill or read and check that it names an observable action.
los.ek: Cues like B.E.E.F. (balance, elbow, eyes, follow-through) compress a model into words a player can act on mid-rep.

los.do: Design an evaluation of a player's decision-making (tagged reads correct / total) separate from shot-making.
los.ek: A right read that misses is still a right read; grade decisions and outcomes separately.

los.do: Set season-level team goals from the four factors and track them per game.
los.ek: Targets for each factor, on both ends, turn analytics into weekly practice priorities.

topics.title: Types of drag and how they scale

los.do: Classify a described resistance (rough suit, wide kick, bow wave at the surface) as skin-friction, form (pressure) or wave drag.
los.ek: Skin friction depends on surface; form drag on frontal area, shape and alignment; wave drag on speed and depth below the surface.

los.do: Explain why gliding and kicking underwater can be faster than swimming at the surface.
los.ek: Wave drag is large at the surface and falls off steeply with depth (most of it gone by roughly 0.5 m).

los.do: Compute how drag and the power to overcome it change when velocity changes by a given factor.
los.ek: D = ½ρC_dAv²; P = Dv ∝ v³ — 5% faster costs ≈ 16% more power.

los.do: Describe a tight streamline and explain each element's effect on drag (stacked hands, arms squeezing ears, head neutral, pointed toes).
los.ek: Each element reduces frontal area or flow separation; a raised head adds form drag.

los.do: Explain why a glide decelerates and when to start kicking off the wall.
los.ek: Glide velocity decays as drag acts on body plus added mass; start kicking when glide speed drops toward kicking speed, not after.

los.do: Contrast Counsilman's lift (Bernoulli sculling) model with the drag-dominant view and state what the evidence supports.
los.ek: 3-D studies of elite swimmers (Cappaert, Rushall, Sanders) found drag > lift through most of the pull in all strokes but breaststroke; hand paths are straighter than once taught, curvature mostly from body roll.

los.do: Explain how the dolphin kick produces thrust from a whole-body wave.
los.ek: A wave travelling head-to-toe with growing amplitude whips the feet; thrust comes mostly on the downkick, with the upkick also propulsive when the feet press water backward.

los.do: Explain propulsion as momentum given to water (Newton III) and say why a high-elbow catch helps.
los.ek: Thrust = rate of backward momentum given to water; a vertical forearm adds paddle area facing backward early in the pull.

los.do: Explain propelling efficiency and why it can matter more than aerobic power.
los.ek: Part of the work goes into moving water, not the body; Toussaint & Hollander modelled efficiency gains as worth more than a 10% rise in aerobic or anaerobic power.

los.do: Describe the phases of the freestyle arm stroke (entry, catch, pull, push, recovery) and the purpose of each.
los.ek: Propulsive force is concentrated from catch to push; entry and recovery set up the next pull and the body line.

los.do: Diagnose a freestyle fault from a description (crossover entry, dropped elbow, scissor kick on breath, lifted head) and choose the correction.
los.ek: Each fault either adds drag or wastes impulse; fix the root cause, usually upstream in head or entry.

los.do: Distinguish catch-up, front-quadrant and opposition timing and match each to distance.
los.ek: More overlap ⇒ longer DPS, lower SR (distance); less overlap ⇒ continuous propulsion, higher SR (sprint).

los.do: Describe the backstroke catch (little-finger entry, bent-arm pull) and why rotation lets the arm catch deep enough.
los.ek: Rotation of ~45° each side keeps the pull under the body instead of sweeping wide at the surface.

los.do: Diagnose a backstroke fault (sitting hips, overreaching past the head, flat body) and choose the correction.
los.ek: Head still and level, hips at the surface; entry in line with the shoulder.

topics.title: Body wave and the axis at the hips

los.do: Describe the butterfly body wave and say where the axis sits and what moves forward vs up and down.
los.ek: The wave pivots near the hips; hips stay at or near the surface; the chest presses to lift the hips; the head leads the wave.

los.do: Explain why over-undulation slows the stroke.
los.ek: Large vertical excursion adds form and wave drag, deepens the catch and lowers tempo; energy goes up and down instead of forward.

los.do: State when each of the two kicks per cycle happens and what each does.
los.ek: Kick 1 at hand entry lifts the hips and balances; kick 2 as the hands push and exit is the more propulsive and lifts the shoulders for recovery.

los.do: Describe the fly pull path from entry to exit and where the high-elbow catch is set.
los.ek: Hands enter in front of the shoulders, set a high-elbow catch just outside them, pull under the body and push past the hips.

los.do: Diagnose kick-kick-pull timing from a description and choose the correction.
los.ek: Both kicks before the catch force an arched back and a downward push; cue one kick, then let the small second kick come as the hands exit — 'kick the hands in, kick the hands out'.

los.do: Describe when the breath starts and ends relative to the pull and recovery.
los.ek: Head lift begins with the pull, the inhale comes as the mouth clears at the push, and the face returns before the hands enter; chin stays near the waterline.

los.do: Diagnose late breathing or a high head lift from a description and choose the correction.
los.ek: A breath that starts at the end of the pull locks neck and shoulders and drops the hips; time the head with the catch and breathe forward, low.

los.do: Choose a breathing pattern (every stroke, 1-up-1-down, 2-down) for a race distance and justify it from drag and oxygen cost.
los.ek: Each breath adds drag and disrupts the wave; fewer breaths for 50s, regular breathing to keep the 200 aerobic.

los.do: Diagnose a fly fault from a description (crashing entry, dropped elbow, bent-knee kick, arms dragging through recovery) and choose the correction.
los.ek: Crashing entry ⇒ place hands and let chest submerge; dropped elbow ⇒ pitch palms and forearms back with fingertips down; bent knees ⇒ think hips at the surface, not 'kick harder'.

los.do: Predict how fly technique degrades over the last 50 of a 200 and which cue protects speed best.
los.ek: Recovery drops, hips sink, kick 2 disappears, SR falls; holding hip height and kick 2 protects DPS.

los.do: Call legal or illegal: a described fly stroke with alternating kick, a breaststroke kick, or arms recovered under water.
los.ek: SW 8.2: both arms forward together over the water, back together under; SW 8.3: leg movements simultaneous, no breaststroke kick (FINA, USA Swimming).

los.do: Call legal or illegal for a Masters butterfly using breaststroke kick, and state how USMS differs from World Aquatics.
los.ek: USMS 101.3.3: breaststroke kick may be used exclusively or interchangeably with dolphin kick, one per arm pull except before turn and finish; illegal under SW 8.3.

los.do: Call legal or illegal: a described fly turn or finish touch (one hand, stacked hands, hands under water, staggered touch).
los.ek: SW 8.4: both hands, separated and simultaneous, at, above or below the surface; 'separated' means not stacked — no visible gap needed.

los.do: Call legal or illegal: body position during fly underwaters (on the side, on the back before the first pull).
los.ek: SW 8.1: from the first arm stroke after start or turn the body stays on the breast; underwater kicking on the side is allowed.

los.do: Describe breaststroke timing (pull, breathe, kick, glide) and explain why it is the most drag-sensitive stroke.
los.ek: The recovery of arms and legs happens under water against the flow; the stroke's speed swings most within a cycle, so a streamlined glide carries the cycle.

los.do: Diagnose a breaststroke fault (knees drawn under the hips, late kick, wide pull past the shoulders) and choose the correction.
los.ek: Heels to seat with knees narrow cuts frontal area; kick as the hands shoot forward.
